entry.title: AWQ: Activation-Aware Weight Quantization
entry.content:
Reference Paper: AWQ: Activation-aware Weight Quantization for LLM Compression and Acceleration Code: mit-han-lab/llm-awq
I read the arXiv v6 version. The core of AWQ is not “one more 4-bit quantizer”. The useful observation is more specific: the importance of a weight cannot be decided from the weight value alone. It also depends on the activation channel multiplied by that weight. That observation has a direct deployment consequence. If we preserve an explicit FP16 outlier path, as in mixed-precision outlier handling, the runtime kernel has to handle both a regular low-bit dense path and an exceptional high-precision path. AWQ takes a more conservative route: keep a regular dense low-bit weight format, and only use activation statistics offline to decide how to scale input channels before quantization.
The paper also ships TinyChat, which is important. AWQ is not presented only as a compression recipe; the authors also show how the resulting W4A16 models run on desktop GPUs, mobile GPUs, ARM CPUs, and edge platforms. The algorithm and the system design are coupled: AWQ is useful for deployment because it preserves a hardware-friendly dense 4-bit weight layout. One SentenceAWQ is activation-aware weight-only quantization:
activations stay in FP16/BF16 at runtime, not INT4; weights are quantized group-wise to INT3/INT4; calibration activations are used only offline to identify important input channels and search per-channel scales; those scales are folded through equivalent transformations, so the final runtime format remains close to a regular dense W4A16 format.
What I like about the paper is that it does not overcomplicate the problem. There is no training loop, no Hessian solver, and no long layer reconstruction process. AWQ mainly trusts one robust statistic: some activation channels have much larger magnitudes, and the weight columns connected to those channels contribute more to the layer output. Motivation: Salient Weights Depend on Activations Figure 2 is the center of the paper. Direct RTN quantization makes OPT-6.7B INT3-g128 perplexity very poor. If 1% salient weights are kept in FP16, perplexity recovers dramatically. The problem is that a mixed FP16/INT3 format is inconvenient for hardware, because the kernel now needs to combine a regular dense low-bit path with an irregular high-precision path. AWQ’s alternative is not to keep actual FP16 outliers. Instead, it scales up salient channels before quantization. After scaling, the weights on those channels occupy a larger range on the quantization grid, so their relative rounding error becomes smaller. The activation is scaled in the opposite direction, so the floating-point computation remains equivalent. The key question becomes: which weights are salient?
Table 1 gives the first strong clue:
randomly keeping a small fraction of FP16 weights is unstable; selecting weights by weight magnitude or weight norm is not enough; selecting channels by activation magnitude is much more effective, and even 0.1%-1% salient channels can reduce perplexity significantly.
This means “important weights” are not simply large values in the static weight tensor. Importance is input-dependent. A weight column may not look extreme by itself, but if its corresponding activation channel is often large, its quantization error is amplified in the output. Formula 0: Fixing the Linear Layer NotationTo stay close to the paper, I write a linear layer as:
Here is the linear layer weight and is the input activation. Many deep learning frameworks write the same computation as ; that is only a layout convention. AWQ scales the input channel direction. Under the notation, that corresponds to the columns of . If we insert a diagonal scale matrix , the floating-point computation satisfies:
This is the equivalent transformation used by both AWQ and SmoothQuant. The goal is different. SmoothQuant mainly uses the transform to smooth activation outliers for W8A8 quantization. AWQ uses the transform to protect selected weight channels in W4A16 weight-only quantization. The important point is that the transform is exactly equivalent only before quantization. Once is applied to , the quantizer sees a different weight distribution, and the quantization error changes. Formula 1: Uniform Weight QuantizerThe paper first defines a standard weight-only quantizer:
Here denotes the weights inside a group or block, is the bit-width, and is the scale for that group. My reading of the formula is:
divide the floating-point weight by to map it to an integer grid; round the mapped value to the nearest grid point; multiply by again to dequantize it back to the floating-point domain.
The error comes from . If the maximum absolute value in a group is large, then becomes large, and ordinary weights in the same group get a coarser effective grid. This is the central tradeoff in group-wise quantization. A larger group size reduces metadata overhead and often gives better kernels, but it also makes unrelated channels share the same quantization scale.
This screenshot contains Equations 1-3 from the paper. I unpack them below because the whole AWQ idea is hidden inside these few lines. Formula 2: Scale Up Salient Weights, Scale Down ActivationsSuppose a salient weight belongs to a channel scaled by . The corresponding activation is multiplied by . Without quantization, the product is unchanged. With quantization, however, the quantizer is applied to the scaled weight:
Here is the new quantization scale after the group has been scaled. There are three pieces to understand:
becomes , so it is represented by a larger coordinate on the integer grid. Small details are less likely to be rounded away. The output is multiplied by , so the floating-point function would remain unchanged if quantization were absent. The risk is that may also grow. If scaling changes the group maximum, the whole group gets a coarser quantization grid, and non-salient weights in the same group can be hurt.
So AWQ is not saying “larger scale is always better”. It is searching for a balance: protect activation-salient channels while not making the group scale too coarse for the rest of the weights. Formula 3: Why the Relative Error Can DropThe paper writes the original quantization error and the scaled quantization error as:
This derivation relies on a few practical approximations:
the expected rounding error is roughly similar before and after scaling; when only a small fraction of salient elements are scaled, the group maximum often does not change much, so ; and are still represented in high precision, so the main new error source is weight rounding.
Under these approximations, the scaled salient weight gets about a reduction in output error:
This is the mathematical intuition of AWQ. Scale up an important channel before quantization, then scale it back at runtime; the floating-point function is preserved, but the relative quantization error on that channel can decrease. The same derivation also explains the failure mode. If is too large, is no longer close to 1. Then the group scale becomes too coarse, and the extra error on non-salient weights can outweigh the benefit on salient weights.
Table 2 verifies this behavior. On OPT-6.7B with 1% salient channels, gives the best perplexity. Increasing the scale to keeps reducing the relative error of salient weights, but it changes more group scales and damages non-salient weights, so total perplexity gets worse. Table 3 shows a related point. A fixed already works, but searching the scale is more stable and can match or exceed the mixed-precision “1% FP16 salient weights” baseline while keeping a regular dense low-bit format. Formula 4: The Real Objective Is Layer Output ErrorThe previous error analysis explains why scaling can help. The actual AWQ search is layer-wise: find an input-channel scale such that the quantized layer output stays close to the FP16 layer output:
Here is the cached activation from a calibration set. I interpret the objective as:
scale the input-channel direction of by ; scale the corresponding channels of by ; quantize the scaled weight; compare the quantized output against the original FP16 output.
If were removed, the loss would be exactly zero because . Therefore the whole loss comes from quantization. AWQ is not changing the model function in floating point; it is changing the distribution seen by the quantizer.
This objective looks like reconstruction, but it is different from GPTQ in spirit. GPTQ uses calibration activations to build an approximate second-order problem, then quantizes weights sequentially with error compensation. AWQ does not run backpropagation and does not invert a Hessian. It searches over a small activation-aware scale family. Formula 5: The Search Space Is Parameterized by Activation MagnitudeOptimizing an independent scale for every channel would be difficult because rounding is non-differentiable and the search space is high-dimensional. AWQ reduces the problem to a one-dimensional hyperparameter:
is the average activation magnitude for each input channel, computed from calibration data. The exponent controls how strongly AWQ trusts the activation statistic:
: , so the method degenerates to RTN/group quantization with no scaling; larger : high-activation channels receive stronger protection; : the scale fully follows the activation magnitude.
The paper performs a fast grid search over . This design is important because it turns a high-dimensional, non-differentiable, and potentially unstable problem into the offline evaluation of a small number of candidate scales. My mental model is: “activation-aware” does not mean AWQ dynamically reacts to activations at runtime. It means calibration activations are compressed into fixed channel scales. Once deployed, each layer already has its chosen scales, and the runtime can still follow a regular W4A16 path. AWQ PipelinePutting the formulas together, the offline quantization pipeline is roughly:
collect a small number of calibration sequences and run the FP16 model; cache the input activations for each linear layer; compute the average activation magnitude per input channel to obtain ; grid search and form candidate scales ; for each candidate, evaluate the output gap between and ; choose the scale with the smallest loss, then apply weight clipping to further reduce group-wise quantization MSE; store the final weights as group-wise INT3/INT4 and run W4A16 dequantization plus matrix multiplication at inference time.
The easy implementation bug is the channel axis. AWQ scales the input channel of a linear layer, which corresponds to the columns of under the notation. If the framework stores weights as [out_features, in_features], the scale is applied along the in_features dimension. Why Weight-Only Quantization Works Well for On-Device Decode Figure 3 is the system motivation. Autoregressive generation at batch size 1 is often memory-bound rather than compute-bound. For every new token, the model reads a large amount of weight data, while the activation footprint is much smaller. W4A16 does not quantize activations, but it can reduce weight bandwidth to about one quarter of FP16, so it is especially useful in the decode stage. This also explains why AWQ and SmoothQuant target different deployment regimes:
SmoothQuant targets W8A8 so both activations and weights can enter INT8 GEMM; AWQ targets W4A16 so memory-bound decode reads much less weight data; if the workload is large-batch prefill, W8A8 or FP8 can be more attractive; if the workload is interactive edge decoding, weight bandwidth reduction is more direct.
TinyChat: Format and Kernels Matter W4A16 is not automatically fast because most hardware does not expose a direct INT4 x FP16 matrix instruction. A real kernel has to read packed 4-bit weights, unpack and dequantize them, and multiply them with FP16 activations. TinyChat handles several engineering details:
on-the-fly dequantization: do not write dequantized FP16 weights back to DRAM; unpack and dequantize inside the matmul loop; platform-aware packing: reorder 4-bit weights for ARM NEON, CUDA, and other backends so unpacking uses fewer SIMD or bitwise instructions; kernel fusion: reduce launches and intermediate memory traffic for operations such as LayerNorm, QKV projection, positional embedding, and KV cache update.
This part is a useful reminder: reporting a compression ratio is not the same as reporting speed. Low-bit formats only accelerate inference if the decode path accounts for unpacking, scaling, metadata loads, and memory traffic. Language Modeling Results Table 4 is one of the main language-modeling results. It compares RTN, GPTQ, GPTQ-R, and AWQ across LLaMA/Llama-2 model sizes. My takeaways:
INT4-g128 RTN is not catastrophically bad, but AWQ is consistently better; INT3-g128 creates a larger gap, which means AWQ matters more when the bit-width becomes aggressive; GPTQ-R’s reordering trick can help on some models, but AWQ does not depend on reordering; AWQ remains close to FP16 even on 70B models, so the method is not a small-model artifact.
I see AWQ as complementary to GPTQ. GPTQ behaves more like a local second-order reconstruction solver. AWQ behaves more like an activation-statistics-guided equivalent transform. Both use calibration data, but they use it in very different ways. Instruction-Tuned Models Instruction-tuned models test generalization. A quantization method that reconstructs a calibration set very well does not necessarily preserve chat or instruction-following behavior. The paper uses GPT-4 pairwise evaluation on Vicuna and shows that AWQ has more quantized wins and fewer quantized losses than RTN/GPTQ under INT3-g128. This should not be overinterpreted as “GPT-4 evaluation is the final answer”. The useful signal is narrower: AWQ avoids heavy fitting to a small calibration set, so it appears less likely to damage instruction behavior under distribution shift. Multi-Modal Models The OpenFlamingo result is useful because VLMs are not pure text-only language models. AWQ quantizes only the language component, yet it clearly outperforms RTN/GPTQ on COCO captioning across few-shot settings. In INT4-g128 32-shot evaluation, the degradation shrinks from RTN’s -4.57 to AWQ’s -1.17.
The VILA table is even more direct: INT4-g128 is nearly lossless across multiple visual-language benchmarks. The point is not only that the numbers are good. It suggests that activation-aware scaling is not tightly bound to one text calibration distribution; it captures a lower-level channel magnitude statistic that transfers across model families and tasks. Code, Math, and Extreme Low-Bit Settings The MBPP and GSM8K results show that AWQ is not merely reducing WikiText perplexity. Code and math tasks are sensitive to generation quality. Under INT4-g128, AWQ stays close to FP16, and some numbers are even slightly higher than FP16. I would not read that as “quantization makes the model smarter”; it is more likely evaluation noise, sampling variance, or a mild regularization effect. The important point is that AWQ does not visibly destroy complex generation behavior.
Table 9 is also important. AWQ can be combined with GPTQ under an extreme INT2-g64 setting and further reduce the gap. This supports a clean division of labor: AWQ is an equivalent-transform or preprocessing step, while GPTQ is a quantization solver. Calibration Robustness Figure 8 best shows the character of AWQ. The left plot shows that AWQ can work with fewer calibration sequences. This makes sense because it mainly estimates average activation scale rather than fitting a complex reconstruction solution. The right plot shows that AWQ is less sensitive to calibration distribution mismatch. When calibration and evaluation domains are swapped between PubMed and Enron, GPTQ has a much larger perplexity gap. AWQ’s degradation is only about 0.5-0.6. This matches the paper’s claim: avoiding backpropagation and heavy reconstruction reduces the chance of overfitting the calibration set. This does not mean AWQ can ignore calibration. Activation magnitude still comes from calibration data. If the target deployment domain has unusual activation patterns, it is still better to recalibrate with representative prompts. Speed Results TinyChat’s speed plot connects the algorithm to actual tokens per second. Compared with HuggingFace FP16, AWQ W4A16 improves throughput on RTX 4090, Jetson Orin, and RTX 4070 laptop GPUs. Some models that run out of memory in FP16 also become runnable in W4A16.
The VILA throughput table shows the same benefit for multi-modal models. VILA-13B is OOM in FP16 on RTX 4090, while AWQ W4A16 runs with a throughput of 99.0.
Figure 10 compares AutoGPTQ, llama.cpp, exllama, and TinyChat. The comparison is not perfectly apples-to-apples because these systems support different model families, packing formats, and kernel backends. The useful message is that TinyChat is not optimized only for a single LLaMA path. It covers StarCoder, StableCode, Mistral, Falcon, and other models, and it runs on edge devices such as Jetson Orin and Raspberry Pi. AWQ vs. GPTQ / SmoothQuant / LLM.int8 / SpQRThese methods address related LLM quantization problems, but their runtime formats are quite different:
LLM.int8() targets mostly INT8 computation with an FP16 outlier path. It demonstrates that LLM activation outliers are real and that naive INT8 quantization is not enough. SmoothQuant targets dense W8A8 INT8. Its key signal is the activation/weight max scale, and its main idea is to migrate activation quantization difficulty into the weights. GPTQ targets dense W3/W4A16 weight-only quantization. Its core signal is calibration-based Hessian/reconstruction, so it behaves like a local second-order rounding solver. AWQ also targets dense W3/W4A16 weight-only quantization, but the key signal is activation magnitude plus scale search. My interpretation is that AWQ protects activation-salient weight channels through an equivalent transform while preserving a kernel-friendly dense layout. SpQR targets low-bit weights plus sparse correction. It stores some sensitive/outlier weights in a sparse path, which is closer to a near-lossless compression format but gives the runtime a more complex format.
AWQ and SmoothQuant look similar at the formula level because both use diagonal scaling as an equivalent transformation. The objective is different:
SmoothQuant mainly wants activations to be representable in INT8; AWQ wants salient weights to have lower error under INT3/INT4 group quantization; SmoothQuant moves difficulty from activations into weights; AWQ uses activation statistics to decide which weight columns deserve protection.
The difference between AWQ and GPTQ is more engineering-oriented:
GPTQ’s strength is precise local reconstruction, especially at low bit-widths; AWQ’s strength is simplicity, speed, and lower risk of calibration overfitting; under extremely low bit-widths, AWQ scaling can be used before GPTQ, which is exactly what Table 9 explores.
Implementation NotesIf I were implementing AWQ from scratch, I would check these details first:
Attach the calibration activation hook to the right tensor. AWQ uses per-input-channel scales, so the axis for linear, attention, and MLP layers must not be flipped. Verify the floating-point equivalent transform. Before quantization, should match up to numerical error. Watch group scale inflation. If many groups have much larger than 1, the scale is too aggressive and non-salient channels will be damaged. Do not judge only by a single-layer MSE. The final model should still be checked by perplexity or task metrics because local layer error is not always aligned with full-model behavior. Account for metadata. INT4 weights still need scales, zero points, and packing padding. The real memory footprint is not just the raw bit-width. Profile the kernel path. W4A16 will not be fast if unpacking/dequantization is slow or if dequantized weights are written back to DRAM.
A practical debug plot is: for each layer, draw channel activation magnitude, selected scale , and per-channel output error before and after quantization. When AWQ works correctly, high-activation channels should receive stronger protection, while ordinary channels should not see a global error increase. LimitationsAWQ is not a universal low-bit quantization answer. First, it mainly reduces weight memory and weight bandwidth. It does not solve KV cache memory. In long-context serving, KV cache can become the larger bottleneck, where KIVI, KV quantization, PagedAttention-style memory management, and related methods belong to a different line of work. Second, AWQ still uses FP16/BF16 activations at runtime, so it does not get all the benefits of W8A8 integer GEMM. Choosing AWQ depends on whether the workload is decode memory-bound or prefill compute-bound. Third, activation magnitude is a calibration statistic. The paper shows that AWQ is less sensitive to calibration distribution mismatch than GPTQ-style reconstruction, but a very unusual deployment input distribution can still require recalibration. Finally, AWQ depends on kernel quality. A smaller model file does not imply faster end-to-end inference unless the W4A16 kernels are actually optimized. TakeawayAWQ’s core contribution can be compressed into one sentence: use activation statistics to identify important weight channels, then protect those channels through equivalent scaling while keeping the final model in a regular dense low-bit weight-only format. This paper is best read between GPTQ and SmoothQuant. GPTQ teaches that calibration activations can guide weight rounding. SmoothQuant teaches that diagonal scaling can move quantization difficulty between activations and weights. AWQ combines both ideas into a lightweight W4A16 recipe and follows the system path all the way to TinyChat. For me, the most valuable part of AWQ is not one particular perplexity number. It is the deployment principle: if protecting outliers would make the kernel irregular, first ask whether an equivalent transform can fold that protection back into a regular dense format.

entry.title: AdaBERT: Task-Adaptive BERT Compression with Differentiable NAS
entry.content:
Paper : AdaBERT: Task-Adaptive BERT Compression with Differentiable Neural Architecture Search. AdaBERT is an early attempt to connect two lines of work: BERT compression and differentiable NAS. The paper’s core claim is not simply “make BERT smaller”. It argues that a single compressed architecture is wasteful because downstream tasks use BERT differently. Sentiment classification, sentence-pair equivalence, and entailment recognition should not necessarily share the same student network. The method searches a small task-specific architecture under three signals: L = (1 - gamma) * L_CE + gamma * L_KD + beta * L_E
Here, L_CE is the supervised task loss, L_KD distills task-oriented knowledge from a fine-tuned BERT teacher, and L_E penalizes inefficient structures. In the experiments, the searched students are about 6.4M to 9.5M parameters, compared with 109M parameters for BERT-base. MotivationMost classical BERT compression methods pick one student shape and reuse it across tasks. That is convenient, but it hides an assumption: the best compressed architecture for SST-2 should also be good for MRPC, QQP, MNLI, QNLI, and RTE. AdaBERT challenges this assumption. Prior probing work had already shown that different BERT layers and attention heads carry different linguistic signals. If each downstream task only needs part of that information, then compression can be task-adaptive: keep the behavior useful for the target task and remove structure that is redundant for that task.
The framework is easy to read from the figure. A fine-tuned BERT teacher gives task-oriented signals, the labeled target dataset gives supervised loss, and the efficiency term pushes the search toward smaller models. The output is not a pruned BERT block. It is a searched small model. Search SpaceThe searched student is CNN-style rather than a shallow Transformer. This choice is important. AdaBERT is not trying to preserve the original Transformer computation graph; it treats the teacher as a source of task behavior and searches a cheaper network that can mimic that behavior.
The architecture has two levels:
Component What is searched Why it matters
Stacked layers K in [1, K_max] Controls depth, capacity, and latency.
Cell structure Operations on directed edges Controls how local/contextual features are encoded.
The cell is a directed acyclic graph. Candidate operations include:
standard 1D convolution with kernel sizes 3, 5, and 7; dilated 1D convolution with kernel sizes 3, 5, and 7; average pooling and max pooling with kernel size 3; skip connection; zero operation.
For single-sentence tasks, the two input nodes can receive the same input sequence. For sentence-pair tasks, the two input nodes correspond to the two texts. This gives the search space a way to express either self-interaction or pairwise interaction. The paper sets K_max = 8, the number of inner nodes N = 3, gamma = 0.8, beta = 4, and searches the architecture distribution for 80 epochs. Distillation As A Search SignalThe distillation design is more specific than ordinary logit matching. AdaBERT freezes a fine-tuned BERT teacher and trains probe classifiers on the hidden layers. These probes turn intermediate teacher states into task-related logits. The student then learns from a hierarchy of teacher signals, not only the final output. This matters because NAS needs a useful search signal early. If the student only sees labels, small GLUE datasets such as MRPC and RTE may not provide enough information to distinguish candidate architectures. The paper’s task-oriented distillation gives the search process a smoother target:
final task labels keep the student grounded; probe-based intermediate logits expose which teacher layers are useful for the task; data augmentation enriches the distillation set; attentive weighting emphasizes teacher probes that predict the sample better.
The differentiable part uses Gumbel-Softmax relaxation for both layer count and operation choices. During forward computation the method uses one-hot sampled choices; during backward propagation it uses continuous relaxed variables through a straight-through estimator. After search, taking argmax over the learned architecture distribution gives the final child model. Efficiency-Aware LossAdaBERT adds an explicit architecture cost: L_E = (K / K_max) * sum_{o in alpha_c}(SIZE(o) + FLOPs(o))
The exact form in the paper normalizes operation size and FLOPs, then uses FLOPs as a proxy for inference time. This is a simple cost model, but it forces NAS to care about deployment. Without this term, the search can choose larger structures that look slightly better in accuracy but lose the point of compression. Compression ResultsThe main result is that AdaBERT trades a small accuracy drop for much smaller and faster models.
The headline numbers:
Model Params Inference speedup Average score
BERT-base teacher implementation 109M 1x 82.4
TinyBERT4 14.5M 9.4x 80.6
AdaBERT 6.4M-9.5M 12.7x-29.3x 80.1
AdaBERT is not the most accurate row in the table. TinyBERT4 and BERT6-PKD have slightly better average scores. The point is the speed/size tradeoff: AdaBERT is much smaller and faster, while keeping the average GLUE score close enough to make the compression credible. The per-task architecture sizes are also useful.
SST-2 gets the smallest model: 3 layers, 6.4M parameters, and 29.3x speedup. MNLI gets the largest searched model: 7 layers, 9.5M parameters, and 12.7x speedup. This matches intuition. Binary sentiment classification is easier than entailment over diverse premise-hypothesis pairs. Task AdaptivenessThe strongest evidence for task-adaptiveness is Table 3. The authors take the structure searched for one task, reinitialize it, train it on another task, and compare performance. If one architecture were universally good, cross-task transfer would work well. It does not.
The diagonal entries are the best in every column. That means the SST-2-searched structure works best on SST-2, the MRPC-searched structure works best on MRPC, and so on. Transfer within related sentence-pair tasks is less harmful than transfer across task types, but the overall pattern supports the paper’s claim: the searched structures are task-specific. The visualized cells make the same point from another angle.
SST-2 uses more aggregation-style operations such as max pooling and smaller convolution filters. MRPC, a sentence-pair equivalence task, has more direct interactions between the two input nodes. QNLI uses a more diverse mix, including skip connections and average pooling, which fits the paper’s explanation that entailment needs more complex interactions. This is the part I find most convincing. The paper is not only reporting a better average number; it shows that the architecture shape changes in a way that roughly matches task structure. AblationThe knowledge-loss ablation explains why AdaBERT is more than a plain DARTS-style search over small CNNs.
Adding probe models improves every task over base KD. Adding data augmentation improves again, especially on smaller datasets such as MRPC and RTE. Adding the supervised cross-entropy term gives the best row. The lesson is that task-oriented compression needs both teacher behavior and target labels. The efficiency-loss ablation is also clean.
With beta = 0, the model becomes larger. With beta = 8, the model becomes smaller but accuracy drops because the search overuses cheap operations such as skip and zero. The middle setting, beta = 4, is the best tradeoff in this experiment. Reading NotesI would read AdaBERT as a compression framework, not as a pure NAS benchmark. Its interesting idea is that the teacher defines task relevance, while NAS decides how much student structure is needed to reproduce that relevance. What I would keep from this paper:
do not assume one compressed BERT architecture fits every task; include an explicit efficiency term in the search objective; use intermediate teacher signals when labels are too weak for architecture search; evaluate whether searched structures transfer across tasks, not only final accuracy.
There are also limitations.
The student search space is CNN-based. This gives speed, but it means the student is no longer a Transformer-like model. The method needs a fine-tuned BERT teacher and a search run per task. The experiments are on six GLUE tasks and BERT-base; the conclusions do not automatically transfer to modern LLM compression. FLOPs and batch-size inference speed are useful proxies, but real deployment still depends on kernels, sequence length, hardware, and batching.
Overall, AdaBERT is useful because it makes task-specific compression concrete. The paper’s numbers are not the final word on BERT compression, but the design principle still holds: if different tasks use different parts of a teacher, the compressed student should be allowed to have different architecture too.

entry.title: AdaRound: Adaptive Rounding for PTQ
entry.content:
Paper: Up or Down? Adaptive Rounding for Post-Training Quantization AdaRound is a small but important PTQ paper. It does not invent a new quantization grid, a new integer kernel, or a full retraining recipe. It asks a narrower question: after the scale is fixed, should each weight round down or round up? The default answer is nearest rounding. That is optimal if the objective is only element-wise weight error. The paper’s point is that the model does not consume weights element by element. It consumes , and different rounding errors interact through activations and loss curvature. MotivationFor a pretrained network with weights , a quantization perturbation changes the task loss approximately by a second-order Taylor expansion:
If the model is already trained, the gradient term is small. The Hessian term remains. The diagonal entries care about the magnitude of each perturbation, but the off-diagonal entries care about how the signs of different perturbations interact. This is the part nearest rounding ignores. The paper makes this concrete by quantizing only the first layer of ResNet18 to 4-bit weights. Rounding every value up or down is catastrophic, but some stochastic rounding samples beat nearest rounding by a large margin.
Table 1 from the paper: nearest rounding reaches 52.29% top-1 accuracy for the first layer, while the best of 100 stochastic samples reaches 63.06%.
The cost from the Hessian proxy correlates with ImageNet validation accuracy. This is the empirical reason the paper treats rounding as an optimization problem instead of a per-weight nearest-neighbor rule. From Hessian To Local ReconstructionFor layer , each quantized weight is constrained to one of two adjacent grid values: Missing or unrecognized delimiter for \left \hat{w}^{(\ell)}_i \in \left{w^{(\ell), floor}_i, w^{(\ell), ceil}_i\right}. The theoretically motivated problem is a QUBO:
This is the right shape, but it is not practical for normal layers: the Hessian is expensive and the binary optimization is NP-hard. AdaRound then makes two important approximations. First, under assumptions on the Hessian with respect to layer preactivations, the problem becomes a local output reconstruction objective. For a fully connected layer row:
In matrix form, this is the familiar calibration loss:
Second, AdaRound replaces the hard binary rounding choice with a continuous relaxation. The soft-quantized weight is:
where represents “round down” to “round up”. Let and denote the quantized layer output. The optimized objective is:
The final method uses asymmetric reconstruction:
where is the layer input after previous layers have already been quantized. This detail matters because the method is applied layer by layer; later layers should see the errors already introduced upstream. Soft RoundingAdaRound uses a rectified sigmoid for the soft rounding variable:
with and . The regularizer is:
The annealing is the useful trick. Early in optimization, the rounding variables stay soft enough to reduce reconstruction error. Later, the regularizer pushes toward exactly 0 or 1 so the final model has real discrete weights.
The regularizer changes shape as is annealed. The target is not a permanently soft quantizer; it is a gradient-friendly path to hard rounding.
After optimization, the learned values collapse close to 0 or 1. The off-diagonal quadrants are the interesting part: those are weights whose final up/down choice differs from nearest rounding. Ablation NotesThe best ablation in the paper is the path from the original Hessian problem to the practical local objective. On ResNet18, the Hessian proxy, local MSE loss, and continuous relaxation all beat nearest rounding by a large margin.
This table is the main justification for the approximations. Nearest rounding on all layers gives 23.99%, while the continuous local relaxation gives 66.56%. The method is not just a convenient relaxation; it preserves most of the benefit from optimizing rounding. The design choices are also worth reading because they explain why AdaRound is not just “train a quantizer with STE”.
The explicit regularizer is more stable than temperature annealing alone, and the rectified sigmoid gives the best all-layer number.
Asymmetric reconstruction is a practical improvement: layer-wise reconstruction gives 66.56%, while adding asymmetric reconstruction and ReLU gives 68.60%.
The STE baseline is strong but still worse. My read is that AdaRound’s restriction is a feature: it only chooses between the two adjacent quantization values, while STE optimization has a biased gradient and a less controlled search space.
The quantization grid still matters, but AdaRound improves all tested grids. The best result here is with the preactivation-MSE grid, but the paper keeps the simpler grid for the remaining experiments. Calibration DataAdaRound is a PTQ method, so the amount and source of calibration data matter. The paper uses unlabeled images and optimizes layer-wise with Adam. The default setup is 1024 ImageNet training images, batch size 32, 10k iterations, and fixed 4-bit symmetric per-layer weight quantization.
The method is not extremely data hungry in this CNN setting. Even 256 images keep the model near the final result, and data from MS COCO or Pascal VOC is close to ImageNet calibration. This does not mean calibration is irrelevant; it means the local reconstruction objective is not overfitted to labels or full-dataset training. Main ResultsThe main ImageNet result is the strongest evidence that the method is useful beyond a first-layer toy case.
For 4-bit weights and FP32 activations, AdaRound reaches 68.71% on ResNet18 and 75.23% on ResNet50, within about 1% of the FP32 baselines in the table. With 8-bit activation quantization added, the numbers barely move for these models. The paper also includes semantic segmentation to show the method is not only an ImageNet classification trick.
On DeeplabV3+ with a MobileNetV2 backend, nearest 4/8 quantization collapses to 6.09 mIOU, while AdaRound with 4-bit weights and 8-bit activations reports 70.86 mIOU versus 72.94 full precision. Implementation ReadingThe layer-wise workflow I would implement is:
Fold batch normalization into neighboring weights. Choose the quantization scale and clipping range before AdaRound. Cache calibration inputs for the current layer. Optimize with the asymmetric reconstruction loss and the annealed regularizer. Convert to hard 0/1 rounding decisions. Move to the next layer with previous layers already quantized.
The important debugging signal is the learned rounding mask. If almost every decision matches nearest rounding, the optimizer is not doing much. If many decisions flip but reconstruction error does not improve, the annealing schedule, calibration cache, or scale choice is probably wrong. Link To Later PTQ WorkAdaRound is one of the bridges from old range-calibration PTQ to solver-style PTQ. Later methods widen or change the local objective, but the core lesson stays the same.
AdaRound optimizes up/down rounding decisions for a layer. BRECQ keeps adaptive rounding but reconstructs larger blocks. GPTQ scales a second-order reconstruction view to LLM weight matrices. AWQ keeps activation-important weight channels accurate through scaling and quantization choices.
The most direct conceptual link is GPTQ. Both methods reject independent nearest rounding. AdaRound uses a soft relaxation and local reconstruction; GPTQ uses a sequential second-order update. Different solver, same warning: the cost of a rounding error depends on how the layer uses that weight. LimitationsAdaRound was evaluated mainly on CNN PTQ. It is not a complete deployment story for modern LLM inference: there is no packed-weight kernel format discussion, no KV-cache issue, and no activation-outlier treatment like SmoothQuant. The layer-wise reconstruction objective is also local. It is much better than per-weight nearest rounding, but it still cannot fully model error interactions across residual blocks or whole networks. This is why BRECQ’s block reconstruction is a natural follow-up. Finally, AdaRound fixes the quantization grid before optimizing rounding. That separation makes the method simple, but it also means a bad scale choice can limit the final result. I would treat scale selection, calibration data, and annealing schedule as the three reproduction knobs to check first. TakeawayAdaRound’s value is not only the 4-bit CNN accuracy. The important idea is that rounding is a discrete optimization problem with structure. Nearest rounding minimizes the wrong objective; calibration-driven reconstruction is a better proxy for what the model actually computes.

entry.title: Attention Is All You Need
entry.content:
ReferencePaper: Attention Is All You Need Code mentioned in the paper: tensorflow/tensor2tensor I want to read this paper as the original Transformer paper, not as a decoder-only LLM paper viewed backward from 2026. The immediate problem in 2017 was sequence transduction, and the main experiments were WMT14 machine translation. The paper’s contribution was not merely “using attention”. Bahdanau attention, Luong attention, memory networks, and several self-attention-like ideas already existed. The important move was making attention the main computational backbone of an encoder-decoder network, then expressing the training graph as large matrix multiplications, softmax, position-wise MLPs, residual connections, and normalization. That change later shaped BERT, GPT, T5, ViT, DiT, MoE Transformers, FlashAttention, KV cache serving, long-context models, and most modern large-model systems. When reading the paper, I find it useful to keep two levels in mind. At the model level, a Transformer block is a precise sequence of tensor operations. At the engineering level, replacing recurrence or convolution with self-attention improves training parallelism, shortens information paths, and gives hardware much larger dense kernels to execute. All figures and tables below are cropped from the original arXiv PDF or the official source package. Problem SettingThe paper studies sequence-to-sequence modeling. Given an input sequence of token representations:
the encoder maps it to a sequence of continuous representations:
The decoder then generates an output sequence:
“Autoregressive” means that the -th output token can depend only on the previous output tokens and the encoder memory:
A typical RNN encoder-decoder computes hidden states along time:
This recurrence is natural for sequence modeling, but it imposes a hard training dependency inside each sample: hidden state cannot be computed before . Batch dimension can be parallelized, but sequence dimension is serialized. Long sequences are therefore constrained by both the recurrent dependency and the smaller kernels used at each step. Convolutional sequence models can process all positions in parallel, but when the kernel size is , distant tokens must communicate through multiple layers; the path length is not constant. The Transformer question is simple: during training, if the full source sequence and the shifted target sequence are already known, can each layer route information directly between all positions instead of stepping through time? Self-attention is the answer used in this paper. Model Architecture Figure 1 is the full encoder-decoder Transformer. The left side is the encoder stack, and the right side is the decoder stack. The default model uses encoder layers and decoder layers. Each encoder layer has two sub-layers: multi-head self-attention and a position-wise feed-forward network. Each decoder layer has three sub-layers: masked multi-head self-attention, encoder-decoder multi-head attention, and a position-wise feed-forward network. Every sub-layer is wrapped by a residual connection and LayerNorm. The paper uses the form now usually called Post-LN:
Here is the sub-layer input, and is the output of either attention or FFN. To make residual addition valid, all sub-layers and embeddings use the same feature width:
The base model can be remembered with the following tensor flow: src = token_embedding(src_ids) * sqrt(d_model) + positional_encodingtgt = token_embedding(tgt_ids_shifted_right) * sqrt(d_model) + positional_encodingfor _ in range(N): src = LayerNorm(src + MultiHeadSelfAttention(src, src, src)) src = LayerNorm(src + FFN(src))memory = srcfor _ in range(N): tgt = LayerNorm(tgt + MaskedMultiHeadSelfAttention(tgt, tgt, tgt)) tgt = LayerNorm(tgt + MultiHeadAttention(query=tgt, key=memory, value=memory)) tgt = LayerNorm(tgt + FFN(tgt))logits = Linear(tgt)prob = softmax(logits)
There are two details worth spelling out. First, in encoder self-attention, all come from the current encoder representation, so every source token can attend to the full source sentence. Second, the decoder has two different attention modules. Masked self-attention looks only at the target prefix and preserves autoregressive training. Encoder-decoder attention uses decoder states as queries and encoder states as keys and values, so it plays the role that alignment attention played in older seq2seq systems. Scaled Dot-Product Attention An attention function maps a query and a set of key-value pairs to a weighted sum of values. The weights are computed from the compatibility between the query and each key. For a single query , the score, normalized attention weight, and output can be written as:
The paper packs all queries into , all keys into , and all values into . This gives the first central formula:
The shapes are useful for implementation. Omitting the batch dimension, let the query length be and the key/value length be :
Then:
and:
The softmax is applied along the key dimension, so for each query the weights over all keys sum to 1. In an implementation, the logits usually have shape [batch, heads, q_len, k_len], and the softmax is taken over the last dimension. Why Scale By sqrt(d_k)The factor is a small but important design. The paper gives the intuition in a footnote. If the components of and are independent with mean 0 and variance 1, then:
The dot product has approximately:
and:
As grows, unscaled attention logits grow in magnitude. Large logits push softmax into a very sharp regime, where many probabilities are close to 0 or 1 and gradients can become small. Dividing by keeps the variance near a constant:
This is why the module is called scaled dot-product attention rather than plain dot-product attention. It keeps the efficient matrix-multiplication form while making the softmax numerically easier to optimize at larger key dimensions. Masked AttentionDecoder self-attention cannot look at future target tokens. The paper handles this by setting illegal logits to before the softmax:
The causal mask can be written as two conditions:
With this mask, target position can attend only to positions . Combined with shifting the output embedding to the right, this lets all target positions be trained in parallel without leaking future ground-truth tokens. Multi-Head AttentionA single attention head forces all relationships through one set of attention weights. Transformer instead projects into lower-dimensional subspaces, applies scaled dot-product attention independently in each head, concatenates the results, and applies one output projection. The paper writes:
where:
The projection matrices have shapes:
The base model uses:
Each head is narrower than the full hidden dimension, so the total compute is similar to a single large attention head. The design trades off representation diversity against per-head resolution. Too few heads force different relations to share the same attention distribution. Too many heads make each head too narrow. Table 3 shows this tradeoff clearly. Transformer uses multi-head attention in three places:
Encoder self-attention: all come from the previous encoder layer. Decoder masked self-attention: all come from the previous decoder layer, with a causal mask. Encoder-decoder attention: comes from the decoder, while come from the encoder output memory.
The third case is the bridge between source and target. In machine translation, a target position can use its current decoder state as a query and retrieve the relevant source positions from the encoder memory. This inherits the purpose of traditional seq2seq attention, but the recurrent hidden-state backbone is gone. Position-Wise Feed-Forward NetworkEach encoder and decoder layer contains a position-wise feed-forward network after attention. The paper defines it as:
Here is ReLU. The same FFN parameters are applied independently to every position within the layer; different layers have different FFN parameters. This is equivalent to a two-layer MLP applied token-wise, or to a pair of 1x1 convolutions over the sequence. In the base model:
and:
So the FFN expands the channel dimension by . Attention handles communication between tokens, while FFN handles nonlinear channel mixing inside each token representation. Modern LLM blocks keep this basic split, although the activation is often GELU or SwiGLU, LayerNorm is often moved to the input side of each sub-layer, and attention gains RoPE, KV cache, GQA/MQA, and other systems-oriented changes. Embedding, Softmax, And Weight SharingTransformer uses learned token embeddings to map source and target tokens into -dimensional vectors. The paper also shares the same weight matrix between the two embedding layers and the pre-softmax linear transformation. The output probability at decoder position can be written as:
Here is the token embedding matrix, and is the final decoder hidden state at position . Before being added to positional encoding, embeddings are scaled by:
That is:
where is the current token id. Many current implementations do not preserve this detail exactly, but in the original Transformer it matters because token embeddings and positional encodings are added directly. Their relative scales affect early training dynamics. Positional EncodingOnce recurrence and convolution are removed, attention itself has no built-in notion of token order. Without position information, self-attention sees a set of token representations and content relations, but it does not know which token came first. The paper injects order by adding positional encoding to token embedding at the bottom of both encoder and decoder:
The original paper uses fixed sinusoidal positional encoding:
Here is the position and is the dimension index. Each pair of even/odd dimensions corresponds to one frequency:
So the same formula can be written as:
One reason for this construction is that for a fixed offset , can be expressed as a linear transform of . For any frequency :
In two-vector form, this is a rotation within each frequency pair. Let . Then:
where:
This does not mean the original Transformer explicitly models relative positions. It means sinusoidal encoding makes relative offsets easier to recover from absolute position vectors. Later methods such as Transformer-XL relative position, T5 relative bias, RoPE, and ALiBi all revisit the same question: how should position enter attention? The paper also tried learned positional embeddings. Table 3 row (E) reports almost the same result: PPL 4.92 and BLEU 25.7, compared with base PPL 4.92 and BLEU 25.8. The paper kept sinusoidal encoding mainly because it might extrapolate to sequence lengths not seen during training. Why Self-Attention Table 1 is one of the most important tables in the paper. It does not just say self-attention is accurate. It compares three properties:
Per-layer computational complexity. Minimum number of sequential operations. Maximum path length between any two positions.
Let sequence length be , hidden dimension be , convolution kernel size be , and restricted self-attention neighborhood size be . The table can be summarized as:
Layer type Per-layer complexity Sequential operations Max path length
Self-Attention
Recurrent
Convolutional
Restricted Self-Attention
Self-attention pays an cost. This later becomes the main bottleneck of long-context Transformers. But in machine translation, sequence length is usually much smaller than hidden dimension . With the base model’s , sentences of a few dozen BPE tokens do not necessarily make more expensive than RNN-style . The more important column is sequential operations: self-attention is across sequence positions during training, while RNNs are . Maximum path length also matters. In an RNN, information from the first token reaches the last token through recurrent transitions. A convolutional model needs enough layers to expand its receptive field. In self-attention, any two positions can interact in one layer, so the path length is . This does not guarantee that long-distance dependencies are always learned, but it makes the optimization path much shorter. Restricted self-attention is mentioned in the conclusion as a future direction. If each token sees only a local neighborhood of size , complexity drops from to , but maximum path length grows to . Longformer, BigBird, Sparse Transformer, Performer, Linformer, and FlashAttention can all be read beside this table: some change the attention pattern, some approximate full attention, and some keep the math exact while improving IO and memory behavior. Training Recipe The training recipe is small by current standards, but it is complete. WMT14 English-German uses about 4.5M sentence pairs with a shared source-target BPE vocabulary of about 37K tokens. English-French uses 36M sentence pairs with a word-piece vocabulary of about 32K tokens. Batches are formed by approximate sequence length and contain about 25K source tokens and 25K target tokens. The hardware is a single machine with 8 NVIDIA P100 GPUs. The base model takes about 0.4 seconds per step, trains for 100K steps, and finishes in roughly 12 hours. The big model takes about 1.0 second per step, trains for 300K steps, and finishes in about 3.5 days. The optimizer is Adam:
The learning-rate schedule is the paper’s third numbered equation. Let be the current step number and be the number of warmup steps:
with:
During warmup, the second term is smaller, so the learning rate grows approximately linearly:
After warmup, the first term is smaller, so the learning rate decays by inverse square root:
This schedule was common in early Transformer training, especially for NMT models trained from scratch. Warmup is not magic. It gives Adam’s moment estimates and the network’s early activation scales time to stabilize before large updates hit a residual stack. The paper uses residual dropout and label smoothing. Dropout is applied to the output of each sub-layer before residual addition and LayerNorm. Dropout is also applied to the sum of token embedding and positional encoding. The base model uses:
Label smoothing uses:
The paper does not expand the label-smoothing distribution, but a common version replaces the one-hot target with:
and:
where is the number of classes and is the correct label. Some implementations distribute over all classes instead. The important observation in the paper is that label smoothing worsens perplexity because the model is trained to be less confident, but improves accuracy and BLEU. This pattern still appears in classification and sequence-generation systems. Inference DetailsThe reported translation results do not come from greedy decoding. The paper uses beam search:
with length penalty:
The maximum output length is:
The base model averages the last 5 checkpoints, with checkpoints written every 10 minutes. The big model averages the last 20 checkpoints. Checkpoint averaging was common in early NMT; it acts like a cheap ensemble and reduces the variance of a single checkpoint. The FLOPs estimate in the results table is also worth reading carefully. The paper estimates training FLOPs from training time, GPU count, and sustained single-GPU FP32 throughput:
The footnote uses estimated sustained rates of 2.8, 3.7, 6.0, and 9.5 TFLOPS for K80, K40, M40, and P100 respectively. The estimate is coarse, but it is enough to show that Transformer was not just winning by spending far more compute. Main Results Table 2 contains the main results. On WMT14 English-to-German, Transformer big reaches 28.4 BLEU, more than 2 BLEU above the best previously published results and ensembles listed in the table. Transformer base reaches 27.3 BLEU, also beating the listed single models and ensembles, with training cost of:
Transformer big costs:
On English-to-French, Transformer big reaches 41.8 BLEU. The ConvS2S ensemble in the table reaches 41.29 BLEU with:
Compared with Transformer big at FLOPs, the compute is roughly two orders of magnitude larger. The key result is not only the BLEU number. Quality, training time, and parallelism all improve together. RNN and CNN models can do machine translation, but Transformer moves the backbone toward the dense matrix operations that GPUs prefer. There is a small textual inconsistency in the paper: one paragraph says the big model achieves BLEU 41.0 on English-to-French, while the abstract and Table 2 report 41.8. I use 41.8 because it is the number in the final main table and abstract. Model Variations Table 3 is the most useful ablation table in the paper. All measurements are on the English-to-German development set newstest2013. PPL is per wordpiece and should not be compared directly with word-level perplexity. The base configuration is:
Hyperparameter Value
6
512
2048
8
64
64
0.1
0.1
Train steps 100K
Params 65M
The base dev result is:
HeadsRow (A) keeps total compute roughly fixed while changing the number of heads and per-head width:
PPL BLEU
1 512 5.29 24.9
4 128 5.00 25.5
8 64 4.92 25.8
16 32 4.91 25.8
32 16 5.01 25.4
One head is 0.9 BLEU worse than 8 or 16 heads, so multiple representation subspaces are useful. But 32 heads also drops, because each head has only 16 dimensions and the compatibility test becomes too narrow. The result is simple but important: Transformer does not use one large attention distribution; it splits representation space into several smaller routing modules. Key DimensionRow (B) reduces :
PPL BLEU Params
16 5.16 25.1 58M
32 5.01 25.4 60M
Reducing hurts quality. The paper suggests that determining compatibility is harder with a lower-dimensional key/query space, and a simple dot product may not be expressive enough. This issue reappears in later systems: reducing KV dimensions, sharing KV across heads, or compressing KV cache can save memory and bandwidth, but it can also reduce token-token discrimination. Depth And WidthRow (C) changes layer count, hidden width, and FFN width:
Change PPL BLEU Params
6.11 23.7 36M
5.19 25.3 50M
4.88 25.5 80M
5.75 24.5 28M
4.66 26.0 168M
5.12 25.4 53M
4.75 26.2 90M
The trend is that larger models usually help, but the gains are not linear. has lower PPL than the base model, but slightly lower BLEU. Increasing to 4096 improves BLEU to 26.2, showing that FFN capacity matters. In modern LLMs, FFN/MLP layers usually dominate parameters and compute; this early ablation already points in that direction. Dropout And Label SmoothingRow (D) changes dropout and label smoothing:
Change PPL BLEU
5.77 24.6
4.95 25.5
4.67 25.3
5.47 25.7
Removing dropout clearly overfits and drops BLEU to 24.6. Label smoothing is more subtle. Without label smoothing, PPL improves to 4.67, lower than the base 4.92, but BLEU gets worse. Stronger smoothing with worsens PPL to 5.47 but yields BLEU 25.7. For generation, NLL/PPL alone can be misleading because it is sensitive to calibration and confidence, while BLEU measures decoded sequence quality. Positional EncodingRow (E) replaces sinusoidal positional encoding with learned positional embeddings:
This suggests that, in this WMT14 setting, the exact positional encoding was not the main bottleneck. Sinusoidal encoding remained attractive because of possible length extrapolation. Modern models often use RoPE or relative position bias instead, because those approaches inject position more directly into attention logits or Q/K rotations. Big ModelThe big configuration is:
Hyperparameter Value
6
1024
4096
16
0.3
Train steps 300K
Params 213M
Its development result is:
This model is small by current standards, but the scaling direction is already visible: wider hidden states, more heads, wider FFNs, stronger regularization, and longer training. English Constituency Parsing The paper also evaluates English constituency parsing. This is not the most cited part of the paper, but it shows that Transformer was not merely tuned for one translation benchmark. The authors train a 4-layer Transformer with on WSJ Penn Treebank. The WSJ-only setting has about 40K sentences. The semi-supervised setting uses additional high-confidence and BerkeleyParser corpora, about 17M sentences. With WSJ-only discriminative training, the 4-layer Transformer reaches:
With semi-supervised training, it reaches:
It does not beat the generative RNNG result of 93.3 or the multi-task result of 93.0, but it is strong without task-specific structural design. This supports the conclusion that attention-based architectures should not be viewed only as translation models; they can transfer to other structured input-output tasks. Attention VisualizationsThe appendix visualizations are often overread as “attention is explanation”. I would treat them as sanity checks instead. If some heads learn sparse and interpretable patterns, then multi-head self-attention is indeed doing structured routing in some places, rather than simply averaging all tokens.
Figure 3 shows attention related to long-distance dependencies in encoder layer 5. In the example, making ... more difficult spans a long range. In an RNN, information has to move through many time steps. Self-attention allows making to connect directly to the later more difficult positions. Different colors indicate different heads, which is the practical meaning of multi-head routing: one query position can use several heads to retrieve different types of information.
The top part of Figure 4 shows the full attention pattern for one head. It is not uniformly spread across the sentence; it has clear line structures. In language tasks, this kind of head may correspond to local syntax, reference resolution, separators, punctuation, or position offsets. Still, each line should not be interpreted as a complete linguistic rule. An attention weight is an internal routing coefficient, not a full causal explanation.
The lower part of Figure 4 isolates its. The attention is sharp and mainly points to Law and application, which looks like anaphora resolution. The example shows that a head can make a concentrated choice for some tokens rather than always spreading weight over the whole sentence.
Figure 5 gives two different head examples. One head looks more like structural cross-token connections, while another looks more local or pattern-based. The important point is not that every head has a clean human-readable label. The important point is that different heads learn different routing patterns in parallel. Later analysis work also finds that some heads can be pruned while others are important for specific positions or tasks, which is consistent with these early visualizations. What Actually ChangedAfter reading the original paper, I would summarize the core change in four layers. First, sequence modeling moves from recurrence to pairwise routing. An RNN’s basic state update is:
The main communication operation in a Transformer layer is:
Each layer recomputes token-token mixing weights from content. The weights are not fixed convolution kernels and not hidden states passed through time. They are dynamically generated from the current representation. Second, the path length becomes short. Any two tokens can interact in a single attention layer. Long-distance dependencies no longer have to pass through recurrent transitions or many convolutional layers. This is friendly to optimization, but the price is the attention matrix. Third, the training graph becomes better matched to hardware. Attention is mostly batched GEMM, softmax, dropout, and another GEMM. FFN is two large matrix multiplications. These operations are easier for GPU/TPU hardware to saturate than small per-time-step kernels. The paper’s statement that the base model trains in 12 hours on 8 P100 GPUs was a strong systems signal at the time. Fourth, the Transformer block separates token communication from token-local computation. Attention mixes information across positions. FFN transforms each position’s channels. Residual connections and LayerNorm make deep stacking possible. This decomposition is simple enough that later work could scale width, depth, head count, context length, FFN form, and parallel training strategies systematically. LimitationsTransformer is not free. The most direct limitation is full self-attention complexity:
Both attention logits and attention probabilities are . For long-sequence training, this creates large memory and bandwidth pressure. For long-context inference, the prefill stage is still quadratic in sequence length. During autoregressive decode, each new token attends to historical KV cache, so per-token complexity grows linearly with context length:
Thus Transformer removes recurrence inside the target sequence during training, but autoregressive generation is still sequential. The conclusion explicitly mentions making generation less sequential as future work. This later grows into non-autoregressive translation, speculative decoding, multi-token prediction, Medusa, EAGLE, and related decoding methods. The second limitation is position modeling. Sinusoidal PE works, but it is not the final answer. It adds absolute position information to embeddings and leaves the model to learn relative patterns. Later relative position methods are more direct, especially for long-context extrapolation, where positional design can determine whether the model remains stable. The third limitation is interpretability. The appendix figures are useful, but attention visualization is not the same as causal explanation. A head with a clean pattern does not prove that the model decision depends only on that line. Attention weights interact with value projections, residual streams, later heads, and FFN layers. They are useful debugging signals, but they are not complete explanations. TakeawayThe paper matters because several decisions close the loop together:
Scaled dot-product attention makes token-token routing expressible as efficient matrix multiplication. Multi-head attention lets the model choose relations in several representation subspaces at once. Positional encoding injects order into a model without recurrence or convolution. Position-wise FFN provides nonlinear channel mixing inside each token. Residual connection, LayerNorm, dropout, label smoothing, and warmup schedule make the 6-layer encoder-decoder train reliably. The whole network greatly reduces sequential operations during training, making it much more suitable for GPU/TPU scaling.
If I remember only one formula, it is:
If I remember only one engineering fact, it is this: Transformer changes the backbone of sequence modeling from time-step recurrence to global matrix routing inside each layer. That change improves model quality, training parallelism, and hardware efficiency at the same time, and it opens the scaling path used by modern large models.

entry.title: Regularized Evolution for Image Classifier Architecture Search
entry.content:
Real E, Aggarwal A, Huang Y, Le Q V. Regularized Evolution for Image Classifier Architecture Search. AAAI 2019.
Paper / Colab AmoebaNet is a useful paper because it separates two things that were often mixed together in early NAS papers:
the search space, which was already made strong by NASNet; the search algorithm, where the paper compares evolution, RL, and random search under similar conditions.
The key algorithmic change is aging evolution. Tournament selection still chooses a good parent from a sampled subset of the population, but the algorithm removes the oldest individual instead of removing the worst one. That sounds like a small queue-management rule, but it changes the failure mode: a model that got lucky early cannot sit in the population forever. The result is AmoebaNet-A, an evolved NASNet-style cell architecture. The paper reports that evolution reaches good candidates faster than the reproduced RL baseline in the early part of the search, and the final AmoebaNet-A transfer result is competitive on ImageNet. MotivationBefore this paper, the strongest automated image classifiers were mostly RL-based NAS results, especially NASNet. That makes the comparison tricky: if an RL controller finds a good model, is the controller the important part, or did the NASNet cell search space already do most of the work? AmoebaNet keeps the NASNet-style search space and changes the optimizer. This is the clean part of the paper. It is not trying to invent a new convolution operator or a new macro skeleton. It asks whether a simpler evolutionary process can compete with an RL controller when both search over the same kind of cells. The historical point also matters. Evolution had been used for neural topology search for a long time, but earlier evolved image classifiers did not clearly beat hand-designed networks. This paper argues that, with a modern cell space and enough compute, evolution is not just a toy baseline. ContributionThe main contributions are:
It proposes aging evolution, also called regularized evolution, for NAS. It compares evolution, RL, and random search in the same NASNet-style search space. It gives a concrete mutation-only implementation: mutate hidden-state inputs or operation labels inside cells. It discovers AmoebaNet-A and reports competitive CIFAR-10 and ImageNet results. It studies aging versus non-aging tournament selection and argues that aging helps under noisy architecture evaluation.
The contribution is not “evolution always beats RL.” The stronger reading is narrower: in this controlled setup, regularized evolution is a very strong and simple NAS baseline. MethodologyNASNet search spaceAll main experiments use the NASNet search space. A model is a stack of two searched cell types:
normal cell: preserves feature-map resolution; reduction cell: reduces spatial resolution, usually by stride-2 operations.
The outer skeleton is fixed. The search only decides the internal wiring and operations of the normal and reduction cells. After the cell topology is selected, two manual scale knobs still exist:
(N): number of normal cells per stack; (F): number of output filters for convolution operations.
Each cell is built from five pairwise combinations. A pairwise combination selects two earlier hidden states, applies two operations, and adds their outputs to create a new hidden state. Unused hidden states are concatenated at the end of the cell. The operation set includes identity, separable convolutions with several kernel sizes, average pooling, max pooling, dilated separable convolution, and a 1x7 then 7x1 convolution. This is a rich enough space for interesting cell topologies, but it is still strongly hand-shaped. Aging evolutionThe search maintains a population of already-trained candidate architectures. In the main setup, the paper uses population size (P=100) and tournament sample size (S=25).
The loop is:
Initialize a population with random architectures. Randomly sample (S) candidates from the current population. Choose the highest-validation-accuracy candidate in that sample as the parent. Mutate the parent architecture to produce a child. Train and evaluate the child. Push the child into the population. Remove the oldest individual from the population.
The last line is the whole regularization mechanism. Standard tournament selection often removes the worst individual. Aging evolution removes by age, so survival requires repeatedly producing descendants that train well. A model that only looked good once because of training noise eventually leaves the queue. This distinction matters because NAS candidate evaluation is noisy. The paper’s interpretation is that non-aging evolution can overfit to lucky trained models, while aging evolution pays more attention to architectures that can reproduce good performance across generations. MutationsA child is produced by applying a random mutation to the parent’s architecture. The paper mainly uses two mutation types:
hidden-state mutation: choose one pairwise combination and replace one of its input hidden states with another valid previous state. operation mutation: choose one pairwise combination and replace one operation label.
There is also an identity mutation with small probability. That is useful in a noisy evaluation setup because sometimes the same architecture deserves another training/evaluation sample. Search and augmentationThe search itself is done on relatively small CIFAR-10 models. The paper withholds 5k CIFAR-10 examples for validation, trains each candidate for 25 epochs during search, and stops after evaluating 20k models. The reported large-scale experiment uses 450 K40 GPUs for about 7 days. After search, the best architectures are augmented by increasing (N) and (F), then trained longer for CIFAR-10 or ImageNet. This is the same basic recipe as NASNet: search a cell cheaply, then scale the discovered cell for the final model. ResultsSearch dynamicsThe first result is the side-by-side search comparison. The paper runs five repeats for evolution, RL, and random search.
Evolution reaches high pre-augmentation CIFAR-10 accuracy earlier than RL in these runs, while both are clearly above random search. This is the part of the result I find most useful: if the search has to stop early because compute is limited, the trajectory matters more than only the final point. There is one caveat. Figure 3 plots accuracy over wall-clock search time, not the compute cost of each discovered model. The paper handles that in the next comparison.
After augmentation, evolved models have better accuracy than random search at similar cost, and lower FLOPs than RL at similar accuracy. Within this case study, evolution lands in the better corner of the accuracy-cost plot. AmoebaNet-A on CIFAR-10The best evolved architecture is named AmoebaNet-A.
The architecture is still recognizably NASNet-style: a repeated normal cell and reduction cell, not a fully free-form model. The found cells use separable convolutions, pooling, identity/none choices, and several skip-like edges. On CIFAR-10, AmoebaNet-A is compared against the published NASNet-A baseline:
Model Params Test error
NASNet-A baseline 3.3M 3.41
AmoebaNet-A, (N=6,F=32) 2.6M 3.40 +/- 0.08
AmoebaNet-A, (N=6,F=36) 3.2M 3.34 +/- 0.06
This table should be read carefully. The paper notes that the NASNet-A comparison is not perfectly controlled because the exact final training code and number of experiments may differ. The cleaner comparison is still the evolution/RL/random-search study above. ImageNet transferThe ImageNet result is where AmoebaNet-A became visible as more than an algorithm toy.
Model Params Multiply-adds Top-1 / Top-5
NASNet-A 88.9M 23.8B 82.7 / 96.2
PNASNet-5 86.1M 25.0B 82.9 / 96.2
AmoebaNet-A, (N=6,F=190) 86.7M 23.1B 82.8 / 96.1
AmoebaNet-A, (N=6,F=448) 469M 104B 83.9 / 96.6
At comparable size, AmoebaNet-A is around the same level as NASNet-A and PNASNet-5. At the very large setting, it reports 83.9% top-1 / 96.6% top-5, but that model is huge: 469M parameters and 104B multiply-adds. This is an accuracy result, not an efficient-deployment result. Aging versus non-agingThe most interesting ablation is aging evolution versus non-aging tournament selection.
Most points are above the (y=x) line, which means aging evolution beats the non-aging variant in these small-compute experiments. The proposed explanation is practical:
non-aging evolution can keep a lucky model alive for a long time; aging evolution removes old models, so useful architectures must keep reappearing through descendants; this acts like regularization against noisy architecture evaluation.
This is why the paper’s title says regularized evolution. The regularization is not a loss term. It is an algorithmic constraint on population lifetime. Reproduction NotesA faithful reproduction should separate three stages:
Search phase: small CIFAR-10 models, 25 epochs per candidate, validation on a 5k holdout split, fixed (P) and (S). Selection phase: choose the best architecture from search history, not just the current population. Augmentation phase: scale (N) and (F), then train the final model from scratch with the full recipe.
I would report at least four things:
validation accuracy during search; final CIFAR/ImageNet accuracy after augmentation; final model cost in FLOPs or multiply-adds; number of evaluated models and actual hardware time.
The hardware number matters here. The search still trains child models independently. This is not an efficient-NAS method in the ENAS/DARTS sense. It is a strong full-training search baseline. TakeawayAmoebaNet’s lesson is that evolutionary NAS should not be dismissed as an older alternative to RL. In the NASNet cell space, a simple tournament-selection loop with age-based removal is enough to compete with a more complex controller. The limitation is also clear. AmoebaNet spends a lot of compute, searches for accuracy rather than latency, and relies on a manually designed cell-based macro skeleton. Later work such as ENAS, DARTS, MnasNet, FBNet, and ProxylessNAS attacks different parts of that cost/deployment problem. I read this paper as a baseline-setting result: if a new NAS method claims better search intelligence, it should beat regularized evolution under a fair search space, budget, and final training recipe.

entry.title: AutoFormer: Searching Transformers for Visual Recognition
entry.content:
Chen M, Peng H, Fu J, Ling H. AutoFormer: Searching Transformers for Visual Recognition. ICCV 2021.
Paper / Code AutoFormer is a one-shot NAS paper for pure Vision Transformers. The interesting part is not only that it searches depth, width, heads, and MLP ratios. The stronger claim is that a trained Transformer supernet can produce many subnets whose inherited weights are already close to retraining from scratch. That is a high bar for one-shot NAS. If inherited accuracy is a poor proxy, the search loop is mostly ranking noise. AutoFormer tries to make the proxy reliable with weight entanglement: candidate Transformer blocks in the same layer are not trained as isolated choices, but share their common parameters in a nested way. MotivationFor ViT, architecture choices are coupled. Increasing one dimension is not always better, and two models with similar parameter counts can behave very differently.
The sensitivity plot is a useful starting point. In this baseline experiment:
Depth improves accuracy until around 14 to 15 layers, then drops. Embedding dimension gives a large jump early, then saturates. MLP ratio peaks around 5 in this setting. Head count is not monotonic when the Q-K-V dimension is fixed.
So the search space is not just “scale the model bigger”. AutoFormer searches a structured set of Transformer choices under parameter constraints. ContributionThe paper contributes three things:
It defines a ViT search space over embedding dimension, Q-K-V dimension, MLP ratio, number of heads, and depth. It proposes weight entanglement for one-shot Transformer supernet training. It searches tiny/small/base AutoFormers and shows that inherited-weight evaluation is close to fine-tuning or full retraining.
The third point is the most important one. If we only look at the final ImageNet table, this is another NAS result. If we look at the inherited-vs-retrained tables, the paper is really arguing that the supernet itself becomes a usable model family. MethodologyOne-Shot SetupAutoFormer follows the usual two-stage one-shot NAS setup. The search space is encoded in a supernet . First the supernet weights are trained:
Then the search algorithm samples or evolves candidate subnets and evaluates them with inherited weights:
This is efficient only if , inherited from , is a faithful proxy for the subnet after retraining. AutoFormer spends most of its method design on making that assumption less fragile.
The left side shows the dynamic AutoFormer supernet: depth can vary, and each layer can choose a Transformer block.
