The right side shows the searchable pieces inside a block, including embedding, Q/K/V, hidden dimension, and attention choices. Search Space AutoFormer builds three independent supernets:
Supernet Parameter range Intended scale
tiny 4-9M mobile/small models
small 14-34M DeiT-S/ViT-S scale
base 42-75M medium/base models
The table notation is (low, high, step). For example, Supernet-small searches embedding dimension from 320 to 448 with step 64, Q-K-V dimension from 320 to 448 with step 64, MLP ratio from 3 to 4 with step 0.5, head number from 5 to 7, and depth from 12 to 14. The paper reports that the combined space contains more than candidate architectures. That explains why the method needs both weight sharing and a search algorithm; enumeration is not an option. Weight EntanglementClassical one-shot NAS often assigns separate weights to different choices in the same layer. AutoFormer argues that this is inefficient for Transformers because the candidate blocks are homogeneous: they are all attention/MLP blocks with different dimensions, not completely different operations like conv/pooling/skip in a DARTS cell.
Weight entanglement makes the smaller block use a subset of the larger block’s weights. For two candidate blocks in the same layer, their weights satisfy a nested relation:
In implementation terms, each layer only needs to store the largest candidate block. Smaller candidates directly slice the corresponding weights. A gradient update from one sampled subnet then trains weights that are also reused by other compatible subnets.
The training curve shows why this matters. Compared with classical weight sharing, weight entanglement converges faster and gives much higher inherited subnet accuracy during supernet training. Search PipelineThe pipeline has two phases:
Train the supernet with weight entanglement by uniformly sampling subnets and updating their selected weights. Run evolutionary search under resource constraints on the trained supernet.
The supernet training recipe is close to DeiT: 500 epochs, AdamW, batch size 1024, cosine LR schedule, weight decay , 20 warmup epochs, label smoothing 0.1, drop path 0.1, RandAugment, CutMix, Mixup, and random erasing. The paper uses 16x16 patches. For evolution search, AutoFormer reserves 10,000 ImageNet training examples as a validation set, starts from 50 random architectures, runs 20 generations, keeps the top 10 as parents, and uses crossover plus mutation. Depth mutation probability is 0.2 and block mutation probability is 0.4. ExperimentsDoes Entanglement Fix The Proxy?This is the key ablation.
The inherited-vs-retrained gap is the part to watch:
Method Inherited Retrain Observation
Classical sharing + random search 69.7% 80.1% inherited score is badly undertrained
Weight entanglement + random search 81.3% 81.4% inherited score is already useful
Classical sharing + evolution search 71.5% 80.4% evolution cannot fix a poor supernet proxy
Weight entanglement + evolution search 81.7% 81.7% search and retrain agree
This table is more convincing than the final top-1 table. It shows that the method improves the quality of the one-shot evaluator, not just the final selected architecture.
Evolution search also matters. The red candidates are consistently above the random baseline during search, which suggests the validation signal from inherited weights is informative enough for selection.
For the final AutoFormer-T/S/B models, inherited accuracy is nearly identical to fine-tuning or retraining:
Model Inherited Fine-tune Retrain
AutoFormer-T 74.7% 74.9% 74.9%
AutoFormer-S 81.7% 81.8% 81.7%
AutoFormer-B 82.4% 82.6% 82.6%
That is the core empirical claim: after weight-entangled training, the supernet is not just a search scaffold. It can directly provide deployable subnets.
The scatter plot makes the same point from another angle. Many high-performing subnets sampled from Supernet-small already land around 80.1% to 82.0% top-1 with inherited weights. ImageNet Results The front-page comparison plots top-1 accuracy against parameter count. It is not a full fairness proof because the models have different training recipes and inductive biases, but it gives a quick picture of where the searched AutoFormers sit among DeiT, ResNet, ResNeXt, and DenseNet references.
The compact comparison against manual Transformer baselines:
Model Params FLOPs Top-1
DeiT-tiny 5.7M 1.2G 72.2%
AutoFormer-tiny 5.7M 1.3G 74.7%
DeiT-S 22.1M 4.7G 79.9%
ViT-S/16 22.1M 4.7G 78.8%
AutoFormer-small 22.9M 5.1G 81.7%
DeiT-B 86M 18G 81.8%
AutoFormer-base 54M 11G 82.4%
AutoFormer-small is the cleanest result: roughly the same scale as DeiT-S and ViT-S/16, but +1.8 and +2.9 percentage points top-1, respectively. AutoFormer-base is also interesting because it beats DeiT-B while using fewer parameters and FLOPs. The table also reminds me not to over-read the result as “Transformers are always more efficient”. EfficientNet-B4 and EfficientNet-B7 are still very strong in this comparison. AutoFormer is competitive among pure Transformers, but CNN/mobile design priors were still hard to beat in this 2021 setup. Transfer And Distillation AutoFormer-S fine-tuned at 384x384 reaches 83.4% ImageNet top-1 with 23M parameters and 16.5G FLOPs. In the same table, DeiT-B at 384x384 uses 86M parameters and 55.4G FLOPs for 83.1% ImageNet top-1. The transfer table is useful because AutoFormer is not only a searched ImageNet classifier. It keeps competitive numbers on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, Flowers, Cars, and Pets under the same fine-tuning style. The paper also reports that knowledge distillation from a RegNetY-32GF teacher improves AutoFormer-T/S/B from 74.7%/81.7%/82.4% to 75.7%/82.4%/82.9%. That means the searched architecture is orthogonal to distillation; the search method is not relying on a teacher to make the main table work. Relation To Other NAS WorkAutoFormer is close in spirit to Once-for-All and BigNAS: train one elastic supernet, then select subnets for different constraints. The difference is that AutoFormer is aimed at pure Transformer blocks. CNN elastic networks vary depth, width, kernel size, and resolution; AutoFormer varies Transformer-specific dimensions such as Q-K-V dimension, heads, and MLP ratio. It is also worth comparing with ViTAS. Both papers care about whether weight sharing is fair enough for Transformer NAS. AutoFormer uses weight entanglement so that compatible candidates train shared slices of the same larger block. ViTAS later emphasizes channel fairness with cyclic sharing. They are attacking the same practical failure mode: inherited subnet ranking can be biased by uneven training. LimitationsThe method is not a free architecture search button.
The search space is still manually designed around a DeiT-style pure ViT. It does not search window attention, hierarchical stages, convolutional stems, or relative position designs. The supernet training is expensive: 500 ImageNet epochs on V100 GPUs is not a small setup. The inherited-weight claim depends on the weight-entangled training recipe. Classical weight sharing in the paper fails badly, so the result should not be generalized to arbitrary supernets. The search objective is mainly ImageNet accuracy under parameter constraints. Real deployment may care more about latency, memory bandwidth, activation size, or hardware-specific kernels.
TakeawayAutoFormer is useful because it makes one-shot Transformer NAS look credible. The searched models are good, but the more reusable lesson is the supernet design: when candidate Transformer blocks are nested and homogeneous, sharing the common weights can make inherited accuracy close to retrained accuracy. For me, the paper’s strongest evidence is Table 2 and Table 4. They show that weight entanglement turns the supernet from a weak ranking proxy into something close to a deployable model family. That is the part worth remembering when reading later ViT NAS papers.

entry.title: BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding
entry.content:
Devlin J, Chang M W, Lee K, Toutanova K. BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding. NAACL 2019.
Paper / Code BERT is the paper that made encoder-only Transformer pre-training the default starting point for NLP understanding tasks. It is not important because the architecture is exotic. It is important because the recipe is clean:
Use a standard Transformer encoder. Pre-train it on large unlabeled document-level text. Make the pre-training objective bidirectional with masked language modeling. Pack single-text and text-pair tasks into one input format with [CLS], [SEP], segment embeddings, and position embeddings. Fine-tune all parameters with a small task head.
That combination made many task-specific NLP architectures look unnecessary. Before BERT, strong systems for NLI, paraphrase, QA, and sequence tagging often had task-specific attention modules, matching networks, CRFs, or hand-designed interaction layers. BERT’s claim is stronger: use one pre-trained encoder, change only the input/output layer, and fine-tune. This note reads BERT as an engineering recipe, not only as a benchmark paper. The details that matter are the pre-train/fine-tune interface, the MLM corruption distribution, the sentence-pair format, and the ablations that justify bidirectionality, NSP, model size, and masking choices. All paper figures and tables below are cropped from the original arXiv PDF. Core IdeaBERT and GPT-1 split early Transformer pre-training into two different directions. GPT-1 uses a decoder-style left-to-right language model:
This is natural for generation. During pre-training and inference, token only depends on tokens before it. BERT instead wants a representation for language understanding. In a classifier, a QA span predictor, or an NER tagger, token should use both left and right context:
The problem is leakage. If a model is trained to predict every token while every token can attend to itself, the task is trivial. BERT solves that by corrupting a subset of tokens and predicting only those selected targets:
where is the set of selected masked positions and is the corrupted input sequence. This gives the encoder full bidirectional self-attention while preventing the selected target from being copied directly from its own input position. The second pre-training task, next sentence prediction (NSP), adds a sentence-pair objective:
where . The final pre-training objective is:
Later work, especially RoBERTa, showed that NSP is not essential under a stronger training recipe. But in the original BERT paper, NSP is part of the full recipe and the ablation suggests it helps QNLI, MNLI, and SQuAD. Pre-Training and Fine-Tuning Figure 1 is the whole BERT interface. The left side is pre-training: the same encoder receives two packed text spans, predicts masked tokens, and predicts whether the second span follows the first. The right side is fine-tuning: the same encoder is initialized from the pre-trained checkpoint, and only the output layer changes. The most important design is that BERT does not use a feature-only transfer setup by default. During fine-tuning, all parameters are updated:
Then the task loss updates both the BERT encoder and the new head:
where is BERT and is the task-specific output layer. The number of newly initialized parameters is small compared with the encoder. This is why the input format matters so much. BERT has to express classification, sentence-pair reasoning, span extraction, and token tagging without changing the encoder architecture. ArchitectureBERT is a multi-layer bidirectional Transformer encoder. It uses the same basic block family as the Transformer encoder from “Attention Is All You Need”: multi-head self-attention, feed-forward layers, residual connections, LayerNorm, and dropout. The paper defines:
: number of Transformer layers; : hidden size; : number of attention heads; feed-forward hidden size: .
The paper uses two main model sizes:
BERT-base: , , , about 110M parameters. BERT-large: , , , about 340M parameters.
BERT-base was chosen to be close in size to OpenAI GPT, so the comparison is not just “larger model wins.” The architectural difference is the attention mask:
Model family Self-attention visibility Natural use
GPT-style decoder token sees generation
BERT encoder token sees all non-masked positions understanding
For a Transformer layer, if the hidden states are , BERT’s self-attention is full sequence attention:
with no causal mask. In GPT, the logits for future positions are masked:
BERT does not apply that causal restriction. This is the direct reason its hidden states are better suited for token classification and extractive QA, but also the reason plain BERT is not an autoregressive generator. Input Representation BERT uses WordPiece tokenization with a 30k vocabulary. A sequence can be either one text span or a pair of spans. The input always begins with [CLS], and sentence pairs are separated by [SEP]. For each position , the vector fed to the encoder is the sum of three embeddings:
The segment embedding identifies whether a token belongs to sentence A or sentence B:
This single design lets BERT represent:
a single sentence: [CLS] sentence [SEP]; a sentence pair: [CLS] sentence A [SEP] sentence B [SEP]; a question and passage: [CLS] question [SEP] passage [SEP]; a tagging sequence: [CLS] tokens [SEP].
The final hidden state of [CLS] is written as . The final hidden state of token is written as . That notation is useful because most BERT task heads are extremely small:
classification uses ; QA span extraction uses ; NER uses token-level .
Pre-Training ObjectivesMasked Language ModelBERT selects 15% of WordPiece positions as prediction targets. Only those positions contribute to the MLM loss. If position is selected, BERT does not always replace it with [MASK]. The corruption rule is:
Corruption Probability among selected positions
replace with [MASK] 80%
replace with a random token 10%
keep unchanged 10%
Then the final hidden vector at that position predicts the original token:
The selected-token loss is:
The 80/10/10 detail is not cosmetic. If BERT always used [MASK], the model would see a token during pre-training that never appears during fine-tuning. Random and unchanged replacements reduce that mismatch:
[MASK] forces the model to infer from context; random replacement teaches robustness to corrupted tokens; unchanged replacement keeps the encoder from treating every selected position as visibly artificial.
Next Sentence PredictionNSP is a binary classification task over a pair of spans:
50% IsNext: sentence B is the actual next span after sentence A; 50% NotNext: sentence B is sampled randomly from the corpus.
The classifier reads , the final [CLS] representation:
The paper reports that the final model reaches 97%-98% NSP accuracy during pre-training. This does not mean is automatically a universal sentence embedding. The authors explicitly note that becomes meaningful for downstream classification after fine-tuning. Pre-Training Corpus and ScheduleBERT uses document-level text:
BooksCorpus: about 800M words; English Wikipedia: about 2.5B words; total: about 3.3B words.
Document-level text matters because NSP needs contiguous spans. A shuffled sentence corpus would damage the sentence-pair signal. The appendix gives the main pre-training details:
Item Setting
batch size 256 sequences
max sequence length 512
tokens per batch 128k
steps 1M
optimizer Adam
learning rate 1e-4
warmup first 10k steps
dropout 0.1
activation GELU
BERT-base hardware 4 Cloud TPUs, 16 TPU chips total
BERT-large hardware 16 Cloud TPUs, 64 TPU chips total
training time about 4 days
There is also a practical sequence-length trick. Because attention cost is quadratic in sequence length, the paper pre-trains with sequence length 128 for 90% of the steps, then uses sequence length 512 for the remaining 10% to learn long-position embeddings. Fine-Tuning Interfaces The fine-tuning design is where BERT’s simplicity shows up. The task-specific model is BERT plus one output layer. Sentence ClassificationFor single-sentence classification such as SST-2 or CoLA: [CLS] sentence [SEP]
The head reads :
Sentence-Pair ClassificationFor NLI, paraphrase, semantic similarity, and multiple-choice scoring: [CLS] sentence A [SEP] sentence B [SEP]
Again, the head reads . The important part is that BERT’s self-attention mixes sentence A and sentence B internally. Older architectures often encoded each sentence separately and then added a cross-attention/matching module. BERT gets bidirectional cross-sentence interaction by simply concatenating the pair. For a -class task:
For SWAG-style multiple choice, each candidate continuation is packed with the context, scored through , and normalized across choices. Extractive QAFor SQuAD: [CLS] question [SEP] passage [SEP]
BERT predicts answer start and end positions using two learned vectors . Start probability:
End probability:
The score for span is:
At prediction time, choose the best valid span with . For SQuAD 2.0, no-answer questions are represented by a span at [CLS]. The no-answer score is:
Then BERT predicts a non-null answer if:
where is tuned on the development set. Token TaggingFor NER, every token representation can receive a label:
The paper uses WordPiece tokenization and uses the representation of the first sub-token for the token-level classifier. ResultsGLUE The GLUE table is the main sentence-level result. The average reported in the table excludes WNLI, following the paper’s note. The compact reading is:
System Avg Main read
OpenAI GPT 75.1 decoder-only baseline
BERT-base 79.6 similar scale to GPT, better transfer
BERT-large 82.1 strongest BERT result in the table
The comparison with GPT is the one to read carefully. BERT-base and OpenAI GPT are close in size. The paper highlights that for MNLI, BERT reaches 86.7/85.9 with BERT-large, and even BERT-base is above GPT. The main difference is not a custom NLI architecture; it is bidirectional encoder pre-training plus the fine-tuning interface. The gains are especially large on tasks that need sentence-pair reasoning or linguistic acceptability:
QNLI: 87.4 to 92.7 from GPT to BERT-large; CoLA: 45.4 to 60.5; RTE: 56.0 to 70.1.
Small datasets also show why pre-training matters. RTE has only about 2.5k examples in the table, but BERT-large still improves substantially. SQuAD 1.1 SQuAD 1.1 is extractive QA where every question has an answer span in the passage.
System Dev EM Dev F1 Test EM Test F1
Human - - 82.3 91.2
BERT-base single 80.8 88.5 - -
BERT-large single 84.1 90.9 - -
BERT-large ensemble 85.8 91.8 - -
BERT-large single + TriviaQA 84.2 91.1 85.1 91.8
BERT-large ensemble + TriviaQA 86.2 92.2 87.4 93.2
The important engineering point is how simple the QA head is. BERT does not add a complex reading-comprehension architecture. Two learned vectors score start and end positions. Most of the work is done by the pre-trained encoder. SQuAD 2.0 SQuAD 2.0 adds unanswerable questions. BERT handles this by letting [CLS] represent the null span.
System Dev EM Dev F1 Test EM Test F1
Human 86.3 89.0 86.9 89.5
Prior single MIR-MRC - - 74.8 78.0
BERT-large single 78.7 81.9 80.0 83.1
The paper reports a +5.1 F1 improvement over the previous best system in this table. Again, the change is mostly the pre-trained encoder and a small output interface. SWAG SWAG is a grounded commonsense multiple-choice continuation task. BERT scores four packed sentence pairs and normalizes over choices.
System Dev Test
ESIM+GloVe 51.9 52.7
ESIM+ELMo 59.1 59.2
OpenAI GPT - 78.0
BERT-base 81.6 -
BERT-large 86.6 86.3
This result is useful because SWAG is not just another GLUE classification task. It tests whether the same sentence-pair interface can handle multiple-choice reasoning. AblationsThe ablation section is the part of BERT that is easiest to under-read. It explains why the recipe is not just “large Transformer plus more data.” Pre-Training Tasks Key numbers from the ablation:
Full BERT-base: QNLI 88.4, MRPC 86.7, SQuAD F1 88.5. No NSP: QNLI drops to 84.9 and SQuAD F1 drops to 87.9. Left-to-right pre-training without NSP: MRPC drops to 77.5 and SQuAD F1 drops to 77.8. Adding a randomly initialized BiLSTM on top of the left-to-right model recovers SQuAD to 84.9, still below full BERT.
There are two separate effects:
Removing NSP hurts QNLI and SQuAD more than it hurts SST-2. Replacing MLM with a left-to-right objective hurts heavily, especially on MRPC and SQuAD.
The SQuAD drop is intuitive. A left-to-right token representation has no right context, which is bad when predicting answer boundaries. Adding a randomly initialized BiLSTM during fine-tuning recovers some SQuAD performance but does not match deep bidirectional pre-training. This is the strongest evidence in the paper that BERT’s bidirectionality matters at the representation level, not just at the task-head level. Model Size The scale trend is almost monotonic in the paper table:
3 layers, , 12 heads: MLM ppl 5.84, MNLI-m 77.9, SST-2 88.4. 12 layers, , 12 heads: MLM ppl 3.99, MNLI-m 84.4, SST-2 92.9. 24 layers, , 16 heads: MLM ppl 3.23, MNLI-m 86.6, SST-2 93.7.
The trend is monotonic in this table: larger pre-trained encoders improve both MLM perplexity and downstream accuracy. This was important in 2018 because many earlier feature-based NLP systems did not clearly benefit from much larger contextual encoders on small tasks. BERT shows that if the whole encoder is fine-tuned, small downstream datasets can still benefit from a much larger pre-trained model. Feature-Based Use BERT is usually remembered as a fine-tuning paper, but it also supports feature extraction. The CoNLL-2003 NER result compares:
full fine-tuning; fixed BERT-base features feeding a task-specific BiLSTM; different layer extraction strategies.
The best feature-based result concatenates the last four hidden layers and reaches 96.1 dev F1, only 0.3 behind BERT-base fine-tuning on dev. This is a practical result: if a task cannot be easily expressed as a pure Transformer encoder fine-tuning problem, BERT features are still useful. Architecture Comparison The appendix compares BERT, OpenAI GPT, and ELMo:
ELMo: separate left/right LSTMs, shallow bidirectional concatenation, feature-based transfer. OpenAI GPT: Transformer decoder, left-to-right self-attention, full fine-tuning. BERT: Transformer encoder, deep bidirectional self-attention, full fine-tuning.
The phrase “deep bidirectional” matters. ELMo combines separately trained left-to-right and right-to-left features. BERT lets every layer condition jointly on both sides through self-attention. Masking Strategy The masking ablation tests whether the 80/10/10 rule matters. The default 80% [MASK], 10% unchanged, 10% random setting reaches MNLI 84.2, NER fine-tuning 95.4, and feature-based NER 94.9. Using 100% [MASK] is similar for MNLI, but feature-based NER falls to 94.0. Fine-tuning is fairly robust, but feature-based NER is hurt by using only [MASK]. That matches the intuition: if the frozen representations were trained with too much visible [MASK] behavior, downstream feature extraction cannot adapt the encoder away from that mismatch. Number of Pre-Training Steps The appendix also compares MLM and left-to-right pre-training over checkpoint steps. MLM converges slightly slower because it predicts only 15% of positions, but its fine-tuned MNLI accuracy overtakes the left-to-right model early and continues improving. The paper notes that BERT-base gains almost 1 point on MNLI from 500k to 1M pre-training steps. What Changed After BERTBERT was not the final word on encoder pre-training. Several later papers changed important parts of the recipe:
Later method What it questions or changes
RoBERTa removes NSP, trains longer, uses more data, dynamic masking
ALBERT parameter sharing and sentence order prediction
ELECTRA replaces MLM with replaced-token detection
SpanBERT masks spans and improves span-level representations
DeBERTa disentangles content and position representations
This does not reduce BERT’s importance. It clarifies what BERT contributed: the unified encoder fine-tuning interface and the proof that bidirectional pre-training scales across many NLP tasks. Reproduction NotesIf I were reproducing BERT, I would separate the checks into four buckets. Data and Packing Use document-level corpora so NSP examples can be sampled correctly. Preserve [CLS], [SEP], segment A/B embeddings, and absolute position embeddings. Verify WordPiece tokenization and special-token handling before training. Make sure MLM target selection is over WordPiece positions, not whole words, if reproducing the original recipe.
MLM CorruptionThe corruption rule should be implemented as target selection plus replacement: orig = input_ids.copy()selected = random_positions(rate=0.15)for i in selected: r = uniform() if r < 0.8: input_ids[i] = mask_id elif r < 0.9: input_ids[i] = random_vocab_id() else: input_ids[i] = orig[i] labels[i] = orig[i]
Only selected positions contribute to the MLM loss. Unselected positions should have ignored labels. Fine-TuningThe original fine-tuning search is small but important:
batch size: 16 or 32; learning rate: 5e-5, 3e-5, or 2e-5; epochs: 2, 3, or 4; dropout: 0.1.
For BERT-large on small datasets, the paper reports instability and uses random restarts. That is a useful warning: a single fine-tuning run can understate the model. ReportingFor a serious reproduction, report:
pre-training data size and document packing; number of tokens and steps, not just epochs; MLM accuracy or perplexity on held-out pre-training data; downstream dev and test metrics; random seed variance for small datasets; whether evaluation uses single models, ensembles, or extra data like TriviaQA.
LimitationsBERT has several limitations that matter in practice. First, MLM is sample-inefficient compared with left-to-right LM because only 15% of positions are prediction targets. This is one reason ELECTRA later became attractive: every token can provide a discriminator signal. Second, BERT is not a natural generator. Its full self-attention encoder is excellent for understanding, retrieval, classification, extraction, and reranking, but it does not define a left-to-right generation process. Third, the original NSP result did not age cleanly. The BERT paper shows NSP helps under its setup, but RoBERTa later showed that removing NSP can improve results when the training recipe is strengthened. So I read NSP as part of the original recipe, not as a permanent requirement. Fourth, the pre-training cost is real. The original BERT-large training used 64 TPU chips for about 4 days. That was large in 2018, and the lesson that scale helps immediately pushed encoder pre-training toward more compute. TakeawayBERT’s core contribution is the interface between pre-training and downstream NLP tasks. A single bidirectional Transformer encoder can be pre-trained with MLM and NSP, then adapted to classification, sentence-pair reasoning, extractive QA, and token tagging with minimal heads. The paper’s most durable lesson is not the exact 80/10/10 masking rule or NSP. The durable lesson is that deep bidirectional representations, full-parameter fine-tuning, and a unified input format can replace a large amount of task-specific NLP architecture design.

entry.title: BART: Denoising Sequence-to-Sequence Pre-training
entry.content:
Paper : BART: Denoising Sequence-to-Sequence Pre-training for Natural Language Generation, Translation, and Comprehension BART is easiest to place as a denoising sequence-to-sequence model. It puts a BERT-style bidirectional encoder and a GPT-style autoregressive decoder into a standard Transformer encoder-decoder, then pre-trains the model by corrupting a document and reconstructing the original one. Given a document and a noising function , the pre-training target is:
This objective gives BART a useful middle ground. If the downstream output is a label, the model still has a bidirectional encoder for understanding. If the output is text, the decoder is already trained to generate a sequence left-to-right. The paper’s experiments are mostly a stress test of that design choice. Motivation Figure 1 is the most useful mental model for the paper. BERT encodes the whole context bidirectionally, but masked tokens are predicted independently, which makes full-sequence generation awkward. GPT is naturally generative, but every position only conditions on the left context. BART encodes a corrupted document bidirectionally and reconstructs the clean document with an autoregressive decoder. The key detail is that encoder input and decoder output do not have to align. That makes it possible to delete tokens, replace variable-length spans, shuffle sentences, or rotate a document. The decoder only needs to recover the original sequence. Noising Functions The paper compares several input corruptions:
Token Masking: randomly replace tokens with [MASK], close to BERT’s MLM setup. Token Deletion: remove tokens entirely, so the model must infer where content is missing. Text Infilling: sample spans and replace each span with a single [MASK]; span lengths are drawn from a Poisson distribution with . Sentence Permutation: split a document into sentences and shuffle their order. Document Rotation: choose a random token as the new beginning of the document.
Text infilling is more generative than ordinary token masking. The model has to recover both the missing content and the missing span length. Based on the ablation results, the large model uses text infilling + sentence permutation, masking 30% of tokens and permuting all sentences. Fine-tuning BART’s fine-tuning recipes mostly follow from the encoder-decoder shape. For sequence classification, the same input is fed to both the encoder and decoder. The hidden state of the final decoder token is used for classification, roughly playing the role that [CLS] plays in BERT, except that it comes from the decoder and can attend to the complete input. For generation tasks, the setup is direct: summarization, abstractive QA, and dialogue response generation are all standard sequence-to-sequence fine-tuning problems. Machine translation is a special case in the paper. To translate into English, the authors add a randomly initialized source encoder that maps the foreign-language input into a space that the pretrained BART model can denoise into English. Training first freezes most BART parameters and updates the new encoder plus a small set of related parameters, then briefly fine-tunes the full model. Objective Ablation Table 1 is the most informative result in the paper. The models are kept at comparable size, trained for 1M steps on books and Wikipedia, and then evaluated across both understanding and generation tasks. The important readings:
Text Infilling is the most consistently strong single corruption: SQuAD 1.1 F1 reaches 90.8, XSum PPL is 6.61, and ConvAI2 PPL is 11.05. Text Infilling + Sentence Shuffling is best on CNN/DailyMail, with PPL 5.41. Document Rotation and Sentence Shuffling perform poorly in isolation. Shuffling structure alone is not a strong enough signal. A pure Language Model is best on ELI5 PPL, but it is weak on SQuAD. That fits the task shape: ELI5 has long, loosely constrained answers, while SQuAD needs bidirectional context.
The point is not that one noising function is universally optimal. The point is that BART’s architecture makes these noising schemes comparable under one framework, and text infilling turns out to be the most robust choice. Large-scale Results The large model uses a 12-layer encoder, a 12-layer decoder, and hidden size 1024. It is trained at a similar scale to RoBERTa for 500k steps. Table 2 answers a practical question: does adding an autoregressive decoder hurt discriminative tasks? The answer is mostly no. On SQuAD 1.1, BART reports 88.8/94.6 while RoBERTa reports 88.9/94.6. MNLI, QQP, QNLI, and RTE are also in the same range. BART keeps generation ability without obviously giving up language-understanding performance.
Summarization is where BART looks most natural. CNN/DailyMail is relatively extractive and the Lead-3 baseline is already strong, but BART still reaches 44.16 / 21.28 / 40.90. XSum is more abstractive, and extractive systems are much weaker there; BART reaches 45.14 / 22.27 / 37.25, roughly six ROUGE points above the previous BERTSUM-style results. This is the cleanest use case for encoder-decoder pre-training: the input is a document, and the output is a new piece of text rather than a label or a copied span. Generation And Translation ELI5 is long-form abstractive QA, and the output is less tightly constrained by the input than in summarization. BART still reports the best ROUGE in Table 5: 30.6 / 6.2 / 24.3. This does not contradict Table 1, where the pure language model had the best ELI5 PPL. PPL and ROUGE measure different things, and the large-scale setup is also different from the base-model ablation.
The translation experiment is more of a probe for BART’s English generation prior. On WMT16 RO-EN with back-translation data, the baseline is 36.80 BLEU. Fixed BART is slightly worse at 36.29, while tuned BART reaches 37.96. The gain is modest, but it shows that the pretrained English denoising model can be attached to a translation system in a useful way. Reading NotesBART is often discussed next to T5 because both models push NLP tasks toward a text-to-text or sequence-to-sequence interface. The emphasis is different, though. BART is mainly about what kind of corruption works well for encoder-decoder denoising. Text infilling is the core design for me. It forces the model to infer content and length, so it is closer to downstream generation than single-token masking. Sentence permutation then adds a document-level ordering signal, which is why the large model keeps it as an auxiliary corruption. BART’s contribution is not a complicated new block. It is a clean composition of ideas that already had evidence behind them:
the encoder handles bidirectional understanding of corrupted input; the decoder handles left-to-right reconstruction; the noising function can be more flexible than MLM; the same model can be fine-tuned for classification, summarization, QA, dialogue, and translation.
The limitations are also visible. If the task is only classification, an encoder-only model such as RoBERTa is cheaper. If the output is only loosely grounded in the input, a pure language model can be competitive. BART is strongest when the input provides real constraints and the output is still natural language. TakeawayBART is not just “BERT + GPT”. The important move is to put a denoising objective inside a sequence-to-sequence architecture. Pre-training teaches the model to recover full documents from damaged ones, and fine-tuning can reuse the same interface for text-in, text-out tasks. My summary after reading the paper:
text infilling is the most important noising function; the bidirectional encoder keeps understanding tasks strong; the autoregressive decoder makes summarization and generation natural; BART is not the lightest classifier, but it is a strong default when the output is text.
The broader lesson is still useful: if the downstream workload is generative, pre-training should look generative too. Recovering damaged text is a better match than predicting isolated masked tokens.

entry.title: BRECQ: Pushing the Limit of PTQ by Block Reconstruction
entry.content:
Paper / Code BRECQ is a useful CNN PTQ paper to read before looking at later LLM quantization work. The paper is not only about collecting activation ranges. It frames PTQ as a local reconstruction problem: given a small calibration set, optimize the quantized model so its internal computation stays close to the full-precision model. The key design choice is the reconstruction unit. Layer-wise reconstruction is too local for modern residual networks. Whole-network reconstruction is too large and easy to overfit when only a small calibration set is available. BRECQ argues that a block is the practical middle point. Reconstruction Granularity Figure cropped from the paper PDF: network, stage, block, and layer granularities, together with the corresponding Hessian/Fisher block structure. The figure explains why the paper prefers block reconstruction. In a residual CNN, a layer does not act alone. Convolutions, nonlinearities, batch norm, and skip connections form a functional block. If PTQ optimizes one layer at a time, it ignores error compensation inside the block. BRECQ compares four granularities:
Granularity What it optimizes Practical issue
Layer-wise one layer output at a time misses cross-layer dependency
Block-wise one residual/building block balances dependency and overfitting
Stage-wise a group of blocks at the same resolution larger search space and harder calibration
Net-wise final network output overfits easily with limited calibration
The Hessian diagram is the paper’s intuition: layer-wise PTQ keeps only the layer-diagonal part, while full-network reconstruction tries to use the full matrix. Block reconstruction keeps the stronger intra-block interactions and drops weaker inter-block terms. Optimization Loop BRECQ optimizes block by block, using calibration inputs, full-precision block outputs, gradients, and optional activation step-size updates. The procedure is still post-training quantization. Labels are not required, and the model is not trained end to end. For each block, BRECQ records calibration input, the full-precision output, and gradient information. It then optimizes the quantized block output to match the full-precision block output. At a high level, the objective is: make quantized_block(x_calib) close to fp_block(x_calib),weighted by second-order/Fisher sensitivity,while optimizing weight rounding and activation step size.
This is the same practical spirit as AdaRound, but the reconstruction target is a block rather than a single layer. The block gives internal layers room to absorb each other’s quantization errors. Why Block, Not Layer The block granularity is the best point in this ablation, especially for MobileNetV2. The ablation is small but important. With 2-bit weight quantization, block reconstruction beats layer, stage, and net reconstruction on both ResNet-18 and MobileNetV2. The MobileNetV2 gap is especially clear: block reconstruction reaches 59.67, while layer-wise reconstruction reaches 52.13 and net-wise reconstruction collapses to 40.76. This also explains why “larger reconstruction unit” is not automatically better. Network-wise optimization has the most dependency information, but with only a small calibration set it can fit the calibration examples instead of improving generalization. Low-bit Results Weight-only ImageNet results. BRECQ remains usable even at 2-bit weights with 32-bit activations. For weight-only quantization, BRECQ is much stronger than range-only or layer-only PTQ baselines. On ResNet-18, the 2/32 result is 66.30 compared with 71.08 full precision. On MobileNetV2, 2/32 reaches 59.67 compared with 72.49 full precision, which is a meaningful result for such an aggressive setting.
Fully quantized ImageNet results. Activations are quantized too, which makes the setting much harder. The fully quantized table is the more deployment-relevant one. At 4/4, BRECQ gives strong results across ResNet, MobileNetV2, RegNet, and MNasNet-style models. At 2/4, most previous PTQ methods fail badly, while BRECQ still produces usable accuracy. Two details are worth keeping in mind when reading the table:
The first and last layers are usually treated more conservatively in low-bit CNN PTQ. The method uses calibration data, but not the full training process required by QAT.
QAT Comparison BRECQ is a PTQ method, but the paper compares it with QAT-style methods to show the cost/accuracy tradeoff. The QAT comparison is the deployment argument. For ResNet-18 at 4/4, BRECQ reports 69.60 top-1 with 1024 calibration images and 0.4 GPU hours. QAT baselines use about 1.2M training images and roughly 100 GPU hours in this table. For MobileNetV2, BRECQ reports 66.57 at 4/4 and 70.74 with mixed precision/8-bit activations. HAQ is still slightly higher in the mixed setting, but at a much higher training/search cost. Mixed Precision Mixed precision uses per-layer sensitivity to spend more bits where they matter most. BRECQ also computes layer sensitivity and uses it for mixed precision. The curve is the useful part: under the same model-size or latency budget, mixed precision sits above uniform precision. That means the method is not only choosing better rounding; it is also learning where low-bit quantization hurts most. This is the same lesson that later becomes common in deployment work: a single bit-width is easy to implement, but it is rarely the best accuracy-cost point. Reading NotesBRECQ’s main idea is modest but durable: choose the reconstruction unit that matches the model’s functional structure. For residual CNNs, that unit is usually a block. The paper also separates two PTQ questions that are often mixed together:
How do we choose quantization parameters for a fixed bit-width? How do we allocate bit-widths under a size or latency budget?
For LLM quantization, BRECQ is not a direct recipe, but it is useful background. GPTQ-style methods target different modules and use different solvers, yet they share the same philosophy: use calibration activations and sensitivity-aware reconstruction instead of minimizing a naive tensor error.

entry.title: BANANAS: Bayesian Optimization with Neural Architectures for NAS
entry.content:
White C, Neiswanger W, Savani Y. BANANAS: Bayesian Optimization with Neural Architectures for Neural Architecture Search. AAAI 2021.
Paper / Code BANANAS is a predictor-based NAS method. It does not build a differentiable supernet like DARTS, and it does not train a controller like early RL-based NAS. The loop is closer to black-box Bayesian optimization: evaluate a small set of architectures, train a predictor from those observations, use an acquisition function to choose the next candidates, and repeat. The useful part of this paper is that it does not treat “neural predictor for NAS” as one vague block. It studies five design choices separately:
Component BANANAS choice
Architecture encoding path encoding
Predictor feedforward neural network ensemble
Uncertainty ensemble variance
Acquisition independent Thompson sampling
Acquisition optimization mutation around strong evaluated architectures
The paper is therefore more valuable as an analysis of the BO + neural predictor framework than as a single named algorithm. BO + Neural Predictor SetupThe search space is a set of architectures. Training an architecture gives its validation error, but this evaluation is expensive. BO tries to spend evaluations where they are likely to improve the best architecture found so far. The practical loop is:
randomly sample and evaluate several initial architectures; encode all evaluated architectures; train an ensemble of neural predictors on architecture/error observations; generate candidate architectures; score candidates with an acquisition function; evaluate the best candidates and update the dataset.
This is attractive because the expensive operation is still actual architecture training, while the predictor is cheap. But the predictor is only useful if the encoding makes architecture similarity visible. That is where path encoding becomes the main idea. Path EncodingMost NAS predictors before this paper used an adjacency matrix plus operation labels. That representation is faithful, but it gives the predictor an awkward feature space: node indices are arbitrary, edges are highly dependent, and an edge can be meaningless if it does not belong to an input-output path. BANANAS instead encodes paths. Each binary feature means that a specific input-to-output operation path exists in the cell.
The left side of the figure is the key intuition. Instead of asking the predictor to infer useful computation from raw adjacency entries, path encoding directly records possible data-flow routes such as: input -> conv 1x1 -> pool 3x3 -> outputinput -> conv 3x3 -> conv 3x3 -> output
The full path encoding can be long. On NASBench-101, the paper gives the full length as: sum_{i=0}^{5} 3^i = 364 bits
But the right side of the figure is important: truncating the encoding can work well. For NASBench-101, the paper reports that the path encoding can be reduced to about 20 bits without hurting the 150-evaluation BANANAS result. Their explanation is practical: many long or rare paths almost never appear under the random graph sampling procedure, so including them can make the predictor overfit noise. This is the reusable idea from the paper. The representation is not only smaller than it first looks; it also matches the structure that determines architecture behavior. Predictor And UncertaintyBANANAS compares several predictor families on NASBench-101: feedforward networks with adjacency encoding, feedforward networks with path encoding, truncated path encoding, Bayesian neural networks, GCNs, and VAEs.
There are three different measurements in this figure:
Plot What it checks What I read from it
left predictor MAE on held-out architectures path encoding and GCN are the strongest predictors
middle RMSCE calibration error ensembles give better uncertainty estimates than the BNN setup used here
right full BO performance predictor quality must still translate into better search
The right plot matters most. A predictor can have low average error but still rank the best candidates poorly. NAS cares about the top of the ranking, not only global regression quality. In the paper’s full BO setting, the path-encoding feedforward ensemble slightly edges the GCN ensemble, while being simpler and less sensitive to GCN hyperparameters. The uncertainty story is also pragmatic. The authors use an ensemble of predictors, not because it is theoretically perfect, but because it gives a simple mean and standard deviation for each candidate architecture. That is enough to drive acquisition functions such as expected improvement, UCB, Thompson sampling, and independent Thompson sampling. BANANAS PipelineThe final predictor is simple: encode architectures with paths, feed the vectors into an ensemble of feedforward networks, then use the ensemble outputs as performance estimates and uncertainty estimates.
The actual search algorithm adds one more strong engineering choice: do not optimize the acquisition function by sampling candidates uniformly from the whole search space. Generate candidates by mutating architectures that already look good.
The mutation step is doing a lot of work. A neural predictor trained on limited observations is usually more reliable near architectures related to what it has already seen. Mutating good architectures keeps the candidate set in that local neighborhood. This also makes the acquisition function easier to optimize than searching the entire discrete architecture space. The final BANANAS recipe in the paper is:
Part Choice
predictor input path encoding
predictor model feedforward neural network ensemble
predictor loss MAPE-style loss that emphasizes low validation error
acquisition independent Thompson sampling
candidate generation mutation from the best evaluated architectures
The name sounds broad, but the algorithm is a specific combination of these components. ResultsThe main experimental result is on NASBench-101, where the paper can run many controlled trials because architecture accuracies are precomputed. The setup uses about 150 architecture evaluations, reported as 47 TPU hours in the NASBench-101 accounting.
The three panels give useful ablations:
acquisition functions are close, but independent Thompson sampling is a strong default; mutation beats random, local search, and evolution as the candidate-generation strategy in this setting; the final BANANAS curve is among the strongest baselines under the same evaluation budget.
The paper also evaluates the DARTS search space. This is less clean than NASBench-101 because it is not a precomputed tabular benchmark, but the comparison is still useful because it checks whether the method can leave a small tabular cell benchmark.
The reported DARTS-space result is:
Method Avg. test error Runtime Note
DARTS, paper 2.76 5 GPU-days gradient-based
DARTS, authors’ rerun 2.68 5 GPU-days same evaluation pipeline
BANANAS 2.64 11.8 GPU-days BO + neural predictor
I would not overread the small difference between 2.68 and 2.64. The more important point is that predictor-based BO remains competitive outside the exact NASBench-101 table, at a cost that is still far below early full-training NAS methods. Reading NotesWhat I would keep from BANANAS:
Architecture representation is not a detail. Path encoding changes the predictor’s job from graph interpretation to data-flow feature learning. Predictor accuracy and uncertainty calibration should be checked together. A calibrated but inaccurate predictor is not useful for NAS. Candidate generation matters as much as acquisition scoring. The mutation strategy makes BO practical in a huge discrete search space. Truncating path encodings is not just a memory trick. It can remove rare-path noise and improve predictor behavior. NASBench-style experiments are good for controlled optimizer comparisons, but DARTS-space or real training checks are still needed before treating a method as generally strong.
My main caveat is that BANANAS still relies on a search-space-specific encoding and mutation operator. That is fine for cell-based NAS, but it means the method is not plug-and-play for every architecture family. For a new space, I would first ask: what is the equivalent of an input-output path, and can mutation stay near architectures where the predictor has support? Overall, BANANAS is a clean paper because it separates the NAS problem into pieces that can be tested: encoding, predictor, uncertainty, acquisition, and candidate generation. The final algorithm works because all five choices are aligned, not because Bayesian optimization alone solves NAS.

entry.title: Big Bird: Transformers for Longer Sequences
entry.content:
Reference Paper: Big Bird: Transformers for Longer Sequences Code: google-research/bigbird
BigBird is a sparse-attention Transformer designed for long sequences. It is usually remembered as “BERT with sparse attention”, but the paper is more interesting than that short description. The main point is not only that quadratic attention is expensive. The paper also asks what kind of sparse graph can replace full attention without collapsing the expressive power that made Transformers useful in the first place. The answer is a three-part pattern: local sliding-window attention, random long-range attention, and a small number of global tokens. Local edges preserve nearby context. Random edges shorten graph distance between far-away positions. Global tokens provide a reliable memory and broadcast path. With these components, each token attends to only a constant or small number of blocks, so the attention cost becomes linear in the sequence length when the sparse parameters are fixed. Problem SettingFor a sequence of length and hidden size , dense self-attention compares every query with every key:
This is acceptable for 512-token BERT-style inputs, but it becomes the bottleneck for 4K-token documents, long QA evidence sets, summarization inputs, and genomics sequences. BigBird instead builds a sparse attention graph. If each token or block attends to random positions, local-window positions, and global positions, then the attention score computation becomes:
When , , and are constants or small task-specific values, the complexity is linear in . The tradeoff is that the attention pattern now matters. A bad sparse graph can make information propagation slow or lose important context. BigBird’s contribution is to argue, both empirically and theoretically, that the random + window + global pattern is a useful sparse graph. Generalized Attention As A GraphThe paper first rewrites attention as a graph problem. Let the input sequence be:
Define a directed graph over vertices . An edge from query position to key position means that token is allowed to attend to token . Let be the out-neighbor set of node . BigBird’s generalized attention is:
Here are the query and key projections, is the value projection, is a scoring function such as softmax, and is the number of heads. The important object is , the matrix formed only by stacking the tokens that position can see. When is the complete directed graph, this reduces to standard full attention. When is sparse, attention only computes the selected inner products. Equivalently, use an adjacency matrix:
Dense BERT-style attention is the all-ones matrix. BigBird replaces it with a structured sparse matrix. The Sparse Pattern Figure 1 is the whole paper in one picture. White entries are missing attention edges. Orange entries are random attention, blue entries are local window attention, and green entries are global attention. BigBird uses all three. Random AttentionFor each query position, BigBird selects random keys:
The graph-theory intuition is that sparse random graphs have short average path length and expansion-like behavior. Even when two tokens are far apart in the original sequence, random edges create shortcuts, so information can travel through fewer layers. This is not the same as saying every random mask is good. The point is that random long-range edges add connectivity that pure local attention lacks. Window AttentionRandom edges alone do not encode the locality that language and biological sequences usually have. BigBird therefore keeps a sliding window:
In words, query position attends to roughly tokens on the left and tokens on the right. This preserves local phrase structure, neighboring evidence, and nearby nucleotide context. A pure window graph is cheap but makes long-range communication slow; it needs many layers for distant tokens to exchange information. Global AttentionThe last component is a set of global tokens. These tokens attend to every position, and every position attends back to them. The paper defines two variants. For internal transformer construction, BigBird-ITC marks existing positions as global. If is the global index set and , then:
For extended transformer construction, BigBird-ETC adds extra global tokens, similar in spirit to adding special memory tokens. If the original attention matrix is , ETC constructs:
The new global rows and columns are fully connected:
The original token-to-token sparse attention is preserved after the offset:
This is a small but important difference. ITC reuses existing tokens as global tokens, while ETC creates dedicated global slots that can store and route context. In the experiments, ETC is often stronger. Putting the pieces together, a regular token attends to:
Therefore the attention matrix has only selected edges instead of dense edges. Why These Three Blocks Table 1 is a small ablation at sequence length 512. It is useful because it shows that sparse attention is not automatically good. A random-only pattern drops from BERT-base’s 64.2 MLM / 88.5 SQuAD / 83.4 MNLI to 60.1 / 83.0 / 80.2. A window-only pattern is worse: 58.3 / 76.4 / 73.1. Combining random and window improves to 62.7 / 85.1 / 80.5, but it still does not fully match dense BERT. This table explains why the paper does not stop at “random edges plus local edges”. Global tokens are not a decorative component. They are used in the theoretical construction and they help empirical performance. My reading is that BigBird’s sparse pattern is a compromise between three graph properties:
local clustering from the sliding window; short global graph distance from random edges; explicit aggregation and broadcast through global tokens.
This is also why BigBird is different from simply pruning the attention matrix. The sparse mask is designed as a communication graph. Theoretical ResultsThe theory section is one reason BigBird was influential. It tries to answer a natural concern: if full attention is expressive because every token can directly inspect every other token, do we lose something fundamental by sparsifying it? Universal ApproximationThe paper follows the sequence-function approximation setup from prior Transformer theory. Let be the set of continuous functions:
For two functions and , define the distance:
The key graph object is a star graph centered at an auxiliary token 0:
The theorem states that if the sparse attention graph contains this star graph, sparse attention can approximate any continuous sequence-to-sequence function:
The proof idea is not that one sparse layer sees everything. Instead, the global token lets the network gradually build a contextual mapping. The paper’s proof has three steps: approximate continuous functions by piecewise-constant functions, use sparse attention plus the global token to construct contextual codes, and then approximate the modified Transformer using ordinary softmax/ReLU Transformer blocks. The practical interpretation is narrower than the theorem statement. It does not say any trained BigBird model will learn every function. It says the sparse graph, if it contains the global-star structure, does not remove universal approximation power in the theoretical model class. Turing CompletenessThe paper also extends a prior result that full encoder-decoder Transformers are Turing complete under arbitrary precision. BigBird’s result is that there exists a sparse attention mechanism using inner products such that the resulting Transformer class is Turing complete. This result has the usual caveat: arbitrary precision is an idealized assumption. Real finite-precision neural networks are finite-state systems. Still, the theorem answers a structural question: full quadratic attention is not the only way to obtain the theoretical simulation result. No Free LunchThe paper also includes a lower-bound style warning. Sparse attention cannot universally replace dense attention without cost. The example task is: given unit vectors in with , return the furthest vector for each vector:
For unit vectors, finding the furthest vector is equivalent to finding the minimum inner product. Full attention can solve it in one layer by embedding:
Use:
Then the attention output can select:
For sparse attention with only edges per layer, the paper argues via the Orthogonal Vectors Conjecture that this task needs roughly layers. In short: BigBird keeps enough power for many long-sequence tasks, but dense all-pairs comparison is still uniquely suited for tasks that genuinely require all pairwise interactions in one layer. Block Sparse ImplementationThe graph view is clean, but a token-level sparse matrix is not automatically fast on GPU/TPU. Hardware likes contiguous dense blocks. Scattered single-token gathers can remove the theoretical speedup. BigBird therefore blockifies the attention pattern.
Instead of deciding attention for individual tokens, BigBird groups queries and keys into blocks of size . If there are tokens, the model has roughly query blocks and key blocks. Random, window, and global attention are then applied at the block level. Let:
After reshaping into block tensors:
The block-diagonal attention scores can be computed as a dense tensor multiplication:
The index selects the block, while and index positions inside a block. This gives the diagonal block scores efficiently. To extend diagonal attention into window attention, BigBird rolls copies of the key-block tensor.
For a window size , the implementation makes copies of the key-block tensor and circularly shifts each copy along the block axis. Multiplying the query-block tensor with these rolled key tensors produces the local-window scores without many scattered gathers. Global blocks can be appended directly because they are fixed. Random blocks still need gather operations, but is small in the paper’s experiments. The final packed key tensor has shape:
Then the sparse attention score computation is again a dense tensor multiplication between:
The resulting score tensor has shape:
and the cost is:
Figure 6 is the implementation summary. The green columns are fixed global keys, the blue columns are local-window keys obtained by rolling, and the orange columns are gathered random keys. The key idea is to turn the sparse pattern into a compact dense tensor layout whenever possible. Pretraining SetupFor NLP, the authors create base and large BigBird variants and pretrain with the masked language modeling objective. In notation, the standard MLM loss is:
where is the set of masked positions. The paper warm-starts from public RoBERTa checkpoints and extends the sequence length to 4096. This matters because BigBird is not trained from scratch in isolation; the sparse long-context model inherits a strong dense short-context initialization. For generative summarization, the paper also uses a Pegasus-initialized large model. The encoder uses sparse BigBird attention for long documents, while the decoder remains full-attention. This is a reasonable engineering choice: the input document is long, but the decoder sequence is much shorter and benefits from dense autoregressive attention. QA Results Table 2 compares base-size models on QA dev sets. Longformer improves over RoBERTa by using longer context, and BigBird improves further on most columns. The strongest base result is usually BigBird-ETC. On Natural Questions, BigBird-ETC reports 73.9 long-answer F1 and 54.9 short-answer F1; on WikiHop it reaches 75.9 accuracy. The key signal is that longer context helps more than just adding parameters.
Table 3 is the test-set comparison. BigBird-ETC reports 77.8 Natural Questions long-answer F1, 84.5 TriviaQA full F1, 92.4 TriviaQA verified F1, and 82.3 WikiHop accuracy. In the paper’s leaderboard snapshot, it sets a new state of the art for Natural Questions long answer, TriviaQA, and WikiHop, while remaining competitive on HotpotQA. The task-specific use of global tokens is worth noting. For QA inputs, global tokens are not just generic CLS tokens. The paper uses global slots for question tokens, paragraph/evidence tokens, or sentence-level structure depending on the dataset. This is one reason ETC can outperform ITC: explicit global slots provide a cleaner interface for task structure. Summarization Results The summarization table is one of the clearest practical arguments for BigBird. Long-document summarization suffers when the encoder only sees a short prefix. BigBird-RoBERTa already improves substantially over a Transformer + RoBERTa baseline, especially on BigPatent. BigBird-Pegasus is stronger still: 46.63 / 19.02 / 41.77 on Arxiv, 46.32 / 20.65 / 42.33 on PubMed, and 60.64 / 42.46 / 50.01 on BigPatent. The important detail is that the model uses sparse attention on the encoder side and full self-attention on the decoder side. This keeps generation quality while making it possible to encode long source documents. It also shows the paper’s practical positioning: BigBird is a long-input encoder technology first, not necessarily a universal replacement for every attention matrix in every part of a sequence model. Genomics ResultsThe genomics section is interesting because it moves away from normal NLP. DNA sequence effects can be non-local, so longer context can matter. The paper uses byte-pair encoding over DNA sequences, trains with MLM, and evaluates both language modeling and downstream biological prediction tasks. A bits-per-character metric can be written as:
Lower is better.
Table 5 shows that BigBird with sequence length 4096 reaches 1.12 BPC, compared with 1.23 for BERT at sequence length 512 and 1.57 for SRILM. This is a clean example where longer context directly improves the representation objective.
For promoter region prediction, BigBird reports 99.9 F1, compared with 95.6 for DeePromoter and 69.7 for CNNProm. The absolute number is almost saturated, so I would not over-interpret the exact decimal, but it supports the paper’s claim that long-context pretraining transfers to biological sequence tasks.
Table 7 evaluates chromatin-profile prediction. BigBird improves TF and HM over the listed baselines, while DeepSea remains slightly higher on DHS. This is a more mixed result than the promoter table, which is useful: sparse long-context attention is helpful, but not a magic dominance claim across every biological endpoint. Relation To LongformerLongformer and BigBird are close relatives. Both reduce attention cost by using a local sliding window and global tokens. The main difference is that BigBird adds random attention and develops theory around the random + local + global pattern. In the implementation, BigBird also emphasizes block sparse packing so the sparse mask is more hardware-friendly. The paper’s appendix makes another distinction: even when BigBird-ETC uses no random tokens in some QA configurations, its global-local design and training of global tokens differ from Longformer. That means the empirical comparison is not “random edges alone beat Longformer”; it is a package of sparse graph design, global token usage, task formatting, and pretraining. My practical takeaway:
If the task is long-document encoding, QA over long evidence, summarization encoding, or genomics, BigBird is a strong candidate. If the task depends on dense all-pairs comparison in a single layer, sparse attention can require more depth or a different architecture. If the sparse pattern is implemented as tiny scattered gathers, the theoretical edge count may not translate into real speed. Block sparse packing is part of the method, not an implementation detail to ignore. Global tokens should be designed with the task structure in mind. Treating them as arbitrary extra tokens leaves performance on the table.
Final TakeawayBigBird’s central idea is simple but carefully balanced:
The window gives local inductive bias, the random edges give long-range shortcuts, and the global tokens give a stable gather/broadcast route. This combination reduces attention from:
while preserving strong theoretical properties in the idealized model and improving several long-context benchmarks in practice. The most useful lesson for me is not merely “make attention sparse”; it is that sparse attention has to be designed as a communication graph and implemented as a hardware-conscious block operation.

entry.title: BinaryBERT: 1-bit BERT Compression
entry.content:
Reference Paper: BinaryBERT: Pushing the Limit of BERT Quantization Code: huawei-noah/Pretrained-Language-Model/BinaryBERT
BinaryBERT is about the point where BERT quantization stops being a simple numeric format change. Going from 32-bit to 8-bit, or even to 2-bit ternary weights, can still be treated as aggressive quantization-aware training. Going to 1-bit weights changes the optimization problem enough that a direct binary student is hard to train. The paper’s main idea is to avoid that direct jump. It first trains a half-width ternary BERT, then splits each ternary weight into binary components to initialize a full-width binary BERT. The binary model starts from a functionally meaningful point instead of from naive binarization. One SentenceBinaryBERT is a training recipe for 1-bit BERT:
train a half-sized ternary BERT as an easier intermediate model; split ternary weights into binary weights while preserving the ternary model as much as possible; fine-tune the resulting binary model with knowledge distillation; optionally choose which modules to split under model-size or FLOPs constraints.
This is different from post-training quantization. At 1-bit, the model is too constrained for calibration-only tricks. Initialization, distillation, and the exact binary parameterization become part of the method. Why 1-bit Is A Different Regime Figure 1 is the first warning. Performance degrades slowly from full precision down to 2-bit weights, then drops sharply at 1-bit. On MRPC, the paper reports a much larger drop when moving from 2-bit to 1-bit than from 32-bit to 2-bit. MNLI-m shows the same shape, although the absolute gap is smaller. This is the main reason BinaryBERT uses ternary BERT as a bridge. A ternary weight can still express negative, zero, and positive states. A binary weight has only sign. Losing the zero state is not a small local perturbation; it changes which computations can be represented. Formula 1: Ternary QuantizationThe paper starts from the Ternary-Weight-Network style quantizer used by TernaryBERT:
with:
Here is the latent full-precision ternary-model weight, and is its ternary quantized value. The threshold decides whether a weight survives or is mapped to zero. The scale is the average magnitude of the surviving weights. My reading: ternary quantization is not only “two signs plus zero”. The zero state is the important part. It lets the quantizer remove small weights rather than forcing every small value into either a positive or negative contribution. This makes the ternary loss landscape much friendlier than the binary one. Formula 2: Binary QuantizationThe binary baseline is Binary-Weight-Network:
Every element keeps only its sign, and the whole tensor shares a scale. This gives a very compact representation, but it also means small weights can no longer become zero. A tiny positive weight and a large positive weight both contribute through the same sign bucket before scaling. This explains why direct BWN-style training is fragile for BERT. Transformer blocks are full of residual paths, attention projections, and feed-forward matrices. If every small weight is forced into a sign, quantization noise is not just large; it is structurally different. Loss Landscape: Why Direct Binary Training Fails Figure 2 visualizes the training loss around full-precision, ternary, and binary BERT parameters. The full-precision surface is low and smooth. The ternary surface is higher but still locally manageable. The binary surface is both higher and rougher. Figure 3 makes the same point quantitatively. The binary model has much larger top Hessian eigenvalue ratios across Transformer parts, especially around MHA-O. This means a similar quantization noise vector can cause a larger increase in loss. The visualization is based on perturbing two weight blocks:
This is not the training algorithm; it is a diagnostic. The authors choose two directions, perturb the latent weights, and plot the resulting loss surface. The purpose is to compare local geometry across precision regimes. The curvature argument is:
This formula is the key to the Hessian discussion. is quantization noise. is the Hessian near a local minimum. measures the steepest local curvature. Even if two quantizers had similar noise norm, the model with larger would suffer a larger loss increase. BinaryBERT’s conclusion is practical: if the binary loss landscape is too steep to optimize directly, start from a nearby ternary solution whose landscape is easier, then transfer that solution into a binary parameterization. Ternary Weight Splitting The workflow is: train a half-width ternary BERT, apply the ternary weight splitting operator, then fine-tune the full-width binary BERT. The split model has twice as many binary branches, so it recovers width while keeping 1-bit weights. The equivalence requirement is:
There are two levels here:
says the latent full-precision ternary weight should be decomposed into two latent binary weights. says the quantized ternary value should also match the sum of the quantized binary values.
The second condition is the hard one. It is easy to split a float tensor into two float tensors. It is much harder to make the post-quantization values preserve the ternary behavior.
Equations 6 and 7 define the two latent binary branches element by element. For the first branch :
if $\hat{w}i^t\ne0w{1,i}^b=a\cdot w_i^t$; if $\hat{w}i^t=0w_i^t>0w{1,i}^b=b+w_i^t$; otherwise set .
For the second branch :
if $\hat{w}i^t\ne0w{2,i}^b=(1-a)w_i^t$; if $\hat{w}i^t=0w_i^t>0w{2,i}^b=-b$; otherwise set .
The cases are easier to understand if we separate nonzero ternary weights from zero ternary weights:
If , the ternary quantizer already decided this weight is important. The latent value is split proportionally into and parts. If but the latent weight is positive, the two binary branches are arranged around and so their quantized binary sum can cancel while their latent sum still equals . The negative zero-ternary case is symmetric.
The constants and are solved by enforcing the quantized equivalence. The paper gives:
where:
My interpretation: controls how the surviving ternary weights are divided between the two binary branches. creates a symmetric cancellation mechanism for weights that were ternarized to zero. This is exactly the missing piece in naive binarization: BinaryBERT creates a way for two binary weights to emulate the ternary zero state. Distillation Objective BinaryBERT still needs distillation after splitting. Equation 9 defines the intermediate-layer objective as :
matches embedding outputs; matches multi-head-attention outputs; matches feed-forward outputs.
is the teacher embedding output, is the teacher MHA output at layer , and is the teacher FFN output. Hatted variables are the quantized student’s corresponding outputs. The prediction-layer distillation loss is:
This is soft cross-entropy between student logits and teacher logits . The split binary student does not only learn labels; it is asked to match internal representations and final predictions. This matters because 1-bit compression is too severe for label-only fine-tuning. Logits preserve task-level behavior, while intermediate losses prevent the Transformer internals from drifting too far after splitting. Adaptive SplittingBinaryBERT also supports adaptive splitting. Instead of splitting every ternary matrix, it can choose which matrices deserve ternary-to-binary expansion under a resource budget. The paper writes the selection problem as:
Here is a sensitivity vector, is a cost vector, is the resource budget, and is the baseline cost of the half-sized binary network. If , the -th matrix is selected for ternary splitting. This is basically a knapsack problem. The method prefers splitting modules that give more performance gain per unit cost. That is why the paper can produce models between the half-width and full-width endpoints.
Figure 7 shows how sensitivity is distributed. FFN-Mid and MHA-QK are more sensitive among Transformer parts, and shallower layers tend to be more sensitive than deeper layers. This matches a common pattern in compression: early layers often carry general representations and are more fragile.
Figure 14 visualizes the selected architecture under different model-size budgets. As the budget increases, more parameters are split, and the earlier layers receive more splitting first. This makes the adaptive policy interpretable instead of just being a black-box search result. Main Results: GLUE and SQuAD Tables 1 and 2 compare BWN and TWS on GLUE development and test sets. The important pattern is consistent:
TWS is better than direct BWN under both 1-1-8 and 1-1-4 settings. The gain is especially visible on sensitive tasks such as CoLA. Data augmentation helps, but TWS remains better even without relying on it.
The notation #Bits (W-E-A) means Transformer-layer weights, word embeddings, and activations. For example, 1-1-8 means 1-bit Transformer weights, 1-bit embeddings, and 8-bit activations.
On SQuAD, TWS again beats BWN in both 8-bit and 4-bit activation settings. The same crop also contains the adaptive splitting curve: maximal gain generally stays above random or minimal-gain splitting at intermediate model sizes.
Table 4 compares BinaryBERT with other compression methods. The headline is the 24.6x compression ratio: BinaryBERT reports 17 MB model size while staying competitive on SQuAD v1.1 and MNLI-m. The comparison is not only against other quantizers; it also includes DistilBERT, LayerDrop, TinyBERT, and ALBERT. I would read this table carefully. BinaryBERT has a very strong size number, but the runtime story depends on whether the deployment backend can exploit binary arithmetic and low-bit activations. If the model is unpacked into ordinary FP16 or INT8 operations, the table mainly proves storage compression rather than proportional latency. Further Fine-tuning and Binarization Ablations Table 5 shows that fine-tuning after splitting improves the binary model. This is expected: TWS gives a meaningful initialization, but the full-width binary model has a new loss landscape, so the old ternary optimum is not necessarily the best binary point. Table 6 compares TWS with other binarization methods such as LAB and BiReal. TWS remains strong, which supports the paper’s claim that initialization through ternary splitting is more important than only swapping the binary quantizer.
Figure 6 is useful because it shows optimization behavior rather than only final scores. TWS has lower training loss than direct BWN and follows a better trajectory on the 2-D loss contour after splitting. This is exactly what the loss-landscape argument predicted. Knowledge Distillation Ablation Table 10 makes the distillation point explicit. Int.+Pred. is better than no distillation and better than prediction-only distillation, especially on CoLA and MRPC. This supports the idea that a binary Transformer student needs internal constraints, not just final logits. The result also explains why BinaryBERT belongs partly to the distillation literature. The quantizer defines the representation, but the teacher defines the training signal that keeps the binary representation aligned with BERT behavior. More Evidence for The 1-bit Drop Figures 8 and 9 repeat the bit-width sweep across more GLUE tasks with 8-bit and 4-bit activations. The same pattern appears: performance is relatively stable down to 2-bit, then 1-bit creates a much sharper drop. This is one reason current LLM inference usually stops at 4-bit weight-only quantization for general deployment. The storage win from 1-bit is huge, but the optimization and kernel requirements become much more specialized. Implementation NotesIf I were reproducing BinaryBERT, I would check these details first:
Keep the stage order intact. Train the half-width ternary model first, split it, then fine-tune the full-width binary model. Skipping the ternary bridge changes the method. Verify the splitting equivalence numerically. Before training, check whether and after applying the quantizers. Separate latent weights and quantized weights. The formulas use both and . Mixing them up makes TWS look simpler than it really is. Log per-task results, not only average GLUE. Binary compression can damage tasks unevenly. CoLA and MRPC often reveal problems that average scores hide. Check activation quantization separately. 1-1-8 and 1-1-4 are different deployment points. 4-bit activations are much harder and need LSQ in the paper. Benchmark the actual binary kernel path. A 1-bit weight file is not automatically a fast model. The runtime must use bit-serial, XNOR-style, or otherwise binary-friendly kernels.
Where It FitsBinaryBERT sits after Q8BERT and TernaryBERT in the BERT quantization timeline:
Q8BERT shows that 8-bit QAT is a practical operating point. TernaryBERT shows that ultra-low-bit BERT needs distillation. BinaryBERT shows that 1-bit weights need both distillation and a special initialization path.
Compared with AWQ/GPTQ-style LLM weight-only PTQ, BinaryBERT is much more training-heavy. That is not a weakness; it is the cost of pushing to 1-bit.
