The closer the bit-width gets to a pure sign representation, the less likely it is that simple rounding or calibration can preserve model behavior. LimitationsThe main limitation is practicality. BinaryBERT is not something to apply to an arbitrary checkpoint in an afternoon. It requires staged training, a ternary intermediate model, distillation, and careful activation quantization. The second limitation is runtime support. A model can be stored as binary weights but still run inefficiently if the backend expands those weights into wider types. The paper reports model size and bit-operation estimates, but real deployment depends on kernels. The third limitation is architecture scope. This is a BERT-era encoder compression paper. Decoder-only LLMs have different bottlenecks: KV cache, long-context attention, autoregressive decoding, and activation outliers. The lesson transfers, but the exact method does not directly become a modern LLM serving recipe. TakeawayBinaryBERT’s core contribution is not just “BERT can be 1-bit”. The stronger lesson is: when the target precision changes the optimization landscape too much, use a better intermediate representation as the initialization bridge. Ternary weight splitting is that bridge. It uses the ternary model’s zero state and smoother landscape to create a full-width binary model that starts from a meaningful point. Distillation then keeps the binary student close to the full-precision teacher. This combination is what makes BinaryBERT more than direct BWN on BERT.

entry.title: BigNAS: Scaling Up Neural Architecture Search with Big Single-Stage Models
entry.content:
Yu J, Jin P, Liu H, et al. BigNAS: Scaling Up Neural Architecture Search with Big Single-Stage Models. ECCV 2020.
Paper BigNAS is a one-shot NAS paper about making the supernet itself good enough for deployment. The claim is stronger than “use a supernet to rank candidates”: after training one single-stage model on ImageNet, child models from about 200 MFLOPs to 1 GFLOP can be sliced out and used directly, without retraining, finetuning, or other post-processing. That is the part worth reading carefully. In many weight-sharing NAS methods, inherited accuracy is only a rough ranking signal and the final architecture still needs stand-alone training. BigNAS tries to remove that last step. The paper is therefore less about a new search algorithm and more about a training recipe that makes shared weights behave like a family of pretrained models. MotivationThe workflow difference is simple:
Traditional one-shot methods train a supernet, search a path, then retrain or finetune the selected child model. OFA-style progressive methods make this more reusable, but still train the elastic model in stages. BigNAS asks whether all child models can be trained simultaneously in one stage and then deployed as-is. The practical reason is deployment cost. If every target latency, FLOP budget, or device class requires another finetuning or retraining pass, the “cheap” NAS loop still leaves a long tail of engineering work. BigNAS wants the output to be a model family, not just an architecture list. Search SpaceBigNAS uses a MobileNetV2-style MBConv search space. The searchable dimensions are input resolution, channel width, depth, and kernel size; expansion ratio is mostly fixed by the MBConv type in the table.
The important details:
Training samples input resolutions from {192, 224, 288, 320}. The supernet contains stage-wise choices for channel count, number of layers, and kernel size. The reported BigNASModels are selected from roughly 200M to 1000M FLOPs, while the single-stage model covers a wider range during training. The paper also notes that after batch-norm calibration, the trained model can generalize to input resolutions not used during training, such as 208, 240, 256, 272, 304, or 336.
This is not a cell-level NAS search space. It is closer to an elastic mobile network family: same backbone grammar, many possible widths/depths/kernels/resolutions. Single-Stage TrainingSandwich Rule And Inplace DistillationBigNAS inherits two useful ideas from Once-for-All:
Sandwich rule: in each step, train the largest child, the smallest child, and sampled intermediate children. Inplace distillation: use the largest child model as the teacher for smaller child models in the same supernet.
This makes sense for the BigNAS goal. The largest child receives normal supervised training, while smaller children learn from a teacher that shares the same weights. The risky part is optimization: small and large child models do not converge at the same speed.
The left plot shows the core dilemma. The big child peaks earlier; the small child keeps improving later. If training stops early, small children are undertrained. If training continues with a decaying learning rate all the way down, the big child can overfit while the small child catches up. Their fix is deliberately small: exponential decay with a constant ending. Once the learning rate reaches a floor, it stays there until the end. In the main ImageNet setting, the paper uses a 5% floor of the initial learning rate. The appendix sweep is also useful:
LR floor Smallest model Biggest model Average
3% 76.5 80.8 78.7
5% 76.4 81.1 78.8
8% 76.3 81.3 78.8
10% 76.3 81.3 78.8
The exact floor is not the whole story, but keeping a non-zero ending learning rate is part of making both ends of the supernet usable. Initialization And Skip TransitionsThe paper spends real space on initialization because the single-stage model changes channel counts and fan-in across child models. A fixed-network initialization rule is not enough when the same residual block can be evaluated under many widths. The BigNAS modification sets the learnable scaling coefficient in the last batch-norm layer of each residual block. This makes the residual branch initially output zeros before the skip connection, so the block starts close to an identity mapping. The paper says this initialization gives around +0.2% in the fixed-network setting, but is much more critical here, with roughly +1.0% improvement in their single-stage setting.
The early-training plot explains why. Naive initialization at the full learning rate can collapse; reducing the learning rate helps but slows training. Modified initialization lets the model keep the original learning rate and still learn quickly. They also add explicit skip connections at stage transitions. When resolution or channel dimensions differ, the skip path uses 2x2 average pooling and/or 1x1 convolution. This keeps the identity path meaningful even when child models choose different stage configurations.
After the modifications, the small child improves more steadily and the large child avoids the earlier degradation. This figure is more convincing than just reporting the final architecture search result, because it shows the recipe improving the shared-weight training dynamics directly. Regularization Only On The Full ModelBigNAS also changes where regularization is applied. A naive recipe applies dropout and weight decay to every sampled child model. BigNAS instead applies regularization only when training the largest/full network.
The reason is capacity mismatch. Small child models are already constrained; regularizing them like the largest model can underfit them. In the paper’s ablation, this modified rule improves the small child by about +0.5 top-1 and the big child by about +0.2. The ImageNet training setup is still heavy: RMSProp, batch size 4096 on TPUs, AutoAugment, Swish, batch-norm post-calibration, weight decay , dropout 0.2 on the full model, and roughly 36 hours of training in the authors’ setup. Architecture SelectionAfter training the single-stage model, BigNAS does not run a complicated controller. It uses a coarse-to-fine selection procedure:
First it evaluates coarse skeletons across resolution, depth, width, and kernel choices. Then it picks promising skeletons and mutates them with a finer grid under the target resource budget. The paper uses FLOPs for the reported selection because FLOPs are easier to reproduce than device-specific latency, but it notes that the evaluation metric could also be latency, memory footprint, or predictive accuracy on a target device. One detail I like: since ImageNet validation is treated as the public “test set” in this community, they use predictive accuracy on the training set for selection after supernet training. That is not a perfect deployment protocol, but it avoids repeatedly tuning on the validation set. Main ResultsThe headline result is the Pareto curve and comparison table:
Compactly, the BigNAS family looks like this:
Model Params FLOPs Top-1
BigNASModel-S 4.5M 242M 76.5
BigNASModel-M 5.5M 418M 78.9
BigNASModel-L 6.4M 586M 79.5
BigNASModel-XL 9.5M 1040M 80.9
The comparisons that matter most are compact enough to write directly:
Around 200M FLOPs, BigNASModel-S reaches 76.5 top-1 at 242M FLOPs, slightly above Once-for-All finetuned at 76.4 top-1 with 230M FLOPs. Around 400M FLOPs, BigNASModel-M reaches 78.9 top-1 at 418M FLOPs, above EfficientNet-B0 at 77.3 top-1 with 390M FLOPs. Around 600M FLOPs, BigNASModel-L reaches 79.5 top-1 at 586M FLOPs, above EfficientNet-B1 at 79.2 top-1 with 734M FLOPs. Around 1000M FLOPs, BigNASModel-XL reaches 80.9 top-1 at 1040M FLOPs, above EfficientNet-B2 at 80.3 top-1 with 1050M FLOPs.
This table should not be read as a perfectly fair training recipe comparison. The paper itself notes that MNasNet and MobileNetV3 are mainly optimized for on-device latency instead of FLOPs, and different model families use different training hyperparameters. Still, the result is strong for the paper’s central claim: directly sliced child models are competitive without an extra training pass. Does Finetuning Help?For me, this is the most important evidence in the paper.
Table 2 tries to finetune selected child models for another 25 epochs with constant learning rates. A too-large finetuning LR hurts badly. A smaller LR mostly changes nothing. For example:
Model Direct slice Finetune LR 0.001 Finetune LR 0.0001
BigNASModel-S 76.5 76.4 76.5
BigNASModel-M 78.9 78.8 78.8
BigNASModel-L 79.5 79.6 79.7
BigNASModel-XL 80.9 80.6 80.8
Table 3 trains the selected architectures from scratch. Even with the better distillation variant, training from scratch remains slightly behind the directly sliced model:
Model Direct slice From scratch From scratch + distill B
BigNASModel-S 76.5 75.3 76.3
BigNASModel-M 78.9 77.4 78.6
BigNASModel-L 79.5 78.2 79.2
BigNASModel-XL 80.9 79.3 80.4
This is the key point. BigNAS is not only saying “our search found good architectures”. It is saying the weight-sharing model has already trained those architectures well enough that the inherited weights beat or match the usual post-processing baselines. Relation To OFABigNAS is close to Once-for-All in spirit: both want one trained network to provide many deployable subnets. The difference is how much staging the training pipeline needs.
Method Training style Deployment claim
Once-for-All Progressive shrinking over elastic dimensions Subnets can be specialized and selected after elastic training
BigNAS Simultaneous single-stage training with a stronger recipe Sliced child models are directly deployable without retraining or finetuning
BigNAS still borrows OFA’s sandwich rule and inplace distillation. The new claim is that progressive shrinking is not strictly necessary if initialization, skip transitions, learning-rate schedule, and regularization are tuned for a very large single-stage model. LimitationsThe result is useful, but it is not a generic proof that all one-shot NAS supernets are deployable.
The search space is manually designed around MBConv mobile CNNs. It does not automatically cover arbitrary operators, attention blocks, or hardware-specific kernels. The recipe is expensive: ImageNet-scale supernet training with batch size 4096 on TPUs is still a serious compute budget. The final comparison is mostly FLOP-based. Real deployment often cares about latency, memory bandwidth, activation size, kernel availability, and device-specific scheduling. The method depends on a carefully tuned training recipe. The paper’s strongest message is that supernet training quality matters; it does not make weight sharing automatically reliable. Batch-norm calibration is still needed when slicing and evaluating child models, especially across different input resolutions.
TakeawayBigNAS is valuable because it changes the question from “which architecture should NAS pick?” to “can a single trained supernet already be the pretrained model family?” The paper’s strongest evidence is Table 2 and Table 3: finetuning and retraining do not meaningfully improve the selected child models. My main takeaway is that one-shot NAS fails or succeeds mostly at the supernet-training level. Search over a weak shared-weight model is ranking noise; search over a well-trained elastic model can produce deployable subnets directly. BigNAS is one of the cleaner demonstrations of that idea for mobile CNNs.

entry.title: CLIP: Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision
entry.content:
Paper / Code CLIP is the paper that made “classification by text prompt” feel practical at scale. The idea is simple to state: train an image encoder and a text encoder on internet image-text pairs, then use text descriptions as classifiers at test time. The important shift is the label space. Instead of predicting one fixed set of dataset labels, CLIP learns a shared embedding space where images and natural-language descriptions can be compared directly. That makes zero-shot classification, retrieval, and open-vocabulary use cases much more natural. Training And Zero-shot Use Figure cropped from the paper PDF: CLIP pre-trains with paired image-text examples, then builds a zero-shot classifier from label text. The training batch contains aligned image-text pairs. The image encoder maps images into a normalized embedding, and the text encoder maps captions into the same embedding space. The model computes all image-text similarities in the batch and uses the matching diagonal as positives. The zero-shot classifier is just the same mechanism reused at inference time:
Convert each class name into a prompt, such as a photo of a {label}. Encode all class prompts with the text encoder. Encode the image with the image encoder. Choose the prompt embedding with the highest similarity.
That means a new label set does not require training a new linear head. It only requires writing label text. Why Contrastive Learning Contrastive training is more data efficient than the caption-prediction baselines in this comparison. The paper compares three objectives on zero-shot ImageNet accuracy as training compute increases. The contrastive bag-of-words variant learns much faster than the caption-prediction alternatives. The result is not only that more data helps. It is that the objective matters. The core implementation is short:
The paper’s numpy-like pseudocode: normalized image/text embeddings, scaled cosine similarities, and symmetric cross entropy. The symmetric loss is worth noting. CLIP trains both image-to-text and text-to-image matching. In a batch of N pairs, each image should match its paired text better than the other N - 1 texts, and each text should match its paired image better than the other N - 1 images. Prompt Engineering Prompt engineering and prompt ensembling improve zero-shot classification without retraining the image model. The paper found that bare class names are often a poor interface to the text encoder. A prompt such as a photo of a {label} gives useful context, and task-specific prompts can help even more. For fine-grained datasets, adding the category type matters, for example writing that the label is a pet, food, aircraft, or satellite image. Prompt ensembling is the same idea repeated with multiple contexts. Encode several prompts per class, average them in embedding space, and use the result as the text classifier. This costs more text-encoder work when building the classifier, but that cost is amortized across many image predictions. Zero-shot Evaluation Zero-shot CLIP versus a fully supervised linear probe on ResNet-50 features across 27 datasets. CLIP’s zero-shot behavior is uneven, which is one of the more useful parts of the paper. It is strong on datasets where natural language names line up well with visual concepts, such as StanfordCars, Country211, Food101, and Kinetics700. It is weaker on some specialized datasets, including EuroSAT, KITTI Distance, PatchCamelyon, GTSRB, and CLEVRCounts. This is a good reminder: zero-shot does not mean uniformly strong. It means the model can attempt a task through language. Whether that language interface contains enough signal depends on the dataset. Few-shot Comparison Zero-shot CLIP is close to a few-shot linear probe on the same feature space in the paper’s aggregate comparison. One surprising result is that zero-shot CLIP can match the average performance of a 4-shot logistic regression classifier trained on the same feature space. This does not mean zero-shot is always better than few-shot. It means language priors can be strong enough that a prompt-based classifier is competitive with a tiny labeled set. The paper also points out a practical research direction: combining the zero-shot classifier as a prior with few-shot learning should be better than treating the two as unrelated methods. Linear Probe And Model Scale CLIP features are competitive with strong supervised and self-supervised vision models under linear probing. The linear-probe results separate two questions:
Are the learned visual features good? Is the text-generated zero-shot classifier good?
CLIP is strong on both, but they are not identical. A feature space can be useful while the zero-shot text interface still loses points because the prompt or label set is imperfect. This distinction is important when debugging CLIP-style systems: sometimes the problem is representation quality, and sometimes the problem is the text classifier specification. Robustness Under Distribution Shift Zero-shot CLIP reduces the ImageNet robustness gap on several natural distribution shifts. The robustness result is one of the paper’s most interesting claims. Standard ImageNet-trained models can do well on ImageNet validation but drop sharply under natural distribution shifts. Zero-shot CLIP narrows that gap, likely because it is not tuned directly to the ImageNet training distribution and because its class interface can be adapted with text. The right side of the figure uses banana examples to make the shift concrete: ImageNet, ImageNetV2, ImageNet-R, ObjectNet, ImageNet Sketch, and ImageNet-A can contain visually different versions of the same semantic class. CLIP handles several of these shifts better than a similarly accurate ImageNet model. Reading NotesCLIP’s influence comes from making the text interface a first-class part of visual recognition:
Labels become natural-language descriptions. Adding a class can be done by adding text. Retrieval and classification share the same embedding space. Prompt design becomes part of model evaluation.
The limitations are also clear. CLIP learns from noisy web image-text pairs, so biases and spurious correlations matter. It is not a full visual reasoning system. It can fail on fine-grained spatial tasks, abstract synthetic tasks, medical/satellite-style domains, and settings where the class names do not describe the visual decision well. The practical takeaway for me: CLIP is not “zero-shot magic.” It is a very strong interface between language and visual representations. The quality of that interface depends on pre-training scale, objective design, prompt wording, and whether the target task can actually be expressed through text.

entry.title: ChamNet: Platform-Aware Model Adaptation
entry.content:
Paper / Code ChamNet is a platform-aware model adaptation paper. It is not mainly about inventing a new operator or cell. It starts from practical building blocks, then reallocates channels, depths, expansion ratios, and input resolution so the resulting model matches a concrete deployment target. That makes it different from reading a pure NAS paper. The core claim is deployment-oriented: FLOPs are not enough. A model that is good on a mobile CPU may not be good on a DSP, GPU, or server CPU, because each backend has different kernel behavior and memory bottlenecks. Chameleon Framework Chameleon separates the main search loop from one-time predictive models for accuracy, latency, and energy. The framework has two parts:
A main search loop using efficient evolutionary search (EES). Predictive models that estimate accuracy, latency, and energy without repeatedly training and measuring every candidate.
The optimization target is straightforward: maximize predicted_accuracy(architecture)subject to predicted_resource(architecture, platform) <= budget
ChamNet folds the resource constraint into a fitness score. Candidates that violate the latency or energy budget get penalized, while candidates inside the budget are ranked mostly by predicted accuracy. This predictor-first design is the paper’s scalability argument. If the accuracy predictor and platform resource predictors are already built, searching for a new use scenario becomes much cheaper than running RL or full hardware-in-the-loop search from scratch. Accuracy Predictor The paper compares several accuracy predictors and reports the best leave-one-out MSE from the Gaussian Process regressor. Only a small number of sampled architectures are fully trained, so the accuracy predictor must work in a low-data regime. ChamNet uses a Gaussian Process regressor because it gives both a prediction and an uncertainty estimate.
The selected samples concentrate near the useful accuracy/FLOPs frontier, while still keeping exploration points. The sampling rule mixes exploitation and exploration:
Exploitation: sample models that look accurate relative to FLOPs. Exploration: sample models where the predictor is uncertain.
This is a practical detail worth remembering. If the predictor only exploits its current belief, it can overfit early mistakes. If it only samples uncertain regions, it wastes training budget. ChamNet deliberately does both. Platform Metrics A 1x1 convolution can have very different latency surfaces on different platforms, even when FLOPs look similar. ChamNet builds an operator latency lookup table from real device measurements. The paper’s latency surface figure is the reason: channel counts create visible discontinuities, and CPU/DSP behavior differs. This is the kind of effect that a FLOPs-only objective misses. Energy is handled with a predictor too, but it is measured directly from device runs. This makes the framework more expensive to set up than a purely analytical model, but much more relevant for deployment decisions. Mobile Results ChamNet-Mobile on Snapdragon 835 CPU.
ChamNet-Mobile on Hexagon v62 DSP. The mobile experiments adapt MobileNetV2-style inverted residual blocks. The search space includes input resolution, channel count, expansion factor, number of repeated blocks, and stride. The headline points are:
Platform Constraint ChamNet top-1
Snapdragon 835 CPU 20 ms 73.8
Hexagon v62 DSP 20 ms 75.3
Snapdragon 835 CPU 4 ms 64.2
Hexagon v62 DSP 4 ms 63.6
The tight-latency points are important. At 4 ms, the method still finds a useful architecture instead of only working at comfortable budgets. Server Results ChamNet-Res on Intel CPU.
ChamNet-Res on Nvidia GPU. For server settings, ChamNet adapts ResNet-style building blocks. The paper evaluates Intel Xeon Broadwell CPU and Nvidia GTX 1060 GPU. The curves differ across CPU and GPU, which reinforces the same point as the mobile results: the best architecture family member depends on the platform, not only on the target FLOPs. Representative reported points:
Platform Constraint ChamNet-Res top-1
Intel CPU 400 ms 78.5
Intel CPU 200 ms 77.2
Nvidia GPU 15 ms 78.6
Nvidia GPU 10 ms 77.7
Energy Results Energy-constrained ChamNet-Mobile on Snapdragon 835 CPU. The energy experiment is a good reminder that latency and energy are related but not identical. The paper reports that MobileNetV2 0.75x at 96x96 gets 58.8 top-1 at 19 mJ per run, while an adapted ChamNet model gets 60.0 top-1 at 14 mJ per run. That is a 26% energy reduction while gaining 1.2 percentage points of accuracy. Comparison And Search Cost Comparison with manual scaling, RL-based NAS, pruning, and related platform-aware methods. The table is useful because it mixes accuracy with scaling complexity. RL-based methods such as MnasNet are listed as O(m * n * k), where the factors correspond to models, platforms, and use scenarios. ChamNet separates model accuracy predictors from platform resource predictors and reports O(m + n). That does not mean ChamNet is free. It still needs a one-time cost for trained architecture samples and platform measurements. The point is that after paying this cost, many platform/budget searches become cheap. Computation Redistribution ChamNet shifts compute across stages instead of using a uniform width multiplier. This is the most concrete design lesson in the paper. The adapted model is not just MobileNetV2 with one global width multiplier. ChamNet moves FLOPs away from some early high-resolution stages and spends more computation later, where it improves the accuracy-latency tradeoff. The paper reports 71.6 top-1 at 15.0 ms for ChamNet-C, compared with 69.8 top-1 at 16.6 ms for MobileNetV2 0.75x. The method is doing stage-wise allocation, not only shrinking the network. Reading NotesChamNet is strongest as a deployment workflow:
Keep proven efficient blocks. Measure the real target platform. Build reusable predictors. Search for stage-wise allocation under the actual budget.
The limitation is also clear. ChamNet depends on the base architecture family and predictor quality. It will not discover a fundamentally new operator class, and it still needs training and profiling samples. But for organizations deploying variants across many devices and budgets, this is a sensible tradeoff: pay the setup cost once, then adapt quickly.

entry.title: CodeBear: Your Personal AI Coding Assitant
entry.content:
Repo: https://github.com/Baytoro/codebear Update2024-04-05 added normal sampling args on web-ui 2024-03-29 changed to deepseek 33b & 6b as base model 2024-03-26 changed to new web-ui developed by gradio 2024-03-10 fused mlp triton kernel Acknowledgement Special thanks to Deepseek team for releasing DeepSeek-Coder models with outstanding performance Special thanks to feifeibear for releasing the implemention of speculative decoding with both Google’s and Deepmind’s versions(LLMSpeculativeSampling ). Special thanks to AutoGPTQ team for implementing GPTQ algorithm and open source the code.
MotivationThis repository combines GPTQ 4-bit quantization and Speculative Decoding to accelerate Large Language Models’ (LLM) inference for code completion tasks in personal usage scenarios (where GPU resources are limited yet there’s a pursuit for better performance and faster speed with larger models). GPTQ is a one-shot weight quantization method based on approximate second-order information, that is both highly-accurate and highly efficient. And Speculative Decoding is a innovative sampling strategy by using a small approximation model to propose sequences of tokens that will later be checked by a larger model. By combining these two techniques, one can even deploy multiple LLMs in a single GPU with limited HBM memory usage. While benefiting from the improved performance brought by larger models, it also helps to accelerate inference speed to some extent. The flowing figures are tested in a single V100(32GB) by deploying 34B and 7B models, with triton-based QuantLinear backend.
3 prefill + 200th decoding
Memory Usage(GB) 27.7
3 prefill + 200th decoding 7B(FP16) 7B(4Bit) 34B(4Bit) Speculative 7B+34B(4Bit)
Inference Speed(Tokens/sec) 14.3 34.1 7.9 9.4
Quick TourRequirementstriton==2.1.0auto_gptq==0.7.0transformers==4.37.2 Step1: QuantizeDownload the float model from official(7B and 34B ), then quantize them. #quntize the 7b model./make_quant.sh -f /PATH/TO/7B/FLOAT/MODEL -q /PATH/TO/7B/QUANT/MODEL#quntize the 34b model./make_quant.sh -f /PATH/TO/34B/FLOAT/MODEL -q /PATH/TO/34B/QUANT/MODEL
The basic config of quantization is set to bits = 4, group_num = 128 (can be changed in ./scripts/quantize.py). Step2: ServingStart serving ./start_server.sh -s /PATH/TO/7B/QUANT/MODEL -l /PATH/TO/34B/QUANT/MODEL -t /PATH/TO/7B/FLOAT/MODEL Default sampling params are set to max_tokens = 500, top_k = 10, top_p = 0.9 (can be changed in ./scripts/serving.py). Send request (the model is specially trained for code completion with python) curl -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"prompt": "def quicksort("}' http://127.0.0.1:5000/codebear
Future plans
Progress
fused_flash_attn_MHA triton implemention todo
fused_flash_attn_GQA triton implemention todo
INT8 KV cache todo

entry.title: Mixture of Experts(MOEs): The Versatile Framework for Scalable AI Solutions
[CUDA] Warp Timeline with NVBit and Modal
entry.content:
Reference GitHub repo: Baytoro/warptrace Main entrypoint: warp_timeline_modal.py NVBit tool: nvbit_tool/warp_timeline_nvbit.cu, nvbit_tool/inject_funcs.cu Example kernel: example/warp_paths.cu Exported viewer: build/warp-timeline/timeline.html NVIDIA NVBit release used by the repo: nvbit-Linux-x86_64-1.8
This note is about a small but useful CUDA profiling project. The repo has one clear goal: run a CUDA executable on a remote Modal B200 machine, inject an NVBit tool with LD_PRELOAD, collect warp-level basic-block timestamps, map those basic blocks back to SASS, and render the result as a local HTML timeline. I like this project because it sits between two common debugging levels. It is lower level than Nsight Systems, because it records warp/basic-block behavior inside a kernel. It is higher level than reading raw SASS, because it groups basic blocks into visible timeline spans: load, compute, sync, and store. It is not a replacement for Nsight Compute metrics. It is closer to an explanatory microscope for one kernel. The final output looks like this:
This screenshot is from the exported timeline.html. The example run has one block, four warps, and one SM. The horizontal axis is raw globaltimer cycles. Each row is a warp row. Green spans are compute, blue spans are load, orange spans are sync, and red spans are store. What The Repo BuildsThe project has four moving parts: warptrace├── warp_timeline_modal.py # profile binary on Modal and render HTML├── build_example_modal.py # build the bundled CUDA example remotely├── build-example.sh # thin wrapper around build_example_modal.py├── nvbit_tool/│ ├── warp_timeline_nvbit.cu # NVBit host-side instrumentation│ ├── inject_funcs.cu # device-side record_bb()│ ├── common.h # event record schema│ └── Makefile # builds warp_timeline_nvbit.so├── example/│ ├── warp_paths.cu # warp-specialized GEMM + SiLU example│ └── CMakeLists.txt└── build/warp-timeline/ ├── trace.json # raw/enriched trace ├── timeline.html # self-contained viewer ├── remote.log # Modal build/run log └── sass.txt # cuobjdump --dump-sass output
The run command is intentionally simple: ./warp_timeline_modal.py build/example/warp_paths
The tool assumes the input is already a Linux x86_64 CUDA executable. That detail matters because the Modal container is x86_64; a local aarch64 binary would not run there. The bundled example avoids this mismatch by building remotely: ./build-example.sh
The outputs are local: build/warp-timeline/trace.jsonbuild/warp-timeline/timeline.htmlbuild/warp-timeline/remote.logbuild/warp-timeline/sass.txt
End-To-End FlowThe whole pipeline can be read as a dataflow: flowchart TB src["CUDA executabletarget_app"] --> modal["Modal B200 container"] toolsrc["nvbit_tool/*.cu"] --> buildtool["build NVBit shared object"] nvbit["warp_timeline_nvbit.so"] --> preload["LD_PRELOAD"] buildtool --> nvbit modal --> preload preload --> run["run target CUDA program"] run --> events["managed event bufferbasic-block records"] events --> trace["trace.json"] run --> sass["cuobjdump --dump-sass"] sass --> enrich["map PC offsets to SASS"] trace --> enrich enrich --> viewer["timeline.html"]
The important design choice is that the CUDA source does not need to be changed. The target program is launched normally, except that the process loads warp_timeline_nvbit.so through LD_PRELOAD. NVBit then instruments the CUDA function at runtime before the kernel launch. The remote runner sets the environment like this: env = { "LD_PRELOAD": str(tool), "NOBANNER": "1", "WARP_TIMELINE_TRACE": str(trace_path), "WARP_TIMELINE_MAX_EVENTS": str(event_capacity),}log += remote_run([str(target), *args], cwd=work_dir, env=env)
After the kernel finishes, the runner also calls: cuobjdump --dump-sass target_app
That SASS dump is not needed to record timing. It is needed to make the timeline human-readable. Without it, a span would only be something like bb_96_pc_0x11b0. With the SASS dump, the viewer can show that this block contains shared-memory loads, integer address arithmetic, branches, and so on. The Example KernelThe bundled example is deliberately small and structured. It launches one block with 128 threads, i.e. four warps: constexpr int kThreads = 128;constexpr int kWarps = kThreads / 32;
The kernel is a warp-specialized GEMM followed by SiLU. The roles are hard-coded: if (warp == 0) { load_a_tile(a, shared_a, k, kt, lane);} else if (warp == 1) { load_b_tile(b, shared_b, k, kt, lane);}__syncthreads();if (warp == 2) { compute_half_tile(shared_a, shared_b, accum, lane, 0);} else if (warp == 3) { compute_half_tile(shared_a, shared_b, accum, lane, 8);}__syncthreads();
This makes the timeline easy to interpret:
Warp Intended role
warp 0 load the A tile into shared memory
warp 1 load the B tile into shared memory
warp 2 compute rows 0..7, apply SiLU, store
warp 3 compute rows 8..15, apply SiLU, store
The default problem shape is small: M = 16N = 16K = 128repeats = 2
That is not meant to be a benchmark. It is meant to produce a trace where warp roles are visible. In the exported trace I inspected, there are 783 raw basic-block events, one kernel, one block, four warps, and one SM: schema: cuda-warp-timeline/v1events: 783kernel: warp_specialized_gemm_silu_kernel(...)blocks: [0]warps: [0, 1, 2, 3]SMs: [142]
What NVBit RecordsThe event schema lives in nvbit_tool/common.h: typedef struct { uint64_t time; uint64_t grid_launch_id; uint64_t pc_offset; uint32_t bb_id; uint32_t num_instrs; int32_t cta_id_x; int32_t cta_id_y; int32_t cta_id_z; int32_t warp_id; int32_t sm_id;} warp_timeline_event_t;
Each record is intentionally small: time: the GPU globaltimer value at basic-block entry. grid_launch_id: a monotonically increasing launch id assigned by the host-side NVBit callback. pc_offset: SASS PC offset of the first instruction in the basic block. bb_id: the tool’s basic-block id inside the function CFG. num_instrs: number of instructions in that basic block. cta_id_*: CUDA block coordinates. warp_id: warp id inside the block. sm_id: SM that executed the recording lane. The device-side injected function is record_bb: extern "C" __device__ __noinline__ void record_bb( uint32_t bb_id, uint32_t num_instrs, uint64_t pc_offset, uint64_t grid_launch_id, uint64_t pevents, uint64_t pcounter, uint32_t capacity) { int active_mask = __ballot_sync(__activemask(), 1); int laneid = get_laneid(); int first_laneid = __ffs(active_mask) - 1; if (laneid != first_laneid) { return; } unsigned long long idx = atomicAdd((unsigned long long*)pcounter, 1ULL); if (idx >= capacity) { return; } warp_timeline_event_t* events = (warp_timeline_event_t*)pevents; int4 cta = get_ctaid(); warp_timeline_event_t* event = &events[idx]; event->time = global_timer(); event->grid_launch_id = grid_launch_id; event->pc_offset = pc_offset; event->bb_id = bb_id; event->num_instrs = num_instrs; event->cta_id_x = cta.x; event->cta_id_y = cta.y; event->cta_id_z = cta.z; event->warp_id = block_local_warp_id(); event->sm_id = get_smid();}
There are two details here that I would keep: First, only one active lane records the event. The function computes the first active lane with __ffs(active_mask) - 1, then returns for all other lanes. This makes each basic-block entry a warp-level event instead of a thread-level event. Second, the timestamp is taken from globaltimer: asm volatile("mov.u64 %0, %%globaltimer;" : "=l"(t));
That gives a single device-wide time base. The viewer does not convert it to seconds. It keeps raw ticks, which is honest for this kind of tool: the relative shape of the timeline matters more than pretending to have calibrated wall-clock units. Where The Injection HappensThe host-side NVBit code instruments the first instruction of each basic block: const CFG_t& cfg = nvbit_get_CFG(ctx, func);uint32_t bb_id = 0;for (auto& bb : cfg.bbs) { if (bb->instrs.empty()) { continue; } Instr* instr = bb->instrs[0]; nvbit_insert_call(instr, "record_bb", IPOINT_BEFORE); nvbit_add_call_arg_const_val32(instr, bb_id); nvbit_add_call_arg_const_val32(instr, bb->instrs.size()); nvbit_add_call_arg_const_val64(instr, instr->getOffset()); nvbit_add_call_arg_launch_val64(instr, 0); nvbit_add_call_arg_const_val64(instr, (uint64_t)events); nvbit_add_call_arg_const_val64(instr, (uint64_t)&event_count); nvbit_add_call_arg_const_val32(instr, max_events); bb_id++;}
This is the core idea of the project. Instead of instrumenting every instruction, it instruments basic-block entries. That has three consequences:
The trace is smaller. The overhead is lower than instruction-level tracing. The timeline loses instruction-by-instruction detail, but keeps the control-flow path and approximate phase shape.
For this project, that tradeoff is reasonable. I usually want to know whether a warp is in a load-heavy region, compute-heavy region, barrier region, or store region. Basic-block granularity is enough for that first pass. The launch callback wires everything together: if (!is_exit) { pthread_mutex_lock(&mutex); instrument_function_if_needed(ctx, func); nvbit_set_at_launch(ctx, func, global_grid_launch_id); nvbit_enable_instrumented(ctx, func, true); event_count = 0;} else { CUDA_SAFECALL(cudaDeviceSynchronize()); const char* func_name = nvbit_get_func_name(ctx, func); append_spans_for_kernel(func_name ? func_name : "kernel"); global_grid_launch_id++; pthread_mutex_unlock(&mutex);}
On launch entry, the function is instrumented and the event counter is reset. On launch exit, the host synchronizes, reads the managed event buffer, converts records into spans, and appends them to the trace. From Records To SpansThe raw event records are point samples: one timestamp per basic-block entry. The viewer needs spans. The conversion is simple:
Sort events by launch id, block, warp, time, and basic-block id. For each event, use the next event from the same block and warp as the end time. If there is no next event, use time + 1.
The relevant logic is in append_spans_for_kernel: uint64_t end = event.time + 1;if (i + 1 < batch.size() && batch[i + 1].grid_launch_id == event.grid_launch_id && flattened_block(batch[i + 1]) == flattened_block(event) && batch[i + 1].warp_id == event.warp_id && batch[i + 1].time > event.time) { end = batch[i + 1].time;}char phase[96];snprintf(phase, sizeof(phase), "bb_%u_pc_0x%llx", event.bb_id, (unsigned long long)event.pc_offset);
At this stage, phase is not yet load or compute. It is still a basic-block identity such as: bb_96_pc_0x11b0
The JSON event then looks conceptually like this: { "kernel": "warp_specialized_gemm_silu_kernel(...)", "block": 0, "warp": 0, "sm": 142, "instructions": 11, "phase": "bb_0_pc_0x0", "start": 1782366955280956192, "end": 1782366955280995264}
This raw format is useful because it keeps the profiler side small. The richer interpretation happens later in Python. SASS EnrichmentThe Python runner parses cuobjdump --dump-sass output. It builds a function list, an instruction list per function, and a PC-index map: FUNCTION_RE = re.compile(r"^\s*Function\s*:\s*(\S+)")SASS_RE = re.compile(r"/\*\s*([0-9a-fA-F]+)\s*\*/\s*(.*)$")OPCODE_RE = re.compile(r"(?:@\!?P\d+\s+)?([A-Z][A-Z0-9_.]*)\b")
For every bb_*_pc_* span, it extracts the PC offset and instruction count, then looks up the corresponding SASS slice: def resolve_sass_instructions(functions, kernel_name, pc, instruction_count): if pc is None or instruction_count <= 0: return [] for function in matching_sass_functions(functions, kernel_name): index = function["pc_index"].get(pc) if index is None: continue return function["instructions"][index : index + instruction_count] return []
The next step is classification. The tool assigns each instruction an opcode category, then assigns the basic block a phase class: def phase_for_basic_block(instructions, category): bases = [opcode_base(str(instr.get("opcode", ""))) for instr in instructions] if any(base.startswith("STG") for base in bases): return "store" if any(base.startswith(("BAR", "MEMBAR", "WARPSYNC", "NANOSLEEP", "DEPBAR")) for base in bases): return "sync" if any(base.startswith(("LDG", "LDGSTS", "STS")) for base in bases): return "load" if category == "sync": return "sync" return "compute"
This heuristic is intentionally practical. It does not try to prove what the block does semantically. It asks: what kind of operations dominate the block enough to color the timeline? That is why the viewer can show four fixed phase colors:
Phase Meaning in this viewer
load data movement or tile staging, including selected shared/global memory instructions
compute arithmetic, address arithmetic, predicate work, and general non-memory execution
sync barriers and synchronization/wait blocks
store global stores
What The HTML Viewer AddsThe HTML renderer normalizes time by subtracting the first event timestamp. It also merges adjacent spans from the same row when they share the same phase class: if ( merged_events and merged_events[-1]["row"] == event["row"] and merged_events[-1]["phaseClass"] == event["phaseClass"] and abs(float(merged_events[-1]["end"]) - float(event["start"])) <= 1.0): merged_events[-1]["end"] = event["end"] merged_events[-1]["bbKeys"].append(event["bbKey"]) merged_events[-1]["bbCount"] += 1
This is why the screenshot reports 332 phase spans, even though the raw trace contains 783 events. The viewer is not hiding information permanently. It is compressing adjacent same-phase basic blocks into readable bars, while still keeping the list of merged basic-block ids for hover/click details. The selected-span view shows the payoff:
After selecting a bar, the viewer can show:
row identity: SM, block, warp; start/end/duration in cycles; merged basic-block count; opcode summary; basic-block id and PC offset; SASS sample for the selected basic block.
This is the part I find most valuable. A normal timeline can tell me that a warp had a long green region. This viewer lets me click into that region and see which basic-block path and SASS sample produced it. Reading The Example TimelineThe overview screenshot is already enough to confirm that the example kernel is behaving as intended. Warp rows: B0 W0 SM142B0 W1 SM142B0 W2 SM142B0 W3 SM142
The rows match one CUDA block, four warps, one SM. In the unzoomed overview, most of the visible time is compute-colored because adjacent compute blocks are merged. In the more zoomed selected-span screenshot, the repeated structure appears: short load segments, compute regions, sync regions, and store at the end. The expected warp-specialized behavior is: W0: mostly data movement into shared memory for the A tile. W1: mostly data movement into shared memory for the B tile. W2 and W3: compute-heavy regions for two row groups, with synchronization between K tiles and stores near the end. One thing to remember: this is basic-block tracing, not occupancy analysis. If a row is green, it does not mean the warp was continuously executing useful floating-point math with perfect efficiency. It means the merged basic blocks were classified as compute. To understand throughput, memory transactions, issue stalls, or cache behavior, I would still use Nsight Compute. Why Basic-Block Level Is A Good CompromiseInstruction-level tracing is tempting, but it can explode quickly. Every instruction from every active lane would create a massive trace and heavy overhead. This tool uses one record per warp per basic-block entry. That keeps the trace small enough for a browser viewer. For kernel understanding, the information I usually need first is: Which warp ran which code path?When did it hit a barrier?Which basic blocks were repeated?Did the loader warps and compute warps follow the roles I expected?Which PC offset should I inspect in SASS?
Basic-block tracing answers those questions. It will not answer: Why did a memory instruction stall?How many sectors did this load touch?Was occupancy limited by registers or shared memory?Did tensor cores reach peak utilization?
That boundary is fine. The tool explains control-flow and phase shape. It does not replace hardware counter profiling. Modal SideThe Modal part is mostly engineering glue, but it is important glue. The runner builds an image from: modal.Image.from_registry( "nvidia/cuda:13.0.2-devel-ubuntu24.04", add_python="3.13",).apt_install("bc", "binutils", "bzip2", "build-essential", "ca-certificates", "make").env({ "CUDA_HOME": "/usr/local/cuda", "PATH": "/usr/local/cuda/bin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin",}).add_local_dir(ROOT / "nvbit_tool", "/workspace/project/nvbit_tool", copy=True).add_local_file(binary, "/workspace/input/target_app", copy=True)
Then the remote function:
checks architecture with uname -m; checks the GPU with nvidia-smi; downloads or reuses the NVBit archive; builds warp_timeline_nvbit.so; runs the target with LD_PRELOAD; captures cuobjdump --dump-sass; returns trace, log, and SASS text to the local machine.
NVBit is cached under /cache/warp-timeline/, and the built tool is keyed by a hash of the nvbit_tool source files. That avoids rebuilding the instrumentation shared object every time if the tool source did not change. This is also why no local GPU is required for profiling. The local machine runs Python and receives artifacts. The CUDA execution and NVBit instrumentation happen remotely. Build And Profile CommandsFor the bundled example: ./build-example.sh./warp_timeline_modal.py build/example/warp_paths
To pass arguments to the example: ./warp_timeline_modal.py build/example/warp_paths 16 4
Those arguments mean: k_tiles = 16repeats = 4K = k_tiles * 16
For another prebuilt CUDA binary: ./warp_timeline_modal.py /path/to/your_cuda_app arg1 arg2
The binary must be Linux x86_64, because the Modal CUDA container is Linux x86_64. Things I Would Improve NextThe current tool is already useful, but the design leaves several obvious next steps. First, I would add an option to record only selected kernels. Right now the NVBit callback instruments launched CUDA functions as they appear. For a larger application, the trace could include setup kernels or library kernels that are not the current target. Second, I would make phase classification configurable. The current opcode heuristic is a good default, but a kernel author may want to label selected PC ranges manually as prologue, tile-load, mma-mainloop, epilogue, or store. Third, I would add a small summary table next to the viewer: warp | load cycles | compute cycles | sync cycles | store cycles
This would make it easier to compare loader warps and compute warps without eyeballing bar widths. Fourth, I would preserve multidimensional block ids as structured fields in the viewer. The current renderer flattens block coordinates into one integer. That is convenient for the first version, but a 2D/3D grid would be easier to inspect if block coordinates stayed as (x, y, z). Fifth, I would add a direct “open source line” mapping only when debug/source information is available. For optimized CUDA kernels, SASS and PC offsets are often the real source of truth, but source correlation would still help during early kernel development. TakeawaysThis repo is a compact example of how to build a custom CUDA introspection tool: NVBit basic-block entry injection-> one event per warp/basic-block entry-> globaltimer timestamp-> host-side span construction-> cuobjdump SASS enrichment-> browser timeline
The strongest part is the workflow. I can run an unmodified CUDA binary, get a trace, open one HTML file, and inspect warp paths with SASS context. The exported timeline is not trying to be a full profiler. It is a focused tool for answering one question:
What did each warp do, in what order, and which SASS basic blocks explain the visible phases?
For warp-specialized kernels, that is exactly the kind of question I want to answer before going deeper into Nsight Compute metrics.

entry.title: End-to-End Object Detection with Transformers
entry.content:
Carion et al. End-to-End Object Detection with Transformers. ECCV 2020.
Paper DETR is worth reading because it changes the shape of the detection problem. Instead of predicting dense anchors, ranking proposals, and cleaning duplicates with NMS, it predicts a fixed-size set of objects and trains the model with a one-to-one matching loss. That sounds simple only after the paper exists. The key engineering move is to make “object slots” explicit through learned decoder queries, then force those slots to compete for ground-truth boxes through Hungarian matching. Motivation The first figure is the whole paper in one diagram. A CNN extracts image features, a Transformer reasons over them, and a fixed number of predictions is matched against the ground-truth set. A query that does not match any object is trained as the no-object class. The important contrast with Faster R-CNN style detectors is not just the use of attention. DETR removes several hand-designed detection components:
no anchor boxes; no region proposal network; no NMS; no class-specific duplicate suppression heuristic.
The model can do that because the loss itself enforces one prediction per object. Architecture The architecture has four parts:
A CNN backbone maps the image to a lower-resolution feature map. A linear projection converts the CNN channels into the Transformer hidden dimension. A Transformer encoder adds global context over the flattened feature map, with positional encodings injected because attention is otherwise permutation-invariant. A Transformer decoder consumes learned object queries and outputs one embedding per query. Each embedding goes through small FFNs for class prediction and normalized box coordinates.
I read the object queries as learned detection slots. They are not proposals with coordinates. They are trainable vectors that ask the decoder to retrieve an object from the encoded image. Since the number of queries is larger than the expected number of objects, unused slots are trained to predict no object. This design is clean, but it also explains why optimization is harder than in anchor-based detectors. Early in training, a query has no obvious spatial prior. The model must learn both where to attend and how to allocate queries to instances. Set Prediction LossDETR trains on unordered sets. If the ground truth has M objects and the model emits N predictions with N >= M, the target set is padded with no-object entries. The matching step searches for the best permutation: best permutation = argmin over permutations sum_i L_match(target_i, prediction_sigma(i))
After this assignment, the Hungarian loss combines classification and box regression: Hungarian loss = classification loss + box loss for matched non-empty objects
The box part uses both L1 distance and generalized IoU: box loss = lambda_iou * GIoU + lambda_L1 * L1 distance
The one-to-one matching is the reason DETR does not need NMS. Two queries can still predict similar boxes, but only one of them receives the object match; the other is pushed toward no-object. COCO Results The main COCO table is more nuanced than “Transformer beats detector.” With ResNet-50, DETR reaches the same AP as Faster R-CNN-FPN+:
Method AP AP50 AP75 APS APM APL
Faster R-CNN-FPN+ 42.0 62.1 45.5 26.6 45.4 53.4
DETR 42.0 62.4 44.2 20.5 45.8 61.1
Faster R-CNN-R101-FPN+ 44.0 63.9 47.8 27.2 48.1 56.0
DETR-DC5-R101 44.9 64.7 47.7 23.7 49.5 62.3
The pattern is clear: DETR is strong on large objects and weak on small objects. That matches the architecture. The model reasons globally, but the original feature resolution and attention pattern are not ideal for dense small-instance localization. Encoder Ablation The encoder ablation makes the global reasoning argument more concrete. Removing the encoder gives 36.7 AP. Six encoder layers give 40.6 AP, and twelve layers give 41.6 AP. The gain is especially visible on large objects:
Encoder layers AP APS APM APL
0 36.7 16.8 39.6 54.2
3 40.1 18.5 43.8 58.6
6 40.6 19.9 44.3 60.2
12 41.6 19.8 44.9 61.9
This is one of the more useful figures for implementation intuition. The encoder is not a cosmetic Transformer block placed after a CNN. It materially improves scene-level reasoning and query assignment. Attention And Segmentation The attention visualization is a good sanity check. Encoder attention follows object boundaries instead of only local texture. That does not prove the model “understands” the scene, but it explains why a global self-attention layer can help with object separation and large-object detection.
The panoptic extension is also important. DETR’s box queries can be reused as instance-level handles: attach mask heads to the decoder outputs, combine them with per-pixel features, and predict segmentation masks. The paper reports competitive panoptic results without changing the core set-prediction idea. TakeawayDETR’s contribution is the combination, not any single component:
object detection as set prediction; learned object queries as fixed prediction slots; Hungarian matching as the training mechanism that removes duplicate predictions; Transformer encoder-decoder for global assignment and scene reasoning.
The original version also has visible costs. It converges slowly, needs long training schedules, and underperforms on small objects. Later work such as Deformable DETR attacks exactly these points with sparse multi-scale attention and faster convergence. Still, DETR is the clean baseline to understand first because it makes the detector pipeline much less hand-engineered.

entry.title: Direct Federated Neural Architecture Search
entry.content:
He et al. Direct Federated Neural Architecture Search. 2020.
Paper DFNAS is a practical follow-up to read after FedNAS. FedNAS already asks how to search architectures when data stays on clients. DFNAS asks a more systems-oriented question: can the search be done directly inside the federated training loop, without a separate retraining stage and without DARTS-style multi-path memory cost? The answer is a DSNAS-like one-path supernet. Each client samples one child network, updates operation weights and architecture parameters locally, and the server averages both. MotivationIn standard federated learning, the global objective is a weighted sum of local client objectives: min_w F(w), where F(w) = sum_i nu_i * F_i(w)
The architecture is usually fixed before training starts. That is a weak assumption in FL:
client data can be non-IID, so a manually chosen architecture may fit some clients better than others; the designer often cannot inspect private client data; a second centralized search or retraining stage is expensive and sometimes impossible; DARTS-style continuous relaxation keeps many candidate operations active, which is a bad fit for memory-limited clients.
DFNAS keeps the goal modest: search one global architecture that is ready to deploy after the federated process finishes. Local Search For client i, the local objective is written around a sampled structure: E_{Z sampled from p_alpha(Z)} [ L_w(x_i, y_i, Z) ]
Here Z is the one-hot architecture decision, alpha parameterizes the sampling distribution, and w is the operation weight. A local step roughly does this:
sample a child network Z from p_alpha(Z); activate only that path in the parent network; update w with a normal batch gradient; update alpha with the estimator tied to the sampled architecture probability; prune weak operations when their architecture weights fall below a threshold.
The memory advantage comes from the one-path execution. If a DARTS cell keeps n candidate operations alive, the forward, backward, and activation memory cost can scale with n. DFNAS trains only one sampled path per step, so the client-side footprint is much closer to training an ordinary child model. Federated Loop The server side is FedAvg with one extra object to average. After selected clients finish local search, the server aggregates both weights and architecture parameters: w_{t+1} = sum_{i in S_t} (n_i / n) * w_{t+1}^{(i)}alpha_{t+1} = sum_{i in S_t} (n_i / n) * alpha_{t+1}^{(i)}
This is the “direct” part of DFNAS. The searched model is produced by the same communication rounds that train it. There is no proxy dataset, no separate architecture-transfer step, and no final retraining pipeline in the method. Search SpaceThe parent network is ShuffleNet-like. That is a good engineering choice for cross-device FL because the candidates are already mobile-friendly. The paper uses:
4 candidates per choice block for cross-silo experiments: ShuffleNet blocks with kernel sizes 3, 5, and 7, plus an Xception block; 3 candidates per choice block for cross-device experiments; a reported 4^20 search space for the cross-silo setting and 3^12 for the cross-device setting.
This is not an open-ended architecture generator. It is a constrained efficient-CNN search space, which makes the one-path federated search realistic. Communication Curves The round-accuracy curves are useful because they show a common NAS-in-FL behavior: DFNAS can look bad early while the sampled architecture is still unstable, then catch the fixed baselines after enough rounds. On non-IID CIFAR-10 with 8 clients and 150 rounds:
Method Final test accuracy
ResNet56 + FedAvg 77.78%
MobileNetV1 + FedAvg 83.41%
DFNAS 88.31%
On non-IID CINIC-10 with 16 clients and 250 rounds:
Method Final test accuracy
ShuffleNetV1 + FedAvg 67.70%
DFNAS 68.35%
The CIFAR-10 gain is the stronger result. CINIC-10 is closer, but still shows that the searched architecture is not just overfitting the small CIFAR setting. Search Cost The main comparison with FedNAS is on CIFAR-10 with 8 non-IID clients:
Method Test accuracy Params Total time Search memory
FedNAS 91.43 +/- 0.13% 0.33M 1 GPU day 10,793 MB
DFNAS 92.11 +/- 0.10% 2.1M 0.18 GPU day 1,437 MB
This table should not be read as “DFNAS gives the smallest model.” It does not. The DFNAS model is larger than the FedNAS model in this comparison. The win is search efficiency: much lower memory and much less total search time.
The IID scaling table reports:
Clients Test accuracy Params Total time
2 93.53 +/- 0.10% 2.1M 0.83 GPU day
4 93.31 +/- 0.12% 2.1M 0.43 GPU day
8 92.79 +/- 0.15% 2.1M 0.18 GPU day
Accuracy drops slightly as more clients are used, while wall-clock search time decreases. I would treat this as an implementation scalability result rather than a full proof of robustness under arbitrary heterogeneity. TakeawayDFNAS makes architecture search look like normal federated optimization:
sample one child model on each client; update weights and architecture parameters locally; average both on the server; derive the final architecture from the learned distribution.
The limitations are also clear. The search space is fixed to efficient CNN blocks, the final model is not always the smallest one, and the method does not add privacy protection beyond ordinary FL. Still, the paper is useful because it attacks the actual bottleneck of federated NAS: client memory and the cost of running search plus retraining as two separate jobs.

entry.title: DeepSeek-V2: Multi-Head Latent Attention and Economical MoE
entry.content:
DeepSeek-AI. DeepSeek-V2: A Strong, Economical, and Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Language Model.
Paper DeepSeek-V2 is not just a bigger MoE model. The paper is useful because it treats model architecture as an inference and training economics problem. The two central choices are Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA), which attacks the KV-cache bottleneck during decoding, and DeepSeekMoE, which keeps the activated compute small while keeping total capacity high. The main numbers are already enough to explain why the report mattered: 236B total parameters, 21B activated parameters per token, 8.1T pre-training tokens, a context window extended to 128K, 93.3% KV-cache reduction compared with DeepSeek 67B, and up to 5.76x maximum generation throughput in the reported setup.
Figure 1 is the paper’s compact claim: DeepSeek-V2 moves the MMLU frontier among open models while reducing the training cost, KV cache, and generation bottleneck relative to DeepSeek 67B. The architecture is therefore best read from the serving path backward: what has to be cached, communicated, routed, and trained? Model Snapshot
Item DeepSeek-V2 setting
Total parameters 236B
Activated parameters per token 21B
Pre-training tokens 8.1T
Default pre-training sequence length 4K
Extended context length 128K
Transformer layers 60
Hidden dimension 5120
Attention heads 128
Per-head dimension 128
KV compression dimension 512
Query compression dimension 1536
Decoupled RoPE dimension per head 64
MoE shared experts per layer 2
MoE routed experts per layer 160
Activated routed experts per token 6
Device-limited routing bound at most 3 devices
The dense baseline view of an LLM usually starts from parameter count. DeepSeek-V2 makes a different trade: keep only a small set of experts active, and make the attention cache much smaller. This is why the model can have 236B total parameters but still activate only 21B parameters per token.
The full architecture figure shows both pieces together. MLA changes the attention block by compressing the KV state into a latent vector. DeepSeekMoE changes the FFN block by mixing always-active shared experts with top-k routed experts. From MHA Cache To MLAThe paper first reviews standard multi-head attention. Let be the attention input at token position . Standard MHA projects it into query, key, and value vectors:
Those vectors are then split into heads:
For each head, causal attention is computed as:
The output projection then mixes heads:
The decoding problem is the cache. If every layer stores every key and value for every token, standard MHA needs:
elements per token, where is the number of layers. This grows with sequence length, batch size, and layer count, and it directly limits the maximum batch size for long-context serving.
The paper compares MHA, GQA, MQA, and MLA visually. GQA and MQA reduce the number of key/value groups. MLA is different: it jointly compresses keys and values into a latent vector and reconstructs what is needed for attention. The core MLA step is low-rank joint compression:
Here is the compressed latent vector for keys and values, and . During inference, the model caches , not the full per-head key/value tensors. Without RoPE complications, the cache would be:
The report also compresses queries for training memory:
This query compression is not what reduces inference KV cache, but it matters for training activation memory. The important inference-side trick is that can be absorbed into , and can be absorbed into , so the model does not have to materialize full keys and values in the same way as standard MHA. Decoupled RoPEThe main subtlety is Rotary Position Embedding. RoPE is position-sensitive for both keys and queries. If RoPE is directly applied to , then the up-projection is coupled with a position-dependent RoPE matrix and can no longer be cleanly absorbed into the query projection during inference. That would defeat the point of MLA, because the prefix keys would have to be recomputed. DeepSeek-V2 solves this by decoupling the RoPE-carrying dimensions from the compressed content dimensions:
Each head concatenates compressed content with the RoPE component:
Attention then becomes:
followed by:
Now the cache has to store both the latent KV vector and the decoupled RoPE key:
This is the formula I find most important in the paper. MLA is not merely “use fewer KV heads”; it changes the cached object. The cache is no longer the expanded per-head K/V state, but a smaller latent state plus a RoPE-specific key component.
Table 1 makes the comparison concrete. With DeepSeek-V2’s settings, MLA has a KV-cache size equal to GQA with only 2.25 groups while preserving stronger capability than MHA in the report’s ablation. DeepSeekMoEThe FFN side uses DeepSeekMoE. The two design ideas are finer-grained routed experts and a set of shared experts. The shared experts are always active and absorb common knowledge; the routed experts are selected per token and specialize. For FFN input , the output is:
The routed gate is top-k:
with affinity:
DeepSeek-V2 uses shared experts and routed experts per MoE layer, with activated routed experts per token. Because all FFNs except the first layer are replaced by MoE layers, this design dominates the model’s capacity and communication pattern. Routing BoundariesFine-grained experts improve specialization, but they also make communication expensive under expert parallelism. If the top-k selected experts are spread across many devices, each token triggers more cross-device communication. DeepSeek-V2 therefore uses device-limited routing. For each token, it first chooses at most devices whose resident experts have the highest affinity scores, then performs top-k expert selection only inside those devices. The paper uses . This is a practical systems constraint inserted into the model’s routing rule: the router is not free to pick an arbitrary global top-k if that choice makes communication too expensive. The paper also uses three auxiliary losses to prevent routing collapse and improve hardware balance. Expert-level balance:
where:
Device-level balance partitions routed experts into device groups :
with:
Communication balance penalizes uneven receive-side traffic:
with:
The actual coefficients are , , and . This is a place where the paper is very implementation-minded: load balance is not only a modeling regularizer; it is also an efficiency condition for expert-parallel training. Training And Long ContextDeepSeek-V2 uses AdamW with , , and weight decay . The maximum learning rate is , with warmup and step decay. The batch size increases from 2304 to 9216 during the first 225B tokens, and the model is trained on 8.1T tokens with a 4K sequence length. For long context, the paper applies YaRN after pre-training to extend the context window from 4K to 128K. Since the RoPE-carrying component is the decoupled shared key , YaRN is applied to that part. The paper uses scale , , , and a target maximum context length of 160K. The entropy scaling factor is described as:
The model is then trained for 1000 additional steps at sequence length 32K with a batch size of 576 sequences. Even though the extension training is done at 32K, the NIAH evaluation is reported up to 128K.
The NIAH figure is important because the paper’s long-context claim is not just a configuration value. The heatmap shows mostly high scores across document depths and context lengths up to 128K, with a few visible weak spots around the middle depths. Results On base model benchmarks, DeepSeek-V2 is compared against DeepSeek 67B, Qwen1.5 72B, Mixtral 8x22B, and LLaMA 3 70B. The interesting point is not that it wins every row. The interesting point is that it is an MoE model with 21B activated parameters per token competing against strong dense and MoE baselines while also reducing KV-cache cost.
The chat tables show a second axis: DeepSeek-V2-Chat and DeepSeek-V2-Chat-RL are evaluated against open-source and closed-source systems, including GPT-4 variants and Claude models. The paper’s own warning is worth remembering: some closed-source results may be underestimated due to limitations of the internal evaluation framework, so I would not over-read small differences. The broad trend is still useful: the architecture is not only a pre-training trick; the chat model is competitive after supervised fine-tuning and RL.
The appendix ablations are the most diagnostic part for MLA. The MQA/GQA/MHA comparison shows that simply reducing KV heads can hurt capability, while MLA keeps a much smaller cache and remains strong. The paper also compares small and large MoE models with MLA and MHA; the point is that MLA is not only a memory optimization but can also be accuracy-neutral or accuracy-positive in their setting.
The code evaluation plot shows DeepSeek-V2-Chat-RL near LLaMA3-70B-Chat and below stronger closed models on HumanEval and LiveCodeBench. I would read this figure as a boundary condition: V2’s architecture gives an efficient model family, but post-training and reasoning data still matter a lot for code and difficult reasoning. TakeawaysMy main takeaway from DeepSeek-V2 is that the paper puts cache design and expert communication into the model architecture itself. MLA reduces the object that must be cached during autoregressive decoding:
DeepSeekMoE reduces activated FFN compute while preserving large total capacity:
Those two choices attack different bottlenecks. MLA helps long-context and high-batch decoding by shrinking memory pressure. MoE helps scaling by separating total capacity from activated compute. Device-limited routing and balance losses then make the MoE trainable on actual hardware rather than just elegant on paper. The limitation is that V2 still relies on auxiliary load-balancing losses, token dropping during training, and a non-trivial hand-designed routing/communication stack. DeepSeek-V3 keeps the same direction but replaces some of this with auxiliary-loss-free balancing, FP8 training, DualPipe, and MTP, which makes V2 a useful bridge between efficient MoE architecture and full-stack LLM training systems.

entry.title: DeepSeek-V3 Technical Report
entry.content:
DeepSeek-AI. DeepSeek-V3 Technical Report.
Paper DeepSeek-V3 should be read as both a model report and a training-systems report. The model keeps the DeepSeek-V2 direction, namely MLA for efficient inference and DeepSeekMoE for economical sparse activation, but the important additions are not only architectural. The report also introduces auxiliary-loss-free MoE load balancing, a multi-token prediction objective, DualPipe pipeline parallelism, and a large-scale FP8 training framework. The headline numbers are unusually explicit: 671B total parameters, 37B activated parameters per token, 14.8T training tokens, 2.788M H800 GPU hours for the full training process, and a stated training cost of about USD 5.576M assuming USD 2 per H800 GPU hour. The paper’s core argument is that frontier-scale capability can come from a co-design of sparse architecture, routing, low-precision training, and communication scheduling.
The first benchmark figure is meant to establish the output side of the story: DeepSeek-V3 is competitive with strong open and closed models on standard benchmarks. The rest of the report explains how that result was made trainable and affordable. Model Snapshot
Item DeepSeek-V3 setting
Total parameters 671B
Activated parameters per token 37B
Pre-training tokens 14.8T
Transformer layers 61
Hidden dimension 7168
Attention MLA
Attention heads 128
Per-head dimension 128
KV compression dimension 512
Query compression dimension 1536
Decoupled RoPE dimension per head 64
FFN architecture DeepSeekMoE
MoE shared experts per layer 1
MoE routed experts per layer 256
Activated routed experts per token 8
Node-limited routing bound at most 4 nodes
MTP depth 1
Training precision FP8 mixed precision
Pipeline parallelism 16-way PP
Expert parallelism 64-way EP across 8 nodes
Data parallelism ZeRO-1 DP
Training cluster 2048 NVIDIA H800 GPUs
The cost table is one of the most cited parts of the report. Pre-training accounts for 2664K H800 GPU hours, context extension for 119K, and post-training for 5K, giving 2788K H800 GPU hours in total. The paper states that one trillion pre-training tokens require about 180K H800 GPU hours under their framework. Continuity From V2DeepSeek-V3 keeps the two structural ideas from DeepSeek-V2:
MLA reduces the decoding cache by storing a compressed latent KV representation plus a small decoupled RoPE key. DeepSeekMoE separates total capacity from activated compute through shared experts and routed experts.
The architecture diagram still has the V2 shape: MLA inside attention, DeepSeekMoE inside FFN. The changes are in the details: V3 uses more routed experts, fewer shared experts per MoE layer, sigmoid affinities with normalized selected gates, node-limited routing, and a different load-balancing strategy. The MLA cache equation from V2 remains the useful mental model:
For V3, , , and . The report does not present V3 as a new attention mechanism; it presents V3 as a larger-scale validation of the same attention design under a much stronger training stack. DeepSeekMoE In V3For the FFN input , DeepSeek-V3 uses the DeepSeekMoE form:
The paper differs from V2 in the affinity and selected-gate normalization. The affinity is:
The unnormalized selected gate is:
The selected gates are then normalized:
This makes V3’s gate slightly different from V2’s softmax affinity. The model has shared expert and routed experts per MoE layer, and activates routed experts for each token. Auxiliary-Loss-Free BalancingThe routing problem in MoE is not only “choose the best experts.” If the router collapses, some experts are undertrained. If routing is balanced poorly across devices, the training system slows down. V2 uses auxiliary losses for expert, device, and communication balance. V3 changes the main balancing mechanism. For each expert, V3 maintains a bias term . This bias is used only for top-k routing, not for the final FFN weight:
At the end of each training step, the expert load is measured over the whole batch. If expert is overloaded, is decreased by ; if it is underloaded, is increased by . The report uses for the first 14.3T tokens and freezes it at for the final 500B tokens. The key modeling choice is that the bias changes selection but does not directly change the expert output weight. The gate value multiplied with the FFN output still comes from the original affinity . This avoids pushing a large auxiliary balance loss into the main language-modeling objective. V3 still keeps a very small complementary sequence-wise loss to avoid extreme imbalance inside a single sequence:
The sequence-level load term is:
The normalized affinity and its sequence average are:
The balance factor is set to only . I read this as the paper’s compromise: batch-level routing is handled dynamically by bias updates, while the tiny sequence-level loss is only a guardrail.
The ablation table shows that auxiliary-loss-free balancing improves most metrics over a purely auxiliary-loss-based baseline at both small and large MoE scales. The strongest gains are visible in code/math style rows such as HumanEval, GSM8K, and MATH for the large MoE setting.
The expert-load figure is also useful because it shows a qualitative difference: auxiliary-loss-free routing allows more domain-specific expert specialization than the auxiliary-loss-based baseline. The point is not simply balanced load; the router can still specialize when the balancing pressure is not injected as a large optimization loss. Node-Limited RoutingDeepSeek-V3 uses node-limited routing, analogous to V2’s device-limited routing. Experts are distributed across 64 GPUs belonging to 8 nodes, and each token is constrained to be sent to at most 4 nodes. This keeps cross-node all-to-all communication bounded. This is an important modeling-system boundary. If the best top-k experts for a token are spread across too many nodes, a naive router would maximize local affinity but hurt global throughput. V3’s router therefore optimizes inside a communication budget. Multi-Token PredictionV3 adds Multi-Token Prediction (MTP). The stated purpose is not only speculative decoding; the report frames it as a training objective that densifies supervision and may encourage the model to plan representations for future tokens.
The implementation uses sequential MTP modules. In the final V3 model, , so each token predicts one additional future token beyond the next-token objective. The paper’s notation is dense; below I use the same structure with slightly cleaned indexing. For the -th MTP depth, the module combines the representation from the previous depth with the embedding of a future token:
The resulting sequence is passed through an MTP Transformer block:
The shared output head predicts the future token distribution:
For each prediction depth, the cross-entropy loss is:
The total MTP loss is:
For V3, the paper sets for the first 10T tokens and for the remaining 4.8T tokens. The MTP modules can be discarded during normal inference, so the main model keeps the same standalone inference shape. They can also be repurposed for speculative decoding, but the report’s primary claim is training improvement.
The MTP ablation is convincing in the practical sense: inference activated parameters are unchanged, but most benchmark rows improve. HumanEval improves from 44.5 to 53.7 in the large MoE ablation, which is large enough to notice even if one does not treat every row as equally stable. DualPipeSparse MoE training creates a communication problem. Cross-node expert parallelism introduces all-to-all dispatch and combine operations. The report states that DeepSeek-V3’s cross-node expert-parallel communication creates an inefficient computation-to-communication ratio of roughly 1:1 unless it is aggressively overlapped. DualPipe is their pipeline schedule for overlapping forward and backward computation with communication. Each chunk is decomposed into attention, all-to-all dispatch, MLP, all-to-all combine, and pipeline communication. Backward computation is further split into backward-for-input and backward-for-weights pieces, following the ZeroBubble idea.
The schedule is bidirectional: micro-batches are fed from both ends of the pipeline. The visual point is that green, yellow, and blue compute regions are interleaved with communication so that all-to-all and pipeline communication can be hidden behind useful work. The paper summarizes pipeline bubble formulas as:
Here is the forward chunk time, is the full backward chunk time, is the backward-for-weights chunk time, and denotes the paper’s F&B term: the time for mutually overlapped forward and backward chunks. The tradeoff is parameter memory: DualPipe keeps two parameter copies, while activation memory is listed as , compared with for 1F1B and ZB1P. The report argues this is acceptable because the large expert-parallel size reduces per-rank parameter pressure. For me, this is one of the paper’s main messages. DeepSeekMoE makes the model economical only if the training system can hide the communication that MoE introduces. DualPipe is part of the architecture story because it makes fine-grained experts across nodes practical. FP8 TrainingDeepSeek-V3’s training stack uses FP8 for most compute-heavy GEMMs while retaining higher precision for sensitive components. This is not a blanket “train everything in FP8” recipe.
