The framework runs the Linear operator’s Fprop, Dgrad, and Wgrad GEMMs in FP8. Outputs are BF16 or FP32, and the optimizer-facing state keeps higher precision where needed. The report keeps embeddings, output head, MoE gating, normalization, and attention operators in higher precision. Master weights, weight gradients, and optimizer states are also retained in higher precision, with optimizer moments tracked in BF16. The most important low-precision issue is outliers. A tensor-wise FP8 scale can be dominated by a few large values, wasting resolution for the majority of elements. V3 uses fine-grained scaling:
Activations are grouped and scaled on a tile basis. Weights are grouped and scaled on a block basis.
Operationally, the quantization can be read as a per-group scaling rule. For a group , with FP8 maximum representable magnitude , the scale is:
The quantized value and dequantized approximation are:
This formula is my operational restatement of the report’s scaling description, not a separately numbered equation in the paper. The important detail is that the group is small: a per-token activation tile or a weight block, not the whole tensor. The report also addresses accumulation precision. It observes that H800 FP8 GEMM accumulation in Tensor Cores effectively retains only about 14 bits, which can produce large errors when the inner dimension is large. Their solution periodically promotes partial results to CUDA Cores for FP32 accumulation. They set the promotion interval to:
elements, corresponding to 4 WGMMAs. This aligns with the fine-grained scaling factors along the GEMM inner dimension. Finally, V3 uses E4M3 for all tensors rather than a hybrid E4M3/E5M2 recipe. The paper attributes the feasibility of this to tile/block-wise fine-grained quantization, which recovers enough dynamic range locally.
The appendix compares FP8 and BF16 training curves at about 16B and 230B MoE scales. The report states that relative loss error remains below 0.25% with high-precision accumulation and fine-grained quantization. Training HyperparametersThe final model is trained with AdamW, , , and weight decay . The pre-training sequence length is 4K. The learning rate schedule is:
Phase Learning rate
Warmup over first 2K steps
Constant until 10T tokens
Cosine decay over 4.3T tokens
First 333B tokens of final 500B
Last 167B tokens
The batch size increases from 3072 to 15360 during the first 469B tokens, then stays at 15360. For node-limited routing, each token is sent to at most 4 nodes. For balancing, the routing-bias update speed is for the first 14.3T tokens and for the final 500B tokens. The sequence-wise balancing coefficient is . These values make the report feel closer to a training recipe than a pure architecture paper. The paper is explicit about the points where stability was engineered: routing bias, small sequence-level loss, LR staging, FP8 precision exceptions, and communication overlap. Long ContextLike V2, V3 extends context with YaRN. The model starts from a 4K pre-training sequence length and then uses two context-extension stages: 32K and 128K. The YaRN configuration remains consistent with V2, with scale , , , and scaling factor:
The NIAH plot is very clean: the heatmap is almost entirely high-score across depths and context lengths up to 128K. This matters because V3 uses MLA with decoupled RoPE; the long-context extension has to work through the RoPE-carrying component rather than a conventional full key representation. Base Model Results The base model table compares DeepSeek-V3 against DeepSeek-V2, Qwen2.5 72B, and LLaMA-3.1 405B. I would read the table by task family rather than by single rows. V3 is especially strong on code and math rows, and it competes with or beats the large dense baseline while activating only 37B parameters per token. The comparison is also an efficiency statement. A 671B total-parameter MoE is not directly comparable to a 405B dense model by total parameters alone. The paper’s preferred lens is activated parameters, training cost, and achieved accuracy. Chat And Post-Training The chat comparison places DeepSeek-V3 against DeepSeek-V2 variants, Qwen2.5, LLaMA-3.1, Claude-3.5-Sonnet, GPT-4o-0513, and other models. Again, small row-wise differences should not be overinterpreted, but the broad result is that V3 becomes competitive with strong frontier chat systems while remaining an open-weight MoE model in the paper’s framing.
The RewardBench table and distillation table connect V3 to the later R1-style line. The report describes distillation from DeepSeek-R1 into V3 during post-training. This is worth separating from the base model story: some final chat/reasoning behavior is not only from architecture and pre-training, but also from post-training data, reward modeling, and distillation. What Changed From V2The shortest useful comparison is:
Area DeepSeek-V2 DeepSeek-V3
Total parameters 236B 671B
Activated parameters 21B 37B
Training tokens 8.1T 14.8T
MoE experts per layer 2 shared, 160 routed 1 shared, 256 routed
Routed experts per token 6 8
Routing communication bound at most 3 devices at most 4 nodes
Load balancing auxiliary losses routing-bias balancing plus tiny sequence loss
Extra objective none MTP
Training precision mainly BF16-style large-scale training FP8 mixed precision
Pipeline system HAI-LLM with overlap optimizations DualPipe plus cross-node all-to-all kernels
V2 proves that MLA and DeepSeekMoE are a strong efficiency pair. V3 makes the training stack mature enough to scale the same pair to a much larger model. TakeawaysMy main takeaway is that DeepSeek-V3 is a systems co-design paper disguised as a model technical report. The model formula alone does not explain the result. The result comes from several constraints being solved together:
MLA reduces decoding memory:
DeepSeekMoE reduces activated compute:
Auxiliary-loss-free balancing keeps batch-level expert load controlled without making a large auxiliary loss fight the language-modeling objective.
MTP adds denser prediction supervision without increasing standalone inference cost, because the auxiliary modules can be discarded.
DualPipe and custom communication kernels hide the all-to-all cost introduced by fine-grained cross-node experts.
FP8 training reduces compute and memory cost, but only after the report adds fine-grained scaling, high-precision accumulation, and precision exceptions for sensitive modules.
The paper is valuable because it does not treat these as independent optimizations. MLA changes what is cached. MoE changes what is computed. Routing changes what is communicated. DualPipe changes when communication happens. FP8 changes what precision the training system can afford. MTP changes how much supervision each token contributes. DeepSeek-V3 is the combination, not any single component.

entry.title: DistServe: Disaggregated LLM Serving
entry.content:
Zhong et al. DistServe: Disaggregating Prefill and Decoding for Goodput-optimized Large Language Model Serving. 2024.
Paper / Code DistServe is a systems paper about taking the prefill/decode split seriously. Many LLM serving engines already know that the two phases behave differently, but they still colocate them on the same worker pool. DistServe asks what happens if prefill and decoding are assigned to different GPU groups and optimized with separate parallelism plans. The paper’s metric is goodput, not raw token throughput. A request only counts if it satisfies both latency constraints. goodput = SLO-satisfying requests / time
For LLM serving, the two SLOs are usually time to first token (TTFT) and time per output token (TPOT). The Interference Problem Figure 1 is the motivating result. On a 13B model with input length 512 and output length 64, colocated serving reaches about 1.6 requests/s per A100 GPU under a 90% SLO attainment target. If the two phases are measured separately, prefill-only can support about 5.6 requests/s and decode-only about 10 requests/s. That gap is the opportunity. The shared worker pool is not only under-optimized; it couples two phases with different bottlenecks and different latency targets.
Chunked prefill helps but does not remove the problem. Adding a long prefill job to a decode batch delays decode steps, increasing TPOT. Adding decode jobs to prefill increases prefill execution time, hurting TTFT. The paper’s point is that better batching still leaves a fundamental resource-coupling issue. Phase Behavior The two phases stress hardware differently:
Phase Computation shape Main pressure SLO link
Prefill many prompt tokens processed together compute and prompt-length throughput TTFT
Decode one new token per active sequence per step memory bandwidth, KV access, queueing TPOT
Prefill benefits from enough parallelism to reduce first-token latency. Decode benefits from batching many active sequences, but each decode step is small and repeated. A single colocated plan has to compromise between these shapes.
Disaggregation lets the system choose different GPU allocation and model-parallel settings for each phase. The tradeoff is that the KV cache produced by prefill must move to the decode side. That KV transfer is the main skepticism point for this paper. The architecture only wins when the benefit from eliminating interference is larger than the communication and orchestration overhead. DistServe Runtime At runtime, DistServe has a centralized controller. A request is sent to a prefill instance, which computes the first token and KV cache. Then the request is assigned to a decode instance, which fetches the KV cache and continues autoregressive generation. The implementation details that matter:
prefill and decode instances can use different parallelism settings; the placement algorithm accounts for inter-node bandwidth; the controller uses queue lengths to dispatch work; KV cache transfer is pull-based, so decode instances fetch cache when they are ready instead of being flooded by prefill workers; workload profiling can trigger replanning when input length, output length, or arrival rate shifts.
This is more than “put prefill on one GPU and decode on another.” The resource plan is a joint choice over phase split, parallelism, replication, and placement. End-to-End Results The chatbot workload uses OPT-13B, OPT-66B, and OPT-175B on ShareGPT. The paper reports that DistServe sustains 2.0x to 4.6x higher request rate than vLLM and 1.6x to 7.4x higher request rate than DeepSpeed-MII under the 90% SLO attainment target. The second row of the figure varies the SLO scale. DistServe handles 1.8x to 3.2x tighter SLOs than vLLM and 1.7x to 1.8x tighter SLOs than DeepSpeed-MII on the chatbot setting. The result makes sense: chat has a strong TPOT component. Colocated systems may satisfy TTFT for many requests but fail because decode steps get delayed by prefill interference.
The code completion and summarization tasks stress different sides of the system:
Code completion on OPT-66B demands low TTFT. DistServe reports 5.7x higher request rate than vLLM and 1.6x higher than DeepSpeed-MII. Summarization on OPT-66B uses long inputs and a looser TTFT SLO, so TPOT becomes more important. DistServe reports 4.3x higher request rate and 12.6x tighter SLO than vLLM, and 1.8x higher request rate and 2.6x tighter SLO than DeepSpeed-MII.
The same figure also includes the latency breakdown. For OPT-175B on ShareGPT, KV transmission is reported as less than 0.1% of total latency, and over 95% of requests have transfer delay below 30 ms in the testbed. That does not mean transfer is always free, but it supports the paper’s claim that bandwidth-aware placement can keep the cost small. Ablation And Planner Cost The ablations separate three ideas:
disaggregate the phases; choose phase-specific parallelism and resource allocation; use bandwidth-aware placement.
The paper argues that all three are needed for high goodput. A naive split can still lose if the KV path is bad or if one phase is over-provisioned while the other queues. The placement algorithm is also designed to be cheap enough for replanning. The paper reports that the largest setting in its evaluation can be solved in under 1.3 minutes, while normal workload shifts happen at a much slower time scale. What I Would Measure FirstBefore implementing this design in another serving stack, I would measure four things separately:
Measurement Why it matters
Prefill execution time vs prompt length estimates TTFT pressure and prefill GPU allocation
Decode step time vs active batch size estimates TPOT pressure and decode batching capacity
KV cache size and transfer time decides whether disaggregation overhead is acceptable
SLO attainment under load prevents raw throughput from hiding missed deadlines
If prefill and decode saturate the same resource in the same way, disaggregation is less compelling. If they bottleneck differently, DistServe’s design gives the scheduler more degrees of freedom. TakeawayDistServe is the architectural counterpart to continuous batching and chunked prefill. Instead of only improving scheduling inside a colocated worker, it changes the worker layout so prefill and decode can be scaled independently. The main win is goodput under latency constraints. The main risks are operational: KV transfer, bandwidth-aware placement, failure coupling between phase instances, and workload drift. I read the paper as a strong argument that production LLM serving should evaluate TTFT and TPOT separately before treating a single token/s number as the capacity metric.

entry.title: DrNAS: Dirichlet Neural Architecture Search
entry.content:
Chen, Wang, Cheng, Tang, and Hsieh. DrNAS: Dirichlet Neural Architecture Search. ICLR 2021.
Paper DrNAS targets the failure mode that makes DARTS-style NAS hard to trust: the search can collapse early into shallow or skip-heavy architectures, and the final cell can be very sensitive to seed, search space, and training length. The paper’s idea is to treat architecture mixing weights as random variables on the probability simplex. Instead of learning one deterministic softmax vector, DrNAS samples operation weights from a Dirichlet distribution and regularizes that distribution around a stable anchor. From Softmax Weights To Dirichlet SamplesDARTS relaxes a discrete edge choice into a deterministic mixture: mixed_op(x) = sum over candidate ops of theta_op * op(x)
DrNAS keeps the mixture view but makes the mixing vector stochastic: theta ~ Dirichlet(beta)
The concentration parameter beta controls how samples behave. A broad distribution keeps exploration alive; a concentrated distribution moves toward confident operation selection. The final discrete architecture is derived from the Dirichlet mean.
Figure 1 shows the range of accuracies from sampled architectures on NAS-Bench-201. The solid line is the architecture selected by the Dirichlet mean. This is a useful diagnostic: the method is not only trying to find one good point, but to keep the architecture distribution well behaved during search. Anchor RegularizationA raw Dirichlet search can still become unstable because the variance of the distribution is hard to control. DrNAS adds an anchor regularizer that keeps the learned concentration parameter near a symmetric Dirichlet anchor: architecture loss = validation loss(w, beta) + lambda * distance(beta, beta_anchor)
The paper also connects this regularization to the Hessian of the validation loss with respect to the architecture parameters. The practical reading is simple: DrNAS tries to avoid the sharp, unstable search trajectory that often appears in DARTS. The gradients still need to pass through samples from a Dirichlet distribution. Since the ordinary reparameterization trick does not directly apply, the paper uses pathwise derivative estimators for Dirichlet samples. Progressive LearningDrNAS also introduces a progressive architecture learning scheme:
start with a cheaper partial-channel search; gradually increase the channel fraction through network transformation; progressively prune weak candidate operations; keep memory usage controlled while searching on larger tasks.
This is important because a probabilistic search method is not useful if it only works on a tiny proxy cell. The progressive schedule is the bridge from NAS-Bench/CIFAR experiments to ImageNet-scale search.
The discovered normal and reduction cells still look like the usual cell-based NAS artifacts. DrNAS is not replacing the DARTS search space. It is changing the optimization dynamics inside that search space. CIFAR-10 Results On CIFAR-10, the paper reports:
Method Test error Params Search cost
DARTS second-order 2.76 +/- 0.09% 3.3M 1.0 GPU day
PC-DARTS 2.57 +/- 0.07% 3.6M 0.1 GPU day
DrNAS without progressive learning 2.54 +/- 0.03% 4.0M 0.4 GPU day
DrNAS 2.46 +/- 0.03% 4.1M 0.6 GPU day
The interesting part is not just the 2.46% number. DrNAS improves while staying in the gradient-based NAS family, which makes the result more comparable to DARTS, PC-DARTS, and SDARTS than to very large RL/evolution searches. ImageNet Mobile Setting On ImageNet mobile classification, DrNAS reports 23.7% top-1 error and 7.1% top-5 error with 5.7M parameters and 4.6 GPU days of search. The non-progressive ImageNet version reports 24.2% / 7.3% with 5.2M parameters. That improvement is small but meaningful in this comparison group. It supports the claim that progressive learning is not only a memory trick; it also improves the final searched architecture. NAS-Bench-201 NAS-Bench-201 is useful because it reduces the ambiguity of retraining and random search-space quirks. In this table, DrNAS reaches strong accuracy on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet16-120. The reported CIFAR-10 test accuracy is 94.36%, with validation accuracy 91.55%. I usually trust this kind of benchmark more for stability claims than for absolute model quality. It tests whether the search method consistently selects good architectures inside a controlled finite space. Regularizer Sensitivity The anchor regularizer table is a good detail. Without the regularizer, the reported NAS-Bench-201 CIFAR-10 accuracy is 93.78%. A range of regularizer strengths reaches 94.36%, while overly large values fall back to 93.76%. This suggests the method is not tuned to one exact lambda, but the regularizer is still doing real work. Too little regularization leaves the distribution unstable; too much prevents useful concentration. TakeawayDrNAS should be read as a stabilization paper for differentiable NAS:
DARTS uses deterministic softmax architecture weights. DrNAS samples architecture weights from a Dirichlet distribution. The anchor regularizer controls the architecture distribution and helps avoid sharp search dynamics. Progressive learning makes the method practical beyond tiny proxy settings.
The limitation is that the search space is still the familiar cell-based NAS space. DrNAS improves how the architecture parameters are optimized; it does not remove the assumptions baked into the candidate operations and cell topology. That is still useful, because instability is one of the main reasons DARTS-style results are hard to reproduce.

entry.title: ELECTRA: Pre-training Text Encoders as Discriminators Rather Than Generators
entry.content:
Paper ELECTRA is a pre-training paper about signal density. BERT’s masked language modeling objective only predicts a small subset of positions, usually 15% of tokens. The other positions provide context, but they do not directly produce prediction loss. ELECTRA changes the task. A small generator first replaces some tokens. Then a discriminator reads the corrupted sequence and predicts, for every token position, whether that token is original or replaced. The downstream model is the discriminator, not the generator. Why MLM Is Wasteful Figure cropped from the paper PDF: replaced token detection reaches stronger validation accuracy than MLM at the same compute budget. Masked language modeling is simple and effective, but it spends most of its forward pass on positions that are not prediction targets. If 15% of tokens are masked, the loss is sparse. ELECTRA’s replaced token detection (RTD) objective gives every position a binary classification target. That does not mean every position is equally informative. Many tokens are easy negatives or easy positives. But the model receives supervision across the full sequence, so the training signal per example is much denser than MLM. The paper’s compute-efficiency curve is the main motivation. ELECTRA is not proposing a new Transformer encoder architecture. It is changing the pre-training problem so the same kind of encoder can learn more from fewer FLOPs. Generator And Discriminator ELECTRA’s pre-training pipeline: a small generator fills masked positions, and the discriminator predicts which tokens were replaced. The generator is trained with a standard MLM loss. Given an input sequence with some positions masked, it predicts distributions over the original tokens at those masked positions: $$\mathcal{L}{\text{MLM}} =-\mathbb{E}\left[\sum{i \in m} \log p_G(x_i \mid x^{\text{masked}})\right].$$ Then ELECTRA samples replacements from the generator. The corrupted sequence is fed to the discriminator, which predicts whether each observed token is the true original token: $$\mathcal{L}_{\text{RTD}} =-\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_t\mathbf{1}(x_t = x_t^{\text{corrupt}})\log D(x^{\text{corrupt}}, t)
\mathbf{1}(x_t \ne x_t^{\text{corrupt}})\log(1 - D(x^{\text{corrupt}}, t))\right].$$
The discriminator is the model kept for downstream tasks. The generator is a training tool. This makes ELECTRA different from a GAN in the usual unstable minimax sense. The generator is not trained to fool the discriminator through discriminator gradients. It is trained as an MLM, and its sampled outputs create realistic negative examples. Generator Size Generator-size and training-algorithm ablations from the paper: a smaller generator is usually the best tradeoff. The generator must be good enough to create plausible corruptions, but not so large that it wastes compute or makes the task too hard. If the generator is too weak, the discriminator learns shallow cues. If the generator is too strong, the corruption distribution becomes expensive and the replaced tokens can be hard to distinguish. The paper’s practical answer is to use a generator that is substantially smaller than the discriminator. This gives the discriminator realistic negatives while keeping most of the training compute focused on the model that will actually be fine-tuned later. There is also a subtle labeling detail. If the generator samples the original token, that position is labeled “original”, not “replaced”. The discriminator is judging the final observed token, not whether the position was selected for masking. Small-Model Results Small-model GLUE comparison from the paper PDF: ELECTRA-Small gets strong accuracy with much lower training compute. Table 1 is the result that makes ELECTRA feel practical. ELECTRA-Small is much cheaper to train than BERT-style baselines and still reaches competitive GLUE performance. This is the strongest evidence for the sample-efficiency claim. The result is not only about model size. It is about objective efficiency. The discriminator learns from every token position, so the same amount of text can produce more supervised decisions than MLM pre-training. For resource-constrained encoder pre-training, this is the core takeaway: if the architecture is fixed and compute is limited, changing the pre-training objective can be as important as scaling the model. Large-Model Results Large-model GLUE dev and test comparisons from the paper: ELECTRA remains competitive when scaled. The large-model tables show that ELECTRA is not only a small-model trick. It scales to base and large settings and remains competitive with strong BERT/RoBERTa-style encoders. The comparison is not perfectly apples-to-apples because large pre-training recipes differ in data, steps, batch size, and tuning tricks. Still, the pattern is consistent: dense RTD supervision gives ELECTRA a strong compute-performance tradeoff. I read this as a pre-training-objective result rather than an architecture result. ELECTRA keeps the Transformer encoder interface that makes BERT convenient, but changes how the encoder is taught before fine-tuning. QA Results SQuAD results from the paper: ELECTRA also transfers to extractive question answering. SQuAD is useful because it tests token-level span prediction instead of sentence-pair classification. ELECTRA’s gains transfer there too, which suggests the discriminator objective is learning generally useful contextual representations rather than only improving GLUE-style classification. The key point is that the discriminator must understand whether each token is plausible in context. That is close to the kind of contextual token understanding needed for span extraction. Compute And Model Scale Compute-efficiency and model-size ablations from the paper: ELECTRA’s advantage is especially visible for smaller models and limited compute. The model-size ablation is a good practical warning. ELECTRA’s relative gains are especially attractive in low-compute settings, but the advantage is not a free replacement for scale. As models and training budgets grow, recipe details matter more. Still, the central idea aged well: do not waste pre-training examples if a denser objective can use them. Many later encoder and generator-discriminator style methods reuse this logic in different forms. Reading NotesELECTRA’s biggest design win is that it removes the train-test mismatch caused by [MASK] tokens. The discriminator sees normal-looking text with replaced words, not a sequence full of artificial mask symbols. Fine-tuning also uses normal text. The main cost is extra machinery. You need a generator, corruption sampling, and a discriminator loss. The generator/discriminator size ratio becomes a real hyperparameter. But that complexity is modest compared with the compute saved when pre-training encoders under a fixed budget. My takeaway: ELECTRA is a clean example of improving pre-training by changing where the supervision lands. BERT asks the model to recover a few hidden tokens. ELECTRA asks it to inspect every token and decide whether it belongs. That makes the same text work harder.

entry.title: EAGLE: Speculative Sampling Requires Rethinking Feature Uncertainty
entry.content:
Paper EAGLE is a speculative decoding paper, but the interesting part is not just “use a smaller model to draft tokens.” Its main claim is more specific: for an autoregressive LLM, the feature right before the LM head is a better draft target than the next token itself. The target model is still the model being sampled. EAGLE only proposes candidate continuations, and the target LLM verifies them with the usual speculative sampling correction. That matters because speedups are only useful if the decoding distribution is preserved. Motivation Figure cropped from the paper PDF: EAGLE improves inference latency on MT-bench across Vicuna and LLaMA2-Chat models under greedy decoding. Speculative decoding tries to reduce the number of expensive target-model forward passes. A draft model proposes several future tokens, then the target model checks them in parallel. If enough draft tokens are accepted, one target forward pass can advance the sequence by more than one token. The usual failure mode is draft quality. A cheap draft model can be fast, but if its proposal distribution is too different from the target model, many drafted tokens are rejected. Then the target model still has to run often, and the acceleration disappears. EAGLE attacks this from inside the target model. Instead of training a draft model to imitate final token probabilities directly, it trains a lightweight autoregressive head to predict the target LLM’s second-to-top-layer feature. The frozen target LM head then converts that feature into token logits. This is a useful framing: token IDs are discrete and jumpy, while high-level hidden features are continuous and usually smoother. If the draft model can predict the next feature well, it can reuse the target model’s own output head rather than learning a separate vocabulary distribution from scratch. Feature Uncertainty The paper’s uncertainty example: the next hidden feature depends on which token was sampled, not only on the previous feature. The paper’s key observation is that feature prediction is ambiguous if the draft model only sees previous features. Suppose two tokens are both plausible under the same distribution. Sampling one token or the other changes the next model state. A feature predictor that does not know which token was sampled is being asked to predict a mixture of futures. That is the “feature uncertainty” in the title. The future feature is not a deterministic function of the old feature alone. It is conditioned on the sampled token:
EAGLE therefore feeds the draft model a shifted token sequence. In plain terms, after a token is sampled, that token is made visible to the feature predictor before it predicts the next feature. This removes a large part of the multi-modal target and makes feature-level autoregression more stable. Draft Model EAGLE’s pipeline: a lightweight draft model predicts features, the frozen LM head produces token candidates, and tree attention lets the method draft multiple branches. The draft model is trained on hidden features extracted from the target LLM. It takes target-model features plus shifted tokens as input and predicts the next second-to-top-layer feature. The loss is applied in feature space, while the target LM head maps predicted features into token logits during generation. This design has two consequences:
The draft model is tied to the target LLM’s representation space. The generated token distribution still passes through the target LLM’s LM head. The final acceptance step still uses the target model, so the accelerated sampler does not become a different model.
The second point is easy to miss. EAGLE is not just a tiny language model trained on the same text. It is a dynamics model over the target LLM’s internal features. Greedy And Non-Greedy Decoding Non-greedy decoding results from the paper: EAGLE keeps useful speedup when sampling is enabled. Greedy decoding is the cleanest case for acceleration because each step has one next token. Sampling is harder. Once token choice is stochastic, the draft model must cope with multiple possible futures, and the acceptance path can branch. EAGLE’s shifted-token input is especially important here. It tells the draft model which branch was actually taken before the next feature is predicted. That makes the method better matched to non-greedy generation than a feature predictor that only sees the previous hidden state. The paper also uses tree-structured drafting. Instead of drafting a single chain only, EAGLE can draft a candidate tree and let the target model verify candidates efficiently. This increases the chance that verification accepts a useful continuation even when sampling produces multiple likely branches. Main Results Main result tables from the paper: speedup, average acceptance length, and generation-speed comparisons across model families and tasks. The reported speedups are strongest when the target model is large and the draft overhead is small relative to a target forward pass. This is the natural regime for speculative decoding: the method is most attractive when target inference is expensive. The tables also show why acceptance length matters. A headline speedup is not just a property of the draft model’s raw latency. It depends on how many drafted tokens survive target verification. Better feature prediction increases the average accepted length, which then reduces the number of target passes needed per generated token. Ablations Input ablation from the paper: using both features and shifted tokens gives the strongest draft behavior. The ablation is one of the most useful figures in the paper. A token-only draft loses the representational advantage of feature prediction. A feature-only draft still suffers from uncertainty because it does not know which sampled token led to the current state. The combination of feature plus shifted token is the point. This is also the best mental model for EAGLE:
Predict in a smoother internal space. Condition on the actual sampled token to avoid ambiguous futures. Use the target LM head and target verification to preserve the original sampler.
Verification Algorithm Algorithm excerpt from the paper PDF: multi-round speculative sampling still performs acceptance and correction through the target model. The verification step is what separates speculative decoding from approximate decoding. The draft model is allowed to be wrong. When it is wrong, the target model corrects the sample according to the speculative sampling rule. That makes EAGLE a serving optimization rather than a model replacement. You pay extra engineering complexity for lower latency, but the semantic contract remains: samples should follow the target LLM distribution. Reading NotesEAGLE is most compelling when the serving stack can access target-model internals. If the target LLM is only available through a black-box API, feature-level drafting is not practical. It also requires training and maintaining a draft model for the target model’s hidden representation. The paper’s useful contribution is the uncertainty argument. Speculative decoding papers often focus on draft-model size or tree width, but EAGLE points out that the draft target itself matters. Token prediction, feature prediction, and feature prediction with shifted tokens are different learning problems. My takeaway: EAGLE works because it treats decoding as short-horizon state extrapolation inside the target model. It is not just faster guessing. It is a model-aware draft that uses the target LLM’s own feature geometry, output head, and verifier.

entry.title: EDD: Efficient Differentiable DNN Architecture and Implementation Co-search
entry.content:
Paper EDD is a useful paper to read after ProxylessNAS and Single-Path NAS. The common hardware-aware NAS recipe is:
Define an architecture search space. Build or measure a latency model on the target hardware. Add latency into the architecture-search objective.
EDD asks for one more step: what if the hardware implementation is not fixed during NAS? For a GPU this may mean precision and measured kernel latency. For an FPGA it may mean quantization, parallel factors, resource sharing, and whether the accelerator is recursive or pipelined. The paper’s main point is to put these implementation variables into the same differentiable search loop as the DNN architecture variables. MotivationHardware-aware NAS improves over pure FLOPs-aware search, but it often assumes a fixed implementation. That is a strong assumption. A model can look good under one implementation schedule and become less attractive after quantization, FPGA resource allocation, or pipeline structure changes. EDD describes the gap as:
Existing hardware-aware NAS searches architecture variables , while implementation variables are fixed. EDD searches together.
The distinction is especially important for FPGA. If the accelerator shares one IP across many layers, the objective is closer to end-to-end latency with resource sharing. If every layer has its own pipelined accelerator, the objective is closer to throughput and resource budgeting across all blocks. These two deployment modes should not necessarily produce the same network. ContributionThe paper contributes a co-search formulation rather than just another MobileNet-like architecture:
Fuse DNN architecture variables and hardware implementation variables into one differentiable search space. Use Gumbel-Softmax to sample both operation choices and quantization choices. Formulate performance and resource terms differently for GPU, recursive FPGA, and pipelined FPGA targets. Search three EDD-Net models within 12 GPU-hours on a P100 GPU. Report similar ImageNet accuracy to prior hardware-aware NAS models, with 1.40x lower GPU latency than Proxyless-GPU and 1.45x higher FPGA throughput than DNNBuilder.
The important engineering idea is not that EDD invents a new operator. It still works inside an MBConv-style search space. The useful part is that the implementation knobs can push the architecture search while the architecture is still being selected. MethodologyCo-search objectiveThe high-level objective combines accuracy loss, performance loss, and a resource penalty:
Here:
is the DNN architecture search space. is the implementation search space. can represent latency, throughput-related loss, energy, or model complexity. is the estimated hardware resource usage. is the target device’s resource upper bound.
The exponential resource penalty is a practical guardrail: when the design exceeds the device budget, the objective becomes much worse. This is closer to FPGA design than ordinary NAS, because a slightly larger model is not merely slower; it may not fit the device at all.
The figure is the paper’s core picture. Blue blocks are architecture search, red blocks are implementation search. EDD connects them before the final performance/resource loss is computed. Architecture variablesThe searched network is made of blocks. Each block has candidate operations:
In the experiments, each candidate is an MBConv-style block. The search choices are:
kernel size in expansion ratio in
So each searchable block has candidates. The architecture sampling parameters form , with one set of parameters for each block and candidate operation. Instead of activating all paths, EDD uses Gumbel-Softmax to sample one operation during forward propagation. This is similar in spirit to other efficient differentiable NAS methods: keep the search differentiable, but avoid paying the full multi-path activation cost every minibatch. Implementation variablesFor each operation , EDD also defines implementation variables . The most general one is quantization. The quantization choices are represented by another set of Gumbel-Softmax parameters:
where is the number of candidate bit-widths.
Given quantization sampling parameters, the expected performance and resource of one operation are:
Then the block-level expectation is taken over operation choices:
This two-level expectation is the cleanest part of the formulation:
chooses which operator a block uses. chooses how that operator is quantized. Device-specific formulas define what performance and resource mean.
Device-specific performance lossEDD changes the last step depending on the hardware target. For end-to-end latency, the performance loss is the sum of block latencies:
For throughput on a pipelined accelerator, the bottleneck is the slowest pipeline stage. Since max is not differentiable, the paper uses LogSumExp as a smooth maximum:
Resource usage also has two cases:
Without sharing, sum resources across blocks. With sharing, count a shared IP once when at least one selected block uses it.
The resource-sharing case is important for recursive FPGA accelerators. The paper uses a differentiable approximation with tanh to avoid repeatedly counting the same shared operation resource. GPU and FPGA detailsFor GPU, the target metric is batch-1 latency. The paper uses measured latency for candidate operations under supported precisions. At the time of the paper, TensorRT support limited the GPU precision choices to 8-bit integer and 16-/32-bit floating point. Mixed precision inference was also not treated as generally supported, so the searched GPU model uses one precision choice across the whole DNN. For FPGA, the implementation variables are richer. The paper models:
operation latency under a selected bit-width DSP usage as the main resource term parallel factors, expressed as powers of two recursive accelerator resource sharing pipelined accelerator throughput
The FPGA quantization choices used in search are 4-/8-/16-bit weights with 16-bit activations. For the recursive FPGA case, EDD optimizes end-to-end latency with shared IP resources. For the pipelined FPGA case, it optimizes throughput with a resource budget across pipeline stages. Search loopThe optimization follows a bilevel differentiable NAS loop:
Fix , , and ; update DNN weights on the training set. Fix ; update , , and by descending the co-search objective on the validation set. Repeat until convergence or a fixed epoch budget.
In the experiments, the search runs for 50 epochs on a randomly sampled 100-class subset of ImageNet. The final searched models are then trained from scratch on full ImageNet with 1000 classes. The paper reports each EDD-Net is produced within a 12-hour search on one P100 GPU. ResultsThe paper searches three models:
EDD-Net-1: low-latency GPU target. EDD-Net-2: recursive FPGA accelerator target. EDD-Net-3: pipelined FPGA accelerator target.
The key rows from Table 1 are:
Model Top-1 Error Titan RTX Latency ZCU102 Latency
MNasNet-A1 24.8 17.94 ms 8.78 ms
FBNet-C 24.9 22.54 ms 12.21 ms
Proxyless-GPU 24.9 15.72 ms 10.79 ms
EDD-Net-1 25.3 11.17 ms 11.15 ms
EDD-Net-2 25.4 13.00 ms 7.96 ms
For GPU, EDD-Net-1 reaches 25.3% ImageNet top-1 error and 11.17 ms latency on Titan RTX. The accuracy is close to Proxyless-GPU (24.9% top-1 error), but the latency is lower than Proxyless-GPU’s 15.72 ms. This is where the paper gets the 1.40x speedup claim. The 1080 Ti TensorRT numbers show the expected precision tradeoff:
Precision Top-1 Error Latency
32-bit floating 25.5% 2.83 ms
16-bit floating 25.3% 2.29 ms
8-bit integer 26.4% 1.74 ms
For the recursive FPGA target, EDD-Net-2 reaches 7.96 ms latency on Xilinx ZCU102 with 25.4% top-1 error. It is faster than the listed FPGA implementations of MNasNet, FBNet, and Proxyless variants under the same CHaiDNN framework. For the pipelined FPGA target, EDD-Net-3 is compared against DNNBuilder on ZC706:
Model Top-1 Error Top-5 Error Throughput
VGG16 on DNNBuilder 29.5 10.0 27.7 fps
EDD-Net-3 25.6 7.7 40.2 fps
The throughput ratio is about 40.2 / 27.7 = 1.45x, while the accuracy is also better. Architectures The searched architectures are visibly hardware-dependent. EDD-Net-3, targeting a pipelined FPGA accelerator, is shallower but uses more channels and larger kernels. That makes sense: more blocks complicate resource allocation and pipeline control, while wider stages can expose parallel work. EDD-Net-1 and EDD-Net-2 stay closer to deeper MBConv chains, but the details still differ because the GPU and recursive FPGA latency/resource models are different. This is the same lesson as ProxylessNAS, but pushed one level deeper. The best architecture is not only hardware-dependent; it is implementation-dependent. TakeawayEDD is most valuable as a formulation paper. It gives a way to ask:
What are the architecture variables? What are the implementation variables? Which parts can be relaxed into differentiable expectations? Which hardware constraints should be modeled as performance loss and resource penalty?
The limitations are also clear. The search space is still a hand-designed MBConv space, not arbitrary DNN discovery. The GPU implementation search is relatively narrow because framework support restricts mixed precision and kernel choices. The FPGA performance/resource models are useful approximations, but the final implementation variables still need to be re-tuned after search. Even with those constraints, the paper makes a good engineering point: hardware-aware NAS should not stop at “add latency to the loss.” If deployment quality depends on quantization, parallelism, resource sharing, or pipeline structure, those variables should influence the architecture while the architecture is being searched.

entry.title: Efficient Neural Architecture Search via Parameter Sharing
entry.content:
Paper / Code ENAS is the paper that pushed weight sharing into the center of NAS. Earlier reinforcement-learning NAS trained each sampled child architecture almost independently, so the controller could only improve after spending a huge amount of GPU time. ENAS keeps the controller idea, but changes the performance-estimation problem: instead of training every child model from scratch, all child models are subgraphs of one large computational graph and share parameters. The important point is not only “use an LSTM controller”. The important point is that architecture search becomes a cheap subgraph-selection problem during search, and only the final selected architecture is trained normally from scratch. One caveat for the released code: the repository is still useful for reading the CIFAR-10 scripts and architecture encoding, but its README warns that the Penn Treebank language-model implementation in that repo is wrong. MotivationThe original NAS result from Zoph & Le and the later NASNet line made the controller-RNN recipe visible, but the cost was hard to ignore. NASNet is reported with hundreds of GPUs for several days. The expensive part is not sampling an architecture string; it is repeatedly training sampled networks well enough to produce a useful validation reward. ENAS asks a very direct question: if two sampled architectures reuse the same operation or edge, why train two separate copies of that parameter during search?
The full graph represents the whole search space. A sampled child model is only a subgraph. Parameters live on the graph and are reused whenever the corresponding computation is active. This turns NAS into a one-shot style training problem: keep a large shared model, sample subgraphs from it, and use validation reward to update the sampler. This is the main cost reduction. ENAS is not making the search space tiny; it is making each architecture evaluation much cheaper. ContributionThe useful contributions are:
Represent the NAS search space as a directed acyclic graph where child architectures share parameters. Train two parameter sets alternately: shared child-model weights omega on training data, and controller parameters theta on validation reward. Apply the same idea to recurrent cells for Penn Treebank and convolutional architectures for CIFAR-10. Keep both macro search over full CNNs and micro search over reusable convolution/reduction cells. Report competitive NAS results with a single GTX 1080Ti in hours instead of hundreds of GPUs for days.
Historically, the first point matters most. Many later NAS methods use some version of a supernet, one-shot model, or over-parameterized search graph. ENAS is one of the clean early examples of that shift. MethodologySubgraphs and shared parameters For recurrent cells, the controller samples a sequence of decisions. At each node, it chooses a previous node and an activation function. The sampled decisions define a small DAG, and unused loose ends are averaged to form the cell output. The paper uses N = 12 recurrent nodes and four candidate activations: tanh, ReLU, identity, and sigmoid. With predecessor choices included, the recurrent-cell search space is about 10^15 models. The large search space is not the bottleneck by itself. The bottleneck is how to score candidates without training 10^15 independent RNNs. ENAS solves this by making the candidate cells share the same matrix pool. If a sampled cell uses an edge from node j to node l, it uses the shared matrix for that edge. If a different sampled cell uses the same edge later, it reuses the same parameter. This is a biased estimate of architecture quality. A child architecture is scored using weights it co-trained with many other architectures, not weights optimized only for itself. But it is cheap enough to make the controller loop practical. Alternating optimizationENAS has two parameter sets:
omega: shared parameters of the child-model graph theta: parameters of the LSTM controller policy
The training loop alternates between them: repeat: freeze theta sample child architectures from pi(theta) update shared weights omega on training minibatches freeze omega sample child architectures from pi(theta) compute validation rewards update theta with REINFORCE
The controller objective is the expected validation reward:
The gradient is estimated with REINFORCE and a moving-average baseline:
The reward is task-specific. For Penn Treebank, the paper uses a constant divided by validation perplexity. For CIFAR-10, it uses validation accuracy on a minibatch. This train/validation split is important: shared weights are trained on training data, but the controller is rewarded for validation behavior. One practical detail is surprisingly aggressive: for the shared-weight update, the paper says M = 1 sampled model works well. So a minibatch update usually trains only one sampled child architecture, not an average over many architectures. CNN search spacesENAS evaluates two CNN search spaces. The macro search space designs the whole convolutional network layer by layer. At layer k, the controller chooses:
one operation among conv 3x3, sep conv 3x3, conv 5x5, sep conv 5x5, avg pool 3x3, and max pool 3x3 skip connections from previous layers
With L = 12, the paper reports about 1.6 x 10^29 possible macro networks.
The micro search space follows the NASNet-style cell idea. Instead of designing the whole network directly, ENAS searches for a convolution cell and a reduction cell, then stacks them into a final network.
For each non-input node inside a cell, the controller chooses two previous nodes and two operations. The operation set is smaller than macro search:
sep conv 3x3 sep conv 5x5 avg pool 3x3 max pool 3x3 identity
With B = 7, the paper reports about 1.3 x 10^11 final cell-based networks.
The cell search space is smaller and more structured than the macro space. That structure is useful: the discovered cell can be repeated, scaled, and compared more directly with NASNet-style baselines. ResultsPenn TreebankThe RNN cell found by ENAS is shown below. The final output averages six loose-end nodes, which is similar in spirit to letting several intermediate states contribute to the next hidden state.
The reported search takes about 10 hours on a single Nvidia GTX 1080Ti. The final ENAS cell reaches 55.8 test perplexity on Penn Treebank without post-training processing.
Model Params Test PPL
LSTM, Zaremba et al. 66M 78.4
LSTM, Merity et al. 24M 57.3
LSTM, Yang et al. + MoS 22M 56.0
NAS, Zoph & Le 54M 62.4
ENAS 24M 55.8
The comparison with MoS should be read carefully: MoS is a strong output-layer technique, while ENAS is changing the recurrent cell. The paper emphasizes that ENAS does not apply MoS to its cell in this result. CIFAR-10On CIFAR-10, ENAS reports both macro and micro search results. The headline number is the micro search space with CutOut: 2.89% test error using 4.6M parameters.
Method GPU Days Params Err
NAS + filters 800 21-28 37.4M 3.65
NASNet + CutOut 450 3-4 3.3M 2.65
ENAS macro+ 1 0.32 38.0M 3.87
ENAS micro 1 0.45 4.6M 3.54
ENAS micro+CutOut 1 0.45 4.6M 2.89
The cost gap is the reason this paper became influential. The micro search takes 0.45 GPU-days in the table, which is roughly 11 hours on one GPU. The result is not better than NASNet-A with CutOut, but it is close enough that the cost reduction becomes the main story. The discovered micro cells are also interpretable as normal NASNet-style cells:
The cell contains mostly separable convolutions, pooling, identity paths, and concatenated loose ends. In other words, ENAS does not discover a fundamentally new operator. It finds a useful wiring pattern inside a constrained operator set. Was the controller doing real work?The paper includes a useful sanity check. If the controller were irrelevant, random sampling from the same search space should be close to ENAS. That is not what the paper reports:
Setting Result
Random recurrent cell on PTB 81.2 PPL
ENAS recurrent cell on PTB 55.8 PPL
Random macro CNN on CIFAR-10 5.86% error
ENAS macro CNN on CIFAR-10 4.23% error
Random micro cells on CIFAR-10 6.77% error
ENAS micro cells on CIFAR-10 3.54% error
They also disable controller training and train only the shared weights. In the macro space, that converges to 8.92% test error; an ensemble of 250 sampled configurations gets 5.49%. That is still worse than the trained ENAS controller. So the controller is not just decoration around a good search space. TakeawayENAS is best understood as a performance-estimation paper. It keeps the RL controller, but the big idea is weight sharing:
train a supergraph instead of thousands of separate child models use validation reward to train the controller retrain the chosen architecture from scratch at the end
The weakness is also clear. Shared weights are a proxy for final architecture quality. A child model may look good because it happened to receive favorable shared-weight training, or look bad because its weights were under-trained by the sampling process. This ranking bias is the main tradeoff behind one-shot NAS. Still, ENAS changed the practical baseline. After this paper, an NAS method that trains every candidate from scratch needs a strong reason. Most later efficient NAS methods either improve the supernet training, make the relaxation differentiable, add hardware-aware objectives, or try to reduce the bias introduced by weight sharing.

entry.title: FQ-ViT: Post-Training Quantization for Fully Quantized Vision Transformer
entry.content:
Lin Y, Zhang T, Sun P, Li Z, Zhou S. FQ-ViT: Post-Training Quantization for Fully Quantized Vision Transformer. arXiv 2021.
Paper FQ-ViT is a post-training quantization paper about a stricter question than normal “W8A8 works” claims: Can the whole Vision Transformer graph be quantized, including LayerNorm and Softmax? That word “fully” matters. If Linear/MatMul layers are INT8 but LayerNorm and Softmax remain floating point, the model still needs float kernels, dequantize/requantize boundaries, and extra memory movement. FQ-ViT focuses on these hard operators instead of only the easy GEMM-heavy parts. The paper proposes two components:
Power-of-Two Factor (PTF) for LayerNorm input quantization; Log-Int-Softmax (LIS) for integer-only Softmax and low-bit attention maps.
All figures and tables below are cropped from the original arXiv PDF. MotivationVision Transformer quantization is not just CNN quantization with bigger matrices. A ViT block contains:
Q/K/V projections; attention-score MatMul; Softmax over attention scores; attention-value MatMul; output projection; MLP layers; LayerNorm; residual additions.
Linear layers are the easy part. LayerNorm and Softmax are the deployment problem.
Figure 1 compares four settings:
full precision; not fully quantized, where LayerNorm and Softmax remain floating point; vanilla fully quantized with standard MinMax treatment; FQ-ViT’s fully quantized method.
The collapse of vanilla fully quantization is the key observation. Some models tolerate it, but large ViT/Swin models can lose most of their accuracy when LayerNorm and Softmax are naively quantized. FQ-ViT tries to make the hard operators quantization-friendly. What “Fully Quantized” MeansFor FQ-ViT, fully quantized means the graph should avoid floating-point islands in the critical path.
Operator Normal PTQ difficulty FQ-ViT treatment
Conv / Linear relatively easy MinMax uniform quantization
MatMul relatively easy integer MatMul
LayerNorm hard Power-of-Two Factor
Softmax hard Log-Int-Softmax
Attention map sensitive log2-style low-bit representation
This is the same engineering pressure that appears in I-BERT for language models: nonlinear and normalization operators decide whether “integer inference” is real or cosmetic. LayerNorm ProblemLayerNorm cannot usually be folded into the previous layer in the same way BatchNorm can be folded into a convolution. It depends on the current input’s mean and variance, so it remains an active operator at inference time. FQ-ViT observes that LayerNorm inputs in ViTs have strong inter-channel variation.
The left plot compares channel-wise ranges for ResNet and Transformer models. The right plot shows channel-wise minimum and maximum values for Swin-B. The transformer activations have much stronger inter-channel variation than the CNN comparison. This breaks simple layer-wise MinMax quantization. A single scale must cover extreme channels, so normal channels receive poor resolution. Channel-wise quantization could help accuracy, but it increases hardware complexity because every channel needs separate quantization parameters. Power-of-Two FactorPTF is a compromise between layer-wise and channel-wise quantization. The idea is:
Keep a layer-wise quantization scale. Give each channel a power-of-two factor. Implement channel adjustment with bit shifts rather than expensive arbitrary scaling.
The paper’s default hyperparameter is K = 3, meaning the per-channel factor is selected from a small set of powers of two. This gives channels enough scale flexibility without turning LayerNorm into a fully channel-wise floating-point operation. At inference, PTF lets the quantized LayerNorm path shift activations to reduce inter-channel range mismatch, compute approximate statistics, and keep the output quantized.
The hyperparameter curve shows that accuracy is mostly saturated when K = 3, which is why the paper uses it as the default. Softmax ProblemAttention maps have a very different distribution from normal activations. Most probabilities are tiny, and a few entries dominate. Uniform quantization wastes too much resolution on large values and gives too little resolution to small positive values.
The figure compares 4-bit bins for uniform quantization and log2 quantization on a ViT-L attention map. Log-style quantization allocates more bins to small values, which is the part of the distribution where attention probabilities are dense. Softmax is also a graph-level deployment issue. If Softmax stays in full precision, attention inference must dequantize before Softmax and requantize afterward.
The left side keeps full-precision Softmax in the attention path. The right side uses Log-Int-Softmax. Instead of producing a normal floating-point attention matrix, LIS keeps the Softmax-related path in integer form and uses bit shifts when multiplying attention by values. This is why FQ-ViT can report attention maps at 4-bit in some settings. The method is not only compressing weights; it is changing how the Softmax path is represented. Log-Int-SoftmaxThe paper builds LIS on integer-only exponential ideas from I-BERT. The high-level route is:
subtract the maximum score before Softmax for numerical stability; approximate exponential in integer arithmetic; use a log2 representation for the reverse Softmax output; combine attention and values with bit shifts instead of floating-point multiply.
The algorithms are useful because they make “fully quantized” concrete. The difficult part is not storing an attention map in fewer bits. The difficult part is computing and consuming that map without falling back to float.
The appendix compares normal exponential with the integer-only approximation. The approximation is designed to be good enough for quantized Softmax while remaining integer-friendly. ImageNet Results Representative ImageNet top-1 results:
Model Full precision FQ-ViT 8/8/8 FQ-ViT 8/8/4
DeiT-T 72.21 71.61 71.07
DeiT-S 79.85 79.17 78.40
DeiT-B 81.85 81.20 80.85
ViT-B 84.53 83.31 82.68
ViT-L 85.81 85.03 84.89
Swin-T 81.35 80.51 80.04
Swin-S 83.20 82.71 82.47
Swin-B 83.60 82.97 82.38
Here W/A/Attn = 8/8/8 means weights, activations, and attention maps are all 8-bit. 8/8/4 keeps weights and activations at 8-bit but uses 4-bit attention maps. The important comparison is not only against full precision. It is against methods that do not fully quantize LayerNorm and Softmax. Those methods can have good accuracy, but the graph still contains floating-point islands. COCO Detection FQ-ViT also evaluates Swin-based detectors on COCO:
Model Full precision FQ-ViT 8/8/8 FQ-ViT 8/8/4
Mask R-CNN w/ Swin-S 48.5 47.8 47.2
Cascade Mask R-CNN w/ Swin-S 52.0 51.4 50.8
The paper reports that current fully quantized baselines perform poorly on these detectors, while FQ-ViT keeps the degradation small. The Cascade Mask R-CNN result at 50.8 mAP with 4-bit attention is one of the headline numbers from the abstract. Ablation The ViT-B ablation isolates PTF and LIS:
Setting Accuracy
full precision 84.53
8-bit baseline, no PTF/LIS 23.64
8-bit baseline + PTF 83.31
4-bit attention baseline + PTF, no LIS 7.96
4-bit attention baseline + PTF + LIS 82.68
This is the cleanest evidence in the paper. PTF is the critical fix for full 8-bit quantization. LIS is the critical fix when attention maps are compressed to 4-bit.
The attention-map visualization makes the same point qualitatively. Uniform low-bit attention loses structure as bit-width drops. Log-Int-Softmax preserves the attention pattern much better. Channel Variation Appendix The appendix plots channel-wise minimum and maximum values across several ResNet and Transformer models. The ViT/Swin plots show the outlier-like channel behavior that motivates PTF. This is a useful diagnostic for any reproduction: before designing a quantizer, look at the tensor distribution that the quantizer must represent. Reproduction NotesFor a serious reproduction, I would report operator coverage explicitly:
Path What to verify
Q/K/V projections integer Linear/MatMul kernels
attention score integer MatMul and scale handling
Softmax LIS path, no hidden float fallback
attention times V integer or bitshift-compatible path
LayerNorm PTF path, no float LayerNorm fallback
residual add compatible scales or explicit requantization
MLP integer Linear/GELU handling or documented fallback
Accuracy alone is not enough. A model can be accurate with quantized weights but still fail the purpose of this paper if LayerNorm and Softmax silently run in float. I would also log:
channel-wise ranges before LayerNorm; the selected PTF factors per layer; attention-map histograms before and after LIS; top-k attention overlap between full precision and quantized models; end-to-end operator dtype coverage in the actual backend.
LimitationsFQ-ViT is post-training quantization, so it avoids retraining cost but depends heavily on calibration quality. The paper samples 1000 training images for calibration in its experiments. Bad calibration can still break low-bit attention or LayerNorm statistics. The deployment benefit also depends on backend support. If the runtime cannot execute PTF LayerNorm or LIS Softmax efficiently, the method may evaluate correctly but not deliver a real integer-only speedup. Finally, the paper focuses on ViT/Swin-style vision transformers. The ideas are relevant to language models, but sequence length, causal masking, KV cache behavior, and activation outliers make LLM deployment a different problem. TakeawayFQ-ViT is valuable because it treats quantization as an operator-coverage problem. Linear layers are not enough. LayerNorm and Softmax decide whether a Vision Transformer can actually run as a fully quantized graph. The two main ideas are easy to remember:
PTF uses power-of-two channel factors to make LayerNorm input quantization tolerate inter-channel variation. LIS uses a log-domain integer-friendly Softmax path so attention maps can be quantized, even to 4-bit in the paper’s experiments.
When reading later quantization papers, I use FQ-ViT as a checklist: show the accuracy table, but also show which operators still run in floating point.

entry.title: FBNet: Hardware-Aware Efficient ConvNet Design via Differentiable Neural Architecture Search
entry.content:
Wu B, Dai X, Zhang P, et al. FBNet: Hardware-Aware Efficient ConvNet Design via Differentiable Neural Architecture Search. CVPR 2019.
Paper / Code FBNet is a practical hardware-aware NAS paper. It does not search arbitrary cell graphs. It searches a constrained MobileNet-style layer space, measures operator latency on the target phone, and makes that latency part of a differentiable search objective. The engineering lesson is simple: if the final user cares about phone latency, the search loop should see phone latency. FLOPs are useful for sanity checks, but they are not the deployment objective. All figures and tables below are cropped from the original CVPR PDF. MotivationFBNet is motivated by three deployment problems.
Efficient ConvNet design has a large combinatorial space. The best architecture depends on input resolution, width, runtime, and target device. FLOPs are a weak proxy for measured latency.
The third point is the important one. Two operators can have similar FLOPs but very different runtime because of memory access, kernel implementation, vectorization, cache behavior, and backend support. This is why hardware-aware NAS papers such as MnasNet, ProxylessNAS, and FBNet measure latency directly instead of only reporting multiply-adds.
Figure 1 summarizes the FBNet loop:
Define a layer-wise search space. Benchmark candidate operators on the target device. Train a stochastic supernet. Sample compact architectures from the learned distribution. Train selected architectures from scratch.
FBNet calls the final models Facebook-Berkeley-Nets. The headline result is FBNet-B: 74.1% ImageNet top-1, 295M FLOPs, and 23.1 ms latency on a Samsung S8 under the reported Caffe2 int8 setup. The paper estimates 216 GPU-hours for search, much smaller than the RL search cost it attributes to MnasNet. Search SpaceFBNet keeps the macro skeleton fixed and searches operator choices inside 22 searchable layers. The first stem and the last projection/classifier layers are fixed.
Each searchable layer chooses from 9 candidates:
Candidate Kernel Expansion Group
k3_e1 3 1 1
k3_e1_g2 3 1 2
k3_e3 3 3 1
k3_e6 3 6 1
k5_e1 5 1 1
k5_e1_g2 5 1 2
k5_e3 5 3 1
k5_e6 5 6 1
skip - - -
So the rough search space size is , around architectures. That is large enough to require an efficient search method, but still structured enough that an additive latency lookup table is plausible. The candidate block is an inverted-bottleneck style block.
The block has:
a first 1x1 pointwise convolution, optionally grouped; a 3x3 or 5x5 depthwise convolution; a final 1x1 pointwise convolution; a residual connection when shape and stride permit it.
This search space is conservative by modern NAS standards, but that is also why the deployment story is credible. FBNet is not searching exotic operators that may be unsupported by mobile runtimes. Differentiable SearchFBNet uses a stochastic supernet. At each searchable layer, the architecture parameter vector controls a probability distribution over candidate blocks. During search, the layer output is a weighted or sampled mixture of candidates. Gumbel Softmax makes the sampling path differentiable enough for gradient-based optimization. The useful mental model:
weights decide how well candidate operators perform; architecture parameters decide which operator each layer prefers; Gumbel temperature controls how close the relaxed choice is to a one-hot discrete choice; after search, FBNet samples/selects a discrete architecture and trains it from scratch.
This is still a supernet proxy. The searched architecture is not deployed directly from the supernet weights. The paper uses the supernet to learn a distribution over good architectures, then does final training separately. Latency-Aware ObjectiveFBNet adds target-device latency to the training objective. Measuring every full architecture would be too expensive, so the paper benchmarks every candidate operator in context and stores the results in a lookup table. The architecture latency is estimated additively: Latency(architecture) = sum of selected block latencies. In the stochastic supernet, the expected latency is the probability-weighted sum over candidate block latencies. Since each lookup-table entry is a constant, this latency estimate is differentiable with respect to the architecture probabilities. That is the paper’s main trick. FBNet makes measured hardware latency usable inside gradient-based NAS. There are two assumptions to remember:
Operator latency is approximately additive across the network. The measured latency table matches the final runtime, device, input shape, and quantization/backend setup.
Those assumptions are reasonable for the paper’s mobile CPU/Caffe2 int8 target, but they are not universal. Search ProtocolFor the main ImageNet experiment, FBNet targets Samsung Galaxy S8 with Qualcomm Snapdragon 835 and Caffe2 int8 inference. The protocol is:
Measure candidate operator latency on the target phone. Train a stochastic supernet for 90 epochs. Use 100 randomly selected ImageNet classes during search. Train operator weights on 80% of the selected training data with SGD. Train architecture parameters on the remaining 20% with Adam. Sample architectures from the learned distribution. Train final models from scratch on ImageNet.
This is a pragmatic compromise. Searching on all ImageNet classes would be more direct, but using 100 classes makes the search cost manageable. ImageNet Results Representative rows from Table 3:
Model Search Search cost FLOPs S8 latency Top-1
1.0-MobileNetV2 manual - 300M 21.7 ms 72.0
MnasNet RL 91K GPUh estimated 317M 23.7 ms 74.0
1.3-MobileNetV2 manual - 509M 33.8 ms 74.4
FBNet-A gradient 216 GPUh 249M 19.8 ms 73.0
FBNet-B gradient 216 GPUh 295M 23.1 ms 74.1
FBNet-C gradient 216 GPUh 375M 28.1 ms 74.9
FBNet-B is the central comparison. It is close to MnasNet latency but slightly better in the reported accuracy/latency point, and the paper estimates a much lower search cost. Compared with 1.3-MobileNetV2, FBNet-B has similar accuracy with far fewer FLOPs and lower latency. I would read the search-cost comparison carefully. The 91K GPUh MnasNet number is an estimate by the FBNet authors, not a perfectly controlled benchmark under identical infrastructure. The more robust takeaway is still strong: differentiable NAS made the search cheap enough that device-specific redesign became plausible. Architecture Patterns The architecture visualization is useful because FBNet is not just selecting one repeated block. Different layers choose different kernel sizes, expansion ratios, grouping, and skip behavior. Two patterns stand out:
Larger models use more high-expansion k5 blocks in later stages. Tiny low-resolution variants skip more layers, which matches the lower need for depth and receptive-field growth.
This is also where FBNet differs from a simple width multiplier. A width multiplier uniformly scales a hand-designed backbone. FBNet changes operator choices layer by layer. Scaling And DevicesFBNet searches again for different input resolutions and channel scaling factors instead of only scaling one discovered model.
Examples from Table 4:
Setting MobileNetV2 baseline FBNet result
224, 0.35 60.3%, 9.3 ms 65.3%, 10.7 ms
192, 0.50 63.9%, 8.4 ms 65.9%, 9.9 ms
128, 0.50 57.7%, 4.8 ms 60.0%, 5.1 ms
96, 0.35 45.5%, 3.8 ms 50.2%, 2.9 ms
The 96, 0.35 setting is the cleanest example: FBNet is both more accurate and faster than the scaled MobileNetV2 baseline. The paper also searches separate models for iPhone X and Samsung S8:
Model iPhone X latency Samsung S8 latency Top-1
FBNet-iPhoneX 19.84 ms target 23.33 ms 73.20
FBNet-S8 27.53 ms 22.12 ms target 73.27
The operator runtime plot explains the non-transferability. Some operator types are faster on iPhone X; others are faster on Samsung S8. A single FLOP count cannot see this difference. Reproduction NotesIf I were reproducing FBNet, I would check five things before trusting the result. First, benchmark latency with the final runtime. A lookup table measured under a different backend, thread count, quantization mode, or batch size can mislead the search. Second, validate the additive latency model. It is usually good enough for a constrained mobile network, but residual adds, memory layout changes, and cache behavior can introduce non-additive effects. Third, separate supernet ranking from final training. The final architecture must be trained from scratch; otherwise the result measures supernet weight sharing more than the architecture. Fourth, record the search split. FBNet trains operator weights and architecture parameters on different slices of the 100-class ImageNet subset. Changing this split changes the proxy. Fifth, report device and runtime details next to accuracy. “23 ms mobile latency” is not meaningful without the phone, backend, quantization type, and measurement protocol. LimitationsFBNet is deployment-oriented, but its scope is still limited.
The search space is manually shaped around MobileNet/ShiftNet-like blocks. The latency model assumes block latencies add cleanly. Search uses a 100-class ImageNet proxy, then final models are trained separately. The reported latency is tied to Caffe2 int8 inference on 2018-era devices. The method optimizes one target runtime at a time; a different device may need a different search.
These are not flaws in the paper so much as the engineering contract. FBNet is useful because it defines that contract clearly. TakeawayFBNet is a clean example of hardware-aware differentiable NAS. The core idea is to benchmark candidate blocks on the real target device, put those latency values into a differentiable objective, and let the supernet learn layer-wise operator preferences. I read FBNet less as a general architecture discovery paper and more as a deployment recipe: constrain the search space to runnable operators, measure the metric the user feels, and make search cheap enough that target-specific redesign is possible.

entry.title: FedMask: Joint Computation and Communication-Efficient Personalized Federated Learning
entry.content:
Li A, Sun J, Zeng X, Zhang M, Li H, Chen Y. FedMask: Joint Computation and Communication-Efficient Personalized Federated Learning via Heterogeneous Masking. SenSys 2021.
Paper FedMask is a personalized FL paper that targets three problems at once: non-IID data, communication cost, and on-device computation. The core idea is not to communicate full model weights. Each device keeps a fixed model weight tensor and learns a personalized binary mask over those weights. During federation, the clients exchange masks instead of dense parameters. This makes FedMask different from ordinary model compression after FL. The sparse model is not a post-training artifact; the mask is the object being optimized and communicated. MotivationClassic FedAvg assumes clients collaborate on one shared global model. That becomes awkward on mobile devices:
Data is non-IID, so one global model may not fit each client. Uploading dense model updates is expensive. Large DNNs are hard to train and run on device.
The paper positions FedMask against several FL baselines:
The table is a good summary of the target. FedAvg gives neither personalization nor communication/computation saving. Top-k compression reduces communication but does not solve personalization. Per-FedAvg personalizes, but it still pays dense training and communication costs. FedMask tries to keep all three columns checked. ContributionThe paper’s contributions are:
It formulates personalized FL as heterogeneous binary mask learning over fixed model weights. It communicates only binary masks, so each parameter is represented by one bit instead of a full floating-point update. It adds structured sparsity through mask learning, reducing runtime computation instead of only communication. It proposes a personalization-preserving mask aggregation rule on the server. It evaluates the method on image classification, human activity recognition, and next-character prediction.
The headline numbers reported in the paper:
Metric Reported improvement
Inference accuracy up to 28.47% higher
Communication cost up to 34.48x lower
Computation cost up to 2.44x lower
Inference speed up to 1.56x faster
Energy per inference up to 1.78x lower
MethodologyMasked local modelFedMask keeps the real-valued model parameters fixed and learns a binary mask . The model used for inference is:
Each mask entry is binary. A mask value of 0 prunes the corresponding parameter or structured unit; a value of 1 keeps it active.
This is why communication becomes cheap. Instead of sending full gradients or weights, a client sends a binary mask. The server and clients already share the fixed parameter tensor, so the mask is enough to reconstruct the local sparse model. Three-stage workflow FedMask has three main stages. First, each client performs one-shot pruning. This initializes a local binary mask from its own data. The goal is to avoid starting every device from the same dense structure. Second, each selected client optimizes its local mask. The mask is trained through a real-valued proxy and then binarized. The model weights stay frozen, so local training is mask optimization rather than ordinary weight training. Third, the server aggregates masks. This is not a simple dense weight average. Since different clients may keep different channels or parameters, the aggregation has to preserve heterogeneity instead of forcing every client into the same subnet. Personalization-preserving aggregation The aggregation rule updates shared mask units when they are comparable across clients, while allowing client-specific mask structures to remain different. The paper also illustrates this by transforming channel masks into mask representations before server-side aggregation:
The important point is that the server is not trying to produce one universal sparse architecture. It is coordinating the masks so clients can still benefit from federation without losing local personalization. Algorithm shape The pseudocode is useful for seeing what is frozen and what moves:
The server initializes model weights and a global mask. Clients download , prune once, and keep a local mask. In each round, selected clients update masks on local data. Clients return masks, not dense model weights. The server aggregates masks and broadcasts the result for the next round.
This is a very different communication object from FedAvg. The learned mask is both the compression mechanism and the personalization mechanism. ExperimentsSetupThe paper evaluates four tasks:
Task Dataset Devices / classes
Image classification EMNIST 2414 / 64
Image classification CIFAR-10 400 / 10
Human activity recognition HAR 30 / 6
Next-character prediction Shakespeare 1129 / 80
The baselines include FedAvg, Top-k, Per-FedAvg, LG-FedAvg, BNN-FedAvg, and standalone local training. This is a useful comparison set because each baseline stresses a different axis: communication compression, personalization, binary networks, or no federation. Accuracy versus communication The red star is FedMask. Across IC-CIFAR10, IC-EMNIST, HAR, and NCP, it sits near the low-communication and high-accuracy corner. This is the core empirical claim: mask communication can be cheap without collapsing accuracy. BNN-FedAvg also communicates cheaply, but the accuracy is much worse in the plots. Standalone local training has no communication, but it usually gives up too much accuracy because each device trains alone. Computation cost The computation-cost plot shows why structured masks matter. If pruning were only unstructured, communication would shrink but inference/training kernels may not become much faster. FedMask tries to learn masks that remove structured units, so the active computation graph is smaller. The figure reports reductions across all four tasks. The gains are largest for HAR in this plot and smaller for NCP, which is a reminder that the benefit depends on the model and layer structure. Memory and inference latency FedMask also reduces model footprint relative to dense baselines:
Application FedMask Baseline
IC-CIFAR10 365.30 MB 537.21 MB
