IC-EMNIST 364.72 MB 538.09 MB
HAR 2.69 MB 4.41 MB
NCP 0.92 MB 1.53 MB
BNN-FedAvg is much smaller than FedMask, but that is not a free win: the earlier accuracy-communication plot shows BNN-FedAvg loses a lot of accuracy. FedMask is a middle point: not as tiny as a fully binarized model, but substantially more accurate. The inference-time bars report speedups around 1.38x to 1.56x over dense baselines across the tested applications. TakeawayThe useful idea in FedMask is that the mask is not just a compression artifact. It is the personalized model. My notes:
Fixing and learning turns FL communication from dense parameter exchange into binary structure exchange. Heterogeneous masks are a natural fit for non-IID clients because each client can keep a different sparse subnet. Structured sparsity is important; otherwise lower communication would not necessarily reduce device computation. The tradeoff is that the method depends on a good fixed weight initialization and a mask aggregation rule that does not erase personalization.
I would read FedMask as an early systems-oriented PFL paper: it is less about finding the best global optimizer and more about choosing the right object to federate. For mobile AI, federating masks can be a better systems interface than federating full models.

entry.title: FBNetV2: Differentiable Neural Architecture Search for Spatial and Channel Dimensions
entry.content:
Wan A, Dai X, Zhang P, et al. FBNetV2: Differentiable Neural Architecture Search for Spatial and Channel Dimensions. CVPR 2020.
Paper / Code FBNetV2 is a follow-up to FBNet, but the problem is different. FBNet searches layer-wise operator choices under a target latency objective. FBNetV2 asks a more structural question: can differentiable NAS search channel width and input resolution directly? Those two dimensions matter a lot for mobile networks. Width changes activation memory, parameter count, kernel efficiency, and FLOPs. Resolution changes early feature-map cost and receptive field behavior. But they are awkward for DNAS because different choices produce tensors with different shapes. FBNetV2’s answer is DMaskingNAS: represent channel and resolution choices with masks and feature-map reuse, so the memory cost stays almost constant as the search space grows. All figures and tables below are cropped from the original arXiv PDF. MotivationStandard differentiable NAS is expensive because the supernet instantiates all candidate operations. If a layer can choose among many blocks, all those blocks must exist in memory during search. This becomes worse when the candidate choices are not just operator types but also tensor shapes. Channel search creates two direct problems:
outputs with different numbers of channels cannot be naively summed; instantiating every width option increases memory and compute.
Resolution search creates similar problems:
feature maps with different spatial sizes cannot be naively summed; padding or upsampling can create pixel/receptive-field misalignment.
The figure compares four cases:
normal DNAS without channel search; naive DNAS with all possible channel counts, which creates shape mismatches and high memory cost; pruning-style search, which explores channel counts sequentially; DMaskingNAS, which keeps all possible channel choices inside one weight-sharing graph.
The abstract gives the headline: with up to 421x less search cost, DMaskingNAS finds models with 0.9% higher accuracy and 15% fewer FLOPs than prior efficient models in one comparison, and it can outperform MobileNetV3 by 2.6% accuracy at comparable model size. Search DimensionsFBNetV2 expands the search space beyond block type.
Dimension Why it matters
operator/block controls kernel type, activation, expansion, and SE
channel width controls activation size, memory traffic, and parameter count
input resolution controls early feature-map cost and receptive field
depth/stage shape changes how computation is distributed across the network
This is closer to how mobile networks are actually designed. A real model family is rarely defined only by “which MBConv block goes here.” Width and resolution dominate the accuracy-cost tradeoff.
The search-space table shows the macro search space and the micro block choices. Macro choices include maximum input resolution, bottleneck type, expansion-rate range, output-channel range, number of blocks, and stride. Micro choices include kernel size, squeeze-and-excitation, and nonlinearity. Channel MaskingThe channel-search idea is to represent width choices with masks. A mask selects the first k active channels from a larger tensor. Instead of training separate convolutions for every channel count, DMaskingNAS uses a shared full-width computation and applies masks to reuse feature maps.
On the left side, channel masking builds a weighted mask from several candidate masks. On the right side, resolution subsampling represents different input resolutions without storing a separate feature map for every candidate resolution. The intuition:
channel choices are nested subsets of a maximum channel tensor; candidate masks have negligible memory cost compared with feature maps; sharing the larger feature map avoids keeping many parallel tensors alive; Gumbel-Softmax weights decide which candidate mask is preferred.
Figure 3 explains why the naive formulation breaks. If each candidate width has a different output channel count, the outputs cannot be summed. Zero-padding makes them summable, but it still computes several separate convolutions. DMaskingNAS approximates this with weight sharing: compute one convolution, then combine masks. This is the main memory trick. The graph can represent many channel options without materializing a full candidate path for each one. Resolution SubsamplingResolution search is harder than “resize input and continue.” If feature maps with different spatial sizes are padded incorrectly, pixels do not align. If a convolution sees a subsampled feature map naively, the effective receptive field changes.
FBNetV2 handles this through resolution subsampling. The smaller-resolution branch is represented as a sampled subset of the larger feature map. Values are placed back into a larger map at the corresponding positions, while missing positions are left as zeros. This avoids building a separate feature map for each resolution candidate. Two details matter:
zero-padding should not contaminate pixels from different resolutions; receptive field should stay consistent, so subsampling must happen before the operation where needed.
The result is a DNAS search space that can include input resolution choices without exploding memory in the same way as naive all-path DNAS. Effective Shape PropagationDuring search, the network is not yet a single discrete architecture. Channel and resolution choices have weights, so the model has an effective shape:
effective output channels; effective height and width; effective FLOPs or parameter cost.
This lets FBNetV2 assign a resource penalty during search even when the current supernet choice is still relaxed. For example, if a 16-channel option has weight 0.8 and a 12-channel option has weight 0.2, the effective channel count is 15.2. That fractional value is not a deployed tensor shape; it is a search-time proxy for cost. This is an important distinction. DMaskingNAS is not saying the final model has fractional channels. It uses effective shapes to guide the continuous search, then samples a discrete architecture and trains it normally. Memory Cost Figure 7 is the most important diagnostic. Conventional DNAS memory rises quickly as the number of channel options grows. With only 8 options per block, the paper reports that conventional DNAS fails to fit in 16GB V100 memory. DMaskingNAS remains roughly constant even with 32 channel options per block. The text reports that DMaskingNAS adds roughly 1MB memory for every two orders of magnitude increase in channel search space, about 0.1% of the total memory cost during training in their setup. That is the concrete reason the method can search wider dimensions than ordinary DNAS. Search SetupThe paper implements DMaskingNAS in PyTorch and uses 8 Tesla V100 GPUs with 16GB memory. It searches architectures under different resource objectives and trains final models from scratch. The naming convention is:
FBNetV2-F: FLOP-efficient models; FBNetV2-P: parameter-efficient models; FBNetV2-L: larger models.
For the FLOP-efficient search space, the maximum input resolution is 224. For larger FBNetV2-L models, the maximum input resolution is 256. The supplementary material lists the final macro-architectures. Results Representative ImageNet results:
Model Search method Search space Cost FLOPs Top-1
MobileNetV3-Small RL/NetAdapt stage-wise >91K GPUh 66M 67.4
FBNetV2-F1 gradient layer-wise 0.2K GPUh 56M 68.3
MobileNetV2-1.0x manual - - 300M 72.0
FBNetV2-F3 gradient layer-wise 0.2K GPUh 126M 73.2
MnasNet-A1 RL stage-wise 91K GPUh 312M 75.2
FBNetV2-F4 gradient layer-wise 0.2K GPUh 238M 76.0
FBNetV2-L1 gradient layer-wise 0.6K GPUh 325M 77.2
The strongest small-model comparison is FBNetV2-F1 versus MobileNetV3-Small: 68.3% versus 67.4% top-1 with fewer FLOPs in the reported table. In the middle range, FBNetV2-F3 reaches 73.2% top-1 at 126M FLOPs, much smaller than many baselines around the same accuracy.
The FLOPs-accuracy curve shows the F-series models on a compact frontier. The black markers are FBNetV2; they sit above many hand-designed and searched baselines at similar FLOPs.
The bottom plots separate two regimes:
parameter-efficient models, where model size matters more than FLOPs; larger models, where FBNetV2-L is compared with EfficientNet, MobileNetV3, and other larger baselines.
The paper’s broader claim is not only that one model is good. It is that searching channel and resolution dimensions opens a better family of tradeoffs. What Changed From FBNetFBNet and FBNetV2 attack different bottlenecks.
Paper Main search dimension Main technical trick
FBNet operator choice under latency stochastic supernet plus latency lookup table
FBNetV2 channel width and input resolution feature-map masks plus effective shape propagation
FBNet asks: which operator should each layer use for this device? FBNetV2 asks: how can DNAS even afford to search over tensor shapes? The second question is more structural. Once channel and resolution are in the search space, the architecture family can move in ways a fixed-width MobileNet-style search cannot. Reproduction NotesA reproduction should not only report final top-1 accuracy. I would check:
maximum GPU memory during supernet search; number of channel and resolution candidates per block; whether masks are nested and aligned correctly; whether the final architecture is sampled and trained from scratch; how effective FLOPs and effective shape are computed during search; whether BatchNorm/statistics are handled consistently when channel masks change.
The most important debugging view is the memory curve. If memory grows linearly with the number of channel options, the implementation is probably instantiating candidate paths instead of using the intended masking formulation. LimitationsFBNetV2 is still constrained by a manually designed mobile search space. It does not discover arbitrary network topologies, and its final quality depends on the candidate ranges for width, resolution, expansion, depth, kernel, SE, and activation. The method also relies on a relaxed search proxy. Effective shapes guide the supernet, but the final model is discrete. The proxy must preserve enough ranking information for the sampled architecture to be good after full training. Finally, the paper emphasizes FLOPs, parameters, and ImageNet accuracy more than direct latency on every target runtime. For deployment, FBNet-style measured latency should still be checked after the final architecture is materialized. TakeawayFBNetV2 is useful because it moves differentiable NAS from operation choice toward shape choice. Channel width and input resolution are central mobile design variables, but they break naive DNAS because tensors no longer match. DMaskingNAS solves this by reusing feature maps with masks, keeping memory nearly constant as the channel/resolution search space expands. That makes layer-wise search over width and resolution practical, and the resulting FBNetV2 models show stronger accuracy-cost tradeoffs than simply scaling a fixed backbone.

entry.title: FedNAS: Federated Deep Learning via Neural Architecture Search
entry.content:
Paper FedNAS is a good baseline to read before DFNAS. It takes a DARTS/MiLeNAS-style differentiable NAS method and puts it inside a federated loop: each client updates both network weights and architecture parameters , the server aggregates both, and the process repeats. The interesting part is that the paper treats NAS as a personalization tool, not only as a way to find one global model. In a non-IID FL setting, two clients may need different local inductive biases even if they start from the same global architecture. FedNAS tries to use architecture search to close that gap. MotivationMost FL papers start with a fixed model: ResNet, DenseNet, MobileNet, or another manually selected architecture. That is convenient, but it assumes the model designer already knows a good architecture for all client distributions. This assumption is weak in federated learning:
The server cannot inspect every client’s local data. Non-IID clients may have very different label or feature distributions. Weight-only personalization can adapt the representation, but the network structure is still frozen.
FedNAS asks a simple question: can clients collaboratively search for the architecture itself while keeping data local?
The loop is close to FedAvg, except the communicated state has two parts: operation weights and architecture parameters . Clients search locally, the server merges the client updates, and the merged are synchronized back. ContributionThe paper’s main contributions are:
It formulates federated NAS as joint optimization over weights and architecture parameters. It adapts MiLeNAS local search to the FL setting. It supports both global architecture search and personalized local adaptation. It implements a distributed AutoFL system on top of FedML/MPI/PyTorch. It compares personalized FedNAS with local adaptation, Ditto, and perFedAvg under non-IID CIFAR-10 splits.
The method is not trying to invent a new search space. It is more about whether a differentiable NAS loop can survive the communication and heterogeneity constraints of FL. MethodologyFederated ObjectiveWith a fixed architecture, a standard FL objective can be written as:
where client has local samples. FedNAS adds architecture parameters to the optimization:
The server does not directly optimize this objective on centralized data. Each selected client performs local search on its private data and sends the updated and back. Search Space The search space follows DARTS/MiLeNAS. The model is built from normal and reduction cells, and each edge is a mixed operation:
So is not a discrete architecture at search time. It is a continuous relaxation over candidate operations. After search, the architecture can be derived by selecting the strongest operations. Local SearchFedNAS uses MiLeNAS as the local optimizer. Each client splits local data into training and validation parts, updates weights on the training loss, and updates architecture parameters using both training and validation losses:
$$\alpha \leftarrow \alpha - \eta_\alpha\left(\nabla_\alpha L_{tr}(w,\alpha)
\lambda\nabla_\alpha L_{val}(w,\alpha)\right)$$
At the end of a local search epoch, the client returns both parameters to the server. The server aggregates by local sample count:
This is the main algorithmic bridge between FedAvg and differentiable NAS. One important detail: after the search stage, the paper still runs an additional evaluation/training stage with a traditional federated optimizer such as FedAvg. So FedNAS is still closer to a two-stage NAS pipeline than to a direct “search and deploy” method. Personalized FedNASFor personalization, the searched global model is not treated as the final model for every client. Each client fine-tunes the received model locally by alternating updates of and . That means personalization happens at both levels:
Weight adaptation changes the learned representation. Architecture adaptation changes which operations are preferred locally.
This is the part that makes FedNAS different from many FL personalization baselines, which usually keep the architecture fixed. ExperimentsSetupThe main experiments use CIFAR-10 with non-IID client partitions. For personalized model search, the paper uses 20 clients and selects 4 clients per round. In the label-skew setting, each client receives images from only five classes, with 3000 images split into 75% training and 25% validation. The paper also evaluates an LDA-style distribution. The baselines use ResNet18 with 11M parameters. FedNAS uses an 8-layer DARTS cell structure with 4M parameters. This matters when reading the numbers: FedNAS is not only changing the optimizer, it is also changing the architecture and parameter count. For global model search, the paper uses a cross-silo setup with 16 clients and one server, all on RTX 2080Ti GPUs. Global test accuracy is measured on the 10,000-image CIFAR-10 test set. Personalized Results The average local validation accuracy is:
Method Params Label skew acc. LDA acc.
FedNAS 4M 0.913 +/- 0.025 0.907 +/- 0.024
Local Adaptation 11M 0.864 +/- 0.028 0.861 +/- 0.0357
Ditto 11M 0.894 +/- 0.035 0.880 +/- 0.032
perFedAvg 11M 0.888 +/- 0.036 0.894 +/- 0.032
FedNAS is strongest in both reported non-IID settings. On label skew, it is about 4.9 percentage points above local adaptation and 1.9 points above Ditto. The paper also notes that FedNAS has the lowest standard deviation in this table, which is useful because personalized FL can look good on average while failing badly for a subset of clients.
The per-client plots show the same pattern: FedNAS is not better for every single client, but its accuracy distribution is shifted to the right and has fewer low-accuracy clients. The paper reports one client with up to 15 percentage points improvement over perFedAvg, while local adaptation is slightly better on two clients. Global Results For global model search, FedNAS is compared with FedAvg on DenseNet under the same fixed non-IID data distribution.
Method Rounds shown Marked test accuracy
FedAvg on DenseNet 100 77.78%
FedNAS 50 81.24%
The paper runs each method three times and tunes hyperparameters for both. The result is a roughly 4 percentage-point gain for the searched FedNAS architecture over the manually designed DenseNet baseline in this setting. System Efficiency The distributed efficiency comparison is:
Method Search time Params Hyperparameters
FedAvg distributed 12 hours 20.01M 100 rounds, 20 local epochs, batch size 64
FedNAS distributed < 5 hours 1.93M 50 rounds, 5 local epochs, batch size 64
This table is useful but should not be over-read. FedNAS is faster in this experiment because the searched model is smaller and the schedule uses fewer rounds/local epochs. It does show that the distributed implementation is practical, but it is not a universal proof that NAS is always cheaper than training a manually designed model. TakeawayFedNAS is convincing as an early federated NAS baseline because it keeps the algorithm close to FedAvg: local clients update , the server averages , and the process repeats. The personalized results are the most interesting part of the paper, since architecture search gives another axis of adaptation beyond local weight fine-tuning. The limitations are also clear:
The search space is a DARTS/MiLeNAS cell space, not a hardware-aware mobile search space. The method communicates architecture parameters in addition to weights, but does not add privacy protection by itself. The comparison changes both optimization method and architecture size, so gains are not purely from personalization. The final searched architecture still needs an additional evaluation/training stage. The strongest reported evidence in the main text is on CIFAR-10 non-IID splits.
Compared with DFNAS, FedNAS is the more DARTS-like method: it searches a mixed-operation supernet and then evaluates the derived architecture. DFNAS later makes a different engineering tradeoff by using one-path sampling and avoiding the extra retraining stage. So I read FedNAS as the personalization-oriented starting point, and DFNAS as the systems-oriented response to its search cost.

entry.title: FlashInfer: An Attention Kernel Engine for LLM Serving
entry.content:
Ye et al. FlashInfer: Efficient and Customizable Attention Engine for LLM Inference Serving.
Paper | Code | Docs FlashInfer is a paper about the layer below the LLM serving runtime. Systems like vLLM, SGLang, and MLC-Engine decide which requests are batched, where KV cache lives, which prefixes are reused, and when CUDA Graphs are replayed. FlashInfer asks a more kernel-level question: given those irregular serving shapes, how should attention kernels read KV cache, specialize attention variants, and keep SMs busy? The key point is that LLM serving attention is not one kernel. A clean training benchmark usually means dense causal prefill with a large query length. Real serving means one-token decode, ragged prompts, paged KV cache, shared prefixes, GQA/MQA, sliding windows, logits soft caps, RoPE fusion, speculative/tree decoding, FP8 KV cache, and changing sequence lengths. FlashInfer is interesting because it treats these differences as first-class API and compiler/runtime inputs rather than as a pile of one-off kernels. The headline numbers from the paper are also concrete: FlashInfer reports 29-69% lower inter-token latency than the Triton backend in SGLang-style serving, 28-30% lower latency for a Streaming-LLM long-context path, and 13-17% speedup for parallel generation with composable formats. I would not read those as universal constants. I read them as evidence that the kernel layer matters once the runtime produces irregular attention layouts.
Figure 1 is the best overview of the design. The left side says FlashInfer wants one logical representation for page tables, radix trees, sparse masks, and related KV-cache structures. The right side says FlashInfer separates compile-time information from runtime information: attention variants, task type, and KV layout feed JIT compilation, while sequence lengths feed a runtime load-balancing scheduler. Serving Attention Is DifferentThe paper starts from FlashAttention, but it is not trying to replace FlashAttention for normal dense training attention. It is trying to adapt FlashAttention-style kernels to the serving regime. For a query length and KV length , the paper summarizes FlashAttention’s operational intensity as:
In prefill, and can both be large, so the kernel has enough matrix work to amortize memory movement. In decode, is often 1 or a small number, while can be thousands or tens of thousands. In that case the expression is dominated by , and decode becomes hard to utilize well:
Grouped-query attention improves this a little because multiple query heads share the same KV heads. If is the number of query/output heads and is the number of KV heads, the group size is:
The paper describes the resulting intensity as roughly:
This is why short-query decode is a kernel-design problem, not just a scheduler problem. The runtime can batch many requests together, but each request may have a different KV length, different page table, different prefix-sharing structure, and different attention variant. FlashInfer’s design is mostly about making that irregularity explicit enough that kernels can still be efficient. Design SnapshotKV layout: paged, ragged, prefix-shared, and sparse KV layouts differ across serving systems. FlashInfer represents them through block-sparse and composable formats. Attention variant: new models add custom masks, logits transforms, RoPE placement, GQA, FP8 KV, and other variants. FlashInfer uses JIT templates and functors instead of maintaining a fixed kernel for every variant. Runtime scheduling: sequence lengths change every generation step, but CUDA Graph prefers static launch shapes. FlashInfer splits planning from execution, dynamically plans work queues, and replays static kernels. Reduction: a long KV range may be split into multiple work tiles. FlashInfer uses attention-state composition over output and log-sum-exp so partial results can be reduced exactly. The rest of the paper can be read as filling in this table. FlashInfer does not only say “use block sparse attention.” It defines a serving boundary: the runtime supplies metadata, the compiler specializes the kernel variant, and the scheduler turns dynamic lengths into deterministic work queues. Attention State CompositionThe mathematical trick that makes splitting work safe is attention-state composition. For a query and an index set over keys and values, define the log-sum-exp scale:
The attention output over the same key set is:
FlashInfer treats the pair as an attention state:
For two disjoint key sets and , their states can be composed without re-reading all keys:
The explicit composition is:
This operator is associative and commutative. That matters because FlashInfer can split a long KV range into chunks, compute partial attention states, and then reduce the partial states later. It is the same family of idea used by Flash-Decoding and RingAttention, but FlashInfer turns it into a standard kernel output/reduction contract for serving. KV Cache As Block Sparse MatrixServing systems do not store KV cache as one neat dense tensor. PagedAttention stores KV in pages. Prefix-cache systems may represent shared prefixes through radix trees. Long-context pruning methods may keep sparse KV pages. A kernel library cannot realistically ask every runtime to convert its cache into one contiguous tensor before attention. FlashInfer’s first move is to view those layouts as block-sparse matrices.
Figure 2 maps a page table into a Block Sparse Row (BSR) view. The row axis is query tiles. The column axis is KV-cache pages. Non-zero blocks mark the physical KV pages that a query tile must attend to. If the query tile size is and the KV page/block size is , the logical sparse attention structure can be viewed as:
This is a useful abstraction because a page table, a prefix tree, and a sparse mask are different metadata structures but similar attention work: for each query tile, load a subset of KV blocks, compute score blocks, apply masks/transforms, and reduce. The cost is that sparse KV loading is not the same as dense KV loading. Tensor Cores want regular tiles. KV pages may be scattered. Hopper TMA is excellent for affine contiguous loads, but sparse page gathering is not a simple TMA load. FlashInfer therefore has to bridge a layout abstraction and the actual global-to-shared memory path. Composable Formats For Shared PrefixesThe second storage idea is composable formats. A single BSR block size is not always ideal. Shared prefixes are a good example. If many requests share the same prefix, it is wasteful for each query row to load the same prefix KV through separate thread blocks. Larger row blocks can reuse shared KV in shared memory/registers, but a larger row block can also create fragmentation when requests do not share enough structure.
Figure 3 shows the decomposition. The shared-prefix part uses a larger block size so several queries can access the same KV cache through faster on-chip storage. The unique suffix part remains in a smaller block format. Importantly, this does not require moving KV cache. It changes the sparse metadata and index arrays that describe which submatrices are executed. I find this design practical because shared-prefix serving is common but irregular. Parallel generation, multi-sample decoding, retrieval reuse, system prompts, and prefix caching all create some overlap, but not necessarily enough to justify one monolithic layout. FlashInfer’s composable format gives the runtime a way to say: this submatrix is shared and should be executed with one block shape; this other submatrix is private and should use another.
Figure 4 is the low-level memory consequence. Dense KV loading can use row-index affine transformations. Sparse KV loading needs indirection through BSR indices. FlashInfer tries to make the post-load computation path converge so that the sparse and dense implementations share most of the attention kernel, while only the data-loading module differs. JIT Attention VariantsAttention variants are not a small detail anymore. Current LLM serving stacks use GQA/MQA, RoPE placement differences, ALiBi, sliding windows, logits soft caps, custom masks, FP8 KV cache, speculative decoding masks, and model-specific score transforms. Maintaining a hand-written CUDA kernel for every combination is not sustainable. FlashInfer’s second major design is a customizable CUDA template with JIT specialization.
The figure uses a FlashSigmoid example to show the compiler path. The user describes an attention variant in Python. The JIT compiler inserts variant functors, additional variables/tensors, data types, and kernel traits into CUDA templates. PyTorch JIT then compiles and registers the result as a custom operator. The paper breaks the attention variant into functor-like hooks: QueryTransform, KeyTransform, ValueTransform: transform Q/K/V before attention. LogitsTransform: transform logits before softmax or an alternative score normalization. LogitsMask: apply custom masking, such as sliding window or sparse patterns. OutputTransform: transform the final attention output. This is a good boundary. A serving runtime should not need to fork a whole kernel just to add a score transform or model-specific mask. The variant should be injected into a stable skeleton that still controls tiling, memory movement, and reduction. There is still an engineering tradeoff. JIT specialization improves performance and supports variants, but serving systems cannot compile during every request. The practical path is compile common variants during initialization, cache them, and make runtime metadata selection cheap. Tile Sizes And Decode KernelsFlashInfer also changes tile-size selection. Traditional FlashAttention-2 tile sizes such as are good for dense prefill on A100-like workloads, but inefficient for short-query decode. FlashInfer supports multiple tile sizes, roughly over query tile sizes and KV tile sizes , then selects based on task and hardware constraints. This is the kernel-level version of a simple serving fact: prefill and decode are different phases. Prefill: and both can be large. The kernel has enough compute to use large Tensor Core tiles. Decode: is tiny while grows over time. The pressure shifts to memory bandwidth, occupancy, and load balance. Incremental/chunked prefill: is moderate and the request already has existing KV. The kernel has mixed prefill/decode behavior. Shared-prefix decode: many queries share prefix KV. The kernel should reuse shared KV and avoid duplicated loading. The tile choice is therefore not a fixed property of the GPU. It depends on the serving shape produced by the scheduler. Load-Balanced Runtime SchedulerThe third major design is dynamic scheduling. Sequence lengths change every generation step. Some requests are short, some are long, and long KV ranges may need to be split into several work chunks. If work is assigned naively, some CTAs finish early while others are stuck processing long contexts. FlashInfer defines a simple cost model for one tile:
Given per-request query/output length , KV length , query tile size , and number of CTAs , it computes a maximum KV chunk size:
Each query tile’s KV range is split into chunks no larger than . The chunks are sorted by length. A priority queue assigns the next largest chunk to the CTA with the currently smallest accumulated cost.
The important detail is determinism. Stream-K-style scheduling is a natural reference, but the paper avoids atomic aggregation because serving attention should be reproducible for identical inputs. FlashInfer instead computes a deterministic work plan and a deterministic reduction map.
Figure 6 shows the runtime flow. The attention kernel writes partial attention states for work tiles. A contraction kernel reduces those partial states into final outputs using the attention-state composition operator. The scheduler produces three pieces of plan information:
the work queue for each CTA; the mapping from partial outputs to final outputs; the reduction map used by the contraction stage.
The plan is generated on CPU for each generation step because sequence lengths change. The paper argues this overhead can be amortized across layers because the same plan information is reusable for every layer in that generation step. CUDA Graph BoundaryCUDA Graphs want static launch shapes. LLM serving wants dynamic request lengths. FlashInfer handles this by separating plan and run.
The key idea is visible in the listing: capture the run path in a CUDA Graph, but call plan outside the graph as sequence lengths change. In conceptual pseudocode: # Compile/capture phaseattn.plan(dummy_sequence_info)with torch.cuda.graph(graph): for layer in layers: attn.run(q, k_cache, v_cache, workspace)# Serving loopwhile not finished: sequence_info.update() attn.plan(sequence_info) graph.replay()
This is a clean serving boundary. Runtime dynamism is not ignored; it is moved into a planning step whose outputs are written into a workspace. The actual persistent attention/contraction kernels keep static launch configurations, which preserves CUDA Graph compatibility. End-To-End Serving ResultsThe first end-to-end experiment integrates FlashInfer into SGLang and compares with a Triton backend.
The paper evaluates Llama 3.1 8B on 1xH100 and Llama 3.1 70B on 4xH100 under ShareGPT and synthetic variable-length workloads. The reported result is consistent speedup in both inter-token latency and time-to-first-token. I read this as a sign that the kernel layer matters even when the runtime is already doing continuous batching and scheduling. One caveat: end-to-end serving numbers depend heavily on request rate, SLO policy, model implementation, CPU overhead, and integration quality. The paper’s SGLang result is useful because it tests FlashInfer inside a real serving engine, but I would still reproduce it under the target workload before assuming the same percentage. Kernel Utilization Under Dynamic LengthsKernel-level results explain why the end-to-end result is plausible.
Figure 8 compares achieved bandwidth utilization for decode and FLOPs utilization for prefill under constant, uniform, and skewed sequence length distributions. FlashInfer improves especially in uniform and skewed distributions. That is exactly where static work assignment struggles: different requests have different KV lengths, and the long ones can create tail CTAs. For prefill, the gains are smaller and depend on hardware and shape. This matches intuition. Dense prefill already exposes enough work for FlashAttention-style kernels. Decode and variable-length serving are where dynamic scheduling and tile-size selection matter more. Customization For Long ContextFlashInfer also evaluates a Streaming-LLM path where RoPE and attention can be fused.
The paper reports 28-30% latency reduction in the Streaming-LLM setting and higher bandwidth utilization for the fused RoPE path. The point is not only that RoPE fusion is good. The point is that serving kernels need a customization mechanism. If the runtime or model wants a special score/key transform, an attention engine should make it possible to fuse that transform instead of launching a separate kernel around attention. This connects directly to the JIT design. A fixed attention kernel library can be fast for common cases, but the long tail of model-specific variants will keep appearing. Parallel Generation And Composable FormatsThe MLC-Engine experiment tests composable formats under parallel generation.
The x-axis is composable-format performance and the y-axis is single-format performance. Points above the diagonal mean composable formats are faster. The reported gains are strongest for moderate parallel generation degrees, especially around in the paper’s setting. When is too small, there is not enough shared-prefix reuse to justify the extra structure. When is too large, other costs dominate and the benefit plateaus. This is a useful result because it shows composable formats are not a universal win. They are a tool for a specific shape: enough shared prefix to benefit from a larger shared block, but not so much extra overhead that the metadata path dominates. GQA Head-Group FusionThe appendix includes one implementation detail I find important: head-group fusion for grouped-query attention.
In GQA, multiple query heads share one KV head. A naive decode implementation can assign separate thread blocks to different query heads and reload the same KV cache repeatedly. FlashInfer fuses query heads into the query-length dimension, so the same shared-memory KV load can serve all query heads in the group. Using the figure’s notation:
The fused row index maps back to a token row and a query/output head. Operationally, this is another example of FlashInfer’s serving mindset: when is tiny, use the head group dimension to create more work per KV load. Sparse Versus Dense KV OverheadSparse KV support is only useful if the sparse gathering overhead does not erase the benefit. The appendix compares sparse and dense KV-cache performance.
For decode, the paper reports negligible difference between sparse and dense KV cache in this experiment. For prefill, sparse KV has an approximately 10% gap. That is a reasonable tradeoff: decode is the phase where scattered KV reads are unavoidable in paged/sparse serving, and keeping sparse decode close to dense decode is valuable. The paper also explains a hardware reason for the remaining gap. Hopper TMA helps dense contiguous KV loading, but sparse gathering needs arbitrary row indices, so FlashInfer falls back to async-copy style loading and pointer arithmetic for sparse paths. FlexAttention And Variant BenchmarksThe appendix compares FlashInfer with FlexAttention on AttentionGym-style variants.
FlashInfer is faster in these tables, especially at longer sequence lengths and on variants such as causal attention, logits soft cap, ALiBi, and sliding window. The paper attributes much of the advantage to Hopper-specific features such as warp specialization and TMA, plus CUTLASS-level resource control compared with Triton. That caveat is important: the gap is not purely algorithmic; it is also an implementation and backend maturity result. Shared Prefix And Load-Balancing AblationsThe shared-prefix table is one of the clearest places where composable formats show up numerically.
For a shared prefix length of 32768, composable format with batch size 16 reports 217.42 us versus 945.67 us for the single format in the same batch-size setting. With batch size 64, it reports 254.54 us versus 4090 us. The exact numbers are workload-specific, but the direction is easy to understand: if the prefix is huge and shared, one format should exploit that sharing instead of reloading the same prefix independently. The load-balancing and vLLM tables are also useful because they show limits.
Tables 6 and 7 show that load balancing helps most when sequence lengths are highly variable and long. In the setting, ITL improves from 13.89 ms without load balancing to 8.63 ms with load balancing. TTFT improves from 421.60 ms to 411.02 ms, while Triton is much worse at 566.30 ms. For ShareGPT and shorter variable lengths, the gains are smaller. Table 8 is a useful warning. In the vLLM integration, FlashInfer with e4m3 KV cache reduces median ITL from 12.56 to 10.92, but the bf16 integration does not improve median ITL because host-side Python overhead offsets the kernel gain. This is exactly why kernel papers should include integration results: a faster kernel can disappear under runtime overhead if the boundary is not engineered carefully. Fine-Grained SparsityThe last appendix table compares fine-grained KV sparsity latency against PyTorch SDPA and FlexAttention.
The scale of the difference is large. At sequence length 32768 and page_budget=64, FlashInfer reports 22.371 us, while PyTorch SDPA is 1711.955 us and FlexAttention is 1169.109 us. This is the strongest evidence that the BSR/sparse-row gathering design is not just a cleaner API abstraction. For sparsity patterns such as long-context KV pruning, the right sparse attention kernel can change the cost model. I would still be careful when generalizing this result. Fine-grained sparsity only helps if the model or runtime can produce a useful sparse KV pattern without hurting quality. FlashInfer supplies the kernel substrate; it does not solve the modeling question of which KV pages are safe to drop. How I Would Place FlashInfer In The Serving StackFlashInfer sits below the scheduler and above raw CUDA templates: Request scheduler: decides which requests are batched and when. It supplies dynamic sequence metadata to FlashInfer. KV-cache manager: decides where KV pages live and which pages are shared. It supplies page, ragged, and sparse layout metadata. Attention variant layer: owns model-specific masks, logits transforms, RoPE placement, FP8 KV, and GQA. These become JIT specialization inputs. FlashInfer runtime: owns work queues, chunking, and partial-state reduction. It plans deterministic CTA work and reductions. FlashInfer kernels: execute the actual global/shared/register/Tensor Core work through specialized attention kernels. The most important contract is that the runtime should describe the layout and variant precisely enough, while FlashInfer owns the optimized execution. If that boundary is leaky, every serving framework ends up maintaining special-case kernels. If the boundary is clean, serving systems can focus on batching, SLOs, memory placement, and prefix reuse. Reproduction ChecklistIf I were reproducing this paper or evaluating FlashInfer for a serving system, I would not start with only one tokens/s benchmark. I would test the following cases separately:
Single-token decode with long KV cache. This is the most memory-bound case and should reveal tile-size and GQA behavior. Ragged prefill. Variable prompt lengths should test dynamic scheduling and packed/ragged metadata handling. Paged KV decode. This checks the page-table path and sparse/dense gather overhead. Shared-prefix parallel generation. This is where composable formats should matter. A custom attention variant. Sliding window, logits soft cap, ALiBi, or fused RoPE can test whether JIT specialization actually avoids extra launches. CUDA Graph replay. Plan/run separation should avoid graph recapture while still adapting to changing sequence lengths. End-to-end integration. Measure TTFT, ITL, throughput, CPU overhead, and graph replay overhead inside vLLM/SGLang/MLC, not only kernel microbenchmarks.
The vLLM appendix table is the reason for the last item. A kernel can be excellent and still fail to improve a serving system if the host/runtime integration adds enough overhead. Limitations And Open QuestionsFlashInfer increases the expressiveness of the attention-kernel layer, but that also increases API surface area. The hard questions are mostly at boundaries:
How many variants should be JIT-compiled and cached ahead of time? How should a serving runtime choose among composable formats without expensive planning? When does sparse KV metadata overhead exceed sparse compute savings? Can the scheduler move more planning work to device without breaking CUDA Graph compatibility? How should kernel libraries expose new hardware features without making runtime integration too fragile?
The paper does not fully answer all of these. It does show a plausible architecture: block-sparse/composable layouts for KV heterogeneity, JIT templates for attention variants, and deterministic load-balanced planning for runtime dynamism. TakeawaysFlashInfer’s core idea is that LLM serving attention should be designed around runtime-generated shapes, not training-time dense attention benchmarks. The useful mental model is:
The paper is valuable because it connects all four:
BSR and composable formats represent paged, sparse, and shared-prefix KV layouts. JIT templates specialize model-specific attention variants without rewriting the whole kernel. Attention-state composition makes split KV chunks reducible exactly. Load-balanced planning keeps CTAs busy under ragged sequence lengths. Plan/run separation preserves CUDA Graph replay while sequence lengths change.
My main takeaway for CUDA work is simple: a beautiful dense attention kernel is not enough for serving. The real kernel has to read the KV cache layout that the runtime actually produces, fuse the transforms that the model actually uses, and survive the dynamic sequence lengths that users actually send.

entry.title: Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pre-Training
entry.content:
Paper / Code GPT-1 is small by modern LLM standards, but the paper is important because it makes the GPT recipe concrete: train a left-to-right Transformer language model on unlabeled text, reshape downstream tasks into token sequences, then fine-tune the same backbone with only a lightweight task head. The paper is not about prompting yet. It still relies on supervised fine-tuning for each benchmark. The interesting part is that most of the modeling burden has already moved into one reusable decoder-only Transformer. MotivationBefore GPT-1, pre-trained word vectors and contextual encoders were already useful, but a lot of NLP systems still had a task-specific architecture: one model for entailment, another for similarity, another for multiple choice QA. GPT-1 tries to remove that split. It asks whether a generative language model can become a general initialization for many natural language understanding tasks. The bet is simple:
Unlabeled text is abundant, so the expensive part of representation learning should happen there. A left-to-right language model is a dense self-supervised objective, because every token becomes a prediction target. If downstream inputs can be converted into sequences, the same Transformer can be reused with minimal changes.
This is why the title says “generative pre-training” even though the benchmarks are mostly understanding tasks. The Two-Stage RecipeThe training pipeline has two stages:
Unsupervised pre-training on BooksCorpus with a standard next-token objective. Supervised fine-tuning on each target dataset with a task-specific input format and a linear prediction head.
The model is a 12-layer decoder-only Transformer with masked self-attention, 768-dimensional hidden states, 12 attention heads, and 3072-dimensional feed-forward layers. It uses a 40k BPE vocabulary and a context size of 512 tokens. These details look modest now, but they matter historically: the paper already has the core GPT shape, just at a smaller scale. Formula Reading: Language ModelingThe pre-training objective is:
Here is the unsupervised token corpus, is the current token, and is the left context window. The model parameters are . My reading of this formula:
It is maximum likelihood estimation for next-token prediction. The model only sees tokens to the left of , so it can be used for generation. Every position in the corpus supplies a training signal, which is why this objective scales naturally with raw text. There is no task label in this objective. The model has to learn syntax, entities, discourse patterns, and world regularities only because those help predict the next token.
This objective is weaker than a supervised task objective in the short term, but it is much easier to scale because the labels are the tokens themselves. Formula Reading: Decoder-Only TransformerThe paper writes the model as:
The first line maps token ids into embeddings and adds learned positional embeddings. is the token embedding matrix and is the position embedding matrix. This is where the model gets both lexical identity and order. The second line applies the same kind of Transformer decoder block repeatedly. Each block contains masked self-attention and position-wise feed-forward layers. Masked self-attention is the important constraint: position can attend to earlier tokens, but not future tokens. The third line projects the final hidden state back to vocabulary logits, then applies softmax. The use of means the output projection is tied to the token embedding space. That coupling is useful because input and output words live in the same vocabulary geometry. The architecture is therefore already the modern GPT skeleton:
token embeddings plus positional embeddings, a stack of causal Transformer blocks, a vocabulary distribution at every position.
Formula Reading: Supervised Fine-TuningAfter pre-training, GPT-1 adapts to a labeled dataset . For an input sequence , the final Transformer activation is passed to a linear classifier:
The notation means the hidden state at the final layer and the selected final position . is the only new task head. This formula hides an important design choice. GPT-1 does not add a bidirectional encoder or a task-specific reasoning module. It simply turns the task input into a sequence, runs the decoder, and reads one hidden vector. The model has to place all task-relevant information into that final representation. The supervised objective is:
This is standard supervised log-likelihood. Compared with , the target is now a task label rather than the next token. The pre-trained model gives a strong initialization; the fine-tuning objective tells it which part of the representation matters for the benchmark. Finally, GPT-1 adds the language-model objective back during fine-tuning:
This is one of the most practical formulas in the paper. makes the model solve the supervised task, while keeps the model close to the language-modeling behavior that made the representation useful in the first place. The paper reports that this auxiliary LM loss improves generalization and speeds convergence. My interpretation: fine-tuning datasets are small compared with BooksCorpus. If the model only optimizes , it can over-specialize quickly. The auxiliary LM loss is a regularizer that says: adapt to the task, but do not forget how language works. Input Transformations Figure: GPT-1 converts different supervised tasks into token sequences that a decoder-only Transformer can process. This figure is the paper’s interface design. Different NLP tasks have different structures, but GPT-1 reduces them to the same computation:
Classification: [start] text [extract] Entailment: [start] premise [delim] hypothesis [extract] Similarity: encode both possible orders, because the relation is symmetric. Multiple choice: encode each candidate answer separately and score the candidates with a softmax.
The special tokens matter. [delim] tells the model where fields change, and [extract] marks the position whose hidden state will be used for prediction. This is an early version of the later “format the task as text” idea. GPT-1 still fine-tunes, but the task adapter is mostly a serialization scheme. Datasets Figure: The benchmark set covers natural language inference, question answering, similarity, and classification. The dataset table is useful because it shows the intended scope. GPT-1 is not tuned for one benchmark family. It is evaluated on NLI datasets such as SNLI and MultiNLI, question answering datasets such as RACE, similarity/paraphrase datasets such as QQP and MRPC, and sentiment/classification datasets such as SST-2 and CoLA. The important point is not that GPT-1 wins every row. The point is that the same pre-trained decoder backbone is reused across all rows with very small task-specific changes. Results: NLI and QA Figure: GPT-1 improves several natural language inference and question-answering benchmarks after generative pre-training. The NLI results are where the method looks especially strong. Entailment tasks require the model to compare two text spans, and GPT-1 handles this by concatenating premise and hypothesis with a delimiter. That is not obviously enough; a decoder-only model reads left to right, so the hypothesis can attend to the premise, but the premise cannot attend back to the hypothesis. The fact that this works is a useful lesson. For many transfer tasks, perfect architectural symmetry is less important than having a strong pre-trained text model and a stable input convention. The sequence format lets the final hidden state summarize both fields. RACE is also interesting because it is a multiple choice reading comprehension dataset. GPT-1 scores each answer candidate independently, then normalizes over candidates. This is still supervised fine-tuning, but the candidate-scoring pattern is close to how later language models handle multiple-choice prompts. Results: Similarity and Classification Figure: GPT-1 also transfers to semantic similarity and single-sentence classification tasks. The similarity setup is one of the more clever parts of the paper. For tasks like paraphrase detection, the relation between sentence A and sentence B should be symmetric. A left-to-right decoder is not symmetric by default, so GPT-1 runs both orders and combines the resulting representations before prediction. This is a small engineering choice, but it shows the paper’s general approach: do not redesign the model unless necessary; reshape the input and output around the same decoder. Analysis: Which Layers Transfer? Figure: More transferred Transformer layers help downstream performance, and more LM pre-training updates improve normalized task scores. The left plot asks how many pre-trained layers should be transferred. If only the embedding layer mattered, transferring deeper Transformer blocks would not help much. The paper shows the opposite: performance improves as more layers are transferred. My interpretation is that the LM is not just learning word lookup tables. Middle and upper Transformer layers contain reusable composition behavior: entity tracking, phrase-level semantics, long-range dependency handling, and patterns that help compare text spans. This is why full-model fine-tuning became the standard recipe. The right plot shows downstream task performance as pre-training continues. The trend is not yet a formal scaling law, but the direction is clear: more language-model pre-training improves multiple downstream tasks. GPT-2 and GPT-3 later turn this observation into a central scaling argument. Ablations Figure: The ablation table separates the effects of pre-training, auxiliary LM loss, and Transformer architecture. The ablation table is the part I would check before trusting the paper’s story. Three lessons stand out:
Removing pre-training hurts badly. That confirms the result is not just a good supervised Transformer. The auxiliary LM objective helps especially on larger datasets and NLI-style tasks. It is not magic, but it stabilizes fine-tuning. Replacing the Transformer with an LSTM under the same framework is weaker. The gain is not only from the two-stage training recipe; the Transformer backbone matters.
The paper is careful here: it does not claim the auxiliary objective always helps. Smaller datasets can behave differently. That is a useful reminder that regularization interacts with data size. What GPT-1 Did Not SolveGPT-1 is still far from a modern instruction-following model. It requires supervised fine-tuning for each task. It uses a 512-token context window. It does not show robust zero-shot or few-shot prompting. The pre-training data is BooksCorpus, not the broad web-scale mixture used later. It also has no RLHF, no instruction tuning, and no chat interface. But those limitations make the contribution clearer. GPT-1 solved the transfer interface for decoder-only language models:
one generative pre-training objective, one causal Transformer backbone, task conversion through token formatting, fine-tuning with a small prediction head.
TakeawayGPT-1 is the bridge between pre-trained representations and the later GPT-style LLM interface. The formulas are simple, but they line up cleanly:
learns a general language model from raw text. The Transformer equations define a reusable causal decoder. adapts that decoder to labeled tasks. keeps language modeling alive during fine-tuning.
The paper does not yet show that a language model can follow arbitrary prompts. It shows the earlier and necessary step: a generatively pre-trained decoder-only Transformer can be a general-purpose initialization for many NLP tasks.

entry.title: Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners
entry.content:
Paper / Code GPT-2 is the paper where the GPT line stops looking like only “pre-train then fine-tune” and starts looking like a general text interface. The model is still a decoder-only Transformer trained with next-token prediction. The important change is how the paper treats downstream tasks: instead of adding a supervised head for every dataset, it asks whether the language model can infer the task from natural language context. The answer is mixed but important. GPT-2 is not a reliable instruction follower, but it shows that scaling a generic language model on broad web text produces measurable zero-shot transfer across many tasks. From Fine-Tuning to Zero-Shot TransferGPT-1 used supervised fine-tuning. GPT-2 tries to remove that dependency. The central idea is that many tasks already appear in text as demonstrations:
translation pairs, question-answer formats, article-summary patterns, cloze questions, multiple-choice patterns, natural language instructions.
If a language model learns these formats during next-token prediction, then at test time the task can be specified as text rather than as a new output head.
Figure: Zero-shot task performance generally improves as GPT-2 scales from 117M to 1.5B parameters. This figure is the paper’s main claim in one picture. The curves are noisy, and some tasks remain weak, but the trend is hard to ignore: larger WebText language models become better zero-shot task solvers. The paper is not claiming that zero-shot is always competitive with supervised SOTA. It is showing that task transfer emerges from the language-modeling objective itself. Formula Reading: Language Modeling as Multitask LearningThe standard autoregressive factorization is:
This is just the chain rule applied to a sequence. GPT-2 trains the model to predict each symbol from its previous context. The interesting reinterpretation is:
In a supervised system, the task is often implicit in the architecture or the dataset. In GPT-2, the task is another part of the sequence. For example, “translate English to French” and a few translation-like examples can all be represented as text. The same next-token objective can learn to continue that pattern. My reading:
The language model objective is unchanged. The training distribution is widened so it contains many naturally occurring task demonstrations. The model has to infer the latent task from context because that helps next-token prediction. Zero-shot transfer is therefore not a new objective. It is a consequence of modeling a broad enough text distribution with enough capacity.
For evaluation, perplexity is still the basic language-model metric:
Lower perplexity means the model assigns higher probability to the observed tokens. The paper repeatedly uses perplexity to check whether scaling is still improving the base language model, not only downstream tasks. WebTextGPT-2 builds WebText from outbound Reddit links that received enough user approval. The point is not that Reddit itself is the corpus; Reddit is used as a filter for linked web pages. The preliminary dataset contains over 8 million documents and about 40GB of text, with Wikipedia removed to reduce overlap with common benchmarks.
Figure: WebText contains naturally occurring task-like patterns, including translation examples. This table is a good reminder that “unsupervised multitask learning” does not mean tasks are absent. It means task supervision is not manually labeled into separate datasets. The web contains many semi-structured examples. A sufficiently large LM can treat those examples as part of its language distribution. This also explains why data quality matters. If the corpus contains clean examples of a task format, zero-shot transfer becomes easier. If a task format is rare, noisy, or adversarial, the model has less to imitate. Input Representation: Byte-Level BPEGPT-2 uses byte-level BPE. This is a practical compromise between character-level and word-level modeling. Word-level tokenization is efficient but has out-of-vocabulary problems. Pure byte-level modeling can represent any string, but long byte sequences make optimization harder. Byte-level BPE starts from bytes and merges frequent byte sequences, so it can represent arbitrary Unicode text without an unknown-token failure mode. The paper also discusses preventing bad BPE merges across character categories, with an exception for spaces. This sounds like a tokenizer detail, but it matters because GPT-2 is evaluated on many datasets with different preprocessing conventions. A robust tokenizer reduces the need for dataset-specific text cleaning. Architecture and Scale Figure: GPT-2 evaluates four model sizes from 117M to 1542M parameters. GPT-2 is architecturally close to GPT-1: a decoder-only Transformer trained left to right. The changes are mostly scale and engineering:
Model sizes: 117M, 345M, 762M, and 1542M parameters. Layers: 12, 24, 36, and 48. Hidden sizes: 768, 1024, 1280, and 1600. Context length: 1024 tokens. Vocabulary size: 50,257 byte-level BPE tokens. LayerNorm is moved to the input of each sub-block, similar to pre-activation residual networks. An extra LayerNorm is added after the final self-attention block. Residual weights are initialized with a factor of , where is the number of residual layers.
The scaling is worth pausing on. In a deep residual network, activations accumulate across many residual branches. If each branch starts too large, the sum can become unstable. Scaling by keeps the residual stream better behaved at initialization as depth grows. GPT-2 therefore did not need a new conceptual architecture. It needed a larger and more stable version of the GPT-1 decoder. Zero-Shot Language Modeling Results Figure: GPT-2 achieves strong zero-shot results on several language-modeling datasets, while still failing badly on some domain-specific settings. Table 3 is a useful sanity check. GPT-2 improves on 7 of 8 tested language-modeling datasets in the zero-shot setting. LAMBADA is the most striking row: the largest model greatly lowers perplexity and raises accuracy, showing better long-range dependency modeling. The weak 1 Billion Word Benchmark result is also informative. That dataset uses sentence-level shuffling, so it removes the kind of long document context that GPT-2 is designed to use. The failure is not just “model too small”; it is a mismatch between evaluation format and training distribution. Cloze and Commonsense Scaling Figure: Children’s Book Test performance improves with scale. CBT is a cloze-style benchmark. The model has to choose a missing word from candidates. The scale trend here supports the same pattern as Figure 1: a larger generic LM becomes better at a task without adding a task head.
Figure: Winograd Schema performance also improves as the WebText LM becomes larger. Winograd-style tasks test pronoun resolution and commonsense. GPT-2 does not solve the problem in a robust way, but the scaling trend matters. It suggests that some commonsense-like behavior can be learned as statistical regularity in text, even without explicit symbolic supervision. Summarization Figure: GPT-2 can imitate summarization format, but ROUGE scores remain far behind supervised systems. Summarization is one of the clearest “capability but not reliability” results. GPT-2 often recognizes that a prompt is asking for a summary. It can produce text with the right shape. But the measured ROUGE scores are weak compared with supervised systems. My interpretation is that GPT-2 learned the genre of summarization before it learned robust content selection. It can generate plausible summary-like text, but it does not consistently preserve the exact information needed for benchmark scoring. This is a pattern that continues in later LLMs: format imitation appears earlier than faithful task execution. Data Overlap and Memorization Figure: GPT-2 measures 8-gram overlap between evaluation datasets and training data. The overlap analysis is one of the more responsible parts of the paper. A web-scale corpus can accidentally include benchmark examples. If a model performs well because it memorized test items, then the zero-shot claim is weaker. The authors build Bloom filters over WebText token 8-grams and compare overlap rates. The result is nuanced:
Some benchmark test sets overlap with WebText. Many benchmarks also overlap with their own training sets. Removing LAMBADA examples with overlap changes the score only slightly. The issue is real enough to measure, but it does not explain all GPT-2 gains.
This section also anticipates a much bigger problem for GPT-3 and later models. As pre-training corpora get larger, contamination is no longer a corner case; it becomes a standard evaluation concern. Is GPT-2 Still Underfitting? Figure: WebText train and test perplexity both improve with model size. This figure is easy to overlook, but it is central to the scaling story. Both train and test perplexity decrease as model size increases. The test curve does not show the model overfitting WebText and getting worse. Instead, the largest model still appears underfit. That means the paper has a clear next step: make the model bigger and train it with more compute. GPT-3 is almost the direct continuation of this plot. Qualitative Generation Figure: GPT-2 generations can preserve the requested format but still drift in factual content and task faithfulness. The qualitative examples are useful because benchmark numbers do not fully describe the model. GPT-2 can write coherent paragraphs and maintain local style. It can also hallucinate, drift, repeat, and confidently produce unsupported details. That distinction matters:
Coherence is not the same as factuality. Recognizing a task format is not the same as following the user’s intent. Good next-token prediction can produce impressive samples without guaranteeing controllability.
This is why later work moves toward instruction tuning and RLHF. GPT-2 proves that the base LM has broad latent capabilities, but it does not make those capabilities easy to steer. What GPT-2 ContributesThe paper’s contribution is not a single new layer or loss function. It is a shift in how to view language modeling. GPT-1 says: pre-train a decoder and fine-tune it for tasks. GPT-2 says: if the pre-training distribution is broad enough, task behavior can be expressed and invoked as text. The technical ingredients are ordinary but aligned:
a causal Transformer, byte-level BPE, a larger context window, WebText as a broad training distribution, larger model capacity, zero-shot evaluation through natural-language formatting.
LimitationsGPT-2 has several clear limitations. First, zero-shot performance is inconsistent. Some benchmarks improve smoothly with scale; others remain weak or depend heavily on prompt phrasing. Second, the model is not instruction-tuned. It continues text. If the continuation happens to match a task, it looks like task solving. If the context is ambiguous, the model has no explicit preference for being helpful, concise, or truthful. Third, web text introduces evaluation and safety problems. It gives broad coverage, but it also carries bias, duplication, low-quality text, and possible benchmark contamination. Fourth, the paper’s strongest evidence is trend-based. Individual scores can be unimpressive, but the trend with scale points toward a new regime. TakeawayGPT-2 is the turning point where the GPT series starts to treat language modeling as an interface for many tasks. The key formula is still next-token prediction, but the interpretation changes:
The model is not yet a dependable few-shot learner. It is not aligned. It is not a robust assistant. But it shows that many tasks can be induced by context without gradient updates. GPT-3 takes that observation and scales it until few-shot prompting becomes the headline.

entry.title: Language Models are Few-Shot Learners
entry.content:
Paper GPT-3 is not important because it changes the Transformer architecture. It is important because it changes the way the model is used. The model is still a decoder-only autoregressive language model, but the task is now placed in the context window as natural language instructions and examples. The parameters do not change at evaluation time. This paper turns the GPT-2 zero-shot observation into a systematic evaluation protocol: zero-shot, one-shot, and few-shot prompting. What Changed from GPT-2GPT-2 showed that a large WebText language model can perform some tasks without supervised fine-tuning. GPT-3 asks a sharper question: if we scale the same idea much further, can the model adapt to a new task from examples in the prompt? The paper’s answer is: often yes, but not uniformly. GPT-3 does very well on tasks where the input-output format can be inferred from examples and where the needed knowledge is likely present in pre-training. It still struggles on tasks requiring robust reasoning, exact symbol manipulation, calibrated truthfulness, and reliable instruction following. That mix is what makes the paper useful: it shows both the strength and the boundary of in-context learning.
Figure: Larger models make more effective use of examples placed in the context window. This figure is the shortest version of the paper’s thesis. The 175B model benefits much more from additional in-context examples than the 13B or 1.3B models. The natural language prompt helps, but scale changes how efficiently the model extracts a task from demonstrations. Formula Reading: The Base LM ObjectiveThe training objective is the same autoregressive negative log-likelihood:
This formula says that every token is predicted from all previous tokens in the context. There is no explicit supervised task label, no special loss for reasoning, and no gradient update for downstream tasks in the evaluation protocol. My interpretation:
The objective is local next-token prediction, but the context can contain task descriptions, demonstrations, and partial answers. If the model learns to use patterns in the prefix to predict the next token, then “learning from examples in the prompt” is a possible behavior under the same objective. GPT-3’s few-shot ability is therefore not a separate training algorithm. It is a behavior induced by a large conditional language model.
That point is easy to miss. GPT-3 is still just optimizing next-token prediction during training. The new thing is that the prefix at inference time becomes a temporary task specification. Evaluation Settings Figure: GPT-3 distinguishes zero-shot, one-shot, few-shot, and traditional fine-tuning. The figure is the interface definition for the whole paper. Zero-shot means the model receives a task description and the test input, but no solved example. One-shot means it receives one solved example before the test input. Few-shot means it receives several solved examples. Fine-tuning is shown for contrast: GPT-3 does not perform gradient updates in the evaluated zero/one/few-shot settings. For a prompt with demonstrations, I read the conditional distribution as:
Here is the sequence of input-output demonstrations and is the query. The model predicts only through a forward pass. The examples change the hidden activations, not the weights. This is the central conceptual shift. In supervised fine-tuning, the model stores task adaptation in parameters. In in-context learning, the model stores task adaptation in the activations induced by the prompt. Scoring CompletionsFor multiple-choice tasks, GPT-3 scores each candidate completion under the language model. A length-normalized score can be written as:
The division by matters because longer completions accumulate more log probabilities and would otherwise be penalized unfairly. For some datasets, the paper also normalizes by an unconditional answer probability:
This is equivalent to the ratio:
My reading: this normalization reduces the advantage of completions that are generally common regardless of the question. The model should prefer a candidate because it fits the context, not because it is a frequent answer string. Model Family Figure: GPT-3 trains a family of decoder-only models from 125M to 175B parameters. The largest model has 175B parameters, 96 layers, hidden size 12288, 96 attention heads, head dimension 128, and a 2048-token context window. All models are trained for 300B tokens. Batch size is measured in tokens, reaching 3.2M tokens for the largest model, while learning rate decreases as model size grows. The table is important because the paper is built around scaling comparisons. GPT-3 is not evaluated as one isolated model. The smaller models show whether a result appears gradually with scale or suddenly only at 175B. Training Data Figure: GPT-3 mixes filtered Common Crawl with WebText2, Books, and Wikipedia. The training mix is not proportional to raw dataset size. Filtered Common Crawl is by far the largest source, but higher-quality datasets are upsampled. This is why the “epochs elapsed” column differs across sources. Wikipedia is only 3B tokens, but it is seen more often than filtered Common Crawl relative to its size. The data recipe matters for interpreting results. GPT-3’s knowledge and task behavior come from a broad web-scale corpus, but that also increases risks:
benchmark contamination, duplicated text, social bias, low-quality pages, memorization of rare strings.
The paper spends real space on these issues, which is necessary for a model trained on this kind of data. Training Compute Figure: GPT-3 175B uses much more training compute than earlier BERT, RoBERTa, and T5-scale models. The compute figure gives the physical meaning of “scale.” GPT-3 175B is not just a bigger checkpoint; it represents a jump in training compute. The model family is also designed so the smaller models act as controlled points on a scaling curve. This matters because the paper is not claiming that 175B parameters alone are magic. It is studying the interaction of parameter count, data, and compute under the same language-modeling objective. Formula Reading: Compute Scaling Figure: Validation loss follows a power-law trend as training compute increases. The figure includes the fitted relation:
Here is validation loss and is compute. The exponent is small, which means loss improves slowly with compute. But on log-log axes, the improvement is smooth over a large range. My interpretation:
There is no obvious saturation at GPT-3 scale in this plot. Scaling is expensive because the exponent is shallow. The smooth curve supports the paper’s decision to extrapolate from smaller models. Many downstream gains are easier to believe when the base LM loss itself follows a predictable scaling trend.
This is why scaling laws became central after GPT-3. The downstream behavior is complicated, but the base loss gives a surprisingly regular signal. Aggregate Performance Figure: Average accuracy across 42 benchmarks improves with model size, and few-shot improves fastest. This figure is the headline result. Zero-shot improves with scale. One-shot improves more. Few-shot improves the most. That pattern supports the in-context learning story: larger models are not only better language models; they are also better at using examples in the prompt. The faint background lines are individual tasks, and they are noisy. The aggregate trend should not be read as every task improving equally. It means the average direction is strong enough to survive the task-level variance. LAMBADA and Completion Tasks Figure: GPT-3 few-shot strongly improves LAMBADA accuracy and lowers perplexity. LAMBADA is useful because it tests whether the model can predict a final word that depends on a long context. The few-shot setting also lets the prompt define the expected answer format. That is important because a raw LM may continue a sentence with multiple words, while LAMBADA expects exactly one word. The result illustrates a recurring GPT-3 pattern: examples in the context do two things at once. They describe the task and constrain the output format. Closed-Book Question Answering Figure: GPT-3 is much stronger on TriviaQA than on Natural Questions or WebQuestions. In closed-book QA, the model cannot retrieve documents. It must answer from parameters and the prompt. GPT-3 performs especially well on TriviaQA, where few-shot reaches 71.2. Natural Questions and WebQuestions are much lower.
Figure: TriviaQA accuracy improves smoothly with model size, with few-shot above one-shot and zero-shot. My interpretation is that this section shows both knowledge storage and task-format sensitivity. Scaling helps the model store more factual associations, but the exact dataset distribution still matters. TriviaQA aligns better with the model’s pre-training distribution and prompt format than the other QA sets. Translation Figure: GPT-3 few-shot translation improves with scale and is strongest when translating into English. Translation is one of the most interesting comparisons with GPT-2. GPT-2 already showed that translation pairs appear in web text. GPT-3 scales that behavior until few-shot translation becomes competitive with previous unsupervised NMT work on several language pairs. The asymmetry matters: translation into English is stronger than translation from English. That makes sense for an English-dominant language model. The model has richer target-language statistics for English output, so decoding into English is easier. Winograd and Commonsense Figure: GPT-3 improves on Winogrande with scale, but still remains below fine-tuned SOTA. Winograd-style tasks are meant to test commonsense disambiguation. GPT-3 improves with scale, especially in the few-shot setting, but the result is not a full solution. The asterisks in the table also remind us that contamination analysis matters for some benchmarks.
Figure: PhysicalQA and related commonsense benchmarks show smoother improvements, with PIQA above fine-tuned SOTA in the reported setting. PIQA is a physical commonsense benchmark. GPT-3 does well here, but the ARC and OpenBookQA rows are more modest. This split is a useful warning: “commonsense” is not one capability. Some questions can be answered from common textual patterns, while others need more structured or grounded reasoning. Reading Comprehension and SuperGLUE Figure: CoQA improves smoothly with scale, and the SuperGLUE table shows a mixed task-by-task picture. CoQA is conversational reading comprehension. The few-shot curve approaches human and fine-tuned model performance but does not fully close the gap. The SuperGLUE table below it is more mixed. Some tasks show strong signs of life, while others remain weak.
