Figure: SuperGLUE improves with both model size and number of in-context examples. This figure is one of the clearest demonstrations of in-context learning. The right panel fixes the model and increases the number of examples in context. Performance rises as more examples are provided. That is exactly what we want to see if examples are being used as task information rather than decorative text. Still, the curve is not a replacement for fine-tuning. It shows that context examples help, but the final score remains below the strongest supervised systems. Arithmetic and Symbol Manipulation Figure: Arithmetic performance is near zero for smaller models and improves sharply at 175B for several tasks. Arithmetic is a good stress test because it is less forgiving than language continuation. Two-digit addition can be memorized statistically, but five-digit arithmetic and multi-step operations require more systematic manipulation. The figure shows a sharp jump at 175B for some tasks, especially two- and three-digit addition/subtraction. But the model is still weak on harder arithmetic. This is not a calculator; it is a language model that has learned some algorithm-like behavior from text.
Figure: GPT-3 175B improves from zero-shot to one-shot to few-shot on arithmetic and word manipulation tasks, but remains brittle. The table makes the limitation concrete. Few-shot helps, but performance drops quickly as digit length or symbolic difficulty increases. Word unscrambling and reversed-word tasks are also uneven. These results are useful because they show where scale alone is not enough for reliable algorithmic generalization. Few-Shot Grammar Correction Figure: A few grammar-correction examples in the prompt are enough for GPT-3 to continue the pattern. This qualitative example is close to how people later used LLMs in practice. The prompt gives several bad-English/good-English pairs, and GPT-3 continues with corrected outputs. There is no gradient update and no explicit grammar correction head. The important point is format induction. GPT-3 is not only answering isolated benchmark questions. It can infer a text transformation from examples and keep applying it for several more lines. Human Detection of Model-Generated Text Figure: Human ability to detect generated news articles decreases as model size increases. This result is not just a capability benchmark; it is a risk signal. Larger models generate text that is harder for humans to distinguish from human-written news-style articles. The curve approaches random chance for the largest model in the tested setup. The paper uses this to motivate misuse concerns. A model that can produce plausible long-form text has obvious benefits, but it also creates detection, attribution, and trust problems. Training Curves Figure: Training and validation loss both continue improving over 300B tokens. The training curves are a useful overfitting check. Validation loss continues to decrease, and the train-validation gap does not explode with scale. This supports the paper’s claim that the models are still learning useful distributional structure rather than merely memorizing the training set. The curves also show why the paper’s conclusions are expensive. Improvements continue, but they require very large compute budgets. Contamination Analysis Figure: Most benchmark changes are small after clean-data filtering, but some tasks are flagged for review. Data contamination is a major concern for GPT-3 because the training corpus is huge and web-derived. The plot compares performance changes when evaluating on verified clean subsets. Most points stay near zero, which suggests contamination does not explain most results. But the flagged tasks still matter. PIQA and Winograd receive special attention, and the paper marks affected results. My reading is conservative: contamination analysis does not invalidate GPT-3, but any web-scale LM benchmark should be treated as an estimate rather than a perfectly isolated measurement. Bias and Social Effects Figure: The 175B model shows gender-skewed descriptive word associations in generated text. The bias table is a reminder that language modeling learns the distribution it is trained on. If the corpus contains skewed associations, the model can reproduce or amplify them. This is not a side issue for deployment; it follows directly from the same objective that gives the model broad capabilities. The paper also discusses misuse, fairness, representation, and environmental cost. Those sections are less mathematically central than the scaling results, but they are technically important. A model that can generalize from prompts can also generalize harmful patterns from prompts. What In-Context Learning Is and Is NotThe phrase “few-shot learner” can be misleading if read too literally. GPT-3 is not running SGD inside the prompt. There is no parameter update. A more precise description is:
The model has learned during pre-training to map certain contexts to likely continuations. When the context contains examples, the continuation can follow the demonstrated mapping. This looks like learning because behavior changes with examples, but the mechanism is forward-pass conditioning. This distinction helps explain both strengths and failures:
It can adapt instantly to formats that resemble text patterns seen in pre-training. It is sensitive to wording, ordering, and example choice. It can fail at systematic rules that are easy to state but rare or hard to infer from surface text. It does not know when the prompt asks for an impossible or underspecified task.
LimitationsGPT-3 is impressive, but the paper is explicit about its limits. First, context length is finite. The 2048-token window typically fits 10 to 100 examples, depending on the task. Many real tasks need more evidence than that. Second, few-shot prompting is unstable. Example selection, ordering, label words, and formatting can change results. Third, the model is not instruction-aligned. It predicts continuations. It does not reliably optimize helpfulness, honesty, or harmlessness. Fourth, symbolic reasoning remains brittle. Arithmetic and word manipulation improve with scale but do not become dependable algorithms. Fifth, evaluation is contaminated by the realities of web data. The paper checks overlap, but perfect isolation is difficult. TakeawayGPT-3’s core contribution is not a new loss or a new block. It is the demonstration that scale changes the interface:
GPT-1 showed that a generatively pre-trained decoder can be fine-tuned for NLP tasks. GPT-2 showed that zero-shot behavior appears when the LM is trained on broad web text. GPT-3 shows that examples in the context can become a practical task interface. The paper also makes the remaining problems visible: alignment, factuality, contamination, bias, and reliable reasoning. Those problems are not footnotes. They are the direct next questions raised by making language models large enough to use through prompts.

entry.title: GPTQ: One-Shot LLM Weight Quantization
entry.content:
Paper: GPTQ: Accurate Post-Training Quantization for Generative Pre-trained Transformers GPTQ is one of the papers that made low-bit LLM deployment feel practical. The target is not a small CNN and not a quantization-aware training recipe. The target is a pretrained decoder LLM with billions to hundreds of billions of parameters, and the constraint is harsh: compress the weights to 3 or 4 bits without full retraining. The paper should be read as a scaling paper for second-order post-training quantization. The core mathematical idea comes from Optimal Brain Quantization (OBQ): when a weight is rounded, update the remaining weights so the layer output changes as little as possible on calibration activations. GPTQ keeps that idea, but changes the implementation enough that it can run on GPT-scale matrices. The ProblemLLM inference is often dominated by moving weights through memory. In batch-1 decoding, each generated token touches a huge number of model weights while doing relatively small matrix-vector work. Weight-only quantization directly attacks this bottleneck: store weights in 3 or 4 bits, dequantize them inside the kernel, and keep activations in FP16/BF16. This is different from full INT8 or W8A8 quantization. GPTQ is primarily a W3A16/W4A16 method:
weights are quantized; activations stay high precision; LayerNorm, attention softmax, residual paths, and KV cache are not the main quantization target; the serving win depends on low-bit weight kernels and memory bandwidth.
The local objective for a linear layer is straightforward. Given a full-precision weight matrix (W) and calibration inputs (X), choose quantized weights (\hat{W}) that preserve the layer output:
If (X) contains representative activations, this objective is a direct proxy for “keep this layer’s behavior unchanged on real model inputs.” Why Round-To-Nearest Is Not Enough Figure cropped from the paper PDF: GPTQ avoids the collapse seen with naive round-to-nearest, especially at 3-bit precision. The first figure is the paper’s main motivation. Round-to-nearest (RTN) can work at mild compression, but it breaks badly when bit width becomes aggressive. For large OPT and BLOOM models, GPTQ stays much closer to the FP16 perplexity curve, while RTN can produce huge perplexity spikes at 3 bits. This is the important point: low-bit quantization error is not just independent noise. Rounding one weight changes the output, but the remaining unrounded weights can compensate for some of that change. Plain RTN throws away this degree of freedom. Second-order PTQ uses the Hessian of the layer reconstruction objective to decide how to compensate. For the least-squares objective above, the relevant Hessian is proportional to
The inverse Hessian tells us how an error in one coordinate can be distributed into the remaining coordinates with minimal output damage. From OBQ To GPTQOBQ quantizes one weight at a time. Suppose (w_q) is the next weight to quantize and (F) is the set of still-unquantized weights in that row. OBQ estimates the loss increase of quantizing (w_q), then applies a compensating update to the remaining weights: $$\delta_F =-\frac{w_q - \operatorname{quant}(w_q)}{[H_F^{-1}]{qq}}(H_F^{-1}){:,q}.$$ This is the right shape of update: the error introduced by quantizing one coordinate is pushed into the remaining coordinates according to inverse-Hessian geometry. The issue is cost. Doing this naively for every weight in a huge transformer matrix is far too expensive. GPTQ keeps the row-wise reconstruction view but makes several implementation changes:
It uses a fixed quantization order instead of an expensive greedy search. It quantizes the same column across all rows together. It batches updates inside column blocks. It uses a Cholesky-based reformulation of the inverse Hessian to improve numerical stability.
GPTQ’s blockwise procedure: columns are quantized recursively, and the remaining weights are updated with Hessian information. The figure is easy to underestimate. It is not just an illustration of “do blocks.” It shows the core scaling trick. A block of columns is processed locally, while global updates are delayed and applied in larger chunks. This improves the compute-to-memory ratio and makes the algorithm usable on very large matrices. Algorithm Details Algorithm excerpt from the paper PDF: GPTQ quantizes a weight matrix using the inverse Hessian and a block size (B). A simplified reading of the algorithm:
Compute the Hessian approximation from calibration activations:
The damping term (\lambda I) improves conditioning. The paper uses a small fraction of the average diagonal as damping.
Compute the Cholesky form used for stable inverse-Hessian updates.
Process columns in blocks. For each column (j), quantize all rows of (W_{:,j}), record the quantization error, and update later columns in the current block.
After a block is done, apply the accumulated block error to the remaining unprocessed columns.
This is why GPTQ is not simply “RTN with a better scale.” The quantized value of a column changes the future unquantized columns. The method is sequential, and the error compensation is part of the quantizer. The paper also reports that arbitrary fixed order works surprisingly well at scale. Later implementations often expose variants such as activation-order sorting, group-wise quantization, and different block sizes. Those options matter in practice, but the central idea remains second-order compensation under a layer reconstruction objective. Why Weight-Only Works HereGPTQ avoids the hardest parts of full-network quantization by keeping activations in high precision. That is not a weakness; it is the deployment tradeoff. For decoder LLM serving, weights are static and huge. Reducing them from FP16 to 4 bits can cut model weight storage by roughly 4x before metadata overhead. At batch-1 decode, that can directly reduce memory traffic. Activations and KV cache still consume memory, but GPTQ is attacking the dominant static weight footprint. This also explains what GPTQ does not solve:
it does not reduce KV-cache memory; it does not make all activations INT8-safe; it does not remove the need for specialized low-bit GEMM/GEMV kernels; it does not guarantee speedup if dequantization overhead dominates.
In deployment language, GPTQ is a strong W4A16 or W3A16 model-compression method. It is not a complete quantized inference stack by itself. Scaling And Runtime Tables cropped from the paper PDF: GPTQ is competitive with prior PTQ on vision models and can quantize the largest OPT/BLOOM models in hours. The runtime table is one of the paper’s most practical claims. GPTQ quantizes 13B/30B models in minutes to under an hour, and 66B/175B-scale models in hours. That is the difference between a method that is mathematically interesting and one that can actually be used on public LLM checkpoints. The comparison with vision PTQ methods is also useful context. GPTQ is not introduced as a weaker LLM-only shortcut. It is positioned as a scalable variant of second-order PTQ that remains competitive on smaller benchmarks while being dramatically more relevant for large transformers. Perplexity Results OPT and BLOOM WikiText2 perplexity results: GPTQ is much more stable than RTN at 3-bit and 4-bit precision. Tables 3 and 4 show the central empirical pattern:
At 4 bits, GPTQ is usually close to FP16 perplexity. At 3 bits, RTN often collapses, while GPTQ remains usable for many models. Larger models are often easier to quantize in perplexity terms, except for model-specific outliers.
This last point is important. A larger model can have more redundancy, so the same bit width may hurt it less than a smaller model. That is why low-bit compression became especially interesting for the largest LLMs: those are the models that most need memory reduction, and they can sometimes absorb quantization error better. Mobile-readable takeaway: the key comparison is not the exact value in every cell, but the gap between RTN and GPTQ. For OPT, 3-bit RTN can jump to unusable perplexity values, while 3-bit GPTQ stays in a range where the model still behaves like a language model. For BLOOM, the same pattern appears: GPTQ tracks the FP16 baseline much more closely than direct rounding. 175B-Scale Summary Summary for OPT-175B and BLOOM-176B: GPTQ keeps 3-bit and 4-bit results much closer to FP16 than RTN. Table 5 is the deployment-facing result. OPT-175B and BLOOM-176B are compressed aggressively, and GPTQ retains reasonable perplexity and LAMBADA accuracy. The group-size rows are especially relevant because practical GPTQ implementations often use group-wise scales and zero points. For the two 175B-class models, the practical reading is:
4-bit GPTQ is close to the FP16 baseline on perplexity and LAMBADA. 3-bit GPTQ is worse but still usable; 3-bit RTN collapses much more severely. grouping with sizes such as 1024 or 128 recovers extra accuracy at the cost of metadata and kernel complexity.
Group size is a tradeoff:
smaller groups usually improve accuracy because each scale covers fewer weights; smaller groups add metadata overhead; smaller groups complicate kernels and memory layout; the effective bits per weight can be higher than the nominal weight bit width.
So “3-bit GPTQ” is not a complete deployment specification. One should always ask about group size, scale/zero overhead, packing format, activation order, and kernel support. Generation Latency Per-token latency table from the paper: speedup comes from lower weight memory traffic and custom low-bit kernels. The paper reports practical generation speedups for a 3-bit OPT-175B setting. The interpretation should be careful. GPTQ reduces weight traffic, but the actual speedup depends on:
whether decoding is weight-bandwidth bound; whether the low-bit kernel is optimized; the batch size and sequence length; how much dequantization work is fused into the matrix-vector operation; whether KV-cache traffic starts to dominate.
The paper’s latency table reports a 4.53x speedup on A6000 and a 3.24x speedup on A100 for the measured batch-1 generation setup. That should be read as a kernel-and-workload result, not a universal property of every GPTQ checkpoint. This is why a GPTQ checkpoint and a fast GPTQ serving path are different things. The checkpoint saves memory. The speedup requires kernels that turn low-bit storage into lower end-to-end latency. Downstream Accuracy LAMBADA accuracy after quantization: GPTQ tracks the FP16 curve much better than RTN, especially at aggressive precision. Perplexity is a useful language-model metric, but downstream tasks reveal whether the compressed model still behaves sensibly. The LAMBADA plot follows the same pattern: GPTQ stays much closer to FP16, while 3-bit RTN can be unstable. The broader appendix results show the same point across PIQA, ARC, and StoryCloze-style evaluations. GPTQ is not perfect, but the second-order update changes the failure mode from “low-bit rounding destroys the model” to “low-bit compression becomes a tunable tradeoff.” Extra Tricks: Grouping And Extreme Quantization The paper’s 2-bit experiment: smaller groups make extreme quantization less destructive.
Group-size comparison at 4 bits: finer-grained groups reduce perplexity loss on medium-sized OPT models. The group-size results are a good reminder that quantization is not only about bit width. A model with 4-bit weights and one scale per large group is different from a model with 4-bit weights and much finer grouping. The second may preserve accuracy better, but it costs metadata and kernel complexity. Extreme quantization around 2 bits is interesting, but it is also where implementation details matter the most. Ternary values, per-group scales, zero points, and packing format can dominate the practical memory/computation tradeoff. For normal LLM serving, 4-bit GPTQ is usually the easier engineering point. 3-bit is attractive when memory is extremely tight. 2-bit is a research and custom-kernel problem unless the hardware/software stack is specifically built for it. Practical Reproduction NotesIf I were reproducing GPTQ, I would track the following separately:
Calibration data: use representative text and enough samples to estimate the layer Hessians. Damping: inspect ill-conditioned layers and dead columns; damping can change stability. Layer order: quantize and evaluate layer reconstruction incrementally. Group size: report effective bits including scales and zeros. Block size: tune for runtime and memory, not only accuracy. Kernel path: benchmark real decode latency, not only model file size.
A useful debugging metric is per-layer reconstruction error:
If one layer spikes, inspect its activation statistics, Hessian diagonal, damping, and quantization range. Full-model perplexity is the final metric, but layer reconstruction tells you where the quantizer failed. Reading NotesGPTQ’s influence comes from combining three facts:
LLM weights are huge and static. Weight-only quantization avoids the hardest activation problems. Second-order compensation is accurate enough if implemented at matrix scale.
The paper is also a useful warning about benchmark wording. “4-bit” is not enough information. A serious comparison needs group size, calibration set, damping, activation ordering, quantization scheme, metadata overhead, and kernel implementation. My takeaway: GPTQ is the practical midpoint between naive rounding and retraining. It does not make quantization free, and it does not solve every inference memory bottleneck. But for W4A16 LLM serving, it is the method that turned second-order PTQ into a usable engineering tool.

entry.title: GDAS: Graph Differentiable Architecture Search
entry.content:
Dong X, Yang Y. Searching for A Robust Neural Architecture in Four GPU Hours. CVPR 2019.
Paper / Code GDAS is a differentiable NAS method that sits between DARTS and stochastic NAS. It keeps the NASNet/DARTS-style cell search space, but changes the search-time computation: instead of evaluating every candidate operation on an edge and mixing their outputs, GDAS samples one operation per edge and trains that sampled subgraph. That makes the searched network closer to the final discrete architecture. It also reduces compute and memory, because one training step does not need to execute all candidate operations. MotivationDARTS made cell search cheap by relaxing each edge into a soft mixture of operations. The weak point is that the relaxed supernet is not the final model. During search, all operations on an edge are active; after discretization, only one operation remains. This can create a gap between search-time optimization and final architecture quality. GDAS attacks that gap directly:
The search space is still a directed acyclic graph. Each node aggregates transformed features from previous nodes. The difference is that GDAS samples a subgraph in every iteration: on each edge, only one candidate operation is active in the forward pass. This has two intended benefits:
The search-time model is closer to the final discrete cell. The search step is cheaper because only sampled operations are computed.
The paper’s headline is the CIFAR-10 search cost: less than four hours on one V100 GPU for the fixed-reduction-cell variant, reported as 0.17 GPU days. Search SpaceGDAS follows the micro-search setup: search for a cell, then stack copies of that cell to build the final network.
For CNN search, a cell is a DAG with ordered nodes. The candidate function set contains 8 choices:
identity, zeroize, 3x3 depthwise separable convolution, 3x3 dilated depthwise separable convolution, 5x5 depthwise separable convolution, 5x5 dilated depthwise separable convolution, 3x3 average pooling, 3x3 max pooling.
The searched cell can be reused in CIFAR-style and ImageNet-style networks. CIFAR uses a simple 3x3 convolution head, then stacks blocks of normal cells with reduction cells between blocks. ImageNet uses a stronger three-layer convolutional stem before the same block idea. Differentiable SamplingFor each edge from node to node , GDAS learns a categorical distribution over candidate functions. If is the architecture logit for the -th function, then:
Directly sampling a categorical variable would block gradients. GDAS uses the Gumbel-Max trick for the forward sample:
where is sampled from Gumbel. For backpropagation, it uses the Gumbel-Softmax relaxation:
The temperature controls discreteness. When , the relaxed sample approaches one-hot. When is large, the distribution becomes smoother. In the CNN search setup, the paper initializes at 10 and linearly reduces it to 0.1. The implementation trick is the key: use the argmax sample in the forward pass, but use the relaxed softmax value in the backward pass. In the paper’s words, this avoids evaluating all candidate functions and reduces memory roughly by the size of the candidate set. Training LoopGDAS uses the usual train/validation split for weight-sharing NAS. Network weights are updated on training data, and architecture parameters are updated on validation data.
The practical loop is:
sample a batch from the training split; sample an architecture from the current distribution; update operation weights using training loss; sample a batch from the validation split; update architecture logits using validation loss; derive the final discrete architecture from and train it normally.
This is close to DARTS’ bilevel motivation, but the search-time computation is different. DARTS trains a soft multi-path graph. GDAS trains one sampled path per edge per iteration. Reduction Cell ChoiceOne surprising part of GDAS is that the paper does not insist on searching everything. It argues that most reduction cells are simple and similar, so jointly searching a normal cell and a reduction cell enlarges the search space without much payoff.
The fixed reduction cell uses simple convolution, max pooling, concatenation, and stride-based downsampling. The ablation later supports this design choice: the fixed reduction cell variant is both smaller and slightly better on CIFAR-10. CIFAR ResultsThe main CIFAR comparison is Table 1:
The compact GDAS rows:
Model Search cost Params CIFAR-10 error CIFAR-100 error
GDAS 0.21 GPU days 3.4M 3.87 19.68
GDAS + CutOut 0.21 GPU days 3.4M 2.93 18.38
GDAS (FRC) 0.17 GPU days 2.5M 3.75 19.09
GDAS (FRC) + CutOut 0.17 GPU days 2.5M 2.82 18.13
FRC means the reduction cell is fixed and GDAS only searches the normal cell. The best CIFAR-10 row reaches 2.82% error with 2.5M parameters and 0.17 GPU days of search. That matches DARTS second-order + CutOut on CIFAR-10 error in this table, while using a much lower reported search cost and fewer parameters. There are two caveats:
The search costs are not normalized across GPU types. The paper explicitly says a Titan 1080Ti run would be about seven GPU hours instead of less than four V100 hours. CIFAR-100 is not the strongest row. DARTS second-order has 17.54% in the table, while GDAS (FRC) + CutOut has 18.13%.
The result is still strong for the paper’s claim: sampled differentiable search can find a competitive CNN cell quickly. ImageNet TransferThe CIFAR-searched cell transfers to ImageNet mobile setting:
The important rows:
Model Search cost Params Multiply-adds Top-1 error Top-5 error
DARTS second-order 1 GPU day 4.9M 595M 26.9 9.0
GDAS 0.21 GPU days 5.3M 581M 26.0 8.5
GDAS (FRC) 0.17 GPU days 4.4M 497M 27.5 9.1
The full GDAS row is better than DARTS second-order on ImageNet top-1/top-5 in this table. The FRC row is smaller and cheaper but loses accuracy. This is a useful tradeoff: fixing the reduction cell helps CIFAR search efficiency and parameter count, but the searched reduction cell still seems useful for ImageNet transfer. RNN ResultsGDAS also searches recurrent cells on PTB and transfers to WikiText-2.
On PTB, GDAS reports 57.5 test perplexity with 23M parameters and 0.4 GPU days of search. DARTS second-order is better in the table, with 55.7 test perplexity and 0.25 GPU days. GDAS is still close to DARTS first-order and ENAS.
On WikiText-2, GDAS reports 69.4 test perplexity, slightly better than DARTS second-order at 69.6 and ENAS at 70.4. The language-modeling section is not the main reason I would cite GDAS, but it shows the differentiable sampler is not limited to CNN cells. What Did It Find?The final discovered cells are more complex than what I would want to design by hand:
The normal cell uses many skip connections and separable convolutions. The FRC normal cell is even more skip-heavy. The recurrent cell uses tanh, relu, and identity paths. This figure is also a reminder that cell search spaces are highly constrained: NAS is not inventing arbitrary networks, it is choosing edges and operations inside a hand-designed grammar. The reduction-cell ablation is worth keeping:
Combination Params CIFAR-10 error
GDAS-N + GDAS-R 3.3M 2.93
GDAS-N + FIX-R 3.0M 2.87
FRC-N + GDAS-R 2.9M 2.84
FRC-N + FIX-R 2.5M 2.82
The fixed reduction cell is not just a shortcut; in this ablation it improves the result. That supports the paper’s practical argument: searching the normal cell may be enough, and searching the reduction cell can add complexity without improving the final model. Relation To DARTS And SNASDARTS, SNAS, and GDAS are attacking the same bottleneck from slightly different angles.
Method Search-time edge behavior Main concern
DARTS soft weighted sum of all candidate operations cheap gradients but larger relaxation gap
SNAS stochastic architecture variables with Concrete/Gumbel-Softmax relaxation optimize a distribution over architectures
GDAS one sampled operation per edge in forward pass, relaxed gradient in backward pass closer discrete subgraph and lower compute
The important GDAS idea is not only “use Gumbel-Softmax”. It is the one-path forward computation. That is what makes the sampled search graph closer to the final architecture and avoids running all operations on every edge. Limitations The search space is still manually designed. GDAS searches inside a NASNet/DARTS-style cell grammar. The method depends on the temperature schedule. Cooling too quickly can make the architecture distribution collapse early; cooling too slowly weakens the discrete signal. The reported search cost is hardware-dependent. The paper gives V100 numbers and explicitly warns that costs are not normalized across GPUs. Directly searching ImageNet with the same hyperparameters failed in their experiments, so the main CNN result still follows the CIFAR-search-then-transfer protocol. The final discrete architecture is derived from learned probabilities using a selection heuristic, so the relaxation gap is reduced but not eliminated.
TakeawayGDAS is best read as a correction to the DARTS relaxation. DARTS made NAS differentiable, but its search-time model executes a soft mixture that does not exist after discretization. GDAS keeps gradient-based optimization while training sampled subgraphs, so each step looks more like the final architecture. For me, the reusable lesson is the forward/backward split: use a discrete one-path sample for computation, but use a differentiable relaxation for gradients. That idea shows up repeatedly in later efficient NAS work, especially when the supernet is too expensive or too biased if every candidate operation is active at once.

entry.title: HAQ: Hardware-Aware Mixed Precision
entry.content:
Paper: HAQ: Hardware-Aware Automated Quantization with Mixed Precision HAQ is a hardware-aware quantization paper. The central point is simple but important: there is no universal best bit-width allocation for a neural network. The right precision for each layer depends on the accuracy sensitivity of that layer and on the hardware target that will run it. This paper is from the CNN/mobile-accelerator era, but the lesson transfers directly to modern model deployment. A quantization format is only useful if it maps to the target hardware and kernels. FLOPs, parameter count, and average bit width are proxies. HAQ puts hardware feedback into the search loop. Motivation Figure cropped from the paper PDF: mixed precision can dominate fixed 8-bit quantization because different layers tolerate different bit widths. Uniform quantization is attractive because it is easy to describe: make all weights 8-bit, or all weights 4-bit. But neural networks are not uniform. Some layers are sensitive and need more precision. Some layers are redundant and can tolerate fewer bits. Some layers dominate memory traffic, while others dominate compute. HAQ asks a more deployment-oriented question:
where (b_l) is the bit-width policy for layer (l), and (C_{\text{hardware}}) can be latency, energy, or model size. The important part is the subscript in (C_{\text{hardware}}). The cost model is not generic FLOPs. It is feedback from the deployment hardware or a simulator calibrated to that hardware. Hardware Dependence The same MobileNet-V1 quantization policy has different latency on different hardware targets. Table 1 is the paper’s simplest argument. A policy optimized for one hardware target is not optimal on another. This is exactly why hand-written rules like “use more bits in early layers” or “compress layers with many parameters” are insufficient. The reason is that hardware cost is shaped by memory hierarchy, parallelism, supported arithmetic, batch size, dataflow, and kernel implementation. A layer that looks expensive in FLOPs can be efficient on one accelerator and awkward on another. A layer with fewer FLOPs can still bottleneck memory traffic. This is the same conceptual issue behind hardware-aware NAS. Architecture search learned that FLOPs are a poor proxy for latency; HAQ makes the same argument for quantization policy. HAQ Framework HAQ overview: an RL agent proposes a quantization policy, the model is quantized, and hardware feedback is returned as part of the reward. HAQ formulates mixed-precision quantization as a sequential decision problem. The controller visits layers one by one. At each step it observes layer information and emits a bit-width action. After a full policy is sampled, the network is quantized, briefly fine-tuned, evaluated, and scored with a hardware-aware reward. The loop has four pieces:
A policy generator chooses per-layer bit widths. The model is quantized according to that policy. A hardware simulator or feedback path reports latency, energy, or model size. Validation accuracy and hardware cost determine the reward.
The controller uses DDPG, an actor-critic reinforcement learning method for continuous actions. The continuous action is later mapped into valid integer bit widths. This is not the only possible optimizer, but it was a reasonable tool for searching a large mixed-precision design space at the time. State, Action, And RewardThe state includes structural information about the current layer: layer index, input/output channels, kernel size, stride, feature-map size, parameter count, and previous action context. This gives the agent enough information to distinguish a depthwise convolution from a pointwise convolution, an early large-feature-map layer from a late compact layer, and a cheap layer from an expensive one. The action is the precision choice for weights and activations. HAQ can search flexible bit widths instead of forcing a global value. The reward depends on the deployment objective:
For latency-constrained search, the policy should maximize accuracy while meeting a latency budget. For energy-constrained search, the hardware energy estimate enters the objective. For model-size-constrained search, storage replaces latency/energy as the resource.
This is the paper’s main abstraction: quantization is not a single-objective compression problem. It is a constrained deployment optimization problem. Hardware Configuration The paper evaluates edge and cloud accelerator configurations with different parallelism and memory resources. The edge and cloud accelerators differ in batch size, processing-element array size, AXI port width, and block RAM. These differences change the best policy. A small edge device may be memory constrained in places where a cloud accelerator is compute constrained, and vice versa. This is why HAQ does not try to learn one “good” mixed-precision pattern for MobileNet. It learns a policy for a model-hardware-objective tuple. Latency-Constrained Results Latency-constrained quantization on BISMO: flexible per-layer precision beats fixed-bit baselines under similar latency budgets. The latency table compares HAQ with fixed-bit PACT baselines on edge and cloud accelerator settings. The result is not just that flexible precision can save latency. The more important result is that it can preserve accuracy under a target latency constraint better than uniform precision. The policy is also interpretable. Under latency optimization, the agent tends to assign different precision patterns to depthwise and pointwise convolutions because those layers stress the hardware differently. Mobile-readable takeaway: under comparable latency budgets, HAQ’s flexible policy usually keeps higher top-1/top-5 accuracy than fixed-bit quantization. The reported latency reduction reaches roughly 1.4x to 1.95x compared with fixed 8-bit baselines in the BISMO experiments.
MobileNet-V1 policy under latency constraints: edge and cloud targets receive different bit allocations. For MobileNet-V1, the paper explains the edge/cloud difference through operation intensity. On the edge accelerator, depthwise convolutions are more memory-bound, so activations in depthwise layers receive fewer bits. On the cloud accelerator, the policy changes because the bottleneck changes. This is a useful result because it is not merely an accuracy table. It tells us what the controller learned about the hardware. The learned policy reflects memory/computation balance rather than parameter count alone.
MobileNet-V2 policy under latency constraints: the same hardware-aware pattern appears in a deeper MobileNet variant. MobileNet-V2 shows the same qualitative lesson. The optimal policy changes across hardware targets, and the depthwise/pointwise distinction remains important. The policy is not a generic “give every depthwise layer fewer bits” rule. It depends on the target accelerator and constraint. BitFusion Energy And Latency BitFusion results: HAQ searches policies for latency and energy objectives instead of relying on one uniform precision. The BitFusion experiments are useful because they separate two deployment metrics that are often conflated. A policy that is good for latency is not necessarily the best for energy. Both can be correlated, but hardware utilization, memory access, and arithmetic precision can make them diverge. HAQ’s framework can swap the resource term in the reward. That means the same search machinery can target latency, energy, or model size. This is more flexible than designing one manual bit allocation heuristic and hoping it generalizes. The headline result in these tables is that HAQ can roughly halve latency or energy relative to the 8-bit baseline while keeping accuracy close. More importantly, the best policy for latency and the best policy for energy are searched as separate objectives. Model-Size-Constrained Results Model-size-constrained quantization: HAQ can preserve accuracy at similar model sizes compared with earlier compression baselines. The model-size objective produces a different policy from the latency objective. This is a key part of the paper. Under a size constraint, the cost of assigning bits is dominated by parameter count. Depthwise convolutions have fewer parameters than pointwise convolutions, so giving them more bits can be cheap while preserving accuracy. The result table is small on mobile, so the main reading is: for MobileNet and ResNet settings, HAQ matches or improves accuracy at similar model sizes compared with the hand-designed compression baseline, especially under aggressive compression.
Under model-size constraints, the learned policy gives more bits to depthwise layers because they have fewer parameters. Compare this with the latency policy. Under latency constraints, depthwise layers may receive fewer bits on some hardware because they are memory-bound. Under model-size constraints, they can receive more bits because they are small. Same model, different objective, different answer. This is the central HAQ lesson:
Any report that only gives “average bit width” misses this structure. Why RL Is Not The Main PointIt is easy to read HAQ as an RL paper, but I do not think RL is the enduring contribution. The lasting idea is hardware feedback in the quantization loop. The controller could be replaced by Bayesian optimization, evolutionary search, differentiable relaxation, integer programming, or a learned cost model plus greedy refinement. The paper’s contribution is the formulation:
policy = per-layer weight/activation bit widths; objective = validation accuracy under a hardware constraint; hardware feedback = latency/energy/size signal from the target platform; result = device-specific mixed precision, not a universal bit schedule.
This framing is still relevant even when the search algorithm changes. Relation To Modern LLM QuantizationHAQ is about CNNs on edge/cloud accelerators, but its deployment lesson maps well to LLM serving. Consider common LLM quantization formats:
W4A16 weight-only quantization can be strong on GPUs with optimized INT4 kernels. W8A8 can be better when hardware has fast INT8 tensor cores and activation quantization is stable. FP8 can be attractive on recent accelerators with native support. KV-cache quantization only helps when KV memory bandwidth or capacity is the bottleneck.
There is no globally best format. The best choice depends on hardware, batch size, sequence length, tensor parallelism, attention implementation, and kernel availability. That is the same problem HAQ identified for CNN quantization, just at a different scale. Practical Reading NotesThe paper gives a good checklist for any mixed-precision result:
What exact hardware target was optimized? Was latency measured, simulated, or approximated by FLOPs? Are weights and activations both quantized? Are first and last layers treated specially? Is the reported model size only raw weights, or does it include scales and metadata? Does the hardware actually support all searched bit widths efficiently? Is the policy evaluated after fine-tuning or immediately after quantization?
These questions matter because mixed precision can look good on paper while failing in deployment if the hardware does not execute the searched formats efficiently. LimitationsHAQ has real limitations:
RL search is expensive compared with a direct heuristic. Hardware simulators must be accurate enough to guide policy search. The paper focuses on CNNs and specialized accelerators, not transformers. Quantization and fine-tuning details can change the final policy. The search space assumes the hardware can benefit from flexible precision.
Those limitations do not weaken the main message. They define where the method needs engineering support. TakeawayHAQ should be remembered as a hardware-aware formulation of mixed-precision quantization. It moves the question from “Should this model be 8-bit or 4-bit?” to “Which layer should use which precision on this hardware under this objective?” That is the right question for deployment. A bit-width policy is not an abstract compression artifact. It is a contract between the model, the quantizer, the kernels, and the device.

entry.title: HAWQ: Hessian-Aware Mixed Precision Quantization
entry.content:
Paper: HAWQ: Hessian AWare Quantization of Neural Networks with Mixed-Precision HAWQ is an early paper that made second-order information practical for mixed-precision neural network quantization. The problem is not simply “use 8 bits or 4 bits.” The problem is deciding which blocks deserve higher precision when the model is pushed into a small weight and activation budget. The paper’s answer is to look at local loss curvature. If quantization perturbs a block in a sharp direction, the loss can increase quickly. If the same magnitude of perturbation lands in a flatter region, the model may tolerate it. HAWQ uses the top Hessian eigenvalue of each block as a sensitivity signal, then uses that signal for two decisions:
which blocks should receive more or fewer bits; which blocks should be fine-tuned first after quantization.
This is a CNN-era paper, but the idea is still useful when reading AdaRound, BRECQ, GPTQ, SpQR, and other later quantization methods. They differ in scale and implementation, but they share the same intuition: rounding error should not be treated as equally harmful in every parameter direction. Motivation Figure cropped from the paper PDF: block-level Hessian spectra are highly non-uniform for ResNet20 and Inception-V3. The first figure is the whole motivation. The top Hessian eigenvalue varies by orders of magnitude across blocks. This means a uniform precision rule is mathematically suspicious. Two blocks may have similar tensor shapes, but if one block has much larger local curvature, the same quantization error norm can cause much larger loss increase. The paper frames this with a second-order Taylor approximation around a trained model:
Near convergence, the first-order gradient term is small. The Hessian term is what tells us whether a perturbation is cheap or expensive. For a block (i), a larger Hessian spectrum means a quantization perturbation in that block is more dangerous.
ResNet20 blocks respond differently when weights are perturbed along the dominant Hessian eigenvector. The 1-D loss landscape makes the eigenvalue interpretation concrete. Blocks with larger top eigenvalues produce steeper curves. The 9th ResNet20 block, for example, is much more sensitive than the final block. This is why a depth-based rule such as “early layers need more bits” is too crude. HAWQ wants a measured sensitivity ranking. MethodHAWQ partitions a neural network into (b) blocks:
For each block (W_i), it estimates the largest eigenvalue of the Hessian (H_i), denoted (\lambda_i). It does not form the Hessian matrix explicitly. Instead, it uses Hessian-vector products and power iteration.
Algorithms cropped from the paper PDF: power iteration estimates the top Hessian eigenvalue, then HAWQ uses Hessian-derived scores for precision and fine-tuning order. The first algorithm is the computational trick. Given the gradient (g_i = \partial L / \partial W_i), the Hessian-vector product can be computed by differentiating (g_i^T v):
This is available through automatic differentiation without materializing (H_i). Power iteration repeatedly applies this product and normalizes the vector until it approximates the dominant eigenvector and eigenvalue. The second algorithm uses two related but different scores. For bit allocation, HAWQ uses:
where (n_i) is the number of parameters in block (i). This score is a curvature-per-parameter signal. A block with high curvature and few parameters is a good candidate for higher precision, because spending bits there is relatively cheap and accuracy-sensitive. A block with many parameters and low curvature can be compressed more aggressively. For block-wise fine-tuning order, HAWQ uses:
This includes the actual quantization perturbation after a bit-width has been chosen. A block can be sensitive because (\lambda_i) is large, or because the quantizer introduces large error. HAWQ fine-tunes blocks in descending (\Omega_i), so the most damaging quantized blocks are repaired first. That separation is important. The precision-ordering score asks, “Where should I spend bits?” The fine-tuning-order score asks, “After quantization, which block should be repaired first?” Inception-V3 Curvature Inception-V3 1-D loss landscapes show the same curvature imbalance at ImageNet scale. The Inception-V3 plot supports the same claim on a larger model and dataset. Some blocks are steep in both directions around the optimum, while later blocks can be almost flat over the same perturbation interval. This matters because mixed precision has a combinatorial search space. If there are (L) layers and several candidate bit-widths per layer, exhaustive search is not realistic. HAWQ does not solve a full discrete optimization problem. It reduces the search by computing a deterministic ordering from Hessian information, then assigning bits according to a target compression level. That is both a strength and a limitation. It is much cheaper than AutoML-style search, but it only gives a relative ordering. It does not magically know the globally optimal bit configuration for every hardware target. ResNet20 Results ResNet20 on CIFAR-10: HAWQ keeps accuracy close to the baseline while using mixed precision and high activation compression. Table I is the cleanest small-model result. The full-precision ResNet20 baseline is 92.37% accuracy. HAWQ reports 92.22% with mixed 2-bit weights and 4-bit activations, while reaching 13.11x weight compression and 8x activation compression. The comparison with “Direct” is the key ablation in the table. Direct quantization uses the same general compression setting but does not use Hessian information. It drops to 90.34%. HAWQ recovers most of that gap. Mobile-readable takeaway: the headline is not just that HAWQ beats uniform 2-bit or 3-bit baselines. The important comparison is HAWQ versus Direct under aggressive mixed precision. The Hessian ranking makes the same bit budget much less destructive. ImageNet Results Inception-V3 on ImageNet: HAWQ improves over direct mixed precision and keeps a much smaller model than the full-precision baseline. For Inception-V3, the full-precision baseline is 77.45% top-1 with a 91.2 MB model. HAWQ reports 75.52% top-1, 12.04x weight compression, and a 7.57 MB model. Direct mixed precision under the same general setup drops to 69.76%, which shows how much the curvature-guided allocation matters. The Inception result is useful because it is not a toy CIFAR-only case. The method still works when the model has more heterogeneous blocks and the dataset is ImageNet.
ResNet50 and SqueezeNext results: HAWQ is competitive with prior quantization and AutoML-style mixed-precision baselines. The ResNet50 table compares HAWQ with Dorefa, PACT, LQ-Nets, Deep Compression, and HAQ. HAWQ reports 75.48% top-1 with a 7.96 MB model, compared with HAQ’s 75.30% at 9.22 MB. This is an interesting comparison because HAQ is hardware-aware and search-based, while HAWQ is sensitivity-based and deterministic. For SqueezeNext, the paper shows two useful cases:
uniform 8-bit HAWQ gets 69.34% top-1, almost matching the 69.38% full-precision baseline; mixed precision reaches a 1.09 MB model with 68.02% top-1, while Direct drops to 65.39%.
SqueezeNext is already compact, so the result is a stress test. HAWQ is not only compressing a redundant large model. It can also guide quantization when the architecture was designed to be small. What Bit Allocation Looks Like ResNet20 final block precision from the appendix: the first and last blocks stay higher precision, while many middle blocks use lower weight bits. The appendix precision table makes the method more concrete. HAWQ does not assign one global bit-width. In ResNet20, some blocks use 6-bit or 8-bit weights, while several middle blocks use 2-bit or 3-bit weights. Activations are mostly 4-bit, with higher precision kept where needed. This is the shape I expect from a useful mixed-precision method: it should produce a policy that can be inspected. If a paper only reports average bit-width, it hides the real deployment artifact.
Inception-V3 final block precision: larger later blocks can still receive low weight precision when the Hessian score allows it. The Inception-V3 table is also a reminder that parameter size and sensitivity pull against each other. Some later blocks are large, so using high precision everywhere would be expensive. HAWQ’s (S_i = \lambda_i / n_i) score lets large, lower-sensitivity blocks absorb more compression while preserving bits for more sensitive regions. Ablations Reversing the Hessian-aware precision order hurts accuracy recovery under the same fine-tuning budget. Figure 4 tests whether the precision ordering matters. HAWQ’s normal ordering recovers quickly and stabilizes around a much higher top-1 accuracy than the reverse-precision variant. This supports the first use of Hessian information: do not assign the low bits to blocks that the Hessian says are sensitive.
Reversing the block-wise fine-tuning order converges more slowly and to a worse final point. Figure 5 tests the second use of Hessian information: fine-tuning order. The normal HAWQ order, based on (\Omega_i), converges faster and reaches higher top-1 accuracy than reverse tuning. This part is easy to miss. HAWQ is not only a bit-allocation paper. It also says the sequence of local repair matters. If a heavily damaged high-curvature block is left unfixed, later fine-tuning may be less useful because the model is already operating through a bad internal representation. Relation To HAQHAQ and HAWQ both produce mixed precision, but they answer different questions:
Method Main signal What it optimizes
HAQ hardware feedback plus validation reward device-specific latency, energy, or size constraints
HAWQ Hessian sensitivity and quantization perturbation loss-aware precision and fine-tuning order
HAQ is deployment-aware. HAWQ is curvature-aware. In practice, these are complementary. A good quantization system needs to know both where the model is sensitive and where the hardware actually benefits from lower precision. For example, a block may be safe to quantize according to HAWQ but still not speed up on a target device if the kernel does not efficiently support that bit-width. Conversely, a hardware search may find a fast policy that damages accuracy if it ignores sensitivity. Modern systems often need both signals. Relation To Later PTQHAWQ is useful background for several later methods:
AdaRound optimizes rounding decisions after the quantization grid is fixed. Its motivation also comes from a Hessian-weighted perturbation objective. BRECQ moves from layer-wise reconstruction to block-wise reconstruction, using second-order or Fisher-style reasoning to preserve internal computation. GPTQ scales second-order PTQ to very large Transformer weight matrices by using calibration activations and inverse-Hessian error compensation. SpQR uses a Hessian view to identify sensitive weights that should become sparse high-precision outliers.
The granularity changes across these papers. HAWQ works at block-level mixed precision. AdaRound works at rounding decisions. GPTQ works inside linear layers. But the shared lesson is the same: quantization error should be weighted by how much the model cares about that direction. Practical Reading NotesIf I were reproducing HAWQ or using it as a baseline, I would check the following:
Block definition. The Hessian score depends on how layers are grouped. A residual block, a convolution, and an Inception module can produce different sensitivity rankings. Eigenvalue estimation cost. The paper avoids forming Hessians, but power iteration still requires Hessian-vector products and extra backpropagation. Calibration and fine-tuning data. The method is not data-free. The Hessian and fine-tuning behavior depend on the examples used. First and last layers. Many quantization papers treat them specially. Comparisons are only fair when this policy is stated. Activation bit-width. HAWQ reports both weight and activation compression. Activation quantization can be harder than weight-only compression because it affects runtime tensors. Kernel support. Mixed precision is only useful at deployment if the hardware/runtime can execute the chosen bit-widths efficiently.
LimitationsHAWQ’s main approximation is aggressive: each block’s Hessian is represented by its top eigenvalue, and sometimes scaled by block size. That captures the sharpest local direction, but it does not model the full spectrum or cross-block interactions. The method also gives a relative ordering, not an exact bit-width solution. A user still needs a target compression ratio and a policy for mapping ranked blocks to concrete bit choices. Finally, the paper is evaluated on CNN image classification. The idea transfers to modern transformer quantization, but the details do not transfer directly. Transformers have activation outliers, attention/KV-cache behavior, layer normalization, and much larger matrix structure. That is why later methods such as GPTQ and SmoothQuant look different even when they share the second-order motivation. TakeawayHAWQ should be remembered for making mixed precision less heuristic. It asks the right question: if two blocks receive the same quantization error, will the loss care equally? The answer is no, and the Hessian gives a usable way to estimate that difference. The paper is not the final word on quantization. It does not solve hardware mapping, it approximates curvature heavily, and it targets CNNs. But it is an important bridge between simple uniform quantization and later reconstruction-based PTQ methods. It turns bit allocation into a sensitivity problem instead of a layer-count or parameter-count rule.

entry.title: I-BERT: Integer-only BERT Quantization
entry.content:
Kim S, Gholami A, Yao Z, Mahoney M W, Keutzer K. I-BERT: Integer-only BERT Quantization. ICML 2021.
Paper / Code I-BERT is the paper I use as a checklist for whether a Transformer quantization method really covers the inference graph. Many BERT quantization methods store weights and activations in INT8, but still run GELU, Softmax, or LayerNorm in floating point. That is useful compression, but it is not integer-only inference. The paper’s claim is stricter:
Embedding and MatMul run with INT8 multiplication and INT32 accumulation. GELU, Softmax, and LayerNorm are approximated with integer-only arithmetic. Intermediate tensors are not dequantized into floating point during inference. The final graph can target hardware where integer logic is the natural execution path.
All figures and tables below are cropped from the original ICML PDF. MotivationBERT inference is dominated by matrix multiplications, but the graph is not only GEMM. A Transformer block also contains:
attention Softmax; GELU in the feed-forward network; LayerNorm before or after sublayers; residual adds and requantization boundaries.
If the runtime dequantizes for every nonlinear operator, then the deployed graph alternates between integer and floating-point execution. This adds casts, memory movement, and backend complexity. It also prevents deployment on integer-only processors.
Figure 1 compares three regimes:
Regime What happens
simulated quantization parameters may be stored as integers, but inference is effectively FP32
partial integer quantization MatMul is integer, but Softmax still forces dequantize and requantize
I-BERT the whole self-attention path avoids floating-point arithmetic
The last case is the important one. I-BERT is not primarily about a new quantizer for linear layers. It is about removing floating-point islands from the Transformer block. Basic QuantizationI-BERT uses uniform symmetric static quantization. A real value is mapped to an integer with bit-width and scale :
The approximate reverse mapping is:
This is a symmetric quantizer: no zero-point appears in the main formulation. The deployment consequence is that scale tracking becomes explicit. Every intermediate integer tensor has a scale, and every operation must return both an integer value and an output scale. For linear operators, the scaling property is friendly:
This is why INT8 MatMul is not the hard part. The hard part is that the same property does not hold for nonlinear functions:
I-BERT’s method starts exactly at this failure point. Integer Polynomial KernelThe paper’s common building block is a second-order polynomial:
A low-order polynomial is attractive because it can be evaluated with additions, multiplications, integer floor operations, and fixed output scales. High-order polynomials would reduce approximation error, but they increase overflow risk and intermediate precision requirements.
Algorithm 1 is the reusable kernel. Given quantized input and scale , it precomputes integer versions of the polynomial coefficients and returns such that:
This is the pattern used later for GELU and Softmax: approximate the nonlinear part by a second-order polynomial, then keep the computation in the integer path. Integer-only GELUBERT uses GELU:
The usual sigmoid approximation,
is not enough for integer-only inference because sigmoid itself is nonlinear. A hard-sigmoid approximation can be computed with integer arithmetic, but the paper shows that it is too loose for BERT accuracy. I-BERT instead approximates the error function with a second-order polynomial:
where the paper uses and . Then:
The left plot shows why h-GELU is not good enough: near the origin, the hard approximation visibly diverges from GELU. The i-GELU curve is much closer around the region where activations often live.
Algorithm 2 makes the scale handling explicit. The integer ERF approximation returns an integer output and a scale. I-GELU then multiplies the original quantized input by the adjusted ERF term and returns a new output scale. The point is not that GELU is magically linear. The point is that the nonlinear part is approximated in a way that the runtime can evaluate without FP32.
The approximation table is small but important:
Method Integer-only L2 distance L-infinity distance
no 0.012 0.020
h-GELU yes 0.031 0.068
i-GELU yes 0.0082 0.018
i-GELU is both integer-only and more accurate than the sigmoid approximation under these error metrics. That is why the paper does not settle for MobileNetV3-style hard sigmoid. Integer-only SoftmaxSoftmax is harder than GELU because exponential grows quickly:
The standard stability trick is still used:
Now every exponent input is non-positive. I-BERT decomposes a non-positive value as:
Then:
The term can be implemented as a bit shift. The remaining only needs to be approximated over a short interval, not over the full real line. I-BERT uses:
The right plot in Figure 2 compares this i-exp approximation with the exact exponential. The paper reports a maximum gap around , smaller than the quantization interval error for an 8-bit unit range. LayerNormLayerNorm is easy to underestimate. BatchNorm can usually be folded into convolution at inference time. LayerNorm cannot be folded in the same way because the mean and variance depend on the current token representation. For input channels :
The mean and variance can be accumulated with integer arithmetic, but the square root is the nontrivial part. I-BERT uses an integer square-root algorithm based on Newton iteration.
The same image contains Algorithm 3 for integer exponential/Softmax and Algorithm 4 for integer square root. I like this placement because it shows the operator-coverage nature of the paper: Softmax needs integer exponential and normalization; LayerNorm needs integer square root. These are exactly the places where a superficially INT8 Transformer often falls back to floating point. End-to-End Inference PathIn I-BERT, the rough inference contract is:
Component Arithmetic
Embedding INT8 representation
Q/K/V and FFN MatMul INT8 multiplication, INT32 accumulation
GELU integer polynomial approximation, INT32 path
Softmax integer exponential approximation and integer normalization
LayerNorm integer mean/variance/square-root path
Requantization output tensors returned to INT8 where needed
This is not the same as saying every intermediate scalar is stored in 8 bits. The nonlinear operators use INT32 intermediate values where needed. The stronger claim is that the graph avoids floating-point arithmetic and dequantization during inference. That distinction matters. INT32 accumulation is normal for INT8 inference. Floating-point fallback is the thing I-BERT is trying to remove. GLUE Results The paper evaluates RoBERTa-Base and RoBERTa-Large on GLUE development tasks. Representative averages:
Model Precision Integer-only Average GLUE
RoBERTa-Base baseline FP32 no 86.0
RoBERTa-Base I-BERT INT8 yes 86.3
RoBERTa-Large baseline FP32 no 89.0
RoBERTa-Large I-BERT INT8 yes 89.5
I would not overread the small average improvements as “quantization is better than FP32.” The robust conclusion is that the integer-only approximations do not create the usual accuracy collapse. For a graph-level quantization paper, preserving full-precision accuracy while removing floating-point nonlinear operators is already the result. The table also shows task-level variation. RoBERTa-Base loses 0.3 on MNLI-m and STS-B, gains 1.3 on CoLA, and gains 1.4 on RTE. RoBERTa-Large is more uniformly positive in the reported run. This kind of movement is normal when quantization-aware fine-tuning and task variance interact. Latency The latency table reports INT8 speedup over FP32 on a Tesla T4 setup:
Model Average speedup Best reported speedup
BERT-Base 3.08x 3.39x
BERT-Large 3.56x 4.00x
This is a useful systems signal, but there is a caveat. T4 is not an integer-only edge processor. The authors choose it because TensorRT and Turing Tensor Cores give usable INT8 deployment support. The paper’s deeper value is that the same arithmetic contract can target hardware where floating point is expensive or unavailable. For reproduction, I would report latency together with:
sequence length; batch size; whether attention kernels are fused; whether nonlinear operators are custom integer kernels; how many dequantize or FP32 nodes remain in the exported graph.
Without that graph-level accounting, “INT8 speedup” can hide important fallback behavior. GELU Ablation The GELU ablation isolates the approximation quality:
Method Integer-only Avg.
GELU no 92.3
h-GELU yes 92.0
i-GELU yes 92.7
This is the best evidence that the polynomial details matter. A crude integer-friendly GELU is not enough. h-GELU is integer-only but loses accuracy, especially on RTE in this table. i-GELU is both integer-only and closer to the true GELU shape. My reading: the method succeeds because it treats numerical approximation as part of model quality, not merely as kernel engineering. If the approximation changes the nonlinear function too much, quantization-aware fine-tuning has to compensate for a shifted model. Reproduction NotesIf I were implementing I-BERT, I would check the following before trusting the result. First, verify operator coverage. The exported graph should not contain hidden FP32 GELU, Softmax, LayerNorm, division, square root, or dequantize nodes inside the Transformer block. Second, log scales at every sublayer boundary. Integer-only inference depends on scale propagation. Residual adds are especially easy to get wrong because two branches may carry different scales. Third, test approximation error independently. Before running GLUE, compare i-GELU and i-exp outputs against their floating references over the expected activation ranges. This catches coefficient, rounding, clipping, and bit-shift mistakes. Fourth, stress LayerNorm. The integer square-root path must handle small variance, large variance, and long sequences without overflow or divide-by-zero behavior. LayerNorm bugs often appear as rare unstable examples rather than as a clean average drop. Fifth, keep latency honest. Measure an actual backend graph. A PyTorch simulation of integer arithmetic is useful for accuracy, but the deployment claim depends on kernels that actually execute the integer path. LimitationsI-BERT is a strong paper, but its scope is clear.
It studies 8-bit integer-only inference, not ultra-low-bit BERT. It evaluates RoBERTa/BERT-style encoders, not decoder-only LLMs with KV cache and causal attention. Nonlinear operators use INT32 intermediate arithmetic, so “integer-only” does not mean every intermediate is INT8. The latency experiment uses a Tesla T4/TensorRT path, not a low-end integer-only microcontroller. Static quantization requires reliable calibration and fine-tuning; bad ranges can still break the graph.
The paper also predates many later LLM quantization constraints: long context, rotary embeddings, activation outliers, group-wise weight-only INT4, KV cache quantization, and mixed backend execution. Still, the operator-coverage lesson transfers directly. TakeawayI-BERT is valuable because it changes the question from “are the weights INT8?” to “can the whole Transformer inference graph run without floating point?” The core recipe is:
use ordinary INT8/INT32 arithmetic for linear layers; approximate GELU and Softmax with low-order integer-friendly polynomials; implement LayerNorm’s dynamic square root with integer arithmetic; preserve scale information across every sublayer and requantization point.
When I read later quantization papers, I-BERT is the baseline for honesty. If GELU, Softmax, LayerNorm, or residual rescaling still dequantize into FP32, the method may still be useful, but it is not making the same integer-only claim.

entry.title: INQ: Incremental Network Quantization
entry.content:
Paper: Incremental Network Quantization: Towards Lossless CNNs with Low-Precision Weights INQ is a useful paper to reread because it makes a simple point that still matters in modern quantization: low-bit conversion is not just a scalar rounding problem. It is also an optimization and scheduling problem. If every weight in a trained model is snapped to a small codebook at the same time, the network receives a large structured perturbation. If only part of the weights are quantized, frozen, and then the remaining weights are allowed to retrain, the model can gradually absorb that perturbation. The paper is from ICLR 2017 and focuses on CNN weight quantization. It does not solve activation quantization, transformer quantization, KV-cache quantization, or post-training LLM compression. Its setting is narrower: start from a pre-trained full-precision CNN, convert all weights into zero or signed powers of two, and use retraining to keep ImageNet accuracy close to the original model. The narrowness is exactly why the idea is clean. What Problem INQ SolvesThe deployment target assumed by INQ is hardware where multiplication by a weight can become a cheap sign change plus a bit shift. That requires the non-zero weights to be powers of two. A normal uniform INT8 or INT4 codebook does not have this property; it is friendly to integer matrix multiply units, but not specifically to shift-based multiplication. So the paper asks for a constrained model:
every final weight is either zero or a signed power of two; the number of candidate values is controlled by an expected bit-width; the final quantized CNN should have little or no accuracy loss compared with the 32-bit reference; retraining is allowed during the quantization process.
The central mechanism is shown below. Gray entries are still full precision, green entries have been quantized and frozen. Each iteration quantizes another portion of the model, then retrains the remaining full-precision entries.
This figure is more important than the exact codebook. INQ’s main contribution is the staged freezing schedule: quantization is treated as a sequence of constrained optimization problems, not as one global rounding pass. Power-Of-Two CodebookLet a pre-trained CNN have learnable layers
where is the weight tensor of layer . The paper writes the formula as if were a matrix, but the same rule is applied to convolutional tensors and fully connected matrices. For layer , INQ maps weights into the following quantization set:
I find it clearer to rewrite the same set as
Here is the largest exponent and is the smallest exponent. The paper’s notation says , so the non-zero magnitudes live between and . Values whose absolute magnitude is too small are mapped to zero. The largest exponent is chosen from the maximum absolute weight in the layer:
Once the expected bit-width is fixed, the smallest exponent is
This equation is easy to miss. A 5-bit INQ codebook does not mean 32 arbitrary scalar values. One code is reserved for zero, and the remaining representable values are signed powers of two. With , the codebook can hold up to non-zero signed values, which means 8 positive magnitudes and 8 negative magnitudes, plus zero. The factor in the definition of is not cosmetic. It aligns the largest observed absolute weight with the nearest power-of-two rounding interval. Without that factor, the maximum layer weight can sit awkwardly near the top boundary of the codebook. Rounding RuleAfter is fixed, each selected weight is mapped to a codebook value by a power-of-two ladder. The paper’s rounding rule can be written in two mobile-friendly pieces. If the interval test holds, the selected value is
Otherwise, the weight is assigned to zero:
The interval test is
where and are adjacent positive elements in the sorted power-of-two ladder. In implementation terms, this is nearest-neighbor rounding in absolute value, followed by restoring the sign:
The paper’s equation is more explicit about the boundaries, while the nearest-codebook view is easier to implement. The important constraint is that can only output zero or a signed power of two. The full method overview from the paper is compact:
Subfigure (a) is the original full-precision model. Subfigure (b) fixes part of the network into quantized values and keeps the rest trainable. Subfigure (c) is the final model where every weight has been quantized. Why Not Quantize Everything At Once?The paper’s failure case is global quantization: take the entire trained model and immediately map every weight to . This introduces a large simultaneous error in all layers. The model cannot compensate because no full-precision parameters are left. INQ instead keeps two groups per layer:
The first group, , contains weights selected for quantization in the current or previous iterations. The second group, , contains the remaining full-precision weights that are still trainable. The paper also defines a binary mask :
So means the weight has been quantized and frozen. means the weight can still move during retraining. Constrained Optimization ViewIf all weights had to be quantized directly, the layer-level objective would be
subject to
Here is the task loss, is the regularization term, and is the regularization coefficient. This constrained problem is difficult to optimize from scratch because the feasible values are discrete. INQ relaxes the problem at each iteration by constraining only the already selected group:
subject to
Now SGD only updates the unfrozen weights:
The mask is doing the real work in this equation. If , the update is exactly zero and the quantized weight remains fixed. If , the weight receives the normal gradient step. This turns quantization into a gradual constrained-training procedure:
freeze some weights into a hardware-friendly codebook; let the remaining weights compensate; repeat until no full-precision weights remain.
AlgorithmThe paper’s Algorithm 1 is short, but it contains several details that matter in reproduction: the base learning rate is reset at each stage, partitioning is layer-wise, and the codebook is determined layer-wise from the selected group.
The input schedule is written as
where is the accumulated portion of weights that should have been quantized by iteration . For example, the schedule means:
after the first stage, 50 percent of weights are quantized; after the second stage, 75 percent are quantized; after the third stage, 87.5 percent are quantized; after the final stage, all weights are quantized.
The “accumulated” wording matters. A stage does not quantize 75 percent more weights; it extends the frozen set until the frozen set reaches 75 percent of that layer. Partition StrategyThe default partition rule is pruning-inspired: quantize larger-magnitude weights first. The paper’s intuition is that large weights define a stable low-precision backbone, while small and medium weights still have room to absorb residual error during retraining. This is related to pruning, but the meaning is different. In pruning, small weights are often removed first because they are assumed to be less important. In INQ, large weights are quantized first because the authors want the main structure of the network to become fixed early. The remaining weights act as a correction buffer. The paper compares this rule against random partition on ResNet-18:
Random partition gives 32.11 percent top-1 error and 11.73 percent top-5 error. The pruning-inspired schedule gives 31.02 percent top-1 error and 10.90 percent top-5 error. Since lower error is better, this is a meaningful gap for such a small design choice. My reading is that this result is less about magnitude being a perfect importance metric and more about ordering. Quantization error is not independent noise. The order in which parameters are frozen changes the optimization path. ImageNet 5-Bit ResultsThe headline result is 5-bit weight quantization on common CNNs:
The numbers are reported as top-1 and top-5 error rates on ImageNet validation center crops. INQ improves or preserves the reference model in all five cases:
AlexNet moves from 42.76 percent top-1 error to 42.61 percent. VGG-16 moves from 31.46 percent to 29.18 percent. GoogLeNet moves from 31.11 percent to 30.98 percent. ResNet-18 moves from 31.73 percent to 31.02 percent. ResNet-50 moves from 26.78 percent to 25.19 percent.
The VGG-16 and ResNet-50 improvements are large enough that I would not read them as “quantization is inherently regularizing” without caution. The baseline models, training recipe, Caffe conversions, and fine-tuning schedule all matter. The safe claim is narrower: after staged retraining, 5-bit power-of-two weights did not hurt these reported ImageNet models. That is still a strong result for 2017. The method is weight-only, but it shows that a very restrictive codebook can work if the conversion schedule gives the model enough adaptation capacity. Lower Bit-WidthsThe next experiment lowers the bit-width on ResNet-18:
The trend is clear:
5-bit INQ: 31.02 percent top-1 error, better than the 32-bit reference. 4-bit INQ: 31.11 percent top-1 error, still better than the reference. 3-bit INQ: 31.92 percent top-1 error, slightly worse than the reference. 2-bit ternary INQ: 33.98 percent top-1 error, now noticeably worse but still much better than earlier ternary baselines in the paper.
The schedule becomes longer as bit-width decreases. The paper uses more incremental stages for 4-bit, 3-bit, and 2-bit ternary models because the codebook becomes more restrictive. This is a useful practical lesson: lower precision does not only need a different codebook; it usually needs a different training schedule. The ternary comparison makes the point more directly:
On ResNet-18, INQ’s 2-bit ternary model reports 33.98 percent top-1 error, compared with 39.20 percent for BWN and 38.20 percent for TWN in the table. The gain is not from inventing ternary weights; the gain comes from the incremental conversion procedure. Compression With DNSThe paper also combines INQ with Dynamic Network Surgery style pruning. The table below uses AlexNet and reports compression ratio with accuracy change:
The best way to read this table is not “INQ wins every row.” Instead:
pruning plus INQ reaches high compression ratios because pruning removes weights and INQ reduces the storage of the remaining weights; 5/5-bit convolution and fully connected weights reach a reported 53x compression ratio with small positive accuracy change; 4/4 and 3/3 settings push compression further but start to trade accuracy for storage; Huffman coding in Han et al. is a different entropy-coding step, so the comparisons mix algorithmic quantization and storage coding.
This is also where the “expected bit-width” terminology matters. A power-of-two codebook can be compactly encoded, but the real model size depends on pruning sparsity, index storage, and any entropy coding used after quantization. Weight Distribution After QuantizationTable 6 is one of the most useful diagnostics in the paper because it shows where the quantized weights actually land:
For AlexNet, every layer in this 5-bit experiment has an actual listed bit-width of 4 in the final row. That does not contradict the expected 5-bit setting. The expected bit-width controls the candidate codebook, while the layer-wise maximum and distribution determine which exponent values are actually used. The table also shows that zero is not rare.
