The paper uses a threshold of alpha = 6.0 for identifying outlier features. The key engineering claim is that the outlier set is tiny. For transformers up to 13B parameters, the paper reports at most 7 outlier feature dimensions, roughly 0.1% of the feature dimensions. That is small enough that the FP16 side path can preserve accuracy without giving up the memory benefit of INT8 weights for the main matrix. This is why the method is practical: it keeps more than 99.9% of values on the low-precision path but refuses to quantize the dimensions that actually break the model. Perplexity Results Table 1 is the most useful accuracy table. On C4 validation perplexity, simple INT8 methods degrade as the model scales. At 13B parameters:
Method 13B C4 perplexity
32-bit float 12.45
INT8 absmax vector-wise 16.48
INT8 zeropoint vector-wise 13.47
Absmax LLM.int8() 12.45
Zeropoint LLM.int8() 12.45
Two details are worth keeping:
Zeropoint quantization helps because the outliers are often one-sided, but it still fails at 13B. Once the outlier dimensions are moved to the FP16 path, zeropoint no longer has much advantage over absmax.
That second point supports the paper’s interpretation: after removing the pathological outlier dimensions from the INT8 path, the remaining distribution is much easier to quantize. Outliers As A Phase Shift The paper defines an outlier feature as a hidden dimension with magnitude at least 6, appearing in at least 25% of layers and at least 6% of sequence dimensions. Figure 3 shows how those features spread with model scale and perplexity. The parameter-scale plot looks like a sharp phase shift around 6B-6.7B parameters. The perplexity plot looks smoother: as C4 perplexity improves, more layers and sequence positions become affected by these large-magnitude features. The interpretation I find useful is: model size is a visible proxy, but not the only cause. Data, training quality, and model family can move the threshold. The real deployment lesson is to check activation statistics on the actual model, not to assume a fixed parameter-count cutoff.
Figure 4 adds another piece: once outliers become systematic, their magnitude grows quickly. This is why normal INT8 quantization breaks. A few very large dimensions stretch the quantization range, leaving too little resolution for ordinary values. Why The Outliers Matter The outlier statistics table is a good sanity check. For the 6.7B fairseq model, outliers affect 100% of layers and 75% of sequence dimensions. For the 13B fairseq model, the table reports 7 outlier dimensions, 100% of layers, and 73% of sequence dimensions. The important line from the paper is not only “outliers exist.” It is that removing them is catastrophic:
at 6.7B scale, the paper reports about 150k outlier values per 2048-token sequence; those values are concentrated in only about 6 feature dimensions; setting the outlier dimensions to zero can reduce mean top-1 attention softmax probability from about 40% to about 20%; validation perplexity can increase by 600%-1000%; removing the same number of random non-outlier dimensions barely changes the result.
That explains why clipping is the wrong mental model. These dimensions are not noise. They are rare in count but central to the model’s computation. Hardware Access The paper’s main deployment win is memory. INT8 storage nearly halves the parameter footprint, while the FP16 side path is tiny. The authors report a 1.96x memory-footprint reduction for BLOOM-176B. Table 2 makes the consequence concrete. With 8-bit inference, an 8x RTX 3090 24GB server can run OPT-175B/BLOOM, while the 16-bit setup listed there only reaches OPT-66B. A 4x RTX 3090 desktop moves from OPT-30B in 16-bit to OPT-66B in 8-bit. This is why LLM.int8() became practically important through bitsandbytes. The method changed which model sizes were loadable on available hardware. Speed Is Not The Main Promise The speed table is easy to misread. Raw INT8 matmul can be faster, but LLM.int8() also pays for quantization, dequantization, outlier extraction, and the FP16 side path. The paper reports that LLM.int8() is slower than FP16 for small GPT-3-sized matrices. In the table, LLM.int8() is 0.64x at the 2.7B shape and 0.86x at the 6.7B shape. It becomes faster at larger shapes: 1.22x at 13B and 1.81x at the 175B shape. The practical reading is:
use LLM.int8() for memory first; expect speedup only when the matmul is large enough and the kernels are good; treat outlier decomposition overhead as a real systems cost, not a free side branch.
The BLOOM-176B end-to-end table reinforces that point. INT8 inference is close to the native per-token latency and can use fewer GPUs, but it is not a universal latency win. For batch size 32, the table reports 9.94 ms/token for the bfloat16 8xA100 baseline, 10.44 ms/token for LLM.int8() on 8xA100, 9.40 ms/token on 4xA100, and 9.11 ms/token on 3xA100. The win is capacity and accessibility. Latency depends on communication, batch size, model sharding, and kernel implementation. Relation To Later Quantization WorkLLM.int8() is a useful reference point for later LLM quantization methods:
Method Main target How it handles activation difficulty
LLM.int8() W8A8-style inference matmul route outlier feature dimensions to FP16
SmoothQuant W8A8 dense inference migrate activation scale into weights before quantization
GPTQ weight-only PTQ keep activations high precision and compensate weight rounding error
AWQ activation-aware weight-only PTQ use activation statistics offline to protect salient weight channels
KIVI KV cache choose different quantization granularity for key and value cache
SmoothQuant can be read as a direct answer to LLM.int8()’s runtime irregularity. Instead of keeping a separate FP16 outlier path, SmoothQuant tries to smooth the activation outliers offline so the final runtime can use a dense W8A8 path. AWQ and GPTQ avoid activation quantization entirely at runtime by staying weight-only. Reproduction NotesIf I were reproducing this paper, I would separate the checks into statistics, accuracy, and systems measurements. For statistics:
plot activation max by hidden dimension across model sizes; count how many feature dimensions exceed the threshold alpha = 6.0; verify whether the same dimensions appear across layers and sequence positions; measure the effect of zeroing outlier dimensions versus random dimensions.
For accuracy:
compare tensor-wise, row-wise, vector-wise, zeropoint, and LLM.int8() variants; report C4 perplexity by model scale, not only one model; run zero-shot tasks at small, medium, and 175B scale if possible; sweep the outlier threshold and report the FP16 side-path size.
For systems:
measure model memory including scales and outlier metadata; report time spent in quantization, INT8 matmul, FP16 outlier matmul, and dequantization separately; benchmark small and large matrix shapes, because the overhead flips the speed conclusion; test end-to-end decoding, not only standalone GEMM.
TakeawayLLM.int8() is important because it names the LLM activation-outlier problem and gives a practical deployment workaround. Vector-wise quantization gives better INT8 precision for normal values, and mixed-precision decomposition protects the tiny set of hidden dimensions that the model cannot afford to quantize. The tradeoff is runtime irregularity. The method is excellent for loading large models with much lower memory, but the FP16 outlier path complicates kernels and does not guarantee latency improvement. That tradeoff explains why later methods either smooth the outliers away, as in SmoothQuant, or avoid activation quantization, as in GPTQ and AWQ.

entry.title: LLMLingua: Compressing Prompts Before Inference
entry.content:
Paper: LLMLingua: Compressing Prompts for Accelerated Inference of Large Language Models Code: https://aka.ms/LLMLingua LLMLingua is an inference acceleration paper, but it does not start from kernels, KV-cache layout, or batching. It starts one layer earlier: if a long prompt can be compressed before it is sent to the target LLM, then prefill latency, KV-cache memory, and API token cost all shrink together. That makes the paper interesting for RAG and agent systems. Those prompts often contain long retrieved passages, many demonstrations, or repeated instructions. A serving stack can optimize the attention kernels perfectly and still waste most of its work on prompt tokens that are not needed for the final answer. MotivationThe method assumes a black-box target LLM and a smaller local language model. The smaller model estimates which prompt tokens or demonstrations are more important, and the compressed prompt is then sent to the target model.
The central idea is not summarization. Summarization asks a model to rewrite the prompt into natural text. LLMLingua treats the prompt as an information source and tries to preserve the parts that keep the target model’s answer distribution close to the answer distribution under the original prompt. The paper defines the compression rate as:
where is the original prompt length and is the compressed prompt length. The compression ratio is . A smaller reduces inference cost, but it also increases the chance of deleting evidence, constraints, or reasoning steps. Coarse-to-Fine CompressionLLMLingua splits a prompt into instruction, demonstrations, and question. These parts do not tolerate compression equally. The instruction and question usually carry task constraints, while multiple demonstrations may contain redundancy. The paper therefore uses a budget controller before token-level compression.
The budget controller first allocates different compression rates to prompt components. For demonstrations, it computes perplexity with the small LM and keeps the higher-perplexity demonstrations first. The paper’s assumption is that these examples are more informative for the target task than low-perplexity or redundant ones. After this coarse filtering, LLMLingua applies iterative token-level prompt compression.
The iterative part matters because one-shot token removal ignores dependency between retained tokens. If a token is removed, the conditional probability of later tokens changes. LLMLingua processes segments iteratively, recomputes conditional probabilities, and selects tokens under an adjusted compression threshold. This is slower than a single scoring pass, but the ablation shows that the extra dependency modeling is not cosmetic. The third piece is distribution alignment. The small LM is only a proxy for the target black-box model. LLMLingua tries to reduce the mismatch between the small LM distribution and the target LLM distribution, because a token that looks unimportant to a small model may still matter to GPT-style or Claude-style models. Main ResultsThe first result table covers ShareGPT conversation and Arxiv-March23 summarization. Both are context-heavy settings where removing prompt tokens should help serving cost, but deleting the wrong context can damage answer quality.
On ShareGPT, LLMLingua keeps stronger ROUGE/BERTScore numbers than the baselines under the reported token budgets. On Arxiv-March23, the paper reports similar behavior: the method reaches higher compression while preserving more of the summarization quality than sentence selection and Selective-Context. The more interesting table for me is GSM8K and BBH, because these tasks punish missing intermediate reasoning details.
On GSM8K, LLMLingua reports 79.08 EM with a 5x compression ratio under the 1-shot constraint, compared with 78.85 for the full-shot prompt. Under heavier compression, it still reports 77.41 EM at 14x and 77.33 EM at 20x. BBH drops more sharply, which is expected: it contains tasks where one deleted condition can change the answer. This is the right way to read the paper. The method is not saying that prompts are always 20x redundant. It is showing that some prompt formats, especially demonstration-heavy ones, contain enough redundancy for aggressive compression to be useful. AblationThe ablation table is the part that makes the method easier to trust. It separates the effects of iterative token compression, budget control, dynamic compression ratio, perplexity-based selection, distribution alignment, and naive stop-word removal.
Removing iterative token-level compression drops GSM8K EM from 79.08 to 72.93. Removing the budget controller gives 73.62. Random selection inside the budget controller gives 72.78. These are large enough drops to show that the method is not just “delete many tokens and hope the LLM survives.” The stop-word row is also useful. Removing stop words gives only 1.3x compression and lower EM. Prompt compression cannot be reduced to a surface-level text-cleaning trick. Serving CostPrompt compression affects serving in two places:
The target model receives fewer prompt tokens, so prefill compute and initial KV-cache allocation decrease. The target model may generate shorter answers because the compressed prompt often contains less redundant context.
The generation-length plot shows a downward trend as the compression ratio increases. This effect is application-dependent, but it matters for end-to-end latency because decode work is paid per generated token. The paper also reports measured latency on GSM8K with a V100-32G GPU.
The reported end-to-end latency moves from 8.6 seconds without LLMLingua to 4.9 seconds at 2x compression, 2.3 seconds at 5x compression, and 1.3 seconds at 10x compression. The small LM compression step is not free, but in this setup it is much cheaper than running the large target model on the original prompt. For serving systems, this makes LLMLingua complementary to KV-cache quantization, paged attention, continuous batching, and fast attention kernels. Those systems reduce the cost of serving a sequence. LLMLingua tries to reduce the sequence before those systems see it. Failure BoundaryThe limitation is semantic rather than numerical. Kernel optimization should not change the model’s input. Prompt compression does. If the compressor removes the one sentence that contains the answer, the target LLM can become confidently wrong. The paper’s compression-ratio curve makes this visible.
Performance stays relatively strong up to moderate compression, then drops when the ratio gets too aggressive. Around very high ratios such as 25x to 30x on GSM8K, all methods degrade. LLMLingua shifts the degradation point later than the baselines, but it does not remove the tradeoff. I would treat the compression ratio as a deployment knob, not as a fixed paper number. A RAG system should tune it against answer faithfulness, citation retention, and failure cases from its own traffic. Practical NotesWhere I would try LLMLingua:
RAG prompts with long retrieved contexts and repeated boilerplate. Agent traces where previous observations contain redundancy. Demonstration-heavy prompts where examples can be ranked and removed. API inference where prompt tokens are a direct cost center.
Where I would be careful:
Legal, medical, or financial prompts where one clause changes the answer. Tool-use prompts where exact JSON schemas or command constraints must survive. Debugging sessions where the model needs the full history, including failed attempts. Any evaluation that only measures compression ratio and not evidence retention.
For production use, I would log both the original prompt and compressed prompt, then diff removed spans during debugging. Without that audit trail, a wrong answer is hard to attribute: it could come from the target LLM, the retrieved context, or the compressor deleting the necessary evidence. TakeawayLLMLingua is useful because it reframes part of LLM serving as input selection. The cheapest prefill token is the one never sent to the target model. The hard part is making sure that deleted tokens are actually redundant for the task, not just low-probability under a small proxy model.

entry.title: LQ-Nets: Learned Quantization for Highly Accurate and Compact Deep Neural Networks
entry.content:
Zhang D, Yang J, Ye D, Hua G. LQ-Nets: Learned Quantization for Highly Accurate and Compact Deep Neural Networks. arXiv:1807.10029.
Paper / Code LQ-Nets is a useful paper to read before LSQ, PACT, and later learned data-type work because it asks a direct question: if the network weights and activations are not uniformly distributed, why should the quantization grid be fixed before training? The answer in this paper is not just “learn a scale.” LQ-Nets learns the quantization basis itself. The quantization levels can become non-uniform, layer dependent, and channel dependent, while still keeping a decomposition that can be evaluated with bitwise dot products. That makes the paper more interesting than a plain learned-codebook method: the quantizer is flexible, but the authors still care about the low-bit inference path. This note reads LQ-Nets as a quantization-aware training design:
represent low-bit values through binary encodings and learned bases; update the quantizer in the forward pass with quantization error minimization; update the network weights with STE-based backpropagation; check whether the extra quantizer flexibility pays off at 1-4 bits.
All figures and tables below are cropped from the original paper PDF. MotivationUniform quantization is attractive because it maps cleanly to integer arithmetic. But a fixed uniform grid is also a strong assumption. The distribution of a convolution filter can be close to symmetric and concentrated near zero; an activation distribution after BN/ReLU can be highly skewed and layer specific. A single handcrafted quantizer cannot be optimal for all of these cases.
Figure 1 shows this mismatch. The left two histograms are weights from different ResNet-20 layers. The right two histograms are activations. The shapes are different enough that “use the same uniform grid everywhere” is more of an engineering convenience than a statistically motivated choice. The paper’s target is very low precision. At 8 bits, many uniform quantizers have enough levels to hide a mediocre grid. At 1-2 bits, every level matters. If a 2-bit quantizer gives only four reconstruction values, the exact placement of those four values can decide whether the model survives. Quantization As A Learned BasisThe core quantizer is simple. For a scalar input , LQ-Nets assigns it to an interval and reconstructs it from a learned basis vector:
Here is the learned basis for a -bit quantizer, and is one of the binary encodings. In the paper’s exposition, . In the implementation note, weights use encodings and activations use encodings. For , the four levels are produced by combinations such as:
For , there are eight combinations. The important part is that the levels are not required to be equally spaced. They are generated by a small number of learned basis scalars.
Figure 2 is the whole idea visually. The left side of each subfigure shows how the codebook is generated by binary basis combinations. The right side shows the resulting staircase quantizer. Compared with a learned arbitrary lookup table, this basis form has a special constraint: each quantized value remains decomposable into bits. That constraint is the reason LQ-Nets can still claim bit-operation compatibility. The codebook is learned, but it is not an unconstrained set of floating-point centroids. Bitwise-Compatible Inner ProductFor low-bit inference, the paper wants the inner product between quantized weights and quantized activations to reduce to bitwise operations. Suppose weights use bits and activations use bits. Their quantized vectors can be decomposed into bit planes:
weight bit vectors: , for ; activation bit vectors: , for ; learned weight basis: ; learned activation basis: .
The inner product becomes:
The bit-plane inner product can be implemented with xnor and popcnt for binary encodings. The learned bases then scale and combine those bitwise partial sums. This is a different deployment contract from ordinary INT8 GEMM:
Quantizer Grid shape Main kernel view
uniform INT quantization fixed uniform grid plus scale integer multiply-accumulate
LSQ-style learned scale uniform grid, learned step size integer multiply-accumulate plus learned scale
arbitrary codebook unconstrained lookup table lookup/decode path
LQ-Nets learned basis-generated codebook several bitwise dot products plus basis mixing
So LQ-Nets is hardware-aware, but not hardware-free. It preserves a bitwise decomposition, yet a real backend still needs kernels that exploit this decomposition efficiently. Training AlgorithmThe training setup keeps floating-point weights during optimization. Before convolution, weights and activations are quantized. After training, the floating-point weights can be discarded; the model keeps the binary encodings and quantizer bases. The difficult part is learning the quantizer. A direct backpropagation update through a piecewise constant quantizer is weak because the derivative is zero almost everywhere. LQ-Nets therefore separates two jobs:
quantizer parameters are updated in the forward pass by QEM; network parameters are updated in the backward pass with STE.
QEM means quantization error minimization. Given full-precision values and bit-width , the quantizer tries to solve:
The exact problem is combinatorial because is binary. The paper uses alternating minimization:
Fix the basis , then assign each scalar to its closest quantization interval. This updates . Fix the binary encodings , then solve the least-squares basis update:
Repeat for QEM iterations. Update the running quantizer basis with a moving average.
Algorithm 1 makes a subtle design choice clear: QEM is a forward-pass quantizer optimization routine, not the backward pass for the network. During training, QEM computes binary encodings and a better basis estimate. During testing, the quantizer simply uses the current basis to encode inputs. The paper uses a moving average factor of 0.9 and sets in the experiments. That sounds surprisingly small, but the basis from the previous training iteration is already a good warm start. How It Is Used In The NetworkThe implementation choices matter because they define how much flexibility the quantizer actually has.
Component Paper setting
weight quantizer channel-wise, one quantizer per convolution filter
activation quantizer layer-wise, one quantizer per layer
first and last layers not quantized in the reported experiments
activation encoding in implementation
weight encoding in implementation
backward estimator STE
quantizer update QEM in forward pass
Channel-wise weight quantization is important. Filters in the same layer can still have different distributions. A single layer-wise basis for all filters would be cheaper, but it would remove much of the flexibility that the paper is testing. Layer-wise activation quantization is a compromise. Per-channel activation quantization would be more flexible, but activations are dynamic and mini-batch sampled. The paper stabilizes activation bases with moving average updates. QEM Versus Naive BackpropagationThe first result to read is not the large ImageNet table. It is the ablation that asks whether QEM is useful at all.
On ResNet-20/CIFAR-10, QEM beats direct BP for quantizer learning:
Bit-width W/A Quantizer optimization Accuracy
2/32 BP 90.0
2/32 QEM 91.8
2/2 BP 88.2
2/2 QEM 90.2
The improvement is not tiny. At 2-bit weights with full-precision activations, QEM gives +1.8 points. At 2-bit weights and 2-bit activations, it gives +2.0 points. The error curves in Figure 3 also show a cleaner gap through training, not just a lucky final checkpoint. This is the paper’s strongest evidence that the quantizer should not merely be treated as another parameter passed through a crude STE. The assignment step and the least-squares basis update use the current tensor distribution more directly. One QEM Iteration Is EnoughThe next ablation checks how many alternating QEM updates are needed per training iteration.
The table reports ResNet-20/CIFAR-10 accuracy over five runs:
W/A T=1 T=2 T=3 T=4
1/2 88.37 88.38 88.45 88.51
2/2 90.16 90.35 90.33 90.25
3/3 91.58 91.55 91.62 91.44
The message is practical: extra inner iterations are not worth much. Because training itself repeats the update thousands of times, one QEM step per mini-batch is enough to track the moving tensor distribution. That matters for runtime. A quantizer that needs a heavy solver inside every forward pass would be difficult to justify. Learned Quantizers Are Non-UniformThe paper then checks the central claim: do the learned quantizers actually look different from uniform ones?
Figure 4 shows weights and activations before and after 2/2 quantization in a ResNet-20 trained on CIFAR-10. The orange diamonds mark the four quantization levels. The learned levels are visibly non-uniform, and they differ across layers. My reading: this figure is more important than it first looks. It proves the method is not just learning a global scale hidden inside a different notation. The quantizer shape changes. For a 2-bit activation distribution that is concentrated near zero with a long tail, spending all four levels uniformly across the full range would be wasteful. LQ-Nets can put more resolution where the data actually sits. That said, non-uniformity is not automatically a win. It is only useful if the backend can still execute the resulting representation efficiently. LQ-Nets earns the right to use non-uniform levels by generating them from bit-compatible bases. ImageNet Sanity CheckBefore the full comparison table, Table 3 compares 1/2 ResNet-18 ImageNet results against DoReFa-Net and HWGQ.
Method W/A Top-1 Top-5
Uniform DoReFa-Net 1/4 59.2 -
Half-wave Gaussian HWGQ 1/2 59.6 82.2
LQ-Nets 1/2 62.6 84.3
This is a clean comparison because HWGQ also targets 1-bit weights and 2-bit activations. LQ-Nets improves top-1 by 3.0 points and top-5 by 2.1 points under the same W/A bit-width. It also beats the DoReFa-Net 1/4 result while using fewer activation bits. The reason I call this a sanity check is that CIFAR-10 results can hide a lot of quantization weaknesses. ImageNet with ResNet-18 is still small by modern standards, but it is much harder to pass with 1-2 bit tensors. Bit-Width BehaviorTable 4 is the best table for understanding the bit-width curve.
Representative numbers, split by model so the table stays readable on mobile. ResNet-20 on CIFAR-10, FP accuracy 92.1:
W/A Acc. Drop
1/32 90.1 -2.0
2/2 90.2 -1.9
3/3 91.6 -0.5
VGG-Small on CIFAR-10, FP accuracy 93.8:
W/A Acc. Drop
1/2 93.4 -0.4
3/3 93.8 0.0
ResNet-18 on ImageNet, FP accuracy 70.3:
W/A Acc. Drop
1/2 62.6 -7.7
3/3 68.2 -2.1
4/4 69.3 -1.0
The table has two lessons. First, weight-only quantization is much easier. ResNet-18 with 4-bit weights and full-precision activations reaches 70.0 top-1, only 0.3 below the full-precision 70.3 reported by the authors. This matches the broader quantization pattern: activations are often the harder part because they are input dependent and layer dependent. Second, activation quantization needs a few bits on ImageNet. The jump from 1/2 to 3/3 on ResNet-18 is large: 62.6 to 68.2 top-1. The learned quantizer helps, but it does not make 1-bit weights and 2-bit activations free. CIFAR-10 ComparisonTable 5 compares VGG-Small against binary and half-wave Gaussian baselines.
Model Method W/A Accuracy
VGG-Small FP-HWGQ 32/32 93.2
VGG-Small FP-ours 32/32 93.8
VGG-Small BNN 1/1 89.9
VGG-Small XNOR-Net 1/1 89.8
VGG-Small HWGQ 1/2 92.5
VGG-Small LQ-Nets 1/2 93.4
The comparison is small but useful. Going from binary activations to 2-bit activations helps, and learning the quantizer helps further. LQ-Nets is within 0.4 points of its full-precision VGG-Small result at 1/2 bits. I would not overgeneralize this result. VGG-Small on CIFAR-10 has enough redundancy that many quantization methods look strong. The ImageNet table below is the harder evidence. ImageNet ComparisonTable 6 is dense, so I split the crop into ResNet models and the other architectures.
For ResNets, the headline numbers are:
Model Setting Top-1 Read
ResNet-18 FP-ours 32/32 70.3 reference for the authors’ run
ResNet-18 LQ-Nets 1/2 62.6 beats HWGQ 1/2 at 59.6
ResNet-18 LQ-Nets 3/3 68.2 closes much of the gap
ResNet-18 LQ-Nets 4/4 69.3 1.0 below FP-ours
ResNet-34 LQ-Nets 1/2 66.6 above HWGQ 1/2 at 64.3
ResNet-34 LQ-Nets 3/3 71.9 1.9 below FP-ours
ResNet-50 LQ-Nets 1/2 68.7 above HWGQ 1/2 at 64.6
ResNet-50 LQ-Nets 4/4 75.1 1.3 below FP-ours
The non-ResNet side has the same pattern:
Model Setting Top-1 Read
AlexNet LQ-Nets 2/32 60.5 close to FP-ours at 61.8
AlexNet LQ-Nets 1/2 55.7 above HWGQ 1/2 at 52.7
DenseNet-121 LQ-Nets 2/2 69.6 above DoReFa-Net 2/2 at 67.7
VGG-Variant LQ-Nets 1/2 67.1 above HWGQ 1/2 at 64.1
GoogLeNet-Variant LQ-Nets 1/2 65.6 above HWGQ 1/2 at 63.0
The broad result is consistent: learned quantizers improve accuracy at the same nominal bit-width. The gain is most visible when both weights and activations are aggressively quantized. The careful reading is also important. These are not all apples-to-apples runtime comparisons. Some baselines use different full-precision references, some rows come from reported numbers in other papers, and first/last layers are not quantized. The accuracy trend is meaningful, but deployment speed still depends on the actual kernel implementation. Training CostThe paper also reports training overhead for ResNet-18. No bitwise operation is used in these training-time comparisons; this is about the cost of the quantization-aware training procedure itself.
W/A Training time
32/32 1.0x
2/32 1.4x
3/32 1.7x
1/2 2.1x
2/2 2.3x
3/3 3.7x
The cost grows with bit-width because the basis solve and the number of bit-plane interactions grow. The paper argues that solving is cheap and solving is small relative to convolution, but the measured overhead is still real. A 3/3 model taking 3.7x training time is not a free ablation. This is one reason later practical QAT methods often prefer lower-dimensional quantizer parameters such as clipping thresholds or step sizes. They give up some codebook flexibility, but they are easier to train and deploy. Relationship To PACT And LSQPACT, LSQ, and LQ-Nets all make the quantizer trainable, but they train different parts of it.
Method What is learned Grid shape Practical bias
PACT activation clipping threshold uniform after clipping simple activation QAT
LSQ step size uniform easy integer deployment
LQ-Nets basis-generated quantization levels non-uniform higher flexibility at low bits
PACT is mainly about learning how much activation range to keep. LSQ is about learning the step size for a uniform grid. LQ-Nets goes further by learning a basis that changes the relative spacing between levels. That extra flexibility is exactly why LQ-Nets is a good conceptual baseline. It shows that “where the levels are” can matter as much as “how many levels exist.” But it also explains why LSQ-style methods became common baselines: uniform grids map more naturally to integer hardware and framework quantization APIs. Reproduction NotesIf I were reproducing this paper, I would check these details first. First, separate QEM from STE. QEM updates the quantizer in the forward pass; STE is only the surrogate gradient used for network training. Mixing these two concepts makes the implementation hard to debug. Second, log the learned basis values per layer or per channel. If the levels remain close to a scaled uniform grid, the method is probably not exercising its main degree of freedom. Figure 4 gives a good qualitative target. Third, reproduce the QEM-vs-BP ablation before chasing the full ImageNet table. Table 1 is a much smaller test of whether the quantizer optimizer is implemented correctly. Fourth, keep the first and last layers consistent with the paper. Quantizing or not quantizing those layers can move low-bit accuracy enough to confuse comparisons. Fifth, measure simulated accuracy and real backend speed separately. A PyTorch simulation can validate QAT, but it does not prove the bitwise inference path is fast. For deployment, the kernel needs to exploit bit packing, xnor, popcnt, and basis mixing. Sixth, watch activation quantizer stability. Activation bases are estimated from mini-batches and then smoothed by moving average. A bad moving average schedule can make the quantizer chase batch noise. LimitationsLQ-Nets is strong, but its scope is narrower than the title might suggest.
The experiments are CNN-focused: CIFAR-10 and ImageNet with AlexNet, VGG, GoogLeNet, ResNet, and DenseNet variants. First and last layers remain full precision in the reported setup, which is common but still part of the accuracy story. The inference format is bit-operation-compatible, but it is not a drop-in replacement for standard INT8 GEMM. Training overhead is nontrivial, especially as both weight and activation bit-widths increase. The paper predates modern deployment stacks, so the accuracy tables do not answer current backend questions such as TensorRT, mobile NPU support, compiler lowering, or mixed-precision fallback.
The main limitation for me is the backend gap. The learned basis is elegant, but a production system needs an efficient implementation of the full dot-product decomposition. Without that, “2-bit” can look better in a table than it behaves in an end-to-end latency benchmark. TakeawayLQ-Nets is the learned-codebook branch of early low-bit QAT, but with an important hardware constraint: the codebook is generated from binary bases so the dot product can still be decomposed into bitwise operations. The paper’s strongest lessons are:
quantization levels should be treated as trainable model components; non-uniform levels can recover accuracy at very low bit-widths; QEM is a better quantizer update than naive backpropagation in this setting; learned codebooks must be judged together with their kernel path.
When reading later quantization work, I keep LQ-Nets as a reference point: if a method learns only a scale, it is choosing deployability over codebook flexibility; if it learns arbitrary levels, it needs to explain the runtime path. LQ-Nets sits in the middle by learning non-uniform levels while preserving a bitwise-compatible decomposition.

entry.title: LSQ: Learned Step Size Quantization
entry.content:
Paper: Learned Step Size Quantization LSQ is a quantization-aware training paper that is easy to underestimate. At first glance, it only makes the quantization step size learnable. That sounds like a small change because many uniform quantizers already have a scale. The important part is not just that is trained. The important part is how the gradient to is defined and scaled. The paper keeps the inference format simple: low-precision integer matrix multiplication followed by a scale multiplication. It does not learn an arbitrary codebook like LQ-Nets, and it does not rely on a post-training reconstruction objective like later PTQ work. LSQ’s bet is more conservative: keep the uniform integer grid, but let task loss tune the bin width. Why LSQ MattersUniform quantization has one central parameter: the step size . If is too small, many values hit the clip boundary. If is too large, the grid is coarse and normal values suffer rounding error. Static calibration can choose a reasonable initial value, but QAT changes weights and activation distributions during training. A fixed scale is a bad place to hide a moving target. LSQ treats the step size as a model parameter, one per weight layer and one per activation layer. The final runtime still looks like a standard scaled integer path:
The figure is the deployment story. During inference, weights and activations are represented by low-precision integer tensors and . The low-precision matrix multiplication produces , and the output is brought back to the real scale by multiplying with learned step-size metadata. That keeps LSQ much more hardware-friendly than a non-uniform learned codebook. Quantizer DefinitionGiven a tensor value , a step size , and quantization bounds and , LSQ first creates an integer-scaled value:
Then it maps the integer value back to the original scale:
For unsigned activations with bits, the paper uses
For signed weights with bits, it uses
The lower bound is written as , so signed weights use the integer range
This is a normal uniform quantizer. LSQ’s novelty is not the forward path. The novelty is the backward path for the scale parameter. Step Size GradientRounding is discontinuous. During QAT, LSQ uses the straight-through estimator for the round operation, but it still differentiates the rest of the quantizer with respect to . The resulting step-size gradient is sensitive to where sits inside the quantization interval. For values inside the unclipped range,
For values below the lower clip point,
For values above the upper clip point,
The intuition is useful: if a value is close to a quantization transition point, a small change in can move it into a different bin. LSQ’s gradient reflects that. This is different from gradients that only care about clipping boundaries.
The left plot shows the quantized output for , , and . The right plot compares the gradient shape used by LSQ, QIL, and PACT. LSQ’s blue sawtooth pattern is the key visual: inside the range, the gradient changes with distance to the nearest integer transition, not just with distance to the clip point. Straight-Through Gradient For ValuesLSQ still uses the usual STE idea for the tensor value itself. During backpropagation, the gradient with respect to is passed through inside the unclipped region and blocked outside it:
Outside the range,
So LSQ has two different gradient stories:
for values, it uses a standard clipped STE; for the step size, it uses a transition-sensitive gradient and then rescales that gradient.
The second part is what makes training stable. Step Size InitializationEach weight layer and activation layer has its own step size stored as fp32. The paper initializes it as
where is computed from the initial weights or from the first activation batch. This is only an initialization. The training loss is allowed to move away from this distribution-fitting value. That last point matters because LSQ later shows that the learned does not necessarily minimize ordinary quantization error metrics such as mean absolute error, mean square error, or KL divergence. It optimizes task loss. Why The Gradient Scale Is NeededIf a layer has one shared step size, then the gradient to that scalar receives contributions from every quantized element in the tensor. A convolution weight tensor may have thousands or millions of elements. Without correction, the update to can become much larger than the update to ordinary weights. The paper frames this with a relative update ratio:
Ideally, should be near 1, meaning the step size and the weights receive updates of comparable relative magnitude. LSQ argues that the expected imbalance grows with both the number of elements sharing the scale and the number of positive quantization levels. For a weight step size, LSQ uses
where is the number of weights sharing that step size. For an activation step size, LSQ uses
where is the number of activation features sharing that step size. The gradient scale is applied to the step-size loss gradient. The forward value of is unchanged; only the backward gradient is scaled. This is why the implementation can be compact even though the training behavior changes a lot. The appendix derivation gives the rough reason:
Taking the inverse gives the weight step-size scale above. Training SetupThe paper trains quantized models from a full-precision initialization. Full-precision weights are stored and updated, while quantized weights and quantized activations are used in the forward and backward computation. The first and last layers remain at 8-bit precision, a common choice in low-bit CNN QAT because those layers are often more sensitive. The main ImageNet setup is:
pre-activation ResNet, VGG-16 with batch norm, and SqueezeNext architectures; 2-bit, 3-bit, 4-bit, and 8-bit quantization for matrix multiplication layers except first and last; 90 epochs for 2-, 3-, and 4-bit networks; 1 epoch for 8-bit networks; cosine learning-rate decay; PyTorch implementation.
This is not post-training quantization. LSQ assumes a real QAT budget. ImageNet ResultsThe main ImageNet comparison is dense, but the pattern is easy to read: LSQ is strongest in the 2-bit to 4-bit region, where step-size errors hurt most.
Some rows worth remembering:
ResNet-18 at 2-bit reaches 67.6 top-1, compared with a 70.5 full-precision baseline. ResNet-18 at 4-bit reaches 71.1 top-1, slightly above the listed full-precision baseline. ResNet-34 at 3-bit reaches 73.4 top-1, close to its 74.1 full-precision baseline. ResNet-50 at 4-bit reaches 76.7 top-1, close to 76.9 full precision. VGG-16bn at 3-bit reaches 73.4 top-1, matching the listed full-precision baseline.
The paper also notes that increasing from 4-bit to 8-bit often gives little or no additional accuracy in these settings. That does not mean 8-bit is useless. It means that with QAT and a learned step size, 4-bit can already be near the full-precision operating point for these CNNs. Weight Decay Changes With PrecisionThe paper includes a small but useful weight-decay sweep:
The result is practical. Lower precision acts like a regularizer, so the best weight decay can be smaller:
2-bit ResNet-18 improves from 66.9 to 67.6 when weight decay is reduced from to . 3-bit improves from 70.1 to 70.2 with . 4-bit and 8-bit are less sensitive in this table.
This is a good reminder for reproductions. If a QAT method looks weaker than reported, the problem may be the training recipe, not only the quantizer. Accuracy Versus Model SizeThe paper also plots accuracy against model size:
This figure gives a deployment-oriented view. Under a fixed memory budget, a larger architecture at lower precision can beat a smaller architecture at higher precision. The paper calls out the 8 MB region: a 2-bit ResNet-50 can be better than a 4-bit ResNet-34. That is a different question from “what is the best bit-width for one architecture?” If the deployment budget is model size, architecture and precision should be chosen together. Gradient Scale AblationThe most important ablation is the gradient scale:
Without scaling, relative updates to are two to three orders of magnitude larger than relative updates to weights. Scaling by reduces the layer-size imbalance, but precision-dependent imbalance remains. Scaling by removes most of both effects. The accuracy table makes the point more concrete:
For 2-bit ResNet-18:
the full scale gives 67.6 top-1 at learning rate 0.01; using only gives 67.3; no scale at learning rate 0.01 does not converge; no scale can train at learning rate 0.0001, but only reaches 64.2; multiplying the proposed scale by 10 or by 0.1 also loses accuracy.
This table is the core of the paper. If I had to summarize LSQ in one sentence, it would be: learn the quantization step size, but normalize its gradient so it behaves like a real parameter rather than a giant accumulator. Knowledge DistillationLSQ also combines well with same-architecture knowledge distillation:
The paper uses a full-precision teacher of the same architecture. The strongest claim is that 3-bit models reach full-precision accuracy in this setting:
ResNet-18 at 3-bit reaches 70.6 top-1, compared with 70.5 full precision. ResNet-34 at 3-bit reaches 74.3, compared with 74.1 full precision. ResNet-50 at 3-bit reaches 76.9, matching the 76.9 full-precision baseline.
This is an important distinction: LSQ alone already gives strong QAT results, and distillation further closes the gap for 3-bit models. LSQ Does Not Minimize Quantization ErrorOne of the more interesting observations is that the learned step size is not the same as the step size that minimizes tensor reconstruction error. For a 2-bit ResNet-18, the paper compares the final learned against a grid of candidate values and checks mean absolute error, mean square error, and KL divergence. The differences are large:
activation layers differ by 50 percent for mean absolute error, 63 percent for mean square error, and 64 percent for KL divergence; weight layers differ by 47 percent for mean absolute error, 28 percent for mean square error, and 46 percent for KL divergence.
The interpretation is important: task-optimal quantization is not necessarily distribution-optimal quantization. A scale that minimizes may not minimize classification loss. This is also why LSQ is a bridge between simple calibration and later reconstruction-based methods. Calibration chooses a scale from tensor statistics. LSQ lets the task loss choose. Implementation PatternThe appendix gives short pseudocode for gradscale, roundpass, and quantize:
The key trick is the detach identity:
In the forward pass, this returns . In the backward pass, the gradient flows through . That lets the implementation return one value in the forward path and use a different surrogate gradient. In PyTorch-style pseudocode, the two helper functions look like: def grad_scale(x, scale): y = x y_grad = x * scale delta = y - y_grad return delta.detach() + y_graddef round_pass(x): y = x.round() y_grad = x delta = y - y_grad return delta.detach() + y_grad
Then LSQ quantization is basically: def quantize(v, s, b, act): if act: qn = 0 qp = 2 ** b - 1 n = num_features(v) else: qn = -(2 ** (b - 1)) qp = 2 ** (b - 1) - 1 n = num_weights(v) gs = 1.0 / math.sqrt(n * qp) s = grad_scale(s, gs) v = v / s v = v.clamp(qn, qp) v_bar = round_pass(v) return v_bar * s
The implementation is small, but small does not mean trivial. The grad_scale line is the difference between a stable learned scale and a scale parameter whose update magnitude is dominated by tensor size. Relation To PACT And LQ-NetsLSQ sits between PACT and LQ-Nets. PACT learns an activation clipping threshold. It improves activation range selection but does not learn a full weight and activation step-size system in the same way. LQ-Nets learns a more flexible quantization basis. That can improve expressivity at low bit-width, but the resulting codebook is less obviously mapped to standard integer kernels. LSQ chooses the middle path:
keep the uniform grid; learn one scale per quantized layer tensor; preserve a simple integer inference path; spend the method complexity in the gradient, not the runtime format.
That is why LSQ became a common QAT baseline. It gives the optimizer a useful degree of freedom without changing the deployed arithmetic too much. Reproduction NotesIf I were reproducing LSQ, I would log these signals:
learned weight step size per layer; learned activation step size per layer; gradient norm of step sizes before and after scaling; clipping ratio for activations and weights; top-1 accuracy under the same weight decay sweep as Table 2.
The likely failure modes are straightforward:
forgetting to scale the step-size gradient; using the wrong convention for signed weights; letting first and last layers become too low precision; treating LSQ as PTQ and expecting it to work without training; comparing against a baseline with a mismatched training recipe.
The paper is compact, but the engineering lesson is durable. In low-bit QAT, the quantizer parameter is part of the model. If that parameter receives gradients on the wrong scale, the model may fail even when the forward quantizer is correct. TakeawayLSQ is not about inventing a new integer format. It is about making the standard uniform format trainable in a controlled way. The part to remember is:
The step size receives gradients from many tensor elements, so the gradient must be normalized by layer size and quantization range. Once that is done, a very simple quantizer becomes a strong low-bit QAT baseline on ImageNet.

entry.title: Linformer: Self-Attention with Linear Complexity
entry.content:
Wang S, Li B Z, Khabsa M, et al. Linformer: Self-Attention with Linear Complexity. 2020.
Paper Linformer is one of the clean efficient-attention papers: it makes a structural claim about self-attention, then turns that claim into a simple layer change. The claim is that the self-attention context mapping is often low-rank, so the model does not need to materialize the full n x n attention map for every head. This is approximate attention. It is not the same kind of optimization as FlashAttention, which computes exact attention with better IO behavior. Why This MattersThe standard Transformer attention pattern has quadratic time and memory in sequence length: full attention: softmax(Q K^T / sqrt(d)) V cost grows like O(n^2)
Linformer projects keys and values along the sequence dimension before attention: Linformer attention: project K from n tokens to k slots project V from n tokens to k slots compute attention against the projected K and V cost grows like O(n k)
If k is treated as a small fixed projection dimension, the layer becomes linear in n.
The comparison table frames Linformer against other sequence models. The pitch is not only lower asymptotic complexity; it also keeps one sequential operation like a standard Transformer layer, unlike recurrent models. Low-Rank Evidence The paper first inspects pretrained Transformer attention matrices from RoBERTa-base and RoBERTa-large. The singular-value curves show that much of the mass is concentrated in a relatively small number of directions, especially in higher layers. This is the empirical basis for replacing the full context matrix with a low-rank approximation. I read this figure as a useful diagnostic, not a universal proof. Some heads, tasks, or positions may need higher-rank interactions. Linformer is betting that the common case can be compressed enough to make the tradeoff worthwhile. Layer Design The layer keeps the usual query projection, but applies learned projection matrices to keys and values across the sequence dimension. In the paper notation, each head can use matrices shaped like k x n to reduce the token axis before attention. The authors also discuss sharing these projection matrices:
Sharing strategy Meaning Practical effect
Headwise sharing heads share projection matrices fewer extra parameters than per-head projections
Key-value sharing key and value projections share parameters reduces the projection overhead further
Layerwise sharing layers share projection matrices smallest projection-parameter footprint
The strongest practical setting in the downstream table uses shared key/value projections and layerwise sharing, which is a useful signal: the benefit is not only from adding more parameters. Pretraining Curves The pretraining plots check several knobs:
larger k improves the approximation; k = 128 works reasonably for n = 512, while k = 256 is stronger for longer settings; sharing projection matrices does not destroy convergence; fixing k = 256 while increasing n still gives similar final validation perplexity.
The last point is the important one for the paper’s linear-time claim. If quality collapsed whenever n increased with fixed k, the asymptotic story would not matter much in practice. Downstream Results The downstream numbers are close to RoBERTa-base on SST-2, IMDB, QNLI, and QQP. The table reports a RoBERTa-base average of 92.25. A Linformer model with n = 512, k = 256, shared key/value projections, and layerwise sharing reaches 92.30. With n = 1024, k = 256, and the same sharing pattern, it reaches 92.18. That is the core empirical bargain: similar benchmark quality while avoiding the quadratic attention map. Efficiency Table 3 measures inference-time speed and memory savings against a standard Transformer on a 16GB Tesla V100. Even at n = 512, k = 128, the paper reports 1.5x faster inference and 1.7x lower memory. At long sequence lengths the savings grow quickly; for example, n = 65536, k = 256 reports 18x faster inference and 52x lower memory. These numbers depend on the benchmark setup and implementation, but the direction is expected. Once the full n x n attention map disappears, the long-sequence memory curve changes substantially. TakeawayLinformer is attractive because the change is easy to understand: compress the sequence axis of keys and values, then attend to the compressed representation. It gives a clean path from quadratic attention to approximate linear attention. The risk is exactly the assumption that makes it work. If a task really needs high-rank token-token interactions, fixed low-rank projections can throw away information before attention has a chance to use it. I would treat Linformer as a strong efficient-attention baseline for long-context experiments, but not as a drop-in replacement for exact attention when output equivalence matters.

entry.title: Longformer: The Long-Document Transformer
entry.content:
Paper: Longformer: The Long-Document Transformer Code: https://github.com/allenai/longformer Longformer is a practical long-context Transformer paper. It does not try to keep full attention and make it slightly faster. It changes the attention pattern so most tokens attend locally, while a small number of task-specific tokens receive global attention. That design gives Longformer two properties that matter in real document tasks:
It scales roughly linearly with sequence length when the local window size is fixed. It can reuse pretrained RoBERTa weights with minimal architectural changes.
Why It MattersThe standard Transformer attention matrix is dense. For sequence length , full self-attention has time and memory complexity. This is tolerable at BERT’s 512-token regime, but it becomes expensive for long QA, document classification, coreference, and summarization.
The paper compares full self-attention with several Longformer implementations. The full attention curve grows quickly and runs out of memory for longer sequences. The vectorized chunk implementation and CUDA implementation keep memory growth much closer to linear. The important engineering point is that sparse attention only helps if the implementation matches the sparsity pattern. A local-window pattern implemented as many tiny inefficient gathers can lose the theoretical advantage. Attention PatternLongformer combines three attention ideas: sliding-window attention, dilated sliding-window attention, and task-specific global attention.
With a fixed window size , each token attends to nearby tokens on both sides. The complexity becomes instead of . Stacking layers expands the receptive field, so a token can indirectly receive information from faraway tokens through multiple local hops. Dilated sliding windows increase the receptive field without increasing the number of attended positions. This is similar to dilated convolutions: the model samples farther positions with gaps between them. Global attention is the task escape hatch. Some tokens need to read or write across the whole document:
[CLS] for classification. Question tokens for QA. Candidate answer tokens for WikiHop. The first token in LED summarization.
Those global tokens attend to the full sequence, and the full sequence can attend back to them. This keeps the model from becoming only a local text smoother. Compared With Prior Long-Document WorkThe paper positions Longformer against earlier efficient Transformer variants and long-document work.
The distinction is not only “sparse attention.” Longformer is designed for transfer learning on document-level NLP tasks. Prior long-sequence models often focused on autoregressive language modeling, or they required task-specific chunking and aggregation. Longformer aims to replace RoBERTa’s self-attention and keep the rest of the pretrained Transformer workflow familiar. Pretraining From RoBERTaThe practical trick is simple but important: start from RoBERTa, replace full attention with Longformer attention, extend the position embeddings, and continue MLM pretraining on long documents. The paper also tests how to configure attention windows.
Increasing the window size from lower to higher layers gives the best BPC in this ablation. Adding dilation on two heads helps in the small autoregressive language-modeling setup, though the paper notes that dilation was not used in the RoBERTa transfer setting because it did not fit the pretrained weights as well. The position embedding story is especially useful. RoBERTa has learned absolute position embeddings up to 512 positions. Longformer extends to 4096 by copying the 512 learned embeddings repeatedly instead of random initialization.
The table shows why this is reasonable. A Longformer initialized with copied position embeddings is far better than one that starts with a random long-position setup, and continued MLM pretraining improves it further. For Longformer-base, BPC moves from 1.957 after copying position embeddings to 1.753 after 2K updates and 1.705 after 65K updates. The Tasks Are Actually LongLongformer is evaluated on tasks where the input length can exceed BERT’s 512-token limit by a large margin.
TriviaQA is the clearest example: the average context length is 6,589 wordpieces and the 95th percentile is 17,126. WikiHop and Hyperpartisan also have long tails. A truncation baseline may work on short examples, but it cannot be trusted as the sequence length grows. This is where Longformer’s design is pragmatic. Instead of chunking the document, running RoBERTa repeatedly, and stitching chunk representations with task-specific logic, the paper can concatenate the available context and process it as one sequence. Finetuning ResultsThe main finetuning table compares Longformer-base with RoBERTa-base.
The strongest gains appear where longer context matters. WikiHop improves from 72.4 to 75.0, and Hyperpartisan improves from 87.4 to 94.8. TriviaQA and HotpotQA improve more modestly because their useful evidence can often be found in shorter local regions or through task-specific pipelines. IMDB also improves slightly, which fits the dataset: many reviews are short, but a nontrivial tail is longer than 512 wordpieces. This result shape is important. Longformer is not a magic upgrade for every NLP benchmark. It helps most when the task has useful information outside the short context window and the model can exploit that information through local plus global attention. What The Ablation SaysThe WikiHop ablation is the best diagnostic table in the paper.
The default Longformer with sequence length 4096 reaches 73.8 accuracy. Training longer reaches 75.0. Reducing the sequence length to 2048 drops to 73.1, and using sequence length 512 with full attention drops to 71.7. This supports the claim that performance is not only coming from extra pretraining; the model benefits from longer context. The most severe row is “no linear projection, no global attention”, which drops to 65.5. Global attention is not a decorative feature. It gives task tokens a direct path to the whole document. Longformer-Encoder-DecoderThe paper also introduces Longformer-Encoder-Decoder (LED) for long-document seq2seq tasks. LED uses Longformer-style local plus global attention in the encoder, while the decoder still attends fully to generated tokens and encoded representations.
On arXiv summarization, LED-large with sequence length 16,384 reports 46.63 ROUGE-1, 19.62 ROUGE-2, and 41.83 ROUGE-L in this table. The useful comparison is not only against prior systems, but also against the shorter LED setting.
Increasing the input size from 1K to 4K and then 16K improves both ROUGE-1 and ROUGE-2. That is the cleanest evidence in the paper that the summarization task benefits from reading more of the source document. Practical NotesLongformer is a good fit when:
The task needs document-level context, not only a short answer span. Most interactions are local, but a few task tokens need global access. You want to reuse pretrained BERT/RoBERTa-style models instead of training a long-context architecture from scratch. The model can tolerate a fixed attention pattern.
The limitation is also clear. Sliding-window attention is an inductive bias. It is efficient because most token pairs cannot directly interact. If a task requires arbitrary token-to-token interactions at many distant positions, a fixed local/global pattern may miss some dependencies unless enough layers or global tokens provide a path. For implementation, I would pay attention to the kernel. The paper separates loop, chunk, and CUDA implementations because the same mathematical sparsity can have very different runtime behavior. The attention pattern and the memory layout have to be designed together. TakeawayLongformer is valuable because it makes long-document modeling feel like a controlled modification of pretrained Transformers. Local windows carry the text stream, global tokens carry the task interface, and copied position embeddings make RoBERTa adaptation practical. The result is not a universal replacement for dense attention, but it is a clean engineering tradeoff for document NLP.

entry.title: Mamba-2: Structured State Space Duality
entry.content:
Paper: Transformers are SSMs: Generalized Models and Efficient Algorithms Through Structured State Space Duality Code: https://github.com/state-spaces/mamba Mamba-2 is not just a faster Mamba kernel. The paper’s main move is to put selective state space models and attention into one algebraic picture, then use that picture to design a sequence mixer that is friendlier to GPU matrix multiplication. The name of the bridge is structured state space duality (SSD). The useful mental model is:
SSM recurrence is a structured lower-triangular matrix transformation. Attention is also a matrix transformation, but usually with a dense or masked query-key matrix. If the attention mask has the right structure, an attention-like quadratic form and an SSM-like linear recurrence can describe the same computation.
That duality matters because implementation details dominate long-context models. A recurrence may be asymptotically linear, but if it is serialized or misses tensor cores, it can lose to a quadratic attention kernel on real hardware. Mamba-2 uses SSD to keep the state-space flavor while making the main training computation look more like block matrix multiplication. Roadmap The paper is organized around the diagram above. It first relates state space models to semiseparable matrices, then generalizes attention into structured masked attention, then shows that the two families overlap. The Mamba-2 architecture is the practical result of that overlap. This is a useful framing because “attention vs SSM” is often discussed as if the two are separate model families. Mamba-2 argues that the boundary is more about structure and algorithms than about a hard mathematical divide. SSMs As Structured MatricesA state space layer can be written as a recurrence:
If we unroll the recurrence over the whole sequence, the layer becomes a lower-triangular matrix multiplication from inputs to outputs . The matrix is not arbitrary. Its off-diagonal blocks have low-rank structure because information has to pass through a finite-dimensional hidden state.
The paper describes this matrix family as semiseparable. That is the first important abstraction: an SSM is not only a recurrence, it is also a structured sequence transformation matrix. This view explains why SSMs have multiple possible implementations:
Recurrent scan: process token by token while carrying the hidden state. Convolution: when parameters are time-invariant or structured enough, use a convolution-like representation. Matrix multiplication: exploit the semiseparable matrix structure in blocks.
Mamba-1 leaned heavily on the scan view. Mamba-2 keeps the recurrence interpretation but makes the matrix view central to the algorithm. Structured Masked AttentionAttention can also be written as a sequence transformation matrix. Standard causal attention computes something like a query-key interaction, applies a causal mask, then uses the result to mix values. Mamba-2 generalizes this idea into structured masked attention:
Here is not just the usual triangular causal mask. It can be any structured mask that gives the attention matrix useful algebraic properties.
This figure is one of the most important in the paper. Different choices of recover different efficient-attention-like mechanisms:
A causal mask gives linear attention style structure. A decay mask connects to RetNet-like behavior. A 1-semiseparable mask gives the SSD case. Other structured masks can produce Toeplitz or Fourier-style attention variants.
The point is not that all of these models are identical. The point is that attention can be constrained with structure, and those structures can be studied with the same matrix tools used for SSMs. State Space DualitySSD is the intersection: a layer that has both an SSM-style recurrent form and an attention-style quadratic form.
This is where the title “Transformers are SSMs” comes from. The paper is not claiming that a vanilla Transformer block is secretly the same as a Mamba block. The narrower and more useful claim is that a family of structured masked attention layers can be represented as state space models, and a family of structured state space models can be computed through attention-like matrix operations. The dual form is useful because each side gives something different:
The recurrent form gives compact inference state. The quadratic matrix form exposes parallel training algorithms. The structured matrix view gives a way to reason about memory, compute, and block decomposition.
That is a better engineering tradeoff than treating recurrence and attention as two unrelated toolboxes. The SSD AlgorithmThe algorithmic problem is straightforward: how can we compute an SSM-like transformation without paying for a fully serial scan during training? Mamba-2 uses a block decomposition of the semiseparable matrix. Diagonal blocks are local within a chunk. Off-diagonal blocks communicate through the hidden state. That creates a mixed algorithm: matrix multiplication inside chunks, state passing between chunks.
The four pieces are:
Compute the diagonal blocks, which correspond to intra-chunk token interactions. Compute each chunk’s contribution to the next hidden state. Scan over chunk states instead of individual token states. Convert the propagated states back into output contributions for later chunks.
This is the part of the paper that feels most like a systems result. The math gives the decomposition, but the reason to care is that the expensive work can be arranged as larger matrix multiplications. That is exactly the kind of operation modern GPUs are built to run well. The complexity comparison in the paper makes the intended tradeoff clear.
In this simplified table, attention keeps a state that grows with sequence length , while SSM/SSD use a state of size . Attention has training FLOPs proportional to , while SSM/SSD have . The difference between SSM and SSD is not the asymptotic FLOP line in the table; it is the ability to use matrix multiplication and reduce naive memory from to in this formulation. For long sequences and moderate state sizes, this is the design goal: compact recurrent state for inference, but training kernels that still use the hardware efficiently. Mamba-2 Block DesignMamba-2 also changes the neural network block around the sequence mixer. This is easy to underplay, but it matters for large model training.
The original Mamba block is sequential: some projections are produced after the input has already passed through part of the block. Mamba-2 treats the SSD layer as a map from to , so it can produce these inputs in parallel at the beginning of the block. The paper highlights three practical changes:
The data-dependent SSM parameters are produced at the beginning of the block. An extra normalization layer is added for stability. The and projections use a single head shared across the heads, analogous to multi-value attention.
This is partly a model-design decision and partly a distributed-training decision. Parallel projections fit existing Transformer-style tensor parallel patterns much better than a strictly sequential block.
The left side of the figure shows tensor parallelism for the Mamba-2 block. The right side shows sequence/context parallelism: each device can handle a segment of the sequence and pass the recurrent state across segment boundaries. That is a cleaner communication pattern than full attention, where query blocks and key blocks interact quadratically across devices. Synthetic RecallThe paper uses multi-query associative recall (MQAR) to test whether the model can remember multiple key-value associations across a sequence. This is a direct stress test for recurrent models because all relevant information must be compressed into the recurrent state.
The result is a good diagnostic for Mamba-2’s larger state sizes. Mamba-1 with a small state struggles on this task. Mamba-2 improves strongly as the state dimension grows from to and . At the shown sequence lengths, the larger-state Mamba-2 curves approach near-perfect accuracy much faster than the small-state recurrent baseline. I would read this figure as evidence for capacity, not as a complete language-modeling result. MQAR is synthetic and narrow, but it exposes a failure mode that recurrent sequence mixers must address before they can be trusted on long-context tasks. Language Modeling ResultsThe scaling-law plot compares Mamba-2 with Mamba and a strong Transformer++ recipe on The Pile at sequence length 8192.
The Mamba-2 line is consistently below the Mamba and Transformer++ lines in this plot, meaning lower perplexity at similar theoretical FLOPs. The paper also states that Mamba-2 is Pareto dominant in wall-clock time in this setting, which is the stronger systems claim. The zero-shot table is useful because it checks whether this efficiency story transfers to normal language-model evaluation.
At the small scale, Mamba-2-780M reaches an average score of 53.5, compared with 53.0 for Mamba-790M and 49.0 for Pythia-1B in the table. At 2.7B, Mamba-2 reaches 60.2 average accuracy, ahead of Mamba-2.8B’s 59.9 and much higher than Pythia-2.8B’s 55.7 under the reported setup.
Model Reported scale Average accuracy
Pythia 1B 49.0
Mamba 790M 53.0
Mamba-2 780M 53.5
Pythia 2.8B 55.7
Mamba 2.8B 59.9
Mamba-2 2.7B 60.2
The result is not a universal win on every single column. For example, Mamba-2-2.7B is slightly behind Mamba-2.8B on ARC-E and OpenBookQA in this table. But the aggregate result supports the paper’s main claim: the new architecture is competitive as a language model, not only as a kernel benchmark. Speed BenchmarksThe efficiency benchmark isolates the SSD algorithm against scan, convolution, and FlashAttention-2 style baselines on an A100 80GB PCIe GPU.
The left plot shows sequence-length scaling. For state dimension 64, SSD is faster than the Mamba fused scan in the reported range and faster than FlashAttention-2 from around sequence length 2K onward. The right plot fixes sequence length at 4K and varies state dimension. The scan implementation slows down roughly linearly as the state dimension grows, while SSD remains much flatter. The important caveat is that this is an algorithm/kernel result, not a full serving-system benchmark. A complete model has projections, normalization, residual paths, memory traffic, batching behavior, and framework overhead. Still, this benchmark explains why the paper cares so much about the matrix view: the same SSM math becomes much more attractive when the implementation reaches tensor-core-friendly operations. Hybrid Attention LayersMamba-2 does not conclude that attention should disappear. The paper tests hybrids that insert a small number of attention layers into a mostly SSD model.
For a 350M model with 48 layers, pure Mamba-2 reports perplexity 8.60 in this table. Adding a few attention layers helps; 6 attention blocks gives the best shown perplexity at 8.26. The paper summarizes this as roughly a 10% attention-layer ratio working well. The 2.7B hybrid table gives the same message in a downstream-evaluation setting.
Mamba-2 alone reaches 60.2 average accuracy, equal to the Transformer++ row in this table. Adding a small number of attention layers improves the best average to 61.0 for Mamba-2-Attention. The Mamba-2-MLP-Attention variant reaches 60.7.
Model Layer mix Average accuracy
Transformer++ Attention + gated MLP 60.2
Mamba-2 SSD only 60.2
Mamba-2-MLP SSD + gated MLP 59.6
Mamba-2-Attention Mostly SSD, 6 attention layers 61.0
Mamba-2-MLP-Attention SSD + MLP + attention 60.7
I like this result because it avoids an ideological conclusion. SSD is useful, but a little attention still helps. A practical long-context architecture may not need to be pure recurrence or pure attention; the better answer can be a controlled mixture. Practical NotesWhere Mamba-2 looks attractive:
Long-context inference where compact recurrent state matters. Training regimes where full attention memory becomes the limiting factor. Models that need better tensor-parallel friendliness than the original Mamba block. Research on hybrid architectures that use attention only where it pays for itself.
Where I would be careful:
Short sequences, where a highly optimized Transformer stack may still be simpler and fast enough. Tasks requiring arbitrary pairwise token interaction in many layers. Production inference stacks that already depend on mature attention-specific kernels, caching, and batching infrastructure. Claims based only on the SSD kernel benchmark without measuring the full model path.
The most useful implementation lesson is that asymptotic complexity is not enough. Mamba-2 improves the algorithmic shape, but the real win comes from matching that shape to GPU primitives. TakeawayMamba-2 is valuable because it explains why the SSM/attention boundary is softer than it looks. Semiseparable matrices give SSMs a matrix form; structured masks give attention a recurrent form; SSD is the overlap where both interpretations are available. The practical result is a sequence mixer with compact inference state, parallel training algorithms, and a block design that fits large-scale training better than Mamba-1. The paper is strongest when read as both theory and systems work: the duality is interesting, but the reason it matters is that it produces a model and kernel path that can actually run well.

entry.title: Medusa: LLM Inference with Multiple Decoding Heads
entry.content:
Cai T, Li Y, Geng Z, Peng H, Lee J D, Chen D, Dao T. Medusa: Simple LLM Inference Acceleration Framework with Multiple Decoding Heads. ICML 2024.
Paper: arXiv PDF Code: FasterDecoding/Medusa
Medusa is an inference acceleration paper that is easy to summarize incorrectly. The superficial summary is “add extra heads and decode more tokens.” The more useful reading is: Medusa replaces the separate draft model in speculative decoding with a set of cheap, target-model-attached heads, then spends one target-model forward pass on a tree of candidate continuations instead of one linear draft. That design is aimed at a very specific bottleneck. During autoregressive decoding, a large model usually emits one token per expensive forward pass. The pass is often memory-bandwidth-bound: every step streams a large amount of model weight data, but only processes a tiny amount of new-token work. Medusa tries to make each pass advance by more than one token while keeping the serving stack simpler than a two-model speculative decoding system. The paper is also more systems-flavored than the title suggests. The final speedup depends on three interacting quantities:
Acceleration rate is the number of accepted tokens per decoding step. Overhead is how much slower each Medusa step is than a vanilla decode step. The method wins only when the candidate tree increases accepted length more than it increases per-step work. One-Pass Overview Figure cropped from the paper PDF: Medusa adds several heads on top of the target LLM hidden state, produces multiple top-k future-token predictions, and verifies a candidate continuation before moving to the next decoding step. The pipeline has three phases, similar to speculative decoding:
Generate candidates. Process those candidates with the target model. Accept a prefix and append it to the sequence.
The difference is where candidates come from. Standard speculative decoding uses a small draft model. Medusa uses the target model’s own last hidden state. If the base model has hidden state at the current position, the original LM head predicts token , while Medusa head predicts token . The paper uses a small residual MLP per head:
The initialization is practical: starts from the original LM head and starts at zero. At initialization, each Medusa head behaves like the original next-token head applied to the same hidden state. Training then specializes head 1 toward the next-next token, head 2 toward the token after that, and so on. This is a nice engineering compromise. The heads are much cheaper than a separate draft LLM, and they live inside the same model checkpoint. There is no separate model-parallel plan, no second KV cache, and no draft model whose tokenizer or distribution needs to be aligned with the target model. Why Separate Draft Models Are AnnoyingSpeculative decoding is attractive because it can be exact under the right rejection-sampling procedure. A draft model proposes several tokens, and the target model verifies them in parallel. If the draft tokens agree with the target distribution, the system can accept several tokens per target forward pass. The deployment pain is the draft model:
Problem Why it matters
Draft quality A tiny model is fast but often rejected. A stronger draft model is slower and harder to serve.
Distribution mismatch The draft may propose text that looks reasonable but is not likely under the target model.
Serving complexity Two models mean two sets of weights, potentially two parallelism plans, and more scheduling logic.
Distributed inference Keeping a draft model synchronized with a sharded target model is not free.
Medusa’s answer is not to make a better standalone draft model. It says: use the target model’s representation as the draft source. The target model still verifies candidates, but the proposal machinery is attached to the same forward pass and can be trained with the model. That is why the method is appealing for local or single-user serving. The paper primarily evaluates batch size 1, which matches local chat or latency-oriented serving better than high-throughput cloud batching. Medusa HeadsEach Medusa head predicts a different future offset. With heads, one decoding position can produce distributions for: original LM head: token t + 1Medusa head 1: token t + 2Medusa head 2: token t + 3...Medusa head K: token t + K + 1
The important limitation is that these heads are not autoregressive inside the draft. Head 3 does not first consume the token proposed by head 1 and head 2. It predicts from the same current hidden state. This makes the heads cheap and parallel, but it also means later heads face a harder, more uncertain prediction task. The loss reflects this: $$\mathcal{L}{\mathrm{Medusa-1}}= \sum{k=1}^{K} -\lambda_k \log p_t^{(k)}(y_{t+k+1}).$$ The paper sets to a decaying weight such as because farther future positions are harder. In the shared experiment settings, they train five one-layer Medusa heads. During inference, they may only use three or four if the optimized tree does not need all of them. My read: five heads is not a magic number. It is a reasonable ceiling for this design because independent future-token prediction gets worse as the offset grows. If the later heads are low quality, they add branches that cost verification time without improving accepted length.
