Tree Attention Tree attention mask from the paper: each candidate node can attend to the prompt and its own ancestors, but not to sibling branches that belong to incompatible continuations. Using only one candidate chain wastes information. Each head can output several plausible tokens. If head 1 has top-2 candidates and head 2 has top-3 candidates, the Cartesian product gives six two-token continuations. Verifying those one by one would be useless, but verifying them as a tree lets shared prefixes reuse work. For head , suppose we keep top predictions. A simple dense tree has:
new candidate nodes, excluding the virtual root. This can grow quickly, so the tree size is a real serving parameter, not a decorative detail. Tree attention changes the attention mask. In ordinary causal decoding, token positions form one linear sequence. In Medusa, candidate nodes form multiple possible futures. A node should see:
the original prompt and generated prefix, its own ancestors in the candidate tree, not its siblings, not nodes from branches that would imply a different previous token.
The paper also adjusts positional indices so the target model evaluates a branch as if it were a normal continuation. After this forward pass, the target model has logits for many candidate positions, and Medusa can choose the longest acceptable prefix. A serving implementation has to be careful here. It is not enough to concatenate all candidates into a batch and call the model. The attention mask and position IDs encode the candidate tree, and after acceptance the runtime must collapse the verified tree back into one linear accepted sequence. Candidate Tree Size Tree-size ablation from the paper: larger candidate trees can increase acceleration rate, but the per-step token/s can decline once the tree becomes too large. This figure is the most useful warning in the paper. More candidates are not automatically better. A bigger tree increases the chance of finding a longer accepted prefix, but it also increases linear-layer and attention work in the verification pass. The left plot shows acceleration rate increasing with more candidate tokens. The right plot shows actual token/s eventually dropping as the tree grows. The optimized sparse tree at 64 nodes beats larger dense trees because it spends candidate budget on likely branches instead of expanding every combination mechanically. The sparse tree is built from calibration statistics. For each Medusa head, the method estimates the accuracy of each top-ranked prediction. If the -th top prediction of head has accuracy , a candidate path can be scored by multiplying the per-node accuracies under an independence approximation. Nodes are then added greedily to maximize expected accepted length under a fixed tree-node budget. This is a small but important point. Medusa is not only “attach heads.” The tree policy is part of the speedup. AcceptanceThere are two acceptance modes to keep separate. For greedy decoding, acceptance is straightforward. The target model verifies the candidate tree, and Medusa accepts the longest prefix whose tokens match the target model’s greedy choices. If the first candidate token fails, the system can still fall back to the target model’s own next token, so decoding always advances. For sampling, exact speculative decoding usually uses rejection sampling to preserve the target distribution. Medusa can use that too, but the paper argues that rejection sampling becomes less efficient at nonzero temperature. Even if the draft and target distributions were identical, independent sampling can reject tokens. Medusa therefore proposes typical acceptance. Instead of insisting on exact distribution matching, it accepts a candidate token when the original model assigns it enough probability: $$p_{\mathrm{original}}(x_{n+k} \mid x_1,\ldots,x_{n+k-1})
\min(\epsilon,\ \delta \exp(-H(p_{\mathrm{original}}(\cdot \mid x_1,\ldots,x_{n+k-1})))).$$ The entropy term matters. When the target model distribution is high entropy, more continuations are plausible. When it is sharp, the threshold becomes stricter. The first token is handled with greedy decoding to guarantee progress, while later tokens use the typical-acceptance criterion.
Typical acceptance ablation from the paper: raising the posterior threshold trades acceleration rate for MT-Bench score under non-greedy generation. I would describe typical acceptance as a quality-preserving heuristic, not a lossless sampler. The paper’s Appendix A explicitly relaxes exact correspondence with the language-model distribution. That is a reasonable systems tradeoff for chat serving, but it should not be confused with exact speculative sampling when distribution preservation is required. Medusa-1Medusa-1 freezes the backbone LLM and trains only the added heads. The backbone hidden states are used as features, but the base model parameters do not change. This has several good properties:
It is the easiest way to add Medusa to an existing model. The original next-token model is not fine-tuned, so its base behavior is not damaged by training the heads. Training memory can be reduced with a quantized backbone, similar in spirit to QLoRA-style setups. The paper reports a few hours of training for Vicuna-7B on a single A100 PCIe GPU using 60k ShareGPT samples.
The downside is head accuracy. The frozen backbone was not trained to make future-token prediction easy from the current last hidden state. Medusa-1 can work, but the heads have to live with the representation they are given. Medusa-2Medusa-2 jointly trains the Medusa heads and the backbone. This gives the heads a better representation to use, but it introduces the risk of degrading the base model. The paper’s recipe has three pieces:
Add the ordinary next-token language-model loss back into training. Use a larger learning rate for the new heads than for the backbone. Warm up the heads before letting their gradients affect the backbone strongly.
The joint loss is: $$\mathcal{L}{\mathrm{Medusa-2}}= \mathcal{L}{\mathrm{LM}} + \lambda_0 \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Medusa-1}}.$$ The engineering reason is simple. At the beginning of training, the Medusa heads are bad, and their losses can be large. If those gradients immediately update the backbone, they can distort the model’s original next-token behavior. A two-stage or warmup recipe lets the heads become useful before co-adapting the model. The shared settings in the appendix are also useful implementation hints: five one-layer heads, 8-bit AdamW, cosine schedule with warmup, LoRA or QLoRA for Medusa-2, head learning rate four times the backbone learning rate, LoRA rank 32, alpha 16, and dropout 0.05. Self-DistillationThe paper assumes a training dataset aligned with the target model. For Vicuna-7B and Vicuna-13B, ShareGPT is close to the SFT data. But many released chat models do not expose their instruction-tuning data, and RLHF or DPO-style alignment can shift the output distribution away from the original SFT corpus. Medusa’s answer is self-distillation:
Start with a public seed prompt dataset from a similar domain. Ask the target model to generate responses. Train Medusa heads on that generated dataset. For Medusa-2, use the original model’s probability distribution as a teacher for the backbone loss.
The LoRA trick is neat. If the backbone is fine-tuned with an adapter, the original model can be recovered by turning the adapter off. That lets the training code get teacher probabilities without keeping a second full model in memory. This is not free. The paper observes that using generated data alone can hurt quality when training the backbone, which is why the distillation loss is needed. In other words, Medusa-2 is not just “generate synthetic data and fine-tune.” The preservation loss is part of the method. Main Results Main MT-Bench result from the paper: on Vicuna-7B and Vicuna-13B, Medusa-1 gives more than 2x speedup, while Medusa-2 reaches 2.83x in this setup. The category-level plot shows higher gains on some tasks, including coding and extraction. The headline results are clear:
Setting Reported result
Vicuna-7B, Medusa-1 2.18x speedup
Vicuna-7B, Medusa-2 2.83x speedup
Vicuna-13B, Medusa-1 2.33x speedup
Vicuna-13B, Medusa-2 2.83x speedup
Vicuna-7B Medusa-2 by MT-Bench category 2.58x to 3.62x
The category split is interesting. Coding is 3.29x and extraction is 3.62x in the figure. Those tasks often have lower-entropy next-token structure than open-ended roleplay. That matches the intuition that multi-token acceptance is easiest when the next few tokens are predictable.
Model comparison table from the paper: Medusa-2 reports acceleration rate, overhead, MT-Bench quality delta, and wall-time speedup against speculative decoding baselines. Table 1 separates acceleration rate from overhead. For example, Vicuna-7B has an acceleration rate of 3.47 but an overhead of 1.22, giving a wall-time speedup of 2.83. That distinction is worth keeping in mind when comparing methods. A decoder can accept many tokens per step and still fail to speed up if the step becomes too expensive. The same table reports Medusa-2 speedups of:
Model Medusa speedup
Vicuna-7B 2.83
Zephyr-7B 2.66
Vicuna-13B 2.83
Vicuna-33B 2.35
The larger and self-distilled cases are not always faster. The paper attributes weaker speedup partly to preserving quality when the true training recipe is unavailable. That is a fair warning: adding Medusa to an arbitrary model depends on how well the heads can learn the target model’s actual output distribution. What Each Technique Adds Technique stack from the paper: heads alone help, tree attention helps more, optimized tree construction helps again, and Medusa-2 training gives the largest reported jump in this ablation. This table is small but useful because it gives a rough decomposition:
Step Effect
Medusa-1 heads without tree attention about 1.5x
Add tree attention about 1.9x
Use optimized tree configuration about 2.2x
Train heads with Medusa-2 about 2.8x
The message is that no single component carries the full method. The heads create future-token proposals, tree attention amortizes target-model verification, tree search spends the candidate budget better, and Medusa-2 improves head accuracy. Sparse Tree Shape Sparse tree visualization from the appendix: a 64-node tree with depth 4. The red path shows the accepted future tokens. The appendix visualization helps explain why a sparse tree beats a dense tree. The tree leans toward high-probability branches instead of spreading budget uniformly. If a top-1 prediction from head 1 is much more reliable than a top-5 prediction from head 3, the tree should reflect that. For implementation, this suggests a calibration step:
Run the model and Medusa heads on a held-out calibration set. Measure how often each top-ranked candidate at each head is correct. Build a fixed sparse tree under a node budget. Use that tree shape during generation.
The tree can be static once chosen. That keeps runtime logic simple, although later work can make tree construction more dynamic. AlpacaEval And Generalization AlpacaEval table from the appendix: Medusa-2 keeps similar acceleration on another dataset, with reported speedups between 2.26x and 3.16x. The AlpacaEval appendix result is useful because it checks whether MT-Bench is the only favorable case. The reported wall-time speedups are:
Model Base speed Medusa speed Speedup
Vicuna-7B 37.07 tok/s 106.76 tok/s 2.88
Vicuna-13B 29.01 tok/s 91.54 tok/s 3.16
Vicuna-33B 17.87 tok/s 40.43 tok/s 2.26
Zephyr-7B 34.21 tok/s 99.50 tok/s 2.91
These are still batch-size-1 style numbers. I would not transfer them directly to a saturated production server with continuous batching. In that setting, decode may already have better hardware utilization, and the Medusa candidate tree competes with batching for the same compute budget. Hardware View Roofline analysis from the appendix: adding candidate tokens moves attention matrix multiplication to higher operational intensity and higher achieved FLOP/s. The hardware appendix is worth reading because it explains why Medusa can help at all. Vanilla decode processes one new token. Many linear layers and attention operations sit near a memory-bandwidth-bound regime. If Medusa verifies many candidate tokens in one pass, it increases the amount of arithmetic per weight movement. The paper reports that, for Llama-33B on an A100-80GB PCIe at batch size 16 and sequence length 1024, using 64 candidate tokens gives much higher FLOP/s and operational intensity for attention matrix multiplication than regular decoding. The direction is the point: candidate verification turns a tiny decode step into a wider parallel computation. But there is a ceiling. If the tree is too large, the step becomes compute-heavy and wall-clock speed drops. If the batch size is already large, the normal decoder may already use the GPU well, leaving less memory-bandwidth slack for Medusa to exploit. This is why the paper’s focus on batch size 1 is not a minor detail. Implementation NotesIf I were adding Medusa to an inference engine, I would treat these as the non-negotiable pieces:
Component Implementation detail
Checkpoint format Store extra Medusa head weights next to the base model.
Head execution Run Medusa heads from the current final hidden state and collect top-k predictions per head.
Candidate tree Use a static sparse tree or a calibrated tree budget; avoid naive dense expansion unless tiny.
Attention mask Build a tree attention mask so branches cannot see incompatible sibling tokens.
Position IDs Make every branch position look like a valid continuation position to the target model.
Verification Use target-model logits on candidate nodes to decide the accepted prefix.
KV update Append only the accepted linear path to the live sequence state.
Sampling mode Choose between exact rejection sampling and typical acceptance depending on quality requirements.
Two failure modes are easy to miss:
If the heads are inaccurate, Medusa can waste target-model work on candidates that are mostly rejected. If the tree is too large, acceleration rate can rise while actual token/s falls.
That makes Medusa more like a calibrated serving optimization than a purely architectural modification. Comparison With EAGLEMedusa and EAGLE are close in spirit because both try to improve speculative decoding without relying on an arbitrary small draft LM. The difference is the draft target. Medusa predicts future tokens directly from the current target hidden state. EAGLE predicts future target-model features and then uses the target LM head to turn those features into token logits. EAGLE’s argument is that hidden features are smoother than discrete token choices, but it has to handle feature uncertainty with shifted token input. Medusa’s advantage is simplicity. Heads are cheap, static, and easy to attach. Its weakness is that the heads are independent future-token predictors. They do not condition on each other inside the draft. That is exactly the gap later draft-head methods try to address. My TakeawayMedusa is a good paper because it turns speculative decoding into an attachable module: add heads -> draft a candidate tree -> verify with tree attention -> accept a prefix
The real insight is not only the heads. The useful system is the combination of lightweight heads, tree verification, calibrated sparse tree construction, and a training recipe that does not ruin the base model. I would use Medusa when:
the workload is latency-oriented or batch size is small, the target model can tolerate an added-head checkpoint format, a small amount of calibration/training data is available, exact sampling distribution is not mandatory, or rejection sampling is acceptable, the serving engine can implement tree attention cleanly.
I would be cautious when:
batch size is already high, output quality must match the original sampler exactly under non-greedy decoding, the model’s training data or output distribution is hard to approximate, the inference stack cannot efficiently build custom attention masks and position IDs.
The paper’s reported 2x to 3x range is credible in the setting it studies, but it is not a universal multiplier. The speedup lives in the balance between accepted tokens and verification overhead. Medusa works when the heads are good enough and the tree is small enough.

entry.title: MnasNet: Platform-Aware Neural Architecture Search for Mobile
entry.content:
Tan M, Chen B, Pang R, Vasudevan V, Sandler M, Howard A, Le Q V. MnasNet: Platform-Aware Neural Architecture Search for Mobile. CVPR 2019.
Paper / Code MnasNet is one of the papers that made hardware-aware NAS feel real. The important change is simple: the search reward uses measured mobile latency, not FLOPs. That sounds obvious now, but it changes the whole NAS problem. If the target is a phone, the architecture is not good because it has fewer multiply-adds on paper. It is good if it runs fast on that phone while keeping accuracy. Kernel implementation, memory access, operator fusion, thread scheduling, and hardware-specific behavior can make two networks with similar FLOPs behave very differently. The paper gives a concrete example: MobileNetV1 has 575M multiply-adds and 113ms latency on a Pixel 1 phone, while NASNet-A has 564M multiply-adds and 183ms latency. FLOPs alone would suggest they are similar. The phone says otherwise. MnasNet combines three ideas:
put real device latency into a multi-objective reward; search a factorized hierarchical space instead of repeatedly stacking one cell; use the resulting model family as a mobile backbone for ImageNet and COCO.
All figures and tables below are cropped from the original paper PDF. Core QuestionThe paper is not only asking “can NAS find a good image classifier?” It asks a more deployment-shaped question:
Which architecture gives the best accuracy-latency trade-off on a specific mobile platform?
This is different from the older NASNet/AmoebaNet-style setup, where the search often optimizes accuracy and reports resource cost afterward. In MnasNet, latency is part of the objective from the beginning.
The search loop has three parts:
a controller samples an architecture from the search space; a trainer estimates its accuracy; a mobile-phone inference engine measures latency.
The controller receives a reward that combines accuracy and measured latency. This means the search can learn that some operators are expensive on the target platform even if their FLOP count looks acceptable. Accuracy-Latency FrontierThe headline plot is the accuracy-latency comparison on ImageNet.
The red MnasNet points form a better frontier than MobileNetV1, MobileNetV2, NASNet-A, and AmoebaNet-A under the reported Pixel 1 latency measurement. The most useful comparison is around the 75-80ms region:
Model Top-1 Latency Read
MobileNetV2 72.0 75ms hand-designed reference
MnasNet-A1 75.2 78ms +3.2 top-1 at similar latency
MobileNetV2 1.4x 74.7 143ms slower and slightly less accurate
NASNet-A 74.0 183ms much slower
MnasNet-A3 76.7 103ms larger searched model
This is the paper’s main empirical claim: optimizing with measured latency can move the Pareto frontier, not merely produce a smaller model. Multi-Objective RewardMnasNet formulates search as a multi-objective problem. For a model :
: validation accuracy; : measured latency on the target phone; : target latency.
The reward is:
The exponent changes depending on whether the model is under or over the latency target:
Two settings are useful:
Setting Meaning
hard-ish latency constraint: models under target are judged mainly by accuracy, models over target are sharply penalized
soft constraint: latency continuously affects reward on both sides of the target
The paper chooses for the main experiments. The heuristic is based on an empirical trade-off: doubling latency often gives roughly 5% relative accuracy gain. Setting the exponent around -0.07 makes those two points receive similar reward, so the search does not over-prefer either side too aggressively. The hard-constraint version is easier to reason about, but it can be too brittle. A soft reward lets the controller explore a wider set of Pareto candidates in one run. Why Search Space MattersEarlier NAS papers often search for a cell, then stack the same cell many times. That makes the search easier, but it is a poor fit for mobile networks. Early layers operate at high resolution and dominate latency; later layers operate at lower resolution and can afford different choices. A single repeated cell cannot express that trade-off well. MnasNet uses a factorized hierarchical search space.
The network is divided into blocks according to resolution and filter size. Inside each block, the searched layer is repeated times. Different blocks can choose different operations. For each block, the controller searches:
Choice Options described in the paper
convolution op regular conv, depthwise conv, mobile inverted bottleneck conv
kernel size 3x3 or 5x5
SE ratio 0 or 0.25
skip op pooling, identity residual, or no skip
output filters relative to MobileNetV2, in {0.75, 1.0, 1.25}
number of layers relative to MobileNetV2, in {-1, 0, +1}
The key engineering compromise is that the search is not fully per-layer. If each block has subspace size , the network has blocks, and each block has around repeated layers, then:
Search style Size
MnasNet block-factorized space
flat per-layer space
The paper’s example uses , , and , giving about candidates instead of . That is still large, but it is searchable with their RL loop. Search AlgorithmThe controller is an RNN that emits architecture tokens. Each sampled architecture is trained briefly, measured on the phone, assigned a reward, and then used to update the controller with PPO. The expected objective is:
The expensive part is that the paper does not search on CIFAR. It searches directly on ImageNet with fewer training steps:
Item Setting
proxy task ImageNet training with 5 epochs
validation split fixed 50K images from ImageNet training set
controller same RNN controller style as NASNet
update method Proximal Policy Optimization
latency device Pixel 1 phone
latency protocol batch size 1, single-thread big CPU core
search cost about 4.5 days on 64 TPUv2 devices
sampled models about 8K architectures
full ImageNet training top 15 searched models
COCO transfer one selected model
This setup is expensive, but it avoids a common trap: if the search is performed on a small proxy task and then scaled up, the latency behavior can change. MnasNet treats mobile latency as part of the target task, not as an afterthought. ImageNet ResultsTable 1 is the main ImageNet comparison.
The most important rows:
Model Top-1 Latency
MobileNetV2 72.0 75ms
MobileNetV2 1.4x 74.7 143ms
NASNet-A 74.0 183ms
AmoebaNet-A 74.5 190ms
MnasNet-A1 75.2 78ms
MnasNet-A2 75.6 84ms
MnasNet-A3 76.7 103ms
The comparison with MobileNetV2 is especially strong. MnasNet-A1 is only 3ms slower than MobileNetV2 in the reported setup, but it is 3.2 points better in top-1 accuracy. It also stays compact: 3.9M parameters and 312M multiply-adds. Compared with MobileNetV2 1.4x, MnasNet-A1 is faster and slightly more accurate. The NAS comparison is also useful. NASNet-A and AmoebaNet-A have similar parameter counts and multiply-adds, but their Pixel latency is much worse. This is exactly the point of measuring latency instead of relying on model-size proxies. Squeeze-and-Excitation AblationMnasNet includes squeeze-and-excitation in the search space. The authors also run a no-SE variant to check whether the whole gain comes from adding SE blocks.
Model SE in space Latency Top-1
MobileNetV2 no 75ms 72.0
NASNet no 183ms 74.0
MnasNet-B1 no 77ms 74.5
MnasNet-A1 yes 78ms 75.2
MnasNet-A2 yes 84ms 75.6
SE helps, but it is not the entire story. Even without SE, MnasNet-B1 reaches 74.5% at 77ms, already ahead of MobileNetV2 and NASNet under the reported mobile latency constraint. Scaling BehaviorA common deployment workflow is to scale a known architecture with width multipliers or input resolution. MnasNet checks whether the searched architecture remains better under those scaling operations.
The left plot varies depth multiplier from 0.35 to 1.4. The right plot varies input image size from 96 to 224. In both cases, the MnasNet curve stays above MobileNetV2. The paper reports up to a 4.1 point accuracy gain across input sizes. This matters because a mobile model is rarely deployed at one fixed point. Product constraints change: 20ms for video, 80ms for interactive camera features, higher latency for offline batch work. A good base architecture should scale gracefully. But scaling is not always enough.
For a tight 22ms target:
Model Top-1 Latency
MobileNetV2 0.35x 60.3 21.4ms
MnasNet-A1 0.35x 64.1 22.8ms
MnasNet-search1 64.9 22.0ms
MnasNet-search2 66.0 23.2ms
All four models are tiny, between 1.66M and 2.0M parameters and between 59M and 68M multiply-adds. Scaling down MnasNet-A1 already beats scaling down MobileNetV2. A fresh search at the new latency target does even better. This is a useful deployment lesson: width scaling is convenient, but a target-specific search can find a better operator allocation for a very different latency regime. COCO TransferThe paper also plugs MnasNet-A1 into SSDLite for object detection.
Representative rows:
Detector mAP Latency
MobileNetV1 + SSDLite 22.2 270ms
MobileNetV2 + SSDLite 22.1 200ms
MnasNet-A1 + SSDLite 23.0 203ms
SSD300 23.2 -
MnasNet-A1 + SSDLite uses 4.9M parameters and 0.8B multiply-adds, close to the MobileNetV2 + SSDLite compute budget. It improves mAP over the MobileNet backbones at roughly the same latency scale. It is also close to SSD300 mAP while using far fewer parameters and multiply-adds. This does not prove MnasNet is universally best for detection, but it shows the searched classification backbone transfers reasonably. Hard Versus Soft LatencyThe paper compares hard and soft latency rewards.
With , the reward behaves more like a hard target. The controller avoids over-target models and samples more tightly on the faster side. With , the controller samples a wider latency range around the target, including models below 40ms and above 110ms. My reading: the soft setup is better if the goal is to get a frontier from one expensive search run. A hard setup is better if violating a latency target is unacceptable, but it can miss useful candidates just above the threshold. Search Space Versus RewardMnasNet has two contributions, so the paper separates them:
use a multi-objective reward with latency; use a factorized hierarchical search space.
Reward Search space Latency Top-1
single-objective cell-based 183ms 74.0
multi-objective cell-based 100ms 72.0
multi-objective MnasNet 78ms 75.2
The reward alone makes the cell-based model faster, but it loses accuracy. The full MnasNet setup is both faster and more accurate. This is the strongest argument that the search space matters, not just the latency penalty. MnasNet-A1 ArchitectureThe selected MnasNet-A1 architecture mixes operation types across stages.
The architecture uses both 3x3 and 5x5 kernels, with different MBConv expansion ratios and SE placements. This is exactly what a repeated-cell search space struggles to express. Early stages, middle stages, and late stages have different resolution, channel count, and latency sensitivity. The paper then tests whether this layer diversity is actually useful.
Variant Top-1 Latency
MnasNet-A1 75.2 78ms
MBConv3 3x3 only 71.8 63ms
MBConv3 5x5 only 72.5 79ms
MBConv6 3x3 only 74.9 116ms
MBConv6 5x5 only 75.6 146ms
The single-op variants show the trade-off. MBConv3 is faster but loses too much accuracy. MBConv6 can recover accuracy but becomes much slower. MnasNet-A1 gets a better balance by mixing choices by stage. Reproduction NotesIf I were reproducing this paper, I would start with the latency protocol, not the controller. First, match the measurement target. The paper reports latency on the big CPU core of a Pixel 1 phone with batch size 1 and single-thread execution. Changing the phone, backend, thread count, warmup, precision, or operator library changes the reward. Second, measure latency repeatedly. Since latency is inside the reward, noisy measurement becomes noisy supervision for the controller. A few milliseconds matter when the target is around 75ms. Third, keep the proxy task honest. The paper searches on ImageNet for 5 epochs rather than CIFAR. That is expensive, but it avoids searching for architectures that only look good after scaling from a toy task. Fourth, separate “reward works” from “space works.” Table 5 is the right sanity check: latency reward on a cell-based space is not enough. Fifth, track the full frontier, not just one checkpoint. The soft reward is designed to recover multiple Pareto candidates from one search run. LimitationsMnasNet is a strong deployment-oriented NAS paper, but its assumptions are clear.
The search is expensive: the paper reports about 4.5 days on 64 TPUv2 devices. The latency target is platform-specific. A Pixel 1 CPU frontier is not automatically the frontier on a GPU, NPU, DSP, or newer phone. The search space is still manually designed around mobile CNN primitives and MobileNetV2-style choices. The RL controller is not the main reusable lesson; later hardware-aware NAS methods often use differentiable search, predictors, or once-for-all supernets. Latency is measured for a fixed inference setup. Real products may care about memory, energy, thermal throttling, startup overhead, and mixed workloads. The paper searches classification backbones and transfers one model to COCO; detection-specific search could make different choices.
The most important limitation is also the main lesson: “hardware-aware” means “aware of this hardware and this runtime.” The result is only as valid as the measurement loop. TakeawayMnasNet changes NAS from a model-design exercise into a deployment optimization loop. The two technical choices that matter are measured latency in the reward and a block-factorized search space that permits layer diversity without exploding into per-layer search. The compact reading:
FLOPs are not reliable enough for mobile latency. Latency should be measured on the target device and included in the reward. A soft multi-objective reward can produce a useful Pareto frontier. Repeated-cell search spaces are too rigid for mobile CNNs. Stage-wise layer diversity is a real accuracy-latency advantage.
When reading later papers such as ProxylessNAS, FBNet, MobileNetV3, Once-for-All, and BigNAS, MnasNet is the reference point: it made the deployment target part of architecture search itself.

entry.title: MobileNetV3: Search-Assisted Engineering for Mobile CNNs
entry.content:
Howard A, Sandler M, Chu G, et al. Searching for MobileNetV3. ICCV 2019.
Paper MobileNetV3 is easy to misread as “NAS found a better MobileNet.” That is not the main lesson. The paper is closer to a deployment engineering log: start from a platform-aware searched model, run a layer-wise adaptation procedure, inspect the expensive pieces, then make operator and layout changes that are outside the search space. The result matters because the metric is not just MAdds. The paper measures single-thread latency on real Google Pixel phones through TFLite. That makes the work a useful bridge between architecture search papers and the kind of model surgery that actually determines mobile runtime. What The Paper Is OptimizingMobileNetV3 keeps the MobileNetV2/MnasNet lineage:
inverted residual blocks remain the basic building block; depthwise separable convolution remains the compute-saving primitive; squeeze-and-excitation is used, but selectively; the final model is evaluated by measured Pixel latency, not only by operation count.
The pipeline has three layers:
Stage Role Why It Is Not Enough Alone
Platform-aware NAS Find a global block-level architecture under a latency-aware reward. The search space still cannot express every useful manual layout change.
NetAdapt Adjust channels layer by layer toward a target latency. It is a local adaptation method and depends on a good seed model.
Manual redesign Change activations, the first layer, the last stage, and SE details. These choices need profiling and implementation knowledge.
That last row is the part I care about most. MobileNetV3 is a strong model because the authors combine automated search with engineering constraints instead of pretending the search algorithm owns the whole design. Accuracy And Real LatencyThe front page result is the Pixel latency frontier. MobileNetV3-Large competes in the 40-100 ms range, while MobileNetV3-Small competes in the 20-40 ms range.
The important comparison is not just “higher accuracy.” The paper reports that MobileNetV3-Large reaches the same 75.2% ImageNet top-1 as MnasNet-A1 while reducing Pixel 1 latency from 71 ms to 51 ms. MobileNetV3-Small reaches 67.4% top-1 at 15.8 ms, compared with MnasNet-small at 64.9% and 20.3 ms.
Model Top-1 Pixel 1 latency
V3-Large 1.0 75.2 51 ms
MnasNet-A1 75.2 71 ms
V2 1.0 72.0 64 ms
V3-Small 1.0 67.4 15.8 ms
MnasNet-small 64.9 20.3 ms
The table makes the paper’s position clear. V3-Large is not merely a slightly larger model with better accuracy. It is a measured-latency improvement over another platform-aware NAS model at the same top-1 point. The MAdds plot is still useful, but it is secondary.
MAdds tells us how many arithmetic operations a model nominally performs. Pixel latency tells us whether those operations map well onto the runtime, memory hierarchy, fused kernels, quantized operators, and thread setup. MobileNetV3 is designed against the second target. From MobileNetV2 Blocks To V3 BlocksMobileNetV2 uses the inverted residual and linear bottleneck block. The narrow representation sits at the input and output of the block, and the expensive work happens in the expanded channel space.
MobileNetV3 keeps this general form, but it brings in MnasNet-style squeeze-and-excitation and changes where nonlinearities are used.
This is not a cosmetic detail. SE is an accuracy booster, but it introduces extra small matrix/vector work and activation functions. Nonlinearity placement also matters because early feature maps are spatially large. An activation that looks cheap in a paper formula can become expensive when it is applied to many pixels. Search StrategyThe paper uses two search/adaptation tools:
Platform-aware NAS for block-wise global architecture search. NetAdapt for layer-wise channel adjustment.
For the large model, the authors reuse MnasNet-A1 as the starting point because the earlier MnasNet search already targets roughly the same 80 ms latency regime. For the small model, they adjust the reward because accuracy changes more sharply with latency in the small-model regime. The MnasNet-style reward is:
Here is validation accuracy, is measured latency, is the target latency, and controls how strongly latency is penalized. The MobileNetV3 paper notes that the original setting was not ideal for small models and uses a smaller weight factor for that regime. NetAdapt then performs a discrete channel search. At each step, proposals reduce either an expansion layer or a bottleneck size shared by residual-connected blocks. A candidate is selected according to the tradeoff slope between accuracy change and latency change:
This is a practical detail. The algorithm is not optimizing an abstract FLOPs proxy; it is trying to spend every millisecond of latency reduction where the accuracy damage is smallest. The Last Stage Was Too ExpensiveOne of the most valuable pieces of the paper is the last-stage redesign. MobileNetV2-like networks often expand to a high-dimensional feature tensor before global pooling. That is expensive because the expansion is still applied at a spatial resolution such as 7x7. MobileNetV3 moves the expensive feature generation after global average pooling. Once the tensor is 1x1, the 1x1 expansion is almost free compared with doing it over a spatial map.
The paper reports that this efficient last stage reduces latency by 7 ms, about 11% of runtime, and removes roughly 30M MAdds with almost no accuracy loss. This is exactly the type of edit a search space may miss: it is not just “choose another kernel size,” it is a structural observation about where expensive features are needed. There is also an early-layer edit. The authors reduce the first convolution filters from 32 to 16 and find that hard-swish preserves accuracy there. That saves about 2 ms and 10M MAdds. Hard-SwishSwish is:
It often improves accuracy over ReLU, but sigmoid is not a friendly primitive on many mobile inference paths. MobileNetV3 replaces it with a piecewise-linear approximation:
This is not just an approximation for mathematical neatness. ReLU6 is widely optimized in mobile frameworks, and hard-swish avoids the precision and implementation variability of approximate sigmoid in quantized inference. The authors also avoid using h-swish everywhere. They use it mainly in the second half of the network because early activations have larger spatial maps and are more expensive. The ablation table shows why the placement matters.
Variant Top-1 Pixel 1 latency
V3-Large 1.0 75.2 51.4
ReLU 74.5 50.5
h-swish @16 75.4 53.5
h-swish @112 75.0 51.0
Using h-swish from the 16-channel point gives a slight accuracy gain but costs more latency. Starting it later at the 112-channel point is closer to the final design tradeoff. The paper’s final choice is not “h-swish is always better”; it is “h-swish is worth it where the accuracy gain buys enough latency budget.” The optimized implementation also matters:
Without an optimized h-swish kernel, the same architecture can move to a worse point on the latency curve. That is a useful warning for reproduction: changing the runtime implementation can change the conclusion. Architecture DefinitionsThe final paper defines two model families. The large model targets higher accuracy under moderate mobile latency, and the small model targets lower-resource cases.
The large architecture has a mixed block layout: 3x3 and 5x5 bottlenecks, selective SE, ReLU in earlier blocks, and h-swish in later blocks. The tail uses the efficient last-stage pattern discussed above.
The small model is not just a width multiplier of the large one. It has its own searched/adapted structure, uses more 5x5 blocks in the middle, and is tuned for a different part of the latency curve. Main ImageNet ResultsThe main floating-point table is the best compact evidence for the paper.
Three observations stand out:
V3-Large 1.0 and MnasNet-A1 both report 75.2% top-1, but V3-Large is 20 ms faster on Pixel 1. V3-Small 1.0 is much smaller in MAdds than MnasNet-small while being both more accurate and faster. V2 1.0 has more MAdds and lower accuracy than V3-Large, and it is slower on Pixel 1.
The last point is a reminder that MobileNetV3 is not only a NAS story. The final-stage edit, activation implementation, SE scaling, and channel adaptation all contribute to the measured latency. The quantized results are worth checking separately because the paper is targeting mobile inference, not just floating-point research models.
For the full-size model, quantized MobileNetV3-Large keeps 73.8% top-1 and runs at 44 ms on Pixel 1, while MobileNetV2 1.0 reports 70.9% and 52 ms. For the small regime, MobileNetV3-Small keeps 64.9% top-1 at 15.5 ms, compared with MobileNetV2 0.35 at 57.2% and 16.7 ms. This is also where the hard-sigmoid/hard-swish choice matters: the activation has to survive the actual inference path. Resolution And Width ScalingMobileNetV3 is also evaluated across width multipliers and input resolutions.
The paper notes that changing input resolution can provide a better accuracy-latency tradeoff than changing the width multiplier. That makes sense: resolution changes the spatial cost of almost every layer, while width changes channel dimensions. But resolution is not always a free tuning knob. Detection and segmentation often need higher spatial detail, so deployment constraints can force a resolution choice before the architecture is selected. The appendix table makes the deployment menu explicit.
Model Accuracy Pixel 1 latency
large 224/1.25 76.6 77.0
large 224/1.0 75.2 51.2
large 160/1.0 71.7 27.8
small 224/1.0 67.5 15.8
small 160/1.0 62.8 8.6
small 96/1.0 51.7 4.4
For a mobile product, this table is more useful than a single headline model. It gives several operating points that can be selected according to latency, battery, memory, and task accuracy requirements. Component ProgressionThe most honest figure in the paper is the component progression plot.
The path is roughly:
Step Effect
MnasNet seed Strong baseline around 75.2% top-1.
SE/4 Improves accuracy with modest parameter cost.
NetAdapt Moves the model to a lower latency region.
Compact / last-stage edits Saves latency without giving up much accuracy.
h-swish and optimized h-swish Recovers or improves accuracy while depending on runtime support.
This figure is why I would not describe MobileNetV3 as a fully automatic NAS method. The final point is reached by a sequence of searched, adapted, and hand-designed changes. Detection TransferThe paper also uses MobileNetV3 as a drop-in SSDLite backbone on COCO.
The interesting detail is the channel reduction between C4 and C5. The last part of the classifier backbone is tuned for 1000 ImageNet classes, but COCO detection has 90 classes and different feature needs. Reducing channels in the late feature layers improves latency with little or no mAP loss.
Backbone mAP Latency
V2 22.1 162 ms
MnasNet 23.0 174 ms
V3 22.0 137 ms
V3 with channel reduction 22.0 119 ms
V3-Small 16.0 52 ms
V3-Small with channel reduction 16.1 43 ms
This is another example of post-search adaptation. A backbone that is good for classification still needs task-specific trimming when transferred to detection. Semantic SegmentationFor segmentation, the paper proposes Lite R-ASPP, a lightweight head designed for MobileNetV3.
The head keeps the ASPP intuition but removes expensive branches. It uses global-average-pooling-like context and a small number of 1x1 convolutions. The authors also use atrous convolution for denser features when output stride is 16.
On Cityscapes validation, the MobileNetV3 rows are broadly similar in mIOU to MobileNetV2 rows but usually faster. The small model is especially useful: MobileNetV3-Small with LR-ASPP reaches 68.38 mIOU at 327 ms half-resolution Pixel 3 latency in the table.
The Cityscapes test table shows the expected tradeoff. Output stride 16 is more accurate and slower; output stride 32 is faster and slightly less accurate. Again, the paper is not claiming one universal best point. It is giving a set of mobile operating points. Reproduction NotesFor a faithful reproduction, I would record these details before comparing results:
Device model: the paper reports Pixel 1/2/3 single large core measurements. Runtime: the paper uses TFLite benchmark tooling. Threading: measurements are single-threaded, not multi-core throughput. Batch size: latency is batch size 1. Input resolution: changing resolution can dominate the measured curve. Operator implementation: optimized h-swish changes the latency conclusion. Quantization path: hard-swish and hard-sigmoid were chosen partly because they are quantization-friendly.
I would also separate five ablations: NetAdapt, SE ratio, efficient last stage, first convolution reduction, and h-swish placement. Without that separation, it is too easy to over-credit the architecture search and under-credit the manual deployment work. LimitationsThe paper is tied to a specific software and hardware stack. Pixel/TFLite latency is a useful target, but it is not a universal latency oracle. A GPU delegate, a different ARM core, a DSP/NPU backend, or a runtime without optimized h-swish can reorder the frontier. The search process is also not cheap or simple to reproduce. The paper reuses MnasNet machinery, runs NetAdapt, and trains models at scale. The engineering lesson transfers more easily than the exact search recipe. Another limitation is that the paper reports a strong final design but not a fully exhaustive decomposition of every design interaction. For example, activation placement, SE placement, and channel adaptation are coupled. A clean ablation of each dimension would be expensive. TakeawayMobileNetV3 is a search-assisted engineering paper. NAS provides a good seed, NetAdapt sharpens the layer widths, and profiler-aware manual edits remove the pieces that the search space did not express. The strongest message is simple: for mobile CNNs, the real objective is not FLOPs, and the best architectures usually come from search plus runtime-aware model surgery.

entry.title: Mooncake: KVCache-Centric LLM Serving
entry.content:
Paper: Mooncake: A KVCache-centric Disaggregated Architecture for LLM Serving Trace / code: kvcache-ai/Mooncake Mooncake is a production serving paper from the Kimi system. I read it as a cluster-level continuation of the KV-cache story started by systems such as PagedAttention, SGLang/RadixAttention, DistServe, and Splitwise. The main point is not only “separate prefill and decode”. The stronger claim is:
In long-context production serving, KV cache is no longer temporary worker-local scratch space. It is the central data object that should drive placement, scheduling, transfer, reuse, overload control, and admission decisions.
The paper is unusually concrete because it is organized around a real service trace. The trace is sanitized, but it still preserves request arrival time, input length, output length, and remapped prefix block hashes. That is exactly the kind of evidence needed for this problem: without repeated prefixes, long prompts, bursty load, and SLO pressure, KV-cache-centric serving looks over-engineered. One-Sentence SummaryMooncake disaggregates prefill workers, decode workers, and a distributed KV-cache pool, then schedules requests by estimating three things together: how much prefix KV cache can be reused, how expensive it is to move that KV cache, and whether the future prefill/decode latency can still satisfy TTFT and TBT SLOs.
Figure 1 from the paper. The important detail is that the Conductor schedules around KV cache state, not only around free GPU slots. Why This Paper MattersFor short prompts, a serving engine can often pretend that KV cache is just part of the runtime’s internal memory allocator. For long-context workloads, that view breaks down:
The prompt can be tens of thousands of tokens. The decode length can be much shorter than the prompt length. The same long prefix may be reused by many requests. KV cache can exceed what is convenient to keep in GPU memory. Moving KV cache across machines can dominate the request path if it is scheduled carelessly. Under overload, accepting a request into prefill can waste a lot of GPU time if the decode stage is already doomed to miss SLO.
The paper uses two service-level metrics:
TTFT: time to first token. This is mostly affected by prefill queueing, prefill execution, prefix cache reuse, and KV transfer before decode can start. TBT: time between tokens. This is mostly affected by decode batching, decode GPU load, and the amount of KV cache decode workers must hold or load.
This distinction is important. A system can have acceptable TTFT but poor TBT if decode is overloaded. It can also have good TBT but terrible TTFT if prefill cannot keep up. Mooncake tries to keep both sides within SLO while maximizing accepted throughput. Formula 1: Why KV Cache Becomes The Main Data ObjectFor one request with context tokens, a rough KV-cache memory estimate is:
My reading of this formula:
The factor is for key and value tensors. is the number of transformer layers. is the number of KV heads. With MHA this equals the number of attention heads; with GQA/MQA it is smaller. is the head dimension. is the number of cached tokens. is bytes per element, for example 2 bytes for fp16/bf16.
The part that matters for serving is the linear dependence on . Long context does not merely increase compute in prefill; it also creates a large state object that survives into decode. If a batch contains requests with different context lengths, the batch-level KV footprint is better viewed as:
This second formula is the reason average prompt length is not enough. A few 128k-token requests can dominate memory and transfer pressure even when many other requests are small. Prefill And Decode Have Different Scaling Laws Figure 2. Prefill gets worse as input length grows; decode throughput improves with larger decode batch size until the system saturates. The prefill phase computes the model over the prompt and produces KV cache. Its cost grows strongly with prompt length. For very long prompts, attention work and KV materialization make prefill expensive, and prefill latency can increase faster than a simple linear mental model. Decode is different. It advances generation one token at a time. The per-step work is usually small enough that batching many decode requests can improve GPU utilization. This is why colocating prefill and decode can be painful: prefill wants large prompt computation, while decode wants stable token-by-token batching. Interference between the two phases can damage both TTFT and TBT. Mooncake’s split is therefore not cosmetic. It reflects a real phase mismatch:
Prefill workers should be scheduled for prompt throughput, prefix reuse, and KV-cache production. Decode workers should be scheduled for continuous batching and TBT stability. KV cache must move between the two sides without becoming the hidden bottleneck.
Formula 2: Effective Throughput Is SLO-Constrained ThroughputThe paper repeatedly evaluates throughput under latency constraints. I use the following mental formula:
My reading of this formula:
is not raw completed requests per second. counts only requests that satisfy both SLOs. and are the configured SLO thresholds. A system that accepts many requests but misses TBT is not actually good for an interactive service.
This is why Mooncake’s result section should be read as a goodput story. The system is trying to increase the number of requests that can be served while still meeting TTFT/TBT constraints. Architecture: Three Pools Plus A KV-Aware ConductorThe architecture in Figure 1 has four central pieces:
Prefill pool: GPU workers that compute prompt prefill and generate incremental KV cache. Decoding pool: GPU workers that run continuous batching for token generation. KVCache pool: CPU DRAM and SSD resources used to store KV cache outside GPU memory. KVCache-centric Conductor: the scheduler that chooses prefill worker, decode worker, KV reuse, KV transfer, and rejection decisions.
The paper’s design objective can be read as three linked constraints:
For prefill: maximize prefix reuse while keeping TTFT acceptable and keeping prefill GPU utilization high. For decode: maximize decode throughput while keeping TBT acceptable and not exceeding GPU KV memory. For KV storage: use cheaper non-GPU memory when possible, but avoid making KV transfer the new latency bottleneck.
This is an important shift from a simple worker-centric serving model. In a worker-centric model, the scheduler mostly asks “which GPU is free?” Mooncake asks “which worker has, or can cheaply obtain, the right KV prefix, and will the downstream decode stage still meet SLO?” KVCache Pool And Prefix Hashing Figure 3. Token blocks are hashed as prefixes, so a reused prefix can be found and loaded before incremental prefill. Mooncake stores KV cache in fixed-size token blocks. The key trick is that block identity is prefix-sensitive. If the block size is and the prompt tokens are , then a simplified prefix-hash recurrence is:
My reading of this formula:
is the hash key for block . is the token slice in the current block. binds the current block to the previous prefix. Two blocks with the same local token content but different preceding prefixes should not be treated as the same KV state.
This is the same reason prefix caching must be careful. KV for a token depends on all previous tokens through attention. A block is reusable only when the prefix before it is also identical. The recursive hash makes that condition easy to test. For one prefill instance , let be the set of prefix block hashes currently available to that instance. The reusable prefix length can be viewed as:
My reading of this formula:
is the contiguous cached prefix length available on instance . It is not enough for some later block to exist; reuse must start from the beginning and remain contiguous. The multiplier converts matched block count to token count.
The figure also shows three block states:
Prefix cache blocks: already reusable by the current request. Incremental cache blocks: newly generated during this request’s prefill. Unallocated blocks: available capacity.
This is a production-oriented cache model. It cares about where blocks are, whether they are hot, whether they should be replicated, and whether moving them is worth the latency. Request Workflow Figure 4. A request reuses prefix KV cache, runs incremental prefill, transfers KV cache, then enters decoding. The workflow is easier to understand as four stages:
KVCache reuse: the selected prefill instance loads the longest useful prefix KV cache from CPU memory to GPU memory. Incremental prefill: the prefill GPU computes only the missing prompt suffix and produces new KV cache. KVCache transfer: the full KV cache needed for decode is transferred to the decode side, usually through CPU memory and RDMA across machines. Decoding: the decode instance asynchronously loads KV cache and adds the request into continuous batching.
The key design detail is overlap. Mooncake does not want prefill to finish all compute and then block on a huge serialized KV store. It stores and loads KV cache layer by layer, overlapping transfer with computation where possible. That matters because for long prompts, the KV object can be large enough that a naive store/load path eats the TTFT gain from prefix reuse. Trace: Why Real Traffic Changes The Problem Figure 5. The public trace has long input prompts and much shorter outputs. The trace has 23,608 entries. The paper reports an average input length around 7,590 tokens and an average output length around 182 tokens. The largest requests are much longer: inputs can reach 128k tokens and outputs can reach 2k tokens. This matters for two reasons. First, prefill dominates many requests. A prompt can be large while the generated answer is small. If decode is short, wasting prefill work on a request that will later miss decode SLO is especially bad. Second, repeated prefixes create a realistic cache opportunity. If many users or internal tools reuse the same long documents, system prompts, retrieval contexts, or conversation prefixes, then prefix KV cache is not a corner-case optimization. Cache Hit Distribution And Eviction Figure 6. Most blocks are cold, while a small number of blocks are hit many times. The CDF says the cache access distribution is skewed. More than half of cached blocks are not reused in this trace window, while a small number of blocks can be accessed many times. That has a direct scheduling implication: hot blocks can become both valuable and dangerous.
Valuable, because moving or replicating them can remove a lot of repeated prefill work. Dangerous, because too many requests chasing the same hot prefix can create a load hotspot on the instance that holds it.
Mooncake therefore needs both cache-aware scheduling and cache-balancing behavior. Pure cache awareness would send every request to the worker with the longest matching prefix. Pure load balancing would ignore expensive prefix reuse. The paper’s scheduler tries to sit between those extremes.
Table 1. On this trace, LRU is slightly better than LFU and length-aware policies at smaller capacities. Table 1 is also interesting because infinite cache still gives about 0.51 hit rate on this sample. I would not read that as “only half of KV cache can ever be useful” in general. I read it as “this trace has a mixture of repeated and non-repeated prefixes, and the public sample is not the entire production universe.” The relative result is more practical:
LRU works well because temporal locality is strong. LFU is not automatically better because old hot blocks can outlive their usefulness. Length-aware eviction is not automatically better because long blocks are expensive but not always reusable.
For a production system, the eviction policy is part of the scheduler. If the cache keeps the wrong blocks, the prefill scheduler will make good-looking decisions using bad state. Multi-Node Prefill And Chunked Pipeline ParallelismLong-context prefill creates a model-parallel problem. A single 8-GPU node may not be enough for very long contexts, but naive cross-node tensor parallelism is expensive because every layer may require RDMA communication. Sequence parallelism helps by splitting the sequence dimension, but it can reduce MFU and competes with the same network resources needed for KV transfer. Mooncake instead proposes Chunked Pipeline Parallelism for the prefill cluster. The idea is:
Group multiple prefill nodes. Split a long prompt into chunks no longer than a configured prefill_chunk. Pipeline chunks across the grouped nodes. Keep communication mainly at pipeline boundaries instead of doing heavy cross-node all-reduce at every layer.
This is different from chunked prefill in systems such as SARATHI, where chunking is mainly used to interleave prefill with decode inside a colocated worker. In Mooncake, the chunking is also about multi-node prefill scaling and about fitting long contexts into a prefill-specific resource pool. Formula 3: Occupation Cost Of KV StorageThe paper describes the KV-cache storage overhead with a simple but useful product:
My reading of this formula:
is the amount of KV cache that must be stored or transferred. is the time during which the KV cache occupies storage or transfer resources. The product captures why large KV objects are painful even when bandwidth is high.
This is a good systems formula because it discourages looking only at peak bandwidth. If a long prompt produces a large KV object and the system serializes storage after prefill, the request may hold memory, queue slots, and transfer resources for too long. Lowering by overlapping layer-wise store/load can be as important as reducing .
Figure 7. Layer-wise KV storage keeps latency almost flat compared with serialized KV storage as sequence length grows. Figure 7 shows the point visually. Serialized KV storage becomes increasingly expensive as sequence length grows, while layer-wise storage stays much flatter. The lesson is that KV movement needs to be pipelined just like compute. KVCache-Centric Scheduling Algorithm 1. The scheduler jointly considers prefix match, prefill queue time, KV transfer time, decode selection, SLO rejection, and hot-spot migration. Algorithm 1 is the core of the paper. I would break it into five decisions. Decision 1: Find The Best Prefix MatchThe scheduler first hashes the prompt into block keys and asks which prefill instance has the best prefix match. Let:
be the prompt length. be the local cached prefix length on prefill instance . be the best prefix length available anywhere in the prefill pool. be the instance holding that best prefix.
The best prefix is useful because it reduces incremental prefill. But it may be on the wrong machine. Decision 2: Estimate Local Cache-Aware PrefillIf instance already has a reasonable prefix, a local estimate is:
My reading of this formula:
is the predicted TTFT if the request runs on prefill instance without importing extra KV cache. is the queueing delay on instance . is the estimated prefill execution time after reusing prefix tokens. A longer usually reduces prefill compute, but it does not help if the worker queue is too long.
This is why simple “largest prefix hit wins” is not enough. A worker with a perfect prefix but a long queue can still produce worse TTFT than a less cached but idle worker. Decision 3: Estimate Transfer-Aware PrefillIf another instance has a much better prefix, Mooncake considers moving KV cache:
My reading of this formula:
is the predicted TTFT if the scheduler imports the better prefix before running prefill on . is the cost of moving the missing reusable KV prefix from to . is the amount of additional prefix reuse that can gain by transfer. is still the queueing delay on the target prefill instance. is lower than because the transferred prefix increases reuse.
This formula captures the central tradeoff. Moving KV cache is good only when the saved prefill compute is larger than the transfer cost and queue cost. In long-context workloads, that condition can often hold; in short-context workloads, it often will not. Decision 4: Use A Balancing ThresholdThe algorithm uses a threshold to avoid overreacting to small prefix differences. A simplified ratio is:
My reading of this formula:
measures how much better the global best prefix is than the local prefix on . The term is my safe way to think about the zero-prefix case; the paper’s pseudocode writes the ratio directly. If is small, local cache-aware scheduling is enough. If is large, the scheduler should consider KV transfer and cache balancing.
The threshold is important because KV-cache transfer is not free. A scheduler that migrates for every tiny prefix improvement will create network traffic and cache churn. Decision 5: Select Decode And Gate By SLOAfter choosing prefill, Mooncake chooses a decode instance and estimates TBT. The acceptance rule can be written as:
My reading of this formula:
The request is useful only if both prefill-side and decode-side predictions pass. The decode side must be checked before the system wastes prefill work. This is admission control, not just scheduling.
This is also where Mooncake differs from a pure cache system. A cache system asks “can I reuse this prefix?” A serving system asks “should I admit this request now, given future decode load?”
Figure 8. KVCache-centric scheduling has much lower TTFT than random, pure load balancing, or cache-aware scheduling alone. Figure 8 is the cleanest scheduler ablation. Random scheduling is bad because it ignores both cache and queue state. Load balancing alone is bad because it throws away prefix reuse. Cache-aware scheduling alone is better, but it can overload hot-prefix workers. KVCache-centric scheduling performs best because it combines prefix reuse, queue time, transfer cost, and balancing. The mean TTFT values shown in the plot are roughly:
Scheduler Mean TTFT shown in the figure
KVCache-centric 6.23 s
Cache-aware 14.36 s
Load-balancing 60.41 s
Random 92.07 s
I would not overfit these exact numbers outside the paper’s workload. The robust lesson is the ordering: cache and load must be optimized together. Overload-Oriented SchedulingDisaggregated serving creates a delayed-load problem. A request accepted into prefill becomes decode load later. If the system only looks at current decode load, it can accept too many requests during a temporary decode valley and then overload decode after prefill completes.
Figure 9. Without prediction-based early rejection, prefill and decode load can fluctuate in opposite phases. The paper’s early rejection idea is straightforward: reject requests before prefill if the system predicts that they cannot meet downstream SLO. This avoids wasting prefill GPU time. The subtle part is prediction. Naive early rejection can create oscillation:
Decode looks overloaded, so the system rejects new prefill work. Later decode drains, but prefill has too little queued work. The system accepts again. Then decode becomes overloaded again after the accepted prefill work arrives.
Figure 10. Prediction-based early rejection smooths the accept/reject behavior by looking at future decode load rather than only current load. I understand the prediction mechanism with this mental model:
My reading of this formula:
is current decode load. is the amount of decode work the system expects to drain over time . is the decode work expected to arrive from requests currently in or entering prefill. The exact paper implementation is system-level prediction rather than accurate per-request output-length prediction.
This distinction matters. Predicting every request’s output length is hard. Mooncake instead estimates whether the decode pool as a whole will remain within a good load range when new requests reach decode.
Table 3. Prediction-based early rejection rejects fewer requests than both baseline and naive early rejection in the overload experiment. The table reports:
Method Rejected requests
Baseline 4183
Early rejection 3771
Early rejection based on prediction 3589
Fewer rejected requests is not automatically better in every system, but here it means the prediction-based policy accepts more requests while still respecting SLO constraints. The key is avoiding wasteful prefill and avoiding oscillatory accept/reject cycles. Evaluation Setup Table 2. The datasets cover no-reuse public data, high-reuse public data, simulated long contexts, and real production-like traffic. The evaluation uses a high-performance cluster where each node has 8 NVIDIA A800-SXM4-80GB GPUs, NVLink, and high-bandwidth RDMA networking. The experiments replay workloads using a dummy LLaMA2-70B-style model architecture. That means the content is not real user content, but the request shapes and cache behavior are meant to reflect realistic serving pressure. The dataset choices are useful:
ArXiv Summarization: long input, moderate output, almost no cache reuse. L-Eval: longer input, short output, high cache reuse. Simulated Data: controlled 16k/32k/64k/128k prompts, 512-token outputs, 50% cache ratio. Real Data: timestamp-based arrivals and around 50% cache ratio.
This is the right evaluation shape. A KV-cache-centric system should be tested under both low-reuse and high-reuse traffic; otherwise it is easy to mistake prefix caching for the whole contribution. Public Dataset Results Figure 11. Mooncake is compared with vLLM on ArXiv Summarization and L-Eval under normalized P90 TTFT/TBT constraints. The public-dataset results show two different regimes. On ArXiv Summarization, cache reuse is almost zero. Mooncake can still outperform vLLM because phase disaggregation reduces prefill/decode interference. The reported improvement is about 20% for the best Mooncake configuration. On L-Eval, cache reuse is high. Mooncake benefits more because prefix caching and KV movement now matter. The paper reports about 40% throughput improvement in the best configuration. The plot also shows a useful warning: the split between prefill and decode workers matters. A configuration such as [2P+2D] can have decode capacity but insufficient prefill capacity, which hurts TTFT. Disaggregation is not magic; it creates a resource allocation problem. Simulated Long-Context Results Figure 12. As prompt length grows, the gap between Mooncake and vLLM becomes much larger. The simulated data is the strongest evidence for the long-context argument. As prompt length grows from 16k to 128k, colocated serving has a harder time protecting decode latency from prefill pressure. Mooncake separates the phases and manages KV movement explicitly, so it can keep TBT under control at higher request rates. The paper reports throughput improvements from about 50% up to 525% over vLLM in these simulated scenarios. I read the 525% number as a stress-case result: it appears when prompt length and cache behavior make the baseline’s colocated prefill/decode interference particularly severe. The general conclusion is still robust: long prompts amplify the value of disaggregation and KV-aware scheduling. Real Workload Result Figure 13. In the real-workload replay, TTFT is similar, but Mooncake has much better TBT SLO satisfaction. The real-workload result is the most production-relevant one. The paper compares Mooncake [10P+10D] against vLLM [20M]. The TTFT CDFs are close. That tells me Mooncake is not simply winning by delaying or rejecting more prefill work. The TBT CDF is the real difference: Mooncake keeps almost all requests within the TBT SLO, while vLLM only satisfies the TBT criterion for about 57% of requests. The paper states that Mooncake enables Kimi to handle about 75% more requests under the same SLO target. This is the central production claim. For an interactive product, stable decode cadence is often more visible to users than a small average TTFT difference. Relationship To Other Serving SystemsI find Mooncake easiest to place by separating the layers of the stack:
System idea Main layer How it relates to Mooncake
PagedAttention GPU-worker KV memory layout Makes KV allocation efficient inside a worker. Mooncake moves the KV-cache question to cluster-level placement and transfer.
SGLang / RadixAttention Program and prefix reuse Exploits reusable prefixes. Mooncake needs similar reuse signals but also schedules storage, transfer, and decode admission.
SARATHI Chunked prefill / decode scheduling Reduces interference by chunking prefill. Mooncake also uses chunking, but its chunked pipeline parallelism targets multi-node prefill and KV movement.
DistServe / Splitwise Prefill-decode disaggregation Separates phases for better goodput. Mooncake adds KV-cache pool, cache-aware scheduling, hot-prefix balancing, and overload prediction.
So I would not describe Mooncake as replacing these systems. It composes several ideas at a production architecture level, then makes KV cache the organizing abstraction. What I Would Measure When ReproducingA weak reproduction would only report average latency. That would miss most of the paper. A useful reproduction should report:
P50/P90/P99 TTFT. P50/P90/P99 TBT. Effective throughput under TTFT/TBT SLO. Rejected request count under overload. Wasted prefill work for requests that later miss decode SLO. Prefix KV-cache hit rate. Cache hit rate by block age and block popularity. KV transfer volume between prefill, KV pool, and decode. RDMA bandwidth utilization and queueing delay. CPU DRAM and SSD KV-cache occupancy. Prefill GPU utilization and decode GPU utilization separately. Hot-prefix load skew across prefill instances.
The workload should include at least three regimes:
Long prompts with little prefix reuse, to test pure prefill/decode disaggregation. Long prompts with high prefix reuse, to test KV-cache-centric scheduling. Bursty overload, to test early rejection and prediction stability.
Without all three regimes, it is hard to tell whether the system is winning because of disaggregation, prefix caching, admission control, or simply a favorable trace. Limitations And QuestionsMooncake is not the first architecture I would build for a small single-node deployment. The operational cost is real:
KV cache becomes distributed state. Cache migration and replication can affect latency. Worker failures now involve request state and KV state. CPU DRAM and SSD cache tiers need eviction, accounting, and backpressure. RDMA bandwidth is shared by KV transfer and other model-parallel communication. Security and isolation matter because KV cache encodes user context. The optimal prefill/decode split can change with workload mix.
I also want more detail on a few engineering questions:
How often do hot-prefix migrations happen in production? What is the failure recovery path if decode-side KV transfer partially completes? How does the scheduler behave when CPU DRAM is full and SSD becomes active? How sensitive are results to block size ? How does the design interact with speculative decoding, prefix compression, or quantized KV cache? Can the prefill/decode split be adjusted online without destabilizing SLO?
These questions do not weaken the paper. They are exactly the questions that appear once KV cache is treated as a first-class distributed object. TakeawayThe sentence I would keep from this paper is:
Long-context LLM serving should be scheduled around KV cache lifecycle, not only around GPU availability.
Mooncake’s contribution is the full lifecycle view: prefix hash, KV-cache pool, layer-wise store/load, prefill-decode disaggregation, cache-aware and cache-balancing scheduling, decode admission, and prediction-based early rejection. The paper is convincing because the pieces are connected by real workload pressure. Long prompts make KV cache large; repeated prefixes make it reusable; overload makes admission control necessary; decode SLO makes phase interference visible. For me, Mooncake is a reminder that the next serving bottleneck is often not a kernel alone. It is the data movement and scheduling policy around the tensors the kernels produce.

entry.title: Better & Faster Large Language Models via Multi-Token Prediction
entry.content:
Gloeckle F, Idrissi B Y, Roziere B, Lopez-Paz D, Synnaeve G. Better & Faster Large Language Models via Multi-token Prediction. ICML 2024.
Paper: arXiv PDF Topic: pretraining objective, future-token heads, code generation, byte-level modeling, self-speculative decoding
This paper is a useful reminder that “next-token prediction” is not the only causal language-modeling objective worth taking seriously. The proposed change is small: at each sequence position, train the model to predict not only the next token, but the next future tokens. The implementation uses a shared Transformer trunk and lightweight output heads. At inference time, the model can either ignore the extra heads and behave like an ordinary autoregressive model, or use the extra heads as draft heads for self-speculative decoding. The main result is not just “more supervision is good.” The interesting part is where the gain appears. Small models can get worse. Large code models improve clearly. Byte-level models improve a lot. Multiple-choice natural language benchmarks do not show the same benefit, while summarization and synthetic reasoning tasks are more positive. So the paper is really about when forcing a model to look ahead changes the representation it learns. One-Picture Summary Figure cropped from the paper PDF. The model predicts four future targets from the same shared trunk state. At inference time the extra heads may be discarded, or reused to accelerate decoding. The upper half of the figure is the architecture idea. Input token produces a shared hidden state. Instead of only supervising token , the model also predicts token , token , and token . The lower half gives an early hint of the scale effect: on MBPP pass@1, 4-token prediction is worse than the next-token baseline for 0.3B and 0.6B models, but better for 1.3B and above, with the biggest gain at 13B. My short read:
Question Answer
Is this an inference-only trick? No. The paper studies multi-token prediction as a pretraining objective.
Does inference require the extra heads? No. The next-token head can be used alone.
Why keep the extra heads? They can serve as draft heads for self-speculative decoding.
Where are the strongest gains? Large code models and byte-level code models.
Is larger always better? No. For 7B token-level code models, is the sweet spot in the main ablation.
Does it help every benchmark? No. Multiple-choice NLP benchmarks are flat or worse.
ObjectiveStandard language modeling trains on one supervised target per position. For a training sequence , the usual next-token objective is:
where the paper writes the history as:
Multi-token prediction changes the target from one future token to a block of future tokens:
If the model could represent the full joint distribution over the future block, this objective would be a direct block-prediction loss. The implementation in the paper makes it tractable by using a shared representation and independent prediction heads. Let the shared trunk produce a latent representation:
Then the paper writes the multi-token loss through the shared latent variable as:
The practical head-factorized form is:
Since is computed deterministically by the trunk in the actual neural network, the training code is best understood as cross-entropy losses sharing one trunk state:
The first head is the ordinary next-token head. The other heads predict farther offsets: head 1: x_{t+1}head 2: x_{t+2}head 3: x_{t+3}...head n: x_{t+n}
The important detail is that the future heads do not consume the future tokens as inputs. They are not doing a mini autoregressive rollout inside the model. They predict different future offsets from the same observed context. This is why the task becomes harder as grows, and why simply increasing is not guaranteed to help. ArchitectureThe architecture is deliberately conservative. There is one shared Transformer trunk , one shared unembedding matrix , and independent heads . The prediction for the -th future token is:
for:
The head is the next-token prediction head:
This matters for inference. A multi-token predictor is still a normal autoregressive LM if we only keep the first head. The future heads are an auxiliary training signal and an optional decoding accelerator. For fair model-size comparisons, the paper does not simply add many new parameters on top of a baseline. When adding future-prediction layers, it removes layers from the shared trunk. This makes the comparison closer to equal-parameter and equal-budget training. The tradeoff is: some capacity moves from the shared trunk into prediction heads that specialize in different lookahead offsets. The appendix also discusses alternative head structures. The main architecture uses independent heads, but causal and anticausal head stacks are possible. In a causal variant, later heads are built on top of earlier heads:
In an anticausal variant, the model starts from the farthest head and refines toward nearer futures:
The paper’s main experiments use the simpler independent-head architecture, which is also the cleanest design if the future heads are later used as parallel draft heads. Memory-Efficient TrainingNaively training future heads can blow up memory. The reason is the unembedding. If the vocabulary size is and the trunk hidden dimension is , materializing logits and gradients for all heads at once can cost:
That is a bad scaling law because is large. The paper’s trick is to run the head losses sequentially while accumulating the gradient at the shared trunk output. This reduces the peak memory to:
Figure cropped from the paper PDF. The trunk state is computed once, detached, used by each head sequentially, and then its accumulated gradient is passed back into the shared trunk. The code sketch in the figure is essentially: z = model.shared(x)d = z.detach()d.requires_grad = Truefor i in range(n): p = model.heads[i](d) loss(p, y[i]).backward()z.backward(gradient=d.grad)
There are two useful engineering points here. First, this is not equivalent to training separate models. The expensive trunk is shared, and the future heads are small relative to the full model. Second, the implementation avoids keeping every head’s unembedding gradients live at the same time. That is why the method can be trained at LLM scale rather than only on toy models. The appendix notes that their actual distributed training implementation had a small overhead because separate backward passes interacted imperfectly with Fully Sharded Data Parallel overlap. I would not read “no overhead” as a law of nature. The stronger claim is that there is no fundamental -times memory blowup if the backward order is implemented carefully. Main Code Results Figure cropped from the paper PDF. Multi-token prediction is worse for the smallest code models but becomes better as model size grows.
