The scaling result is the most important empirical part of the paper. The authors train code models from 300M to 13B parameters and evaluate MBPP and HumanEval. The behavior is not monotonic in the naive sense. At 0.3B and 0.6B, 4-token prediction often hurts. Around 1.3B the trend starts to flip. At 6.7B and 13B, the gains are clear. This is a plausible reason the idea has not become standard earlier. If one only runs small ablations, multi-token prediction looks fragile or negative. The paper’s claim is that the representation-level benefit is mostly visible once the model has enough capacity to use the lookahead signal.
Table cropped from the paper PDF. The bold entries mark the best values within each setting. Table 1 gives a denser view of the main 7B results. The token-level code setting trains 7B models on 200B tokens with a 32k-token vocabulary and tests:
The best token-level model in that setting is usually :
Benchmark Baseline Best main token setting Observation
MBPP pass@1 30.0 33.8 at clear gain
MBPP pass@10 53.8 55.9 at smaller but positive
MBPP pass@100 73.7 76.9 at positive
HumanEval pass@1 22.8 24.0 at positive
HumanEval pass@10 36.4 40.1 at strong gain
HumanEval pass@100 62.0 66.1 at strong gain
The paper summarizes the same ablation as:
for pass@1, pass@10, and pass@100, and:
APPS/Intro behaves differently. In the 200B-token setting, is best for APPS/Intro. That is an important caveat: the best prediction window depends on the data distribution and evaluation task. There is no universal “four tokens is optimal” rule. The byte-level result is even more dramatic. With byte tokenization, the next-token objective has to learn many local byte transitions that are easy but not semantically useful. Multi-byte prediction forces the model to look past some of those local byte patterns. In Table 1, the 313B-byte setting has:
Model MBPP pass@1 HumanEval pass@1 APPS/Intro pass@100
next-byte, 19.3 18.1 2.4
8-byte, 32.3 21.8 14.0
The authors describe this as more MBPP pass@1 problems solved and more HumanEval pass@1 problems solved compared with next-byte prediction. My interpretation is that byte-level training exposes the weakness of pure next-token supervision most clearly: the model can spend too much training signal on tiny local continuations instead of learning larger program structure. How Many Future Tokens?The paper’s answer is empirical, not theoretical. For 7B token-level code models trained on 200B tokens:
is the strongest setting across MBPP and HumanEval in the main table. But wins APPS/Intro in the same training regime, and is best for byte-level models. So I would treat as a modeling hyperparameter tied to token granularity:
Tokenization More local redundancy? Useful in paper
32k BPE tokens lower for MBPP/HumanEval
bytes much higher in main byte ablation
The intuition is simple. A byte is a smaller semantic unit than a BPE token, so looking eight bytes ahead may correspond to a similar semantic horizon as looking a few tokens ahead. But this is only an intuition. The actual optimum still depends on model size, data, and task. Faster InferenceThe future heads can be used as draft heads. This is not exactly the same story as Medusa, because the heads are trained during pretraining rather than attached afterward. But the serving idea is similar: use cheap lookahead predictions to propose several tokens, then verify them with the next-token head.
Figure cropped from the paper PDF. With more heads used during self-speculative decoding, throughput increases and relative latency decreases across batch sizes. In the appendix experiment, the authors use a 4-token prediction model and vary how many heads participate in self-speculative decoding. The speedup is stable across batch sizes in their setup. This matters because many speculative decoding results are strongest at small batch sizes and fade when batching grows. Here, the future heads are attached to the same model, so the overhead profile is different from running a separate draft model.
Table cropped from the paper PDF. Token-level 4-token models reach about 2.7x to 3.0x relative speedup when using four heads. For the token-level 4-token model:
Domain Heads used Relative speedup Tokens per forward
Wikipedia 4 2.74 3.12
Books 4 2.67 3.09
Code 4 3.05 3.50
The code setting is the strongest. With four heads, the model retrieves 3.50 tokens per forward on average and reaches a 3.05x relative speedup. The speedup is lower than the theoretical maximum of four because not every proposed token is accepted and each speculative step has overhead. The byte-level results can go higher because byte predictions are more local and often easier to accept:
Table cropped from the paper PDF. Byte-level self-speculative decoding reaches much larger speedups when many byte heads are used. For the byte model, using eight heads gives 6.39x relative speedup. For , using all thirty-two heads gives 10.84x relative speedup and 15.35 tokens per forward. These are byte tokens, so the numbers are not directly comparable to BPE-token speedups, but they show why multi-byte prediction is appealing: byte-level training normally hurts inference length, and self-speculative decoding can recover much of that cost. Finetuning Figure cropped from the paper PDF. A model pretrained with 4-token prediction remains better after CodeContests finetuning. The paper also checks whether the multi-token pretraining benefit survives finetuning. The setup compares:
Pretraining Finetuning target Legend
next-token next-token
4-token next-token
4-token 4-token
Both finetuned versions of the 4-token pretrained model beat the next-token baseline on CodeContests pass@k. The strongest line is , meaning: pretrain with the auxiliary lookahead task, then strip or ignore the future heads and finetune with the classical next-token objective. This is a useful pattern. It suggests the future-token loss is valuable as a representation-shaping pretraining signal, even if the downstream finetuning objective returns to ordinary next-token modeling. Natural Language Results Are MixedThe paper does not claim universal improvement on all natural language benchmarks.
Figure cropped from the paper PDF. On six standard multiple-choice NLP benchmarks, 2-token prediction is roughly on par with the baseline and 4-token prediction is worse. This negative result is important. Multiple-choice and likelihood-based evaluations reward calibrated preferences over fixed answer options. A lookahead objective may help generation and reasoning without improving this particular evaluation format. Or the natural language setting may simply require a different , larger model scale, or more data before the benefit appears. For generative natural language, the paper reports a more positive summarization result:
Figure cropped from the paper PDF. On eight abstractive summarization benchmarks, 2-token and 4-token models improve average ROUGE-L F1 over the next-token baseline. The average ROUGE-L F1 gains are not huge, but they are consistent in the plotted summarization aggregate. The gap shrinks at 500B training tokens, which fits the broader theme: multi-token prediction can improve sample efficiency, but the advantage may shrink as the baseline sees more data. My read is that natural language results are task-dependent. If the benchmark is mostly about choosing among given labels, the extra lookahead supervision is not clearly useful. If the benchmark requires generating structured output, the result is more promising. Synthetic DiagnosticsThe authors use synthetic tasks to probe why lookahead might help. These experiments are not meant to replace large-scale evaluations, but they make the paper easier to reason about.
Figure cropped from the paper PDF. On a controlled induction task, 2-token prediction helps small models learn the second token of repeated two-token names. The induction task asks whether a model can complete repeated patterns. If a story has already mentioned a two-token name, predicting the second token of a later occurrence is mostly an induction problem. The figure shows that 2-token prediction helps small models substantially. The advantage disappears around 100M nonembedding parameters. That disappearance is not a contradiction. Once a model has enough capacity, or once the data makes induction easy enough, next-token training can learn the required feature. Multi-token prediction seems most useful when the model would otherwise underinvest in such longer-range features. The arithmetic task pushes this further:
Figure cropped from the paper PDF. Multi-token prediction improves accuracy on a polynomial arithmetic task, including out-of-domain expressions with more operations than seen during training. The task works in the polynomial ring:
Training expressions contain one to five operations. Evaluation includes both in-domain cases and harder out-of-domain cases with more than five operations. The absolute out-of-domain accuracy is still low, but multi-token prediction improves it more than increasing the small model size from 30M to 100M in the related appendix comparison. The useful lesson is not that multi-token prediction solves arithmetic. It does not. The lesson is that forcing lookahead can change which algorithmic features the model learns under the same parameter budget. Why Might It Work?The paper gives two related explanations. I find both useful, but neither should be read as a complete theory. Choice PointsSome token decisions matter much more than others. In code, choosing a function name, branch condition, API call, loop bound, or variable update can constrain many future tokens. Other tokens are local formatting or syntactic glue. A next-token objective gives every target one direct loss term. A multi-token objective gives more indirect weight to tokens whose consequences affect the future.
Figure cropped from the paper PDF. If the hard transition is , then future-token losses also penalize earlier predictions that should have anticipated . For an -token objective, the paper argues that a consequential choice point receives:
loss terms through its future correlates. An inconsequential transition receives only:
reinforcements. The relative emphasis on choice points is therefore:
For , that is a 2.5x relative emphasis on consequential decisions in this simplified counting argument. This connects nicely to code generation. One wrong high-level token can derail the entire solution even if the next few syntax tokens remain locally plausible. The appendix gives a more formal reinforcement-learning style definition of a choice point. Let be the current partial sequence and be the generation policy. In shorter notation, define a state value $V_\pi(s_t)=\mathrm{E}\pi G_tG_t=\sum{j\ge0}R(s_{t+j})\sigma_\pi(s_t)=\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(V_\pi(s_{t+1}))}\sigma_\pi(s_t)$ is large. This formalization is not directly used as a training objective, but it clarifies what the paper means by a token whose choice matters for the future trajectory. Information-Theoretic ViewThe second explanation is about mutual information between adjacent future tokens. Let be the next token and be the second-next token, with the observed prefix omitted from notation. Next-token prediction focuses on:
Two-token prediction adds the next future token:
The paper decomposes the single-token entropy as:
For two-token prediction:
The interpretation is that two-token prediction increases the relative weight of the mutual information term . In plain terms, the model is pushed to learn features of that are useful for predicting , not just features that make locally likely. The appendix makes this argument closer to the actual cross-entropy loss. Let be the empirical data distribution and be the model distribution. The conditional cross-entropy is:
The relative mutual information term is defined as:
Then the relative version of the one-token decomposition is:
And the relative two-token decomposition is:
I would not over-interpret this as a complete proof of better reasoning. It is still an explanatory decomposition. But it gives a precise way to say what the objective changes: the future-token loss makes the model pay more attention to information that couples nearby future tokens. Relation to Medusa and DeepSeek-V3This paper sits between training objectives and inference systems. Medusa also attaches future-token heads to a model, but its main framing is inference acceleration. The heads propose candidates and a tree attention pass verifies them. Multi-token prediction is more fundamental: the heads are part of pretraining, and the main question is whether the objective improves the base model even when the heads are discarded. DeepSeek-V3 later uses an MTP module as part of its training recipe. The connection is direct at the conceptual level: force the model to predict more than one future token. The difference is implementation scale and integration with the rest of the model recipe. I read this paper as one of the clearest controlled studies showing why MTP is not just a decoding trick. The clean mental model is:
Method Main role of future heads
Medusa inference-time candidate generation
Multi-token prediction paper pretraining objective and optional self-speculative decoding
DeepSeek-style MTP large-scale recipe component for stronger training signal
Practical NotesIf I were trying to reproduce or reuse this idea, I would watch the following details. First, compare at a fixed parameter and compute budget. If we simply add heads and parameters to the baseline, the result is harder to interpret. The paper removes trunk layers when adding future head layers, which makes the comparison more meaningful. Second, tune for tokenization. The right window for byte-level code is not necessarily the right window for BPE-token natural language. Larger creates harder prediction targets and can inject noisy gradients. Third, keep the memory schedule. The method is appealing only if it avoids materializing all vocab-sized outputs at once. The difference between and is the difference between a neat idea and a trainable LLM recipe. Fourth, evaluate both direct model quality and decoding speed. The future heads can help in two separate ways: they may improve the representation learned by the trunk, and they may provide high-quality drafts for self-speculative decoding. Those are related but not identical claims. Fifth, do not expect every benchmark to improve. The multiple-choice result is a useful warning. Multi-token prediction seems especially aligned with generation, code, byte-level modeling, and synthetic tasks where local next-token correctness is not enough. TakeawaysThe paper’s strongest contribution is showing that multi-token prediction is a serious pretraining objective at scale. The gains are not universal, but they are large enough on code and byte-level modeling to matter. The method also creates a natural bridge from training to inference: the same future heads that shape representations during pretraining can later draft tokens for self-speculative decoding. The part I like most is the choice-point interpretation. Next-token prediction treats every position as a local prediction problem under teacher forcing. Multi-token prediction asks the representation to carry information that will still matter a few steps later. That is a small objective change, but for code and algorithmic sequences, it changes the training pressure in exactly the place where one bad local decision can derail the whole continuation.

entry.title: Neural Architecture Optimization
entry.content:
Luo R, Tian F, Qin T, et al. Neural Architecture Optimization. NeurIPS 2018.
Paper / Code / PyTorch Code NAO is an interesting NAS paper because it does not search directly in the discrete architecture space, and it also does not relax every edge operation into a DARTS-style mixture. It learns a separate continuous representation of architecture strings. Once an architecture is embedded into that space, NAO uses a performance predictor to define a differentiable surface, moves the embedding in the direction of higher predicted accuracy, and then decodes the moved point back into a discrete architecture. The useful mental model is:
a discrete cell is serialized as a token sequence; an encoder maps that sequence into continuous hidden states; a predictor learns a dev-accuracy surface over the hidden states; a decoder reconstructs a valid architecture from hidden states; search is done by gradient ascent on the predictor, not by sampling a controller action.
Figure 1. The core loop of NAO: encode a cell architecture, move its embedding on the learned predictor surface, then decode the optimized embedding into a new architecture. The paper is from the same era as ENAS, PNAS, AmoebaNet, and DARTS, so the reported compute is not directly comparable to modern NAS practice. But the formulation is still worth reading. NAO makes a concrete attempt to turn “architecture search” into “architecture representation learning plus gradient optimization”. Problem SettingNAS has a difficult search space: the architecture is discrete, the evaluation is expensive, and a local edit in the string representation may or may not be a local edit in model behavior. Earlier methods typically used reinforcement learning, evolutionary search, Bayesian optimization, or progressive search. NAO asks a different question: can we learn an embedding space in which gradient steps are meaningful? The architecture is represented as a fixed-length string:
How I read this formula: is not a tensor of weights. It is a sequence of discrete architecture tokens. is fixed by the number of nodes in the cell, and is the set of legal tokens at position . The valid-token set is position dependent because some positions represent input indices, while others represent operation types or operation sizes. For a CNN cell, the paper follows the common cell-based search space. A full network is built by stacking normal and reduction cells. Each cell contains nodes. Each node has two branches, and each branch selects an earlier node and applies an operation:
How I read this formula: branch chooses a source activation , runs operation , and the node output is the sum of the two branch outputs. The final cell output is the concatenation of all intermediate nodes that are not consumed by later nodes. In the non-weight-sharing CNN search, the operation set contains 11 choices: identity, 1x1 conv, 3x3 conv, 1x3+3x1 conv, 1x7+7x1 conv, 2x2/3x3/5x5 max pooling, and 2x2/3x3/5x5 average pooling. In the weight-sharing setting, it uses the ENAS-style 5-operator space: identity, 3x3 separable conv, 5x5 separable conv, 3x3 average pooling, and 3x3 max pooling. For the RNN cell, NAO also reuses the ENAS search space. Each node chooses a previous node and an activation function:
How I read this formula: for node , is the selected predecessor and is one of tanh, ReLU, identity, or sigmoid. The first node is special because it combines the current input and the previous hidden state . The output of the whole recurrent cell is the average of all node outputs. Encoder, Predictor, DecoderNAO has three learned components. They are trained together, but each has a different job. The encoder maps a discrete architecture string into a continuous representation:
How I read this formula: the architecture is first treated like a sentence. A single-layer LSTM reads the token sequence, and the hidden state at every token position is kept. NAO does not collapse the architecture into one scalar or one one-hot vector. It keeps a sequence of hidden states so the decoder can attend to different parts of the original structure. The predictor maps the architecture embedding to predicted dev performance:
How I read this formula: the predictor only sees a mean-pooled version of the encoder hidden states. This makes the predictor simpler than the decoder. It does not need to reproduce the architecture token by token; it only needs a representation good enough to rank or regress performance. The target is the measured dev-set accuracy after training that child architecture. The decoder maps the continuous representation back to a valid discrete sequence:
How I read this formula: the decoder is autoregressive. It predicts token using the embedding and previously generated tokens. This is important because the decoder is not just producing a vector. It must output a complete architecture string that satisfies the grammar of the search space. The decoder’s token distribution is masked by valid choices:
How I read this formula: is the decoder LSTM state, is the attention context over encoder hidden states, and is the valid token set at this position. The denominator only sums over legal tokens. This detail matters: without the mask, the decoder could emit invalid cell descriptions such as an operation token where an input-index token is expected. The model is trained by a joint objective:
How I read this formula: the first term trains the predictor to match measured performance. The second term is the negative log-likelihood reconstruction loss, written with a minus sign because training minimizes . controls the balance. If is too small, the encoder can become a copy-friendly representation for the decoder without organizing architectures by performance. If is too large, the decoder may not preserve enough structural information to reconstruct valid architectures after gradient steps. The paper also uses a small but important symmetry trick. If two architecture strings only differ by swapping the two branches inside a node, they describe the same computation. NAO augments training data with such symmetric strings and the same score. This pushes the encoder and predictor toward permutation invariance and gives roughly a 2% pairwise-accuracy gain in their CIFAR-10 predictor diagnostic. Search AlgorithmOnce the encoder-predictor-decoder model is trained, NAO improves a seed architecture by moving its hidden states along the predictor gradient:
How I read this formula: every token-level hidden state is nudged in the direction that locally increases the predictor output. is the step size. The statement is only locally believable when is not too large and the predictor is smooth enough. After the update, is not itself an architecture. The decoder still has to turn it into a valid sequence .
Algorithm 1. NAO alternates between evaluating architectures, fitting the encoder-predictor-decoder model, selecting top seeds, moving their embeddings, and decoding new candidates. The algorithm has a clean outer loop:
start from an initial candidate set; train and evaluate those architectures to get real dev scores; train , , and with the joint loss; choose the top- architectures as seeds; apply the gradient step to their embeddings; decode the moved embeddings into new architectures; evaluate the new architectures and repeat.
One practical detail I like: if the decoded architecture is exactly the same as the seed, the paper increases the step size until the decoder emits a different architecture. That is a heuristic, but it exposes a real problem. The latent update is only useful if it crosses a decoder decision boundary without jumping into a nonsensical region. DiagnosticsNAO needs two things to be true: the predictor must rank architectures usefully, and the decoder must reconstruct architecture strings reliably. The paper checks both. For the predictor, it uses pairwise ranking accuracy:
How I read this formula: is the number of held-out architectures used for the diagnostic. This metric asks whether the predictor orders two architectures the same way as the true dev-set scores. For NAS, ranking can be more relevant than absolute regression error because search mostly needs to know which candidate is better. For the decoder, it measures average Hamming distance between the decoded string and the original string:
How I read this formula: this is a reconstruction check. If the decoder cannot recover the original architecture from its own encoder output, then decoding a moved point is even less trustworthy. The paper reports that with about 500 evaluated architectures, the predictor reaches more than 78% pairwise accuracy and the decoder’s average Hamming distance is below 0.5 tokens out of 60.
Figure 2. Left: predictor pairwise accuracy rises while decoder reconstruction distance drops. Right: the mean dev accuracy of generated candidates improves over NAO iterations, and predicted mean accuracy tracks the real value. The right plot is the more important sanity check. It shows that candidates generated in later NAO iterations have higher measured dev accuracy, not just higher predicted accuracy. That does not prove the learned space is globally smooth, but it supports the claim that the local gradient step is doing useful work within the explored region. Weight Sharing VariantThe original NAO loop still trains many child architectures from scratch. The authors also combine NAO with ENAS-style weight sharing. The idea is simple: keep the ENAS one-shot training pipeline, but replace the RL controller with the NAO encoder-predictor-decoder. This attacks a different part of the cost:
NAO reduces the search algorithm’s dependence on random controller sampling by optimizing in embedding space. Weight sharing reduces child-model evaluation cost by reusing parameters in a supernet.
This distinction matters when reading the result tables. “NAONet” usually means the architecture was searched without weight sharing and then trained normally. “NAONet-WS” means the architecture was found with weight sharing. CIFAR-10 Results Table 1. CIFAR-10 comparison. The paper reports both the expensive non-weight-sharing NAONet and the much cheaper NAONet-WS variant. The headline number is strong: NAONet + Cutout with reaches 1.93% CIFAR-10 error. But that row uses 144.6M parameters and a reported 200 GPU days. I would not read it as “NAO is always cheap.” I read it as “the discovered cell scales well when made very large.” The smaller rows are more useful for method comparison:
NAONet with gets 3.18% error with 10.6M parameters after evaluating 1000 architectures. NAONet + Cutout with gets 2.48% error. NAONet-WS gets 3.53% error in 0.3 GPU days. NAONet-WS + Cutout gets 2.93% error in 0.3 GPU days.
The non-weight-sharing search uses 600 random initial architectures and then two more rounds of 200 decoded candidates, so 1000 architecture evaluations in total. This is far fewer than AmoebaNet’s reported 20000 to 27000 evaluated models, but still expensive because each candidate is trained as a small standalone network. Transfer To CIFAR-100 And ImageNetThe paper transfers the best CIFAR-10-discovered CNN cell to CIFAR-100 and ImageNet. This is important because NAS methods can overfit to a benchmark’s search/evaluation protocol. Transfer is a better test of whether the cell is a useful architecture pattern rather than a CIFAR-10 artifact.
Table 2. CIFAR-100 transfer. NAONet + Cutout reaches 14.75% error when scaled to . On CIFAR-100, the best NAONet + Cutout row reports 14.75% error with 128M parameters. The smaller version reports 15.67% with 10.8M parameters. The large model beats the comparison rows in this table, but again the parameter count should be kept in mind.
Table 3. ImageNet transfer. NAONet gets 25.7% top-1 error and 8.2% top-5 error. On ImageNet, NAONet is competitive but not dominant. It reports 25.7% top-1 error, close to PNAS and AmoebaNet-A, worse than AmoebaNet-C, and better than the DARTS row shown in the paper. It also uses 11.35M parameters, which is larger than many rows in the table. My takeaway is that the discovered cell transfers, but the comparison is not just accuracy; parameter count and search budget both matter. Language Modeling ResultsNAO also searches an RNN cell on Penn Treebank. This part is useful because it shows the method is not tied to convolutional cells. The search string changes, but the encoder-predictor-decoder framework is the same.
Table 4. Penn Treebank language modeling. NAONet reaches 56.0 test perplexity, while NAONet-WS reaches 56.6 with much lower search cost. The PTB results have the same tradeoff pattern as CIFAR-10. Full NAONet reports 56.0 test perplexity with 300 GPU days. NAONet-WS reports 56.6 perplexity with 0.4 GPU days. DARTS is very close at 56.1 with 1 GPU day. So the best NAO number is strong, but the weight-sharing version is the more practical row. The paper also transfers the PTB-discovered RNN cell to WikiText-2:
Table 5. WikiText-2 transfer. The PTB-searched NAONet reports 67.0 test perplexity. On WikiText-2, NAONet reaches 67.0 test perplexity. It is better than ENAS in this table and close to DARTS, but it does not beat strong hand-designed language-modeling recipes such as Mixture of Softmax. That is a reasonable outcome: NAO searches the recurrent cell topology, not the full language-modeling training recipe. Discovered ArchitecturesThe appendix plots the final CNN and RNN cells. These pictures are useful because they remind me that NAS papers are often searching within a very specific grammar. NAO does not invent an arbitrary neural network. It searches wiring and operation choices inside a cell template.
Figure 3. CNN cells discovered by NAO. The upper graph is the normal cell, and the lower graph is the reduction cell. The CNN cells contain many pooling and asymmetric-convolution choices. The normal cell has several skip-like paths and concatenates unused nodes at the output. The reduction cell has a different routing pattern and more pooling operations, which makes sense because reduction cells are expected to change spatial resolution.
Figure 4. RNN cell discovered by NAO for Penn Treebank. The RNN cell is mostly ReLU nodes, with tanh at the entry and another internal node, plus a sigmoid node near the upper middle. The final output is an average over the node outputs. I would not try to over-interpret every edge, but the figure is still helpful: the searched cell is a sparse directed computation graph, not a standard LSTM gate layout. What I Would Watch CarefullyNAO is conceptually clean, but its success depends on several fragile assumptions. First, the predictor gradient is only useful if the predictor learned a smooth local surface. A high predictor score after the update is not enough; the decoded architecture must also evaluate well. This is why Figure 2(b) is more convincing than only reporting predictor loss. Second, decoder reliability is central. If the decoder has high reconstruction error, then the latent space is not a stable architecture space. A moved embedding may decode to an arbitrary valid architecture rather than a small improvement over the seed. Third, the search cost accounting needs attention. NAONet without weight sharing evaluates 1000 architectures for CIFAR-10 and uses a large GPU pool. NAONet-WS is much cheaper, but then the comparison is partly about the ENAS-style weight-sharing setup. Fourth, the final model scale changes the story. The best CIFAR-10 number uses a very large model with 144.6M parameters. The smaller rows are more informative when comparing cell quality under realistic parameter budgets. TakeawayThe core contribution of NAO is not just “use an accuracy predictor.” The key idea is to train a reversible-ish architecture representation: encode a discrete cell, learn a performance surface over the embedding, take a gradient step, and decode the result back to a legal architecture. I see NAO as a bridge between black-box NAS and differentiable NAS. Unlike RL or evolution, it explicitly optimizes a learned continuous space. Unlike DARTS, the continuous variables are not operation mixture weights inside a supernet; they are architecture embeddings learned by an encoder-decoder model. That makes the method more flexible, but also puts a lot of pressure on representation quality. The paper is worth remembering for this design pattern: if a discrete object is hard to optimize directly, learn a continuous space that can reconstruct the object and supports a task-specific gradient.

entry.title: NAS-Bench-101: Towards Reproducible Neural Architecture Search
entry.content:
Ying C, Klein A, Christiansen E, Real E, Murphy K, Hutter F. NAS-Bench-101: Towards Reproducible Neural Architecture Search. ICML 2019.
Paper: https://arxiv.org/pdf/1902.09635.pdf Code: https://github.com/google-research/nasbench
NAS-Bench-101 is a benchmark paper rather than a new NAS optimizer. Its main contribution is to turn a large but still controlled cell search space into a queryable table. The table maps each valid architecture to fixed training results, so an optimizer can be evaluated without retraining thousands of CIFAR-10 models. That sounds simple, but it fixes a real problem in early NAS papers: algorithm comparisons were often dominated by GPU budget, implementation choices, and hidden training recipes. NAS-Bench-101 changes the experiment into a cleaner question: under the same query budget, which optimizer finds better architectures, and how stable is that behavior over many independent runs? Search SpaceNAS-Bench-101 uses the familiar cell-based CNN setup. A macro skeleton repeats a learned cell several times, and the cell itself is a directed acyclic graph. The original encoded space contains about 510 million possible graphs before validity checks and canonicalization. After removing invalid and isomorphic cases, the benchmark contains 423k unique valid architectures.
The cell has at most 7 vertices and at most 9 edges. The input and output nodes are fixed, while intermediate nodes select one of three operations:
3x3 convolution; 1x1 convolution; 3x3 max pooling.
This is intentionally narrower than a production architecture search space. It does not include inverted residual blocks, device latency choices, width multipliers, activation choices, or Transformer-style dimensions. The point is controlled diagnosis, not direct deployment search. Query ProtocolFor every architecture, NAS-Bench-101 stores multiple training budgets: 4, 12, 36, and 108 epochs. Each architecture is trained and evaluated three times, so the API can return either repeated observations or a particular trial index. This matters because a realistic search algorithm should see noisy observations, not an oracle with the exact mean performance. The paper is also explicit about validation and test usage. During search, the optimizer should use training and validation metrics. Test accuracy should only be queried offline after the search has selected an architecture. If an algorithm uses test accuracy during search, it is no longer measuring generalization; it is optimizing the benchmark’s hidden answer key. The stored metrics include:
training time; train accuracy; validation accuracy; test accuracy.
The cleanest evaluation is a best-so-far curve under a fixed budget. Reporting only the final architecture hides whether the method was sample efficient or just used enough queries to eventually stumble into a good cell. Dataset ShapeThe ECDF plots show two useful properties. First, most valid architectures are not terrible after 108 epochs; a large fraction already exceeds 90% validation and test accuracy. Second, stochastic training noise shrinks with longer training budgets, which is why early-epoch signals are useful but not equivalent to final ranking.
The best architecture in the table reaches 94.32% mean test accuracy. The paper compares this with two hand-designed cells: a ResNet-like cell at 93.12% and an Inception-like cell at 92.95%. The final validation and test accuracies are almost perfectly correlated at 108 epochs, with correlation around 0.999. That makes NAS-Bench-101 a good place to study optimizer behavior without getting too distracted by validation/test mismatch. Training time is not just a function of parameter count. The plot below shows that more parameters usually cost more time, but topology still matters: two cells with similar parameter counts can have different runtime because of branching and operation placement.
That is one reason a benchmark table is useful. If the only feedback is accuracy, an optimizer may overfit to expensive cells. If the table also exposes time, one can evaluate regret over estimated wall-clock time instead of only over number of queries. Architecture DiagnosticsThe operation replacement experiment is one of the most useful parts of the paper. The authors replace one operation type with another across architectures and measure the average effect on validation accuracy and training time.
Replacing 3x3 convolution with 1x1 convolution drops average validation accuracy by about 1.16%, while replacing it with max pooling drops it by about 1.99%. The training-time changes go in the opposite direction: 1x1 convolution and max pooling are cheaper. A simple search algorithm can therefore get an apparent speed benefit while moving into a weaker region of the space. The depth/width analysis is also a useful sanity check. In this benchmark, average validation accuracy peaks around depth 3, while increasing width helps up to the maximum width considered in the space.
This is a reminder that “deeper is better” is not a universal claim inside a constrained DAG cell. The combine semantics and edge constraints shape the distribution of architectures. A benchmark should be interpreted together with its encoding rules. LocalityNAS algorithms often assume locality: a small architecture edit should usually cause a small performance change. NAS-Bench-101 lets the paper test that assumption directly.
The random-walk autocorrelation and fitness-distance correlation suggest locality up to a rough edit distance of about 6. The paper also notes that high-performing cells are rare in the encoded space: the chance of sampling one of the top graphs is roughly 1 in 50,000, while about 35.4% of the search space lies within distance 6 of the closest top graph. This explains why local search can be meaningful here, but also why pure random search needs many queries. Search Algorithm BenchmarkingThe benchmark section compares random search, regularized evolution, reinforcement learning, SMAC, TPE, BOHB, and Hyperband-like methods. Each algorithm is run 500 times, and performance is plotted as test regret over estimated wall-clock time.
This presentation is more informative than a single best score. The left plot captures convergence speed. The right ECDF shows how often an optimizer ends near the optimum. A method with a strong median but a bad tail may be unreliable, while a method with slower median progress but high robustness may be preferable for expensive real searches. The comparison also highlights a subtle issue: algorithms that exploit lower training budgets, such as Hyperband and BOHB, are using a different kind of signal from optimizers that query only 108-epoch results. That is legitimate, but it must be stated. Otherwise “query count” is not a fair budget unit. Mini-Benchmark and Early EpochsThe paper bootstraps a smaller NASBench-Mini with at most 6 vertices, giving around 64.5k cells instead of the full 423k. The relative ranking of random search, non-regularized evolution, and regularized evolution remains consistent across the smaller and larger tables.
This is useful because it suggests that a reduced space can still preserve some optimizer-ordering signal. It does not mean every algorithm conclusion transfers, but it gives evidence that the benchmark is not completely brittle to space size. Early-epoch correlation is more complicated. The appendix reports Spearman rank correlations between early and final accuracies under different percentile slices.
The full-space 36-to-108-epoch correlation is high, around 0.902. But within the top 10% of architectures it drops sharply, to about 0.495. That is exactly the regime where strong NAS algorithms operate. Early training is useful for pruning weak models, but it is much less reliable for sorting the best models. How I Would Use ItFor a new black-box NAS optimizer, I would use NAS-Bench-101 as a first diagnostic step:
Fix a query budget and wall-clock budget model. Run at least dozens of independent seeds, not just one or three. Use validation accuracy for search and reserve test accuracy for post-search reporting. Report best-so-far curves, not only the final best cell. Compare against random search and regularized evolution. State whether the optimizer can query 4/12/36-epoch results or only 108-epoch results. Check whether improvements survive on NAS-Bench-201 or a larger surrogate benchmark.
The important part is not to claim too much. A win on NAS-Bench-101 says that the optimizer navigates a small CIFAR-10 cell space well. It does not prove that the method will discover strong ImageNet, mobile, language, or hardware-aware architectures. LimitationsNAS-Bench-101 is deliberately constrained:
only CIFAR-10 is used; the operation set has only three choices; the macro skeleton is fixed; latency and memory are not first-class objectives; the benchmark is small enough that repeated querying can turn into table exploitation; the top region is narrow enough that early-epoch ranking becomes noisy.
These limitations do not make the benchmark weak. They define what the benchmark is for: controlled, reproducible optimizer analysis. TakeawayNAS-Bench-101 made NAS evaluation much more scientific. It replaced many expensive and hard-to-reproduce claims with a shared table, a clear query protocol, and enough repeated runs to study robustness. I would treat it as a unit test for NAS optimizers. Passing that unit test is not enough for real architecture design, but failing it is a strong warning sign.

entry.title: NAS-Bench-201: Extending the Scope of Reproducible Neural Architecture Search
entry.content:
Dong X, Yang Y. NAS-Bench-201: Extending the Scope of Reproducible Neural Architecture Search. ICLR 2020.
Paper: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2001.00326.pdf Code/API: https://github.com/D-X-Y/NAS-Bench-201
NAS-Bench-201 is the natural follow-up to NAS-Bench-101. NAS-Bench-101 made a large cell space queryable, but it used only one dataset and imposed graph constraints that excluded some NAS algorithms. NAS-Bench-201 chooses a smaller fully enumerated space, then spends the saved budget on cleaner diagnostics: multiple datasets, more operations, and better support for different optimizer families. The result is one of the most useful sanity-check benchmarks for NAS. It is small enough to be completely tabular, but rich enough to expose failure modes such as skip-connection collapse, weak transfer across datasets, and misleading early validation signals. Search SpaceNAS-Bench-201 uses a four-node cell. Every directed edge chooses one operation from a fixed set:
zeroize; skip connection; 1x1 convolution; 3x3 convolution; 3x3 average pooling.
There are 6 edges and 5 possible operations per edge, so the encoded search space has architectures.
The macro network repeats the searched cell inside a fixed skeleton. Compared with NAS-Bench-101, the cell is smaller, but the operation set is broader and the graph is unconstrained enough to support reinforcement learning, evolution, differentiable NAS, and hyperparameter-optimization-style search. The paper also reports fewer unique topologies after accounting for equivalence: 12,751 if skip-connection isomorphism is considered, and 6,466 if both skip and zeroize isomorphisms are considered. That is a good reminder that an encoded search space and a semantic search space are not always the same thing. What It Adds Over NAS-Bench-101The paper includes a concise comparison table. The main differences are not only size. NAS-Bench-201 is multi-dataset, supports more NAS families, and exposes more diagnostic information.
NAS-Bench-201 stores results on:
CIFAR-10; CIFAR-100; ImageNet16-120.
For each architecture, it stores training, validation, and test loss/accuracy, plus compute-related properties such as parameter count, FLOPs, and latency. The latency measurement in the released benchmark was collected on a GTX 1080 Ti with batch size 256 for the non-CIFAR-10 settings. This changes the kind of question the benchmark can answer. Instead of asking only “which method wins on CIFAR-10?”, we can ask whether a search method finds architectures that transfer across datasets and whether its behavior is stable when the target distribution changes. Distribution of ArchitecturesThe full enumeration gives a view of the entire space, not just the subset visited by a search algorithm.
The scatter plots show training, validation, and test behavior over all 15,625 architectures on all three datasets. The orange ResNet marker is a useful anchor. It is competitive, but not optimal: the paper notes that there is still about a 2% gap to the best architecture on CIFAR-100 and ImageNet16-120, and about a 1% gap among models with comparable parameter count. The benchmark therefore has room for search algorithms to improve over a hand-designed baseline, while still being small enough that we can know the actual optimum. Cross-Dataset TransferOne of the strongest reasons to use NAS-Bench-201 is cross-dataset analysis. The paper sorts architectures by CIFAR-10 ranking and then shows where the same architectures rank on CIFAR-100 and ImageNet16-120.
The rankings are broadly correlated, but not identical. This matters for NAS claims. An optimizer that looks strong on CIFAR-10 may be exploiting a region that does not transfer cleanly to the other two datasets. The correlation matrices make the same point more explicitly.
Within-dataset validation/test correlation is high. Cross-dataset correlation is lower, and it becomes weaker when focusing only on high-performing subsets. That is the practical regime of NAS: after a method filters out weak models, it still needs to rank good models, and that ranking is much harder to transfer. Dynamic Ranking During TrainingNAS-Bench-201 also records training curves, which makes it possible to ask how early validation accuracy relates to final test ranking.
The rank ordering becomes clearer as training progresses. At 1 epoch, the ranking is noisy. By 150 to 200 epochs, the validation ranking is much closer to final test ranking. This is the same lesson as NAS-Bench-101: early signals are useful, but using them as exact rank labels for the top architectures is risky. Search Algorithm ResultsThe paper evaluates ten search algorithms, including random search, regularized evolution, REINFORCE, BOHB, DARTS variants, GDAS, SETN, ENAS, and random search with parameter sharing.
The table is valuable because it includes both search time and final validation/test performance across all three datasets. A few points stand out:
Random search is already a strong baseline in this compact space. Regularized evolution is consistently competitive and extremely cheap when evaluated through the benchmark API. Differentiable and parameter-sharing methods can fail badly if their search dynamics collapse to degenerate cells. The optimal row is known, so the gap to the true best architecture is visible.
The paper also runs 500 trials for several non-weight-sharing search methods and plots trajectories across datasets.
This plot is closer to how NAS optimizers should be compared: many runs, explicit distribution, and both validation and test behavior. A single lucky search run is not enough evidence. Parameter-Sharing Failure ModeNAS-Bench-201 is especially useful for diagnosing parameter-sharing methods. In the reported experiments, DARTS-V1 and DARTS-V2 quickly move toward architectures dominated by skip connections, causing poor final performance.
The batch-normalization statistic strategy also matters. When using batch statistics instead of keeping running estimates for BN layers in each searched cell, the trajectories change.
This is a good example of why benchmarks need fine-grained traces. If a paper reports only the final architecture, we cannot tell whether the method failed because the search space is bad, the optimizer is bad, or the shared-weight evaluation protocol is biased. Early Training CorrelationThe appendix compares early-budget correlations with full-budget metrics.
Twelve-epoch training already gives a useful signal. For example, the 12-epoch diagnostic setting has strong correlations with full validation/test metrics across the three datasets. But the correlations are not perfect, especially for transfer to ImageNet16-120. Early stopping is a useful accelerator, not a replacement for final evaluation. API ShapeThe released API makes the benchmark easy to use from a script. The paper includes a short example showing architecture lookup, metric access, compute-cost access, and query by architecture string.
A typical use should keep the protocol explicit: from nas_201_api import NASBench201API as APIapi = API("NAS-Bench-201-v1_0-e61699.pth")arch_index = api.query_index_by_arch( "|nor_conv_3x3~0|+|nor_conv_3x3~0|nor_conv_3x3~1|")info = api.query_meta_info_by_index(arch_index)metrics = info.get_metrics("cifar10", "valid")cost = info.get_compute_costs("cifar10")
When reporting results, it is worth stating the dataset split, search budget, number of seeds, whether validation or test accuracy was queried during search, and whether any training-curve information was allowed. LimitationsNAS-Bench-201 is controlled and compact, which is exactly why it is useful. But the same design also limits its scope:
the search space has only 15,625 encoded architectures; all tasks are image classification; the macro skeleton is fixed; latency is measured in a limited hardware setting; operation choices are small compared with modern mobile or Transformer spaces; parameter-sharing results can depend strongly on implementation details.
Success on NAS-Bench-201 is therefore not proof that a method will work on every large real search space. It is evidence that the method survives a clean, fully observable diagnostic environment. TakeawayNAS-Bench-201 is a stronger NAS sanity check than a single-dataset benchmark. It tests whether a search algorithm beats simple baselines, avoids degenerate skip-heavy cells, and transfers across CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet16-120. I would use it after NAS-Bench-101 and before moving to larger surrogate or real-training benchmarks.

entry.title: NAS-Bench-301 and the Case for Surrogate NAS Benchmarks
entry.content:
Siems J, Zimmer L, Zela A, Lukasik J, Keuper M, Hutter F. NAS-Bench-301 and the Case for Surrogate Benchmarks for Neural Architecture Search. ICLR 2022.
Paper: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2008.09777.pdf Code: https://github.com/automl/nasbench301
NAS-Bench-301 attacks the scaling limit of tabular NAS benchmarks. NAS-Bench-101 and NAS-Bench-201 are exact lookup tables, which is excellent for reproducibility, but their spaces are deliberately small. Real NAS spaces such as DARTS or FBNet can contain to architectures. Exhaustive training is impossible. The paper’s solution is a surrogate NAS benchmark. Instead of evaluating every architecture, it samples a large but finite set of architectures, trains them with a fixed recipe, fits performance predictors, and uses those predictors as cheap benchmark oracles. The tradeoff is clear: a tabular benchmark is exact but small; a surrogate benchmark is approximate but much larger. Why Surrogate BenchmarksThe motivating experiment uses NAS-Bench-101 itself. A graph neural network surrogate is trained on subsets of the NAS-Bench-101 table and compared with single tabular observations. Once enough architectures are used for training, the surrogate can beat a one-seed table lookup because it smooths out evaluation noise.
The crossover happens around 21,500 NAS-Bench-101 architectures in the paper’s experiment. That is the conceptual hook: if architecture evaluations are noisy, a learned predictor can sometimes provide a better estimate of expected performance than a single real training run. This does not mean surrogates are automatically safe. It means they can be useful if their ranking behavior, uncertainty, and optimizer trajectories are validated carefully. Benchmark ConstructionThe general pipeline is:
Choose a large search space, such as DARTS or FBNet. Sample architectures with a mixture of random search and NAS optimizers. Train and evaluate those architectures with a controlled recipe. Fit surrogate models from architecture encoding to validation performance. Validate the surrogates with error metrics, rank metrics, and optimizer trajectory tests. Release both the benchmark oracle and enough data to audit it.
The main dataset is SNB-DARTS, built on the DARTS search space and CIFAR-10. The paper collects roughly 60k architectures. The sampling mixture includes random search and optimizer traces from methods such as BANANAS, DARTS, PC-DARTS, GDAS, DrNAS, regularized evolution, TPE, differential evolution, and COMBO. The second dataset is based on FBNet and CIFAR-100. The FBNet space is even larger: the paper describes 22 searchable layers, each with 9 operation choices, giving roughly possible architectures, around . Surrogate Model ChoiceThe paper compares several surrogate families, including graph neural networks and gradient-boosted trees. The strongest models include graph isomorphism networks, LightGBM-style boosting, and XGBoost-style boosting. The authors evaluate both prediction quality and ranking quality. Mean absolute error is useful, but for NAS the ranking is often more important. A surrogate that predicts exact errors poorly but preserves the ordering of architectures can still be useful for optimizer comparison. Conversely, a low average error can hide bad behavior in the high-performing tail. The noise-modeling table is important because architecture evaluations are stochastic. The paper compares a tabular single-observation baseline with learned surrogate ensembles on 500 architectures evaluated five times.
The GIN surrogate has the best MAE in this table and a much better KL divergence than the boosting models, suggesting better uncertainty modeling. This is one reason the paper does not rely on a single surrogate type. Multiple surrogate families reduce the chance that a NAS optimizer simply exploits one model’s bias. True Benchmark vs Surrogate TrajectoriesThe central validation question is not only “does the surrogate predict held-out architectures?” It is “does an optimizer behave similarly on the surrogate as it does on the expensive real benchmark?”
The figure compares trajectories on the real benchmark with trajectories on GIN and XGBoost surrogate benchmarks trained with optimizer data. The broad convergence behavior is preserved. BANANAS improves strongly, random search stagnates, and the surrogate trajectories follow the same qualitative ordering. The paper then repeats the experiment using surrogates trained only on random-search data.
Random-only training still gives plausible trajectories, but it is weaker in the best-performing regions. That makes sense: random sampling covers the global space, but strong optimizers concentrate in small regions that random search may undersample. A robust surrogate benchmark needs broad coverage and enough data near both good and bad boundaries. Optimizer Data DistributionThe appendix gives an ECDF of validation error by optimizer.
The distribution is not uniform across optimizers. BANANAS samples many strong architectures; PC-DARTS, DrNAS, differential evolution, GDAS, and regularized evolution occupy different quality regions; TPE is only slightly better than random search in this plot; COMBO and DARTS include many weak architectures. This is useful for training surrogates because different optimizers expose different parts of the space. The t-SNE visualization makes the coverage issue more concrete.
Random search covers the main cloud, while individual optimizers often explore specific regions. COMBO goes into areas less covered by random search. BANANAS concentrates outside the main cloud. Differential evolution finds a strong central region. This explains why leave-one-optimizer-out validation is necessary: a surrogate trained on one distribution may not extrapolate well to another optimizer’s candidates. Leave-One-Optimizer-OutThe paper validates this directly with leave-one-optimizer-out experiments. The surrogate is trained without data from one optimizer and then tested on that held-out optimizer’s architectures.
The table shows a pattern that is easy to miss if one only reports average . Leaving out DARTS can hurt badly because DARTS contributes unusual skip-heavy architectures, but sparse Kendall tau can remain reasonably high. In other words, the surrogate may still rank bad DARTS architectures as bad even if it cannot predict exactly how bad they are. The trajectory plot gives the practical version of the same test.
This is the kind of validation a surrogate benchmark needs. If a new optimizer searches in a region not represented in the training data, the surrogate may be overconfident or wrong. Holding out optimizer families is a stronger test than a random train/test split. FBNet Surrogate BenchmarkThe paper also constructs a surrogate benchmark for the FBNet search space on CIFAR-100. Here the authors use an XGBoost surrogate trained on randomly sampled architectures. The scaling plot shows that more training data reduces MAE and improves rank correlation.
With transferred hyperparameters from the DARTS surrogate, the FBNet surrogate reaches about and sparse Kendall tau around 0.75 on the test set. That is not perfect, but it is enough to reproduce broad optimizer trajectories.
This part of the paper is important because it argues that surrogate NAS benchmarks are not a one-off trick for DARTS. The same methodology can be applied to a different, much larger search space, as long as the data collection and validation protocol are careful. Failure Cases and Boundary ChecksThe paper does not pretend that surrogates are exact. It studies a constrained DARTS failure case where DARTS can diverge toward cells with only skip connections.
The surrogate can capture the broad divergent trajectory, especially when the relevant data is included. But uncertainty grows when the surrogate is asked to extrapolate into regions it has not seen. This is the main operational risk of surrogate benchmarks: a NAS method can optimize the benchmark model rather than the real architecture performance. The parameter-free operation analysis is another useful boundary test.
The ground truth and surrogate predictions both show that too many parameter-free operations, especially skip connections, lead to worse validation error. This is exactly the kind of degenerate region that differentiable NAS methods can exploit if the benchmark or search objective is not robust. The one-shot optimizer trajectory plot checks whether the surrogate can monitor methods such as DARTS, PC-DARTS, and GDAS through the search process.
The curves are not a perfect replacement for real training, but they are informative enough to diagnose behavior at much lower cost. How I Would Use ItFor benchmarking a new NAS method, I would use NAS-Bench-301 differently from a tabular benchmark:
Report both GIN and XGBoost surrogate results when possible. Use validation performance during search and reserve final real training checks for selected candidates. Track uncertainty or at least avoid making claims from a single surrogate prediction. Compare against random search, regularized evolution, BANANAS, and simple Bayesian optimization baselines. Inspect whether the method visits regions covered by the surrogate training data. Run a small number of real evaluations for final architectures if the claim is about actual model quality. Treat surprising superhuman surrogate scores as suspicious until verified.
The last point is the most important. A surrogate benchmark is a model. It can be exploited. LimitationsNAS-Bench-301 expands the search space dramatically, but it introduces new limitations:
surrogate predictions are approximate; training data coverage affects every conclusion; strong optimizers can search out-of-distribution regions; random train/test splits can overestimate reliability; one surrogate family can bias the benchmark; final deployment claims still need real training and hardware checks.
These limitations are not a reason to avoid the benchmark. They define the right level of evidence. NAS-Bench-301 is excellent for comparing optimizer behavior in a large search space. It is not a final oracle for architecture quality. TakeawayNAS-Bench-301 is the bridge between exact tabular NAS benchmarks and expensive real architecture search. It keeps the reproducibility benefit of benchmarks while moving into search spaces that are orders of magnitude larger than NAS-Bench-101 or NAS-Bench-201. The price is approximation, so the benchmark must be used with surrogate validation, optimizer holdout tests, and real checks for final claims.

entry.title: NAS-BERT: Task-Agnostic and Adaptive-Size BERT Compression with Neural Architecture Search
entry.content:
Reference Paper: NAS-BERT: Task-Agnostic and Adaptive-Size BERT Compression with Neural Architecture Search Venue: KDD 2021
NAS-BERT is a BERT compression paper, but the interesting part is not simply that it produces a smaller encoder. The paper changes the compression setting:
the compressed models should come in many sizes, not one fixed student; the search should happen at the pre-training stage, not separately for every downstream task; the final model should be selected under parameter and latency constraints; the search space is allowed to change the block type, not only width and depth.
This makes the paper closer to Once-for-All / BigNAS than to ordinary BERT distillation. NAS-BERT trains a supernet once, then selects subnets such as 60M, 30M, 10M, and 5M parameter models for different deployment budgets. One SentenceNAS-BERT is a task-agnostic, adaptive-size BERT compression framework:
build a supernet over MHA, FFN, separable convolution, identity, and hidden-size choices; train it block by block using a BERT teacher; progressively shrink weak candidate architectures while preserving different model-size bins; approximate latency and loss with lookup tables; select a subnet that satisfies a target size and latency budget, then pre-train/fine-tune it.
My short reading: the paper is valuable because it treats compressed BERT as a model family, not as a single distilled model. Why This Setting MattersMost BERT compression papers choose a single student. DistilBERT, TinyBERT, MiniLM, and BERT-PKD each define one typical compressed size around 60M to 66M parameters. That is convenient for comparison, but deployment usually has more than one target:
Scenario Constraint that matters
online service latency and throughput
mobile device memory, energy, and CPU latency
offline batch inference total compute cost
edge device strict parameter and memory budget
A fixed compressed model cannot be optimal for all of these. A 60M model may be fine for server inference but too large for an embedded device. A 5M model may fit memory but sacrifice too much accuracy for a normal CPU service. The other issue is task-specific compression. AdaBERT and DynaBERT can adapt to downstream tasks, but that means extra work per task. NAS-BERT tries a different tradeoff: do the expensive compression/search work during pre-training, then reuse the resulting model family across downstream tasks. The phrase “task-agnostic” needs a careful reading. In this paper it mainly means the architecture search and compression are not repeated for each downstream task. The authors still evaluate optional downstream knowledge distillation. Their ablation later shows a stricter setting without fine-tuning-stage distillation. Search Space The search space is chain-structured. A supernet has layers, and each layer chooses one operation from a candidate set :
Here is one architecture path through the supernet. is the operation selected at layer . If there are candidate operations per layer and no further restrictions, the number of possible paths is:
This formula is simple but important. The architecture count grows exponentially with depth. NAS-BERT uses searchable layers because BERT-base has 12 Transformer layers, and each Transformer layer can be viewed as two sub-layers: MHA and FFN. With 26 operation choices, direct full-supernet search would have:
candidate paths. That number explains why the rest of the method is mostly about making supernet training and selection feasible. The candidate operation set is:
The terms mean:
1 for MHA; 1 for FFN; 3 for separable convolution with kernel size 3, 5, or 7; 5 hidden sizes: 128, 192, 256, 384, and 512; +1 for identity.
MHA and FFN keep the search space connected to the original Transformer. SepConv adds a cheaper non-attention operation with local context. Identity allows shallow networks because an identity operation can be removed after selection. The hidden-size table is also structured. MHA uses 2, 3, 4, 6, or 8 heads as hidden size grows from 128 to 512. FFN uses intermediate sizes from 512 to 2048. This means the search is not merely “drop layers from BERT”; it can choose a different computation type and a different width at each block. Why SepConv Appears HereThe appendix gives the practical reason for adding separable convolution. A standard 1D convolution with kernel size and hidden size has parameter scale:
A depthwise separable convolution has scale:
The first formula grows with both kernel size and the square of hidden size. The second separates channel mixing from depthwise local filtering. For BERT compression, this matters because a larger kernel can increase local receptive field without paying the full cost of standard convolution. My interpretation: SepConv is a way to let the search escape the pure Transformer template while still remaining cheap. If the task does not need a full attention/FFN pair at every layer, the architecture can replace some blocks with local convolutional mixing. Block-Wise Supernet Training Directly training the entire supernet is too expensive. Weight sharing gives many paths access to the same operations, but with a search space around , random single-path optimization would give each architecture too little training signal. NAS-BERT therefore divides the 24-layer supernet into blocks. Each block has 6 searchable layers. The BERT-base teacher is also divided into 4 corresponding blocks. For the -th student block, the training target is the output hidden state of the -th teacher block. The paper’s block-wise distillation loss is:
Meaning of the terms:
is the teacher hidden state before block . is the teacher hidden state after block . is the student search block. is the output of the student block when it receives the teacher’s input hidden state. The squared norm is a mean-square style matching loss.
The formula says: “given the teacher’s input to this block, make the student block reproduce the teacher’s output.” This is not task-label supervision. It is representation matching inside the pre-trained BERT computation graph. There is one extra engineering detail: student hidden size may be 128, 192, 256, 384, or 512, while the BERT-base teacher hidden size is 768. The paper uses learnable linear transformations before and after each student block to map hidden dimensions into the teacher-compatible space. Without these transformations, block-wise hidden-state matching would not be dimensionally valid. Search Space Reduction From BlockingBlocking changes the search problem from one enormous path to a composition of smaller sub-architectures. Inside each block, NAS-BERT keeps the hidden size consistent across the 6 layers. The rough number before removing redundant identity-order variants is:
The 5 is the number of hidden-size choices. The term comes from 6 operation choices per layer over 6 layers, where the operation categories are MHA, FFN, SepConv3, SepConv5, SepConv7, and identity. The paper then removes redundant identity permutations. For example: FFN -> identity -> FFN -> identity
and: FFN -> FFN -> identity -> identity
represent the same effective architecture after identity layers are removed. Keeping identities only at the end of a block reduces each block from 233,280 to 97,650 candidate sub-architectures. The full combination count becomes:
This is still huge, but much smaller than . The key is that block-wise training lets NAS-BERT evaluate and prune candidate sub-architectures per block, then assemble full models later. Progressive ShrinkingBlock-wise training reduces the search space, but each block is still large. NAS-BERT uses progressive shrinking: after training epochs, it evaluates sampled architectures and removes weak candidates. This gives surviving architectures more training budget.
The figure is a useful sanity check. Progressive shrinking starts at epoch 4. After that, the red curve drops lower than the no-shrinking baseline. The interpretation is not that shrinking magically improves the model; it improves the allocation of training. Weak candidates are removed, so the remaining candidates receive more effective optimization. Naive pruning has a problem: it may remove large models early because they are harder to train, and remove small models late because they have less capacity. Then the final supernet would lose the ability to serve different deployment budgets. NAS-BERT solves this by dividing each block’s architectures into bins by parameter size and latency. For bin , the maximum parameter and latency thresholds are:
Here:
is the number of bins; is the largest model in the search space; is the parameter-size function; is the latency function; and define the upper boundary of bin .
An architecture belongs to bin only if:
This formula is the diversity guardrail. Pruning is performed inside each bin, so the method does not collapse into only one size range. If the binning works, the final supernet keeps candidates for small, medium, and large budgets. The paper uses bins. It first trains for 3 epochs without progressive shrinking as a warm start. Then at the end of each later epoch, it samples architectures for validation and removes architectures per bin. The process stops when only architectures remain in each bin. Model SelectionAfter progressive shrinking, each block contains sub-architectures. A complete architecture is formed by choosing one sub-architecture from each of the blocks, so the final candidate count is:
With , , and , this is:
Measuring full validation loss and actual latency for candidates is still not practical. NAS-BERT builds a lookup table with approximate metadata: architecture, parameter count, latency, and loss. Latency is approximated additively:
This says the latency of the whole architecture is estimated by summing the measured latency of its operations. It is not perfect because real systems have memory effects, kernel launch overhead, batching behavior, and cache behavior. But it is cheap and hardware-specific: one can measure the 26 candidate operations on a target device and use that device’s latency table. Loss is also approximated additively from block-wise losses:
This is my notation for the paper’s procedure. The method evaluates sub-architectures in each block on the dev set, then adds those block losses to estimate a complete architecture’s quality. The approximation is only valid if block-wise losses are informative enough after teacher-guided training. This is exactly why the earlier block-wise distillation matters. The final selection pipeline is:
build the architecture lookup table; filter candidates that violate parameter or latency constraints; choose the top candidates with low approximate loss; evaluate those full architectures on the dev set; select the best compressed model.
The paper uses . Two-Stage Distillation NAS-BERT’s architecture search is task-agnostic, but the paper also evaluates knowledge distillation during both pre-training and fine-tuning. The appendix summarizes the two-stage pipeline:
pre-train the teacher; pre-train the student with distillation from the pre-trained teacher; fine-tune the teacher on the downstream task; fine-tune the student with distillation from the fine-tuned teacher.
The paper uses a general distillation objective:
In MathJax form:
The terms are:
and are student and teacher parameters. is the normal supervised or language-modeling loss for the student. matches the teacher output distribution and the student output distribution. and are teacher and student predicted distributions. balances ground-truth supervision and teacher matching.
The formula is not unique to NAS-BERT, but it matters for interpreting the experiments. The paper’s main claim is about architectures; the distillation objective helps train and evaluate them. The ablation later is important because it asks whether the searched architectures remain useful when one distillation stage is removed. Training CostThe training setup is large but not absurd for BERT-era compression:
Item Setting
Teacher BERT-base
Searchable layers 24
Blocks 4
Search bins per block 10
Warm start 3 epochs before shrinking
Validation samples during shrinking 2000 architectures
Stop condition 10 architectures per bin per block
Corpus English Wikipedia + BookCorpus
Supernet training 3 days on 32 NVIDIA P40 GPUs
Teacher training in paper 5 days
The cost story is central. Training a supernet on masked language modeling is expensive, but the cost is amortized over many final model sizes. If one needed to repeat the entire search per downstream task or per device, the method would be much less attractive. Results: Adaptive Sizes Table 2 is the cleanest evidence that the search space is doing something useful. The hand-designed baselines are BERT-like models with similar size and latency. NAS-BERT is compared at four sizes and two training settings:
PF: pre-training and fine-tuning; KD: pre-training and fine-tuning with two-stage distillation.
The average GLUE score improvements are:
Size Setting BERT avg NAS-BERT avg Difference
60M PF 82.5 83.2 +0.7
60M KD 83.5 84.2 +0.7
30M PF 79.2 80.0 +0.8
30M KD 79.7 80.3 +0.6
10M PF 74.0 75.2 +1.2
10M KD 74.6 75.5 +0.9
5M PF 68.4 72.3 +3.9
5M KD 68.5 72.7 +4.2
The gap is much larger at 5M. This is the most interesting part of the table. When the model is still fairly large, a hand-designed BERT-like stack is competitive. When the budget becomes tiny, allowing the search to mix SepConv, MHA, FFN, identity, and width choices becomes more valuable. The 5M result is also faster in the paper’s latency proxy: NAS-BERT5 reports 23.6x speedup, while BERT5 reports 20.7x. So the smaller model is not gaining accuracy by secretly becoming slower. Comparison With Prior Compression Work The common-size comparison uses NAS-BERT60 against previous 60M to 66M models. On the dev set:
Teacher: 84.4 average. DynaBERT with augmentation: 82.7 average. NAS-BERT: 84.2 average. NAS-BERT with augmentation: 84.8 average.
On the GLUE test set:
BERT-of-Theseus: 79.4 average. TinyBERT with augmentation: 80.6 average. NAS-BERT: 81.1 average. NAS-BERT with augmentation: 81.7 average.
This table should be read with some caution. Compression papers often differ in teacher strength, data augmentation, distillation details, and training budgets. The authors explicitly do not compare with MobileBERT in this table because MobileBERT uses a stronger teacher. Still, the table supports the main claim: NAS-BERT60 is competitive with strong BERT compression methods while being produced from an adaptive architecture search framework. Extremely Small Models Table 4 compares NAS-BERT5 with AdaBERT in a stricter small-model setting. The paper removes some sophisticated task-specific tricks for fairness: no two-stage distillation and data augmentation for NAS-BERT5, and no data augmentation or probe classifiers for AdaBERT. The reported numbers:
Task AdaBERT NAS-BERT
QNLI 82.0 / 7.9M 83.9 / 5.0M
MRPC 77.2 / 7.5M 80.0 / 5.0M
RTE 56.7 / 8.6M 67.0 / 5.0M
This is where NAS-BERT’s task-agnostic design looks strongest. AdaBERT searches task-specific students, but NAS-BERT5 uses a single searched architecture family from pre-training and still obtains better scores with fewer parameters in these comparisons. My reading: the absolute numbers are from the 2021 BERT compression ecosystem, but the qualitative lesson is useful. At very small sizes, architecture matters more than simply scaling down a Transformer template. Ablations The ablations answer three questions. First, does progressive shrinking help? Table 5 says yes:
Setting AVG
without progressive shrinking 83.1
with progressive shrinking 84.2
The gain is +1.1 average GLUE points for NAS-BERT60. The explanation matches Figure 3: without shrinking, each candidate path is under-trained; with shrinking, the remaining paths receive more useful optimization. Second, should shrinking prune whole architectures or operations? Table 6 favors pruning architectures:
Setting AVG
PS-arch 84.2
PS-op 82.8
This makes sense. Operation-level pruning is too coarse. Removing an operation globally from a layer can damage many potentially good paths. Architecture-level pruning keeps the operation set alive but removes weak paths inside each bin. Third, how much does distillation matter? Table 7 compares pre-training distillation (PD) and fine-tuning distillation (FD). NAS-BERT60 stays better than the BERT60 baseline in all corresponding settings:
Setting BERT60 AVG NAS-BERT60 AVG
PD + FD 83.5 84.2
PD only 82.9 83.5
FD only 82.6 83.1
The PD only row is especially important. Without fine-tuning-stage distillation, the compressed model is closer to the fully task-agnostic story: search and compression happen during pre-training, and each downstream task only needs normal fine-tuning. NAS-BERT60 still reaches 83.5 average. SQuAD Results NAS-BERT is evaluated beyond GLUE on SQuAD v1.1 and v2.0. For the 60M model, the compact comparison is:
Model EM F1
TinyBERT on SQuAD v1.1 79.7 87.5
NAS-BERT on SQuAD v1.1 80.5 88.0
NAS-BERT dagger setting on SQuAD v1.1 81.2 88.4
Model EM F1
TinyBERT on SQuAD v2.0 69.9 73.4
NAS-BERT on SQuAD v2.0 73.2 76.3
NAS-BERT dagger setting on SQuAD v2.0 73.9 77.1
The dagger setting uses a larger training budget for fair comparison with MiniLM’s larger pre-training run. The important point is not only that NAS-BERT beats several baselines; it also transfers from classification-style GLUE evaluation to span extraction QA. That supports the paper’s task-agnostic claim. The architecture family is not searched for one GLUE task and then overfit to that task. What The Selected Architectures Look Like Table 10 is useful because it shows the selected architectures are not just shallow BERTs. The notation is:
E: embedding size; M: MHA; F: FFN; S3, S5, S7: SepConv with kernel size 3, 5, or 7; the subscript is the hidden size.
Several observations stand out:
Large models such as 60M and 55M still contain many MHA and FFN operations. Middle-size models start mixing in more SepConv while keeping some MHA/FFN. Very small models use mostly SepConv and a few MHA operations. Embedding size also shrinks: the 5M model uses E64, while larger models use E512, E384, E256, or E128.
This is the core architectural result. NAS-BERT is not only choosing “how many BERT layers”. It is changing the composition of the encoder under size constraints. My Reading NotesThe paper is strongest when read as an amortized deployment method. If I only need one 60M BERT student, a strong distillation method may be simpler.
