If I need many models under different latency and memory budgets, a trained supernet becomes more attractive. The most important engineering ideas are:
Block-wise distillation turns a huge pre-training search into smaller block searches. Progressive shrinking improves training allocation and search accuracy. Size/latency bins preserve diversity so the supernet does not collapse into one budget range. Lookup-table selection makes final architecture selection cheap enough. Mixed operations let tiny models move away from pure Transformer structure.
The limitations are also clear:
The supernet still costs 3 days on 32 P40 GPUs in the paper. Latency lookup is hardware-specific and approximate. The results are for BERT-base-era encoder compression, not decoder-only LLMs. The “task-agnostic” claim has a practical caveat: optional fine-tuning-stage distillation still uses downstream-task teachers, although the architecture search itself is task-agnostic. The search space is manually designed. NAS decides within that space; it does not invent arbitrary efficient Transformer blocks.
Overall, I would place NAS-BERT between AdaBERT and Once-for-All. Compared with AdaBERT, it moves compression earlier and avoids per-task search. Compared with Once-for-All, it brings the elastic-supernet idea into BERT compression and adds block-wise teacher supervision to make the pre-training search feasible.

entry.title: Learning Transferable Architectures for Scalable Image Recognition
entry.content:
Paper NASNet is the paper that turns the expensive NAS-RL idea into a more transferable design pattern. Instead of searching a whole ImageNet-scale network directly, it searches for small convolutional cells on CIFAR-10, then stacks those cells to build larger ImageNet models. The important contribution is the search space. Once the cell is found, the number of cell repeats and filter counts can be scaled without changing the cell topology. MotivationThe original NAS-RL paper could discover good architectures, but searching directly over a large full network is expensive. NASNet asks a more reusable question:
Can we search for a small building block on CIFAR-10 and transfer that block to ImageNet?
The answer depends on constraining the search space. If the controller searches arbitrary whole networks, transfer is fragile. If it searches repeated motifs, the learned component can be reused at different depths, resolutions, and compute budgets. ContributionThe paper contributes:
The NASNet search space: architectures are built from repeated Normal Cells and Reduction Cells. A transfer recipe: search the cell on CIFAR-10, then stack it for ImageNet. ScheduledDropPath, where the probability of dropping a path increases during training. Strong results on CIFAR-10, ImageNet classification, and COCO detection with NASNet features.
The headline numbers:
Task Result
CIFAR-10 2.40% error
ImageNet 82.7% top-1 / 96.2% top-5
ImageNet mobile-scale setting 74.0% top-1
COCO detection 43.1% mAP test-dev
MethodologyNormal and reduction cellsNASNet fixes the macro layout and searches the repeated cell structure. There are two cell types:
Normal Cell: keeps the feature map resolution. Reduction Cell: reduces spatial resolution by using stride-2 operations.
For CIFAR-10, cells are stacked between a few reduction points. For ImageNet, the image is larger, so the network uses more reduction stages. The topology of each cell is learned; the number of repeats and initial filters are scaling knobs. Controller blockEach cell is built from blocks. In the paper’s main NASNet-A search, . For each block, the controller predicts five decisions:
Select the first hidden state. Select the second hidden state. Select an operation for the first hidden state. Select an operation for the second hidden state. Select how to combine the two outputs.
The operation set includes identity, pooling, standard convolution, factorized convolution, dilated convolution, and depthwise-separable convolution. At the end of the cell, unused hidden states are concatenated to form the output. NASNet-A cell The found NASNet-A cells contain many separable convolutions and learned skip-style connections. There are no manually inserted residual links between cells; the searched cell already learns its own internal connectivity. ScheduledDropPathThe authors found ordinary DropPath was not enough. ScheduledDropPath drops paths in a cell with a probability that increases linearly over training. This is a small but practical detail: without strong regularization, these searched cells can overfit. ResultsCIFAR-10
Model Params Error
NAS v3 + more filters 37.4M 3.65%
NASNet-A (6 @ 768) 3.3M 3.41%
NASNet-A (6 @ 768) + cutout 3.3M 2.65%
NASNet-A (7 @ 2304) + cutout 27.6M 2.40%
NASNet-C (4 @ 640) 3.1M 3.59%
The large NASNet-A with cutout reaches 2.40% error averaged across 5 runs, and the best single run reported in the paper is 2.19%. ImageNet transferThe key claim is transfer: the cells are searched on CIFAR-10, then all ImageNet models are trained from scratch with those cells.
Model Params Mult-Adds Top-1
Inception ResNet V2 55.8M 13.2B 80.1
NASNet-A (7 @ 1920) 22.6M 4.93B 80.8
SENet 145.8M 42.3B 82.7
NASNet-A (6 @ 4032) 88.9M 23.8B 82.7
NASNet-A reaches 82.7% top-1 and 96.2% top-5 on ImageNet with fewer mult-adds than SENet in the comparison table. Smaller compute settingFor the <1.5B mult-add regime, the paper reports:
Model Params Mult-Adds Top-1
MobileNet-224 4.2M 569M 70.6
ShuffleNet (2x) ~5M 524M 70.9
NASNet-A (4 @ 1056) 5.3M 564M 74.0
This is one reason NASNet mattered: the same cell family could scale down and still beat mobile-oriented baselines from that period. Detection transferThe paper also plugs NASNet-A ImageNet features into Faster R-CNN on COCO. The best reported test-dev mAP is 43.1%, which supports the claim that the learned features transfer beyond classification. TakeawayNASNet’s main lesson is that the search space can matter more than the controller. By forcing architectures to be made of reusable cells, the paper makes search results transferable across scale. There are still limitations. The search is expensive, and the method assumes a hand-designed macro skeleton with normal/reduction cell placement. But the cell-based formulation became the template for many later NAS papers because it turns an architecture into something you can scale, compare, and reuse.

entry.title: NATS-Bench: Benchmarking NAS Topology and Size
entry.content:
Paper: NATS-Bench: Benchmarking NAS Algorithms for Architecture Topology and Size Code and data: https://xuanyidong.com/assets/projects/NATS-Bench NATS-Bench is a NAS benchmark paper, not a new search algorithm. Its main contribution is to make two usually mixed questions separable:
Is a NAS method good at searching cell topology? Is it good at searching architecture size, especially channel allocation?
This distinction matters because architecture quality is not only a graph problem. Width, channel schedule, FLOPs, and training recipe can move accuracy as much as the cell topology. If two NAS papers use different search spaces and retraining setups, it is hard to tell whether the search algorithm improved or whether the evaluation protocol changed. Search SpacesNATS-Bench defines two spaces, both under the same macro skeleton.
The topology space searches the operation assigned to each edge in a 4-node cell. The operation set has 5 choices:
zeroize skip connection 1x1 convolution 3x3 convolution 3x3 average pooling
This gives candidate cells. Each architecture in stacks the searched cell in the fixed macro skeleton. The size space fixes the cell topology and searches channel numbers. Each layer chooses one value from:
With 5 channel decisions, this gives candidates. This is the part I find most useful: it makes width and capacity allocation a first-class NAS benchmark instead of treating them as post-search tuning. Compared With NAS-Bench-101The paper positions NATS-Bench as broader than NAS-Bench-101 in three ways: more datasets, more diagnostic information, and an additional size search space.
NAS-Bench-101 has many more unique architectures, but only one dataset and a topology-style space. NATS-Bench is smaller in topology count but evaluates both and on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet16-120. It also provides fine-grained information such as accuracy/loss curves, parameter counts, and FLOPs. That makes the benchmark useful for more than ranking final methods. It can also answer diagnostic questions:
Does validation ranking track test ranking? Does a good architecture on CIFAR-10 transfer to CIFAR-100 or ImageNet16-120? Does a method behave differently on topology search and size search? Does an algorithm beat simple baselines under the same query budget?
What Is StoredFor each candidate, NATS-Bench stores training logs and evaluation metrics instead of only final test accuracy. The paper lists training accuracy, test accuracy, training loss, test loss, parameters, FLOPs, latency-like cost information, and trained parameters for each architecture/run. The practical effect is that a NAS algorithm can query a benchmark table instead of retraining each sampled architecture. That makes repeated algorithm comparison feasible, especially for methods where the search itself must be run many times to estimate variance. The authors evaluate architectures under a unified split and training setup on:
CIFAR-10 CIFAR-100 ImageNet16-120
This is still small-image classification, but using three datasets is important. A benchmark that only rewards a CIFAR-10-specific architecture can quietly encourage overfitting to that one table. Dataset Ranking BehaviorThe first diagnostic result checks how architecture rankings transfer across datasets.
The left plot is the topology search space. Rankings are sorted by CIFAR-10, then plotted against CIFAR-100 and ImageNet16-120. The trend is fairly diagonal, which means topology rankings are somewhat consistent across datasets. The right plot is the size search space. The scatter is much wider. That is the strongest motivation for having at all: the best channel allocation is more dataset-dependent than the best topology under this benchmark. Performance LandscapeThe full performance landscape is also useful. It shows training/test accuracy against parameters and FLOPs for every candidate.
Two points stand out:
Architectures with similar parameter counts or FLOPs can have very different accuracy. Human-designed reference patterns such as ResNet or pyramid channel schedules are competitive, but not always Pareto optimal.
For topology search, the vertical bands reflect discrete operation choices and fixed macro sizes. For size search, the bands and curved fronts make channel allocation visible. This is exactly the sort of structure a NAS optimizer can exploit or overfit. Validation And Test CorrelationThe benchmark depends on validation accuracy being a reasonable search signal. If validation and test rankings were unrelated, a NAS method that queries validation performance would not be meaningful.
The paper reports that validation rankings and test rankings are similar in both spaces. That supports the usual NAS workflow: search on validation, then report test performance of the selected architecture. But this should not be read as “validation is perfect.” The correlation is strong enough for benchmark use, while still leaving room for methods to overfit validation quirks. Cross-Dataset TransferThe Kendall rank correlation heatmaps show a more nuanced picture.
For , the all-candidate rank correlations are high. But when the paper only keeps high-accuracy candidates, correlations drop. For , the correlations are weaker, especially when focusing on top candidates. This is a good warning for NAS papers. A method that selects the best architecture for one dataset may not transfer cleanly to another. The top of the ranking is exactly where NAS methods operate, and that region is noisier than the whole-space average suggests. Search Curves: Multi-Trial MethodsThe paper benchmarks 13 NAS algorithms. It separates methods that train/evaluate many candidates from weight-sharing methods.
For multi-trial methods, the comparison includes REA, REINFORCE, RANDOM, and BOHB. The curves are best read as best-found architecture quality over estimated wall-clock search time. REA and BOHB are strong in many settings, but the exact ordering depends on dataset and search space. The important benchmark lesson is not “always use one method.” It is that the same algorithms can be compared under the same architecture table, training recipe, and repeated-run protocol. Search Curves: Weight SharingWeight-sharing methods are evaluated separately because they use a supernet and do not pay full training cost for every sampled architecture.
The topology-space curves show instability for several weight-sharing methods. DARTS variants and GDAS can swing heavily before converging or failing. In the size-search curves, channel-wise interpolation is much more stable than masking-based strategies in the paper’s implementation. This matches a common NAS observation: weight sharing buys search speed, but it can distort the ranking signal. As the search space grows, a shared set of weights may not represent each candidate accurately enough. Main Result TableThe main benchmark table gives the numeric summary across spaces, method families, and datasets.
Some rows I would keep in mind:
Space Method CIFAR-10 test CIFAR-100 test ImageNet16-120 test
REA 94.02 72.23 45.77
RANDOM 93.86 71.55 45.28
GDAS 93.23 68.17 39.40
ENAS 93.76 70.67 41.44
optimal by validation 94.37 73.51 46.20
channel-wise interpolation 93.40 70.72 47.17
largest candidate 93.40 70.72 47.17
The gap between searched methods and the optimal row is the room a better search method could still use. The gap between weight-sharing and multi-trial methods is also a reminder that fast search is not automatically accurate search. Training Budget SensitivityThe appendix includes an interesting sanity check: lower-fidelity training can change the search dynamics.
For REA on CIFAR-10, using fewer training epochs can converge faster at the beginning but may not dominate after enough search time. This is a standard multi-fidelity tradeoff. Short training is cheap and informative early, but it can bias the ranking of final architectures. For benchmark users, this means that “query cost” should be part of the experimental claim. A method that wins under cheap proxy training may not win when the benchmark asks for higher-fidelity estimates. How I Would Use ItNATS-Bench is good for algorithm diagnosis:
Compare search methods under a controlled query budget. Plot best-so-far curves instead of reporting only the final architecture. Separate topology search from channel-size search. Check variance across repeated runs. Test whether a method’s ranking behavior transfers across datasets.
It is less suitable as a final deployment benchmark:
The tasks are small image-classification datasets. The architectures are CNN-style cell networks, not modern ViTs or LLMs. Hardware latency is not the main objective, even though FLOPs and cost metadata are available. Since all architecture results are tabulated, benchmark overfitting is a real risk.
The paper explicitly discusses this risk. If a new NAS method uses operation-specific rules designed after inspecting the best NATS-Bench architecture, it can look strong on the table without generalizing. A fair use of NATS-Bench should keep the algorithm generic and report multiple runs. TakeawayNATS-Bench is valuable because it expands NAS benchmarking beyond topology search. The topology space is useful for comparing cell-search algorithms, while the size space exposes how important channel allocation can be. The strongest lesson for me is that NAS benchmarks should be diagnostic, not just leaderboards. Search curves, cross-dataset ranking, validation/test correlation, FLOPs/parameter landscapes, and repeated-run variance tell more about an algorithm than one final accuracy number.

entry.title: OmniQuant: Omnidirectionally Calibrated LLM Quantization
entry.content:
Shao W, Chen M, Zhang Z, Xu P, Zhao L, Li Z, Zhang K, Gao P, Qiao Y, Luo P. OmniQuant: Omnidirectionally Calibrated Quantization for Large Language Models. ICLR 2024.
Paper: arXiv PDF Code: OpenGVLab/OmniQuant Topic: post-training quantization, learnable clipping, equivalent transformation, low-bit LLM deployment
OmniQuant is a useful paper because it sits between lightweight PTQ and expensive QAT. It does not update the full-precision model weights like quantization-aware training. It also does not rely only on handcrafted calibration rules like plain MinMax, SmoothQuant-style fixed migration strength, or grid-searched scaling. The main idea is narrower and more practical: freeze the original LLM weights, add a small set of learnable quantization parameters, optimize those parameters block by block on calibration samples, then fold the learned parameters away so the exported model has no extra runtime modules. That design matters most in the hard cases. W4A16 is already reachable by strong weight-only methods such as GPTQ and AWQ. W8A8 is the target of SmoothQuant. OmniQuant tries to cover a wider set of formats, especially W2A16 and W4A4, where ordinary PTQ collapses. The method has two knobs:
Learnable Weight Clipping, or LWC, learns relative clipping strengths for weights. Learnable Equivalent Transformation, or LET, learns scale/shift transformations that move activation quantization difficulty into weights while preserving the floating-point function before quantization.
The paper’s name is a little grand, but the technical point is concrete. “Omni” means the same calibration framework is used across weight-only, weight-activation, and attention/KV-related quantization positions. One-Picture Summary Figure cropped from the paper PDF. OmniQuant tries to keep PTQ-level calibration cost while getting much closer to QAT-quality low-bit results. Figure 1 is the best starting point. The left panel compares three points for LLaMA-7B W4A4:
Method Calibration data Time Average accuracy
SmoothQuant 128 samples 10 min 38.41%
LLM-QAT 100k samples 90 h 46.43%
OmniQuant 128 samples 1.6 h 52.65%
The two right panels show why the paper focuses on low bit widths. In the weight-only curve, GPTQ is reasonable at W4A16 and W3A16, then breaks badly at W2A16. In the weight-activation curve, SmoothQuant is fine around W8A8/W6A6 but degrades sharply at W4A4. OmniQuant’s claim is not that every quantization setting becomes lossless. The claim is that optimizing a small number of calibration parameters gives much better low-bit behavior than fixed rules, while staying far cheaper than QAT. Quantization TargetThe notation WbAa means: Wb: b-bit weightsAa: a-bit activations
So:
Format Meaning Typical deployment reading
W4A16 4-bit weights, FP16/BF16 activations weight-only compression
W3A16 3-bit weights, FP16/BF16 activations more aggressive weight-only compression
W2A16 2-bit weights, FP16/BF16 activations extreme weight-only compression
W8A8 8-bit weights and activations dense INT8 inference target
W6A6 6-bit weights and activations low-bit activation quantization
W4A4 4-bit weights and activations very hard low-bit compute target
For weight-only quantization, reducing the weight bit width attacks model memory and weight bandwidth. The approximate raw weight storage ratio against FP16 is:
ignoring scale, zero-point, group metadata, and packing overhead. This is why W4A16 is attractive: a nominal 4x weight-size reduction is possible before metadata. W2A16 is even more attractive on paper, but the accuracy loss is usually severe. For weight-activation quantization, the goal is broader. If both weights and activations are low-bit, the matrix multiplication itself can move toward low-bit kernels. This is also where outliers are most damaging. LLM activations often have large channel-wise outliers, and naive per-token activation quantization must choose a scale large enough to cover them, wasting resolution on ordinary values. A generic affine uniform quantizer can be written as:
The hard part is not writing this formula. The hard part is choosing the scale, zero point, clipping range, and equivalent transformations so that the quantized block still behaves like the original block on real activations. PTQ, QAT, And Where OmniQuant Fits Figure cropped from the paper PDF. The paper positions OmniQuant as learning a small set of quantization parameters with 128 calibration samples on a single A100-40G. The practical tension is:
Approach What is optimized Cost Low-bit behavior
Plain PTQ fixed quantization parameters low often fails at W2A16/W4A4
Heuristic PTQ scales/clips searched by proxies low to medium better, but limited by proxy quality
QAT all model weights under quantization simulation very high strong but expensive
OmniQuant only quantization parameters medium PTQ-like strong in low-bit settings
OmniQuant’s calibration setup in the paper is intentionally small: 128 randomly selected 2048-token segments from WikiText2, batch size 1, AdamW, and block-wise optimization. The original FP weights are frozen. The learned parameters are:
The central implementation question is whether these parameters stay in the runtime graph. OmniQuant’s answer is no: clipping affects the final quantized weights, and equivalent transformations are folded into adjacent normalization or linear layers. If these parameters remained as extra floating-point operations during serving, the method would be much less attractive. Block-Wise Reconstruction ObjectiveOmniQuant calibrates one transformer block at a time. For a block mapping , full-precision weights , and calibration activations , the paper writes the optimization objective as:
I read this as a local reconstruction loss. The full-precision block output is the teacher, and the quantized block output is the student:
The important engineering choice is the block boundary. Optimizing an entire 7B-70B model with differentiable quantization would be too large. Optimizing only a layer or a small operator can miss error propagation across residual paths, attention, and MLP sublayers. A transformer block is a reasonable middle point: large enough to see the effect of several quantized operators, small enough to calibrate sequentially. The gradient is applied to quantization parameters, not to the original pretrained weights:
As usual for differentiable quantization, the rounding operation itself needs a straight-through-style gradient in practice. The paper’s contribution is not a new rounding estimator; it is the choice of learnable parameters and where they are inserted. Learnable Weight ClippingWeight quantization fails when a few extreme values force the quantization range to become too wide. MinMax quantization uses the observed min and max as the clipping range. OmniQuant keeps the MinMax structure but learns relative clipping strengths for the upper and lower bounds. The LWC quantizer is:
Here:
Symbol Meaning
target bit width
original full-precision weights
quantized integer weights
normalization factor / scale
zero point
learnable upper clipping strength
learnable lower clipping strength
The constraints are:
The paper instantiates them through a sigmoid:
So the trainable variables can be unconstrained, while the actual clipping strengths stay in . If and , LWC reduces to the ordinary MinMax range. If either value becomes smaller, the effective range shrinks and extreme weights are clipped. The dequantized weight can be read as:
This design is more stable than directly learning absolute clipping thresholds, because the threshold is parameterized relative to the current weight range. That matters when LET changes the equivalent weight distribution during calibration. Learnable Equivalent TransformationLWC helps weights. LET targets activations. The core observation is the same one used by SmoothQuant: activation outliers can be made smaller by an equivalent transformation that moves scale into weights. OmniQuant makes the transformation learnable and extends it beyond ordinary linear layers. For a linear layer:
OmniQuant inserts channel-wise shifting and scaling:
where:
The operators and are elementwise division and multiplication with channel-wise broadcast. The equality is exact in floating point:
After transformation, quantization is applied to the transformed activation and weight:
The intuition is simple:
divide hard activation channels by so they become easier to quantize; multiply the corresponding weight channels by so the floating-point function is unchanged; let LWC handle the harder transformed weight distribution; learn and through block reconstruction, instead of choosing them only by a fixed heuristic.
SmoothQuant uses a scale initialized from activation and weight maxima. A common form is:
where is a channel index and controls how much difficulty moves from activations to weights. OmniQuant uses SmoothQuant-style scaling as an initialization, but then optimizes the equivalent parameters with the block-wise loss. LET Inside AttentionThe attention score matrix is:
OmniQuant applies an equivalent transformation to the affinity multiplication:
Define:
The quantized attention-affinity computation becomes:
The paper notes that the scale factors in and can be absorbed into the query and key projection weights. The explicit transformation for is omitted because the inverse transformation associated with the output projection already changes the value distribution. This attention LET is one of the reasons the method is broader than a direct SmoothQuant clone. It touches the Q/K path and therefore relates to the difficulty of quantizing attention computation and KV-cache-related tensors. Transformer Block Placement Figure cropped from the paper PDF. Red modules are learnable during calibration, blue snowflake markers are fixed, and pink modules can be eliminated after quantization. The placement diagram is dense, but it is the most useful implementation figure in the paper. The learnable pieces appear around:
weight clipping before weight quantization; normalization-to-projection transformations; Q/K transformations before attention affinity; value/output projection transformations; MLP transformations around fc1.
The paper explicitly avoids LET on the second FFN linear layer. Its explanation is that the activation after the nonlinear layer is sparse, which can make LET gradients unstable there. That is a good reminder that equivalent transformations are not free to place everywhere. They need numerically stable statistics and a neighboring operation where the transform can be folded. Calibration Algorithm Algorithm cropped from the paper PDF. OmniQuant runs a full-precision stream and a quantized stream through blocks, optimizing LWC/LET parameters for each block before moving on. The algorithm keeps two activation streams: X_fp: activations produced by the full-precision modelX_q : activations produced by the progressively quantized model
For each transformer block :
Run the full-precision block to update . Initialize LWC parameters and LET parameters . For several epochs, transform the block, quantize it, run it on , and minimize . Fold the learned LET parameters and quantize the block with LWC. Run the final quantized block to update for the next block.
A simplified pseudocode view: X_fp = X_calibX_q = X_calibfor block in model.blocks: X_fp = block.fp_forward(X_fp) theta_lwc = init_lwc() theta_let = init_let() for epoch in range(num_epochs): block_equiv = apply_let(block, theta_let) block_quant = quantize_with_lwc(block_equiv, theta_lwc) X_q_trial = block_quant(X_q) loss = mse(X_q_trial, X_fp) loss.backward() optimizer.step() block = fold_let_and_quantize(block, theta_let, theta_lwc) X_q = block(X_q)
This sequential design is important because errors accumulate. If every block were calibrated only against the original full-precision input distribution, later blocks would see a cleaner distribution than they will see at inference time. By updating after each quantized block, the next block calibrates on the actual quantized prefix distribution. Main Weight-Only Results Table cropped from the paper PDF. WikiText2 perplexity for LLaMA-1 and LLaMA-2 weight-only quantization. Table 1 is the most important weight-only result. The easy setting is W4A16, where GPTQ/AWQ/RTN are already close to FP16. The interesting setting is W2A16. Some representative rows:
Setting Model GPTQ PPL AWQ PPL OmniQuant PPL
W2A16 LLaMA-1-13B 5.5e3 - 13.21
W2A16 LLaMA-1-30B 499.75 - 8.71
W2A16 LLaMA-2-70B 77.95 - 7.81
W2A16g128 LLaMA-1-13B 15.60 2.8e5 7.93
W3A16 LLaMA-1-13B 6.76 7.45 5.68
W4A16g128 LLaMA-2-70B 3.42 - 3.40
The pattern is:
At W4A16, the gap is small because the format is not extremely hard. At W3A16, OmniQuant is consistently strong but the baseline methods remain usable. At W2A16, the learned clipping becomes crucial; GPTQ and AWQ can collapse depending on model and grouping, while OmniQuant keeps perplexity in a usable range.
I would not read this table as “OmniQuant replaces GPTQ everywhere.” For ordinary W4A16 deployment with mature kernels, GPTQ/AWQ may still be simpler. The reason to care about OmniQuant is the lower-bit frontier and the fact that the same calibration machinery also supports weight-activation quantization. Weight-Activation Results Table cropped from the paper PDF. Six zero-shot task accuracy for LLaMA W6A6 and W4A4 quantization. W4A4 is the table I care about most. Once activations are also 4-bit, activation outliers become unavoidable. SmoothQuant helps at W8A8, but W4A4 is much harsher. For average zero-shot accuracy:
Model SmoothQuant W4A4 OS+ W4A4 OmniQuant W4A4 FP16
LLaMA-1-7B 38.41 48.43 52.65 64.09
LLaMA-1-13B 49.36 49.86 54.37 66.33
LLaMA-1-30B 44.83 52.62 56.63 67.44
LLaMA-1-65B 47.71 52.52 59.22 71.04
The 7B row also includes LLM-QAT:
Method LLaMA-1-7B W4A4 average accuracy
SmoothQuant 38.41
LLM-QAT 41.27
LLM-QAT + SmoothQuant 46.43
OS+ 48.43
OmniQuant 52.65
This is the headline result: with 128 calibration samples and 1.6 hours for LLaMA-7B, OmniQuant beats the listed QAT baseline in that W4A4 comparison. The reason is not that tiny PTQ optimization is more expressive than full QAT in general. It is that optimizing the right local quantization parameters can be a better use of calibration budget than doing broad weight updates under a limited QAT setup. W6A6 is less dramatic. It is usually close to FP16 and SmoothQuant/OS+ are already reasonable. Again, OmniQuant is most interesting where handcrafted parameters stop being enough. Instruction-Tuned Models Figure cropped from the paper PDF. Vicuna-Bench pairwise comparison for LLaMA-2-chat W3A16g128. The instruction-tuned experiment is useful because perplexity is not the whole story. On Vicuna-Bench, the authors compare RTN, AWQ, and OmniQuant with GPT-4 judging over both answer orders. For LLaMA-2-7B-chat:
AWQ vs RTN: 69.4% win rate for AWQ. OmniQuant vs RTN: 80.3% win rate for OmniQuant. OmniQuant vs AWQ: 50.0% win rate.
For LLaMA-2-13B-chat:
AWQ vs RTN: 46.6% win rate for AWQ. OmniQuant vs RTN: 54.4% win rate for OmniQuant. OmniQuant vs AWQ: 56.2% win rate for OmniQuant.
The result is not an overwhelming sweep, but it supports the claim that the calibration is not only overfitting WikiText2 perplexity. For instruction-tuned models, OmniQuant remains competitive or better in a pairwise chat evaluation. Deployment Result Table cropped from the paper PDF. Weight-only quantized LLaMA models deployed through MLC-LLM on an NVIDIA A100-80G. The deployment table matters because a quantization method can look good in perplexity and still be awkward to serve. OmniQuant’s learned parameters are designed to be folded, so weight-only models can be exported into existing low-bit deployment stacks. The paper reports memory and generation speed through MLC-LLM. For LLaMA-7B:
Setting Weight memory Running memory token/s
FP 12.6G 14.4G 69.2
W4A16g128 3.8G 5.7G 134.2
W3A16g128 3.2G 5.1G 83.4
W2A16g128 2.2G 4.1G 83.9
For LLaMA-65B, the FP model is OOM under the measured setup, while quantized variants run:
Setting Weight memory Running memory token/s
W4A16g128 33.0G 41.0G 24.3
W3A16g128 27.0G 35.1G 15.2
W2A16g128 18.0G 25.6G 24.8
The speed numbers are not monotonic with bit width because kernel support matters. INT3/INT2 support was weaker in the reported MLC-LLM stack. This is a deployment lesson: lower bits reduce memory, but latency depends on packing, dequantization, kernel quality, and hardware support. The paper only demonstrates deployment for weight-only quantization. It explicitly notes that W4A4 and W6A6 lacked out-of-the-box hardware support in that study. So OmniQuant’s W4A4 accuracy result should be separated from actual production W4A4 serving speed. Why LWC And LET Need Each Other Table cropped from the appendix. LET and LWC work best when optimized together under the same differentiable block-wise framework. Table A2 is one of the most useful ablations:
LLaMA-7B W4A4 method Average PPL Average accuracy
SmoothQuant 28.78 38.41
LET 16.97 48.83
LET + grid-searched weight clipping 15.82 49.59
SmoothQuant + LWC 15.80 50.15
LET + LWC 12.87 52.65
The point is not simply “clipping helps” and “equivalent transformation helps.” LET changes the activation and equivalent weight distributions. LWC then has to clip the transformed weights, not the original weights. If clipping is found by a separate grid search or if the equivalent transform is fixed, the two knobs are not co-adapted. This is the most convincing argument for OmniQuant’s differentiable setup. It is not learning many parameters, but it is learning coupled parameters. Component Ablation Table cropped from the appendix. Removing LET is catastrophic for W4A4; removing LWC is also harmful. The component ablation is blunt:
Model / setting LWC+LET without LWC without LET without both
LLaMA-13B W4A4 10.87 20.75 5.4e3 1.8e3
LLaMA-13B W3A16 5.65 7.65 5.68 10.68
OPT-13B W4A4 11.65 15.23 7.8e3 7.8e5
OPT-13B W3A16 10.87 12.98 11.29 4.6e3
For W4A4, removing LET causes a collapse because activation quantization remains unsolved. For W3A16 weight-only quantization, LET is less important for LLaMA, which is why the paper often uses only LWC for LLaMA weight-only settings to save time. OPT is more sensitive to LET even in weight-only W3A16. This is a good practical rule:
If activations are quantized, LET is not optional. If only weights are quantized, LWC is the core component, and LET may or may not pay for itself depending on the model family.
LET Design Choices Tables cropped from the appendix. Channel-wise shifting, attention transformation, and LET placement each affect W4A4 quality. Table A4 compares the two additions beyond a basic scale-only linear transformation:
Method LLaMA-13B W4A4 PPL OPT-13B W4A4 PPL
LWC + LET 10.87 11.65
without shifting 11.47 13.64
without attention LET 11.34 11.79
Channel-wise shifting helps, especially on OPT-13B W4A4. Attention LET helps too, though less dramatically in this table. That matches the paper’s explanation that the largest outliers often appear after normalization layers, so linear-layer LET carries most of the gain. Table A5 removes LET at different positions in LLaMA-7B W4A4:
Removed LET position Average PPL Average accuracy
none 12.87 52.65
[ln1, (q_proj, k_proj, v_proj)] 19.87 46.79
[v_proj, out_proj] 13.03 51.68
[Q,K] 13.34 51.47
[ln2, fc1] 14.47 51.04
The most sensitive placement is the transform after the first LayerNorm and before Q/K/V projections. This is consistent with the activation-outlier story: if a normalization output has severe channel outliers, every downstream projection inherits the quantization problem. Calibration Time Table cropped from the appendix. Most configurations improve quickly; W2A16 needs more epochs. The training-time ablation uses LLaMA-7B and reports WikiText2 perplexity:
Epochs W4A16 W3A16 W2A16 W6A6 W4A4
0 6.29 24.04 1.1e5 6.16 33.93
10 5.87 6.51 27.49 5.96 12.04
20 5.85 6.49 17.46 5.95 11.26
40 5.86 6.47 15.47 5.95 11.23
80 - - 14.77 - -
The fast convergence is important. W4A4 drops from 33.93 to 12.04 in 10 epochs, then only improves modestly. W2A16 is harder and keeps benefiting from longer calibration. This is exactly what I would expect: 2-bit weight quantization leaves so little representational room that the clipping parameters need more optimization. The main paper uses 20 epochs for most settings and a longer schedule for W2A16. The deployment implication is that calibration cost is not zero, but it is still in the PTQ family rather than QAT. What LWC Learns Figure cropped from the appendix. Learned clipping strengths differ by bit width and grouping. The learned clipping-scale visualization is a useful sanity check. LWC is not always clipping aggressively. In grouped quantization, many groups have clipping strengths close to 1, meaning little clipping. At lower bit widths, the distribution shifts toward more clipping because the quantizer has fewer representable values. This fits the role of LWC. The method is not trying to erase all outliers. It is deciding where the quantization range should stop so that the block output is preserved on calibration data. The appendix also reports that LWC reduces both weight distance and final activation distance. That second part matters more than the first. A small weight reconstruction error is not enough if it produces a large downstream activation error. OmniQuant’s block-wise loss directly sees that downstream effect. What LET Changes Figure cropped from the appendix. LET makes activation channels more homogeneous than the original distribution and the SmoothQuant-transformed distribution. Figure A2 shows the activation-outlier story visually. Original activations have a few channels with much larger magnitude. SmoothQuant reduces the largest outliers, but the transformed distribution still has visible channel imbalance. LET reduces the disparity further because it is optimized under the block reconstruction objective rather than chosen by a fixed migration rule. This is the activation-side reason W4A4 improves. If the activation quantizer must cover a few huge channels, ordinary channels lose resolution. LET reshapes the distribution before quantization, and LWC absorbs the corresponding weight-side difficulty. Block-Wise Error Figure cropped from the appendix. Gradient-based calibration produces lower block-wise error than grid-search-based methods in the reported settings. Figure A3 compares block-wise quantization error against AWQ-style or OS+-style grid-search baselines. The curves make the main optimization argument concrete: a handcrafted proxy can find a useful scale, but directly optimizing block reconstruction can reduce the error more consistently across blocks. This does not mean gradient-based PTQ is automatically better for every model. It means the optimization target is better aligned with what we care about: preserving the block’s actual output on representative activations. Bit-Level Scaling Law Figure cropped from the appendix. With stronger PTQ, 3-bit quantization can approach the tradeoff usually associated with 4-bit quantization. The bit-level scaling plot is a more speculative but interesting result. Earlier empirical work often argues that 4-bit quantization is a good universal balance between total model bits and accuracy. OmniQuant’s appendix suggests that, with better calibration, 3-bit models can approach a similar tradeoff for perplexity. I would read this cautiously. It depends on the quantizer, metadata, kernels, and model family. A 3-bit checkpoint with poor kernel support may be slower than a 4-bit checkpoint. Still, the result is important because it says the “4-bit is the natural floor” intuition is partly a method limitation, not only a model property. LWC Versus PACT And LSQ Table cropped from the appendix. LWC is compared against MinMax, PACT, and LSQ inside the same OmniQuant-style pipeline. The paper compares LWC with older learnable clipping methods:
Method W3A16 PPL W4A4 PPL
MinMax 25.73 14.49
PACT 6.95 18.25
LSQ 6.63 15.03
LWC 6.47 11.26
PACT and LSQ were originally designed in a QAT context. They can help weight-only quantization, but W4A4 is different because LET changes the equivalent weight distribution during calibration. LWC’s relative clipping parameterization adapts better to that changing distribution.
Figure cropped from the appendix. LWC tracks changing weight ranges during training more stably than absolute-threshold clipping methods. Figure A5 reinforces the same point. If the effective weight range changes during LET optimization, an absolute clipping threshold can become stale. Relative clipping strengths are a better parameterization when the scale of the transformed weights is moving. Relation To Other LLM Quantization Methods Table cropped from the appendix. OmniQuant differs from SmoothQuant/AWQ/OS+ by learning scale-and-shift transformations and applying them to both linear layers and attention.
Method Main target Calibration signal Runtime shape
LLM.int8() INT8 matmul with outlier rescue activation outlier detection INT8 path plus FP16 outlier path
SmoothQuant W8A8 activation/weight maxima, fixed smoothing strength dense INT8-friendly path
GPTQ W3A16/W4A16 second-order layer reconstruction weight-only low-bit kernels
AWQ W4A16 activation-aware salient weight protection weight-only low-bit kernels
OmniQuant W2A16/W3A16/W4A16/W6A6/W4A4 gradient-optimized block reconstruction over LWC/LET parameters folded quantized model
The closest conceptual relatives are SmoothQuant and AWQ:
Like SmoothQuant, OmniQuant uses equivalent transformations to migrate activation difficulty into weights. Like AWQ, OmniQuant cares about activation-aware weight quantization and avoids updating the full original model. Unlike both, OmniQuant directly optimizes the calibration parameters with gradients under a block-wise reconstruction loss.
Compared with GPTQ, OmniQuant is less about Hessian-based rounding compensation and more about making the quantization range and transformed distributions easier before quantization. They attack different parts of the PTQ problem. Practical Reproduction NotesIf I were reproducing OmniQuant, I would not start with all settings at once. I would stage it like this:
Implement LWC only for one linear layer and verify the LWC formula against MinMax when . Calibrate one transformer block in W4A16 or W3A16 and confirm the block reconstruction loss decreases. Add LET for a linear layer and verify exact floating-point equivalence before quantization:
Check that folding removes the runtime transformation. The exported graph should not contain extra LET modules. Move from W4A16 to W3A16, then W2A16. Do not debug W2A16 first. Add activation quantization and test W6A6 before W4A4. Track both layer/block reconstruction and end metrics. A lower local loss is useful only if perplexity and task accuracy follow.
The calibration data also deserves attention. The paper uses 128 2048-token WikiText2 segments. That is enough for the reported setting, but deployment prompts may have different activation statistics. For a production model, I would calibrate on representative prompts and hold out a similar set to detect overfitting of the learned quantization parameters. TakeawayOmniQuant is best read as differentiable PTQ for LLMs. It keeps the original weights frozen, learns only a small set of quantization parameters, and calibrates them block by block. LWC learns how much weight range to clip. LET learns how to reshape activation distributions through equivalent transformations. Together, they make difficult formats such as W2A16 and W4A4 much more stable than fixed PTQ rules. The caveat is systems support. Weight-only OmniQuant can be deployed through existing low-bit stacks after folding. W4A4 accuracy is promising, but real W4A4 serving also needs mature kernels and hardware support. In that sense, the paper is both a quantization-method paper and a reminder that quantization quality and quantized inference are related but separate engineering problems.

entry.title: Once-for-All: Train Once, Specialize Everywhere
entry.content:
Cai H, Gan C, Wang T, Zhang Z, Han S. Once-for-All: Train One Network and Specialize it for Efficient Deployment. ICLR 2020.
Paper / Code Once-for-All (OFA) is a deployment paper disguised as a NAS paper. The problem is not only “can we find one efficient CNN?” The real problem is that deployment has many targets: different phones, CPUs, GPUs, FPGAs, battery modes, batch sizes, and latency budgets. Repeating neural architecture search and full training for every target is expensive and slow. OFA changes the cost model. It trains one elastic network once, then specializes subnetworks for each deployment scenario without retraining from scratch. All figures and tables below are cropped from the original paper PDF. Core IdeaThe first figure is the whole paper in one picture.
The left side is the model view: train a large elastic supernet and deploy different subnetworks for cloud AI, mobile AI, or tiny AI. The middle plot is the cost view: classic NAS has design cost that grows with the number of deployment scenarios, while OFA tries to make the expensive training step a one-time cost. The right plot shows the accuracy-latency menu produced by one trained OFA network. The important phrase is “direct deploy.” OFA does not train a separate model after every architecture is selected. A subnet inherits weights from the once-for-all network. This is why the method is interesting for product deployment: many operating points can be shipped from one shared training run. Why This Is Different From Ordinary NASClassic hardware-aware NAS usually does three things for every target:
Define a search space and latency target. Search an architecture under that target. Train the selected architecture.
That workflow is fine for a paper with one benchmark setting. It is awkward for deployment. A model team may need one variant for Pixel latency, another for Samsung latency, one for CPU batch size 1, one for GPU batch size 64, and another for an FPGA accelerator. If every target needs search plus training, the cost is linear in the number of targets. OFA decouples the expensive part:
Train one elastic once-for-all network. Train cheap accuracy predictors and use hardware-specific latency lookup tables. Run evolutionary search over subnet choices for each target. Deploy the inherited subnet weights.
This turns NAS from “find one model” into “train a reusable model family.” ImageNet FrontierThe paper’s headline ImageNet comparison is not a tiny-model result. OFA reaches 80.0% top-1 at 595M MACs, below the paper’s mobile setting threshold of 600M MACs.
This plot is useful because it compares against both hand-designed networks and AutoML-designed networks. OFA moves to the upper-left region: high ImageNet accuracy with low MACs. The result is not just “NAS found another point.” OFA can produce a family of points by selecting subnetworks from the same trained weights. Elastic Search SpaceOFA makes four dimensions elastic:
Dimension Choices used in the paper
Resolution 128 to 224, stride 4
Kernel size 3x3, 5x5, 7x7
Depth 2, 3, or 4 layers per unit
Width expansion ratio 3, 4, or 6
The training objective can be written as:
Here is the once-for-all weight set, ranges over architecture configurations, and selects the subnet corresponding to that configuration. The paper estimates roughly:
architecture choices, and each can be paired with 25 input resolutions. The point is not that the search space number is impressive by itself. The point is that all of these candidates share one set of trained weights, so storing and deploying many candidates does not require storing independently trained models. Progressive ShrinkingTraining such a large shared-weight space naively is unstable. Small subnetworks and large subnetworks interfere with each other. OFA’s answer is progressive shrinking: start from the largest network, then gradually introduce smaller choices.
The order is:
Train the full network. Support elastic resolution. Add elastic kernel size. Add elastic depth. Add elastic width.
Resolution is sampled throughout training. Kernel size, depth, and width are introduced progressively so smaller subnetworks inherit useful weights from already trained larger subnetworks. The paper also uses knowledge distillation after training the largest network: smaller subnetworks learn from both the real labels and soft labels from the largest network. Relation To PruningProgressive shrinking is easy to confuse with pruning. The similarity is that both start from a large model and shrink it. The difference is the training target.
Network pruning usually produces one smaller model. OFA tries to keep a large family of subnetworks valid at the same time. It also shrinks across four dimensions, not only width. That distinction matters. A pruned model is a single deployment point. OFA is closer to a trained architecture space: after training, a search procedure can choose a subnet for a new constraint without running full training again. Elastic Kernel And DepthThe kernel and depth mechanisms are simple but important.
For elastic kernel size, the center of a larger kernel is reused by smaller kernels. A 7x7 kernel contains a 5x5 center, and the 5x5 contains a 3x3 center. OFA adds transformation matrices so the smaller centered kernels do not have to share raw weights blindly with the larger kernel. For elastic depth, OFA keeps the first layers in a unit and skips the later layers. This is more structured than randomly dropping layers. It preserves a clear prefix-sharing pattern, which makes the inherited subnet easier to reason about. Elastic WidthWidth shrinking uses channel sorting.
The paper sorts channels by importance and keeps the most important channels when shrinking width. In the toy example, a 4-channel layer can shrink to 3 or 2 channels by preserving the highest-ranked channels. The practical benefit is that a smaller subnet starts from the most useful subset of the larger subnet instead of an arbitrary slice. This is one of the reasons progressive shrinking is more stable than random subnet sampling. The smaller networks are not fighting the largest model from scratch; they are initialized as structured subsets. Does Progressive Shrinking Help?The ablation says yes. OFA compares subnetworks trained with progressive shrinking against subnetworks from a once-for-all network trained without it.
Across the sampled configurations, progressive shrinking improves top-1 accuracy by about 2.5 to 3.7 points. One concrete row is especially useful: at , , , OFA with progressive shrinking reaches 74.8% top-1 with 226M MACs, while the version without progressive shrinking reaches 71.5%. This is the main training lesson. The elastic search space is only useful if inherited weights preserve ranking and accuracy. Progressive shrinking is what makes the inherited weights good enough to search over. Cost ComparisonTable 1 is the clearest evidence for the deployment story.
Some rows to keep in mind:
Model Top-1 MACs Mobile latency Total cost when N = 40
MobileNetV3-Large 75.2 219M 58 ms 7.2k GPU hours
OFA w/o PS 72.4 235M 59 ms 1.2k GPU hours
OFA w/ PS 76.0 230M 58 ms 1.2k GPU hours
OFA w/ PS #25 76.4 230M 58 ms 2.2k GPU hours
OFA w/ PS #75 76.9 230M 58 ms 4.2k GPU hours
OFA large w/ PS #75 80.0 595M - 4.2k GPU hours
The #25 and #75 rows fine-tune the selected subnet for 25 or 75 epochs after inheriting weights. The no-retraining OFA row is already strong: 76.0% at 230M MACs and 58 ms, which beats MobileNetV3-Large in the table while keeping similar mobile latency. The cost plot makes the scaling argument more obvious.
For 40 deployment scenarios, the paper reports OFA as 16x lower in CO2 emission than ProxylessNAS, 19x lower than FBNet, and 1300x lower than MnasNet. The exact accounting assumptions can be debated, but the direction is hard to miss: if deployment has many targets, training once and specializing later changes the economics. Resource-Constrained FrontiersOFA is not only cheaper. It also produces better trade-off curves under MAC and measured latency constraints.
The left plot compares MAC-constrained models. OFA reaches 79.1% top-1 at 389M MACs and 80.0% at 595M MACs. The right plot compares Pixel 1 latency. OFA reaches 80.1% at 143 ms and is reported as 2.6x faster than EfficientNet-B2 at a similar accuracy point. The green curve, “OFA - Train from scratch,” is also important. It shows that the architecture alone is not the whole story. The inherited once-for-all weights matter; training the same selected architecture from scratch does not reach the same accuracy in the plotted setting. Mobile Device TransferMobile latency is not a single number. Different phones can rank architectures differently.
The six plots show Samsung, Google, and LG devices. OFA produces a dense accuracy-latency curve on each device, while MobileNetV3 is shown as a smaller set of reference points. This is where the once-for-all setup pays off: the method can search a new subnet for a new device using a measured latency table, without training a new supernet. This is more useful than a single headline model. A deployment team often needs a curve, not one checkpoint. Beyond PhonesThe paper also evaluates CPU, GPU, mobile GPU, and FPGA platforms.
The key observation is that “efficient” is hardware-dependent. A model that is good on a phone CPU is not automatically good on an FPGA or GPU. OFA’s specialization step can choose different subnetworks for different latency models. The FPGA analysis makes this concrete.
OFA improves arithmetic intensity and FPGA utilization compared with MobileNetV2 and MnasNet in the reported setup. This is a useful reminder that FLOPs are not enough. If an architecture has poor memory access behavior or poor accelerator utilization, fewer operations may not translate into faster inference. Different Hardware Selects Different ArchitecturesThe final architecture figure is one of the most practical parts of the paper.
The FPGA-specialized model heavily prefers 3x3 mobile blocks. The CPU and GPU examples use wider blocks and sometimes larger kernels. That matches the cost model intuition: an FPGA pipeline can favor simple point-wise/depth-wise structure, while CPU and GPU parallelism can make wider blocks or larger kernels worthwhile. This is the strongest argument against one-size-fits-all mobile scaling. Changing only a width multiplier cannot express all hardware-specific trade-offs. What I Would Use OFA ForOFA is useful when the product needs a model family:
multiple latency targets for the same task; different devices with different kernels and runtimes; a need to ship many checkpoints without retraining each one; a hardware-aware search loop where latency measurement is cheap but training is expensive.
It is less useful when the architecture family itself is wrong. The paper is about CNNs for ImageNet-style vision models. It does not directly solve Transformer or LLM serving constraints, where KV cache, sequence length, batching, tensor parallelism, and memory bandwidth dominate the runtime story. There is also a supernet ranking assumption. The selected subnet is only good if inherited weights and the accuracy predictor correlate with standalone performance. OFA improves this with progressive shrinking and distillation, but the assumption still needs validation when moving to a new task or search space. TakeawayOFA’s main contribution is not a clever single architecture. It is a reusable deployment workflow:
Train one elastic network. Keep many subnetworks accurate through progressive shrinking. Build cheap accuracy and latency feedback. Select specialized subnetworks for each hardware and latency target.
That makes the expensive part of NAS amortized. For deployment, this is often more valuable than finding one more point on an ImageNet leaderboard.

entry.title: PACT: Parameterized Clipping Activation
entry.content:
Paper: PACT: Parameterized Clipping Activation for Quantized Neural Networks PACT is a quantization-aware training paper about one specific question: how should a network choose the clipping range for activations when the activation tensor only has a few bits? That sounds like a calibration detail, but it is usually where low-bit activation quantization starts to break. If the clipping threshold is too low, the model throws away large feature values. If the threshold is too high, the quantizer spreads the same small number of levels across a wide range and common activations get coarse resolution. PACT turns that threshold into a learnable parameter, trains it with the task loss, and keeps the final inference path close to ordinary uniform quantization. The paper is worth reading together with LSQ. PACT learns the activation clipping value ; LSQ later learns the quantization step size directly. Both papers make the same practical point: for QAT, the important quantization constants should not only be chosen by pre-training statistics. ProblemWeight quantization is relatively stable because weights are fixed tensors after training. Their ranges can be inspected layer by layer, and many schemes can use per-channel scales or learned weight distributions. Activation quantization is less forgiving. Activations are input-dependent, layer-dependent, and often have a long tail because ReLU is unbounded. The failure mode is visible in the paper’s first experiment.
Figure 1 compares ReLU, clipped activation, and quantized clipped activation on CIFAR10-ResNet20. Weight quantization alone is not the main source of damage here. The validation error jumps when activations are quantized without a good clipping policy. Clipping helps, but the clipping point cannot be arbitrary. For a -bit unsigned activation quantizer, there are only representable codes. After ReLU, one code is naturally used for zero and the positive range is represented by a small grid. At 2 bits or 4 bits, the clipping threshold largely decides the model behavior:
Threshold choice Main effect Failure mode
Small Fine resolution near zero Useful large activations saturate
Large Less saturation Ordinary values suffer large rounding error
Learned Task loss searches the tradeoff Requires QAT and regularization
PACT is built around this tradeoff. PACT ActivationPACT replaces ReLU with a clipped activation:
Equivalently:
The parameter is learned during training. Once the activation is clipped into , PACT applies uniform quantization:
So the quantization interval is:
This makes the role of very concrete. Increasing increases the clipping range but also increases . Decreasing gives a denser grid near zero but clips more values. During backpropagation, the round operator is handled with the straight-through estimator. The paper gives the gradient of the clipped activation with respect to as:
This is the useful part of the design. The model can push down when the quantization grid is too coarse, but samples that saturate at the upper bound can still push back. Alpha Is Trained, Not CalibratedThe paper initializes to a large value and then uses an L2 regularizer on :
The point is not simply to make small. The point is to prevent the learned activation from drifting back toward an almost unbounded ReLU. Without that pressure, a large can reduce clipping error while making low-bit rounding error worse.
Figure 2 shows the learned values for different layers of CIFAR10-ResNet20. They start high and then settle to layer-specific values. This already argues against a single global clipping constant. Early, middle, and late activations do not need the same dynamic range. Two implementation details matter here:
The paper uses one per activation layer in its main setting. It finds that setting to the same coefficient used for weight L2 regularization works well in practice.
That is a fairly simple recipe. It is also hardware-friendly because the inference graph only needs a clipped activation scale, not a learned non-uniform codebook. Alpha SweepBefore trusting a learned parameter, the paper checks whether the parameter is actually important. The alpha sweep experiment is the most useful diagnostic.
Figure 3 evaluates CIFAR10-ResNet20 with different fixed values of . The full-precision forward pass is relatively tolerant of large because it does not pay much rounding cost. The quantized forward pass is different: when is too large, the quantizer wastes bins on the tail and the cross-entropy rises. The third plot includes the regularization term. It removes flat plateaus in the training objective and gives the optimizer a cleaner preference for smaller activation ranges. This explains why the paper treats as part of the method rather than as a cosmetic training trick. The important reading is that “good clipping” is not a property of the tensor distribution alone. It is a property of the quantized network under task loss. Experimental SetupPACT is evaluated as a QAT method for CNNs. The paper tests:
Dataset or model Network
CIFAR10 ResNet20
SVHN ResNet20
ImageNet AlexNet
ImageNet ResNet18
ImageNet ResNet50
The paper quantizes activations with PACT and weights with DoReFa-style weight quantization. The main experiments follow the common convention of keeping the first and last layers unquantized, because these layers are unusually sensitive. The appendix later studies what happens when those layers are quantized. This setup matters because PACT is not a post-training quantization method. It assumes the network is trained, or at least fine-tuned, while the quantization operators are present in the forward pass. Accuracy ResultsThe main result is that learnable activation clipping makes very low activation precision much less brittle.
Figure 4 shows training and validation curves across CIFAR10, SVHN, AlexNet, ResNet18, and ResNet50. The high-level pattern is consistent: as activation precision increases, PACT approaches the full-precision baseline. The paper reports that validation error is within about 1 percentage point of full precision once activations use at least 4 bits. The degradation plot in Figure 4 is also important. On ImageNet ResNet18 and ResNet50, PACT has lower top-1 accuracy degradation than the compared activation quantization schemes at the same activation bitwidths.
Figure 5 compares PACT with prior quantization schemes on AlexNet, ResNet18, and ResNet50. The exact experimental settings differ across earlier papers, so this should not be read as a perfectly controlled ablation. Still, it shows the practical motivation: activation clipping was one of the missing pieces for making 4-bit activations usable on larger CNNs. The paper also provides a direct DoReFa versus PACT table.
A few numbers are worth keeping:
Model Full precision DoReFa 4b PACT 4b
CIFAR10-ResNet20 0.916 0.905 0.913
SVHN-ResNet20 0.978 0.975 0.978
AlexNet 0.551 0.549 0.557
ResNet18 0.702 0.681 0.692
ResNet50 0.769 0.714 0.765
The ResNet50 line is the clearest. DoReFa-style activation quantization at 4 bits reaches 0.714 top-1 accuracy, while PACT reaches 0.765, close to the 0.769 full-precision reference used in the table. At 5 bits, PACT reaches 0.917 on CIFAR10, 0.979 on SVHN, 0.557 on AlexNet, 0.698 on ResNet18, and 0.767 on ResNet50. The method is not only saving memory; it is making the low-bit activation path trainable enough that the model can recover most of the lost accuracy. System MotivationPACT is a training method, but the paper also includes a hardware analysis to explain why sub-8-bit activations are worth the trouble.
Figure 6 studies a precision-configurable MAC design and a ResNet50 inference system model. The main observation is that reducing bit precision can improve both compute density and memory behavior. The paper reports about 14x MAC density improvement when moving from 16-bit to 2-bit precision. The system-level result is not limited to peak FLOPs. Under a 64 GBps memory bandwidth setting, moving from 16 bits to 4 bits gives a 4x peak FLOP increase but a 4.5x performance improvement. The extra gain comes from memory behavior: lower precision lets the same on-chip memory hold more data and reduces off-chip traffic pressure. The paper keeps first and last layers at 8 bits for the 4-bit and 2-bit configurations in this analysis. It estimates that quantizing those layers too could add another 1.24x performance improvement, which motivates the appendix experiments on first and last layer sensitivity. Ablation: Scope Of AlphaPACT needs to decide how many clipping parameters to learn. The paper compares three choices:
Scope Meaning
Per channel Different for each activation channel
Per layer One for each activation layer
Per network One global shared by the network
Figure 7 shows that per-layer and per-channel clipping behave similarly, while per-network clipping is worse. The paper chooses per-layer clipping because it is simpler for hardware. With one activation scale per layer, the scaling factor can be applied after accumulation rather than changing inside the inner MAC loop. This is a useful engineering compromise. Per-channel clipping might be slightly more expressive, but activation per-channel scaling is more intrusive than per-channel weight scaling. PACT chooses the simpler runtime contract. Ablation: Alpha RegularizationThe regularizer on is not optional in spirit. Without it, the learned threshold can stay too large and the low-bit quantizer behaves too much like a naive ReLU quantizer.
Figure 8 compares different values on CIFAR10-ResNet20. The paper’s practical recommendation is simple: use L2 regularization on and set its coefficient to the same value as the weight L2 coefficient. That makes PACT relatively easy to add to a normal training recipe. The plot also shows why this is not just “make alpha small.” Too much regularization can damage validation error because it forces excessive clipping. The useful range is the range where is small enough to give a dense quantization grid but large enough not to erase important activations. First And Last LayersThe main experiments keep first and last layers in full precision. The paper then checks how risky that assumption is.
Table 2 reports CIFAR10-ResNet20 validation error when the middle layers use 2 to 5 bits and the first and last layers use different precisions. The pattern is clear: quantizing first and last layers to 8 bits causes little damage, but using 2 or 4 bits there is much more dangerous.
Figure 9 gives the same message from training curves. Quantizing only the first layer or only the last layer already hurts. Quantizing both hurts more. This is why many practical quantization papers leave those layers at a higher precision even when most of the network is aggressively quantized. For PACT, this means the headline “4-bit activations” should be read carefully. The middle layers can use low precision, but deployment recipes often keep the boundary layers special. Implementation NotesA minimal PACT module only needs three pieces:
A learnable positive clipping parameter. A clipped activation function. A fake-quantized forward path during training.
In PyTorch-like pseudocode: class PACTActivation(nn.Module): def __init__(self, bits: int, alpha_init: float = 10.0): super().__init__() self.bits = bits self.alpha = nn.Parameter(torch.tensor(float(alpha_init))) def forward(self, x): alpha = torch.clamp(self.alpha, min=1e-6) y = torch.clamp(x, min=0.0, max=alpha) qmax = (1 << self.bits) - 1 scale = alpha / qmax q = torch.round(y / scale).clamp(0, qmax) # In real QAT code, this should use an STE-friendly fake quant op. return q * scale
Real training code should be more careful than this snippet:
Use an STE or framework fake-quant operator so gradients through rounding are defined as intended. Keep positive. The paper initializes it high and regularizes it; implementations often clamp it or parameterize it through a positive transform. Add to the training loss. Decide explicitly whether first and last layers are left full precision, quantized to 8 bits, or included in the same low-bit policy.
At inference time, PACT does not require a complicated activation function. The learned gives the activation scale . The activation tensor is clipped, quantized to an unsigned integer range, and consumed by the low-precision layer. Relation To Later Quantization WorkPACT is a CNN-era QAT method, but the idea keeps reappearing. LSQ learns the step size instead of directly learning the clipping bound. For unsigned activations, these are closely related because . LSQ also adds a careful gradient scaling rule for the learned step size, which PACT does not emphasize. Post-training LLM quantization methods attack a harder version of the same activation range problem. LLM.int8() isolates activation outliers, SmoothQuant migrates activation magnitude into weights, and OmniQuant learns clipping and equivalent transformations during calibration. Those methods are different because full QAT is usually too expensive for large language models, but the pressure is the same: activation ranges cannot be treated as passive min/max statistics. PACT is therefore best read as a clean early example of learnable activation range control. It is not the direct recipe for a 70B LLM, but it is one of the simplest papers showing why the activation range belongs inside the optimization problem. LimitationsPACT has several important limits:
It requires quantization-aware training. That is fine for CIFAR or ImageNet CNNs, but expensive for large pretrained models. The paper mostly uses one activation clipping value per layer. That is simple and hardware-friendly, but less expressive than per-channel, per-token, or group-wise activation control. The method needs an extra regularization coefficient for , even if the paper finds a simple default. The strongest results rely on keeping first and last layers unquantized or at higher precision. The experiments are from the CNN quantization setting. Transformers and LLMs have different activation outlier structure and often need PTQ-friendly methods.
These limitations do not weaken the main contribution. They define where the contribution applies. TakeawayPACT turns activation clipping from a fixed calibration choice into a trained model parameter. That is the whole paper, and it is enough. The best way to remember it:
The clipping threshold controls both sides of that sum. PACT lets the task loss choose the balance.

entry.title: PTQ4ViT: Post-Training ViT Quantization
entry.content:
Z. Yuan, C. Xue, Y. Chen, Q. Wu, and G. Sun, “PTQ4ViT: Post-Training Quantization for Vision Transformers with Twin Uniform Quantization.”
Paper: arXiv:2111.12293 Code: hahnyuan/PTQ4ViT PTQ4ViT is an early and useful ViT quantization paper because it does not treat a Vision Transformer as “a CNN with larger matrix multiplications”. The paper starts from two concrete observations:
post-softmax attention probabilities are extremely unbalanced; post-GELU activations are asymmetric, with long positive tails and a narrow negative range.
Those two tensors sit exactly on important paths in a transformer block. A single symmetric uniform grid can either waste many quantization levels near empty ranges or collapse the small but important values. PTQ4ViT addresses this with twin uniform quantization and a Hessian-guided metric for calibration. One important boundary: PTQ4ViT is not a fully quantized ViT inference recipe in the later FQ-ViT sense. In the experiment setting, it quantizes weights and inputs of fully-connected layers and matrix multiplications in self-attention, but it does not quantize softmax and normalization layers. The paper is mainly about better post-training calibration for ViT MatMul/Linear operands and for the difficult activations around softmax/GELU. The ProblemThe transformer block has two major compute-heavy parts:
attention: , softmax, and ; MLP: two linear layers with GELU between them.
For quantization, the usual starting point is symmetric uniform quantization:
For a matrix multiplication , the base PTQ method quantizes both operands and reconstructs the output:
Then it searches for scaling factors that make close to :
This is reasonable for CNN-style PTQ, where many layers have activation distributions that are close enough to symmetric or bell-shaped. ViTs break that assumption in two places.
The paper’s overview is compact but informative: twin uniform quantization is applied to the post-GELU and post-softmax activation patterns, while a Hessian-guided metric is used to search scaling factors layer by layer. Post-Softmax And Post-GELU Are SpecialThe key empirical figure is the distribution plot below.
The post-softmax values are almost all close to zero, but a few values can be close to one. These large values correspond to strong token-patch relations. If the scaling factor is too small, those important large values get clipped or represented poorly. If the scaling factor is too large, most small probabilities collapse to zero. The post-GELU tensor has a different failure mode. GELU keeps a small negative range but allows positive values to have a much longer tail. A symmetric quantizer has to cover both sides with one grid, so either the positive tail gets harmed or many levels are wasted on the negative side. PTQ4ViT makes this concrete by comparing different scaling factors.
For post-softmax, a “large” protects large probabilities but destroys many small probabilities. A “small” keeps small probabilities visible but cannot represent large attention entries well. For post-GELU, the same tension appears across sign and magnitude: the negative side and positive side need different treatment. This is the main reason PTQ4ViT is not just another layer-wise reconstruction paper. It identifies which transformer tensors violate the implicit distribution assumptions behind common PTQ recipes. Twin Uniform QuantizationThe proposed quantizer keeps the hardware-friendly idea of uniform grids, but it uses two ranges instead of one. For a -bit tensor, PTQ4ViT uses one bit as a range flag and the remaining bits for the quantized value inside that range.
The formulation is:
For post-softmax activations:
uses a small scale to represent the dense near-zero region; covers the whole range, so large attention probabilities remain representable.
For post-GELU activations:
covers the negative range; covers the positive range; the paper searches the positive scale while fixing the negative range to cover all negative values.
The hardware detail is also important. Two independent floating-point scales would be awkward inside matrix multiplication. PTQ4ViT constrains the scales as:
Then values from the two ranges can be aligned with a bit shift:
That is a pragmatic design choice. It is not as flexible as arbitrary non-uniform quantization, but it avoids custom codebooks and avoids expensive scale alignment by multiplication. This is why the method is “twin uniform” rather than generic non-uniform quantization. Hessian-Guided CalibrationThe other problem is calibration. Earlier PTQ methods often choose scaling factors by minimizing MSE, cosine distance, or Pearson-style correlation between the original output and the reconstructed output. PTQ4ViT argues that these local metrics can pick the wrong scale for ViTs. The paper plots common reconstruction metrics against the real task-loss change.
The curves show that MSE, cosine distance, and Pearson correlation can prefer scaling factors that do not match the cross-entropy loss curve. This is exactly the calibration trap: a tensor can be locally close under an easy metric while still moving the model output in a sensitive direction. PTQ4ViT uses a second-order view. With a quantization perturbation , the expected loss change can be approximated by Taylor expansion: $$\mathbb{E}[L(\hat{W})] - \mathbb{E}[L(W)]\approx\epsilon^T \bar{g}^{(W)}
\frac{1}{2}\epsilon^T \bar{H}^{(W)}\epsilon.$$
The paper then uses a layer-output approximation. For layer output and quantized output , the calibration objective becomes a gradient-weighted reconstruction error:
In plain terms: do not weight every output coordinate equally. Coordinates with larger output gradients should matter more because perturbing them changes the loss more. There is a subtle PTQ issue here: calibration data is unlabeled. The paper approximates the label with the full-precision model prediction, so the loss is computed against the FP32 model’s own output. This is a common PTQ trick: use the teacher model to define what “do not change the behavior” means. This is also where the old shorthand “ranking-aware calibration” would be wrong for PTQ4ViT. Ranking loss appears in prior ViT PTQ work that PTQ4ViT compares against. PTQ4ViT’s own main metric is Hessian-guided, based on output gradients. FrameworkAlgorithm 1 is simple but useful because it shows the actual calibration flow.
The framework has two phases:
Run the full-precision model on calibration images and store each layer output . Run backward propagation to get . Search scaling factors layer by layer. For each layer, evaluate candidate scales with the Hessian-guided objective. Alternate the search over activation scale and weight scale for several rounds.
The paper stores outputs and gradients in CPU memory after generation, then moves them back to GPU memory layer by layer during search. Candidate outputs are evaluated in batches to make use of GPU parallelism. This is not just an implementation footnote. Without this memory movement, storing all layer outputs and gradients for ViT calibration can be expensive. The reported experiment setting is:
ImageNet classification; 32 randomly selected training images as unlabeled calibration data; models from timm; search range parameters alpha = 0, beta = 1.2, n = 100; search round #Round = 3; separate quantization parameters for different attention heads; different scaling factors for , , and ; no quantization for softmax and normalization layers.
The last point matters when comparing this paper to later fully quantized ViT work. ImageNet ResultsTable 1 is the central result.
At W8A8, PTQ4ViT keeps all tested models within roughly 0.5 percentage points of FP32. The drops are small across ViT, DeiT, and Swin. At W6A6, the gap between base PTQ and PTQ4ViT becomes much larger. The paper reports that base PTQ has a 9.8 percent average drop, while PTQ4ViT reduces the average drop to 2.1 percent. A few numbers make the pattern clear:
Model FP32 Base PTQ W6A6 PTQ4ViT W6A6
ViT-S/224 81.39 70.24 78.63
ViT-B/224 84.54 75.66 81.65
DeiT-S/224 79.80 72.26 76.28
DeiT-B/384 83.11 68.44 81.55
Swin-B/384 86.44 85.22 85.38
Swin is less sensitive than plain ViT/DeiT in these results. The paper’s explanation is plausible: Swin computes self-attention within local windows, so the softmax distribution is less extreme because fewer patches participate in each attention operation. There is also a model-size trend. Larger ViTs are less sensitive than smaller ones. For example, at 8-bit PTQ4ViT, the reported drops for ViT-S/224/32, ViT-S/224, ViT-B/224, and ViT-B/384 are 0.41, 0.38, 0.29, and 0.17. At 6-bit they are 4.08, 2.75, 2.89, and 2.65. This is a common compression pattern: larger models often have more redundancy, though that is not a guarantee. Comparison With Prior PTQThe method comparison table is useful because it separates calibration image count, mixed precision, model size, and top-1 accuracy.
