PTQ4ViT uses only 32 calibration images, while EasyQuant and the Liu et al. baseline in the table use 1024. At W8A8 and W6A6, PTQ4ViT is stronger than the listed prior methods despite using fewer images. The 4-bit result is more nuanced. On DeiT-B:
Liu et al. W4A4 mixed precision reaches 75.94; PTQ4ViT W4A4 reaches 60.91; PTQ4ViT with bias correction reaches 64.39.
So PTQ4ViT is a strong 8-bit and 6-bit PTQ method, but it is not a complete answer for 4-bit ViT quantization. Mixed precision still matters at lower bit-widths because sensitivity is not uniform across layers and tensors. AblationThe ablation table is the part I would check first when judging whether the two proposed components really matter.
The main reading:
Hessian-guided calibration alone helps, especially at 6-bit. Twin uniform quantization helps only when the calibration metric is strong enough. Combining Hessian-guided calibration with twin uniform quantization gives the best results.
For ViT-S/224 at W6A6:
base row: 70.24; Hessian-guided only: 77.20; Hessian + softmax twin: 78.57; Hessian + GELU twin: 76.93; Hessian + both twin quantizers: 78.63.
The warning is visible too. Twin uniform quantization without the Hessian-guided metric can degrade accuracy. On ViT-S/224 W8A8, using both twin quantizers without Hessian gives 79.25, which is worse than the 80.47 base row. That makes sense: a more flexible quantizer gives the search more ways to choose a bad scale if the objective is misaligned. Calibration CostTable 4 gives a practical view of calibration time.
With 32 calibration images, most models are quantized in a few minutes on one Nvidia Tesla V100. Increasing calibration images to 128 raises time substantially, especially for larger high-resolution models. For example, Swin-B/384 goes from 25 minutes to 69 minutes. Accuracy does not change much when moving from 32 to 128 images. That is important for PTQ deployment: if the method needed 1024 images and long calibration time, it would lose much of the appeal of post-training quantization. Relation To FQ-ViTPTQ4ViT and FQ-ViT solve related but different problems. PTQ4ViT focuses on post-training calibration for the main matrix multiplications and difficult ViT activations. It explicitly leaves softmax and normalization layers unquantized in the reported setting. Its central ideas are twin uniform quantization and Hessian-guided scale selection. FQ-ViT goes after fully quantized inference, including parts that PTQ4ViT leaves floating point. That requires different tricks, such as special handling for LayerNorm and Softmax. If the deployment target requires every operation to run in integer or low-bit arithmetic, PTQ4ViT is not enough by itself. If the target allows some FP operations and the main bottleneck is Linear/MatMul quantization, PTQ4ViT is a cleaner fit. Relation To LLM QuantizationI read PTQ4ViT as an early transformer quantization warning:
architecture-specific activation distributions matter; local reconstruction error is not always aligned with task loss; calibration objectives should weight sensitive directions more heavily; low-bit quantization needs tensor-specific treatment, not only a global bit-width.
Those themes later reappear in LLM quantization. LLMs have activation outliers, attention/KV-cache behavior, and strong layerwise sensitivity differences. The exact PTQ4ViT design does not directly transfer to language models, but the diagnostic mindset does: first inspect the tensor distribution and tensor role, then choose the quantizer and calibration metric. Reproduction NotesIf I were reproducing this paper, I would not start with all models. I would use DeiT-S/224 or ViT-S/224 first and build the checks in this order:
verify FP32 top-1 with the exact timm checkpoint; implement base PTQ with symmetric quantization for Linear/MatMul operands; confirm that W6A6 base PTQ loses a large amount of accuracy; add Hessian-guided calibration and check whether the selected scales move closer to the CE-preferred scales; add twin uniform quantization only for post-softmax and post-GELU; reproduce the ablation table before scaling to all ViT/DeiT/Swin models.
The most important debug artifacts would be:
activation histograms for post-softmax and post-GELU; candidate scale curves for MSE, cosine, Pearson, Hessian, and CE; layerwise chosen scales before and after Hessian weighting; attention-head-specific quantization parameters; top-1 results under W8A8 and W6A6 for a fixed 32-image calibration set.
I would also run several random calibration sets. The appendix says the paper observes slight accuracy variation with different calibration image counts, but PTQ methods can still have calibration-set variance. A single lucky 32-image set is not enough to understand robustness. LimitationsPTQ4ViT has several clear boundaries:
It does not quantize softmax and normalization layers in the reported experiments. It is much stronger at 8-bit and 6-bit than at 4-bit. Twin uniform quantization adds format logic and range handling, even if it stays shift-friendly. The Hessian-guided metric needs gradients and stored layer outputs, so calibration is heavier than pure min/max or MSE calibration. The method is evaluated on ImageNet classification; downstream dense prediction tasks may expose different sensitivity.
None of these make the paper weak. They define what problem it solves: practical post-training quantization for ViT-family classifiers when 8-bit or 6-bit Linear/MatMul quantization is the target. TakeawayPTQ4ViT is valuable because it connects three things that should be considered together: tensor distribution, tensor semantics, and calibration objective. The twin uniform quantizer addresses the weird activation distributions around softmax and GELU. The Hessian-guided metric addresses the fact that local reconstruction error is not always the right proxy for task loss. The broader lesson is simple: transformer PTQ is not solved by copying CNN PTQ. The difficult tensors are different, and the calibration metric has to know which errors the model actually cares about.

entry.title: PagedAttention and vLLM: KV Cache Paging for High-Throughput LLM Serving
entry.content:
Paper: Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention Code: vllm-project/vllm PagedAttention is one of those serving papers where the main idea is easy to say but easy to under-read. The one-line summary is “use virtual-memory-like paging for KV cache.” The important part is why this becomes a throughput primitive for online LLM serving:
The KV cache is large enough to be a first-class memory object, not a small side buffer. Its lifetime and size are dynamic because output lengths are unknown. Fine-grained batching only helps if the runtime can pack many live sequences into GPU memory. Advanced decoding methods, such as parallel sampling, beam search, and shared prefixes, create sharing opportunities that contiguous KV allocation cannot exploit cleanly.
The paper is not claiming that the PagedAttention kernel is faster than a contiguous attention kernel. In fact, its attention kernel is slower in the microbenchmark. vLLM wins because better memory packing lets the system admit a larger effective batch before latency explodes. The Serving ProblemFor autoregressive decoding, every token stores key and value vectors for all transformer layers. With standard multi-head attention, a rough KV cache size for one sequence is:
where is the number of layers, is the number of attention heads, is the head dimension, is the sequence length, and is bytes per element. For grouped-query or multi-query attention, replace with the number of KV heads. The important scaling is still linear in sequence length and number of live requests. The paper gives a concrete OPT-13B example:
That is about 800 KB of KV cache per token. At 2048 tokens, one request can consume about 1.6 GB of KV cache. This is why serving throughput can become memory-capacity-bound even when the GPU has enough compute for more tokens.
Figure 1 in the paper: for a 13B model on an A100 40GB GPU, model weights are static, while KV cache is dynamic and consumes a large fraction of memory. Smoother KV growth translates into larger effective batches. The hardware trend makes this worse. The paper points out that from A100 to H100, FLOPs grow much faster than maximum GPU memory capacity. If compute grows but the number of requests that fit in memory does not, memory management becomes the limiter. Why Existing Allocation Wastes MemoryExisting systems before vLLM typically keep the KV cache of a request in a contiguous memory region. Because output length is unknown, the system must either reserve for a maximum length, reserve for a predicted length, or allocate/copy as the sequence grows. All three choices are awkward in an online server. The paper separates the waste into three buckets:
Waste type Meaning Why it hurts batching
Reservation Memory reserved for future tokens that might be generated Other requests cannot use it while the current request is alive
Internal fragmentation Allocated slots that will never be used because the final output is shorter than the reserved length Memory is permanently unavailable until the request finishes
External fragmentation Free space exists, but not in a shape that can satisfy a contiguous allocation Total free memory is misleading because it cannot be packed
Figure 2 in the paper: in the evaluated existing systems, only 20.4%-38.2% of KV cache memory stores actual token states. vLLM raises that fraction to 96.3%. The graph is the key motivation for the paper. The gap is not a small allocator inefficiency. If most KV memory is not storing useful token states, the scheduler cannot form a large batch, and throughput collapses at a lower request rate.
Figure 3 in the paper: contiguous KV regions create reserved slots, internal fragmentation, and external fragmentation. The same token content at different positions also has different KV states, so the runtime cannot simply deduplicate token strings. This is why “just use continuous batching” is not enough. Continuous batching changes which requests are executed together at each decoding iteration. It does not by itself solve the physical memory layout. If finished requests leave holes that cannot be reused by growing requests, the batch scheduler has logical capacity but no usable KV memory. The Core AbstractionPagedAttention borrows the address-translation idea from virtual memory. A sequence sees a logical KV address space, split into fixed-size logical blocks. The runtime maps each logical block to a physical KV block from a GPU memory pool. For token position and block size , let be the logical block id and be the offset inside that block:
The block table then gives the physical location: bid = floor(t / B)off = t % Bpid = block_table[bid]slot = pid * B + off
Only the last logical block of a sequence can be partially empty. Therefore, with block size , the unused KV slots per live sequence are bounded by less than one block, instead of being proportional to the difference between maximum sequence length and actual generated length.
Figure 5 in the paper: the query attends over K/V vectors stored in non-contiguous physical blocks. The attention kernel follows the block table instead of assuming one contiguous KV array. The OS analogy is useful, but it is not a copy-paste of CPU virtual memory. vLLM uses application semantics:
All KV blocks of a sequence are read together during attention, so eviction can be sequence-level. The runtime knows when a sequence forks, appends a token, or finishes. Copy-on-write is applied at KV block granularity for decoding algorithms. Recovery can use recomputation, which is not a normal OS page fault strategy.
vLLM Runtime ArchitecturevLLM wraps PagedAttention in a serving runtime. The architecture has a centralized scheduler, a KV cache manager, GPU/CPU block allocators, and distributed workers that execute model shards.
Figure 4 in the paper: the scheduler coordinates requests, the KV cache manager owns block tables, and workers use cache engines to read/write physical KV blocks. The control flow during serving is roughly:
The scheduler chooses which sequences or sequence groups to run in the next iteration. The KV cache manager allocates new physical blocks only when a logical block needs storage. The scheduler sends input token IDs and block tables to GPU workers. The model executes the next step. Attention layers read past KV through the block table. Newly generated K/V tensors are written into the allocated physical blocks. Finished sequences release their blocks; forked sequences may share blocks with copy-on-write.
This runtime design makes memory management explicit. KV cache is not a tensor hidden inside a framework allocator; it is a managed serving resource. Block TablesThe block table is the most important data structure in the paper. It records, for each sequence, which physical block stores each logical block and how many slots in the current block are filled.
Figure 6 in the paper: a request has logical KV blocks, while physical KV blocks can live anywhere in GPU DRAM. The block table translates logical block ids to physical block ids. In the example, the prompt “Four score and seven years ago our” is split into logical blocks of four tokens. Its logical blocks do not have to be adjacent in GPU memory. The first logical block can map to physical block 7, the second to physical block 1, and a newly generated token can later trigger allocation of another physical block. This solves the reservation problem directly:
At prompt time, vLLM allocates just enough blocks for the existing prompt and generated tokens. During decoding, it allocates more blocks only when the current final block is full. When a request completes, its physical blocks return to the free pool and can be reused by any other request.
Figure 7 in the paper: two requests can use interleaved physical blocks without needing neighboring logical blocks to be contiguous in GPU memory. This is the memory-side requirement for high-throughput continuous batching. The batch can change every iteration because the KV memory layout can also change every iteration. PagedAttention KernelThe kernel has to compute attention while K/V blocks are non-contiguous. The paper rewrites attention over blocks. If the block size is , the -th key block is:
and similarly for . The attention score for a query over one block is computed block by block, then combined across all previous blocks. This has a real cost. Compared with a contiguous attention kernel, PagedAttention needs to:
Load block table entries. Follow non-contiguous physical block ids. Handle variable sequence lengths in the same batch. Execute extra branches around block boundaries and partially filled blocks.
The paper reports 20%-26% higher attention kernel latency than FasterTransformer in the kernel microbenchmark. That sounds bad if attention is evaluated in isolation. It is acceptable at the serving-system level because the memory savings allow much larger batches. Implementation details from the paper:
Fused reshape and block write: new K/V tensors are split, reshaped, and written to physical blocks in one kernel. Fused block read and attention: the attention kernel reads K/V according to block tables and computes attention on the fly. Warp-level block read: a GPU warp is assigned to read each block for coalesced memory access. Fused block copy: copy-on-write block copies are batched into one kernel launch instead of many small cudaMemcpyAsync calls.
Copy-On-Write For Parallel SamplingMany generation requests ask for multiple samples from the same prompt. Without sharing, each sample would duplicate the prompt KV cache even though the prompt part is identical. PagedAttention makes this natural. Multiple sequences can map their logical prompt blocks to the same physical blocks. Each physical block has a reference count. When a sequence needs to write into a shared block, vLLM allocates a private physical block and copies the old content once.
Figure 8 in the paper: two samples share prompt blocks. When one sample writes to a shared final block, copy-on-write creates a private block only for the modified block. The subtle point is the final block. If the prompt length is not a multiple of the block size, the last prompt block has empty slots. When different samples begin generating different tokens, they may need to write into that same logical final block. That is where copy-on-write is needed. Earlier full prompt blocks can remain shared. This is a block-level version of process fork: fork(seq): child.table = seq.table inc_ref(child.table)append(seq, token): old = current_block(seq) if refcount(old) > 1: new = alloc_block() copy(new, old) dec_ref(old) seq.table[last] = new write_kv(seq, token)free(seq): dec_ref(seq.table) release_zero_ref_blocks()
The paper presents fork, append, and free as the common API for supporting different decoding algorithms. That is a clean abstraction: the model execution kernel only sees physical block ids, while the scheduler and block manager handle sharing. Beam Search SharingBeam search creates even more sharing than parallel sampling. Candidates share the original prompt, and many candidates also share intermediate prefixes. As beams are pruned and expanded, the sharing pattern changes dynamically.
Figure 9 in the paper: beam candidates share prefix blocks. When candidates are pruned, their blocks are released; when new candidates are created, they reuse shared prefix blocks and allocate only new suffix blocks. The old way to implement this often involves copying KV cache between beam candidates when a candidate inherits another candidate’s prefix. With PagedAttention, inheritance is mostly block-table manipulation plus reference-count changes. Only a shared block that is being modified requires an actual block copy. This matters because beam search multiplies the number of live candidate sequences. If each candidate duplicated its full KV history, the KV budget would shrink quickly. If most prefix blocks are shared, the same GPU can keep more beams alive. Shared PrefixesShared prefix is the prompt-engineering version of the same idea. Many requests may share a long system prompt, task description, or few-shot examples. The service provider can precompute the shared prefix KV cache and map user requests to those physical blocks.
Figure 10 in the paper: multiple translation prompts share the same instruction and examples, while each user input adds a different suffix. For shared prefixes, vLLM can reserve physical blocks for the prefix, then map the prefix part of many requests to those cached blocks. The final prefix block may still need copy-on-write when user-specific suffix tokens are appended. This is distinct from semantic prompt caching. The paper does not solve how to discover arbitrary reusable prefixes across traffic. It shows that once a shared prefix is known, the block table makes the memory sharing mechanism straightforward. Scheduling And PreemptionPagedAttention also affects request scheduling. When GPU KV blocks are exhausted, vLLM has to preempt some work. The paper chooses FCFS fairness: earlier requests are served first, and later requests are preempted first. The eviction policy is all-or-nothing at sequence granularity. This is different from normal virtual memory, where an OS may evict individual pages. In LLM decoding, attention needs all previous KV blocks for a sequence, so evicting only some blocks of a sequence is not useful. Sequence groups, such as beam candidates in one request, are gang-scheduled. They are preempted and resumed together because they may share blocks. The paper studies two recovery options:
Recovery method What happens Tradeoff
Swapping Copy evicted KV blocks from GPU memory to CPU RAM, then copy them back later Can be expensive with many small block transfers
Recomputation Discard evicted KV blocks and regenerate them when the sequence is resumed Uses GPU compute, but prompt-phase recomputation can be efficient
Recomputation is possible because the generated tokens can be concatenated with the original prompt and processed as one prompt during recovery. That generates KV cache for all positions in a prompt-like pass instead of replaying one token at a time. Distributed ExecutionThe paper supports Megatron-LM style tensor parallelism. Each worker stores the shard of KV cache corresponding to its attention heads, but the workers share the same logical-to-physical block mapping from the centralized scheduler. At each decoding iteration:
The scheduler builds a control message with input token IDs and block tables. The scheduler broadcasts it to all GPU workers. Each worker executes the model shard and reads local KV blocks according to the shared block table. Workers synchronize intermediate tensors through all-reduce as in tensor parallel inference. Workers send sampled tokens back to the scheduler.
The key observation is that model parallelism shards the content of KV tensors, but not the sequence positions. All shards still need the same block-table structure. Evaluation SetupThe paper evaluates OPT-13B, OPT-66B, OPT-175B, and LLaMA-13B on A100 GPUs. The configurations show how KV memory changes with model and GPU setup.
Table 1 in the paper: model sizes, GPU memory, parameter memory, KV cache memory budget, and maximum KV cache slots. Two workload traces are synthesized from ShareGPT and Alpaca. ShareGPT is much longer and more variable. Alpaca is shorter and therefore less memory-stressing.
Figure 11 in the paper: ShareGPT has average input length 161.31 and output length 337.99, while Alpaca has average input length 19.31 and output length 58.45. The baselines are:
Baseline Description
FasterTransformer Highly optimized inference engine, with a custom dynamic batching scheduler in the paper
Orca (Max) Reserves KV space up to the model maximum length, such as 2048 tokens
Orca (Pow2) Reserves output space rounded to the next power of two, at most 2x the real output length
Orca (Oracle) Knows the true output length in advance, which is not feasible but gives an upper bound for contiguous allocation
The main metric is normalized latency:
The curves should be read as capacity curves. When request rate exceeds what the system can sustain, the queue grows and normalized latency shoots up. Basic Sampling ResultsFor single-sequence generation, vLLM sustains much higher request rates at similar normalized latency.
Figure 12 in the paper: vLLM shifts the latency explosion point to higher request rates across OPT models and both datasets. On ShareGPT, the paper reports:
vLLM sustains 1.7x-2.7x higher request rates than Orca (Oracle). vLLM sustains 2.7x-8x higher request rates than Orca (Max). vLLM sustains up to 22x higher request rates than FasterTransformer.
The comparison to Orca (Oracle) is the most interesting. Orca (Oracle) already knows the actual output length, so it removes one source of over-reservation that real systems do not know. vLLM still wins because block-level allocation removes fragmentation and makes live KV packing denser.
Figure 13 in the paper: for OPT-13B, vLLM batches more live requests. On ShareGPT at 2 req/s, it batches 30.42 requests on average versus 13.62 for Orca (Oracle) and 7.00 for Orca (Max). The Alpaca results follow the same pattern, but the OPT-175B Alpaca case has a smaller gap against Orca (Oracle) and Orca (Pow2). The paper’s explanation is important: OPT-175B in the evaluated configuration has a large KV memory budget, while Alpaca sequences are short. The system becomes more compute-bound, so better memory packing has less room to improve throughput. This is the right way to read PagedAttention: its benefits are largest when the workload is memory-bound because KV cache capacity constrains the batch. Parallel Sampling And Beam Search ResultsPagedAttention becomes more valuable when generation creates multiple related sequences per request.
Figure 14 in the paper: vLLM improves throughput for parallel generation and beam search. The gain grows as parallel size or beam width increases. For OPT-13B on Alpaca:
In basic sampling, vLLM improves over Orca (Oracle) by about 1.3x. In beam search with beam width 6, the improvement over Orca (Oracle) grows to 2.3x.
This difference makes sense. Beam candidates share prefixes beyond the original prompt. The block table and reference counts turn that sharing into memory savings.
Figure 15 in the paper: sharing saves 6.1%-9.8% memory for parallel sampling and 37.6%-55.2% for beam search on the Alpaca trace. The paper also reports larger memory savings on ShareGPT:
Parallel sampling: 16.2%-30.5%. Beam search: 44.3%-66.3%.
Longer prompts and longer continuations increase the amount of reusable KV history. Shared Prefix And Chatbot ResultsFor shared-prefix translation prompts, vLLM reuses the prefix KV blocks. The paper evaluates one-shot and few-shot translation prefixes.
Figure 16 in the paper: when prompts share an 80-token one-shot prefix, vLLM reaches 1.67x higher throughput than Orca (Oracle). With a 341-token five-shot prefix, the gain becomes 3.58x. Again, the longer the reusable prefix, the more useful block sharing becomes. The chatbot workload is also memory-heavy because each prompt includes conversation history. The paper truncates prompts to the last 1024 tokens for OPT-13B and lets the model generate up to 1024 tokens.
Figure 17 in the paper: vLLM sustains about 2x higher request rates than Orca baselines on the chatbot workload. The reason Orca variants behave similarly here is that long prompts force large reservation behavior. vLLM can still allocate only the blocks needed and recycle them at block granularity. AblationsThe ablation section is important because it shows the cost of the abstraction.
Figure 18 in the paper: PagedAttention has higher attention kernel latency than FasterTransformer, but block size 16-128 works well on ShareGPT and 16/32 works best on Alpaca. Two details matter:
PagedAttention’s attention kernel is 20%-26% slower than FasterTransformer’s attention kernel in the microbenchmark. The end-to-end system is still faster because the extra kernel overhead is outweighed by better memory utilization and larger batches.
Block size controls a tradeoff:
Block size choice Benefit Cost
Smaller blocks Less internal fragmentation, more precise sharing More block-table entries and weaker kernel parallelism per block
Larger blocks Better block-level compute efficiency More wasted tail slots and less sharing granularity
The paper sets the default block size to 16. That is small enough to keep fragmentation low for short sequences, but large enough to use GPU parallelism reasonably well.
Figure 19 in the paper: swapping is expensive for small blocks because it creates many small CPU-GPU transfers. Recomputation is more stable across block sizes, and both methods are comparable around medium block sizes. This result is a good reminder that paging on GPU is not the same as paging on CPU. PCIe/NVLink transfer granularity, kernel launch overhead, and recomputation throughput all matter. What The Paper Actually ContributesMy reading is that the paper has three contributions, ordered by importance:
It identifies KV cache memory waste as a primary throughput bottleneck for LLM serving. It introduces a block-table abstraction that makes KV cache allocation dynamic, packed, and shareable. It implements the abstraction in a full serving runtime with kernels, scheduling, preemption, tensor parallel execution, and support for complex decoding algorithms.
PagedAttention is not just “attention over paged KV.” The serving runtime matters. Without a scheduler, block manager, refcounts, and kernels that understand block tables, the abstraction would not translate into throughput. Limitations And CaveatsThe paper is very strong, but the technique has boundaries. First, PagedAttention adds indirection. If a workload is compute-bound and KV memory is not limiting batch size, a slower paged attention kernel can reduce performance. This is why the Alpaca OPT-175B case shows less advantage against strong baselines. Second, block size tuning is workload-dependent. Short sequences punish large blocks because the tail waste becomes large relative to the useful KV. Very small blocks reduce waste but increase metadata and memory-access overhead. Third, preemption is not free. Swapping has bandwidth and small-transfer overhead. Recomputation consumes GPU cycles. The best recovery policy depends on interconnect bandwidth, GPU compute, model size, sequence length, and current load. Fourth, prefix sharing requires the runtime to know which prefix is shared. PagedAttention gives the memory mechanism, not a full semantic cache discovery system. Fifth, the centralized scheduler and block manager become critical runtime components. At very high request rates, CPU-side scheduling, block-table construction, and metadata transfer can matter, even if the paper’s evaluated workloads are dominated by GPU memory capacity. Reproduction ChecklistIf I were reproducing this paper or debugging an implementation, I would not start with end-to-end throughput. I would first test the memory behavior directly.
Build a synthetic trace with varied prompt and output lengths. Compare contiguous allocation, max-length reservation, power-of-two reservation, and block allocation under the same KV memory budget. Track useful token-state slots versus reserved, internal-fragmented, and external-fragmented slots. Measure average active sequences per decoding iteration. Add parallel sampling and verify that prompt blocks are shared. Add beam search and verify that pruned candidates decrement refcounts and free physical blocks. Sweep block sizes and plot both memory waste and attention-kernel latency. Stress preemption and compare recomputation with CPU swap.
The expected signal is not merely lower memory usage. The expected signal is a later latency explosion point because more live sequences fit in GPU memory. TakeawayPagedAttention changed the framing of LLM serving. Before this paper, it was natural to think about throughput mainly through batching and kernel speed. vLLM shows that the KV cache itself needs an OS-like memory manager. The central insight is simple but deep: a sequence should have a logical KV address space, and physical KV memory should be allocated, shared, copied, evicted, and freed at block granularity. Once that is true, continuous batching, parallel sampling, beam search, shared prefixes, and preemption all become much easier to support in one runtime. That is why this paper sits underneath so much later LLM serving work. It turns KV cache from an implementation detail into a first-class systems object.

entry.title: PC-DARTS: Partial Channel Connections for Memory-Efficient Architecture Search
entry.content:
Xu Y, Xie L, Zhang X, et al. PC-DARTS: Partial Channel Connections for Memory-Efficient Architecture Search. ICLR 2020.
Paper: https://arxiv.org/pdf/1907.05737.pdf Code: https://github.com/yuhuixu1993/PC-DARTS
PC-DARTS is one of the most practical follow-ups to DARTS. The paper does not replace the differentiable NAS formulation. Instead, it attacks the part that makes DARTS awkward to scale: every candidate operation on every edge is kept alive during search, so the supernet has to store and backpropagate through many operation outputs that will mostly be discarded when the final discrete cell is derived. The key idea is deliberately simple. On each edge, PC-DARTS sends only a fraction of the input channels through the expensive mixed operation and lets the remaining channels bypass that operation. This reduces search memory and computation roughly in proportion to the channel sampling factor. Since partial-channel sampling can make the edge ranking noisy, the paper adds edge normalization parameters to learn which incoming edges should dominate each node. The result is a DARTS-family method that is much easier to run: 0.1 GPU-days on CIFAR10 and 3.8 GPU-days for direct ImageNet search in the reported experiments, while keeping competitive final accuracy. MotivationDARTS makes neural architecture search differentiable by relaxing a discrete operation choice into a weighted mixture. That relaxation is elegant, but its implementation is expensive. Suppose an edge has 8 candidate operations and an activation tensor with channels. During search, the supernet has to evaluate those 8 operations on the full -channel tensor and keep their intermediate activations for gradient computation. This is much heavier than training the final architecture, where each edge keeps only one operation. This creates two practical problems:
The search batch size is small because the supernet is memory-heavy. The over-parameterized supernet can overfit its own search dynamics, especially by preferring cheap or weight-free operations such as skip-connect.
PC-DARTS treats these two problems as coupled. If only channels are used for the operation mixture, the search stage can use a batch size about times larger. At the same time, the sampled-channel path acts as a regularizer because each operation is trained and evaluated through a partial view of the feature tensor instead of a full deterministic input. The important caveat is that partial evaluation changes the signal used to rank edges. The paper therefore adds edge normalization so that the final topology decision does not depend only on the operation weights inside an edge. DARTS RecapPC-DARTS inherits the DARTS cell search space. A cell is a directed acyclic graph. Each node is a feature tensor. Each directed edge carries an operation selected from a candidate set , usually including separable convolutions, dilated separable convolutions, pooling, skip-connect, and zero. Before discretization, DARTS replaces each categorical operation choice with a mixed operation:
Here is the architecture parameter for choosing operation on edge . The operation weights inside are the usual network parameters. The output of node is the sum of all incoming mixed operations:
The output of the whole cell concatenates the intermediate nodes:
The high-level optimization is the same bilevel problem as DARTS. Network weights are trained on the training split, and architecture parameters are trained on the validation split:
PC-DARTS keeps this formulation. The contribution is not a new objective, but a cheaper and more stable way to evaluate the relaxed cell during search. Partial Channel ConnectionThe main operation-level change is partial channel connection. Instead of applying the mixed operation to the full tensor , PC-DARTS samples a channel mask and applies candidate operations only to . The unselected channels bypass the operation mixture and are concatenated or added back into the edge output.
PC-DARTS evaluates operation mixtures on a subset of channels and uses edge-level normalization to rank incoming edges. The paper writes the partially connected mixed operation as:
The mask selects channels. If , only one quarter of the channels go through the expensive mixed operation. The remaining three quarters are passed forward directly. This is why the method is memory-efficient: the dominant activation storage for the candidate operations is reduced from full channels to partial channels. A useful approximation is:
The bypass is cheap compared with evaluating all candidate convolutions on all channels, so the search stage gets a large reduction in memory and FLOPs. On CIFAR10, the paper uses , increasing the search batch size from 64 to 256 while keeping memory below 12GB. On ImageNet, it uses a less aggressive sampling rate, , to preserve more information. There is also an implementation detail that matters. The conceptual formula samples channels, but the practical implementation does not need to randomly sample a different subset every time an operation is called. The paper uses the first channels for the operation mixture and then shuffles the output channels before the next computation, similar to ShuffleNet. This avoids costly dynamic indexing and makes the partial-channel path GPU-friendly. Edge NormalizationPartial-channel search makes operation evaluation cheaper, but it introduces a new source of uncertainty. If each edge is evaluated through only part of the feature tensor, the relative strength of incoming edges may become noisier. DARTS already has a known instability problem where the relaxed supernet and the final discrete cell do not always agree. PC-DARTS tries to prevent partial-channel sampling from making that gap worse. The fix is to add edge-level parameters . These parameters normalize incoming edges to node :
It is helpful to separate the two probabilities:
The final score for choosing operation on edge is:
This small change is important. In vanilla DARTS, the operation softmax only compares operations on the same edge. It does not explicitly say whether one incoming edge should be stronger than another incoming edge. PC-DARTS learns both the within-edge operation distribution and the across-edge topology distribution, then multiplies them when deriving the final cell. Search And DiscretizationThe search loop is still DARTS-like: initialize winitialize alpha and betafor each search epoch: update w on a training minibatch update alpha and beta on a validation minibatchderive cells from q_{i,j} * p_{i,j}^{o}train the derived architecture from scratch
The paper uses a warm-up stage where architecture parameters are frozen. This is a practical detail I like because early architecture gradients are usually noisy before the shared operation weights have learned anything useful. In the reported setting, and are frozen for the first 15 epochs on CIFAR10 and for the first 35 epochs on ImageNet. After search, PC-DARTS follows the DARTS extraction rule. For each intermediate node, keep the strongest non-zero incoming edges according to the final score:
Then the continuous supernet is discarded. The selected normal and reduction cells are trained from scratch as a normal network. This point is important because the search-time partial channel connection is not the final inference architecture. It is a cheaper estimator used to find the cell. Results On CIFAR10The CIFAR10 result is the headline demonstration that PC-DARTS keeps DARTS-level quality while reducing search cost.
CIFAR10 comparison. PC-DARTS reports 2.57 +/- 0.07% test error with 0.1 GPU-days search cost on a GTX 1080Ti. The compact view:
Method CIFAR10 test error Params Search cost
DARTS first order + cutout 3.00 +/- 0.14% 3.3M 0.4 GPU-days
DARTS second order + cutout 2.76 +/- 0.09% 3.3M 1 GPU-day
P-DARTS + cutout 2.50% 3.4M 0.3 GPU-days
PC-DARTS + cutout 2.57 +/- 0.07% 3.6M 0.1 GPU-days
The important comparison is not only the final error. DARTS second order is already strong, but PC-DARTS reaches a better reported error while using one tenth of the listed search cost. The paper also notes that the 0.1 GPU-day number was measured on a single GTX 1080Ti and can be shortened to 0.06 GPU-days on a Tesla V100. The searched CIFAR10 cells are shown below. They still look like DARTS-family cells: separable convolutions dominate, with skip connections and pooling appearing where useful.
Cells found on CIFAR10 and ImageNet. The ImageNet-searched normal cell is deeper than the CIFAR10-searched normal cell. Results On ImageNetPC-DARTS is more interesting when moving beyond CIFAR10 because DARTS-style methods often search on CIFAR10 and only evaluate transfer to ImageNet. PC-DARTS reports both transferred and directly searched ImageNet architectures.
ImageNet mobile setting comparison. PC-DARTS reports both CIFAR10-searched transfer and direct ImageNet search results. The key accuracy rows are:
Method Search data Top-1 err. Top-5 err.
DARTS second order CIFAR10 26.7% 8.7%
P-DARTS CIFAR10 24.4% 7.4%
PC-DARTS CIFAR10 25.1% 7.8%
PC-DARTS ImageNet 24.2% 7.3%
And the compute side:
Method Params MAdds Search cost
DARTS second order 4.7M 574M 4.0 GPU-days
P-DARTS 4.9M 557M 0.3 GPU-days
PC-DARTS, CIFAR10 5.3M 586M 0.1 GPU-days
PC-DARTS, ImageNet 5.3M 597M 3.8 GPU-days
The direct ImageNet search setting uses eight V100 GPUs, batch size 1024, and a sampling rate of . The paper reports that search takes 11.5 hours. This is the point of the method: if the supernet is cheap enough, direct search on ImageNet becomes practical instead of being treated as too expensive. Ablation: Channel Sampling RateThe channel sampling rate is controlled by . A larger means fewer channels go through the mixed operation, so search is cheaper but the operation-quality estimate is noisier.
Sampling-rate ablation on CIFAR10. The paper compares full channels, 1/2, 1/4, and 1/8 channel sampling. The pattern is exactly what I would expect:
uses the full tensor and is expensive. reduces cost and improves the final error. gives the best tradeoff in the reported CIFAR10 setting. is cheaper, but the final test error becomes much worse.
This is a good sign that partial channel connection is not just a hardware trick. Moderate sampling regularizes the supernet; too much sampling throws away too much information. Ablation: Partial Channel And Edge NormalizationThe paper separates the effect of partial channel connection (PC) and edge normalization (EN).
Component ablation. PC reduces search cost and improves accuracy; EN stabilizes edge selection. The numbers are clear:
PC EN CIFAR10 test error CIFAR10 search cost
no no 3.00 +/- 0.14% 0.4 GPU-days
no yes 2.82 +/- 0.05% 0.4 GPU-days
yes no 2.67 +/- 0.11% 0.1 GPU-days
yes yes 2.57 +/- 0.07% 0.1 GPU-days
And on ImageNet with the 100-epoch ablation setting:
PC EN ImageNet test error ImageNet search cost
no no 26.8 +/- 0.1% 7.7 GPU-days
no yes 26.3 +/- 0.1% 7.7 GPU-days
yes no 26.2 +/- 0.1% 3.8 GPU-days
yes yes 25.8 +/- 0.1% 3.8 GPU-days
This ablation is probably the most convincing part of the paper. Partial channel connection is responsible for the big search-cost reduction, but it also improves accuracy. Edge normalization has almost no extra computation, but it consistently improves the final architecture. The combination is better than either piece alone. StabilityDARTS-family methods are sensitive to seeds, search epochs, and search-space size. PC-DARTS evaluates this explicitly.
Stability comparison across independent runs, search epochs, and number of nodes. Across five independent search runs, the reported standard deviations are:
Method Five-run behavior
DARTS-v1 +/- 0.15%
DARTS-v2 +/- 0.21%
PC-DARTS +/- 0.07%
The table also varies the number of search epochs and the number of nodes in the cell. PC-DARTS is not perfectly invariant, but it is visibly less erratic than the DARTS variants. This supports the paper’s interpretation that partial channel sampling works as a regularizer and edge normalization reduces the instability caused by sampling. My reading is slightly more cautious: the stability result is strong within this DARTS search space, but it does not prove that the partial-channel estimator will rank operations well in every search space. If operations have very different cross-channel behavior, the subset may be a biased estimator. Still, for convolutional DARTS cells, the evidence is solid. Transfer To Object DetectionThe paper also tests whether the ImageNet-searched backbone transfers to MS-COCO object detection with SSD.
MS-COCO test-dev 2015 detection results using the PC-DARTS backbone inside SSD. The PC-DARTS with SSD row reports:
Model Input FLOPs AP
PC-DARTS with SSD 320x320 1.2B 28.9
The same row reports AP50 = 46.9 and AP75 = 30.0. The backbone is the PC-DARTS architecture searched directly on ImageNet. This is not the main contribution, but it is a useful transfer sanity check. The discovered ImageNet backbone is not only a CIFAR/ImageNet classification artifact; it can serve as a lightweight detection backbone too. What PC-DARTS Actually FixesI see PC-DARTS as fixing three practical weaknesses of vanilla DARTS:
Full-channel mixed operations make search memory-heavy. Small search batch sizes make the supernet optimization noisy. Operation softmax alone is not enough to rank incoming edges robustly.
Partial channel connection addresses the first two issues. Edge normalization addresses the third. The paper is effective because these changes are small and local. They do not require a new controller, a new reward, a new surrogate benchmark, or a complicated progressive search schedule. The method also exposes a useful NAS lesson: the search supernet should not be optimized too well in a way that is disconnected from the final discrete architecture. PC-DARTS deliberately weakens each operation’s search-time view of the input tensor. That sounds like losing information, but the ablation suggests it can reduce overfitting to the supernet. LimitationsThere are still limitations worth keeping in mind.
Partial-channel evaluation is an estimator. It can misrank operations if the sampled channels are not representative. The best is task-dependent. CIFAR10 uses , while ImageNet uses . The final cell extraction rule is still heuristic, just like DARTS. The method remains tied to a DARTS-style cell search space. The reported stability is much better than DARTS, but the paper still evaluates a limited family of convolutional spaces.
I would not treat PC-DARTS as a universal NAS solution. I would treat it as a very strong engineering improvement to differentiable cell search. TakeawayPC-DARTS keeps the main appeal of DARTS: architecture search is differentiable and cheap enough to iterate on. Its contribution is making the relaxed supernet cheaper and less brittle. The formula is simple:
The most important numbers are also simple:
Setting Result
CIFAR10 2.57 +/- 0.07% error, 0.1 GPU-days
ImageNet transfer from CIFAR10 search 25.1% top-1 error, 0.1 GPU-days
Direct ImageNet search 24.2% top-1 error, 3.8 GPU-days
Detection transfer 28.9 AP on COCO with SSD
My main note after reading the paper: PC-DARTS is valuable because it improves the estimator used during search, not the final architecture class. The final network is still an ordinary DARTS-style cell. The difference is that the search process is cheaper, uses larger batches, and is less likely to overfit the full supernet. That is exactly the kind of detail that decides whether a NAS method is merely elegant or actually usable.

entry.title: Performer: Linear Attention With FAVOR+
entry.content:
Choromanski K, Likhosherstov V, Dohan D, et al. Rethinking Attention with Performers. ICLR 2021.
Paper Code Performer is an efficient-attention paper, but it is different from the sparse-attention line represented by Reformer, Longformer, and BigBird. It does not choose a fixed sparse pattern or assume that the attention matrix is low-rank. Instead, it treats softmax attention as a kernel and estimates that kernel with random features. The important promise is:
where is a positive random feature map. If this approximation is good enough, the attention computation can be reassociated so the full attention matrix never needs to be materialized. The LinearizationRegular bidirectional attention can be written as:
The expensive object is . Performer replaces the softmax kernel entries with random feature dot products:
Let and , with feature dimension . Then the numerator can be computed as:
instead of:
That ordering is the whole trick. Compute first, which is only , then multiply by every transformed query.
The paper states the resulting approximate attention as:
If is treated as a fixed or modest random-feature dimension, this changes the layer from quadratic in sequence length to roughly time and memory. Why Positive Features MatterA naive random Fourier feature view would suggest using trigonometric features, because the Gaussian kernel has the usual random feature representation. The paper’s warning is that attention is not just a kernel approximation problem. Attention normalizes scores into a convex combination of values. Negative random feature coordinates can create unstable score estimates. This is especially bad when the true softmax kernel value is near zero, because small positive weights are common and still matter after normalization. Performer uses positive random features for the softmax kernel. A simplified form is:
This keeps the random feature map positive and gives an unbiased softmax-kernel estimator in the setting described by the paper. The paper also discusses a hyperbolic variant and a regularized softmax kernel, but the practical message is simpler: positive features are much more stable than trigonometric features for attention.
The figure visualizes why. In regions where the softmax kernel value is small, the trigonometric estimator can have much larger mean squared error. Positive random features behave better exactly in the low-score regions that would otherwise create normalization trouble. The ORF Part Of FAVOR+The full method is FAVOR+: Fast Attention Via positive Orthogonal Random features. There are two separate ideas:
Part Role
FA Reassociate kernel attention so is computed before multiplying by .
R+ Use positive random features for softmax, avoiding negative score estimates.
O Make the random projection vectors orthogonal to reduce estimator variance.
The orthogonal part is easy to underweight when reading the paper. It is not just an implementation detail. For a fixed random feature budget, orthogonal random features reduce approximation error compared with IID Gaussian features, which means the model can use fewer features for the same quality target.
The MSE plots match the theory: orthogonal features beat IID features, and positive features beat features by a large margin in this attention-output experiment. Causal Attention Uses Prefix SumsFor autoregressive attention, token can only attend to keys and values at positions . The same reassociation still works, but the accumulators must be prefix sums:
Then:
This is useful because it keeps causal attention linear in sequence length while preserving the streaming structure. The implementation has to be careful with numerical stability and feature redraws, but the algebra is clean. Speed And MemoryThe speed figure is the first sanity check. Performer should not merely have better asymptotic notation; it should change the observed long-sequence curve.
The regular Transformer curves hit memory limits as grows. Performer tracks much closer to the paper’s “OPT” reference, where attention simply returns . That is not a real model, but it is a useful lower bound for attention overhead. The figure supports the claim that the method removes most of the quadratic attention bottleneck in this benchmark. The caveat is that this is a JAX implementation benchmark from the paper’s setup. Modern exact-attention kernels such as FlashAttention attack a different problem: they preserve exact softmax attention and reduce memory traffic. Performer changes the mathematical computation through approximation. Approximation Is Not FreeThe paper is honest about error propagation. A single attention approximation may be tight, but a Transformer stacks many attention heads, MLPs, nonlinearities, and residual paths. Small layer errors can compound. The pretrained-model experiment is therefore important.
On LM1B, the authors transfer a pretrained Transformer into a Performer and recover accuracy through fine-tuning. On PG-19, the difference between feature choices becomes more visible: trigonometric softmax approximation is unstable, while positive softmax features with redrawing can match the Transformer curve. I read this as the paper’s best practical warning. “Linear attention” is not one thing. Kernel choice, feature count, redraw schedule, and numerical treatment are part of the model. Protein Sequence ModelingThe TrEMBL experiments are useful because they test long biological sequences rather than only synthetic attention approximations.
The setup uses 36-layer models with sequence length . In the unidirectional case, Performer-ReLU is close to or better than the Transformer and clearly ahead of Reformer. In the bidirectional case, Performer-RELU is strongest in the plotted runs; Performer-SOFTMAX tracks the regular Transformer closely, while Linformer is much worse. This is where generalized kernel attention matters. FAVOR+ is not only a way to approximate softmax. It also lets the model use other kernelizable attention functions, such as ReLU features, while retaining the same linear-time structure. Long Sequence ExperimentsThe paper also includes tasks where a regular Transformer is no longer a practical baseline at the same scale.
On ImageNet64, the sequence length is . Performer with fewer layers can match deeper Reformer variants in the plotted BPD curves. On concatenated TrEMBL with , the regular Transformer has to be shrunk heavily to fit, while Performer can train the larger standard architecture. That is the deployment-shaped argument: linear attention is valuable when it lets you use a model size that quadratic attention cannot run. Long Range ArenaThe appendix includes Long Range Arena results. This table is worth reading carefully because it prevents an overly clean story.
Performer is not the best average-quality model in this table. BigBird has the strongest average score, and the vanilla Transformer average is also higher. Performer is best on Pathfinder and near the top on Text/Image, but weak on ListOps. So the result is not “Performer dominates long-range modeling.”
Model LRA Avg Useful Detail
Transformer 54.39 Strong quality, but high memory and low speed at long length.
BigBird 55.01 Best average score in this table.
Performer 51.41 Best Pathfinder score, strong speed-memory point.
Linear Transformer 50.55 Similar speed region, slightly lower average score.
The speed and memory table gives the other half of the picture.
Performer is among the fastest rows and has very low memory usage. At 4K tokens, the table reports 8.0 steps/s for Performer versus 1.4 for the vanilla Transformer, with peak memory 1.06 GB versus 9.48 GB. This is the tradeoff I would remember: Performer is a strong speed-memory point, not a guaranteed accuracy upgrade.
Model 4K Steps/s 4K Peak Memory
Transformer 1.4 9.48 GB
Linformer 7.7 0.99 GB
Linear Transformer 7.8 1.03 GB
Performer 8.0 1.06 GB
The scatter plot makes the tradeoff visible. Performer sits far to the right, with high speed and moderate LRA score. BigBird scores higher but is slower in this benchmark. Practical NotesIf I were reproducing Performer, I would track these details before judging the method:
random feature dimension ; positive feature variant and whether SMREG is used; orthogonal versus IID feature construction; feature redraw schedule; causal prefix-sum numerical stability; exact attention baseline implementation; whether the task rewards approximation or needs exact token-token scores.
The last point matters. Performer and FlashAttention answer different questions. Performer asks: can I replace full attention with a linear-time approximation? FlashAttention asks: can I compute exact attention with much better IO behavior? They can both be useful, but they should not be compared as if they preserve the same operator. TakeawayPerformer is valuable because it gives kernelized attention a concrete, mathematically motivated implementation path. FAVOR+ makes softmax attention approximable with positive orthogonal random features, and the reassociation of removes the explicit attention matrix. The limitation is the same thing that makes it fast: it is an approximation. Feature design, redraws, numerical stability, and task distribution decide whether the approximation is harmless. I would treat Performer as a strong long-sequence baseline when memory is the blocker, but not as a drop-in replacement when exact softmax behavior is required.

entry.title: PowerInfer: Fast LLM Serving on a Consumer GPU
entry.content:
Song et al. PowerInfer: Fast Large Language Model Serving with a Consumer-grade GPU. SOSP 2024.
Paper: PowerInfer: Fast Large Language Model Serving with a Consumer-grade GPU PowerInfer is a local LLM serving paper. It is not trying to beat datacenter serving systems under large batches. It asks a narrower and very practical question:
If the model is too large for a single consumer GPU, can we use CPU memory without making every token wait on CPU-GPU weight transfer?
The paper’s answer is to exploit activation locality. A small subset of MLP neurons is activated frequently across inputs. PowerInfer treats these as hot neurons and keeps them on the GPU. The remaining cold neurons stay in CPU memory and are computed on the CPU only when an online predictor says they are needed. This is different from quantization and different from layer-level offloading. Quantization shrinks all weights. Layer offloading moves whole Transformer layers between GPU and CPU. PowerInfer instead works at neuron granularity inside layers. The Local Serving ProblemConsumer GPUs have much less memory than datacenter GPUs. An RTX 4090 has 24 GB of VRAM. That is large for games, but not large enough for many FP16 LLMs, and still tight for some quantized large models once runtime buffers are included. The naive offloading solution is simple: keep part of the model in CPU memory and move weights to GPU when needed. The problem is that autoregressive decoding runs the full model for every generated token. If a token step repeatedly transfers large weights over PCIe, latency becomes dominated by data movement. PowerInfer’s key claim is that LLM inference has enough neuron-level locality to use the GPU as a hot-neuron cache and the CPU as a cold-neuron executor. What Is A Neuron Here?The paper defines a neuron as a row or column in a weight matrix. In an MLP block, the simplified shape is:
For ReLU-style activations, many entries of are zero or near-zero for a given token. If an intermediate activation entry is inactive, the corresponding work in the following projection can be skipped.
Figure 1 shows this at the MLP level. The activation function gates FC1 outputs, and only the activated rows or columns contribute to the FC2 computation. The paper reports substantial MLP sparsity even outside pure ReLU models.
Table 1 is the quick motivation:
Model Activation Reported MLP sparsity
OPT-30B ReLU 97%
LLaMA2-13B SwiGLU 43%
Yi-34B SwiGLU 53%
For ReLU-based models, sparsity means zero activation. For SwiGLU-based models, the paper measures the proportion of neurons that can be dynamically pruned with less than 1% perplexity impact. That distinction matters: PowerInfer is strongest on ReLU-family models, but the authors also test lower-sparsity non-ReLU settings. Why Existing Offloading Is SlowThe paper separates two common approaches.
GPU-centric offloading stores overflow parameters in CPU memory, then transfers needed weights to GPU at runtime. This can make a large model fit, but every token can pay PCIe transfer cost. Hybrid CPU-GPU offloading splits layers between CPU and GPU. This reduces transfer volume, but it gives the CPU too much compute when the GPU cannot hold enough of the model.
Figure 3 shows the failure on OPT-30B with an RTX 4090. FlexGen and DejaVu with unified memory are dominated by CPU-GPU movement. The paper states that more than 99.5% of FlexGen processing time is spent transferring LLM weights from CPU to GPU. The llama.cpp-style hybrid path avoids much of that transfer, but for OPT-30B on a 24 GB 4090 only about 37% of the model is on GPU, and the CPU ends up handling most of the computation time. PowerInfer is trying to get the best of both:
Keep the most frequently useful weights in GPU memory. Avoid moving cold weights to GPU for each token. Compute cold activated neurons directly on CPU. Skip inactive neurons entirely.
Insight 1: Power-Law ActivationThe central observation is not only “activations are sparse.” It is that activation frequency is highly skewed.
Figure 4 profiles about 1M tokens from Wikipedia. In one MLP block, the paper reports that 26% of OPT-30B neurons, 43% of LLaMA2-ReGLU-70B neurons, and 69% of LLaMA2-SwiGLU-70B neurons account for 80% of activations. Across the entire model, the corresponding proportions are 17%, 26%, and 75%. This is the hot/cold split:
Group Meaning Placement intuition
Hot neurons Frequently activated across many inputs Keep on GPU
Cold neurons Input-dependent and less frequently activated Keep on CPU, compute only when predicted active
The split is useful only if it is stable across tasks. The paper checks that too.
Figure 5 shows OPT-30B activation frequency by layer and across tasks. The paper reports more than 90% overlap in the top 20% most frequently activated neurons across the profiled downstream domains. That is the key evidence behind the offline placement step. If the hot set changed completely between tasks, static placement would be fragile. Insight 2: CPU Computation Can Beat Weight TransferIf a cold activated neuron lives in CPU memory, there are two options:
Load the neuron’s weights to GPU and compute there. Compute the neuron directly on CPU and transfer only the result.
For small local-serving batches, PowerInfer chooses the second path.
Figure 6 compares load-then-execute with direct CPU execution for OPT-30B. For batch sizes under 32, direct CPU computation is faster than transferring those weights to the RTX 4090 and computing on GPU. This is the second reason the design is neuron-level rather than layer-level: the CPU should not own whole layers, but it can handle a small set of cold activated neurons. System OverviewPowerInfer has an offline part and an online part.
The offline part profiles activation statistics, classifies neurons as hot or cold, trains adaptive activation predictors, and solves a placement problem under GPU memory and bandwidth constraints. The online part loads the selected hot neurons on GPU, keeps cold neurons on CPU, predicts active neurons per input, and runs GPU and CPU work concurrently. The high-level workflow is: offline: profile neuron activation frequency on a general corpus train per-layer activation predictors solve hot/cold placement under GPU memory and transfer constraints load hot neurons on GPU and cold neurons on CPUonline for each token step: predict active neurons run active hot neurons on GPU run active cold neurons on CPU transfer cold-neuron outputs to GPU merge GPU and CPU results
The model is still the same model. PowerInfer is changing the runtime path, not replacing the LLM with a smaller model. Single-Layer ExecutionThe single-layer example is the easiest way to understand the runtime.
In the example, neurons 3, 5, and 7 are classified as hot offline and are stored on GPU. At runtime, the predictor says neurons 3, 4, and 5 are active. The GPU computes 3 and 5. The CPU computes 4. Neuron 7 is hot but predicted inactive, so it is skipped. After CPU computation finishes, its output is transferred to GPU and merged with the GPU result. This is why PowerInfer needs three pieces to work together:
The offline hot/cold split controls memory placement. The online predictor controls which neurons are computed for a particular token. The hybrid executor overlaps CPU and GPU work and merges partial results.
If any piece is weak, the design loses its advantage. A bad predictor computes too much or misses useful neurons. A bad placement policy leaves hot work on CPU. A bad executor spends the saved compute on synchronization. Adaptive PredictorsPowerInfer inherits the idea of activation predictors from DejaVu, but local deployment changes the predictor budget. Fixed-size predictors can be too large. The paper gives a concrete example: predictors for OPT-175B would require around 27 GB of GPU memory, more than an RTX 4090 has. The paper’s solution is to size predictors according to layer sparsity and skewness. Sparse, highly skewed layers need smaller predictors because the active set is easier to identify. Dense or less skewed layers need larger predictors.
Figure 9 shows the relationship for OPT-175B at a guaranteed 95% predictor accuracy level. Higher sparsity generally permits smaller predictors, while the error bars reflect skewness differences inside layers. Later, the evaluation reports predictor sizes for several models.
The predictor ratio is not free, but it is bounded. The paper reports that predictor parameters are about 7.09% of model weights on average, and predictor execution contributes less than 10% of total inference time. Placement PolicyThe placement policy is more subtle than “put the hottest neurons on GPU.” The GPU has limited memory and high bandwidth. The CPU has more memory and lower compute throughput. PCIe transfer is expensive. A placement policy therefore needs to balance:
Factor Why it matters
Activation frequency Hot neurons are likely to be used often
Neuron impact Some neurons matter more to model output
GPU memory capacity The hot set cannot exceed available VRAM
CPU-GPU transfer Too much split work can create communication overhead
Layer structure Partial placement inside a layer must still be executable efficiently
The paper formulates this as an integer linear programming problem. The objective is to maximize the impact of neurons placed on GPU while satisfying memory and communication constraints. That offline solver is what turns the activation profile into an actual memory layout. The practical reading: PowerInfer is a cache placement system for neurons, but the cache item is not only chosen by frequency. It also needs to respect layer-level execution cost. Neuron-Aware OperatorsNormal sparse kernels are not automatically a good fit here. The sparsity is dynamic, neuron-granular, and split across CPU and GPU. Converting dense matrices into generic sparse formats at runtime can erase the win. PowerInfer implements neuron-aware operators that directly compute activated neurons and their weights. On GPU, the operator maps individual activated neurons to thread blocks. On CPU, the operator assigns activated neuron work to available CPU cores.
Figure 16 compares PowerInfer’s operators with dense computation, PyTorch sparse on CPU, and PIT on GPU. The CPU result is the most striking: PyTorch sparse does not beat dense computation until sparsity is above 87%, while PowerInfer’s CPU operator beats dense even below 10% sparsity. On GPU, PowerInfer is close to PIT, but PowerInfer’s advantage is that the same framework supports hybrid CPU-GPU execution. Evaluation SetupThe evaluation uses two local PC configurations.
Setup CPU Host memory GPU PCIe
PC-High Intel i9-13900K, eight 5.4 GHz cores 192 GB, 67.2 GB/s RTX 4090, 24 GB PCIe 4.0, 64 GB/s
PC-Low Intel i7-12700K, eight 4.9 GHz cores 64 GB, 38.4 GB/s RTX 2080Ti, 11 GB PCIe 3.0, 32 GB/s
The tested models cover ReLU, ReGLU, SwiGLU, and dReLU variants.
Table 3 is useful because it explains the result spread. OPT and Falcon are highly sparse. LLaMA2-ReGLU is less sparse but still favorable. SwiGLU models have lower sparsity, so PowerInfer still helps but with smaller speedups. The baselines are llama.cpp and SpecInfer. The paper also analyzes FlexGen and DejaVu earlier, but they are not the main end-to-end baselines because their latency is poor in this local, batch-small setting. FP16 ResultsThe main FP16 result is batch size 1 generation speed, which matches the local interactive setting better than a throughput-oriented server benchmark.
On PC-High with RTX 4090, the paper reports an average PowerInfer generation speed of 8.32 tokens/s and a peak of 16.06 tokens/s. It reports average speedups of 7.23x over llama.cpp and 6.19x over SpecInfer, with Falcon-40B reaching up to 11.69x over llama.cpp.
On PC-Low with RTX 2080Ti, PowerInfer still improves performance, but the margin is smaller because the 11 GB GPU can host fewer hot neurons. The paper reports average speedups of 4.71x over llama.cpp and 5.97x over SpecInfer, with peaks of 7.06x and 7.47x. This is a useful boundary condition. PowerInfer benefits from GPU memory even though it is designed for limited VRAM. If the GPU is too small relative to the model, more hot neurons spill to CPU and the CPU becomes the bottleneck. Where The Work RunsFigure 12 explains why PowerInfer is faster than layer-level hybrid offloading.
The paper defines neuron load as the proportion of activated neuron computations executed by each device. On PC-High, PowerInfer increases the GPU’s share from about 20% in llama.cpp to about 70%. This is the runtime effect of hot-neuron placement: the GPU gets the common work even though the whole model does not fit in VRAM. On PC-Low, the GPU share can fall. The paper gives the example of running a roughly 60 GB model on an 11 GB RTX 2080Ti, where the GPU handles about 42% of the neuron load because it cannot hold enough hot neurons. Long Input And INT4Long prompts change the behavior. During prefill, many tokens are processed together, and their combined active-neuron set is less sparse. PowerInfer switches to dense GPU computation in prefill, then uses sparse hybrid execution during generation.
For 1.5K input length and 256 output length on PC-High, the paper still reports 3.47x to 5.69x speedup over llama.cpp. This is not as clean as single-token decode, but it shows that the system is not only a short-prompt trick. The paper also evaluates INT4 models.
With INT4 quantization, PC-High reaches 13.20 tokens/s on average and 29.08 tokens/s at peak. The average speedup over llama.cpp is 2.89x, with a maximum of 4.28x. On PC-Low, the average speedup is 5.01x and the peak is 8.00x. The OPT-175B result is especially interesting: PowerInfer nearly reaches 2 tokens/s on PC-High and is 2.66x faster than llama.cpp. Quantization and PowerInfer are complementary. Quantization reduces the memory footprint of every weight. PowerInfer changes where and whether neuron computations happen. Batching BoundaryPowerInfer is aimed at small-batch local serving. The batch-size result makes that explicit.
On Falcon-40B with PC-High, the paper reports strong speedups when batch size is below 32, with an average 6.08x improvement over llama.cpp. At batch size 32, PowerInfer still reports 4.38x speedup, but the ratio declines as batch size grows. The reason is joint activation. With more requests in a batch, the union of active neurons grows. Eventually the batch activates enough of the model that sparsity is less useful. This is why PowerInfer should not be read as a replacement for high-throughput datacenter batching systems. It is a local, latency-sensitive path. AblationThe ablation separates three ideas:
+PO: add predictors and neuron-aware operators, but keep layer-wise execution. +Engine: allow GPU and CPU to process neurons from the same layer concurrently. +Policy: add the optimized placement policy from the offline solver.
The paper reports:
Variant Bamboo-7B speedup Falcon-40B speedup
+PO 1.87x 3.32x
+Engine 2.60x 7.80x
+Policy 3.62x 11.69x
The large jump from +PO to +Engine shows that neuron sparsity alone is not enough. The runtime must split work inside a layer so the GPU and CPU are both useful. The final jump from +Engine to +Policy shows that random neuron placement wastes GPU memory and creates bad communication patterns. Predictor Overhead And AccuracyPrediction is not free, but it is small enough in the measured setting.
Figure 17 shows predictor overhead on PC-Low. The paper reports that online predictor execution is less than 10% of total inference time on average. This matters because a perfect sparsity plan would be useless if the predictor cost were comparable to the skipped MLP work. The paper also evaluates model accuracy after using predictors. The short version is that the reported benchmark averages remain close to the original models. This does not mean misprediction is harmless. It means the missed neurons tend to have small contribution in the evaluated tasks, and the predictors were sized to keep perplexity close to baseline. RTX 4090 Versus A100The headline comparison is not “4090 beats A100.” It is more careful: PowerInfer narrows the gap between a local consumer GPU setup and a server GPU that can hold the whole model.
The paper compares PowerInfer on RTX 4090 with vLLM on an 80 GB A100 for OPT-30B and Falcon-40B. With input length 1, llama.cpp on 4090 is 93% and 92% slower than vLLM on A100, while PowerInfer reduces the gap to 18% and 23%. With input length 64, PowerInfer reduces the gap to 28% and 29%. This result is the strongest systems message in the paper. The 4090 does not magically become an A100. The CPU still becomes a bottleneck in some cases. But neuron-level locality makes the consumer-GPU setup much closer than layer offloading can. What I Would Check In A ReproductionFor a real reproduction, I would measure these items separately:
Measurement Why it matters
Per-layer activation sparsity Decides whether PowerInfer is applicable
Hot-neuron overlap across tasks Tests whether offline placement generalizes
Predictor false negatives Missed active neurons can hurt accuracy
Predictor runtime and memory Predictor overhead can consume the saved budget
GPU/CPU neuron load split Shows whether the GPU is actually doing the common work
PCIe transfer volume Verifies that the system is not secretly transfer-bound
Prefill versus decode latency Sparsity is much cleaner during token-by-token generation
Batch size sweep Finds where joint activation destroys sparsity
The most important test is distribution shift. If a new workload activates a different hot set, an offline policy from Wikipedia may be less effective. The paper’s task-overlap result is encouraging, but a deployment should still profile on representative prompts. LimitationsPowerInfer has clear boundaries:
It works best when MLP activation sparsity is high. ReLU-family models are the best fit. Larger batches reduce the advantage because the union of active neurons grows. Long prefill is less sparse than single-token decode, so the generation phase carries most of the win. The system needs an offline profiling, predictor training, and placement step per model. Predictor errors are acceptable only if missed neurons have low output impact. CPU execution can become the bottleneck when the GPU cannot host enough hot neurons. The design is more complex than quantization or simple layer offloading.
The paper is therefore not a universal serving recipe. It is a strong design for one important corner: large-model, low-latency, small-batch inference on a local machine with limited GPU memory and enough CPU memory. TakeawayPowerInfer reframes local LLM serving as a locality problem. Instead of asking only “how do I make the model smaller?”, it asks:
Which parts of the model are usually needed for the next token, and where should those parts live?
That makes the paper complementary to quantization, KV-cache paging, and speculative decoding. PowerInfer’s useful lesson is that activation sparsity is not only an arithmetic shortcut. When the hot set is stable, it becomes a memory-placement primitive.

entry.title: Primer: Searching Transformer Primitives
entry.content:
So D R, Mańke W, Liu H, Dai Z, Shazeer N, Le Q V. Primer: Searching for Efficient Transformers for Language Modeling.
Paper Primer is a useful AutoML paper because its output is not an opaque architecture that only works inside one search codebase. The search finds two small Transformer block changes that are easy to reimplement: squared ReLU in the feed-forward network and depthwise convolution in the attention projections. That makes the paper more interesting than a normal “NAS beats baseline” result. The search acts as an idea generator, and the real contribution is the evidence that the discovered primitives transfer across codebases, datasets, hardware, and larger model sizes. All figures and tables below are cropped from the original paper PDF. Search Over ProgramsPrimer searches over decoder-block programs written from TensorFlow-style primitives. A candidate architecture is represented as a DNA. The DNA contains subprograms, each subprogram contains instructions, and those instructions are translated into TensorFlow code.
This is a lower-level search space than most NAS work. Instead of choosing only a layer type or a macro cell topology, the search can compose primitive operations inside the Transformer block. That is why the final result can look like a small local edit rather than a brand-new model family. The search objective is still pragmatic: evaluate candidates on an auto-regressive language modeling proxy task, then keep the architectural ideas that improve compute efficiency without requiring a new optimizer recipe. The Two Useful ChangesThe paper names the simpler, easy-to-adopt variant Primer-EZ. It keeps the two changes that explain most of the gains:
Replace feed-forward ReLU with squared ReLU. Add spatial depthwise convolution after the Q, K, and V projections in multi-head attention.
The left diagram is Multi-DConv-Head Attention, or MDHA. After each per-head Q, K, and V projection, Primer applies a causal 3x1 depthwise convolution along the sequence dimension. This injects a small amount of local mixing before attention. It does not remove attention, and it does not change the global attention path. The middle diagram is the feed-forward change. The ordinary activation is replaced with . The shape is simple, but it changes the activation’s asymptotic behavior and overlaps with some of the benefits that gated linear unit variants try to capture.
The right plot in this figure is the part I would pay attention to. In the paper’s C4 language-modeling comparison, squared ReLU is better than ReLU, GELU, Swish, ReGLU, and SwiGLU under the reported setup. That does not mean squared ReLU dominates everywhere, but it explains why the authors considered it a reusable primitive instead of a search artifact. Search-Task EvidenceThe first empirical check is the LM1B proxy task with roughly 35M-parameter models. The paper compares vanilla Transformer, Transformer+GELU, Transformer++, Primer, and Primer-EZ across Tensor2Tensor, T5, TPUv2, and V100 settings.
Speedup here means compute needed to reach the same quality as the vanilla Transformer baseline trained for the full budget. On the search task, Primer and Primer-EZ are consistently above 1.7x.
Some exact rows from the table:
Tensor2Tensor on TPUv2: vanilla Transformer reaches 35.44 PPLX, Primer reaches 33.77, and Primer-EZ reaches 33.53 with a 2.34x speedup. Tensor2Tensor on V100: vanilla Transformer reaches 37.19 PPLX, Primer reaches 35.06, and Primer-EZ reaches 35.16 with a 2.03x speedup. T5 on TPUv2: vanilla Transformer reaches 23.30 PPLX, Primer reaches 22.71, and Primer-EZ reaches 22.62 with a 1.75x speedup.
Two details matter. First, Primer-EZ is not slower because of the extra depthwise convolution; its step rate is slightly lower in some rows, but the quality gain more than pays for it. Second, the result transfers from Tensor2Tensor to T5. That is a stronger signal than a single-codebase search win. Scaling-Law ViewThe authors then ask whether the gain survives when model size and training compute vary. They sweep layer count, model width, feed-forward projection ratio, and training budget, then plot validation loss versus TPUv2 hours.
The key visual claim is that the lines remain roughly parallel in log-log space. Primer is not just better at one point; it shifts the loss-compute curve. When curves are parallel, a vertical improvement can be interpreted as a compute reduction at a fixed target quality. This is also where the paper’s argument becomes more deployment-relevant.
