A fixed final perplexity target is common in real training decisions: if a model variant reaches that target earlier, it saves accelerator time even if each step is not dramatically faster. Transfer Beyond The ProxyProxy-task NAS results often fail when moved to larger data, larger budgets, or different implementation stacks. Primer spends a lot of the paper showing the opposite direction: the same primitives continue to help on C4, PG19, Switch Transformer, and Synthesizer variants.
The C4 and PG19 bars are the cleanest transfer result. Primer and Primer-EZ remain more efficient than the baselines after moving from the small LM1B search setup to larger datasets and longer training. The Switch and Synthesizer cases are also useful because they show the primitives are not only compatible with vanilla dense Transformers. The larger T5-scale comparison is especially direct. The paper copies the original T5 auto-regressive language-modeling setup at 537M parameters and compares the compute needed to hit target perplexities.
Target PPLX Model Steps TPUv3 hours
13.25 Original T5 1M 15.7K
13.25 T5++ 251K 4.6K
13.25 Primer 207K 3.8K
12.69 T5++ 1M 16.5K
12.69 Primer 480K 8.3K
12.35 Primer 1M 17.3K
At the original T5 quality target, Primer reaches parity with about 3.8K TPUv3 hours instead of 15.7K. The paper reports this as roughly 4.2x less compute than the original T5 architecture.
The compute-saving curve is worth reading carefully. The saving factor grows as training continues because the Primer and T5 perplexity curves separate asymptotically. This also means the reported saving depends on the target quality. The higher the quality target, the more important the shape of the whole training curve becomes. One-Shot Transfer At Larger ScaleThe last main experiment moves to 1.9B parameters and one-shot downstream evaluation, following the style of GPT-3-style pretraining evaluation. This is not a direct GPT-3 comparison; it is a controlled comparison between Transformer+GELU and Primer under the paper’s setup.
Primer with 24K TPUv4 hours roughly matches Transformer+GELU with 72K TPUv4 hours on the averaged pretraining and one-shot bars. With the same 72K-hour budget, Primer is ahead.
The per-task grid is noisier than the averaged figure, as expected. The useful conclusion is not that Primer wins every task. The useful conclusion is that the training-efficiency gain is not limited to validation perplexity; it mostly carries into downstream one-shot task scores. Which Pieces Actually Matter?One reason I like this paper is that it does not stop at “the searched model is better.” It runs insertion and ablation studies to see which modifications are robust.
In the insertion study, each modification is added to a vanilla Transformer. In the ablation study, each modification is removed from Primer. Positive values mean the modification is beneficial under the paper’s normalization. The result separates “found by search” from “worth recommending.” A larger 12x feed-forward projection helps at this small scale, but the paper does not recommend it as the simple transferable recipe. The two robust and easy pieces are MDHA and squared ReLU, which become Primer-EZ. Full Program ViewThe appendix expands the full Transformer and Primer programs into primitive operations. This figure is dense, but it is a useful reminder of what the search actually changed.
The orange nodes are Primer’s differences. Some of them are more complicated than the two Primer-EZ edits. That is the reason Primer-EZ matters: it turns a searched program into a small recipe a practitioner can implement without importing the whole search system. Engineering Notes And LimitsPrimer is strongest as evidence for primitive-level architecture search, not as a universal Transformer replacement.
The search task is small: about 35M parameters, LM1B, and short sequences. The paper does run larger transfer experiments, but the discovered primitives still come from a proxy setting. The main focus is decoder-only auto-regressive language modeling. The paper’s appendix discusses masked language modeling, but the authors explicitly treat encoder or encoder-decoder search as future work. Depthwise convolution inside attention projections is not free. Whether MDHA helps wall-clock latency depends on the runtime kernel, sequence length, batch size, and hardware. The paper reports training compute savings, but an inference system still needs direct measurement. Squared ReLU is simple enough to try almost anywhere, but activation changes can interact with initialization, normalization, optimizer settings, and mixed precision.
The broader lesson is that NAS can be most useful when it returns simple hypotheses. Primer’s search found candidates, but the paper’s value comes from the follow-up: transfer tests, ablations, scaling curves, and a simplified recipe. TakeawayPrimer is not important because it discovered a mysterious architecture. It is important because it shows that searching at the primitive level can surface small Transformer edits that humans can understand, ablate, and reuse. The practical recipe is Primer-EZ: use squared ReLU in the feed-forward block and add causal depthwise convolution after Q, K, and V projections. The practical caution is that the recipe should be benchmarked in the target codebase. The paper makes a strong case that it transfers, but the real unit of evidence is still measured compute, not architectural elegance.

entry.title: Q8BERT: 8-bit Quantization-Aware Training for BERT
entry.content:
Paper: Q8BERT: Quantized 8Bit BERT Code: NLP Architect Q8BERT is a compact paper, but it is a useful baseline for reading later BERT quantization work. The main question is practical:
If we are allowed to run quantization-aware fine-tuning, can BERT’s dominant matrix multiplications and embedding tables be moved to INT8 with small task accuracy loss?
The answer is mostly yes. Q8BERT quantizes the weights of BERT’s embedding and fully connected layers to 8-bit integers, simulates the quantized path during fine-tuning, and keeps higher-risk nonlinear operators such as Softmax, LayerNorm, and GELU in FP32. That makes Q8BERT different from I-BERT:
Q8BERT is an 8-bit quantization-aware training baseline for the GEMM-heavy parts of BERT. I-BERT later asks for integer-only inference and replaces Softmax, GELU, and LayerNorm with integer approximations. BinaryBERT later goes to the opposite extreme: 1-bit weight compression with distillation and special initialization.
All crops below are taken from the original 2019 PDF. The ProblemBERT-Base has about 110M parameters. BERT-Large has about 334M parameters. In FP32, that means large memory footprint, high bandwidth demand, and expensive feed-forward computation during inference. For latency-sensitive NLP services, this is not just a training cost problem; it is a production deployment problem. Q8BERT’s target is conservative: stay at 8 bits, keep the original BERT architecture, and use quantization-aware training during downstream fine-tuning.
The abstract already states the scope: compress BERT by 4x with minimal accuracy loss and make the resulting model suitable for hardware with optimized 8-bit integer arithmetic. The 4x number is straightforward. Moving most model weights from FP32 to INT8 reduces storage from 4 bytes per parameter to 1 byte per parameter. Since the paper quantizes all fully connected and embedding weights, which account for more than 99% of the model weights, the total model footprint approaches this 4x reduction. What Is QuantizedThe implementation goal is narrow and clear:
Component Q8BERT treatment
Embedding layer weights Quantized to INT8
Fully connected layer weights Quantized to INT8
FC input activations Fake-quantized during training; INT8 path for inference
GEMM accumulation INT32 accumulation
Bias Quantized to INT32
Softmax Kept in FP32
LayerNorm Kept in FP32
GELU Kept in FP32
This is why I read Q8BERT as a practical partial-integer inference paper, not an integer-only inference paper. It attacks the dominant memory and GEMM cost, but it does not eliminate floating-point islands from the Transformer block.
The implementation section is explicit: quantized embedding and FC layers replace the original layers, while Softmax, LayerNorm, and GELU remain FP32 because they require higher precision. Why 8-bit GEMM Is The Main TargetBERT inference is dominated by dense matrix multiplications:
Q/K/V projections in self-attention; output projection after attention; the two feed-forward network linear layers; embedding lookup storage and movement.
INT8 helps in two ways:
Weight memory shrinks, reducing model footprint and memory bandwidth. Matrix multiplication can use integer hardware paths, such as VNNI-style instructions or other accelerator INT8 kernels.
The paper cites prior transformer INT8 GEMM work reporting 3.7x speedup over FP32 matrix multiplication on Intel Xeon Cascade Lake VNNI. Q8BERT does not prove a universal end-to-end 3.7x BERT speedup; it uses that hardware fact to justify targeting the GEMM-heavy parts of BERT. This distinction matters. End-to-end latency depends on operator coverage, layout conversion, dequantization/requantization boundaries, memory movement, batch size, and backend implementation. Q8BERT’s accuracy result is strong evidence that BERT tolerates this INT8 GEMM path under QAT, but deployment speed still depends on the runtime. Symmetric Linear QuantizationQ8BERT uses symmetric linear quantization for weights and activations. The paper writes the integer quantizer as:
with:
For 8-bit signed quantization, . The paper’s is a multiplicative scaling factor from real value to integer value. This is the reciprocal convention of the common “real = scale * integer” notation.
The weight scale is computed from the max absolute weight:
The activation scale is based on values observed during training:
The symmetric choice removes the zero-point term. This simplifies integer GEMM because the quantized value is centered around zero: asym: q = round(x / s) + zsym: q = round(x * S)
In an asymmetric formulation, matrix multiplication may need correction terms involving zero points. Q8BERT intentionally uses the symmetric case to simplify the inference path. QAT During Fine-tuningThe central training choice is to insert fake quantization into the fine-tuning graph. Forward propagation sees quantized values, but the underlying trainable parameters remain floating point. Fake quantization creates the same rounding/clipping noise that the model will see at inference. During backpropagation, Q8BERT uses the straight-through estimator:
This is the standard QAT compromise. Rounding is not differentiable, but if the backward pass treats it as identity, the model can adapt its FP32 latent weights to produce quantization-friendly forward activations. The practical pipeline is:
Start from a pre-trained BERT checkpoint. Replace embedding and FC layers with quantized versions. During fine-tuning, run fake quantization for weights and activations. Keep latent weights in FP32 for optimization. Export INT8 weights and INT8 activation scales for inference. Run quantized embedding/FC/GEMM while keeping Softmax, LayerNorm, and GELU in FP32.
QAT is done during downstream fine-tuning, not during the original large-scale pre-training. This is why the paper is practical: it does not require pre-training BERT again. Dynamic Quantization BaselineThe paper compares QAT with a dynamic quantization baseline. In this baseline, activations are quantized during inference, and the activation scale is computed from each incoming activation tensor using a max-absolute rule, similar to the weight scale. The distinction is:
Method Scale source Why it behaves differently
DQ Current tensor max abs at inference The task fine-tuning stage never sees quantization noise
QAT EMA statistics from training Fine-tuning adapts to rounding and clipping noise
The authors find that dynamic quantization is consistently worse. This is not surprising: BERT is fine-tuned for a downstream task, and the quantized model needs that fine-tuning stage to see the same perturbations it will face at inference. Main ResultsThe paper evaluates on GLUE tasks and SQuAD v1.1. It reports the mean and standard deviation over five runs. Most experiments use BERT-Base, with selected BERT-Large rows marked as Large.
The important pattern is that QAT stays close to FP32 while DQ often drops more:
Task FP32 baseline QAT INT8 DQ INT8
CoLA 58.48 58.48 56.74
MRPC F1 90.00 89.56 87.88
QNLI 90.30 90.62 89.34
QQP F1 87.84 87.96 84.98
RTE 69.70 68.78 63.32
SST-2 92.36 92.24 91.04
STS-B 89.62 89.04 87.66
SQuAD v1.1 F1 88.46 87.74 80.02
QAT sometimes slightly exceeds the baseline due to run variance, for example QNLI and QQP in the table. I would not over-interpret those small gains. The main claim is that QAT preserves accuracy, not that INT8 improves BERT. Relative ErrorTable 2 is a cleaner way to read the result because it reports the relative accuracy drop from quantization.
QAT has less than 1% relative error on every listed task except RTE:
Method Typical behavior
DQ Often multiple percent relative drop; 9.13% on RTE and 9.54% on SQuAD
QAT Usually below 1% relative drop; 1.32% on RTE and 0.81% on SQuAD
RTE is a small dataset and tends to have higher variance. The QAT row still improves substantially over DQ, but the relative drop is larger than the other GLUE tasks. What The Paper Does Not ClaimQ8BERT is easy to overstate. The paper does not claim:
post-training quantization is enough for BERT; every Transformer operator runs in INT8; Softmax, LayerNorm, and GELU are solved in integer arithmetic; end-to-end latency must improve by the same ratio as INT8 GEMM; 4-bit or 2-bit BERT is covered by the same recipe.
The actual claim is narrower and more defensible:
With quantization-aware downstream fine-tuning, the GEMM-heavy embedding and fully connected layers of BERT can be quantized to INT8 while preserving most task accuracy.
This is why Q8BERT is still useful. It establishes a strong simple baseline for 8-bit QAT. Any more complex BERT quantization paper should explain what extra constraint it solves: lower bit-width, no task fine-tuning, integer-only nonlinear ops, better latency, or smaller memory. Relationship To I-BERTI-BERT directly addresses Q8BERT’s main limitation. Q8BERT leaves Softmax, LayerNorm, and GELU in FP32. I-BERT replaces them with integer-friendly approximations and keeps the whole inference path in integer arithmetic. The comparison:
Aspect Q8BERT I-BERT
Main goal 8-bit BERT with QAT Integer-only BERT inference
Linear layers INT8 GEMM INT8 GEMM
Embeddings INT8 INT8
GELU FP32 Integer polynomial approximation
Softmax FP32 Integer exponential approximation
LayerNorm FP32 Integer sqrt and normalization
Practical message 8-bit QAT is enough for accuracy Operator coverage matters for integer-only deployment
So Q8BERT is not obsolete; it is a different operating point. If the backend already handles mixed INT8/FP32 efficiently, Q8BERT is a simple baseline. If the target hardware prefers integer-only execution, I-BERT’s stricter graph coverage becomes necessary. Implementation NotesA faithful reproduction should pay attention to quantization boundaries. It is not enough to say “BERT is INT8.” The questions are:
Are embedding tables stored and returned as INT8? Are Q/K/V, attention output, and FFN matrix multiplications using INT8 inputs and weights? Are accumulators INT32? How are bias tensors quantized? Where does the graph dequantize before Softmax, LayerNorm, or GELU? Are activation scales static from training EMA, dynamic per batch, or calibrated post-training? Does the exported graph run on an actual INT8 backend, or only evaluate fake quantization?
The last point is important. Fake-quantized evaluation measures numerical robustness. It does not by itself measure speed. Speed requires an execution backend that maps the quantized FC layers to optimized INT8 kernels. Reproduction ChecklistFor a clean reproduction, I would separate accuracy, model size, and runtime:
Check What to measure
Accuracy GLUE/SQuAD metrics for FP32, DQ, and QAT over multiple seeds
Model size Serialized parameter footprint before and after INT8 export
Operator coverage Which layers run INT8, INT32, or FP32
GEMM speed Isolated FC/GEMM latency on the target hardware
End-to-end latency Full BERT request latency with tokenization excluded and included
Dequant overhead Cast/requant time around Softmax, LayerNorm, and GELU
The expected result is not just “the model is 4x smaller.” A deployment-oriented reproduction should show whether the model is also faster under the intended batch size and hardware backend. TakeawayQ8BERT is the clean 8-bit QAT baseline for BERT. It shows that if downstream fine-tuning is available, BERT’s embedding and fully connected layers can tolerate INT8 quantization with small accuracy loss across GLUE and SQuAD. The most important caveat is operator coverage. Q8BERT quantizes the parts that dominate parameters and GEMM compute, but it keeps Softmax, LayerNorm, and GELU in FP32. That makes it practical and accurate, but not integer-only. Later papers like I-BERT should be read as tightening this exact gap.

entry.title: Q-BERT: Hessian Based Ultra Low Precision Quantization of BERT
entry.content:
Paper: Q-BERT: Hessian Based Ultra Low Precision Quantization of BERT Q-BERT is an early but still useful paper for understanding why transformer quantization cannot be treated as a simple “pick one bit-width for every matrix” problem. The paper studies fine-tuned BERTBASE models with second-order information, then uses that signal to decide where low precision is safe and where the model needs more bits. The two main tools are Hessian-aware mixed precision and group-wise quantization. My reading focus is not only the headline compression number. The important part is the failure mode: BERT layers, attention heads, feed-forward blocks, word embeddings, and position embeddings do not react to quantization in the same way. Q-BERT is valuable because it makes that statement measurable. MotivationThe deployment problem in the paper is straightforward. BERTBASE is accurate on downstream NLP tasks, but it is expensive for edge inference. The paper reports the full-precision parameter footprint as roughly 91 MB for the embedding table, 325 MB for the encoder stack, and only about 0.01 MB for the output/classifier layer. Since the classifier is negligible, Q-BERT focuses on quantizing the embedding and encoder parameters. The paper evaluates four task families:
Task Dataset Metric used in the paper
Sentiment classification SST-2 Accuracy
Natural language inference MNLI Matched / mismatched accuracy
Named entity recognition CoNLL-03 F1
Machine reading comprehension SQuAD EM and F1
The baseline approach, called DirectQ in the paper, quantizes BERT without Hessian-aware mixed precision or group-wise quantization. DirectQ is useful as a sanity check because it shows how much accuracy is lost when the quantization recipe ignores transformer structure. The gap is huge at low bit-widths, especially on SQuAD. BERT Quantization SetupThe fine-tuned BERT model is written as an embedding module, a stack of encoder layers, and an output layer. For an input sentence and label , the paper writes the training loss as:
Here is the embedding table, are the Transformer encoder layers, is the classifier, and denotes the collection of these parameters. Q-BERT leaves in full precision because its size is too small to matter. The quantizer maps a real value to one of discrete values:
The paper uses uniform quantization rather than a learned non-uniform codebook. This is a hardware-minded choice: uniform quantization is easier to implement with integer arithmetic and dequantization tables. For a tensor , the forward quantization process in the appendix is:
The interval does not have to be the full min-max range of the tensor. It can be a clipped range that sacrifices outliers to represent the majority of values more accurately. During quantization-aware fine-tuning, the paper uses the straight-through estimator to backpropagate through the non-differentiable quantization operator. The second-order intuition is the usual local loss approximation:
If a layer has a sharper local curvature, the same perturbation from quantization should cause a larger loss increase. This is why Hessian information can guide bit allocation. Hessian-Aware Mixed PrecisionQ-BERT builds on the HAWQ idea: layers with larger Hessian spectrum are more sensitive to quantization and should receive more bits. The challenge is that each BERTBASE encoder layer has millions of parameters, so explicitly materializing a Hessian matrix is not practical. Q-BERT does not form the Hessian. It estimates the top eigenvalue with Hessian-vector products and power iteration. For the first encoder layer, let be the gradient with respect to , and let be a random vector with the same dimension. The Hessian-vector product is computed by differentiating :
The middle term disappears because is independent of . This makes the computation matrix-free: one can get through automatic differentiation, then iterate.
Algorithm 1 in the paper. The method repeatedly computes an inner product , backpropagates it to get , and normalizes the vector for the next power-iteration step. The paper computes the top Hessian eigenvalue distribution for each encoder layer using 10 runs, each run using 10 percent of the training dataset. This detail matters. A single average top eigenvalue is not stable enough for BERT tasks, especially SQuAD.
Top Hessian eigenvalue distributions across the 12 BERTBASE encoder layers. Middle layers tend to have larger values and larger variance; the last few layers are often less sensitive. Instead of using only the mean top eigenvalue, Q-BERT defines the layer sensitivity score as:
Here is the empirical distribution of top eigenvalues for encoder layer . Taking both mean and standard deviation is a practical change from earlier Hessian-aware CNN quantization. The paper observes that NLP tasks can have high variance in eigenvalues across data subsets, so assigning bits from the mean alone can be misleading. The loss landscape figures make the same point visually. Flatter layers can be pushed to lower precision, while sharper or unstable layers need protection.
MNLI and CoNLL-03 loss landscapes along the first two dominant Hessian eigenvector directions. The flatter basins are the layers where aggressive quantization is less damaging. SQuAD is the outlier. The paper reports that the fine-tuned SQuAD model has not reached a clean local minimum: the visualized landscape contains negative curvature directions, and the eigenvalue distribution is much more unstable. This is one reason SQuAD suffers the largest drop under ultra-low-bit quantization.
SQuAD loss landscapes. The stopping point is not sitting in the same kind of local quadratic bowl as the other tasks, which helps explain why SQuAD is harder to quantize. Once is computed, Q-BERT sorts the encoder layers by sensitivity and assigns higher precision to more sensitive layers. The bit assignment is task-specific because the Hessian statistics are task-specific.
The appendix bit assignment for 2/3-bit Q-BERTMP. The common pattern is that middle encoder layers receive more 3-bit assignments, while early and late layers can often stay at 2 bits. This is a useful table to read slowly. For SST-2, layers 4 to 9 are assigned 3 bits while layers 1 to 3 and 10 to 12 are assigned 2 bits. For MNLI, layers 5 to 8 get 3 bits. For CoNLL-03, the higher-bit region shifts toward layers 2 to 5. SQuAD gives 3 bits to layers 4 to 9. The bit pattern is not universal; it is derived from the downstream fine-tuned model. Group-Wise QuantizationMixed precision decides how many bits a layer or module gets. Group-wise quantization decides what dynamic range those bits should cover. The core problem is that a Transformer attention matrix is not homogeneous. In multi-head self-attention, each head has its own key, query, value, and output projections. For a sequence with tokens and embedding dimension , the paper writes the attention computation for one head as:
For BERTBASE, and the number of heads . Each head has hidden dimension . Across , , , and , the multi-head attention block contains:
output-neuron groups that can have different value ranges. If the entire matrix shares one quantization range, a few high-magnitude groups can dominate the scale and reduce resolution for the rest. Q-BERT therefore partitions matrices into groups, each group having its own quantization range and lookup table.
Group-wise quantization illustrated on value matrices. Layer-wise quantization gives the whole tensor one range; group-wise quantization gives each head or sub-head group its own range. There are three granularity levels in the figure:
Layer-wise: the whole 3D tensor uses one quantization range. Head-wise: each attention head matrix uses one range. Finer group-wise: each head matrix is further partitioned along output neurons.
The paper evaluates the number of groups directly.
Group-count ablation with 4-bit weights, 8-bit embeddings, and 8-bit activations. The paper uses 128 groups for the main experiments. The numbers are clear:
Number of groups SST-2 MNLI-m/mm CoNLL-03
Baseline 93.00 84.00 / 84.40 95.00
1 85.67 76.69 / 77.00 89.86
12 92.31 83.30 / 83.55 94.42
128 92.66 83.89 / 84.17 94.90
768 92.78 84.00 / 84.20 94.99
Layer-wise quantization, which corresponds to one group, loses about 7 points on these tasks. Moving to 12 groups recovers most of the loss. Moving from 12 to 128 still helps. Moving from 128 to 768 gives almost no additional accuracy. The paper chooses 128 because it balances accuracy with metadata and lookup-table overhead. This is one of the most transferable lessons from Q-BERT. The exact architecture is BERT, but the idea reappears in modern LLM weight-only quantization: group size is not cosmetic. It controls how much local dynamic-range information survives. Main ResultsAll non-baseline results in the main table use 8-bit activations. Q-BERT uses 128 groups in each layer. The table compares three ideas:
DirectQ: direct quantization without group-wise quantization or mixed precision. Q-BERT: group-wise quantization with a fixed bit-width. Q-BERTMP: group-wise quantization with Hessian-aware mixed precision.
Main BERTBASE quantization results on SST-2, MNLI, CoNLL-03, and SQuAD. A compact reading of the table:
Task Baseline Strong low-bit Q-BERT result DirectQ failure mode
SST-2 93.00 Acc 92.08 Acc with 2/3-bit Q-BERTMP, 48.1 MB 2-bit DirectQ falls to 80.62
MNLI 84.00 / 84.40 Acc 81.75 / 82.29 with 2/3-bit Q-BERTMP, 46.1 MB 2-bit DirectQ falls to 53.29 / 53.32
CoNLL-03 95.00 F1 94.37 F1 with 2/3-bit Q-BERTMP, 45.0 MB 2-bit DirectQ falls to 54.50
SQuAD 81.54 EM / 88.69 F1 79.29 EM / 86.95 F1 with 2/3-bit Q-BERTMP, 48.1 MB 2-bit DirectQ falls to 4.77 / 10.32
Several observations matter more than the average compression ratio. First, 4-bit direct quantization is already weak. On SQuAD, DirectQ with 4-bit weights and 8-bit embeddings gives 66.05 EM / 77.10 F1, while Q-BERT under the same bit-width gives 80.95 EM / 88.36 F1. That is the effect of group-wise quantization and quantization-aware tuning. Second, uniform 2-bit Q-BERT is still too aggressive. Group-wise quantization helps, but it does not remove the need for mixed precision. For example, CoNLL-03 uniform 2-bit Q-BERT gets 91.06 F1, while 2/3-bit Q-BERTMP recovers to 94.37 F1. SST-2 moves from 84.63 with uniform 2-bit Q-BERT to 92.08 with 2/3-bit Q-BERTMP. Third, SQuAD is consistently harder. Even with Q-BERT, SQuAD sees the largest degradation. The Hessian analysis gives a plausible reason: the fine-tuned SQuAD model has unstable curvature and negative curvature directions, so quantization is perturbing a model that is not sitting in a clean minimum. The paper’s headline claim is that Q-BERT reaches up to 13x weight compression, 4x activation-size reduction, and 4x embedding-size reduction with at most 2.3 percent performance degradation. Reading the table, this claim is credible but conditional: it depends on QAT, group-wise quantization, task-specific Hessian analysis, and mixed precision. Why Reversed Mixed Precision FailsThe most convincing ablation is the reversed mixed-precision assignment. If Hessian-aware sorting matters, then assigning lower bits to sensitive layers and higher bits to insensitive layers should be worse at the same model size.
Reversed mixed-precision assignment. Q-BERTMP-rev uses the same total size pattern but flips the bit allocation against the Hessian-aware assignment. That is exactly what happens. On SQuAD, uniform 2-bit Q-BERT gives 69.68 EM / 79.60 F1. The reversed 2/3-bit assignment gives 69.71 EM / 79.39 F1, basically no improvement. The Hessian-aware 2/3-bit Q-BERTMP reaches 79.29 EM / 86.95 F1. The same trend appears on SST-2, MNLI, and CoNLL-03. This ablation matters because mixed precision can otherwise look like a parameter-budget trick. The reversed setting shows that the allocation signal is doing real work. Module SensitivityQ-BERT also studies which BERT modules are fragile. This section is more useful than it may look, because it separates “quantizing BERT weights” into multiple different problems.
Module sensitivity experiments. The top table isolates word and position embeddings; the bottom table compares multi-head attention with feed-forward layers. The embedding results are sharp:
8-bit word embedding and 8-bit position embedding are safe: SQuAD F1 is 88.47, close to the 88.69 baseline. 4-bit word embedding with 8-bit position embedding is still tolerable: SQuAD F1 is 87.55. 8-bit word embedding with 4-bit position embedding is bad: SQuAD F1 drops to 72.38. 4-bit word and 4-bit position embedding together are catastrophic: SQuAD F1 drops to 61.70.
The interesting part is not just that embeddings are sensitive. Position embedding is much smaller than word embedding, but it is more fragile in this experiment. The paper interprets this as evidence that positional information is especially important for natural language understanding tasks. From an engineering perspective, this is a reminder that model-size contribution and quantization sensitivity are different axes. A small module can be worth keeping at higher precision. The attention-vs-FFN experiment also has a clear conclusion. With embeddings and activations kept at 8 bits, the paper reduces either self-attention or fully connected layers by one extra bit:
1/2-bit mixed precision for self-attention and 2/3-bit mixed precision for FFN gives SQuAD F1 75.81. 2/3-bit mixed precision for self-attention and 1/2-bit mixed precision for FFN gives SQuAD F1 68.71. 2/3-bit mixed precision for both gives SQuAD F1 86.95.
So in this setup, self-attention is more robust than the feed-forward network. Reducing FFN precision hurts more. Mixed Precision for EmbeddingsThe main table uses 8-bit embeddings, so after encoder compression the embedding table becomes a large part of the remaining model size. The appendix explores a mixed embedding setting: 4-bit word embeddings and 8-bit position embeddings.
Embedding mixed-precision results. The paper uses 4-bit word embedding and 8-bit position embedding, with 128 groups for both encoder weights and embeddings. This is a good compromise if the memory target is very strict. For example:
Task 2/3-bit weights + 8-bit embeddings 2/3-bit weights + 4/8-bit embeddings
SST-2 92.08 Acc, 48.1 MB 91.51 Acc, 36.9 MB
MNLI 81.75 / 82.29 Acc, 46.1 MB 81.00 / 81.65 Acc, 34.9 MB
CoNLL-03 94.37 F1, 45.0 MB 94.45 F1, 34.4 MB
SQuAD 79.29 EM / 86.95 F1, 48.1 MB 78.68 EM / 86.49 F1, 36.9 MB
The drop is not free, but it is small enough that this setting is realistic for a tight memory budget. The key is that Q-BERT does not push position embeddings to 4 bits in this setting. It keeps the more sensitive position component at 8 bits. Attention Distribution AnalysisThe paper also checks whether the quantized model preserves attention behavior. It computes KL divergence between the attention distribution of the quantized model and the full-precision baseline, for coordinated heads on the same input. Lower KL means the quantized attention pattern is closer to the baseline.
KL divergence over attention distributions. Q-BERT stays closer to the full-precision baseline than DirectQ across tasks and layers. The qualitative result aligns with the accuracy tables. Q-BERT has consistently lower KL distance than DirectQ. This does not prove that attention distributions are the whole reason accuracy is preserved, but it is useful supporting evidence: group-wise quantization and QAT are not merely matching final labels; they also preserve more of the internal attention behavior. Implementation NotesA practical Q-BERT pipeline looks like this:
Fine-tune a full-precision BERT model on the downstream task. Compute top Hessian eigenvalue distributions per encoder layer using matrix-free power iteration. Compute . Sort layers by and assign mixed precision under the target model-size budget. Apply group-wise uniform quantization, typically with 128 groups in the paper’s experiments. Use quantization-aware fine-tuning with STE. Keep small or sensitive modules at higher precision when the memory benefit is not worth the accuracy loss.
The method is not a pure post-training quantization method. It relies on quantization-aware fine-tuning, task-specific calibration, and Hessian-vector products. It is therefore heavier than modern one-shot weight-only LLM quantization methods. The upside is that the analysis is explicit: Q-BERT tells us which layers and modules are sensitive instead of only reporting a final compressed checkpoint. There is also a hardware caveat around 3-bit execution. The paper notes that 3-bit arithmetic is not usually directly supported. A practical implementation may pack 3-bit values in memory and cast them to 4-bit or 8-bit execution units, preserving some memory-bandwidth benefit but not necessarily delivering ideal low-bit compute speedup. The 2/4-bit mixed-precision alternative is included partly for this reason. LimitationsQ-BERT should be read as a BERT-era quantization paper, not as a complete recipe for current decoder-only LLM deployment. First, the method is task-specific. The Hessian statistics are computed after downstream fine-tuning, and the bit assignment changes across SST-2, MNLI, CoNLL-03, and SQuAD. This is reasonable for fine-tuned BERT services, but it is less convenient for general-purpose foundation models that serve many tasks. Second, the paper uses QAT. That makes the results stronger than simple PTQ, but it also means extra training cost and access to task data. Third, group-wise quantization introduces scale/range metadata and lookup-table overhead. The paper’s group-count ablation is important because it shows why 128 groups is a reasonable point: 768 groups only improves accuracy by about 0.1 point while increasing overhead. Fourth, the SQuAD analysis is a warning. If the full-precision model is not at a stable local minimum, second-order quantization sensitivity becomes harder to interpret and the quantized result is worse. The paper tried changing fine-tuning hyperparameters but found SQuAD quickly overfit, so fixing that training issue was outside its scope. TakeawayThe core lesson of Q-BERT is that ultra-low-bit transformer quantization needs both sensitivity measurement and the right granularity. Hessian-aware mixed precision answers “which layers deserve more bits”; group-wise quantization answers “which sub-tensors deserve their own dynamic range.” For this paper, the most reusable ideas are:
Use curvature or another sensitivity proxy before assigning bits. Do not assume identical encoder layers have identical quantization sensitivity. Treat word embedding, position embedding, self-attention, and FFN separately. Group-wise ranges can recover most of the loss from low-bit quantization. Very low memory size does not automatically imply practical acceleration unless the hardware path supports the chosen bit format.
Q-BERT is not the final form of LLM quantization, but it is one of the clean early papers showing that transformer compression is a structured problem. The model is not one tensor; it is a set of modules with different curvature, different value distributions, and different failure modes.

entry.title: QLoRA: 4-bit LLM Fine-Tuning
entry.content:
Paper: QLoRA: Efficient Finetuning of Quantized LLMs Code: artidoro/qlora , bitsandbytes QLoRA is one of those papers that looks simple after it becomes infrastructure. The headline is “fine-tune a 65B model on one 48GB GPU”, but the useful idea is more specific: keep the pretrained base model frozen in a 4-bit storage format, dequantize it only when it participates in BF16 computation, and train LoRA adapters through that frozen quantized model. That makes QLoRA a training-memory paper more than an inference-speed paper. It does not say that every serving stack should run NF4 directly. It says that the expensive part of adapting a large language model can be moved from full-precision optimizer state over all weights to low-rank adapter updates plus a carefully quantized frozen backbone.
Figure 1 from the paper. Full fine-tuning stores and updates the whole model; LoRA freezes the base model but still keeps it in 16-bit; QLoRA freezes a 4-bit base model and trains adapters through it. Why QLoRA matteredBefore QLoRA, the common memory story was already clear:
Full fine-tuning is high quality but expensive because model weights, gradients, optimizer states, activations, and temporary buffers all have to fit. LoRA reduces trainable parameters by inserting low-rank adapter matrices, but the frozen base model still consumes 16-bit memory. Post-training quantization can reduce inference memory, but earlier low-bit training attempts often lost quality or became unstable at large LLM scale.
QLoRA connects those pieces. It keeps the large base model in a 4-bit representation, but it does not update those base weights. Gradients flow through the dequantized base computation into LoRA adapters, and only the adapters receive optimizer updates. The paper gives the strongest motivation number in the introduction: regular 16-bit fine-tuning of LLaMA-65B requires more than 780GB of GPU memory, while QLoRA brings the 65B fine-tuning footprint below 48GB without observed degradation against the 16-bit fine-tuning baselines they can compare to. That is not a minor engineering tweak; it changes the class of experiments a small lab can run. The memory accountThe model weight reduction is the obvious part, but QLoRA is careful about the full training footprint. The important buckets are:
Base model weights: frozen, stored in NF4, dequantized to BF16 for compute. LoRA adapters: trainable BF16 parameters, small compared with the base model. Adapter gradients: still need memory, but far smaller than full-model gradients. Optimizer states: only for the adapters, with paged allocation to survive spikes. Activations and temporary buffers: managed with checkpointing and paged optimizer behavior.
The appendix memory breakdown is useful because it prevents a common misunderstanding: LoRA parameters are not the only memory that matters. Even in parameter-efficient fine-tuning, gradients and activations can dominate specific steps, and the 4-bit base model is still the largest persistent object.
Figure 6 from the appendix. The paper reports QLoRA training footprints of about 6.9GB, 11.3GB, 24.7GB, and 45.0GB for 7B, 13B, 33B, and 65B LLaMA models under the stated setup. The practical reading is:
7B and 13B fine-tuning become routine on single consumer GPUs. 33B is close to a 24GB boundary, so transient memory spikes matter. 65B fits the single professional-GPU story, but only because the paper attacks weight storage, scale metadata, and optimizer spikes together.
The QLoRA layerFor one linear layer, standard LoRA starts from a frozen projection:
where is the frozen base weight, and are low-rank trainable matrices, and is the LoRA scaling factor. QLoRA changes the storage path for . The base weight is stored as NF4 plus quantization constants; when used, it is double-dequantized into the BF16 compute type. Let be the dequantized base weight:
Then the QLoRA layer is:
The key distinction is storage type versus compute type:
Storage type: usually 4-bit NF4 for the frozen base weight. Compute type: usually BF16 for the matrix multiplication and backward pass. Trainable type: LoRA adapters are trained in BF16.
This is why QLoRA is not “training a 4-bit model” in the naive sense of updating 4-bit weights. It is training adapter weights through a frozen quantized model. NF4: 4-bit storage for normally distributed weightsThe first technical contribution is NormalFloat4, or NF4. The motivation is that pretrained neural network weights are usually roughly zero-centered and normal-looking after blockwise scaling. If that assumption is good enough, then a uniform int4 grid is not the most efficient way to spend 16 representable values. NF4 uses quantile-based levels for a standard normal distribution, then normalizes the values into a fixed range. In other words, it puts more representational resolution where normal weights are likely to appear. The paper also forces an exact zero representation, which matters for padding and exact zero values. The exact NF4 codebook in the appendix is: [-1.0, -0.6961928, -0.52507305, -0.39491749, -0.28444138, -0.18477343, -0.09105004, 0.0, 0.0795803, 0.1609302, 0.2461123, 0.33791524, 0.44070983, 0.562617, 0.72295684, 1.0]
That list is a useful reminder that NF4 is not the same thing as ordinary signed int4. It is a small floating-style codebook specialized for zero-centered normal weights.
Table 2 from the paper. On Pile Common Crawl perplexity across OPT, BLOOM, LLaMA, and Pythia models, NF4 plus double quantization has the best mean perplexity among the tested 4-bit formats. The table is small but important. The reported mean perplexities are:
Int4: 34.34 Float4 (E2M1): 31.07 Float4 (E3M0): 29.48 NFloat4 + DQ: 27.41
Lower perplexity is better, and NF4 wins before any downstream instruction tuning story is added.
Figure 3 from the paper. For LLaMA models, NF4 gives better bit-for-bit zero-shot accuracy than the tested FP4 baseline, while double quantization keeps the memory budget tighter. The reason this result matters for training is simple: LoRA has to learn through the frozen base model. If quantization destroys too much signal, the adapter update has less useful information to work with. NF4 reduces that damage enough that the later LoRA stage can recover 16-bit behavior in the tested setups. Double quantization: quantize the scales tooBlockwise low-bit quantization needs scale constants. With a small block size, those constants are not free. In the paper’s main setup:
The base weight block size is 64. A 32-bit scale per 64 parameters costs bits per parameter. Double quantization stores those scale constants in an 8-bit second quantization with block size 256. The amortized scale cost becomes bits per parameter. The saving is bits per parameter, about 3GB for a 65B model.
This is an easy detail to skip, but it is one of the reasons the method actually fits large models. At 65B scale, metadata is no longer bookkeeping noise. The dequantization path is two-level:
The base weights stay in NF4 storage, the first-level quantization constants are themselves quantized, and the final matrix multiplication uses BF16 values after dequantization. Paged optimizers: protect against spikesThe third contribution is less mathematical but very practical. Paged optimizers use NVIDIA unified memory to let optimizer state move between CPU and GPU memory when a training step has an unusual memory spike. This is not advertised as a speed optimization. The paper says paging is critical for 33B and 65B QLoRA tuning on single 24GB and 48GB GPUs, but also notes that paging happens only when memory pressure appears. In their 65B analysis with batch size 16, paged optimizers had the same training speed as regular optimizers. The right mental model is:
NF4 lowers persistent model memory. Double quantization lowers quantization metadata memory. LoRA lowers trainable parameter and optimizer memory. Paged optimizers make the remaining spikes survivable.
If a method fits on average but crashes on long examples, it is not useful. QLoRA treats peak memory as the real constraint. LoRA placement matters more than rankA subtle but important result is that “use LoRA” is not enough. The paper finds that the default practice of adding LoRA only to query and value projection matrices does not match full fine-tuning for larger base models.
Figure 2 from the paper. Applying LoRA broadly across transformer layers is necessary to match the stronger 16-bit baseline on Alpaca. The practical conclusion is that adapter coverage matters. Because the LoRA parameter memory is small compared with the frozen base model and activation-related costs, QLoRA can afford to place adapters on all linear layers rather than only on a narrow subset. The rank ablation is also useful:
Figure 4 from the appendix. Once LoRA is applied broadly, the tested LoRA rank values are not strongly predictive of final performance. The paper’s default large-scale instruction tuning setup uses:
LoRA rank LoRA alpha LoRA modules on all linear layers NF4 storage with double quantization BF16 computation paged optimizers
This is the part that many reproductions get wrong: rank alone is not the main knob if adapter placement is too sparse. Does 4-bit fine-tuning recover 16-bit quality?The strongest scientific question is not whether QLoRA saves memory. It obviously does. The important question is whether training through the quantized backbone loses quality. The paper checks this in two stages:
Smaller established benchmark setups where full 16-bit fine-tuning is feasible. Larger LLaMA instruction-tuning experiments where 16-bit LoRA is used as the comparison.
Table 3 from the paper. On GLUE and Super-NaturalInstructions, 4-bit QLoRA variants replicate the 16-bit LoRA and full fine-tuning baselines. The main observation from Table 3 is not that NF4 wins every cell by a large amount. It is that the 4-bit adapter-tuning path stays in the same performance band as 16-bit fine-tuning and LoRA. That is the result QLoRA needs: the memory savings should not force a visible quality tax.
Table 4 from the paper. On LLaMA 7B to 65B models fine-tuned on Alpaca and FLAN v2, NF4 plus double quantization matches the BFloat16 LoRA mean MMLU score. The MMLU dtype comparison is concise:
BFloat16 mean: 53.0 Float4 mean: 52.2 NFloat4 + DQ mean: 53.1
This supports two separate claims:
4-bit QLoRA can match 16-bit LoRA in the tested instruction-tuning setup. NF4 is a better 4-bit storage format than the tested FP4 alternative.
Guanaco: QLoRA as an instruction-tuning toolThe paper then uses QLoRA to train a family of chat models called Guanaco. These are not just quantization benchmarks; they are instruction-tuned models trained across model sizes and datasets. The dataset result is worth reading carefully because it separates “MMLU is high” from “chatbot is good”.
Table 5 from the paper. Different instruction datasets move MMLU differently across model sizes. FLAN v2 is strong on MMLU, while OASST1/Guanaco is the stronger chatbot direction later in the paper. The important lesson is that benchmark similarity and data quality matter. FLAN v2 performs well on MMLU, but it is not the best chat dataset in the Vicuna-style evaluation. OASST1 is much smaller but better aligned with multi-turn assistant behavior. This is one reason the paper’s conclusion is stronger than “4-bit works”. QLoRA made it cheap enough to run more than 1,000 fine-tuning experiments, and that scale exposed data effects that would have been difficult to study with full fine-tuning. Vicuna benchmark resultsThe headline Guanaco result comes from the Vicuna benchmark. GPT-4 scores model responses relative to ChatGPT, and the paper reports both prompt orders because GPT-4 has an ordering bias.
Table 6 from the paper. Guanaco 65B reaches 99.3% of ChatGPT’s Vicuna benchmark score while using 4-bit model weights and 41GB of memory. Key numbers from Table 6:
Guanaco 65B: 41GB, 99.3% mean score relative to ChatGPT. Guanaco 33B: 21GB, 97.8%. Vicuna 13B: 26GB, 94.9%. Guanaco 13B: 10GB, 90.4%. Guanaco 7B: 5GB, 87.0%.
The comparison with Vicuna 13B is especially interesting. Guanaco 33B uses more parameters but lower precision, so its memory footprint is 21GB compared with Vicuna 13B at 26GB, while scoring higher in this evaluation. That points to a broader scaling tradeoff: given a fixed memory budget, it can be better to use a larger lower-precision base model than a smaller higher-precision one, as long as the quantization error is controlled. Elo ranking and evaluation caveatsThe authors do not rely only on absolute GPT-4 scores. They also run pairwise tournaments and aggregate Elo ratings from human or GPT-4 judgments.
Table 7 from the paper. Guanaco 65B and 33B are near the top of the tournament rankings, but the judge and benchmark choice still matter. The table makes Guanaco look very strong, but the caveats are part of the result:
GPT-4 is ranked first overall. Guanaco 65B has median rank 2. Guanaco 33B has median rank 4. ChatGPT-3.5 Turbo has median rank 5. The OpenAssistant benchmark favors ChatGPT more than the smaller Vicuna prompt set.
The paper reports only moderate agreement between GPT-4 and humans on the Vicuna benchmark: system-level Kendall tau is 0.43, Spearman rank correlation is 0.55, and example-level agreement with human majority vote has Fleiss kappa 0.25. That means the chatbot claim should be read as “very competitive under these evaluation protocols”, not as a universal proof of model quality.
Table 13 from the appendix. Pairwise GPT-4 judgments induce an ordering where Guanaco 65B and 33B rank ahead of Vicuna, ChatGPT-3.5 Turbo, Bard, and smaller Guanaco variants. The evaluation section is also useful as a warning for later LLM papers. When the judge is another model, prompt order and self-preference can move scores. Averaging both orders and supplementing with human ratings is not optional polish; it changes how much the result can be trusted. Training recipe detailsThe appendix gives enough training detail to make the method concrete.
Table 9 from the appendix. QLoRA training hyperparameters across model sizes and datasets. The core setup is:
NF4 with double quantization. BF16 computation. LoRA , alpha . LoRA on all linear layers. Adam beta2 . max grad norm . constant learning rate schedule. group-by-length batching. dropout 0.1 up to 13B, dropout 0.05 for 33B and 65B.
Learning rate and batch size change with scale:
7B and 13B use learning rate , usually batch size 16. 33B and 65B use learning rate , with larger batch sizes for some datasets. OASST1 keeps batch size 16 and 1,875 steps across model sizes.
A compact reproduction checklist would look like this: base_model: weights: frozen storage_dtype: NF4 quantization: blockwise, double_quantized_scales compute_dtype: BF16adapter: method: LoRA target_modules: all_linear_layers r: 64 alpha: 16optimizer: type: paged_adamw beta2: 0.999 max_grad_norm: 0.3 schedule: constant_lr
The most important reproduction trap is adapter coverage. If LoRA is only attached to the query and value projections, the result is not the paper’s main QLoRA recipe. Target-only training and data qualityFor instruction tuning, the paper studies whether to train on both source and target text or only on the target response.
Table 10 from the appendix. Training only on the target response improves mean MMLU in this ablation. The target-only result is modest but consistent in the reported setup:
Train on source and target: mean 37.5. Train on target: mean 38.6.
That matches a common supervised fine-tuning practice: do not spend loss on reproducing the user instruction when the goal is to improve assistant response behavior. The data-size ablation is more important:
Table 11 from the appendix. Increasing dataset size and epochs helps less than choosing a better-suited dataset. The authors report that increasing dataset size or epochs only marginally improves MMLU, while differences between datasets are much larger. This explains why a small high-quality chat dataset can beat a much larger but less suitable instruction mixture on chatbot evaluations. For practical work, this is one of the strongest takeaways from the paper:
Use QLoRA to make iteration cheap. Spend the saved budget on dataset selection, cleaning, and evaluation. Do not assume that more instruction data is automatically better.
What QLoRA is notQLoRA is sometimes casually described as “4-bit fine-tuning”, but a few boundaries matter. First, the base weights are frozen. QLoRA is not doing full 4-bit weight updates. If the task requires changing the whole model distribution in ways LoRA cannot express, QLoRA may not match full fine-tuning. Second, NF4 is primarily a training-memory storage format. The paper dequantizes to BF16 for computation. For production inference, the fastest representation may be INT4, FP8, AWQ/GPTQ-style layouts, or a custom kernel format depending on the serving stack. Third, the paper does not fully prove 33B and 65B equality to full 16-bit fine-tuning. The resource cost of those baselines is too high, so the large-scale comparison is mostly against 16-bit LoRA and task evaluations. Fourth, chatbot evaluation is noisy. The Guanaco results are strong, but GPT-4-as-judge is not a perfect measurement instrument. My readingThe clean technical contribution is the combination, not any single isolated trick:
NF4 preserves enough information in the frozen model. Double quantization makes the 4-bit representation honest at large scale by accounting for metadata. Paged optimizers address peak memory instead of average memory. Broad LoRA placement recovers quality because adapter memory is cheap compared with the base model.
QLoRA became popular because it matched the way people actually work: download a strong base model, adapt it to a dataset, and do not buy a cluster for every experiment. The method also made a useful empirical point: for many adaptation tasks, the base model capacity is more valuable than keeping every base weight in 16-bit precision. If I were reproducing the paper today, I would track three numbers for every run:
Peak GPU memory, not just steady-state memory. Evaluation quality on the target behavior, not just MMLU or perplexity. Adapter target modules, because a “LoRA” run with sparse targets is not comparable to the paper’s all-linear-layer recipe.
TakeawayQLoRA is best understood as a practical memory system for supervised adaptation of large language models. It does not make low-bit training magically free, and it does not remove the need for good data or careful evaluation. What it does is move 33B and 65B fine-tuning from “cluster-only” into the range of single-GPU experiments, while preserving 16-bit quality in the paper’s tested settings. That change is why this paper matters: it turned quantization from a deployment-only trick into a core part of the fine-tuning workflow.

entry.title: QuaRot: Rotated 4-Bit LLM Inference
entry.content:
Ashkboos et al. “QuaRot: Outlier-Free 4-Bit Inference in Rotated LLMs.” NeurIPS 2024.
Paper: arXiv:2404.00456 Code: spcl/QuaRot QuaRot is a rotation-based answer to the LLM activation-outlier problem. SmoothQuant rescales channels. LLM.int8() routes outlier dimensions through a high-precision side path. QuaRot changes the coordinate basis with orthogonal Hadamard rotations so the same hidden state becomes less axis-aligned and easier to quantize. The target setting is hard: A4W4KV4. That means activations, weights, and KV cache are all stored or moved through 4-bit paths where possible. This is different from W4A16 methods such as GPTQ or AWQ, which keep activations high precision, and different from W8A8 methods that only need INT8-level robustness. The key reading of the paper is:
rotations preserve the model function before quantization; Hadamard structure makes those rotations cheap enough; the rotated tensors have fewer coordinate outliers; after that transformation, ordinary low-bit quantizers become much less fragile.
The Outlier ProblemThe first figure is the whole motivation.
The left panel shows the input activation distribution of a Llama-2-7B FFN block before QuaRot. Some hidden dimensions have much larger ranges than the rest. If a per-token INT4 activation quantizer has to cover those spikes, most ordinary dimensions lose resolution. The right panel shows the same kind of tensor after QuaRot processing. The total vector energy is not removed, but it is spread across coordinates. That is exactly what a uniform quantizer wants: a smaller coordinate-wise maximum for the same semantic signal. For an orthogonal matrix :
So rotation preserves the vector norm but changes which coordinate carries which part of the signal. If outliers are sparse in the original basis, a randomized Hadamard basis can make the maximum coordinate smaller. Why This Can Preserve The ModelFor a plain linear layer, the algebra is simple:
The model can therefore consume a rotated activation if the corresponding weight matrix is pre-multiplied by . The nontrivial part is that transformer blocks have RMSNorm, residual streams, attention, RoPE, and multi-head structure. QuaRot relies on a computational invariance property: if the residual stream is transformed by an orthogonal matrix and adjacent weights are updated consistently, the full-precision model output stays the same. The RMSNorm interaction is important. Ignoring the learned scaling term for a moment, RMSNorm divides each row by its norm. Since orthogonal rotation preserves the row norm:
In practice, QuaRot absorbs the RMSNorm scale parameters into adjacent weights first, then uses rotations around the remaining norm-only operation. This is the main conceptual move: make the network compute in a rotated hidden basis without changing the FP16 function, then quantize the easier tensors. Hadamard RotationsQuaRot uses randomized Hadamard matrices rather than dense random orthogonal matrices. A Walsh-Hadamard matrix can be built recursively:
A randomized Hadamard transform multiplies by a random sign diagonal:
The point is not that Hadamard is the only possible orthogonal matrix. The point is that it is fast. A dense orthogonal rotation would be too expensive on the inference path. A Hadamard transform can be implemented with structured add/subtract operations, and many rotations can be folded into weights offline. QuaRot In The FFNThe FFN diagram is the cleanest place to see the method.
QuaRot first rotates the residual stream, so the hidden state becomes . Then it updates the FFN weights so the original function is preserved:
absorb RMSNorm scale into adjacent matrices; use and for the two input projections; insert an online Hadamard transform before the down projection; fold the inverse side into the down projection as .
The diagram also makes the precision boundary clear. Activations immediately before linear weights are quantized to INT4. The INT4 matmul accumulates into INT32, then the result is dequantized/cast back to FP16 for the surrounding model operations. QuaRot is not claiming every scalar operation is INT4. It is targeting the expensive matrix multiplications and the cache/memory path. QuaRot In AttentionAttention is more delicate because the KV cache must remain useful across decoding steps, and RoPE prevents all key/query rotations from being folded into weights.
The value path has a useful structure. Inside one attention head, the value projection and output projection appear together:
For one head, . QuaRot can rotate values head-wise and fold the corresponding inverse into the output projection:
For keys and queries, RoPE is the blocker. If positional encoding sits between and the attention score, a rotation cannot simply be absorbed into and . QuaRot instead rotates queries and keys online after RoPE with the same head-wise Hadamard:
The attention logits are preserved because the same orthogonal matrix appears on both sides:
For decoding, the paper chooses post-RoPE caching. That avoids repeatedly rotating the whole old key cache for each new query. New keys/values are rotated and quantized as they are appended, while attention dequantizes cache segments when loading them. Quantization SetupQuaRot has two stages:
Rotate and modify the model in high precision. Fold rotations into weights where possible and insert the small number of online Hadamard transforms that remain. Quantize weights, activations, and cache. The paper uses GPTQ by default for weights, round-to-nearest for online activations, and group-wise asymmetric quantization for KV cache.
The experiment details are worth keeping:
activation quantization: symmetric per-token INT4; activation clipping ratio: 0.9; activation scale: row maximum divided by 7 for INT4; KV cache quantization: asymmetric, group size 128; KV clipping ratio: 0.95; weight quantization: GPTQ by default, RTN in ablations; GPTQ calibration: 128 WikiText-2 samples with sequence length 2048; implementation: PyTorch/Hugging Face, CUTLASS INT4 GEMM, FlashInfer for KV cache; performance hardware: NVIDIA RTX 3090.
For Llama-2-70B, the paper reports about 5 minutes for the QuaRot model modification and about 2 more hours for GPTQ quantization on a single A100. So this is still PTQ-style work, not QAT, but it is not a zero-cost conversion. Main Accuracy ResultsTable 1 is the most important result because it compares end-to-end 4-bit quantization on WikiText-2.
QuaRot with GPTQ has no high-precision outlier features and keeps Llama-2 perplexity close to FP16:
Model FP16 QuaRot GPTQ A4W4KV4 PPL increase
Llama-2-7B 5.47 6.10 +0.63
Llama-2-13B 4.88 5.40 +0.52
Llama-2-70B 3.32 3.79 +0.47
That is the headline: the 70B model, which is usually more forgiving under quantization, loses only 0.47 WikiText-2 perplexity while weights, activations, and cache are all in the 4-bit target regime. The comparison against SmoothQuant and OmniQuant is also revealing. Those methods were not designed around this exact 4-bit activation/cache setting, and their table entries degrade badly. QUIK-4B keeps 256 outlier features, while QuaRot keeps zero. This supports the paper’s claim that rotation can remove the need for a high-precision outlier side path. Group-wise quantization narrows the gap further. With 128-group quantization, QuaRot reaches 5.93 on 7B, 5.26 on 13B, and 3.61 on 70B. Zero-Shot AccuracyThe zero-shot table checks whether the perplexity story transfers to common LM-eval tasks.
The average drops are:
Model FP16 avg QuaRot avg Drop
Llama-2-7B 69.82 65.64 -4.18
Llama-2-13B 72.59 69.79 -2.80
Llama-2-70B 77.07 75.98 -1.09
This is a useful pattern: 4-bit end-to-end quantization is more painful for smaller models, and the 70B model retains most of its average zero-shot score. The paper summarizes this as preserving about 99% of zero-shot performance for the largest Llama-2 case. Kernel And Memory ResultsQuaRot is not only a mathematical transform. Its deployment value depends on whether the remaining online Hadamard operations and quantized cache path are cheap enough.
For a single transformer block on RTX 3090:
prefill speedup on Llama-2-7B is about 1.97x to 2.16x at sequence length 2048; prefill speedup on Llama-2-70B reaches 3.16x to 3.33x; decode peak memory saving is at least 3.63x; Llama-2-70B decode memory saving is about 3.89x across the shown sequence lengths.
The memory result is the most directly useful for long-context serving, because decode is often cache-capacity and memory-bandwidth constrained. The speedup result is also encouraging, but it depends heavily on kernel quality and batch/sequence shape. The layer microbenchmark gives another view.
For the FFN down-projection-like layer sizes, the paper reports:
Llama-2-7B shape: FP16 2.57 ms, INT4+Hadamard 0.80 ms; Llama-2-13B shape: FP16 3.98 ms, INT4+Hadamard 1.14 ms; Llama-2-70B shape: FP16 12.45 ms, INT4+Hadamard 2.91 ms.
The Hadamard transform adds only a small overhead over the INT4 path in this benchmark. That matters because QuaRot would be much less compelling if every rotation erased the INT4 GEMM win. For decode memory, the detailed table is even more concrete.
For example, on Llama-2-7B with batch size 16 and sequence length 4096, the single-block decode memory drops from 1.416 GB to 0.378 GB, a 3.75x saving. On Llama-2-70B, the shown cases stay near 3.89x saving. RTN And Group Size AblationsThe paper also checks how far simple round-to-nearest can go after rotation.
RTN is nearly lossless at 8 bits after QuaRot, but 4-bit RTN is still worse than GPTQ, especially on smaller models. For Llama-2-7B, 4-bit RTN has perplexity 8.37, while the GPTQ-based QuaRot result in Table 1 is 6.10. For Llama-2-70B, the RTN gap is smaller: 4.14 versus the GPTQ-based 3.79. My reading is that rotation fixes the outlier geometry, but it does not make all rounding choices harmless. GPTQ still matters for 4-bit weights, especially in smaller models. Group size shows the usual accuracy/metadata tradeoff.
Smaller groups improve perplexity:
Method 7B 13B 70B
QuaRot 6.10 5.40 3.79
QuaRot-256G 5.98 5.28 3.63
QuaRot-128G 5.93 5.26 3.61
QuaRot-64G 5.88 5.25 3.58
But smaller groups require more scale metadata and can complicate kernels. This is a common practical boundary: a paper table can prefer smaller groups, while a production runtime may choose the group size that best matches packing and GEMM layout. KV Cache QuantizationKV cache quantization is a separate pressure point from weight quantization. The cache grows with sequence length and batch size, so it matters most in long-context decode.
The cache ablation keeps the rest of the model high precision and changes only K/V precision. A few readings:
4-bit K and 4-bit V are almost lossless: 5.51 vs 5.47 on 7B, 3.33 vs 3.32 on 70B. 3-bit K and 3-bit V are still close: 5.68 on 7B and 3.39 on 70B. 2-bit cache is much harder, especially on 7B: K2/V2 gives 9.23. keys are more sensitive than values in the shown comparisons: K4/V3 is better than K3/V4 on 7B.
This matches KIVI/KVQuant-style observations: the key cache has structured outlier behavior and directly affects attention logits, so key precision/granularity deserves special care. Relation To Other Quantization MethodsQuaRot sits in a useful line of equivalent-transform methods:
Method Main target What it does with outliers
LLM.int8() W8A8-ish matmul keeps outlier dimensions in FP16
SmoothQuant W8A8 dense inference migrates activation scale into weights
GPTQ/AWQ W4A16 weight-only avoids activation quantization at runtime
KIVI KV cache uses asymmetric grouping for K and V
QuaRot A4W4KV4 inference rotates the basis to remove coordinate outliers
The important distinction is that QuaRot changes the basis, not just the scale. Scaling can make one channel easier by making the paired weight channel harder. Rotation mixes coordinates so sparse outliers become less concentrated. That is a stronger transformation, but it also requires more careful placement around RMSNorm, RoPE, and the cache. Compared with QuIP/QuIP#, QuaRot uses related incoherence-processing ideas but applies them to end-to-end activation/cache quantization and tries to fold most rotations into the model so runtime overhead stays small. Reproduction NotesI would reproduce QuaRot in layers, not all at once. First, test function preservation in floating point:
apply the residual-stream rotation and fold / into adjacent weights; verify full-precision block outputs match the original within numerical noise; add the FFN online Hadamard before down projection; add attention value rotation; add post-RoPE key/query rotation and confirm attention logits are unchanged before quantization.
Then test the quantization path:
plot activation max per hidden dimension before and after rotation; quantize activations per token and measure reconstruction error; enable GPTQ weights and compare against RTN; quantize KV cache separately and reproduce the K/V bit-width ablation; measure kernel overhead of each online Hadamard block separately.
The last step is important. A mathematically equivalent transform can still be a bad deployment idea if it adds latency on the decode path. QuaRot’s claim depends on the rotations being either folded into weights or implemented with very cheap structured kernels. LimitationsThe paper is strong, but the boundary should be clear. First, “4-bit inference” does not mean every operation is INT4. RMSNorm, online Hadamard transforms, softmax-related work, query handling, dequantization, and some attention arithmetic still use higher precision. The claim is better read as: all major matrix multiplications and KV cache storage are pushed into the 4-bit regime. Second, QuaRot is a kernel-aware method. Without CUTLASS/FlashInfer-style support for low-bit GEMM, packing, cache quantization, dequantization, and online Hadamard transforms, the paper’s accuracy result would not automatically translate into speed or memory savings. Third, GPTQ is still used for the strongest 4-bit weight results. Rotation makes the tensors easier, but it does not remove the need for a good weight quantizer at 4 bits. Fourth, the method has several engineering knobs: group size, clipping ratio, Hadamard precision, cache format, and rotation placement. The paper shows these are manageable, but they are still part of the deployment surface. TakeawayQuaRot is useful because it reframes activation outliers as a basis problem. Instead of preserving a few large coordinate directions in high precision, it rotates the model into a basis where those directions are spread out and ordinary low-bit quantization works better. The idea is elegant, but the practical value comes from the details: RMSNorm scale folding, FFN and attention-specific Hadamard placement, post-RoPE key rotation, cache-aware quantization, and kernels where the online rotations are cheap. That is why this paper belongs in the full-stack LLM quantization path rather than only in the algebraic-transform bucket.

entry.title: RPTQ: Reorder-Based LLM Quantization
entry.content:
Paper: RPTQ: Reorder-based Post-training Quantization for Large Language Models Code: hahnyuan/RPTQ4LLM RPTQ is a layout-aware post-training quantization paper. Its main claim is more specific than “LLM activations have outliers.” The paper argues that activation quantization fails because different channels have very different value ranges. Some channels have large outliers, but even channels without extreme outliers can occupy incompatible intervals. If those channels are forced to share one quantization scale, the smaller or shifted ranges lose precision. The method is simple in spirit:
Run calibration data through the model. Record each activation channel’s minimum and maximum. Cluster channels whose ranges look similar. Reorder channels so each quantization group contains similar channels. Quantize each cluster with its own scale and zero point. Fold the reorder into layer norm writes and linear weights so inference does not pay an explicit shuffle.
That makes RPTQ a useful bridge between SmoothQuant and later rotation-based methods such as QuaRot. SmoothQuant rescales coordinates. RPTQ permutes coordinates. QuaRot rotates coordinates. All three try to make the tensors seen by low-bit quantizers less hostile. The Activation ProblemThe first figure is the motivation. Each dot is one activation channel, plotted as (channel maximum, channel minimum) on calibration data.
Figure 1 from the paper. Different OPT activation channels occupy very different min/max ranges across layers and projection sites. Two things show up in this plot:
Some channels are outliers with much larger maxima or minima. Many channels have different ranges even when they are not isolated outliers.
The second point is the one RPTQ focuses on. Suppose two channels are both important, but one lives mostly in [-100, -50] and another in [80, 100]. A single asymmetric quantizer covering [-100, 100] wastes resolution for both channels. If the quantizer has only 4 bits, this waste is not a small rounding issue. This matters because activation quantization is the hard part for LLM PTQ. By the time this paper appeared, weight-only 4-bit methods such as GPTQ were already usable. Turning activations and KV cache into low-bit tensors is harder because runtime tensors vary with data and sequence state. Where RPTQ SitsThe paper compares four ways to handle activation quantization difficulty.
Figure 2 from the paper. LLM.int8() isolates outliers, SmoothQuant rescales channels, VSQ uses local vector scales, and RPTQ clusters and reorders channels before grouped quantization. The differences are useful:
LLM.int8() keeps outlier features in high precision. This protects accuracy, but it adds a side path. SmoothQuant moves activation difficulty into weights through equivalent per-channel scaling. It can make activation INT8 practical, but the paper argues that scaling alone does not fully solve range differences at lower bit widths. VSQ gives nearby values their own quantization parameters, but that can increase parameter storage and runtime overhead. RPTQ changes which channels share a quantization group. It tries to get most of the benefit of finer granularity without per-channel or per-vector overhead.
The key observation is that group-wise quantization is not permutation-invariant. If a group shares a scale, channel order decides which ranges are forced to share that scale. Reordering is therefore a quantization parameter. Uniform Quantization SetupThe paper uses uniform quantization because it maps better to ordinary hardware than non-uniform codebooks. For a k-bit integer quantizer:
Here, s is the scale and z is the zero point. With 4-bit signed integers, the integer range is [-8, 7]. The dequantized value is approximately:
For asymmetric min-max quantization over a tensor or group:
RPTQ’s contribution is not a new quantization formula. It changes the group assignment used before these ordinary scale and zero-point values are computed. Clustering Channels By RangeLet the calibration activation tensor be , where B is calibration batch count, N is token count, and C is hidden channel count. RPTQ computes channel-wise calibration statistics:
For each channel i, the paper forms a 2D point:
Then it runs K-means over those points. Channels in the same cluster are placed next to each other in memory order, and each cluster gets its own asymmetric quantization parameters. This is a small algorithmic step but an important systems detail:
If g = 1, RPTQ becomes ordinary shared-scale quantization. If g = C, each channel can get its own scale, but metadata and kernels become expensive. With a small number of clusters, RPTQ tries to keep quantization groups homogeneous while keeping overhead moderate.
The paper uses 32 clusters for R1, R4, and R5, and 4 clusters for R2 and R3 in the main experiments. R2 and R3 are per-head self-attention reorder indices, so their overhead grows with head count. Avoiding Runtime ShuffleA naive implementation would physically reorder activation channels at runtime. That would add memory movement, temporary buffers, and latency. RPTQ tries to avoid that. The full transformer-layer flow is shown below.
Figure 3 from the paper. Reorder indices R1 to R5 are inserted around layer norm, attention projections, attention matmul, output projection, and FFN projections. The paper uses two main tricks. First, it fuses reordering into layer norm. Layer norm already writes its output back to memory. RPTQ changes the write address according to the reorder index, so the activation is produced in reordered layout without a separate shuffle kernel. Second, it pre-reorders linear weights. For a linear layer, the permutation view is:
If both sides are permuted consistently, the full-precision function is unchanged. In practice, RPTQ rearranges columns according to the input activation order and rows according to the output activation order. The weight reorder can be done before deployment. Alignment ConstraintsThe hard part is not the single linear layer. It is keeping the whole transformer block consistent. RPTQ has to handle several alignment constraints:
Residual additions require matching channel order. The paper therefore avoids reordering the output of the attention output projection and final FFN output in ways that would break residual paths. Query and key channels meet in QK^T. They must use compatible reorder indices, otherwise attention scores become wrong. The paper computes R2 and R3 for each self-attention head, and for query/key it clusters a combined point containing both Q and K min/max statistics. LayerNorm output can be reordered because the following weights are adjusted to accept that order.
This is why the method is more than a sorting heuristic. It is a static layout transformation that must be propagated through the transformer graph. Experiment SetupThe experiments focus on OPT models from 1.3B to 175B. Since RPTQ focuses on activations, the paper combines it with GPTQ for weight quantization. The setup details:
weights and input activations use static quantization; activation clusters use asymmetric min-max quantization; layer norm output and softmax output are quantized to 8-bit precision; calibration uses 256 samples randomly selected from WikiText2, Penn Treebank, and C4; metrics include perplexity, zero-shot accuracy, memory consumption, and cluster-number ablations; experiments run on a server with 8 NVIDIA A6000 GPUs.
The naming convention is important:
W4A16: 4-bit weights, 16-bit activations. W4A8: 4-bit weights, 8-bit activations. W4A4: 4-bit weights, 4-bit activations. W4A4KV: 4-bit weights and 4-bit KV cache, with ordinary activations less aggressively quantized. W3A3KV: 3-bit weights and 3-bit KV cache.
The KV variants exist because KV cache becomes a dominant memory cost at long sequence length and large batch size. Perplexity ResultsTable 1 is the main accuracy table for perplexity on WikiText2, Penn Treebank, and C4.
Table 1 from the paper. RPTQ is evaluated across OPT-1.3B to OPT-175B under W4A16, W4A8, W4A4, and KV-cache-focused settings. The easiest way to read the table is to compare OPT-175B:
FP16: WIKI 8.34, PT 12.01, C4 10.13. W4A16: WIKI 8.37, PT 12.31, C4 10.26. W4A8: WIKI 8.43, PT 12.24, C4 10.49. W4A4: WIKI 10.60, PT 15.59, C4 12.28. W4A4KV: WIKI 8.40, PT 12.38, C4 10.54. W3A3KV: WIKI 10.03, PT 13.82, C4 11.30.
Two lessons stand out. First, full activation W4A4 is much harder than W4A8. The perplexity increase is still manageable on the largest model, but it is not free. Second, KV-focused quantization is attractive. W4A4KV stays close to FP16 on OPT-175B while reducing memory pressure in the part of the model that grows with sequence length and batch size. Zero-Shot TasksThe zero-shot table checks whether perplexity trends transfer to downstream multiple-choice tasks.
Table 2 from the paper. The evaluated tasks are LAMBADA(OpenAI), PIQA, ARC(Easy), ARC(Challenge), OpenBookQA, and BoolQ. The table is dense, but the pattern is consistent with Table 1:
