W4A16 is usually close to FP16. W4A8 loses some accuracy but remains usable. W4A4 is more fragile, especially on smaller models and harder tasks. KV-focused schemes preserve more quality than fully quantizing all activations to the same low bit width.
This is a useful distinction for deployment. If the memory bottleneck is KV cache, then pushing every activation to 4-bit may not be the best first move. A KV-focused design can buy a lot of memory reduction with less quality loss. Memory ResultsThe memory table is the practical reason activation and KV quantization matter.
Table 3 from the paper. Memory consumption is reported for OPT-30B, OPT-66B, and OPT-175B across batch sizes and sequence lengths. The headline result from the paper:
W4A8 reduces memory by about 63%. W4A4 reduces memory by about 75%. W4A4KV reduces memory by about 73%. W3A3KV reduces memory by about 80%.
For OPT-175B at batch size 64 and sequence length 8192:
W16A16: 2750.1GB. W4A16: 2505.6GB. W4A8: 1311.6GB. W4A4: 714.6GB. W4A4KV: 759.6GB. W3A3KV: 593.7GB.
The W4A16 number is a good sanity check. Weight-only quantization helps, but in this long-context large-batch setting it does not solve the problem because activations and KV cache dominate. The appendix breaks this down by memory component.
Table 6 from the appendix. As batch size and sequence length grow, KV cache and dynamic activation memory become much larger fractions of total memory. This table explains why activation quantization is worth the trouble. At small batch and short sequence, weights dominate. At large batch and long sequence, the KV cache and runtime tensors can become the main memory problem. Cluster Count AblationRPTQ has a knob: the number of clusters. More clusters mean channels share scales with more similar channels, but also increase bookkeeping and possibly kernel complexity.
Figure 4 from the paper. Perplexity generally improves as the number of clusters increases, but the curves differ across reorder locations. The paper reports that:
increasing clusters generally decreases perplexity; R2 has fluctuations, which the authors suspect may come from limited calibration data; larger models are more sensitive to too few clusters; using only one cluster can make larger networks fail badly; the main experiments choose 32 clusters for R1/R4/R5 and 4 clusters for R2/R3.
The appendix adds a larger calibration comparison.
Figure 7 from the appendix. Calibration sample count changes the stability of the cluster-number ablation, especially for R2 and R3. This makes sense: RPTQ depends on channel min/max statistics. If calibration data misses rare activation ranges, the clusters can be poorly placed. Comparison With SmoothQuant And PEGThe paper also compares against SmoothQuant and PEG under low-bit settings.
Table 4 from the appendix. SmoothQuant degrades badly in several W4A4 cases, while RPTQ remains in a usable perplexity range. The most dramatic entries are in W4A4 on larger OPT models. For OPT-30B, SmoothQuant has extremely large perplexity values on all three datasets, while RPTQ stays at WIKI 11.15, PT 14.11, and C4 13.48. That supports the paper’s claim that range differences are not fully solved by simple channel scaling.
Table 5 from the appendix. Under W4A4, RPTQ is generally better than PEG on the tested OPT models. PEG is also a permutation-style idea, but the paper argues that its grouping is less suitable for LLM activation range patterns. The RPTQ advantage is strongest on OPT-30B in this table, where PEG has PT 34.94 and C4 45.43 while RPTQ has PT 14.11 and C4 13.48. Large-Model Channel DistributionsThe appendix includes larger distribution plots for OPT-30B and OPT-66B.
Figure 5 from the appendix. OPT-30B channel ranges show repeated structured differences across layers.
Figure 6 from the appendix. OPT-66B shows even more structured channel-range patterns. These plots make the “range difference” argument concrete. The outlier problem is not one isolated channel that can be routed around. The distributions form structured clouds, curves, and separated groups. A clustering-based layout transform is a reasonable response to that geometry. Implementation NotesThe main implementation trap is alignment. A local permutation can preserve one matrix multiplication, but a transformer block has multiple consumers and residual joins. The safest way to think about RPTQ is: calibrate: collect min/max per activation channel cluster channels by range choose reorder indices R1...R5rewrite model: fuse reorder writes into LayerNorm output reorder linear weight columns for input layouts reorder linear weight rows only when the output layout is also expected keep residual-add outputs aligned force Q and K to share compatible reorder indicesquantize: use cluster-specific activation scale and zero point combine with GPTQ for weight quantization use lower-bit KV cache variants when memory is dominated by long context
In algebra, a permutation is harmless:
In a real transformer, a wrong permutation silently corrupts residual additions or attention scores. That is the difference between a nice figure and a working implementation. What RPTQ Is Good AtRPTQ is strongest when:
activation quantization is required, not only weight-only compression; group-wise quantization is used, so channel order controls scale sharing; the reorder can be folded into existing operations; calibration data is representative enough to estimate channel ranges; the deployment target benefits from lower activation or KV-cache memory.
It is less compelling if the runtime has to execute explicit gather/scatter operations for every token, or if the hardware cannot efficiently run the chosen low-bit integer format. The appendix notes that 3-bit values are not supported on most GPUs and may need to be cast to 4-bit or 8-bit datatypes. Relation To Later WorkRPTQ permutes channels. QuaRot rotates channels. The conceptual connection is direct: both treat the coordinate basis as part of the quantization problem. The difference is expressive power:
A permutation can only group existing coordinates differently. A scaling transform can shift quantization difficulty between activations and weights. A rotation can spread outlier energy across many coordinates.
RPTQ is cheaper and easier to reason about than rotations, but less flexible. That makes it a good intermediate point in the LLM quantization story. It shows that low-bit activation quantization is not only a numeric-type problem; it is also a data-layout problem. TakeawayRPTQ’s main lesson is that channel grouping matters. If a group-wise quantizer uses one scale for a set of channels, then the order of those channels can decide whether the group is easy or impossible to quantize. The method is not just “sort channels.” It uses calibration statistics, clusters channels by min/max range, propagates compatible reorder indices through transformer layers, and folds the layout change into layer norm and linear weights. That combination lets RPTQ push OPT activation and KV-cache quantization into lower-bit regimes while keeping perplexity and zero-shot accuracy usable in the paper’s experiments.

entry.title: Reformer: The Efficient Transformer
entry.content:
Reference Paper: Reformer: The Efficient Transformer Code: google/trax Reformer
Reformer is one of the early long-context Transformer papers that is still useful to read carefully. It does not only say “attention is quadratic” and then replace attention with a sparse pattern. It separates the memory problem into several pieces:
attention scores scale as in sequence length; activations have to be kept for every layer during training; the feed-forward hidden dimension is often much larger than ; long sequences make even “linear-looking” activation tensors enormous.
The paper’s answer is three-part:
use locality-sensitive hashing attention to avoid comparing every query with every key; use reversible residual layers so intermediate activations can be reconstructed during backpropagation; chunk feed-forward and output computations so large intermediate tensors do not have to be materialized at once.
This post is mainly a formula-by-formula reading. I care less about memorizing the exact Reformer implementation and more about understanding which tensor causes which cost. One SentenceReformer is a Transformer variant for long sequences: LSH attention attacks the attention matrix, reversible layers attack the per-layer activation cache, and chunking attacks the large feed-forward intermediates. This is a different route from FlashAttention. Reformer changes the attention pattern and therefore gives an approximate attention mechanism. FlashAttention keeps exact dense attention but changes the kernel schedule and memory traffic. That distinction matters when deciding whether a method is an algorithmic approximation or an implementation-level optimization. Why Long Context HurtsThe paper gives two simple memory estimates that are worth keeping in mind. First, a batch of long hidden states is already large before attention:
That is 0.5 billion floating-point values for sequence length , hidden size , and batch size . In fp32 this is about 2 GB for one activation tensor. If a normal Transformer stores activations for many layers, the layer count multiplies this cost. Second, dense attention creates a score matrix:
For , this is a matrix. Even for batch size 1 and one head, that is already too large to casually materialize. The paper cites roughly 16 GB for the raw fp32 attention matrix. This is the core reason Reformer needs to change attention itself. Formula Reading: Standard AttentionThe usual scaled dot-product attention is:
My reading of each term:
, , and are projected token representations. compares every query position with every key position. keeps dot-product magnitudes from growing with the head dimension. The softmax converts similarities into a distribution over keys. Multiplying by forms a weighted average of value vectors.
The expensive object is not the final output. The expensive object is the pairwise score matrix inside the softmax. If the sequence length is , every head has an attention map. That is why saving only the final attention output is not enough; the algorithm has already paid the quadratic comparison cost. Reformer asks a specific question: softmax is dominated by the largest logits, so can we cheaply find likely large dot products without checking every pair? Shared Query-Key SpaceLSH attention needs queries and keys to live in the same space, so Reformer uses a shared query-key projection:
The value projection remains separate. The reason is practical. Locality-sensitive hashing puts vectors into buckets. If query vectors and key vectors were produced by unrelated projections, “same bucket” would be less meaningful. With shared , a query and a key are comparable as points in one space. The paper also normalizes key vectors and prevents a token from attending to itself except when it has no other valid context. This self-attention rule is easy to miss. In shared , a token’s dot product with itself is almost always very high, so without masking it can waste attention mass on copying itself. Formula Reading: Angular LSH Figure: Angular LSH maps nearby vectors to the same bucket with high probability by using random rotations and signed projections. The hash function in the paper is:
where:
and denotes concatenation. I read this as a random hyperplane scheme written in a compact batched form. The matrix produces random projections. Concatenating and creates signed directions. The hash bucket is the direction with the largest projection. Why this helps:
similar vectors tend to have similar projections; after normalization, angular closeness corresponds to large dot product; nearby vectors are likely to share at least one hash bucket; vectors in different buckets are not compared, which saves attention work.
The hash is approximate. If two tokens should attend to each other but land in different buckets for a given hash round, that pair is missing. Reformer compensates by using multiple hashing rounds. From Full Attention To LSH AttentionThe paper first rewrites normal causal attention for one query position:
Here is the set of keys that position is allowed to attend to. In a causal decoder, those are the current and previous positions. The term is the log normalizer for the softmax over that set. This formula is useful because it makes attention a set restriction problem. Dense causal attention says is all previous positions. Sparse or approximate attention changes . For batched computation, the paper uses a larger set and masks invalid keys:
with:
The mask formula is just softmax masking written explicitly. If is not allowed, subtracting makes its contribution zero after exponentiation. This is the same idea used in causal masks and padding masks, but here it is part of the LSH batching story. LSH attention changes the allowed set to:
Now a query can attend only to keys in the same hash bucket. This is the central approximation. Instead of “all previous tokens”, the model sees “tokens that hash near me”, plus the causal mask and implementation details needed for batching. Sorting, Chunking, And Local Batches Figure: Reformer hashes tokens, sorts by bucket, splits the sorted sequence into chunks, and runs attention inside nearby chunks. Hash buckets have two engineering problems:
bucket sizes are uneven; different examples and heads may produce different bucket layouts.
The paper handles this by sorting tokens by bucket id. After sorting, items from the same bucket become adjacent in memory. The sorted position of token is written as . Instead of forming a separate ragged attention problem for every bucket, Reformer chunks the sorted sequence. A query chunk attends to itself and one previous chunk:
The paper sets:
where is sequence length. The intuition:
sort-by-bucket makes same-bucket tokens local; fixed-size chunks make the computation dense enough for accelerators; attending one chunk back catches bucket boundaries that were split across chunks; the causal mask still removes illegal future positions.
This is why Reformer is not just “group by hash and run tiny attentions”. It is a sorted dense batching trick around the hash grouping. Multi-Round LSHOne hash can miss a true neighbor. Reformer repeats hashing with independent random rotations:
where:
This union is the recall mechanism. More rounds mean a higher chance that two similar vectors collide at least once. The cost also grows with , so the paper treats it as a quality-speed knob. I like this formula because it makes the approximation tunable. LSH attention is not a single fixed sparse pattern. At evaluation time, the paper can increase the number of hashes to improve accuracy, which shows up clearly in the synthetic task and imagenet64 experiments. Attention Complexity Figure: Table 1 compares scaled dot-product attention, memory-efficient attention, and LSH attention. The key row is LSH attention. The dense attention term is replaced by a term controlled by chunk size and hash rounds:
where is batch size, is number of heads, is number of hash repetitions, is sequence length, and is number of chunks. This is still not magically free. If chunks are too large or the number of hash rounds is too high, the constant can be large. But the structure is better than dense because Reformer controls the local attention window after hashing and sorting. The phrase “memory-efficient attention” in Table 1 is also important. It reduces materialization but still has the same asymptotic dense pairwise comparison. LSH attention is the row that changes which pairs are compared. Synthetic Duplication Task Figure: Table 2 tests whether LSH attention can solve a task that requires non-local copying. The task is deliberately simple: duplicate a sequence. A model has to retrieve information from far away, so local attention is not enough. This is a good sanity check for LSH attention because the method claims to preserve important non-local links through content similarity, not through fixed distance. The table has two useful lessons:
A full-attention model evaluated with LSH loses accuracy as hashes decrease. This means the LSH approximation is real, not free. Models trained with LSH attention become robust to LSH evaluation. A model trained with LSH-4 gets almost perfect accuracy when evaluated with LSH-4 or more hashes.
The most interesting row is not the full-attention row. It is the LSH-trained rows. They show that if the model learns under the approximate attention mechanism, it can adapt its representations so relevant tokens collide more reliably. Reversible LayersAttention memory is only one part of the problem. A normal Transformer also stores activations for every layer so backpropagation can use them later. Reformer borrows reversible residual layers from RevNets to remove most of that activation storage. The standard residual block is:
This is not reversible in general. Given , we cannot recover unless we can invert . RevNet-style blocks split the hidden state into two parts:
The reverse direction is:
Figure: The reversible residual equations from the paper. The important detail is the dependency order. To reconstruct:
and are available from the next layer. Compute . Compute .
So the forward activations do not need to be stored at every layer. During the backward pass, they can be recomputed layer by layer from the output and the parameters. This saves memory but costs extra compute because parts of the forward pass are repeated. Formula Reading: Reformer BlockReformer maps the reversible residual idea onto attention and feed-forward sublayers:
Figure: The paper’s reversible Transformer block and the chunked feed-forward expression. This is a clean design:
becomes the attention layer; becomes the feed-forward layer; layer normalization is moved inside the residual blocks; and each have size , so the reversible model keeps comparable capacity.
My interpretation: reversible layers do not make attention cheaper. They make training deep stacks cheaper in activation memory. LSH attention and reversible layers solve different parts of the cost model. Chunked Feed-Forward ComputationReversibility removes the layer-count factor from activation storage, but the feed-forward network can still create a large intermediate tensor because is usually much larger than . The paper uses the fact that a Transformer feed-forward layer is position-wise. Each token can be processed independently. So the sequence can be split into chunks:
This formula is not changing the model’s function. It is changing the schedule. Instead of materializing feed-forward activations for all positions at once, process a chunk, release memory, then process the next chunk. The same idea is used for large output vocabularies. Computing log probabilities for every token at every position can also be chunked. Whole-Model Complexity Figure: Table 3 shows how each Reformer component removes one cost factor. Table 3 is the best summary of the paper. I read it from top to bottom:
Transformer: memory has both the feed-forward term and the attention term , multiplied by layers. Reversible Transformer: removes the multiplier from activation memory, but dense attention remains. Chunked Reversible Transformer: replaces the large feed-forward activation term with a smaller term. LSH Transformer: changes dense attention to an LSH chunk term, but still stores per-layer activations. Reformer: combines both sides, so memory is dominated by and the LSH attention term rather than layer-wise dense attention and feed-forward caches.
The final Reformer memory expression in the table is:
where summarizes the squared chunk width used by LSH attention. This is the paper’s intended endpoint: memory grows much more gently with depth and sequence length than in a standard Transformer. Experiments: Shared QK And Reversibility Figure: Figure 3 compares shared query-key space and reversible layers on enwik8 and imagenet64. This figure checks two risks:
Does sharing query and key projections hurt quality? Does making the Transformer reversible hurt quality?
The plots say mostly no. Shared QK performs similarly to separate Q and K. Reversible layers also track the regular Transformer closely. This matters because both are structural changes. If either one caused a large accuracy drop, the memory savings would be less convincing. One small detail I like: the paper tests these changes before combining them with LSH attention. That keeps the ablation clean. Shared QK and reversibility are not justified only by final Reformer performance; each component is separately checked. Experiments: Machine Translation Figure: Table 4 evaluates reversible Transformers on WMT14 English-German. This table is not about LSH attention. WMT14 sentences are usually short enough that the paper does not use LSH attention here. The purpose is narrower: prove that reversible layers can work in a standard encoder-decoder Transformer setting. The reversible Transformer reaches BLEU scores in the same range as the Vaswani et al. baselines. The big reversible model gets 29.1 BLEU in the paper’s table. My takeaway is that reversibility is not only a trick for character-level long-context tasks; it can be applied to regular sequence-to-sequence models without obviously destroying translation quality. Experiments: Number Of Hash Rounds Figure: Figure 4 shows LSH attention performance as the number of hashes increases on imagenet64. This plot is the empirical version of the union formula:
More hash rounds improve the chance of recovering the neighbors that full attention would have used. In the plot, 2 hashes are clearly worse. 8 hashes and 16 hashes approach full attention much more closely. The knob is easy to interpret:
fewer hashes: faster and cheaper, but lower recall; more hashes: closer to dense attention, but more computation.
The paper notes that already almost matches full attention in this setup. That is a useful practical point: the approximation can be tuned rather than accepted as a fixed loss. Experiments: Depth And Speed Figure: Figure 5 compares depth scaling on enwik8 and attention speed as sequence length grows. The left plot shows that deeper Reformers improve enwik8 performance up to around the tested 12-20 layer range. This is important because memory-efficient models sometimes save memory by becoming too constrained. Here the model can still benefit from depth. The right plot is the speed argument. Full attention slows down as sequence length increases. LSH attention stays much flatter because it does not compare every pair. The plot keeps total token count fixed and varies sequence length versus batch size, so it isolates the attention-length effect. This is one of the clearest figures in the paper: Reformer is not merely fitting into memory by recomputation. LSH attention changes the runtime trend with length. What I Would Check In An ImplementationIf I were implementing or debugging Reformer, I would focus on these failure points:
Hashing must be deterministic enough within a forward pass, but independent across hash rounds. Shared QK self-attention needs the self-mask; otherwise tokens over-attend to themselves. Sorting and unsorting must preserve token order for residual paths and output alignment. Chunk boundaries need one chunk of overlap or look-back, otherwise same-bucket tokens split across chunks are lost. Multi-round duplicates need careful handling; the same key can be found by more than one hash. Reversible layers save activation memory only if the implementation actually avoids caching intermediate activations. Chunked feed-forward is a scheduling optimization; it should not change numerical results except for small floating-point order differences.
These are the places where the paper’s math turns into engineering risk. LimitationsReformer is elegant, but it is not a universal replacement for dense attention. First, LSH attention is approximate. The model may miss relevant pairs if they do not collide in a hash bucket. Multiple hash rounds reduce the risk but increase cost. Second, the implementation is more complicated than dense attention. Hashing, sorting, chunking, duplicate removal, causal masking, and reversible recomputation all interact. Third, later long-context methods took different paths. Some methods use fixed sparse patterns, some use retrieval, some use state-space or recurrent structure, and FlashAttention-style kernels preserve dense exact attention while improving memory traffic. Reformer is best understood as one important branch of the design space, not the final answer. TakeawayThe part I want to remember is the decomposition:
causes the attention bottleneck. LSH attention replaces all-pairs comparison with content-based bucketed comparison. Multiple hash rounds trade compute for neighbor recall. Reversible layers remove the need to store every layer’s activation. Chunking keeps feed-forward and output intermediates from exploding.
The paper is valuable because each formula points to a concrete tensor. It does not just say “efficient Transformer”; it says which memory term is being removed, which approximation is being introduced, and which engineering schedule makes the method practical.

entry.title: RoBERTa: A Robustly Optimized BERT Pretraining Approach
entry.content:
Paper: RoBERTa: A Robustly Optimized BERT Pretraining Approach Code: fairseq RoBERTa is a paper about experimental hygiene. It does not introduce a new Transformer block, a new attention mechanism, or a new pretraining loss. Instead, it asks a sharper question:
How strong is BERT if we train it with a better-controlled recipe?
The answer is uncomfortable for many post-BERT papers. A carefully tuned BERT-style masked language model, trained longer with larger batches and more data, can match or exceed several methods that appeared to improve the objective or architecture. The paper’s main contribution is therefore not “remove NSP” in isolation. It is the systematic demonstration that pretraining data, optimization budget, masking strategy, input packing, and hyperparameters are all large enough to change the conclusion of an NLU comparison. All tables below are cropped from the original arXiv PDF. The ClaimRoBERTa starts from BERT and keeps the same broad model family:
Transformer encoder only; masked language modeling pretraining; task-specific fine-tuning; BERTBASE and BERTLARGE-sized configurations.
The improved recipe is:
use dynamic masking instead of fixed preprocessed masks; remove the Next Sentence Prediction objective; pack full-length sequences rather than sentence-pair fragments; train with larger mini-batches; use byte-level BPE with a 50K vocabulary; train on much more text; train for more update steps.
This matters because BERT was widely used as a baseline, but the original BERT training recipe was not necessarily a fully optimized baseline. RoBERTa argues that some reported gains from newer objectives were entangled with stronger compute and data settings. BERT Setup Being RevisitedBERT takes one or two text segments and packs them into a single input:
The segment lengths are constrained by the maximum pretraining sequence length:
The original BERT pretraining uses two objectives. The first is masked language modeling. BERT selects 15 percent of input tokens for prediction. Among those selected positions, 80 percent are replaced with [MASK], 10 percent are left unchanged, and 10 percent are replaced by a random vocabulary token. The model is trained with a cross-entropy loss on the selected positions. The second objective is Next Sentence Prediction. NSP is a binary classification loss that asks whether the two packed segments are contiguous in the original document. Positive examples use consecutive text; negative examples pair segments from different documents. The original optimization recipe also matters. The paper summarizes BERT as using Adam with:
weight decay 0.01, peak learning rate , 10K warmup steps, dropout 0.1, maximum length , 1M updates, and batch size 256 sequences. RoBERTa keeps the architecture fixed during the main ablation section, using BERTBASE with , hidden size , attention heads , and roughly 110M parameters. This is the right experimental move: change the recipe before changing the model. DataBERT’s original pretraining data is BookCorpus plus English Wikipedia, about 16GB of uncompressed text. RoBERTa expands this to about 160GB by adding CC-News, OpenWebText, and Stories.
Corpus Size Role in the paper
BookCorpus + Wikipedia 16GB Original BERT data
CC-News 76GB Large news crawl collected by the authors
OpenWebText 38GB Open recreation of WebText-style Reddit-linked web data
Stories 31GB CommonCrawl subset filtered for story-like text
Total about 160GB Used for the strongest RoBERTa runs
The paper is careful about this point: increasing data size and increasing data diversity are conflated in these experiments. It proves that the stronger data mixture improves the model, but it does not fully separate “more tokens” from “better domain coverage.” Static vs Dynamic MaskingThe original BERT implementation applies masking during preprocessing. To reduce exact repetition, the data is duplicated 10 times with different masks, but across 40 epochs each sequence still reappears with the same mask several times. RoBERTa switches to dynamic masking: every time a sequence is fed to the model, a fresh mask pattern is sampled. The difference is small in the short BERTBASE comparison, but dynamic masking is the more sensible choice for longer training and larger datasets.
Static vs dynamic masking on BERTBASE. Dynamic masking slightly improves SQuAD 2.0 and SST-2, while MNLI-m is essentially unchanged. The table should not be over-read as a huge accuracy jump. The important point is that fixed masking becomes increasingly awkward as the number of training steps grows. If the model sees the same sentence many times, changing the corruption pattern is a cheap way to create a richer denoising signal. Removing NSP Is Not The Whole StoryThe most remembered RoBERTa change is “remove NSP”, but Table 2 shows that the input format is just as important as the loss term.
Input format and NSP ablation. Sentence-pair training with NSP is worse; packed full-sentence training without NSP matches or improves the original BERT-style setting. The paper compares four formats:
Format NSP? Description
Segment-pair Yes Original BERT format: two multi-sentence segments, paired as positive or negative NSP examples
Sentence-pair Yes Two individual natural sentences; usually much shorter than 512 tokens
Full-sentences No Consecutive full sentences packed up to 512 tokens; may cross document boundaries
Doc-sentences No Similar packing, but examples never cross document boundaries
The bad result is sentence-pair + NSP: it drops to 88.7/76.2 on SQuAD 1.1/2.0, 82.9 on MNLI-m, 92.1 on SST-2, and 63.0 on RACE. The paper argues that this format is too short and prevents the model from learning longer-range dependencies. The stronger no-NSP settings are full-sentences and doc-sentences. Doc-sentences is slightly better in this table, but it produces variable-length examples and variable batch sizes. RoBERTa therefore uses full-sentences for easier comparison and implementation. The reading I take from this table: NSP is not rescued by better input packing, and removing NSP is not useful if the replacement format destroys sequence length. The recipe is “packed long sequences without NSP”, not merely “delete one loss.” Large Batch TrainingThe original BERTBASE pretraining cost can be expressed in several equivalent ways. Training for 1M steps with batch size 256 sequences sees roughly the same number of examples as 125K steps with batch size 2K, or 31K steps with batch size 8K.
Large-batch ablation under similar data passes and compute. The 2K batch setting improves held-out MLM perplexity and downstream scores in this comparison. The 2K batch row has the best held-out perplexity, 3.68, and the best MNLI-m/SST-2 scores, 85.2 and 92.9. The 8K row is close but not better in this table. RoBERTa still uses very large batches later because large-batch training is easier to parallelize over many GPUs, and the authors tune learning rate and Adam settings for stability. The lesson is not that any arbitrary large batch works. The paper notes that large-batch training requires appropriate learning-rate scaling and optimizer tuning. In particular, they found Adam helpful for stability in large-batch settings. Byte-Level BPEThe original BERT uses a character-level BPE vocabulary of about 30K units after heuristic tokenization. RoBERTa uses byte-level BPE with 50K subword units, following GPT-2 style tokenization. The byte-level choice has two practical benefits:
it can encode arbitrary text without an unknown-token fallback; it reduces dependence on language-specific preprocessing rules.
The paper says early experiments showed only slight task differences, and byte-level BPE was sometimes slightly worse. RoBERTa still adopts it because the robustness of a universal encoding scheme is useful when pretraining on diverse web-scale data. This is a small but durable engineering choice. Many later LLM tokenizers inherit this preference for byte-level or byte-fallback behavior because production text is messy. The RoBERTa RecipeThe core RoBERTa configuration combines the ablations:
dynamic masking; full-sentence packing; no NSP objective; large mini-batches; byte-level BPE; BERTLARGE architecture for the final model.
The final BERTLARGE-sized model uses , , , and about 355M parameters. The paper first controls for data by training on Books + Wiki, then adds the 160GB data mixture, then increases the number of pretraining steps.
The main RoBERTa scaling table. Each RoBERTa row accumulates one more improvement: more data, then longer pretraining. This table is the paper’s strongest evidence. The key rows are:
RoBERTa with Books + Wiki, trained for 100K steps: SQuAD 1.1/2.0 is 93.6/87.3, MNLI-m is 89.0, and SST-2 is 95.3. Adding the 160GB data mixture at the same 100K steps gives 94.0/87.7 on SQuAD, 89.3 on MNLI-m, and 95.6 on SST-2. Training the 160GB model for 300K steps gives 94.4/88.7 on SQuAD, 90.0 on MNLI-m, and 96.1 on SST-2. Training for 500K steps gives 94.6/89.4 on SQuAD, 90.2 on MNLI-m, and 96.4 on SST-2. The originally reported BERTLARGE row is much lower: 90.9/81.8 on SQuAD, 86.6 on MNLI-m, and 93.7 on SST-2. XLNetLARGE with additional data is strong but still slightly behind the final RoBERTa row on MNLI-m and SST-2.
The first RoBERTa row already beats the originally reported BERTLARGE result while staying on comparable Books + Wiki data. That validates the recipe ablations. The later rows show that more data and longer training continue to improve downstream results. The 500K-step RoBERTa row beats the listed XLNetLARGE + additional data row on MNLI-m and SST-2, and is close on SQuAD. This is why the paper is important. It does not say new objectives are useless. It says that if the baseline is undertrained, a new objective can look better than it really is. GLUE ResultsThe GLUE table has two parts. The top part compares single-task single models on development sets. The bottom part compares leaderboard test ensembles as of July 25, 2019.
GLUE results. RoBERTa uses the same MLM objective family as BERT but is much stronger under the improved recipe. On single-task dev, RoBERTa improves over both BERTLARGE and XLNetLARGE on every listed task. The most visible gains over BERTLARGE are:
MNLI rises from 86.6 to 90.2/90.2. QNLI rises from 92.3 to 94.7. RTE rises from 70.4 to 86.6. SST-2 rises from 93.2 to 96.4. CoLA rises from 60.6 to 68.0. STS-B rises from 90.0 to 92.4.
The leaderboard part reports RoBERTa at 88.5 average, slightly ahead of XLNet’s 88.4 in the table. The paper emphasizes that the submission uses ensembles of single-task models rather than multi-task fine-tuning. It does use task-specific details for QNLI and WNLI, and for RTE/STS/MRPC it helps to fine-tune from an MNLI model. That is worth remembering: the pretraining story is clean, but the leaderboard submission still includes task-level engineering. The appendix gives a more direct incremental view over GLUE dev results:
Appendix GLUE development results for RoBERTaBASE and RoBERTaLARGE configurations. The RoBERTaLARGE progression is useful: MNLI improves from 89.0 to 90.2, QNLI from 93.9 to 94.7, SST from 95.3 to 96.4, CoLA from 66.3 to 68.0, and STS from 91.6 to 92.4 as the recipe accumulates more data and longer training. SQuAD and RACERoBERTa also performs strongly on SQuAD without extra QA data.
SQuAD results. RoBERTa uses only the provided SQuAD data, while dagger-marked rows depend on additional external training data. On SQuAD 2.0 dev, RoBERTa reaches 86.5 EM and 89.4 F1, improving over XLNetLARGE’s 86.1 EM and 88.8 F1 in the table. On the SQuAD 2.0 test leaderboard, RoBERTa reaches 86.8 EM and 89.8 F1 without the extra-data dagger, just below XLNet + SG-Net Verifier’s 87.0 EM and 89.9 F1, which is marked as depending on additional external training data. For RACE, RoBERTa is also ahead:
RACE test results. RoBERTa improves the overall, middle-school, and high-school subsets. The jump from BERTLARGE to RoBERTa is large: 72.0 to 83.2 overall accuracy. XLNetLARGE is much closer at 81.7, but RoBERTa still improves to 83.2 overall, 86.5 on middle-school questions, and 81.3 on high-school questions. HyperparametersThe appendix tables are useful because RoBERTa is a recipe paper. If the point is training setup, the setup itself should be visible.
Pretraining hyperparameters for RoBERTaLARGE and RoBERTaBASE. Important pretraining details:
RoBERTaLARGE uses 24 layers, hidden size 1024, FFN size 4096, and 16 attention heads. RoBERTaBASE uses 12 layers, hidden size 768, FFN size 3072, and 12 heads. Both use attention head size 64, dropout 0.1, attention dropout 0.1, batch size 8K, weight decay 0.01, max steps 500K, linear LR decay, Adam , and Adam . Peak learning rate is for RoBERTaLARGE and for RoBERTaBASE.
Fine-tuning hyperparameters for RACE, SQuAD, and GLUE. Fine-tuning is not one-size-fits-all. The paper uses learning rate for RACE, for SQuAD, and searches over for GLUE. It uses batch size 16 for RACE, 48 for SQuAD, and for GLUE. Warmup ratio is 0.06 across these tasks. This is one reason RoBERTa is more than a slogan. “Train longer and remove NSP” is not enough to reproduce the result. The paper is a bundle of training choices. What RoBERTa Changes ConceptuallyRoBERTa changes the default interpretation of BERT results in three ways. First, BERT’s MLM objective is stronger than it looked in early comparisons. If the baseline is undertrained, replacing the objective can look like a bigger breakthrough than it is. Second, pretraining evaluations must control for data and compute. XLNet and other post-BERT systems often used more data, bigger batches, or longer training. RoBERTa makes those variables visible. Third, “simple” recipe choices can be architecture-level in effect. Dynamic masking, long packed sequences, and byte-level tokenization do not change the Transformer equation, but they change the distribution of training examples and the optimization path. LimitationsRoBERTa is a strong paper, but it should be read with its scope in mind. The experiments do not fully disentangle data size from data diversity. The 160GB setting improves results, but the paper explicitly leaves a more careful separation of those variables to future work. The strongest models are compute-heavy. Training the 100K-step large model uses 1024 V100 GPUs for roughly one day, and the later 300K/500K runs are correspondingly expensive. RoBERTa is not a cheap baseline; it is a strong baseline. The GLUE leaderboard submission contains task-specific choices and ensembling. The paper is clear about this, but when using RoBERTa as evidence, it is better to distinguish the cleaner single-task dev results from leaderboard engineering. Finally, RoBERTa is still an encoder-only masked-LM pretraining paper. It does not address autoregressive generation, instruction tuning, retrieval, long-context attention, or modern decoder-only LLM serving. Its lasting value is methodological: train the baseline properly before attributing gains to a new modeling idea. TakeawayRoBERTa turns BERT from a model checkpoint into a stronger training baseline. The recipe is not glamorous, but it is decisive:
dynamic masks reduce repeated corruption patterns; packed full-length examples are better than short sentence pairs; NSP is unnecessary under the stronger input format; large batches and tuned optimization make pretraining scalable; more diverse data and longer training keep improving downstream tasks; byte-level BPE makes the tokenizer more robust for large web corpora.
The paper’s practical message is still relevant: before claiming a new architecture or objective is better, first check whether the baseline had enough data, enough steps, a fair batch size, and a tuned fine-tuning procedure. RoBERTa is a reminder that many “model” improvements are really recipe improvements until proven otherwise.

entry.title: S3: Searching Vision Transformer Search Spaces
entry.content:
Chen M, Wu K, Ni B, Peng H, Liu B, Fu J, Chao H, Ling H. Searching the Search Space of Vision Transformer. NeurIPS 2021.
Paper S3 is a meta-NAS paper for Vision Transformers. Most NAS papers start with a fixed search space and then optimize architectures inside it. S3 moves one level up: first ask whether the search space is good, evolve that space, and only then run architecture search inside the evolved space. That question matters because search quality is bounded by the space. A weak space can make a strong optimizer look bad, while a carefully designed space can make even simple search methods competitive. For ViTs, this is especially visible because depth, embedding width, Q-K-V dimension, MLP ratio, window size, and stage layout are tightly coupled. What Is Being Searched The left side of the figure is the main idea:
decompose a search space by dimensions; estimate the quality tendency of each dimension; move each dimension toward a better region; compose the updated dimensions into a new search space.
The right side is the ViT family explored by the paper. It is not a flat DeiT-style sequence of identical blocks. It is a four-stage hierarchical transformer with patch embedding, downsampling between stages, window self-attention, and FFN blocks. The searched dimensions include:
stage depth, written as the number of blocks in each stage; embedding dimension per stage; per-block Q-K-V dimension; MLP ratio; window size; number of attention heads.
The important detail is that S3 does not require the same choice in every stage. A shallow stage can shrink while a deeper stage grows. That is where most of the paper’s architecture insight comes from. Problem FormulationOrdinary NAS can be written as:
The search space is fixed. S3 changes the setup by explicitly searching for a better first:
Then it trains a supernet over and searches for the best architecture inside that searched space. This separation is useful. If the search space is poor, optimizing is trying to win inside a bad game. S3 instead tries to improve the game board before selecting a model. E-T ErrorThe paper needs a way to score a search space. It uses E-T Error, which averages two terms:
The expected error term is:
where is ImageNet top-1 error and is the resource constraint. This term measures the average quality of the space. The top-tier term is the average error of the top 50 candidates under the same constraint. This term estimates the upper end of the space. I like this metric because it catches two different failure modes:
Failure mode Why E-T helps
The space has one good model but most candidates are bad remains high
The average candidate is fine but the best models are not strong remains high
A dimension looks useful only because a few lucky samples work both terms must improve
The metric is still only as good as the performance proxy. S3 does not train every candidate from scratch. It trains a once-for-all supernet, following the AutoFormer style, and evaluates many inherited-weight subnets. That makes the search-space metric practical, but it also means the supernet ranking quality is critical. Search-Space Evolution The algorithm alternates between supernet optimization and space evolution. For a current space , S3 trains a supernet and samples architectures from it. For each search dimension, it groups candidates by the value of that dimension and computes E-T Error for each group. Then it fits a simple linear tendency between dimension value and E-T Error. If larger values make the error better, the dimension moves upward. If larger values make the error worse, it moves downward. This is deliberately simple. The paper is not trying to learn a complex controller over search spaces. It uses the supernet to answer a local question: for this dimension, which direction improves the space? Some implementation details are worth keeping:
space search runs for 3 iterations; the threshold for space evolution is 0.4; evolution step sizes are 1 block, 64 embedding channels, 0.5 MLP ratio, 64 Q-K-V channels, and 7 window-size units; supernet training uses AdamW, weight decay 0.05, batch size 1024, 20 warmup epochs, stochastic depth 0.2, and a 300-epoch DeiT-like recipe on 16 V100 GPUs; sandwich training samples the largest, smallest, and two middle models per iteration; the authors avoid in-place distillation because it collapses for their transformer training.
So this is not a cheap search procedure. The claim is not “free NAS”. The claim is that spending compute on the search space can give a better architecture family. What The Space Learns Figure 2 is the most useful part of the paper for manual model design. It starts from a deliberately symmetric space and lets each stage evolve. The discovered tendencies are:
Stage 3 gets deeper. The number of blocks in stage 3 grows during search, while stages 1, 2, and 4 shrink. Later stages get wider. Embedding and Q-K-V dimensions increase in the deeper stages, especially stage 4. Q-K-V can be smaller than embedding. The searched Q-K-V dimension is often below the embedding dimension, with a larger gap in deeper layers. MLP ratio increases with depth. Shallow layers prefer smaller MLP ratios, while deeper layers can use larger ratios. Window size is stage-dependent. Shallow layers move toward smaller windows, while deeper layers prefer larger windows.
The third-stage observation is interesting because it mirrors CNN backbones: much of the representational budget sits in the middle/high-resolution stage, not evenly across all stages.
The block-number plots tell the same story from the E-T Error side. For stage 3, adding blocks improves the top-tier region. For the other stages, fewer blocks are often enough. This is the kind of signal that a manually fixed uniform space would hide. Why Window Size Changes With DepthThe paper gives a small diagnostic to justify the window-size trend.
The attention maps use the top-left patch as the reference position. Earlier blocks concentrate attention near the reference. Deeper blocks attend farther away, and the top-5/top-10 relative-distance box plots shift right. This does not prove that every ViT should use the exact S3 window schedule, but it explains the search result: shallow layers benefit from local windows, while deeper layers can use larger windows because their useful attention region has expanded. ImageNet Results The headline ImageNet numbers are strong for a 2021 hierarchical ViT search paper:
Model Params FLOPs Resolution Top-1
Swin-T 28.3M 4.5G 224 81.3
S3-T 28.1M 4.7G 224 82.1
Swin-S 50M 8.7G 224 83.0
S3-S 50M 9.5G 224 83.7
S3-S-384 50M 33G 384 84.5
Swin-B 88M 15.4G 224 83.3
S3-B 71M 13.6G 224 84.0
S3-B-384 71M 46G 384 84.7
The most direct comparisons are against Swin at similar scale. S3-T improves Swin-T by 0.8 points with similar FLOPs. S3-S improves Swin-S by 0.7 points. S3-B is also smaller than Swin-B while reporting higher top-1 accuracy.
Figure 7 is a constraint view of the same result. S3 sits on a strong accuracy-parameter and accuracy-FLOP curve compared with ViT, DeiT, Swin, ResNet, and RegNet references. The throughput plot is more nuanced because real speed depends on kernels and implementation, not just FLOPs. I read it as evidence that the searched models are not only parameter-efficient, not as a final hardware-latency study. Does The Supernet Proxy Work? S3 depends on inherited-weight evaluation. If the supernet proxy is wrong, E-T Error becomes noise. Figure 5 checks 10 sampled architectures and compares inherited performance with fine-tuned or retrained performance. The points are close to the diagonal, which supports the proxy in this setting. It is not a complete statistical proof, but it is the right sanity check. Figure 6 compares three search spaces:
Space A: initial space; Space B: one-step evolved space; Space C: two-step evolved space.
The error distribution shifts left from A to C, meaning sampled candidates become better on average. Table 5 gives the top searched architecture in each space:
Space Params FLOPs Top-1
A 28M 4.7G 65.5
B 29M 4.7G 78.0
C 28M 4.7G 82.1
That gap is the core empirical argument for S3. The final architecture is not merely the result of a better evolutionary search. The search space itself has changed enough that the same resource level becomes much more productive. Downstream Transfer The paper also transfers S3 backbones to detection, segmentation, and VQA. For COCO with Cascade Mask R-CNN and FPN, the 3x schedule results are:
Backbone Box AP Mask AP Comparison
Swin-T 50.4 43.7 baseline at tiny scale
S3-T 50.5 43.8 slightly higher
Swin-S 51.8 44.7 baseline at small scale
S3-S 52.6 45.5 +0.8 box AP, +0.8 mask AP
Swin-B 51.9 45.0 baseline at base scale
S3-B 52.5 45.4 +0.6 box AP, +0.4 mask AP
This matters because searched classifiers can overfit to ImageNet. Here the architecture choices transfer to dense prediction under the Swin-style downstream setup.
The ADE20K and VQA results are smaller tables but useful:
Task S3 result Reference comparison
ADE20K UperNet S3-T 44.87 mIoU / 46.27 ms+flip above Swin-T 44.51 / 45.81
ADE20K UperNet S3-S 48.04 mIoU / 49.31 ms+flip above Swin-S 47.60 / 48.87
VQA v2.0 S3-T 67.84 test-dev / 68.00 test-std above Swin-T 67.13 / 67.40
The gains are not huge everywhere, but they are consistent enough to support the paper’s point: the searched space does not only produce an ImageNet-specific classifier. Relation To AutoFormer And ViTASS3 is closely related to AutoFormer. AutoFormer shows that a weight-entangled ViT supernet can evaluate and deploy subnets. S3 reuses that idea as an estimator for search-space quality, then changes the space before the final architecture search. The distinction is:
Paper Main target Reusable idea
AutoFormer search architectures in a fixed ViT space weight-entangled transformer supernet
S3 search the ViT search space, then search architectures E-T Error and dimension-wise space evolution
ViTAS improve supernet fairness for ViT NAS cyclic channel sharing
S3 also has a RegNet flavor. RegNet studied design-space quality for CNNs, but it relied on training many sampled models for a short time. S3 instead uses a trained once-for-all transformer supernet to get many performance estimates more cheaply. Reproduction NotesIf I were reproducing S3, I would not start from the final ImageNet table. I would first validate the measurement loop:
implement the hierarchical search-space encoding; train a small supernet on a reduced setting; sample subnets and check inherited accuracy against a few retrained models; compute , , and E-T Error by dimension value; verify that one evolution step moves a dimension in the predicted direction; only then scale to the 300-epoch recipe and evolution search.
The final architecture search uses evolutionary search under resource constraints. The supplementary algorithm uses a population of 50, 20 generations, and the top 10 candidates as parents. That is a small part of the total cost compared with repeated supernet training. The dangerous failure mode is a misleading supernet. If inherited accuracy is biased toward certain widths, depths, or channel slices, S3 may evolve the space toward whatever the supernet trained best, not toward what would retrain best. This is why Figure 5 is more important than it first appears. LimitationsS3 improves search-space design, but it still has clear boundaries.
The “infinite” space is still hand-structured as a four-stage window-attention transformer family. It does not discover new attention operators, convolutional stems, normalization variants, or training recipes. The E-T metric depends on inherited-weight evaluation. If the once-for-all supernet has ranking bias, the search-space update can be biased too. The compute budget is substantial. Space evolution requires training supernets, and the reported recipe uses 300 epochs on 16 V100 GPUs. The optimization target is mainly ImageNet accuracy under parameter/FLOP constraints. Real deployment may care about latency, memory traffic, activation size, and kernel availability. The design observations are tied to this hierarchical ViT setting. “Stage 3 should be deeper” is a strong clue, not a theorem for every transformer backbone.
TakeawayS3 is useful because it makes search-space design measurable. Instead of treating the ViT search space as a fixed human prior, it evaluates whether each dimension is moving the candidate distribution in a better direction. The paper’s lasting value is not only that S3-T/S/B beat several 2021 baselines. The more general lesson is that NAS has two coupled problems: how to search, and what space to search in. For Vision Transformers, S3 shows that the second problem is large enough to deserve its own optimization loop.

entry.title: SARATHI: Piggybacking Decodes with Chunked Prefills
entry.content:
Paper: SARATHI: Efficient LLM Inference by Piggybacking Decodes with Chunked Prefills SARATHI is a paper about the execution shape of LLM inference. The key observation is not just that prompts can be long. It is that the prefill phase and the decode phase stress the GPU in opposite ways:
prefill has many tokens per request, so it can form large matrix-matrix multiplications and saturate compute quickly; decode has one new token per active request, so it is often a small vector-matrix-like workload dominated by loading weights and KV cache state; pipeline parallelism makes this worse, because consecutive micro-batches can have very different runtimes and leave pipeline stages idle.
SARATHI’s answer is simple but subtle: split prefill into chunks, and schedule each chunk with as many decode tokens as possible. The prefill chunk keeps the GPU compute-bound; the decode tokens reuse the weight loads and “piggyback” on that work. In pipeline-parallel deployments, the same chunking also makes micro-batches more uniform, reducing bubbles.
Figure 1. Orca-style iteration-level scheduling can still create non-uniform pipeline work. SARATHI cuts prefills into smaller chunks and mixes them with decode tokens, making the per-iteration work more regular. The Problem ShapeAn autoregressive LLM request has two major phases. The prefill phase consumes all prompt tokens. If the prompt length is , the hidden size is , and the batch size is , a transformer block sees tensors shaped like . The model can run many token positions in parallel. The decode phase generates one token per iteration. The same block now sees for most linear operations. Attention still needs to read the previous KV cache, but the new query side is tiny.
Figure 2. SARATHI studies a standard decoder-only transformer block: attention projections, attention, output projection, and the FFN.
Table 1. In decode, for most operations. Attention is the exception because it still depends on all cached previous keys and values. This difference matters because GPU efficiency is not decided by token count alone. A prefill batch can do large dense GEMMs. A decode iteration may touch the same large weight matrices for only a few tokens, which gives poor arithmetic intensity. The paper profiles LLaMA-13B on an A6000 with sequence length 1024. Prefill per-token time is almost flat across batch sizes because even one long prompt can saturate compute. Decode behaves very differently: at batch sizes 1, 2, and 18, decode per-token cost is about 200x, 100x, and 16.7x the prefill per-token cost, respectively.
Figure 3. Prefill cost per token is almost constant; decode becomes cheaper only as the active decode batch grows. Figure 4 explains why this happens. Prefill reaches high throughput when is large enough. For LLaMA-13B on A6000, the paper reports that prefill throughput saturates around 180 tokens/ms once . Decode throughput grows with batch size, but practical full-model decode batches are limited by model weights and KV cache memory.
Figure 4. Prefill operations have high arithmetic intensity at small batch sizes. Decode operations remain memory-bound until impractically large batches. The immediate consequence is a bad serving tradeoff:
run big prefill batches, and active decodes can wait too long; prioritize decode-only iterations, and the GPU spends too much time doing low-arithmetic-intensity work; use pipeline parallelism, and variable prefill/decode runtimes create bubbles between stages.
Pipeline BubblesPipeline parallelism splits the model by layers. It is attractive when tensor parallel all-reduces are too expensive across nodes, but it depends on a stream of similarly sized micro-batches. SARATHI points out that LLM inference violates this assumption.
Figure 5. Even with iteration-level scheduling, different prompt lengths and decode contexts create pipeline bubbles. The paper names three bubble sources:
PB1: varying prefill length. Consecutive micro-batches can contain different numbers of prompt tokens. PB2: prefill/decode mismatch. A prefill-heavy micro-batch and a decode-heavy micro-batch have different runtimes. PB3: decode context mismatch. Decode runtime changes with accumulated context length because attention reads more KV cache.
The usual fix in training is to increase the number of micro-batches, but inference has no backward pass and a constantly changing mix of request states. If the serving engine cannot make each unit of work more uniform, pipeline stages still go idle. SARATHI’s core idea is to manufacture uniform units of work:
cut large prefills into chunks that are still compute-efficient; add decode tokens to each chunk until the batch is decode-maximal; make each micro-batch close to the same compute cost.
Chunked PrefillsChunked prefill means a long prompt is not processed as a single monolithic prefill. Instead, the prompt is split into chunks, and each chunk is scheduled in a separate iteration. The key correctness issue is attention masking. A token in a later chunk must be allowed to attend to all previous chunks, but it must not attend to future tokens. With the right mask and KV cache updates, chunked prefill is mathematically equivalent to full prefill.
Figure 6. Each prefill chunk can attend to all earlier prompt tokens and the earlier tokens inside the same chunk, but not to future tokens. Chunking is useful only if each chunk is still large enough to run efficiently. The paper gives two reasons this is often possible:
LLaMA-13B on A6000 reaches peak prefill throughput once the number of prefill tokens is around 512 or higher; using 256 tokens costs only about 12.5% of peak prefill throughput. Larger hidden sizes need fewer tokens to saturate compute. For GPT-3 with hidden size 12288 on A100, a single layer peaks around chunk size 256.
There is overhead. Smaller chunks reduce arithmetic intensity. They also reread old KV cache in attention: if a prompt is split into chunks, the first chunk’s KV cache is read by later chunk attentions many times. SARATHI argues this is acceptable because attention is a smaller part of the full forward pass than the linear layers, but the ablation later shows that very small chunks can still be expensive. Decode-Maximal BatchingChunking alone only creates more prefill scheduling units. The important scheduling rule is decode-maximal batching. Each SARATHI batch contains:
one prefill chunk; as many decode tokens as the remaining batch slots can hold.
The maximum decode batch size is constrained by GPU memory. The paper writes it as:
where:
is GPU memory; is model parameter memory per GPU; is the maximum sequence length; is the memory required for the KV pair of one token; is the maximum batch size that fits.
In a decode-only baseline, the decode batch can use up to requests. In SARATHI, a decode-maximal batch uses one slot for the prefill request and at most decode tokens. The compute trick is in the linear layers. Prefill and decode run the same weight matrices. Baseline decode loads those weights for only a tiny number of new tokens. SARATHI concatenates the prefill chunk tokens and the decode tokens for linear operations, so the decode tokens reuse the same weight loads. Attention still runs separately for prefill and decode because their attention shapes are different.
Table 2. In the LLaMA-13B/A6000 example, decode-only costs 12.49 ms/token. In a decode-maximal batch, the marginal decode cost falls to 1.2 ms/token. This table is the cleanest numerical explanation of the paper. The decode-maximal batch has almost the same total time as a prefill-only batch, but it also advances decode tokens. The decode tokens are not free, but their marginal cost is much lower because the expensive weight movement is already paid for by the prefill chunk. This also explains why the paper’s headline improvements differ by metric:
decode throughput can improve by up to an order of magnitude; end-to-end throughput improves less, because SARATHI mostly improves decode and does not make pure prefill much faster.
Picking Chunk SizeThe chunk size is not a universal constant. It depends on workload mix, model size, GPU, KV memory, and matmul tile behavior. The paper uses the P:D ratio, the ratio between prefill tokens and decode tokens. For a prefill length , output length , chunk size , and max batch size , perfect piggybacking happens when the number of chunks matches the number of decode iterations that can be covered:
or:
Small chunks create more opportunities to piggyback decode tokens, but they reduce prefill efficiency. Large chunks keep prefill efficient, but they create fewer mixed batches and may leave decode tokens uncovered. There is another hardware detail: tile quantization. GPU matmuls are partitioned into tiles. If the relevant matrix dimension is just over a tile multiple, the kernel may do a lot of wasted work.
Figure 7. Adding one token past a tile-friendly boundary can cause a large runtime jump. The paper reports 69.8 ms at 256 tokens and 92.33 ms at 257 tokens in this example. The practical rule is:
choose a chunk size that gives acceptable prefill efficiency; make prefill_chunk_tokens + decode_tokens align with the matmul tile size.
For example, if the target combined token count is 256, the max batch size is , and a decode-maximal batch carries decodes, the actual prefill chunk used in the fused linear operation should be tokens. Implementation SetupSARATHI is implemented on nanoGPT with support for chunked prefills and decode-maximal batching. For fair comparison with Orca-style iteration-level scheduling, the authors use the same mixed batching mechanism but remove SARATHI’s constraints for the baseline. They also use xFormers attention because it was fastest in their setup, and they pre-allocate KV cache for the maximum sequence length to avoid per-iteration allocation overhead.
Table 3. The paper evaluates single-GPU physical deployments for LLaMA-13B/A6000 and LLaMA-33B/A100, and a profile-driven 64xA100 GPT-3 simulation. The model configurations are standard:
LLaMA-13B: 40 layers, 40 attention heads, hidden size 5120; LLaMA-33B: 60 layers, 52 attention heads, hidden size 6656; GPT-3: 96 layers, 96 attention heads, hidden size 12288.
Single-GPU ResultsThe first experiment measures decode-only speedup on LLaMA-13B with chunk size 256. SARATHI computes decode speedup by comparing the marginal decode time inside a decode-maximal batch against the baseline decode-only iteration.
Figure 8. SARATHI gives the largest decode speedup at smaller batch sizes, where baseline decode is most memory-bound. The reported decode speedup ranges from about 2.8x to 10x. It decreases as batch size grows because baseline decode becomes less inefficient. It also decreases as sequence length grows because attention becomes a larger fraction of total decode time, and SARATHI mostly improves linear layers. The end-to-end throughput gains are smaller but still meaningful:
The peak cases in Table 4 are:
LLaMA-13B on A6000: 1K/2K/3K sequence lengths reach 1.33x, 1.26x, and 1.22x throughput gain, with decode speedups of 5.45x, 3.26x, and 2.51x. LLaMA-33B on A100: 1K/2K/3K sequence lengths reach 1.25x, 1.22x, and 1.14x throughput gain, with decode speedups of 3.83x, 4.25x, and 3.51x.
Two things stand out. First, the A6000 gains are higher than the A100 gains. The paper attributes this to the A100’s higher FLOPs-to-memory-bandwidth ratio. On A100, a larger chunk size or larger hidden dimension is needed to avoid losing prefill efficiency. Second, a 5x to 10x decode speedup does not become a 5x to 10x serving speedup. That is expected. SARATHI attacks the decode inefficiency; the remaining prefill work still costs real time. P:D Ratio BehaviorFigure 9 is one of the most useful graphs for implementation. It shows that each chunk size has a sweet spot, and the sweet spot moves with sequence length and batch size.
Figure 9. Throughput peaks when prefill chunks and decode iterations balance. Too few prefill chunks or too few decode tokens both reduce SARATHI’s advantage. For sequence length 1K and batch size 18:
chunk size 256 peaks around , matching ; chunk size 512 peaks around , matching ; chunk size 128 gives more opportunities to overlap decode, but it loses too much prefill efficiency.
The paper’s useful takeaway is that a scheduler should not blindly use the smallest possible chunk. If the request mix is decode-heavy, smaller chunks can help. If the request mix has a higher P:D ratio, larger chunks are often better. If the mix is far away from the selected chunk’s balance point, SARATHI can fall back toward normal prefill-only or decode-only behavior. The operation breakdown supports the same point.
Figure 10. Linear layers, especially the FFN, benefit most from decode-maximal batching. Attention is not the main source of speedup. The FFN sees the largest runtime reduction, around 1.3x to 1.6x in the paper’s reported cases. Pre-projection and post-projection improve less, around 1.05x to 1.38x. This matches the mechanism: SARATHI improves the linear operations by turning tiny decode work into a larger fused matrix multiplication. Attention remains a different shape and is less affected. Comparison With Orca-Style Iteration-Level SchedulingOrca, vLLM, and TGI use iteration-level scheduling: requests can enter or leave the batch at iteration boundaries. This avoids padding all requests to the longest sequence and lets completed requests exit early. But iteration-level scheduling does not guarantee a good prefill/decode composition. A batch can contain:
only prefills; only decodes; a random mixture of full prefills and decodes.
Orca may overlap a newly arriving full prefill with ongoing decodes, but that overlap is incidental. It still submits the entire prompt as one prefill unit. SARATHI’s difference is that it creates many chunked prefill units, each of which can carry decodes.
Figure 11. SARATHI consistently beats the baseline and Orca best case in these experiments because it actively creates piggyback opportunities instead of relying on arrival timing. The paper compares Orca in two scenarios:
best case: a full prefill overlaps with ongoing decodes; worst case: requests begin and end together, so there is little useful overlap.
For LLaMA-13B on A6000:
best-case Orca gets about 1.11x throughput at 1K sequence length, then drops closer to baseline at longer sequence lengths; SARATHI reaches 1.27x, 1.25x, and 1.23x for 1K, 2K, and 3K sequence lengths.
The reason is coverage. A full prefill provides only one overlap opportunity. Chunked prefill turns one long prompt into many opportunities, so more decode iterations can piggyback. Pipeline-Parallel ResultsSARATHI’s second major contribution is applying the same uniform-work idea to pipeline parallelism. The GPT-3 experiment is simulated but carefully profile-driven:
64 A100 GPUs across eight servers connected with InfiniBand; 8-way tensor parallelism inside a node plus 8-way pipeline parallelism across nodes; comparison against eight 8-way tensor-parallel replicas; max batch size 27 for TP+PP and 11 for TP-only; P:D ratio fixed at 10; request sequence lengths sampled between 1K and 4K from a Zipf distribution with ; chunk size 256; simulator predictions validated within 5% on an 8-GPU 80GB A100 DGX box.
Figure 12. SARATHI reduces pipeline bubble time and improves request completion time for GPT-3 in the 64xA100 simulation. The reported result is strong:
median bubble time per request drops by 6.29x; SARATHI’s TP+PP setup is 1.91x faster than the TP+PP baseline with Orca-style scheduling; it is also 1.48x faster than the TP-only replica setup.
The TP-only setup is already 1.28x faster than the baseline TP+PP setup because the baseline suffers from large pipeline bubbles. SARATHI changes that conclusion by making pipeline-parallel work units much more uniform. This is the part of the paper that connects scheduling to cluster architecture. Without uniform micro-batches, PP can waste enough time that TP-only replicas look better despite smaller batch capacity. With chunked-prefill and decode-maximal batching, PP can use its memory advantage without paying as much bubble overhead. Chunking OverheadThe ablation asks whether chunked-prefill overhead cancels the decode gain.
Figure 13. Very small chunks hurt prefill efficiency, but moderate chunks can still improve the full batch because decode gets cheaper. The main numbers:
chunk size 64 causes around 3x attention overhead and about 5x total prefill overhead; chunk sizes 256 and 512 keep end-to-end prefill loss within about 20% and 10%; chunk size 64 can still roughly match baseline overall because it piggybacks more decodes; chunk size 128 can reach up to 1.16x overall throughput even though prefill is more than 2x slower; tile quantization appears again: chunk size 256 does better than 320 because 256 aligns with the tile size.
This is the clearest warning for implementers. Chunked prefill is a scheduler parameter, not a magic constant. It needs profiling on the actual model and GPU. Relationship To PagedAttention And DistServeSARATHI sits between memory management and cluster-level phase separation. PagedAttention / vLLM solves KV cache allocation and fragmentation. It lets the serving engine fit more active requests and avoid wasting memory on over-reserved KV blocks. SARATHI assumes a serving engine can maintain active decode requests and KV state, then asks: given those requests, how should prefill and decode work be composed in each iteration? DistServe separates prefill and decode onto different workers. It argues that the two phases have different parallelism and latency requirements, so they should be scaled independently. SARATHI keeps the phases colocated and improves the mixed execution schedule. This avoids cross-phase KV transfer, but it also means the same workers still handle both phase types. So the boundary is:
PagedAttention: “How do I store KV cache efficiently enough to support many active requests?” SARATHI: “How do I mix prefill chunks and decode tokens so decode becomes cheap and pipeline bubbles shrink?” DistServe: “Should prefill and decode live on separate resource pools?”
These ideas are complementary in principle. A production serving stack could use paged KV memory, SARATHI-like chunked prefill scheduling, and some form of phase-aware placement or disaggregation. Implementation Notes I Would CheckIf I were implementing SARATHI in an inference runtime, I would start with these invariants. The scheduler state needs to distinguish:
waiting prefill requests; active decode requests; partial prefill chunks that have already written KV cache; per-request generated length and remaining decode budget; max sequence length and current KV allocation.
The batch builder should be decode-maximal: def build_sarathi_batch(waiting_prefills, active_decodes, max_batch, target_tokens): decode_slots = max_batch - 1 decodes = pick_decodes(active_decodes, limit=decode_slots) # Keep the fused linear dimension tile-friendly. prefill_tokens = target_tokens - len(decodes) prefill_chunk = pick_prefill_chunk(waiting_prefills, tokens=prefill_tokens) return Batch(prefill_chunk=prefill_chunk, decodes=decodes)
The real version needs more policies:
what to do when there is no waiting prefill; what to do when there are too few active decodes; how to age waiting prefills to avoid TTFT starvation; how to choose chunk size when P:D changes over time; how to preserve fairness when some requests have very long prompts; how to account for partial chunks near the end of a prompt; how to handle memory pressure if KV cache allocation fails.
The paper mainly optimizes execution efficiency. A production engine still needs admission control, SLO-aware queuing, preemption behavior, and fairness. SARATHI is the compute layer mechanism, not the whole serving policy. LimitationsThe paper is explicit about several limitations. First, SARATHI focuses on throughput and execution efficiency. Real serving systems also care about TTFT, TPOT, queueing delay, fairness, cancellation, and request priorities. A decode-maximal scheduler that ignores these can still create bad user-visible latency. Second, chunk size selection is workload-dependent. The paper can choose good values for the evaluated P:D ratios, models, and GPUs, but a production workload may have changing prompt and output distributions. Dynamic chunk-size selection is left open. Third, many experiments assume requests in a batch have similar prefill and decode token counts. The pipeline simulation adds variable sequence lengths, but real traffic can be more irregular. Fourth, the paper focuses on sequence lengths up to about 3K for most experiments and P:D ratios from 1 to 200. Very long-context serving changes the attention cost substantially. When attention dominates, SARATHI’s linear-layer piggybacking has less room to help. Finally, SARATHI does not replace KV memory management. If KV cache fragmentation or over-reservation prevents large active batches, the scheduler may not have enough decodes to piggyback. TakeawayMy mental model for SARATHI:
Decode is inefficient because it is too small to amortize weight movement. Prefill is efficient because it is large enough to make the GPU compute-bound. SARATHI slices prefill into enough compute-saturating chunks, then attaches decode tokens to those chunks so decode inherits prefill’s efficiency.
The paper is valuable because it turns a vague serving intuition into a concrete execution rule:
one prefill chunk per batch; fill the rest with decodes; align the combined token count with GPU tile behavior; use chunking to create uniform pipeline micro-batches.
That is why SARATHI improves both single-GPU decode efficiency and pipeline-parallel utilization. It is not just “interleave prefill and decode”; it is “interleave them in the shape that the GPU wants.”

entry.title: SGLang: Efficient Execution of Structured Language Model Programs
entry.content:
Paper: SGLang: Efficient Execution of Structured Language Model Programs Code: sgl-project/sglang SGLang is easy to under-read if it is described as “a prompting language” or “a prefix cache.” My reading is different:
SGLang is a paper about making LLM application structure visible to the serving runtime.
That visibility is the real contribution. A normal OpenAI-style completion API receives strings. It does not know that several calls are branches of the same program, that the same few-shot prefix is reused by all options, that a tree-search branch inherits a search history, or that a JSON literal has only one valid continuation for the next several tokens. SGLang’s frontend exposes those relationships through a small Python-embedded DSL. Its backend then turns them into concrete runtime optimizations: KV-cache reuse through RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, parallel execution inside one program, compressed finite-state-machine decoding, and speculative execution for black-box APIs. The important lesson is not only “use a radix tree for prefix caching.” The stronger lesson is:
If the serving runtime sees a workload as unrelated strings, it can only optimize generic batching. If it sees the workload as a structured program, it can optimize the graph of shared prefixes, forks, joins, and constraints.
All figures below are cropped from the original arXiv PDF. The System In One Figure Figure 1. SGLang has a frontend language and a backend runtime. The runtime optimizations are not bolted on after the fact; they depend on the frontend exposing program structure. The frontend contains language primitives for prompt state, generation, selection, multimodal input, and parallelism. The backend runtime includes three main optimizations:
RadixAttention for automatic KV-cache reuse across calls and program instances. Compressed FSM decoding for faster structured output generation, such as JSON under a regex constraint. API speculative execution for API-only models where the runtime cannot modify the model backend.
The paper reports up to 6.4x higher throughput and up to 3.7x lower latency compared with the evaluated systems across workloads such as MMLU, ReAct agents, tree-of-thought, skeleton-of-thought, LLM-as-judge, HellaSwag, JSON decoding, multi-turn chat, and DSPy RAG. I would summarize the paper as a three-layer system:
Layer What it sees What it can optimize
String API independent prompt strings batching and generic model execution
SGLang frontend prompt state, gen, select, fork, join, constraints dependency order, intra-program parallelism, frontend hints
SGLang runtime token prefixes, KV pages, FSM states, batch queues prefix reuse, eviction, scheduling, constrained decoding
The last two rows are inseparable. The runtime optimization works because the frontend gives the runtime a better shape of the computation. What Is A Language Model Program?The paper uses “language model program” for applications that are no longer a single prompt and a single completion. Examples include:
an agent loop that repeatedly calls an LLM and a tool; a few-shot benchmark where all questions share the same demonstrations; self-consistency sampling where several generations branch from the same prompt; tree-of-thought search where nodes share search history; an LLM judge that evaluates several dimensions in parallel and then merges them; a RAG pipeline where many queries share retrieved context or examples; a JSON decoder that must obey a schema.
The two common properties are:
