Multiple dependent LLM calls: there is control flow, branching, and synchronization. Structured inputs or outputs: multimodal inputs, schemas, choices, tool results, or downstream parsers.
If these calls are submitted as independent strings, the backend cannot exploit the application structure. It can still do continuous batching, but it misses two categories of reuse:
Prefix reuse: repeated prompt tokens should reuse the same KV cache. Program-level parallelism: independent branches should execute concurrently rather than serially through Python glue code.
This is why SGLang belongs in the serving-system family. It is not only a nicer syntax for writing prompts. It changes what information the runtime can use. The KV-Cache Cost ModelFor one request with cached tokens, a rough KV-cache memory estimate is:
Here:
is for key and value tensors. is the number of transformer layers. is the number of KV heads. is the head dimension. is the number of cached tokens. is bytes per element.
The linear dependence on is why prefix reuse matters. If a long system prompt, few-shot prefix, retrieved document, chat history, or tree-search context is recomputed many times, the cost is paid in both prefill compute and KV-cache memory. For a set of requests , let be the prompt-token sequence for request . Without reuse, the prefill token work is roughly:
If those prompts form a prefix tree, and each edge represents a token span that needs to be computed once, the lower bound for reusable prefix computation is:
The gap between and the tree cost is exactly the redundant prefill work. SGLang’s RadixAttention tries to make the runtime approach that tree cost online, under memory pressure and continuous batching. This mental model also explains why this paper is not identical to PagedAttention. PagedAttention is mainly about representing live KV memory efficiently inside a serving runtime. RadixAttention is about retaining and matching KV prefixes across calls and program instances. The two are compatible, but they answer different questions. Programming Model Figure 2. The running example is a multi-dimensional essay judge. The red primitives are SGLang operations that expose generation, selection, constraints, and parallel branches. The frontend is a Python-embedded DSL. The core object is a prompt state, usually named s. Strings and primitives are appended to it. The primitives that matter most are:
gen: generate text and store it under a variable name. select: choose the highest-probability option from a list. += or extend: append text to the prompt state. s["name"]: fetch a generated variable and synchronize if needed. fork: create parallel copies of the prompt state. join: merge prompt states. image and video: add multimodal inputs. regex: constrain gen output to match a regular expression.
A simplified shape of the example is: dimensions = ["Clarity", "Originality", "Evidence"]@functiondef judge(s, image_path, essay): s += system("Evaluate an essay about an image.") s += user(image(image_path) + "Essay:" + essay) s += assistant("Sure!") s += user("Is the essay related to the image?") s += assistant(select("related", choices=["yes", "no"])) if s["related"] == "no": return forks = s.fork(len(dimensions)) for f, dim in zip(forks, dimensions): f += user("Evaluate based on: " + dim) f += assistant("Judgment:" + gen("judgment", stop="END")) judgment = "\n".join(f["judgment"] for f in forks) s += user("Return a summary and a grade in JSON.") s += assistant(judgment + gen("output", regex=schema))
The code is not the full contribution. The runtime consequences are:
The fork call tells the runtime that several branches share the same prefix. The generated judgments can run in parallel. Fetching f["judgment"] is a synchronization point. The final regex tells the backend that constrained decoding is possible. The image input can be hashed and reused if the same image appears again.
This is a useful programming model because it does not hide the prompt from the user. SGLang is closer to LMQL and Guidance than to high-level agent frameworks such as LangChain or DSPy. The user still controls the low-level prompt state, but the runtime sees more structure than a raw completion server would see.
Table 1. Compared with LMQL and Guidance, the paper emphasizes SGLang’s Python syntax, multimodal primitives, fork and join, and the dedicated SGLang Runtime backend. My reading of this comparison: SGLang is not trying to be the most abstract programming layer. It is trying to be low-level enough that runtime optimization remains possible. RadixAttentionSGLang’s most important backend idea is RadixAttention. The observation is simple:
The KV cache for a token prefix depends only on that exact prefix.
If two token sequences share the prefix , then their KV tensors for those first positions can be reused. The catch is that this is exact prefix reuse, not semantic similarity. “Same text after a different earlier context” is not the same KV state, because self-attention conditions on all previous tokens. RadixAttention stores reusable KV cache in a radix tree keyed by token prefixes. A radix tree is a compressed trie: edges can contain token spans rather than one token per edge. This is a good fit because prompts often share long segments such as:
a system message; few-shot demonstrations; a retrieved document; earlier chat turns; a tree-search path; a common schema or instruction block.
Figure 3. RadixAttention maintains a radix tree under an LRU eviction policy. It handles chat history, few-shot sharing, branching, splitting, insertion, and eviction. The runtime operations are:
Prefix match: find the longest cached prefix for an incoming token sequence. Reuse: load/use the cached KV prefix and prefill only the unmatched suffix. Reference counting: protect nodes used by currently running requests. Insertion: after a request finishes, insert its prompt and generated continuation into the tree. Edge splitting: if two prompts share only part of an edge, split the edge so the shared prefix becomes reusable. Eviction: when memory is needed, evict least-recently-used leaves first.
The leaf-first eviction detail matters. If a leaf is removed, common ancestors remain cached and can still be reused. If the runtime evicted internal shared nodes first, it would destroy reuse for many descendants. The paper defines cache hit rate as:
This is a prefill-centric metric. A higher hit rate means fewer prompt tokens must be recomputed. It can also reduce memory pressure because shared KV cache allows a larger effective batch. One implementation detail I like: cached tokens and currently running requests share the same memory pool. There is no fixed cache quota. When the waiting batch needs memory, cached tokens can be evicted in favor of active execution. That is the right serving tradeoff. A cache is useful only if it helps throughput or latency; it should not block new work indefinitely. Frontend HintsThe paper notes a subtle but important frontend-runtime interaction. During fork, the frontend can send the shared prefix first as a hint, then send the remaining branch prompts. This helps ensure the shared prefix is inserted correctly and gives the runtime a cleaner scheduling/matching structure. This is the “co-designed” part of the system. The backend can do prefix matching on full strings by itself, but the frontend can make the relationship explicit earlier. That matters when execution is asynchronous and when multiple branches arrive around the same time. My interpretation: frontend hints are not an implementation convenience. They are the mechanism by which the programming model becomes scheduling information. Cache-Aware SchedulingPrefix caching is not enough if the scheduler destroys locality. Suppose the waiting queue contains many requests from several prefix groups. A first-come, first-served schedule may keep switching groups and evict useful prefixes before all related requests are processed. SGLang schedules requests by matched prefix length. Requests with longer cached prefixes are prioritized, approximating a depth-first traversal of the implicit request tree.
Algorithm 1. The scheduler matches waiting requests against the radix tree, sorts by prefix length, selects requests that fit available memory, protects prefix nodes with reference counters, evicts if needed, runs the batch, and inserts finished requests back into the tree. The paper proves an offline result:
For a batch of requests, if cache size is at least the maximum request length, visiting the request radix tree in depth-first order achieves the optimal cache hit rate. Longest-shared-prefix-first is equivalent to a DFS order.
The proof’s lower bound is:
DFS achieves equality because when an edge is computed, the scheduler then processes the whole subtree under that edge while the shared prefix remains hot:
The resulting hit rate can be written as:
This is the cleanest theoretical part of the paper. It says the optimal offline schedule is not mysterious: keep walking the tree so the active prefix stays hot. The online setting is messier:
requests arrive over time; decode lengths are unknown; active requests cannot have their referenced nodes evicted; memory pressure changes with current batches; latency-sensitive serving cannot reorder requests arbitrarily.
The paper acknowledges a fairness issue: greedy cache-aware scheduling can cause starvation. That is a real production concern. A scheduler that always favors hot prefixes may delay cold-prefix requests too long. In a real service, I would want a combined policy:
Here p(r) is matched prefix length, w(r) is waiting time, and m(r) is memory risk. The paper does not present this exact formula; this is my mental model for how I would extend it. Prefix locality is valuable, but it should be balanced against fairness and memory risk. What Patterns Does RadixAttention Cover? Figure 9. The appendix shows common KV sharing structures: few-shot learning, self-consistency, multi-turn chat, and tree-of-thought. The four examples are worth reading separately. Few-shot learning: all questions share the same demonstrations. If the demonstrations are long, caching them once saves a large amount of prefill. Self-consistency: several answers are sampled from the same prompt. The prompt KV cache is shared, while generated answers diverge. Multi-turn chat: later turns share earlier chat history. This is a natural prefix reuse pattern, but the reusable prefix grows over time. Tree-of-thought: branches share search history. This is the irregular case where a simple one-level prefix cache is not enough. A tree is the natural representation. This is why a radix tree is a better abstraction than a flat hash table. A table can cache full prompts, but it does not naturally represent multi-level partial sharing or subtree locality. Compressed FSM For Structured OutputsSGLang’s second runtime optimization targets constrained decoding. When a model must output JSON or another structured format, a common method is:
Convert the regex or grammar into a finite state machine. Track the current FSM state. At each decode step, mask out invalid next tokens. Generate one token. Update the FSM state and repeat.
This is correct but slow when the next several characters or tokens are deterministic. For example, after the model begins a JSON object, the literal prefix {"summary": " may have only one valid continuation for many positions. A normal FSM still steps token by token.
Figure 4. A compressed FSM merges deterministic chains, allowing the runtime to jump forward through forced text instead of decoding one token at a time. Formally, view a regex-derived FSM as:
where is the set of states, is the character or string alphabet, is the transition function, is the initial state, and is the set of final states. At decoding state , the normal constrained decoder can define an allowed-token set:
Then it masks all other vocabulary tokens:
The compressed-FSM idea is to find singular transition chains. If a state has only one legal outgoing transition and that next state also has only one legal continuation, those edges can be merged into one compressed edge. The runtime can then perform a jump-forward step through the deterministic string.
Figure 10. The appendix gives the background: regex is converted into an FSM, and the FSM guides decoding by masking invalid continuations.
Figure 11. Compressed FSM can jump through deterministic substrings, while normal FSM decoding spends a forward pass on every small step. The paper reports that compressed FSM increases JSON-decoding throughput by 1.6x. It also notes an important engineering detail: FSM preprocessing should be reused across a batch. Redoing the preprocessing for every request makes throughput 2.4x lower. There are two caveats I would keep in mind. First, regex is character/string-level, while LLM decoding is token-level. The runtime must retokenize carefully so the jump-forward text aligns with the tokenizer’s behavior. Bad partitioning can create invalid token boundaries. Second, compressed choices can distort probabilities. If a broad textual choice maps onto several tokenizations, comparing choices is not always equivalent to comparing one next-token probability. The paper mentions this as future work. For schema enforcement, compressed FSM is very practical; for exact probability accounting over choices, I would be more cautious. API Speculative ExecutionSGLang also supports API-only models, where the runtime cannot modify the backend or access KV cache. The paper proposes API speculative execution for multi-call templates. The example pattern is: s += contexts += "name:" + gen("name", stop="\n")s += "job:" + gen("job", stop="\n")
Naively, the two gen calls require separate API calls and repeat the input context. SGLang can let the first call continue a few extra tokens past the stop condition, cache the extra generated text, and match it against later primitives. If the model follows the template correctly, later calls can reuse the speculative output. The input-token cost difference can be approximated as:
while speculative execution tries to move toward:
where is the shared context, are per-field prompt fragments, and extra is the additional speculative continuation. The paper reports about a threefold input-token cost reduction in a GPT-3.5 field-extraction example. This optimization is more fragile than RadixAttention because it depends on the model following a predictable template. I would treat it as a useful API-cost trick, not as a correctness-preserving compiler transformation in every program. End-To-End EvaluationThe evaluation covers:
Models: Llama-2 7B/70B, Mixtral-8x7B, LLaVA image/video models, and GPT-3.5 for API experiments. Hardware: mainly AWS G5 instances with A10G 24GB GPUs, plus A100G 80GB for some larger experiments. Baselines: Guidance, vLLM, and LMQL. Workloads: MMLU, HellaSwag, ReAct agents, generative agents, tree-of-thought, skeleton-of-thought, LLM judge, JSON decoding, multi-turn chat, and DSPy RAG. Metrics: maximum throughput in programs per second, and average single-program latency.
Figure 5. Normalized throughput on Llama-7B. SGLang is normalized to 1.0, so smaller bars indicate slower baselines.
Figure 6. Normalized latency on Llama-7B. Lower is better. SGLang has the smallest latency on most workloads in this figure. The results should be interpreted by workload type:
MMLU benefits because the 5-shot examples are shared. HellaSwag benefits from both few-shot reuse and common question-prefix reuse across choices. ReAct and generative agents reuse agent templates and previous calls. Tree-of-thought and skeleton-of-thought benefit from parallel branches and shared search/skeleton prefixes. JSON decoding benefits mainly from compressed FSM. Multi-turn chat short outputs benefit because prefill reuse matters more when decode is short. Multi-turn chat long outputs benefits less because decode dominates and different sessions have less sharing. DSPy RAG benefits from shared context examples.
This breakdown is more useful than the headline speedup. SGLang is strongest when the workload has visible structure: shared prefixes, branches, short outputs, constrained literals, or repeated context. It is less special when requests are independent and decode dominates.
Figure 7. Normalized throughput on Mixtral-8x7B with tensor parallelism. The same trend largely holds on a larger MoE model.
Figures 12 and 13. Appendix results for Llama-2-70B throughput and achieved versus optimal cache hit rate. The appendix cache-hit figure is important. The paper reports cache hit rates from 50% to 99% across workloads, and says cache-aware scheduling reaches about 96% of the optimal hit rate on average. That is strong evidence that the scheduler is doing more than opportunistic prefix matching. Multimodal Results And Production Deployment Table 2. SGLang improves throughput on LLaVA image and video workloads, using image/video primitives and cache reuse for repeated visual inputs. For multimodal models, the paper hashes image inputs and uses that hash as part of the radix-tree key, allowing reuse of image-token KV cache when the same image appears across questions. This is a practical detail. Multimodal prompts often contain expensive visual tokens, and repeated questions about the same image are common in evaluation and applications. The production deployment note is also useful. In Chatbot Arena, after one month, the paper reports:
52.4% RadixAttention cache hit rate for LLaVA-Next-34B. 74.1% cache hit rate for Vicuna-33B. 1.7x average first-token latency reduction for Vicuna-33B.
I like this result because it grounds the paper in real traffic. Cache hits came from common system messages, reused example images, and multi-turn chat histories. Those are exactly the repeated prefixes one would expect in a serving product. Ablation Study Figure 8. Higher cache hit rate improves batch size, throughput, total latency, and first-token latency. The component ablation shows that cache, tree structure, scheduling, frontend parallelism, and frontend hints all matter. Figure 8 is the best evidence for the system design. The left two plots show that as cache hit rate increases:
batch size increases; throughput increases; total latency decreases; first-token latency decreases.
That aligns with the cost model: fewer prefill tokens mean less compute and memory pressure, which allows larger batches. The right plot is more interesting. Disabling different components hurts different workloads:
No cache removes the main prefill reuse benefit. No tree structure weakens multi-level sharing. FCFS or random scheduling loses locality and cache-hit rate. No frontend parallelism loses parallel branches inside one program. No frontend hint makes runtime matching and scheduling less effective.
This ablation supports the paper’s central claim: the frontend and runtime must be designed together. A backend-only prefix cache helps, but it does not recover the full effect. The overhead result is also important. On a ShareGPT benchmark without KV-cache reuse opportunities, the paper reports 74.3 seconds for 100 requests, with only 0.2 seconds spent managing RadixAttention data structures. That is less than 0.3% overhead. This justifies turning RadixAttention on by default, at least for the evaluated implementation. Compiler ModeThe main paper uses interpreter mode, but the appendix also discusses compiler mode. SGLang can trace a program into an intermediate representation with streams, nodes, and dependencies.
Figure 14. An SGLang program and its corresponding dataflow graph. The graph exposes streams, constants, generated values, and synchronization dependencies. This is conceptually important even if the paper’s main results are interpreter-based. Once the program becomes an IR graph, the system can apply compiler-like transformations:
reduce interpreter overhead; serialize programs; schedule streams more aggressively; move code to increase prefix sharing; plan memory and execution statically.
The paper’s code-movement case study is deliberately aggressive. It asks GPT-4 to reorder natural-language prompt components to increase the constant prefix length. On 15 test templates, GPT-4 successfully rewrote 12 without changing semantics by manual inspection, increasing shareable prefix length by 60 tokens on average. I would treat this as a research direction, not a production-safe transformation. Natural-language code motion can silently change meaning. But the idea is valuable: once prompts are represented as a graph, prompt layout becomes an optimization target. How SGLang Fits With vLLM, FlashInfer, And MooncakeI would place these systems at different levels of the serving stack:
System Main abstraction What it optimizes
vLLM / PagedAttention KV blocks inside a worker memory fragmentation, continuous batching, copy-on-write
SGLang / RadixAttention structured LM programs and prefix trees prefix reuse across calls, branch parallelism, constrained decoding
FlashInfer serving attention kernels irregular KV layouts, dynamic scheduling, JIT variants
Mooncake distributed KV-cache lifecycle prefill/decode disaggregation, KV movement, SLO-aware scheduling
SGLang is closest to vLLM in implementation space, but its conceptual level is higher. It asks: what if the runtime sees program structure before it sees token tensors? The systems are complementary:
SGLang can use paged KV memory layouts. FlashInfer can accelerate the irregular attention shapes produced by SGLang. Mooncake can extend KV-cache-aware thinking to cluster-level placement and transfer.
The throughline is that KV cache has become a first-class serving object. PagedAttention manages it as pages, SGLang manages it as a reusable prefix tree, FlashInfer consumes it through layout-aware kernels, and Mooncake schedules it as distributed state. What I Would Measure In A ReproductionA normal tokens-per-second benchmark is not enough for this paper. I would reproduce SGLang with metrics that separate the mechanisms:
Prefix cache hit rate: measured in prompt tokens, not request count. Saved prefill tokens: compare naive prompt tokens with actually computed prompt suffix tokens. First-token latency: should improve when prefill is saved. Inter-token latency: should not regress from extra cache management. Effective batch size: cache reuse should allow larger batches under the same memory budget. KV memory occupancy: split active-request KV and cached reusable KV. Eviction rate: high hit rate with excessive eviction may still create instability. Tree operation overhead: CPU-side match, split, insert, ref-count, and eviction time. Fairness and tail latency: cache-aware scheduling can starve cold-prefix requests. Frontend contribution: compare full SGLang, no frontend parallelism, no frontend hints, and backend-only prefix caching. Constrained-decoding speed: separate FSM preprocessing cost from per-token decode cost. Correctness under regex: verify tokenization edge cases and probability behavior.
The workload suite should include both high-reuse and low-reuse cases. Otherwise the benchmark only proves that prefix caching helps when prefixes repeat, which is true but incomplete. The more interesting question is whether the runtime can detect reuse, exploit it without harming unrelated traffic, and keep overhead low when reuse is absent. LimitationsSGLang is strong, but its assumptions matter. First, RadixAttention helps most when prompts share exact prefixes. It does not help semantically similar prompts unless the token prefix is identical. The paper mentions fuzzy semantic matching as future work, but that would be a different correctness/performance tradeoff. Second, cache-aware scheduling can conflict with fairness. A hot prefix group may keep getting priority, while cold-prefix requests wait. This is not a small issue in user-facing services. A production scheduler needs aging, SLO constraints, or admission control around the prefix-locality objective. Third, memory pressure can erase cache benefits. Cached tokens and active requests share the pool. Under high load, cached prefixes may be evicted to admit larger active batches. That is the right behavior, but it means the speedup depends on workload shape and memory headroom. Fourth, compressed FSM decoding is not free from modeling caveats. Regex constraints live at a string level; LLMs decode tokens. Retokenization and probability distortion are real edge cases. Fifth, API speculative execution is heuristic. It can reduce API cost when templates are predictable, but if the model deviates from the assumed structure, the system must fall back or validate carefully. Sixth, compiler-mode prompt rewriting is risky. Moving natural-language text can change semantics in ways a traditional compiler would not allow. The paper frames it as a case study, and I think that is the right level of confidence. Finally, distributed prefix caching opens consistency and placement questions. The appendix discusses a weakly consistent meta-tree for data parallelism, but the full production design space includes replication, eviction propagation, worker failure, privacy isolation, and cross-node KV movement. TakeawaySGLang’s core contribution is the connection between a structured frontend and an optimized runtime. The frontend primitives expose where a program branches, synchronizes, reuses context, and constrains outputs. The backend uses that information to reuse KV cache, schedule for prefix locality, run branches in parallel, and skip deterministic constrained-decoding steps. The paper’s practical message is:
do not submit structured LLM workflows as unrelated strings if you want the serving stack to optimize them; exact prefix reuse is a runtime resource, not just an application convenience; a tree-structured cache is a better fit than a flat cache for agents, self-consistency, multi-turn chat, and tree search; constrained decoding should exploit deterministic spans, not only mask one token at a time; frontend/runtime co-design can matter as much as a faster kernel.
For me, SGLang is the missing middle layer between prompt programming and serving infrastructure. It is above PagedAttention-style memory management and below high-level agent frameworks. That is exactly where many real LLM applications now live: not one prompt, not a full distributed service by itself, but a structured program whose execution shape is rich enough to optimize.

entry.title: Single-Path NAS: Designing Hardware-Efficient ConvNets in Less Than 4 Hours
entry.content:
Paper: Single-Path NAS: Designing Hardware-Efficient ConvNets in less than 4 Hours Code: dstamoulis/single-path-nas MotivationThe paper targets a very specific bottleneck in hardware-aware NAS: one-shot NAS methods usually build a multi-path supernet. For each searchable layer, every candidate operator is inserted as a separate trainable path, and the search learns which path to keep. That formulation is easy to understand, but expensive to maintain. If a MobileNet-like model has 22 searchable layers and each layer has 5 candidate choices, the discrete space is about architectures. A multi-path supernet avoids training every architecture from scratch, but it still keeps separate path weights in memory and updates them during search. Single-Path NAS changes the question from:
Which operator/path should this layer choose?
to:
Which subset of weights inside one over-parameterized kernel should this layer use?
The left side is the common multi-path view: separate operators and separate path weights. The right side is the paper’s core idea: put the candidates into one larger “superkernel”, then select a subset of its weights. ContributionThe paper’s contribution is not just “NAS becomes faster”. The useful part is the encoding:
A single-path search space for MobileNetV2-style MBConv blocks. Kernel size, expansion ratio, and skip-op decisions are all encoded inside one searchable superkernel. The latency objective remains differentiable by using a profiled runtime model for Pixel 1. The final result reaches 74.96% ImageNet top-1 accuracy at 79.48ms on Pixel 1. The search uses 8 epochs, reported as 3.75 hours on TPUv2, or 30 TPU-hours.
The last point is the reason this paper is interesting. The method is not searching an arbitrary operator graph; it is carefully redesigning the search space so the search itself becomes cheap. MethodologySearch SpaceThe macro-architecture follows a MobileNetV2/MnasNet-like layout. The model has several blocks, and each block contains MBConv layers. For each searchable MBConv layer, NAS chooses:
depthwise kernel size: expansion ratio: optional skip-op when the layer shape allows residual connection
The largest candidate can represent the smaller candidates. A larger kernel contains the smaller kernel as its inner core; a larger expansion ratio contains the lower expansion ratio as a subset of channels. That observation is what makes the one-path formulation possible. Superkernel EncodingThe paper uses a searchable depthwise convolution kernel as the superkernel. For a simplified 3x3 vs 5x5 choice, the 5x5 kernel can be decomposed into:
If the search chooses 3x3, only the inner core contributes. If it chooses 5x5, both the inner core and the outer shell contribute.
The same idea is used for expansion ratio. A 6x expansion contains the 3x part plus an extra channel subset. The architecture decision becomes a decision over whether to keep or drop these extra subsets. In the actual formulation, the hard indicator is relaxed during search. The model learns threshold variables for kernel-size and expansion-ratio decisions, and uses a sigmoid relaxation so gradients can still flow. Conceptually: 𝟙 For skip-op, the layer can be dropped by zeroing the kernel contribution and forwarding the input directly when the tensor shape is compatible. Runtime-Aware ObjectiveThe search objective includes both cross entropy and runtime:
Here is a latency model for the target hardware. The authors profile candidate MBConv operations on Pixel 1, then approximate total network runtime as the sum of per-layer runtimes:
This is not a FLOPs proxy. It is explicitly optimized for the phone runtime target. The paper reports an average latency-model prediction error of 1.76%, which is good enough for the search loop. ResultsThe headline result is easy to summarize:
Method Top-1 Acc (%) Top-5 Acc (%) Pixel 1 Runtime (ms) Search Cost
MobileNetV2 1.0x 72.00 91.00 75.00 -
MnasNet 1.0x 74.00 91.80 76.00 40,000 epochs
ProxylessNAS-R 74.60 92.20 78.00 200 epochs
FBNet-B 74.1 - - 90 epochs
Single-Path NAS 74.96 92.21 79.48 8 epochs / 3.75 hours
The accuracy improvement over ProxylessNAS-R is modest, around +0.31 top-1, but the search-cost reduction is the real result. The paper reports 8 search epochs, compared with much larger search budgets in previous mobile NAS work.
The search curve is also useful: cross entropy decreases, while the runtime term is eventually pulled down toward the 80ms target. The early noisy runtime region is caused by dropout over kernel subsets.
The final architecture is still a MobileNetV2-style network. Most layers are MBConv variants with different kernel size and expansion ratio. This matters because the method is not discovering arbitrary operators; it is searching a compact and hardware-aware MBConv design space. TakeawayI think the main value of this paper is the reframing of NAS from path selection to weight-subset selection. Multi-path supernets pay memory and optimization cost for maintaining many candidate branches. Single-Path NAS avoids that by forcing candidate operators to share one superkernel. The limitation is also clear: this trick works because the candidate operations are nested. A 3x3 kernel is naturally contained in a 5x5 kernel, and a lower expansion ratio is naturally contained in a higher one. If the search space contains very different operators, such as attention, pooling, deformable conv, or arbitrary graph motifs, this encoding is not directly applicable. So this is not a universal NAS recipe. It is a clean engineering solution for a constrained MobileNetV2-like space, and that constraint is exactly why it is fast.

entry.title: SmoothQuant: W8A8 LLM Quantization
entry.content:
Reference Paper: SmoothQuant: Accurate and Efficient Post-Training Quantization for Large Language Models Code: mit-han-lab/smoothquant
SmoothQuant is one of the cleanest LLM quantization papers because the main idea is only a diagonal rescaling, but the consequence is large: it turns difficult W8A8 quantization into a regular INT8 GEMM problem. The paper should be read as a system paper as much as an algorithm paper. LLM.int8() preserves activation outliers with a mixed INT8/FP16 decomposition. Weight-only methods such as GPTQ or AWQ reduce weight bandwidth but leave activations in high precision. SmoothQuant chooses a different target: both weights and activations are INT8 for the expensive matrix multiplications, so the runtime can use dense hardware-friendly kernels.
Figure 1 gives the deployment pressure. Model size grew faster than single-node accelerator memory. A GPT-3-size model already needs hundreds of GB in FP16, and MT-NLG 530B is far beyond a single accelerator. Weight quantization alone helps memory, but W8A8 also makes the main GEMMs faster when the hardware has strong INT8 support. One SentenceSmoothQuant is a training-free post-training quantization method that:
observes that LLM activations are much harder to quantize than weights; divides each activation input channel by a calibrated scale ; multiplies the matching weight channel by the same ; keeps the floating-point function exactly unchanged before quantization; then quantizes the smoothed activations and scaled weights to INT8.
The important phrase is “migrating difficulty”. SmoothQuant does not delete outliers, and it is not just clipping. It uses an algebraic equivalence to move some dynamic range from activations into weights. Since weights are usually easier to quantize, this trade is profitable.
Figure 2 is the whole paper in one picture. The activation matrix has a few huge columns. If one global INT8 scale is used, those columns determine the quantization step, and ordinary activation values receive very few effective levels. SmoothQuant makes those columns smaller and compensates by making the corresponding weight rows larger. Formula 1: Uniform INT8 QuantizationThe paper starts with the standard symmetric quantizer:
Here is the bit width. For INT8, , so the signed integer range is roughly . The scale maps the largest absolute floating-point value to the edge of that integer range. My reading of the formula:
Find the maximum absolute value in the quantization group. Use it to set the grid spacing . Divide every value by . Round the result to the nearest integer.
This is why outliers are painful. If one element has magnitude and most values are around , the scale must still cover . The normal values now live close to zero on the integer grid, so many distinct FP16 values collapse to the same INT8 value. The formula also explains why quantization granularity matters. The set used by can be the whole tensor, one token, one channel, or a smaller group. A finer group gives a better local scale but may break the fast kernel layout. Linear Layer NotationFor a Transformer linear layer, the paper writes:
is the number of tokens, is the input channel dimension, and is the output channel dimension. This orientation matters. An activation outlier in input channel multiplies the whole row of the weight matrix. If we divide activation channel by a scale , we must multiply the corresponding weight row by to keep unchanged. Different frameworks may store a linear weight as and compute . That is just a layout convention. The conceptual axis is the same: SmoothQuant scales the input-channel direction. Hardware-Friendly Granularity Figure 3 separates three choices:
per-tensor quantization: one scale for the whole activation or weight tensor; per-token activation quantization: one activation scale per token row; per-channel weight quantization: one weight scale per output channel.
The key hardware point is not just accuracy. For INT8 GEMM, the inner product dimension should use regular INT8 values, and scale factors should sit outside the dense integer multiplication. Per-token activation quantization and per-output-channel weight quantization satisfy this. Per-input-channel activation quantization would put a different activation scale inside the reduction dimension, which no longer maps cleanly to a standard INT8 GEMM. The paper expresses the hardware-friendly case as:
This formula is worth unpacking carefully.
is the real dense integer GEMM. This is the part we want to keep regular. applies one activation scale per token after the GEMM. applies one weight scale per output channel after the GEMM. The scale matrices are on the outer dimensions of , not the inner reduction dimension.
So the formula says: quantize in a way that lets the expensive matrix multiply happen completely in INT8/INT32, then dequantize with cheap row/column scaling. Why Per-Channel Activation Quantization Is Not Enough Table 1 is a useful negative result. If the activation is quantized per-channel, OPT accuracy is almost preserved even at 175B. But per-channel activation quantization is not compatible with efficient INT8 GEMM in the usual layout. Per-tensor or per-token activation quantization is hardware-friendly, but it collapses accuracy once activation outliers become large. This table gives the central problem statement:
activation quantization accuracy kernel story
per-channel good bad for standard INT8 GEMM
per-token or per-tensor bad on large LLMs good for standard INT8 GEMM
SmoothQuant tries to get both sides: make the activation easier so that the hardware-friendly per-token/per-tensor activation scales become accurate enough. Observation: Activation Outliers Are Structured Figure 4 gives three observations. First, weights are already relatively flat. Their channel maxima do not vary wildly, so INT8 quantization of weights is not the main blocker. Second, activations contain a small number of channels with very large magnitude. The paper describes these activation outliers as about two orders of magnitude larger than typical channels in some cases. Third, the outliers are persistent by channel. They are not random isolated elements. If channel is an outlier, it tends to be an outlier across many tokens. This is exactly the structure that a per-channel smoothing factor can exploit. A useful way to read the outlier effect is:
where is the maximum magnitude in channel and is the maximum magnitude over the whole tensor. If , channel receives only a small fraction of the available INT8 levels. The outlier channel consumes the range; normal channels become low effective-bit channels. SmoothQuant does not need to know every token value at runtime. It only needs the calibration-time channel maxima to choose smoothing scales. Formula 2: Equivalent Channel SmoothingThe core formula is:
This is the most important formula in the paper. Let be a positive scale vector. Then:
For channel :
activation values are divided by ; the corresponding weight row is multiplied by ; the product contribution stays the same:
The floating-point layer output is therefore exactly unchanged. The change appears only after quantization, because the quantizer now sees different activation and weight distributions. This is the same family of equivalent transformation that also appears in AWQ, but the objective is different:
SmoothQuant scales down activation outlier channels to make W8A8 possible. AWQ scales up activation-salient weight channels to reduce W4A16 weight quantization error.
Same algebra, different quantization target. What “Migrating Difficulty” MeansBefore smoothing, activation channel may have a huge maximum. If we choose , the smoothed activation maximum becomes smaller:
The corresponding weight channel becomes larger:
This is not free. We are making the weights harder to quantize. SmoothQuant works because the original weights have enough quantization headroom. The paper’s practical claim is not “scaling is always good”; it is “LLM weights can absorb some activation difficulty better than activations can”.
Figure 5 shows the balanced case. When the activation has a large outlier channel and the corresponding weight channel is not extreme, a moderate can reduce the activation range while keeping the weight range still quantizable. Formula 3: Choosing The Smoothing ScaleThe paper first discusses two extreme choices. If we choose:
then every activation channel is normalized by its own maximum. This makes activations very easy to quantize, but it can push too much scale into the weights. If we choose:
then weight channels are normalized, but activations keep the original outlier problem. SmoothQuant interpolates between the two:
Here is the migration strength.
Larger means larger for activation-outlier channels. Larger means activations are divided down more. But larger also means the corresponding weights are multiplied up more.
So is the knob that decides where quantization difficulty lives. Let:
Then:
and:
When , both become:
This is the cleanest way to understand Figure 5. With , the activation and weight ranges for the same input channel are balanced around the geometric mean of their original maxima. If the activation maximum was huge and the weight maximum was moderate, the activation range shrinks while the weight range grows to a still manageable level. The paper uses for OPT and BLOOM, and for GLM-130B because GLM activations are harder to quantize. Later results on Llama, Falcon, Mistral, and Mixtral use model-specific alpha values, shown in Table 7 below. Applying SmoothQuant To Transformer Blocks Figure 6 is important because it draws the deployment boundary. SmoothQuant does not quantize every single operator to INT8. It quantizes the compute-heavy linear layers and attention BMMs. Lightweight or numerically sensitive operations such as LayerNorm, Softmax, ReLU, and residual additions stay in FP16. That is a pragmatic design. The speed and memory bottleneck is dominated by large matrix multiplications. Keeping small elementwise operations in FP16 avoids unnecessary accuracy risk and kernel complexity. The smoothing scale can often be folded offline:
multiply the weight-side scale into the weight tensor before quantization; fuse the activation-side inverse scale into the previous linear layer or nearby normalization when possible; when a residual branch makes fusion awkward, keep a small extra scaling operation.
This is why the final runtime still looks like a regular INT8 model. The awkward part is calibration and folding, not a special outlier branch inside the main GEMM. O1, O2, O3: Accuracy And Kernel Tradeoffs Table 2 defines three SmoothQuant operating points.
setting activation scale weight scale expected runtime
SmoothQuant-O1 per-token dynamic per-tensor safest among SmoothQuant variants
SmoothQuant-O2 per-tensor dynamic per-tensor faster, less adaptive
SmoothQuant-O3 per-tensor static per-tensor most efficient, needs good calibration
O1 is closer to a conservative quantization recipe because activation scales are still dynamic per token. O3 is the system-friendly endpoint because scales can be calibrated statically. The paper’s strongest result is that O3 still preserves accuracy on very large models. The calibration procedure is lightweight:
collect activation maxima from 512 random sentences from the Pile validation set; compute smoothing scales from activation maxima and weight maxima; calibrate static quantization step sizes once; no weight update, no gradient descent, no reconstruction training.
The calibration data matters. The transform is exact before quantization, but the quantizer depends on the observed activation range. If calibration prompts miss deployment outliers, O3 can under-estimate scales. OPT-175B: The Main Accuracy Table Table 3 is the main accuracy proof for OPT-175B. The naive W8A8 baseline collapses: LAMBADA becomes 0.0%, average accuracy is 35.5%, and WikiText perplexity explodes to 93080. ZeroQuant also fails at this scale. Outlier Suppression fails similarly. LLM.int8() preserves accuracy, but it uses an FP16 outlier path. SmoothQuant-O3 reaches:
LAMBADA: 74.6% vs FP16 74.7%; average over seven tasks: 66.8% vs FP16 66.9%; WikiText perplexity: 11.17 vs FP16 10.99.
This is the core result: the most aggressive SmoothQuant setting keeps almost the same OPT-175B accuracy while using regular W8A8 quantization for the expensive layers. I read this table as a separation between “quantization format” and “quantization recipe”. W8A8 itself is not enough. Naive W8A8 has the right hardware format but the wrong statistics. SmoothQuant keeps the same target format but changes the distributions seen by the quantizer. Different Large Models Table 4 shows OPT-175B, BLOOM-176B, and GLM-130B. SmoothQuant works across all three, but the details are not identical. For OPT-175B, O3 is close to FP16. For BLOOM-176B, O1/O2 are nearly exact and O3 drops somewhat more. For GLM-130B, the authors use a larger , because activation quantization is harder. This is a useful reminder that alpha is a real model-dependent knob, not a universal constant.
Figure 7 shows the scaling story across OPT sizes. Naive W8A8 and ZeroQuant become unreliable as the model grows. SmoothQuant-O3 stays close to FP16 from smaller OPT models up to OPT-175B. That trend matters more than any single benchmark number: activation outliers become more severe with scale, and SmoothQuant specifically attacks that scaling failure mode. Newer LLM Results The paper also includes LLaMA results. With and per-token activation quantization, W8A8 SmoothQuant keeps WikiText perplexity almost unchanged from 7B to 65B. This is useful because LLaMA-style models differ from OPT/BLOOM and generally have less severe activation outliers.
Table 7 extends the method to Llama-2, Falcon, Mistral, and Mixtral. The alpha values vary:
Llama-2-7B and 13B use ; Llama-2-70B uses ; Falcon uses lower values around -; Mistral and Mixtral use .
This table is a practical warning against treating the smoothing strength as a fixed hyperparameter. The formula is simple, but the best migration point depends on architecture, activation statistics, and the selected quantization granularity. System Results: PyTorch Figure 8 compares FP16, LLM.int8(), and SmoothQuant-O3 in PyTorch on A100. SmoothQuant gives up to 1.51x speedup and around 1.96x memory reduction. LLM.int8() can preserve accuracy, but the mixed INT8/FP16 outlier path often slows inference in this benchmark. This is the system reason the paper cares so much about regularity. If the quantized model needs exceptional high-precision paths, the hardware may not deliver the expected speedup. SmoothQuant spends complexity offline so that the online path stays dense.
Table 8 focuses on autoregressive decoding. This stage is often memory-bound and latency-sensitive. SmoothQuant reduces per-token decoding latency and memory footprint for OPT-30B and OPT-175B. The memory savings are close to the expected halving, while latency speedup ranges roughly from 1.19x to 1.42x depending on model size, batch size, and sequence length. System Results: FasterTransformer And 530B Serving Figure 9 shows the FasterTransformer integration. This is the more deployment-oriented result. SmoothQuant-O3 can reduce latency by up to 1.56x and nearly halve memory usage. It also reduces the GPU count for large OPT models: the figure reports OPT-66B on one GPU instead of two, and OPT-175B on four GPUs instead of eight.
Table 9 shows MT-NLG 530B accuracy. FP16 and INT8 SmoothQuant both report the same average, 73.1, over LAMBADA, HellaSwag, PIQA, and WinoGrande. This is a small table, but it supports the biggest deployment claim: W8A8 can be accurate even beyond 500B parameters.
Table 10 is the memory result for MT-NLG 530B. FP16 serving uses 16 GPUs, while INT8 SmoothQuant uses 8 GPUs. Latency is comparable and memory drops from roughly one TB to about half a TB depending on sequence length. This is exactly the regime where W8A8 matters: the method changes not only speed, but also whether the model fits within a single node. Ablation: Why O3 Is Fastest Table 11 compares O1, O2, and O3 latency. The trend is straightforward:
dynamic per-token activation quantization is more adaptive but more expensive; per-tensor dynamic quantization removes some overhead; per-tensor static quantization is fastest because runtime scale computation is minimized.
O3 is therefore the strongest system setting. The risk is calibration quality, because static scales have less opportunity to adapt to runtime inputs. Ablation: Understanding Alpha Figure 10 directly validates the role of . If is too small, the activation side is under-smoothed. The activation outlier problem remains, so W8A8 accuracy fails. If is too large, too much difficulty is migrated to the weights. The weights become harder to quantize, and accuracy also drops. The sweet spot for OPT-175B is around -, matching the default . This is exactly what the formula predicts: the best point is not at either extreme, but where activation and weight quantization errors are balanced. Implementation NotesA minimal SmoothQuant implementation should first verify the floating-point equivalence before adding INT8 quantization. For a layer with paper-style weight layout : # X: [tokens, input_channels]# W: [input_channels, output_channels]# act_max[j] = calibration maximum of abs(X[:, j])# weight_max[j] = maximum of abs(W[j, :])s = act_max**alpha / weight_max**(1 - alpha)X_hat = X / s[None, :]W_hat = W * s[:, None]Y0 = X @ WY1 = X_hat @ W_hat
Before quantization, Y0 and Y1 should match up to floating-point roundoff. If they do not, the scale axis is probably wrong. This check is simple and catches the most common implementation mistake. After that, quantize X_hat and W_hat according to the chosen O1/O2/O3 setting. For deployment, fold as much of s as possible into neighboring weights so the runtime path remains a normal INT8 linear or BMM kernel. I would also plot these three quantities for several layers:
act_max[j]; weight_max[j]; s[j].
The expected pattern is visible in Figure 4: channels with large activation maxima receive larger smoothing scales, and the corresponding weight ranges grow. If the plot is flat, the calibration collection is wrong. If scales are extreme everywhere, alpha or clipping probably needs attention. LimitationsSmoothQuant is not a universal answer to all LLM compression problems. First, it targets W8A8. If the bottleneck is pure weight memory and the hardware has excellent W4A16 kernels, a weight-only method such as AWQ or GPTQ may be more attractive. Second, O3 depends on calibration. Static activation scales are efficient, but they assume calibration maxima cover deployment prompts well enough. Third, SmoothQuant reduces the main linear/BMM cost, but it does not solve KV cache memory by itself. For long-context decoding, KV cache quantization is a separate issue. Fourth, the method relies on the empirical asymmetry that weights are easier to quantize than activations. That is true for the models in the paper, but the exact alpha and quantization granularity should still be validated per model family. TakeawayThe key contribution of SmoothQuant is not the existence of a diagonal rescaling. The key contribution is identifying that LLM activation outliers are channel-structured, persistent, and movable into weights without changing the floating-point function. The formulas tell a clean story:
uniform INT8 quantization is controlled by the maximum absolute value; activation outliers waste effective quantization levels; a diagonal transform can divide activation channels and multiply weight channels equivalently; controls how much difficulty is migrated.
That is why the method is elegant. The runtime model is simple, but the calibration step reshapes the distributions so that simple INT8 kernels become accurate enough for very large LLMs.

entry.title: SNAS: Stochastic Neural Architecture Search
entry.content:
Xie S, Zheng H, Liu C, Lin L. SNAS: Stochastic Neural Architecture Search. ICLR 2019.
Paper: https://arxiv.org/pdf/1812.09926.pdf Code: https://github.com/SNAS-Series/SNAS-Series
SNAS is a useful paper to read right after DARTS and ENAS. It keeps the familiar cell-based NAS search space, but changes the variable being optimized. Instead of training a deterministic soft mixture of operations like DARTS, SNAS samples architecture decisions from a learned distribution and makes that sampling differentiable with a Concrete, or Gumbel-Softmax, relaxation. The paper’s claim is not just “use Gumbel noise”. The claim is that NAS can be written as optimizing the expected loss of sampled child graphs, while still allowing gradients to flow through both operation weights and architecture distribution parameters in the same backpropagation pass. That makes SNAS sit between three families:
RL NAS samples discrete architectures but uses delayed rewards. DARTS uses direct gradients but trains a deterministic supernet mixture. SNAS samples stochastic child graphs and uses a differentiable relaxation to update the sampling distribution.
The practical result is a search method that reports competitive CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-transfer results with about 1.5 GPU days of search, while preserving the search-time validation accuracy much better than DARTS in the paper’s own comparison. Core IdeaThe search space is a directed acyclic cell. Each edge can choose one operation from a candidate set, including a zero operation that removes the edge. SNAS represents each edge decision by a one-hot random vector :
Here is the vector of candidate operation outputs on edge . If the third entry of is one, the third operation is selected. If the zero operation is selected, that edge is effectively dropped.
The distribution over all edge decisions is written as . SNAS assumes it is fully factorizable across edge decisions, so the architecture parameter controls a set of categorical distributions rather than a sequential controller policy. Writing E_Z as expectation under , the objective is:
This is the key difference from DARTS. DARTS avoids sampling by replacing each edge with a weighted sum over operations. SNAS keeps a stochastic architecture variable and optimizes expected sampled-architecture loss. The paper argues that this makes the search objective better aligned with the final child graph, because the training graph is already a sampled graph rather than a full deterministic mixture. Concrete RelaxationDirect categorical sampling blocks gradients through . SNAS uses the Concrete distribution to create a differentiable approximation to a one-hot categorical sample. For operation on edge :
where is Gumbel noise and is the temperature. When is high, samples are soft. When approaches zero, the sample becomes close to a one-hot categorical draw. This temperature is not just a cosmetic hyperparameter. If it is too high, the search behaves like a soft supernet and the sampled child graph may not match the search model. If it is too low too early, the architecture distribution can collapse before operation weights have learned enough. SNAS therefore uses the relaxation as a bridge: differentiable enough for gradient updates, but stochastic enough to keep the objective close to discrete child graphs. The training loop is conceptually simple: initialize operation weights thetainitialize architecture distribution parameters alphafor each minibatch: sample relaxed architecture masks Z from p_alpha run the sampled cell compute task loss, optionally with a resource cost update theta and alpha in the same backward passderive the discrete child cell from the learned distributiontrain the derived child network for final evaluation
The “same backward pass” point matters. DARTS usually uses bilevel optimization: network weights on a training split and architecture parameters on a validation split. SNAS instead uses a single-level objective in its main experiments. That choice is part of the paper’s argument: if the sampled architecture objective is less biased, the search-time validation accuracy should better reflect the final child network. Why SNAS Is Not Just DARTSDARTS relaxes an edge into a soft weighted operation: mixed_edge(x) = sum_o softmax(alpha)_o * op_o(x)
That mixed operation is easy to differentiate, but it is not the final architecture. After search, DARTS removes weak operations and keeps a small number of incoming edges per node. The training-time graph and final child graph are therefore different objects. SNAS frames the problem as a distribution over child graphs instead:
The sampled graph is still relaxed during search, but the random variable corresponds directly to the discrete choice that will exist after derivation. That is why the paper repeatedly uses the word “complete”: architecture sampling, parameter learning, validation, credit assignment, and search update are all present in the same differentiable pipeline. The appendix figure makes the gradient difference visual:
This is the part I find most reusable. DARTS says: “replace the discrete decision by a deterministic expectation.” SNAS says: “keep the decision as a random variable, then relax the random variable.” Those two choices lead to different biases. Credit AssignmentThe paper connects SNAS to policy-gradient NAS, but with a more local signal. In RL NAS, the controller receives a reward after a sampled architecture has been trained or validated. That reward is delayed and coarse. SNAS uses the differentiable training loss itself, so the architecture parameter receives gradients through the actual computational graph. A high-level policy-gradient view has the familiar score-function shape: grad_alpha E[L(Z)] = E[L(Z) * grad_alpha log p_alpha(Z)]
but the Concrete reparameterization gives a pathwise gradient rather than relying only on a scalar terminal reward. The paper interprets this as more efficient credit assignment: operation and topology decisions receive feedback from how they affect the differentiable loss, not only from a final architecture-level score. This is also where SNAS differs from ENAS. ENAS shares weights and samples architectures, but its controller is still a sequential decision process trained by reinforcement learning. SNAS removes the controller MDP assumption and directly parameterizes a factorizable architecture distribution over cell edges. Resource ConstraintSNAS also adds a resource-aware objective. The paper wants the search to decide topology instead of relying on hand-designed rules such as “keep two inputs per intermediate node.” Since the zero operation is part of the candidate set, a resource penalty can encourage sparse cells. The augmented objective is:
where is a resource cost such as computation. The important engineering property is decomposability. If the global cost can be written as a sum of local edge or operation costs, then the resource term can be assigned to the same structural decisions that SNAS is already optimizing. In the experiments, the authors search with three levels of resource constraint:
mild constraint, moderate constraint, aggressive constraint.
The mild constraint produces a DARTS-like sparse cell where each intermediate node effectively uses two inputs.
The aggressive constraint pushes harder on topology and drops more edges.
The appendix also shows the moderate constraint cells:
This progression is useful because it shows the resource term is not only changing a scalar objective. It changes the actual discovered graph structure. Search BehaviorThe search-stage comparison is one of the strongest pieces of evidence in the paper. SNAS is compared with DARTS and ENAS across randomly generated seeds.
The paper’s interpretation is:
DARTS reaches high search validation accuracy quickly, but the final derived child graph can be very different from the relaxed parent network. ENAS improves more slowly and plateaus lower in this plot. SNAS keeps a stochastic child-graph objective, so its search validation accuracy is more meaningful after derivation.
The table below is the clearest version of that claim.
The numbers are stark:
Method Search validation accuracy Child-network validation accuracy Search cost
DARTS, second-order bilevel 87.67 54.66 1 GPU day
SNAS, single-level, mild constraint 88.54 90.67 1.5 GPU days
This does not prove every DARTS run collapses this badly. It does show the exact failure mode SNAS is designed around: a relaxed supernet can look good before discretization and then lose quality when converted to a child graph. SNAS tries to make the search-time model closer to the thing that will be evaluated. CIFAR-10 ResultsThe main CIFAR-10 comparison is Table 2.
The compact rows I care about are:
Method Test error Params Search cost Pipeline
ENAS + cutout 2.89 4.6M 0.5 GPU days complete
DARTS first-order + cutout 3.00 +/- 0.14 3.3M 0.4 GPU days incomplete
DARTS second-order + cutout 2.76 +/- 0.09 3.3M 1 GPU day incomplete
DARTS single-level + cutout 3.56 +/- 0.10 3.0M 0.3 GPU days incomplete
SNAS mild + cutout 2.98 2.9M 1.5 GPU days complete
SNAS moderate + cutout 2.85 +/- 0.02 2.8M 1.5 GPU days complete
SNAS aggressive + cutout 3.10 +/- 0.04 2.3M 1.5 GPU days complete
The moderate constraint row is the best SNAS row in the table: 2.85 +/- 0.02% test error with 2.8M parameters. It does not beat second-order DARTS on error, but it uses fewer parameters and is much better than single-level DARTS. That is the fair comparison for the paper’s optimization claim, because SNAS is also using a single-level setup. The aggressive constraint row is also worth keeping. It gives up accuracy, moving to 3.10 +/- 0.04%, but shrinks the searched model to 2.3M parameters. That supports the idea that the resource constraint is a real knob, not only a regularizer. ImageNet TransferSNAS follows the usual NASNet/DARTS protocol: search on CIFAR-10, then transfer the discovered cell to ImageNet mobile setting.
The SNAS row reports:
Method Top-1 error Top-5 error Params MAdds Search cost
DARTS 26.9 9.0 4.9M 595M 1 GPU day
SNAS, mild constraint 27.3 9.2 4.3M 522M 1.5 GPU days
This is a reasonable transfer result, not a dominant one. DARTS is slightly better on top-1 and top-5 error. SNAS is smaller and uses fewer multiply-adds. The useful takeaway is that the stochastic cells are not CIFAR-only artifacts; they transfer about as well as the DARTS-family cells in this mobile ImageNet setting. Relation To DARTS, ENAS, And GDASSNAS is easiest to place by comparing the training graph each method uses.
ENAS samples discrete child graphs from a controller and trains them with shared weights. Its weak point is delayed RL reward and controller training. DARTS trains a deterministic soft mixture of all candidate operations. Its weak point is the mismatch between the relaxed supernet and the derived child graph. SNAS samples relaxed edge masks from a Concrete distribution. Its weak point is that temperature scheduling and final discretization still matter. GDAS samples one operation per edge in the forward pass. Its weak point is still the final discretization rule and the hand-designed search space.
SNAS and GDAS are especially close in spirit. Both use differentiable stochastic sampling to reduce the DARTS relaxation gap. The emphasis is different:
SNAS is framed around optimizing a distribution over child graphs and connecting search gradients to policy gradients. GDAS is framed around sampling one differentiable subgraph per step to reduce memory and make search computation closer to the final architecture.
So I would not read SNAS as “the final answer” to differentiable NAS. I would read it as one of the papers that makes the DARTS relaxation less naive. LimitationsSeveral caveats matter when using SNAS as a baseline.
The search space is still hand-designed. SNAS searches inside a NASNet/DARTS-style cell grammar. The fully factorizable distribution ignores correlations between edge decisions. That makes optimization simpler, but it is not a universal architecture prior. The Concrete temperature schedule can change the result. A bad schedule either makes the model too soft or collapses the distribution too early. The reported ImageNet result is transfer from CIFAR-10, not direct ImageNet search. Search cost comparisons are hardware- and implementation-dependent. The paper uses NVIDIA TITAN Xp GPUs for the main search setting. The final architecture is still derived by turning a learned stochastic distribution into a discrete cell, so the relaxation gap is reduced but not eliminated.
TakeawaySNAS matters because it separates two ideas that are often conflated in differentiable NAS. Gradients do not require a deterministic soft mixture over all operations. You can keep architecture choices as stochastic variables, relax the samples for backpropagation, and optimize the expected loss of child graphs. My main practical lesson from the paper is about objective alignment. If the final model will be a discrete child graph, the search-time computation should look as much like a child graph as possible. SNAS pushes in that direction with Concrete-relaxed sampling and a decomposable resource penalty. Later one-path and hardware-aware NAS methods keep returning to the same theme: the supernet is only useful if its training signal predicts the quality and cost of the model you will actually deploy.

entry.title: SpQR: Sparse-Quantized LLM Weight Compression
entry.content:
Paper: SpQR: A Sparse-Quantized Representation for Near-Lossless LLM Weight Compression Code: Vahe1994/SpQR SpQR is a post-training weight compression method for LLMs. The short version is simple: most weights are stored in a dense 3-4 bit group-wise format, while a very small set of high-sensitivity weights is stored separately in a sparse high-precision component. That makes SpQR different from a plain W4 quantizer. It is a representation format:
a dense low-bit matrix for the common case; compressed quantization metadata for scales and zero points; a sparse matrix of sensitive outlier weights; a kernel path that must combine the dense and sparse parts efficiently.
The paper’s target is “near-lossless” compression: keep the quantized model within roughly 1% relative perplexity degradation compared with the 16-bit model, while reducing model memory by more than 4x. Why This Paper MattersThe useful observation is not merely that outliers exist. The useful observation is that the outlier budget can be tiny if the detector measures the right thing.
Figure 1 from the paper. SpQR gets a better quality-size tradeoff than RTN and GPTQ on LLaMA models, both for WikiText2 perplexity and zero-shot accuracy. On the left plot, lower is better. On the right plot, higher is better. The green SpQR curve is usually closer to the fp16 frontier for the same model size. This is the core reason the method is interesting: it does not just squeeze the same dense quantizer harder, it changes the storage format so that difficult weights do not ruin the dynamic range of normal groups. Sensitivity, Not MagnitudeA tempting outlier rule is “large absolute value means outlier”. SpQR uses a stricter criterion: a weight is important if quantizing it causes output error that cannot be compensated well by nearby weights. The paper defines sensitivity through the layer reconstruction objective:
Using the same second-order view as GPTQ, this becomes tied to the squared rounding error and an inverse-Hessian term:
The exact constant is not the important part for reading the paper. The important part is that sensitivity depends on both quantization error and how much the rest of the layer can compensate for that error.
Figure 2 from the paper. Weight log-sensitivities in a LLaMA-65B attention layer show row outliers, column outliers, attention-head patterns, rotary-position structure, and unstructured sensitive weights. This figure is the strongest motivation for the sparse component. Sensitive weights are not only clean columns. Some are row-like, some are head-local, some follow RoPE-related structure, and some are simply unstructured. A channel-only rule would miss part of the picture. RepresentationSpQR has three compression ideas that must be read together. First, it uses very small groups for normal weights. A typical first-level group size is 16 contiguous weights. Small groups reduce local dynamic-range waste, which is helpful at 3-4 bits. Second, it compresses the quantization statistics themselves. If every 16-weight group stores high-precision scale and zero-point values, metadata becomes too expensive. SpQR therefore quantizes those statistics with a second-level grouping scheme. In the paper’s example, a 256-weight block can be split into 16-weight first-level groups, and the scale/zero statistics for those groups are themselves quantized with compact second-level statistics. Third, it extracts high-sensitivity weights into a sparse high-precision path. These outliers are usually less than 1% of all weights. The sparse representation stores a 16-bit value and a 16-bit column index for each outlier, plus a row-prefix structure. The average cost is about 32 bits per outlier, so the method only works if the sparse set stays small.
Figure 3 from the paper. The stored tensor consists of quantized weights, first-level quantized scales/zeros, second-level statistics, and a sparse outlier component. One subtle implementation detail matters: an outlier still has a low-bit value in the dense matrix, and the sparse path stores a correction-like high-precision value. This keeps the dense memory layout regular. The outlier value is also affected by GPTQ-style error compensation, so it should not be read as merely “copy the original fp16 weight into sparse storage”. The conversion procedure follows this high-level flow:
Algorithm 1 from the paper. SpQR detects sensitive weights, quantizes the remaining dense weights, quantizes quantization statistics, and gathers sparse outlier values. The algorithm is closest in spirit to GPTQ: it processes layers with calibration data, estimates reconstruction error, and performs error compensation. SpQR adds an outlier-detection step and a storage format that can actually keep those outliers. Main ResultsThe headline result is near-lossless compression for LLaMA and Falcon models at about 4.4-4.7 average bits per parameter. The average-bit number includes weights, quantization statistics, and sparse metadata.
Table 1 from the paper. LLaMA perplexity on WikiText2, C4, and Penn Treebank. Selected LLaMA rows:
7B fp16: 16.00 average bits, 5.68 WikiText2, 7.08 C4, 8.80 PTB. 7B SpQR near-lossless: 4.63 average bits, 5.73 WikiText2, 7.13 C4, 8.88 PTB. 7B GPTQ W4: 4.00 average bits, 6.13 WikiText2, 7.43 C4, 9.27 PTB. 7B SpQR low-bit: 3.94 average bits, 5.87 WikiText2, 7.28 C4, 9.07 PTB. 65B fp16: 16.00 average bits, 3.53 WikiText2, 5.62 C4, 6.91 PTB. 65B SpQR near-lossless: 4.71 average bits, 3.57 WikiText2, 5.64 C4, 6.93 PTB. 65B GPTQ W4: 4.00 average bits, 3.83 WikiText2, 5.80 C4, 7.07 PTB. 65B SpQR low-bit: 3.90 average bits, 3.68 WikiText2, 5.70 C4, 6.99 PTB.
The near-lossless rows are the important ones for the paper’s main claim. For LLaMA-65B, SpQR at 4.71 average bits moves WikiText2 from 3.53 to 3.57 and C4 from 5.62 to 5.64. The lower-bit SpQR row is also useful: at 3.90 average bits, it still beats the 4-bit GPTQ baseline in this table.
Table 2 from the paper. Falcon perplexity results show the same pattern: near-lossless SpQR is close to fp16, while the lower-bit setting remains competitive with 4-bit GPTQ. The Falcon table is a good sanity check because the calibration and model family differ from LLaMA. For Falcon-40B, fp16 gets 5.23 on WikiText2 and 7.76 on C4. SpQR at 4.46 average bits gets 5.26 and 7.79, while the 3.90-bit SpQR setting gets 5.29 and 7.85. AblationsThe ablation table answers two practical questions:
Does compressing quantization statistics hurt? Are unstructured sensitive weights actually better than row/column-style outliers?
Table 3 and Figure 4 from the paper. Quantized statistics remain effective, and unstructured SpQR outliers reduce perplexity faster than row or column outlier choices. The 65B ablation is useful because it shows why metadata compression is not optional. With 3-bit quantized statistics, SpQR reports 3.74 WikiText2 perplexity at 3.63 average bits. Using 16-bit statistics is not better in this setting: it reports 3.84 at 3.67 average bits. In other words, spending more bits on metadata is not automatically the right allocation. The outlier-type plot also supports the sensitivity-based design. The unstructured SpQR outlier rule gives the best perplexity improvement as the sparse share increases. Row outliers and the Dettmers et al. column outlier criterion help less for this weight-only setting. Bit AccountingSpQR should always be compared by effective bits per parameter, not only by the dense weight bit-width. The stored model includes:
low-bit dense weights; first-level scales and zero points; second-level statistics used to quantize those scales and zero points; sparse outlier values; sparse outlier indices and row-prefix metadata.
The paper defines average bits as:
For a 3-bit dense configuration with 3-bit quantized scales, 3-bit quantized zero points, first-level group size 16, second-level group size 32, and a 0.4% outlier rate, the rough accounting is:
This is why the outlier fraction must be small. A sparse value is expensive relative to a 3-bit dense weight, but it can be worth the cost if it prevents a much larger dense accuracy loss.
Figure 8 from the appendix. Perplexity improves as average bits increase, but the useful region depends on dense bit-width and outlier share. The figure also shows diminishing returns. Outliers are valuable at low rates, but after some point each additional sparse weight buys less perplexity improvement while still paying the index/value cost. InferenceThe runtime story is more complicated than the compression story. A naive sparse correction path can erase the benefit of smaller weights. The paper therefore implements a custom sparse matrix multiplication path instead of relying only on a standard PyTorch sparse operator.
Table 4 from the paper. Batch-1 A100 decoding speed in tokens per second. Selected numbers:
7B scratch: fp16 47, PyTorch sparse 30, optimized SpQR 57 tokens/s. 7B prefix 1024: fp16 46, PyTorch sparse 27, optimized SpQR 55 tokens/s. 13B scratch: fp16 37, PyTorch sparse 24, optimized SpQR 44 tokens/s. 13B prefix 1024: fp16 31, PyTorch sparse 21, optimized SpQR 37 tokens/s. 30B scratch: fp16 19, PyTorch sparse 8.8, optimized SpQR 22 tokens/s. 30B prefix 1024: fp16 17, PyTorch sparse 6.5, optimized SpQR 22 tokens/s. 65B scratch: fp16 OOM, PyTorch sparse OOM, optimized SpQR 12 tokens/s. 65B prefix 1024: fp16 OOM, PyTorch sparse OOM, optimized SpQR 11 tokens/s.
Two points stand out. First, the PyTorch sparse path is slower than fp16 even though the model is compressed. This is the warning sign: a sparse-plus-dense format is not automatically fast. Second, the optimized SpQR path is faster than fp16 for the model sizes that fit, and it runs 65B where the fp16 baseline is out of memory. This is the real systems contribution: the representation needs a kernel implementation that respects GPU memory behavior. The paper still leaves a limitation here. Dense low-bit matrix multiplication and sparse correction are not fully fused. A fused implementation could be faster, but it is also harder to engineer. Relation To Other Quantization WorkGPTQ is the closest ancestor. It uses a second-order reconstruction objective and layer-wise error compensation, but stores the final result as dense low-bit weights. SpQR keeps the GPTQ-style sensitivity signal and adds a sparse high-precision escape path. AWQ protects activation-salient channels by rescaling weights before quantization. That is attractive because the runtime can remain a regular dense quantized path. SpQR is more explicit about storing exceptions, which can preserve quality but requires sparse metadata and kernels. SqueezeLLM is conceptually nearby because it also studies weight sensitivity and compressed low-bit storage for LLMs. The design details differ: SpQR emphasizes group-wise uniform quantization, bilevel statistics, and a sparse outlier representation. LLM.int8() should not be confused with SpQR. LLM.int8() isolates activation outlier dimensions during matrix multiplication. SpQR isolates weight outliers in the stored model. Reproduction ChecklistIf I were reproducing this paper, I would track these items explicitly:
Start from a working GPTQ-style layer reconstruction implementation. Verify the calibration data path first. The paper uses RedPajama for LLaMA and RefinedWeb for Falcon. Plot sensitivity maps for a few late transformer layers. If the detector only finds clean columns, something may be too simplistic. Tune the outlier threshold by target outlier rate, not by raw threshold value alone. Report effective bits per parameter, including statistics and sparse indices. Compare three variants: dense-only GPTQ, SpQR with sparse storage disabled at runtime, and full SpQR. Benchmark the sparse correction path separately from dense dequantization. Report both perplexity and zero-shot tasks. Perplexity alone is useful but not enough to understand downstream behavior.
The easy mistake is to celebrate low dense bit-width while hiding metadata. SpQR is convincing because the paper keeps the average-bit accounting visible. LimitationsSpQR is not the simplest deployment format. A regular W4 group-wise model has easier kernels, easier packing, and fewer metadata edge cases. SpQR buys quality by accepting an irregular sparse path. The sparse path can also become a failure mode. If a model, target bit-width, or calibration setup requires too many outliers, the index/value cost and irregular memory access can dominate. At that point the representation is no longer “dense with rare exceptions”; it becomes two competing formats. The evaluation also focuses on predictive metrics such as perplexity and zero-shot accuracy. The paper explicitly does not settle open-ended generation quality. For a serving system, I would still run task-specific generation checks after perplexity looks good. TakeawaySpQR is a good example of quality-oriented compression. It treats a small number of sensitive weights as first-class citizens instead of forcing them through the same dense low-bit quantizer as everything else. The tradeoff is engineering complexity. If the serving stack has an optimized sparse correction path, SpQR can deliver near-lossless compression with useful speedups. If the sparse path is slow or poorly integrated, a simpler dense W4 format may be less accurate but easier to run well.

entry.title: SqueezeLLM: Dense-and-Sparse Quantization
entry.content:
Reference Paper: SqueezeLLM: Dense-and-Sparse Quantization Code: SqueezeAILab/SqueezeLLM Related notes: GPTQ, AWQ, SpQR
I read the arXiv v4 / ICML 2024 version. SqueezeLLM belongs to the same weight-only quantization family as GPTQ, AWQ, and SpQR, but it makes a different bet: if decoding is memory-bandwidth bound, we can afford a slightly more complicated dequantization format as long as it cuts weight traffic and preserves perplexity. The method has two pieces:
