sensitivity-based non-uniform quantization, where each output channel gets a small LUT of quantized values chosen by weighted k-means; Dense-and-Sparse decomposition, where a tiny set of outliers and highly sensitive weights is kept in an FP16 sparse matrix.
The headline is mainly a 3-bit story. On LLaMA-7B C4 perplexity, uniform RTN at 3-bit collapses to 28.26, dense-only SqueezeLLM gets 7.75, and the 0.45% sparse variant gets 7.56. The FP16 baseline is 7.08, so the remaining gap is small enough that the kernel and format details become the real deployment question. Why Weight-Only Quantization MattersFor batch-1 autoregressive decoding, most large linear layers behave like matrix-vector products. The same weight matrix is streamed for every generated token, and there is not much batch reuse to amortize that read. That is the setting where W3A16 / W4A16 formats are attractive: keep activations in FP16/BF16, but store weights in a few bits.
Figure 2 is a useful sanity check. The paper models LLaMA-7B on an A5000 and shows that reducing only the weight precision from 16-bit to 8-bit and 4-bit lowers normalized runtime substantially for sequence lengths 128 and 2048. This does not mean every LLM workload is memory-bound. Prefill, large-batch serving, attention kernels, and KV-cache pressure can shift the bottleneck. But for single-batch generation, weight bandwidth is a good first target. Sensitivity-Based Non-Uniform QuantizationThe simplest non-uniform quantizer for one output channel is k-means over the weights. For a codebook , the dense quantized value is selected by nearest centroid:
Plain k-means minimizes unweighted reconstruction error:
SqueezeLLM changes the objective. The paper starts from the second-order perturbation of final loss:
assuming the first-order gradient term is close to zero after training. Computing the full Hessian is too expensive, so the method approximates it with a diagonal Fisher estimate from calibration samples:
This is weighted k-means. A weight with large pulls the centroid harder, because quantizing that value badly is expected to hurt final loss more.
This figure is the core intuition. The green bars are uniform quantization levels, while the purple levels from sensitivity-aware non-uniform quantization cluster around sensitive values. The paper’s ablation is pretty decisive here: for 3-bit LLaMA-7B on C4, sensitivity-agnostic non-uniform quantization gives 18.08 perplexity, while sensitivity-based non-uniform quantization gives 7.75 before adding any sparse values. One detail I like: SqueezeLLM optimizes for final loss perturbation rather than only layer-wise output perturbation. GPTQ/AWQ/SpQR mostly protect layer outputs or activation-weighted layer behavior. SqueezeLLM’s Fisher score is more expensive because it needs gradients through the model, but it is closer to the quantity we actually evaluate. Dense-And-Sparse DecompositionNon-uniform centroids help, but outliers still waste codebook capacity. If a few very large weights stretch the range, the 8 centroids available in a 3-bit codebook spend too much capacity on values that almost never occur. SqueezeLLM handles this directly:
where is the dense matrix after removing selected values, and stores those selected values in sparse FP16 form.
The sparse matrix stores two kinds of values:
outlier weights selected by percentile thresholds; highly sensitive weights selected by Fisher scores.
The default setting in the main experiments is small: 0.45% sparse values, split as 0.05% sensitive values plus 0.4% outliers.
Figure 5 explains why this works. Across output projection and down projection layers in LLaMA-7B, most weights are packed into a narrow range, while the full range is stretched by rare outliers. Removing less than 1% of values can shrink the dense range enough that the same 3-bit codebook becomes much more useful. This is close in spirit to SpQR, but the emphasis is different. SpQR is a sparse-quantized representation with a strong outlier/sensitivity story. SqueezeLLM first makes the dense part better with non-uniform Fisher-weighted codebooks, then uses the sparse part as a small correction path. That difference matters for runtime because sparse paths are not free. Main Results The most useful slice for me is LLaMA-7B at 3-bit. First, the quality numbers:
Method Bits C4 Wiki2
FP16 16 7.08 5.68
RTN 3.00 28.26 25.61
GPTQ 3.00 9.55 7.55
SqueezeLLM 3.02 7.75 6.32
AWQ g128 3.24 7.90 6.44
SqueezeLLM 0.45% 3.24 7.56 6.13
And the corresponding serving numbers:
Method Speed Mem
FP16 1.0x 12.7 GB
RTN 2.3x 2.9 GB
GPTQ 2.3x 2.9 GB
SqueezeLLM 2.1x 2.9 GB
AWQ g128 2.0x 3.0 GB
SqueezeLLM 0.45% 1.9x 3.1 GB
The comparison I care about is not just “lower perplexity”. It is lower perplexity at similar average bit-width and measured memory. The 0.45% sparse setting has the same average bit-width as grouped GPTQ/AWQ in this table, but better C4 and WikiText2 perplexity. At 4-bit, the picture is more compressed. Several methods are already close to FP16, so the extra method complexity is harder to justify unless the deployment target really needs the smaller gap. At 3-bit, the gap is large enough that sensitivity-aware non-uniform quantization is doing real work.
Figure 6 is a better way to read the 3-bit result than a single row. The x-axis is relative model size, adjusted by group size for GPTQ/AWQ and by sparsity level for SqueezeLLM. SqueezeLLM stays below GPTQ/AWQ across 7B, 13B, 30B, and 65B. The separation is most visible on smaller models, where 3-bit quantization has less redundancy to absorb mistakes. Kernel NotesSqueezeLLM’s dense path stores packed 3-bit or 4-bit indices. Each index points into a per-output-channel FP16 LUT, and the CUDA kernel dequantizes values while performing matrix-vector multiplication. Arithmetic stays FP16; the saving comes from reading fewer weight bits. The sparse path is implemented with CSR-style storage and a balanced sparse kernel. The balanced part matters because sparse nonzeros are skewed across output channels. A naive one-row-per-thread CSR kernel gives poor load balance; the paper instead assigns a fixed number of nonzeros per thread.
On 128-token generation with an A6000:
LLaMA-7B FP16 takes 3.2 s and 12.7 GB. dense-only 3-bit SqueezeLLM takes 1.5 s and 2.9 GB. 0.45% sparse SqueezeLLM takes 1.7 s and 3.1 GB.
That is the tradeoff in one line: the sparse correction improves 7B C4 perplexity from 7.75 to 7.56, and the latency cost is 1.5 s to 1.7 s in this benchmark. The GPTQ g128 row is also a warning. With activation ordering, GPTQ gets good perplexity but very poor latency in this implementation because the kernel has to handle distributed group scales and memory accesses. Accuracy tricks that look cheap in a table can become expensive once the packed layout is real. Reproduction ChecklistIf I were reproducing this paper, I would separate the algorithmic gain from the format gain:
Run RTN, GPTQ/AWQ, and dense-only non-uniform quantization at the same average bit-width. Estimate diagonal Fisher scores from the same calibration sample budget used by the paper. Compare ordinary k-means against Fisher-weighted k-means before introducing sparsity. Add the sparse path in two steps: sensitive values only, then outliers plus sensitive values. Report effective bits including codebooks, sparse values, and sparse indices. Benchmark generation with the final packed kernels, not only fake-quantized PyTorch matmuls.
The important control is step 3. Without it, it is too easy to attribute all improvement to the sparse FP16 escape hatch. The paper’s ablations show that the dense non-uniform codebook is already responsible for most of the recovery from RTN collapse. TakeawaySqueezeLLM is a strong paper because it treats 3-bit LLM quantization as both a numerical problem and a layout problem. The numerical side says: uniform bins are a bad fit when only 8 values are available, and sensitive weights should influence centroid placement more than ordinary weights. The layout side says: a small sparse FP16 path is acceptable only if the dense LUT kernel and sparse kernel are implemented carefully. I would reach for this idea when the target is near-lossless 3-bit weight-only inference and custom kernels are acceptable. If a plain 4-bit AWQ/GPTQ format already meets the quality and latency target, the simpler dense format is probably easier to ship. The value of SqueezeLLM is the low-bit corner where the extra format complexity buys back enough perplexity to matter.

entry.title: Swin Transformer: Hierarchical Vision Transformer using Shifted Windows
entry.content:
Paper Swin Transformer is one of the papers that made vision Transformers feel practical as a backbone instead of only as an image classification model. The design is not mysterious: it keeps the Transformer block, but changes the token layout and the attention pattern so that the network looks more like a CNN pyramid. The two core ideas are:
build hierarchical feature maps by progressively merging neighboring patches; compute self-attention inside local windows, then shift the window partition between adjacent blocks so information can cross window boundaries.
This sounds small, but it fixes two major problems of the original ViT: the feature map is no longer stuck at one low resolution, and attention is no longer quadratic in the full image size. MotivationPlain ViT treats an image as a sequence of non-overlapping patches. For image classification this is acceptable: a class token or pooled feature is enough. For object detection and semantic segmentation, however, the model needs dense feature maps at multiple scales. A detector usually wants something like a feature pyramid, where early stages preserve spatial details and later stages carry high-level semantics.
The figure compares the two feature layouts. ViT keeps a single-scale token grid after patch embedding. Swin starts from small patches and repeatedly merges them, so the network naturally produces feature maps at resolutions similar to C2, C3, C4, and C5 in a CNN backbone. This is why Swin became useful outside ImageNet classification. The paper evaluates it as a drop-in backbone for ImageNet classification, COCO detection, and ADE20K segmentation, instead of only reporting a classification number. Hierarchical Patch MergingThe input image is first split into non-overlapping patches of size . For an RGB image, each raw patch contains values. A linear embedding maps each patch into a feature vector with dimension . After this patch embedding, Swin has four stages:
Stage 1: resolution , channel size . This is the high-resolution low-level feature level. Stage 2: resolution , channel size . This is the first downsampled feature level. Stage 3: resolution , channel size . This is the main semantic feature level. Stage 4: resolution , channel size . This is the lowest-resolution high-level feature level.
Patch merging performs the downsampling between stages. It groups every neighboring patches, concatenates their channels, and applies a linear layer:
So the spatial resolution is reduced by , while the channel dimension is doubled. This is very close to the intuition of CNN downsampling: reduce the map size, increase the representation width, and keep a pyramid that downstream heads can consume.
The architecture figure is worth reading carefully. The patch merging layers are not a side detail; they are what let Swin replace a ResNet in detection and segmentation frameworks. The Transformer blocks operate inside each stage, and the stage outputs can be attached to FPN, UperNet, Mask R-CNN, Cascade Mask R-CNN, and similar heads. Window AttentionThe expensive part of global self-attention is the attention matrix. If the feature map has size , then the number of tokens is . Global multi-head self-attention compares every token with every other token, so the attention matrix has entries. The paper writes the complexity of global MSA as:
My understanding of the two terms:
is the linear projection cost. We project tokens into , , , and project the attention output back to channel dimension . This part grows linearly with the number of tokens. is the actual global attention cost. It includes computing and multiplying the attention map with . This is the term that explodes when the image resolution grows.
Swin replaces global attention with window-based attention. Split the feature map into non-overlapping windows of size , and only run self-attention inside each window. The complexity becomes:
The first term stays the same because all tokens still pass through the projection layers. The second term changes from to . If is fixed, this term is linear in image size. For the default window size , each window has only tokens. That is much cheaper than letting every token attend to all tokens in a high-resolution feature map. Shifted WindowsLocal windows alone create a new problem: tokens in different windows cannot communicate. If every layer uses exactly the same window partition, the model becomes a set of isolated local Transformers. Swin solves this by alternating between regular window partitioning and shifted window partitioning.
The left side is regular window attention. The right side shifts the partition by half a window size, so each shifted window contains tokens that came from several previous windows. After two consecutive blocks, information can move across the original window boundary. This is a nice compromise:
within one block, attention is still local and cheap; across two blocks, neighboring windows exchange information; the model does not need global attention at every layer.
The paper writes two consecutive Swin Transformer blocks as:
This is a pre-norm Transformer layout. The first block uses normal window attention. The second block uses shifted window attention. Both blocks keep the standard residual connection and MLP sub-layer. The formula is simple, but the alternation is the important part. is efficient but has no cross-window communication. keeps the same local attention cost while letting each new window overlap several old windows. Efficient Shifted Window ImplementationA naive implementation of shifted windows would create more windows near the feature boundary. The paper gives an example where a window layout becomes a layout after shifting, which means more attention windows and more padding. The efficient implementation uses cyclic shift:
Cyclically shift the whole feature map toward the top-left. Partition the shifted feature map into the same number of windows as before. Apply an attention mask so tokens from non-adjacent wrapped regions cannot attend to each other. Reverse the cyclic shift after attention.
The mask is not a minor engineering trick. Without it, tokens wrapped from the opposite side of the feature map would be treated as if they were spatial neighbors. With the mask, cyclic shift becomes a batching trick: the implementation keeps the same number of windows while preserving the intended shifted-window attention pattern. This is also why Swin is fast in practice. The theory says window attention is cheaper, but the cyclic-shift implementation makes the shifted case close to the non-shifted case in actual latency. Relative Position BiasSelf-attention by itself does not know the relative position between two tokens. Swin adds a learnable relative position bias to the attention logits:
Here for one window, so the full bias matrix would be . But Swin does not learn each entry independently. For a window of size , the relative offset along each axis ranges from to . Therefore the number of possible 2D relative offsets is:
The paper learns a smaller bias table:
Then each pair of query and key positions indexes into this table according to their relative offset. This gives the model local geometric information without using a fixed absolute position embedding tied to a specific image size. The ablation table later shows that relative position bias is not just decorative. It improves ImageNet, COCO, and ADE20K, and the gain is especially visible for dense prediction. Model Variants The paper defines several model sizes. The most common ones are:
Swin-T: , blocks per stage . Swin-S: , blocks per stage . Swin-B: , blocks per stage . Swin-L: , blocks per stage .
All four use the default window size and head dimension in the paper’s main configurations. Swin-T is the small practical backbone, roughly comparable to ResNet-50 scale in downstream usage. Swin-B and Swin-L are larger models where ImageNet-22K pre-training becomes important. One useful detail: the deeper stage is Stage 3, not Stage 4. That matches CNN backbone design as well. Stage 3 usually has enough spatial resolution to matter for dense prediction, so spending more blocks there gives a better compute-accuracy tradeoff. ImageNet Results On ImageNet-1K, Swin-T reaches 81.3 top-1 accuracy with 4.5G FLOPs and 755.2 images/s throughput. Swin-S reaches 83.0, and Swin-B reaches 83.5 at input. The comparison with DeiT is the most relevant Transformer baseline:
At input, DeiT-S gets 79.8 top-1 with 4.6G FLOPs, while Swin-T gets 81.3 with 4.5G FLOPs. At input, DeiT-B gets 81.8 top-1 with 17.5G FLOPs, while Swin-B gets 83.5 with 15.4G FLOPs. At input, DeiT-B gets 83.1 top-1 with 55.4G FLOPs, while Swin-B gets 84.5 with 47.0G FLOPs.
Swin is not always faster in throughput than DeiT at the small scale, but it gives better accuracy at similar FLOPs. After ImageNet-22K pre-training, Swin-L reaches 87.3 top-1 at input. That was a strong result for a general-purpose backbone. COCO Detection Results The COCO table is more important than the ImageNet table for understanding this paper. Swin is presented as a backbone, so the real question is whether it improves standard detection frameworks. A few examples from the table:
Framework CNN backbone Swin backbone Gain
Cascade Mask R-CNN R-50: 46.3 box AP Swin-T: 50.5 box AP +4.2
ATSS R-50: 43.5 box AP Swin-T: 47.2 box AP +3.7
RepPointsV2 R-50: 46.5 box AP Swin-T: 50.0 box AP +3.5
Sparse R-CNN R-50: 44.5 box AP Swin-T: 47.9 box AP +3.4
This is the strongest argument for the design. If the model only improved ImageNet classification, it could be seen as another ViT variant. The COCO results show that the hierarchical features and window attention are useful for dense prediction. The system-level number is also strong: with larger models and stronger training, Swin-L reaches 58.7 box AP and 51.1 mask AP on COCO test-dev. ADE20K Segmentation Results On ADE20K semantic segmentation, Swin is used with UperNet. The validation mIoU numbers are:
Backbone mIoU
Swin-T 46.1
Swin-S 49.3
Swin-B 51.6
Swin-L 53.5
Again, this is where the backbone design matters. Semantic segmentation needs detailed spatial output. The hierarchical structure gives the segmentation head multi-scale features, while shifted windows allow local regions to communicate without paying global attention cost. Ablation: Shift, Position Bias, and Speed The shifted-window ablation is very direct. Removing the shift drops Swin-T from 81.3 to 80.2 on ImageNet, from 50.5 to 47.7 box AP on COCO, and from 46.1 to 43.3 mIoU on ADE20K. My reading: the shift is more important for dense prediction than for classification. Classification can tolerate some locality because the final representation only needs a global category. Detection and segmentation need object boundaries, context, and cross-window consistency, so the lack of communication hurts more. The position encoding ablation is also useful:
no position embedding: 80.1 ImageNet, 49.2 box AP, 43.8 mIoU; absolute position embedding: 80.5 ImageNet, 49.0 box AP, 43.2 mIoU; relative position bias: 81.3 ImageNet, 50.5 box AP, 46.1 mIoU.
Relative position bias works better because it is local and window-compatible. Absolute position embeddings are more tied to a specific image grid, which is less convenient when image sizes vary across detection and segmentation pipelines.
The speed table compares different attention implementations. The important row is shifted window with cyclic implementation. It is much faster than naive shifted-window padding and close to normal window attention. For Swin-T, the paper reports:
Attention implementation Throughput
Sliding window, naive MSA 183 images/s
Performer 638 images/s
Window, no shift 770 images/s
Shifted window, padding 670 images/s
Shifted window, cyclic 755 images/s
This explains why the cyclic shift and mask trick matters. The shifted-window idea would be less attractive if it created many extra windows or padding overhead. With cyclic shift, the implementation keeps the number of windows stable. Input Resolution Tradeoff Swin can use larger input sizes because the dominant attention cost is linear in image size when the window size is fixed. The table shows the expected tradeoff: larger input improves accuracy but reduces throughput. For Swin-T:
Input size Top-1 Throughput
81.3 755.2
81.6 580.9
82.1 342.0
82.2 219.5
The gain from to is only +0.9 top-1, while throughput drops by about 3.4x. For pure classification this may not always be worth it. For dense prediction, larger input resolution can be more valuable because the output spatial quality matters. TakeawaySwin Transformer is important because it adapts the Transformer to the normal shape of vision backbones:
patch merging creates a feature pyramid; window attention makes high-resolution features affordable; shifted windows allow cross-window communication; relative position bias gives local spatial inductive bias; cyclic shift and masking make the design efficient enough to use in real detection and segmentation systems.
The paper is not just proposing another attention variant. It is packaging several architectural and implementation choices into a backbone that fits existing vision pipelines. That is why Swin had such a large downstream impact: it could be plugged into the same places where people were already using ResNet, ResNeXt, and ConvNeXt-style backbones.

entry.title: Switch Transformers: Scaling to Trillion Parameter Models with Simple and Efficient Sparsity
entry.content:
Paper Switch Transformer is a very practical MoE paper. It does not start from a complicated routing algorithm. It takes the Transformer FFN, replaces it with multiple FFN experts, and routes each token to only one expert. That top-1 choice is the central simplification. Compared with earlier top-2 MoE designs, Switch reduces expert computation, reduces communication, makes the dispatch tensor easier to implement, and still preserves the main benefit of MoE: the model can have many more parameters without activating all of them for every token. The paper is important because it makes sparse scaling look like an engineering path rather than only a modeling idea. The authors scale from T5-style baselines to 395B and 1.6T parameter Switch variants, while keeping the per-token compute close to dense baselines. One SentenceSwitch Transformer increases total model capacity by adding many FFN experts, but keeps token-level compute controlled by routing each token to a single selected expert.
The scaling curve gives the main intuition. As the number of experts increases, parameter count grows, but each token still activates one expert. The result is a new scaling axis: more sparse parameters at roughly fixed per-token FLOPs. From Dense FFN to Switch FFNIn a standard Transformer block, every token passes through the same FFN. Switch keeps the attention block unchanged and replaces the dense FFN with a Switch FFN layer.
For every token representation , the router computes logits:
Here is the router weight matrix. If there are experts, then has entries. Each entry is the router’s score for sending this token to one expert. The router then applies softmax: $$p_i(x) = \frac{\exp(h(x)i)}{\sum{j=1}^{N}\exp(h(x)_j)}$$ My understanding of this formula:
is the probability mass assigned to expert for token . The denominator normalizes all expert scores so the probabilities sum to 1. The router is still differentiable through , even though the final dispatch decision is discrete.
In a general top-k MoE layer, let be the selected expert set. The output is:
This means the token output is a weighted sum of selected expert outputs. Earlier MoE work often used , so each token was processed by two experts and then combined. Switch changes this to :
Only the best expert is executed. The gate value still multiplies the expert output, so the router probability is not thrown away. The key practical win is that the layer no longer needs to run two FFNs per routed token. Why Top-1 Routing MattersTop-1 routing looks almost too simple, but it changes the system behavior:
The expert computation per token is reduced because only one FFN expert runs. The expert capacity can be smaller because each token consumes one expert slot instead of two. The all-to-all communication pattern is simpler because each token has only one destination expert. The implementation has fewer combine paths because the output comes from one selected expert.
This is the core reason the paper calls the layer “Switch”. Each token is switched to one expert rather than softly mixing several experts. Expert CapacityThe hard part of sparse routing is not the softmax. The hard part is batching tokens efficiently on accelerators. TPU/XLA-style systems need statically shaped tensors, but the number of tokens sent to each expert is dynamic. Switch solves this with a fixed expert capacity:
Every expert gets a fixed number of token slots. The first fraction is the average number of tokens each expert would receive under perfectly balanced routing. The capacity factor adds extra buffer.
The figure shows the tradeoff. With capacity factor 1.0, there is no extra buffer. If the router sends too many tokens to one expert, some tokens overflow. In the paper’s implementation, an overflowed token skips the expert computation in that layer and continues through the residual connection. With capacity factor 1.5, there is extra room, so fewer tokens overflow. But the empty slots still occupy compute and memory. This is the main capacity tradeoff:
lower capacity factor: faster and less memory, but more risk of dropped tokens; higher capacity factor: fewer dropped tokens, but more wasted slots and communication.
The paper reports that dropped tokens are typically below 1% when the load balancing loss is strong enough. Load Balancing LossIf the router is trained only through the main language modeling loss, it may collapse toward a small number of experts. That is bad for two reasons. First, overloaded experts drop tokens. Second, unused experts waste parameters. Switch adds one auxiliary loss per Switch layer:
This formula is compact but important. is the number of experts. is the fraction of tokens actually dispatched to expert :
is the number of tokens in batch . The indicator is 1 if token chooses expert , and 0 otherwise. So measures the actual hard routing load. is the average router probability assigned to expert :
is differentiable because it uses the soft router probabilities. is not differentiable because it depends on the argmax dispatch. The loss multiplies these two vectors, so the differentiable probability mass is pushed to match the hard token allocation. Under ideal uniform routing, both vectors are:
Then:
Multiplying by keeps the loss scale roughly independent of the number of experts:
This explains the factor. Without it, the uniform-routing loss would shrink as the expert count grows, changing the effective strength of the auxiliary objective. The paper uses .
The pseudocode is a useful implementation view. It computes two density vectors:
density_1: the hard fraction of tokens sent to each expert; density_1_proxy: the soft probability mass assigned to each expert.
The loss is their dot product multiplied by num_experts ** 2 in code. This is equivalent to the paper’s scaled loss up to the chosen coefficient and averaging convention. Benchmark Against MoE Table 1 compares T5, top-2 MoE, and Switch under the same hardware setting. The important comparisons:
At capacity factor 1.0, Switch-Base reaches the quality threshold in 62.8 hours, while MoE-Base needs 80.1 hours. Switch-Base at capacity factor 1.0 runs at 1000 examples/sec, faster than MoE-Base at 860 examples/sec. Switch-Base+ gets the best 100k-step quality in this table, -1.534 negative log perplexity, while still reaching the threshold in 67.6 hours.
The interesting point is that lower capacity factors help Switch. This matters for large sparse models because memory is limited. A design that only works with a large capacity factor is less attractive at scale. Stability TricksSparse expert models add hard routing decisions inside the network. That makes training less stable than a dense Transformer. The paper uses several practical fixes. Selective Precision Pure bfloat16 training is fast but unstable in the router: the table shows bfloat16 diverging. Full float32 is stable but slower. Switch uses selective precision:
cast the router computation to float32; compute router probabilities, dispatch, and combine tensors; cast the dispatch/combine path back to bfloat16 for the rest of the layer.
The result is almost the same speed as bfloat16, but with float32-like stability. In the table, selective precision reaches -1.716 quality at 1390 examples/sec, while full float32 reaches -1.718 at 1160 examples/sec. Smaller InitializationThe paper initializes weights with a truncated normal distribution with mean 0 and a standard deviation controlled by a scale parameter :
is the number of input units. Reducing reduces the initial weight scale. The paper recommends reducing the default Transformer scale from 1.0 to 0.1.
The effect is large. At 3.5k steps, the 0.1x initialization has average quality -2.72 with standard deviation 0.01, while the 1.0x initialization has average quality -3.60 with standard deviation 0.68. The mean improves and the run-to-run variance becomes much smaller. Expert DropoutSwitch has many more parameters than a FLOP-matched dense model. During fine-tuning on smaller downstream tasks, this can overfit. The paper therefore uses larger dropout inside expert FFNs than in the rest of the model.
The useful setting is not “increase dropout everywhere”. The better pattern is lower regular dropout on non-expert layers and higher dropout inside experts, for example standard dropout 0.1 and expert dropout 0.4. Scaling With ExpertsThe number of experts is the cleanest scaling dimension in Switch. If the model still routes each token to one expert, adding more experts increases total parameters without proportionally increasing FFN compute per token. The router has extra cost:
This is the cost of producing router logits over experts. It is not free, but it is small compared with running a large FFN expert, especially at the expert counts studied in the main experiments.
Figure 4 shows two things:
Increasing experts from 1 to 256 improves the sparse-parameter scaling curve. On a step basis, Switch-Base with more experts learns faster than T5-Base under the same per-token compute budget.
The paper notes that Switch-Base with 64 experts reaches the same quality around 60k steps that T5-Base reaches around 450k steps. That is about a 7.5x step-efficiency gain. Wall-Clock SpeedStep efficiency alone is not enough. Sparse routing adds communication, and communication can erase theoretical compute savings. The paper therefore also measures wall-clock training time.
The 64-expert Switch-Base reaches the same quality in about one seventh of the time of T5-Base. This is the result that makes the paper feel practical: despite router overhead and all-to-all dispatch, the sparse model is still faster in real training time. The paper also compares against scaling the dense model itself.
T5-Large uses about 3.5x more FLOPs per token than T5-Base, but Switch-Base is still more sample-efficient and gives a 2.5x wall-clock speedup over T5-Large in this setup. This is a stronger comparison than only beating T5-Base, because it asks whether the same resources should be spent on dense width/depth or sparse experts. Downstream Results The downstream table checks whether pretraining gains transfer after fine-tuning. They generally do:
Switch-Base improves over T5-Base on GLUE, SQuAD, SuperGLUE, Winogrande, XSum, ANLI, ARC Easy, and closed-book QA tasks. Switch-Large improves over T5-Large on many of the same tasks. Some tasks are not uniformly better, for example ARC Challenge is tied or worse in some comparisons.
This matters because a sparse model could in theory only improve the upstream language modeling metric. The table shows that the gains often survive task fine-tuning, although the behavior is not perfectly uniform. Multilingual Pretraining The multilingual setting uses 101 languages. The plotted result shows Switch improving over the dense multilingual baseline across all languages in the experiment.
The speedup histogram is also useful. The paper reports a mean step speedup around 5x over the dense mT5-Base baseline, and 91% of languages get at least 4x speedup to reach the final mT5-Base perplexity. Parallelism and CommunicationSparse models are not just “bigger dense models”. They stress the system differently. Dense scaling mainly adds model-parallel tensor operations. Expert scaling adds routing, token packing, dispatch tensors, and all-to-all communication.
The figure separates data parallelism, model parallelism, expert parallelism, and combinations of them. Switch can use expert parallelism by placing different experts on different devices. But once tokens are routed to experts, the system must move token representations to the device holding the selected expert, then move outputs back. The practical bottlenecks are:
whether each expert gets enough tokens to form efficient matmuls; whether the all-to-all communication is hidden or exposed; whether expert capacity creates too many padded slots; whether the router distributes tokens evenly enough.
This is why the paper spends so much space on load balancing, capacity factor, and static tensor shapes. Trillion-Parameter Models Table 9 is the large-scale result. A few numbers stand out:
T5-XXL has 11B parameters and 6.3T FLOPs/sequence. Switch-XXL has 395B parameters and the same 6.3T FLOPs/sequence. Switch-C has 1.571T parameters, 2048 experts, and 890B FLOPs/sequence.
Switch-C is interesting because it uses expert parallelism without model parallelism in the same way as Switch-XXL. It has far more parameters than T5-XXL, but lower FLOPs/sequence in the table. The paper reports that Switch-C is 4x faster than T5-XXL to a fixed perplexity under the same compute budget. The result also shows a limitation: not every sparse scale-up is equally stable. The paper notes that Switch-C showed no training instability, while Switch-XXL was sometimes unstable despite having better step-basis performance. Implementation SketchThe router logic can be summarized like this: router_logits = x @ W_rrouter_logits = router_logits.float()router_probs = softmax(router_logits, dim=-1)expert_gate, expert_index = top1(router_probs)expert_mask = one_hot(expert_index, num_experts)aux_loss = load_balance_loss(router_probs, expert_mask)position_in_expert = cumsum(expert_mask, dim=tokens) * expert_maskexpert_mask = expert_mask * (position_in_expert < expert_capacity)dispatch_tensor = build_dispatch(expert_mask, position_in_expert)combine_tensor = build_combine(expert_gate, expert_mask, position_in_expert)
The important operations are:
top-1 selection chooses the destination expert; cumulative position assigns each token a slot inside that expert’s fixed capacity; overflow tokens are masked out; dispatch tensor sends tokens to experts; combine tensor brings expert outputs back and multiplies by the gate value.
This is the implementation side of the paper’s main idea. The model is sparse, but the tensors are shaped so accelerators can still run large batched operations. TakeawaySwitch Transformer is important because it takes MoE from “powerful but complicated” toward “simple enough to scale”. The main technical choices are:
replace dense FFN layers with expert FFN layers; route each token to one expert using top-1 routing; use fixed expert capacity to make shapes static; add a load balancing loss to avoid expert collapse; use selective precision so router softmax stays stable; reduce initialization scale for sparse-model stability; use expert dropout during fine-tuning; combine data, model, and expert parallelism for very large models.
The tradeoff is also clear. Switch increases parameter capacity without linearly increasing per-token compute, but it introduces routing and communication complexity. The paper’s contribution is showing that this tradeoff can be favorable in real pretraining runs, not only in theory.

entry.title: Exploring the Limits of Transfer Learning with a Unified Text-to-Text Transformer
entry.content:
Paper: Exploring the Limits of Transfer Learning with a Unified Text-to-Text Transformer Code and models: google-research/text-to-text-transfer-transformer T5 is easy to remember as “the text-to-text model”, but that slogan undersells the paper. The paper is closer to a large engineering study of transfer learning for NLP. It fixes a common interface, runs many controlled ablations, and then scales the best recipe into the final T5 family. The important part is not only that classification can be written as generation. The important part is that the authors make architecture, objective, data, fine-tuning, task mixing, and scaling decisions comparable under one framework. T5 is a model, but the paper is also a benchmark harness for pretraining research. All figures and tables below are cropped from the original arXiv PDF. One InterfaceT5 casts every task as conditional text generation.
Figure 1. The central interface: all tasks consume text and emit text. The input contains a task prefix and the example content. The output is also text: translate English to German: That is good.=> Das ist gut.cola sentence: The course is jumping well.=> not acceptablestsb sentence1: The rhino grazed on the grass. sentence2: A rhino is grazing in a field.=> 3.8summarize: state authorities dispatched emergency crews...=> six people hospitalized after a storm in attala county.
The model no longer needs a classification head, a span head, a translation-specific head, or a summarization-specific head. It always estimates a conditional sequence probability:
Training is ordinary teacher-forced maximum likelihood:
This is mechanically simple, but it changes what the experimental pipeline looks like. GLUE, SuperGLUE, SQuAD, WMT translation, and CNN/Daily Mail summarization all become the same kind of supervised example. For classification, labels are strings such as entailment, not_entailment, positive, or not acceptable. For STS-B, the regression target is rounded to a string such as 3.8. There is an engineering cost hidden in this elegance. A classifier with a fixed label set cannot emit an invalid label, but a text generator technically can. The paper says this did not happen in their trained models, but the possibility matters in production. If I were reproducing this today, I would still track invalid-output rate separately from accuracy, especially for small models, long labels, or multilingual label strings. The larger lesson is that the task description becomes part of the input distribution. The prefix is not decorative. It is the routing mechanism that tells the same model which conditional distribution to learn. Baseline RecipeThe baseline model is a standard encoder-decoder Transformer, close in spirit to the original sequence-to-sequence Transformer. The encoder reads the corrupted or task-prefixed input. The decoder autoregressively generates the output. The baseline uses:
12 encoder layers and 12 decoder layers; hidden size ; feed-forward size ; 12 attention heads; a shared SentencePiece vocabulary of 32K wordpieces; roughly 220M parameters; pretraining on C4 for steps; fine-tuning for steps.
The baseline is deliberately not the final T5. It is the experimental control used throughout the paper. The authors first ask which design decisions are worth keeping, then scale the resulting recipe. The dataset is also part of the contribution. T5 introduces C4, the Colossal Clean Crawled Corpus, a filtered English Common Crawl dataset. The filtering rules remove boilerplate, non-English pages, duplicated spans, pages with bad words, pages with too little punctuation, and other obvious low-quality web text. This is not a minor detail. A pretraining objective can only learn from the distribution it is fed, and C4 became a standard dataset largely because it made web text usable enough for broad transfer experiments. Span CorruptionT5’s default unsupervised objective is span corruption.
Figure 2. T5 replaces each corrupted span with a sentinel token and trains the decoder to emit only the missing spans. Take a token sequence . Sample several contiguous spans whose total length is about a fixed corruption rate . T5 uses and later settles on average span length . The rough number of corrupted spans is:
If the corrupted spans are , the encoder input replaces each span by a unique sentinel token:
The decoder target is the concatenation of sentinel markers and missing text:
This differs from BERT-style masked language modeling in two important ways. First, T5 is sequence-to-sequence. The decoder is trained to generate a target string, not independently classify masked positions. Second, the decoder target is short. It contains only the dropped spans plus sentinel tokens, not the entire original sequence. If the full sequence has length , then a rough target length is:
With and , this is about , much shorter than reconstructing all tokens. That is why span corruption is not only a modeling choice. It is also a compute choice. My reading is that T5’s objective is a compromise between BERT and seq2seq denoising. It keeps BERT’s bidirectional encoder signal, but makes the decoder do a generation task that resembles the downstream text-to-text interface. Attention Masks And Architecture ChoicesThe paper compares encoder-decoder, decoder-only language model, and prefix-LM structures. Before the architecture comparison, it makes the masking patterns explicit.
Figure 3. Fully visible, causal, and causal-with-prefix attention masks. In Transformer attention, a mask can be viewed as an additive matrix. Let denote the attention output:
Here when position may attend to position , and when it may not.
A fully visible mask lets every position see every input position. A causal mask lets each output position see only previous positions. A causal-with-prefix mask gives a bidirectional prefix, then causal generation after the prefix.
The architecture variants map naturally onto these masks.
Figure 4. Encoder-decoder, decoder-only language model, and prefix-LM variants. The encoder-decoder version has a bidirectional encoder and a causal decoder. The decoder-only language model concatenates input and target and applies a causal mask everywhere. The prefix LM allows the input prefix to be fully visible while keeping output generation causal. The table result is clear:
Table 2. Encoder-decoder with denoising is the strongest baseline among the tested architectures. Several observations matter:
Denoising beats plain language modeling for every architecture family. The standard encoder-decoder with denoising has the best overall baseline average. Sharing encoder and decoder parameters cuts parameters roughly in half and remains surprisingly competitive. Decoder-only language modeling is weak in this text-to-text setting, especially on SQuAD and SuperGLUE. Prefix LM closes much of the gap to encoder-decoder, but not all of it.
This is one of the paper’s useful historical points. In 2019, encoder-only BERT and decoder-only GPT-style models were both rising. T5 does not argue that encoder-decoder is universally superior. It argues that, under a text-to-text transfer setup covering classification, QA, summarization, and translation, encoder-decoder is a strong default because it gives the input bidirectional processing while preserving autoregressive output generation. Today, decoder-only LLMs dominate many general-purpose systems because scale, prompting, KV-cache serving, and instruction tuning changed the tradeoff. But for supervised seq2seq transfer, T5’s architecture result still makes sense. Objective SurveyThe objective section is the densest part of the paper. The authors compare many objectives under the same text-to-text framework.
Table 3. Different unsupervised objectives produce different input/target pairs from the same text. The objectives differ in two dimensions:
what corruption is applied to the input; how much text the decoder must reconstruct.
For example, BERT-style denoising asks the model to reconstruct the original text. MASS-style masking also reconstructs the original text. T5’s “replace corrupted spans” objective only predicts the corrupted spans, delimited by sentinels. The “drop tokens” variant removes corrupted tokens instead of inserting a sentinel placeholder. The first high-level comparison is between prefix language modeling, BERT-style denoising, and deshuffling:
Tables 4 and 5. Denoising wins over prefix LM and deshuffling; among denoising variants, several short-target objectives are close. Table 4 says BERT-style denoising is a better high-level family than prefix language modeling and deshuffling. Table 5 then narrows the question: if we are already doing denoising, should the decoder reconstruct the full original text, or only the corrupted pieces? The answer is not a dramatic accuracy story. Several denoising variants are close. The practical difference is target length. Reconstructing the full original segment gives the decoder a long target. Predicting only the corrupted spans keeps the target much shorter. That is the kind of tradeoff I care about in pretraining: if two objectives are close in accuracy, the one that uses less target-side computation is usually the better default. The paper then varies span length:
Table 7. Average span length 3 is a strong default; very long spans are slightly worse in this setup. The paper’s chosen default, average span length 3 with 15% corruption, is not magic. The results are close for span lengths 2, 3, and 5. Span length 10 is weaker in several non-translation settings. The practical interpretation is that the objective should remove meaningful chunks but not make the reconstruction problem too coarse. The paper summarizes this search as a flow chart:
Figure 5. The objective search narrows from high-level families to corruption strategies, corruption rate, and span length. My takeaway is that T5’s objective is important, but the paper does not prove that it is uniquely optimal. It proves something more useful: many denoising variants work, so one should choose the version that is accurate, simple, and computationally efficient. C4 And Data EffectsThe dataset section is easy to overlook because the model name became famous, but C4 is one of the paper’s lasting artifacts.
Table 8. C4 is a strong general-purpose source, while domain-matched corpora help specific downstream tasks. The table compares C4, unfiltered C4, RealNews-like data, WebText-like data, Wikipedia, and Wikipedia plus Toronto BookCorpus. C4 is not the best on every metric. Wikipedia plus BookCorpus is strong on SuperGLUE because some SuperGLUE tasks have book-like or Wikipedia-like domains. Wikipedia helps SQuAD because SQuAD passages come from Wikipedia. RealNews-like data helps ReCoRD-like reading comprehension. This is a useful reminder: “better pretraining data” is not a single scalar. A dataset can be better because it is cleaner, larger, more diverse, or closer to the downstream domain. These are different axes. T5’s C4 is a strong general-purpose compromise, not a universal optimum. The authors also study dataset size by artificially truncating C4:
Figure 6. Smaller repeated datasets can show lower pretraining loss, which is a warning sign for memorization rather than better transfer. The curve is counterintuitive at first: smaller datasets can produce lower pretraining loss because the model repeatedly sees the same examples. This does not imply better transfer. It suggests memorization of the unlabeled data. For pretraining, a low loss on repeated data can be less valuable than a slightly higher loss on fresh, diverse data. I would track at least three data-side metrics in a modern reproduction:
number of unique tokens seen during pretraining; repetition rate across training steps; downstream transfer by domain, not only an averaged benchmark score.
Fine-Tuning: Full Updates Still MatterThe paper also compares fine-tuning strategies that update fewer parameters.
Table 10. Full fine-tuning is strongest in this experiment; adapters and gradual unfreezing are competitive but not universally better. Full fine-tuning wins in the baseline setup. Adapter layers can be useful, especially when parameter storage or deployment constraints matter, but their performance depends on adapter dimension and task size. Gradual unfreezing is close in some metrics but still weaker than updating all parameters. This result predates modern LoRA and instruction-tuning practice, so I would not overgeneralize it. The important point is experimental: parameter-efficient tuning is not automatically free. It changes the optimization problem, and the right adapter capacity depends on the task. Multi-Task MixingBecause every task is text-to-text, it is natural to ask whether all tasks can be trained together.
Table 11. Multi-task results are sensitive to sampling strategy. If dataset has examples, examples-proportional sampling with an artificial cap can be written as:
Temperature-scaled mixing starts from a base sampling distribution and flattens or sharpens it:
The table shows why this matters. Equal mixing over-samples small tasks and under-samples large tasks. Pure examples-proportional mixing can let large datasets dominate. Temperature and caps are attempts to balance these forces. The next table compares broader training strategies:
Table 12. Unsupervised pretraining plus fine-tuning remains the strongest general baseline. The result is conservative. Multi-task learning helps in some places, but the standard recipe, unsupervised pretraining followed by fine-tuning, remains robust. “Leave-one-out” multi-task pretraining is interesting because it trains on many supervised tasks while withholding the target task, then fine-tunes on the held-out task. It is only slightly worse in several metrics, suggesting that supervised tasks can transfer some useful behavior. But supervised multi-task pretraining alone is weaker overall, especially outside translation. My reading: the text-to-text interface makes multi-tasking possible, but it does not solve mixture design. Dataset mixture is an optimizer input. If the mixture is wrong, the unified interface simply gives the model a unified way to learn the wrong balance. ScalingSection 3.6 asks a practical question: given more compute, should we train longer, use a bigger model, increase batch size, or ensemble?
Table 13. Scaling model size and training time both help; ensembling is a separate way to spend compute. A rough training-compute proxy is:
This proxy is incomplete because architecture, sequence length, optimizer state, parallelism, and hardware utilization matter. But it captures the key tradeoff: spend compute on more tokens, more parameters, or multiple models. The table suggests:
training longer improves the baseline; increasing batch size is also useful in this setup; larger models add gains beyond longer training alone; 2x size with 2x training and 4x size with 1x training are both strong; ensembling is useful on some metrics, especially summarization and translation.
The paper’s interpretation is close to the “bitter lesson”: general methods improve with compute. But T5 also shows that compute is not the whole story. The final recipe includes interface design, data cleaning, objective choice, and fine-tuning choices. Scaling makes those decisions more valuable; it does not replace them. Final T5 VariantsAfter the ablation study, the authors train the final T5 family:
Variant Parameters Role
T5-Small 60M Small baseline
T5-Base 220M Comparable size to the baseline, but with final recipe
T5-Large 770M Larger encoder-decoder
T5-3B 3B Large-scale model
T5-11B 11B Largest reported model
The final table is large, so I split it into two crops.
Table 14, part 1. T5 variants on GLUE, SQuAD, and the first part of SuperGLUE.
Table 14, part 2. Remaining SuperGLUE tasks, WMT translation, and CNN/Daily Mail summarization. The large model is strong:
GLUE average reaches 90.3. SQuAD reaches 91.26 EM and 96.22 F1. SuperGLUE average reaches 88.9. CNN/Daily Mail reaches 43.52 ROUGE-1, 21.55 ROUGE-2, and 40.69 ROUGE-L.
The translation story is more mixed. T5 does not beat the listed previous best WMT English-to-German, English-to-French, or English-to-Romanian systems. That is not surprising: the model pretrains primarily on English C4, while translation benefits from large parallel corpora and multilingual pretraining. The most important final comparison is Table 15.
Table 15. T5-Base beats the original baseline and a longer-trained baseline, so recipe changes matter beyond token count. Baseline-1T trains the original baseline for 1 trillion tokens. T5-Base uses the final recipe at the same 220M parameter scale. T5-Base wins across all summarized metrics. This is the strongest evidence that the ablation study was not just decoration. More tokens help, but the final T5 recipe helps beyond merely training longer. What T5 AnticipatedT5 is not instruction tuning in the modern chat-model sense. It does not use RLHF, preference optimization, tool calls, or conversational alignment. But it clearly anticipates several later ideas:
task instructions are input text, not model architecture; one model can cover classification, generation, QA, and regression through a shared interface; labels can be verbalized; the pretraining/fine-tuning pipeline can be phrased as conditional generation; benchmark mixtures and task prefixes become part of model design.
The difference is that T5 is still mainly a supervised fine-tuning framework. It does not rely on in-context learning as the primary adaptation mechanism. A T5 checkpoint is meant to be adapted to tasks; a modern instruction-tuned decoder-only model is often expected to perform many tasks directly from prompting. That difference matters. The T5 interface is unified, but not necessarily open-ended. The model is trained to map known prefixes to known output styles. General instruction following requires a broader distribution of task descriptions, demonstrations, dialogue states, and preference signals. What I Would Measure In A ReproductionIf I were reproducing T5 today, I would not only report benchmark averages. I would measure the mechanisms separately:
Target length per objective: compare decoder-token cost for full reconstruction versus span-only reconstruction. Invalid label rate: especially for small models and classification tasks with string labels. Prefix sensitivity: evaluate whether small changes to task prefixes affect accuracy. Domain transfer: separate in-domain gains from general transfer gains for C4, Wikipedia, books, and news. Data repetition: measure unique tokens and repeated-example rate, not just total tokens. Mixture entropy: quantify how concentrated the multi-task sampling distribution is. Parameter-efficient tuning: revisit adapters with modern LoRA-style baselines. Compute-normalized objective comparison: compare objectives at matched wall-clock or FLOP budget, not only matched steps. Decoder latency: text-to-text classification requires generation; measure whether label generation is a deployment bottleneck. Scaling law fit: fit loss and downstream score against parameters and tokens instead of comparing only a few sizes.
The paper already gives unusually good experimental coverage for its time. These extra checks would make the conclusions sharper under today’s infrastructure and serving constraints. LimitationsT5 is a strong paper, but several assumptions matter. First, text-to-text unification can hide task-specific structure. A classifier’s label space is small and discrete, while T5 treats labels as text. This is elegant, but it may waste computation and introduces invalid-output concerns. Second, the task prefix is a learned convention. It works because training data consistently uses prefixes. It is not automatically robust to arbitrary natural-language instructions. Third, C4 is English-centric and heavily heuristic-filtered. The paper’s translation results make this limitation visible. A model pretrained mostly on English web text is not automatically a strong multilingual model. Fourth, the ablation study is large but still finite. Many results are close, especially among denoising objectives. The exact winning objective may change with model size, tokenizer, sequence length, training tokens, optimizer, or data mixture. Fifth, final performance depends heavily on scale. T5-11B was large for 2019, and the strongest conclusions rely on compute that many labs could not reproduce then and many small teams still cannot reproduce now. Sixth, a unified interface does not solve evaluation. Averaging over GLUE, SuperGLUE, QA, summarization, and translation can blur very different failure modes. TakeawayT5’s core contribution is not only “use text-to-text”. It is the combination of:
a universal text-in/text-out interface; an encoder-decoder Transformer baseline; C4 as a large cleaned web corpus; span corruption with short decoder targets; systematic ablations across architecture, objective, data, fine-tuning, mixture, and scale; final large models trained from the resulting recipe.
For me, the paper is best read as a recipe paper with a simple interface. The interface made the study possible. The ablations made the recipe credible. The scale made the final results impressive. The most durable lesson is that unification is useful when it exposes comparisons. T5 did not merely force every task into one format; it used that format to ask controlled questions about transfer learning. That is why the paper still matters.

entry.title: TE-NAS: Training-Free Architecture Search
entry.content:
Chen W, Gong X, Wang Z. Neural Architecture Search on ImageNet in Four GPU Hours: A Theoretically Inspired Perspective. ICLR 2021.
Paper: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2102.11535.pdf Code: https://github.com/VITA-Group/TENAS
TE-NAS is a training-free NAS paper. The question is simple: can we rank and prune architectures before doing any gradient descent? The paper answers yes, at least inside NAS-Bench-201 and DARTS-style cell spaces, by combining two initialization-time signals:
trainability, estimated by the condition number of the neural tangent kernel; expressivity, estimated by the number of linear regions induced by ReLU activations.
The method is not a predictor trained on many evaluated architectures, and it is not a supernet trained with weight sharing. It builds a full search graph, measures these two properties at random initialization, and prunes low-value operators edge by edge. The headline result is a DARTS-space ImageNet search in about four GPU hours on one GTX 1080Ti. The part I find most useful is the framing. TE-NAS does not claim that initialization-time theory fully explains generalization. It uses theory as a cheap diagnostic: a network should be trainable enough for gradients to make progress and expressive enough to fit nontrivial functions. A search procedure that ignores either side can select pathological cells. Why Training-Free NASMost NAS methods spend their budget evaluating architectures. They either train sampled candidates, train a weight-sharing supernet, or train a predictor from architecture-performance pairs. All three routes introduce cost or bias:
Full candidate training is expensive. Early stopping gives a noisy ranking. Weight sharing can make the supernet ranking disagree with standalone training. Learned predictors need a dataset of already trained architectures.
TE-NAS tries to remove this evaluation loop. For each candidate or supernet state, it only needs a minibatch of inputs and randomly initialized weights. No labels are required for the two main indicators. This is a strong assumption. A zero-cost proxy is only useful if the search space is constrained enough that the proxy signal is comparable across candidates. TE-NAS is therefore best read together with its search spaces: NAS-Bench-201 and DARTS cells. Trainability: NTK Condition NumberThe neural tangent kernel describes how output changes with respect to parameter updates. For a finite network, the empirical NTK can be written as:
where is the Jacobian of network output with respect to parameters. The paper uses the conditioning of this kernel as a proxy for trainability:
The intuition is ordinary numerical conditioning. If the largest and smallest eigenvalues of the training NTK differ too much, gradient descent fits some directions quickly and some directions slowly. A smaller condition number means the architecture is expected to be easier to optimize.
In NAS-Bench-201, the paper reports a negative Kendall-tau correlation between NTK condition number and test accuracy. It is not a perfect predictor. The scatter has obvious outliers. But it is useful enough to reject many bad candidates without training them. Expressivity: Linear RegionsTrainability alone can prefer networks that are easy to optimize but weak. TE-NAS adds an expressivity signal based on ReLU linear regions. For a ReLU network, the input space is partitioned into regions where the network behaves as an affine function. More distinct activation patterns suggest richer piecewise-linear behavior.
TE-NAS estimates this without training. It samples inputs, forwards them through a randomly initialized network, records activation patterns from ReLU layers, and counts unique patterns as an approximation to the number of linear regions.
The paper reports a positive Kendall-tau correlation around 0.50 on NAS-Bench-201. Again, this is not a complete theory of accuracy. It is a search signal. The useful part is that it points in a different direction from the NTK condition number. The Two Signals Prefer Different OperatorsThe paper’s operator-composition plot explains why TE-NAS uses both indicators.
In NAS-Bench-201:
Both indicators like a large amount of conv3x3. The NTK condition number prefers more skip_connect, which helps gradient flow. The linear-region count prefers more conv1x1, which increases expressive variation. Average pooling is not favored by either signal in the top-ranked group.
This is the main design reason for combining the two ranks. If the search only minimizes the NTK condition number, it can become too biased toward easy-to-train structures. If it only maximizes linear regions, it can select expressive but poorly conditioned structures. Pruning By ImportanceInstead of sampling many complete cells, TE-NAS starts from a supernet containing all operators and prunes it.
For each pruning step:
Consider removing each candidate operator from the current supernet. Measure how NTK condition number changes. Measure how the linear-region count changes. Rank removals by the two changes. Combine the ranks and prune one operator on each edge. Repeat until the search space becomes a single-path architecture.
The criterion is easy to state:
Prefer removals that improve trainability, meaning they reduce the NTK condition number. Prefer removals that preserve expressivity, meaning they do not reduce linear regions too much.
This is different from DARTS. DARTS learns continuous operation weights by optimizing a validation objective. TE-NAS does not train a supernet at all. It repeatedly asks: “If this operator disappeared, would the untrained network look more trainable and still expressive?” Search TrajectoryThe pruning trajectory figure is useful because it shows the behavior of the two signals during search.
The starting supernet has high expressivity because it contains all operations, but it has poor trainability. Early pruning sharply improves the NTK condition number. Later steps fine-tune the architecture while trying not to sacrifice too much expressivity. This matches a practical intuition about oversized search graphs. The full supernet is not necessarily a good architecture. It can be expressive and badly conditioned at the same time. Search needs to remove structure, not only choose the largest function class. NAS-Bench-201 ResultsNAS-Bench-201 is a good place to test zero-cost search because every architecture in the space has a standardized evaluation. TE-NAS is evaluated on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet-16-120.
The compact comparison is easier to read as triples: CIFAR-10 / CIFAR-100 / ImageNet-16-120.
GDAS: 93.61 / 70.70 / 41.84, with 28925.91 GPU seconds of search. NAS without training: 91.78 / 67.05 / 37.07, with 4.8 GPU seconds of search. TE-NAS: 93.90 / 71.24 / 42.38, with 1558 GPU seconds of search. Optimal in space: 94.37 / 73.51 / 47.31 from benchmark lookup.
The interesting comparison is with “NAS without training” from Mellor et al. That method is faster, but the accuracy gap is large. TE-NAS spends more zero-cost evaluation time, still far below trained NAS methods, and gets much closer to the best architectures in the benchmark. DARTS-Space CIFAR-10 ResultsThe DARTS cell space is more realistic than NAS-Bench-201. It is also more fragile: cells need to be derived and then trained from scratch.
Key rows:
DARTS second-order: 2.76 test error, 3.3M parameters, 1.0 GPU day of search. SNAS: 2.85 test error, 2.8M parameters, 1.5 GPU days of search. GDAS: 2.82 test error, 2.5M parameters, 0.17 GPU days of search. PC-DARTS: 2.57 test error, 3.6M parameters, 0.1 GPU days of search. TE-NAS: 2.63 test error, 3.8M parameters, 0.05 GPU days of search.
TE-NAS is not the absolute best CIFAR-10 error in this table. PC-DARTS reports a better 2.57 error. But TE-NAS is competitive while using roughly 0.05 GPU days of search, which is about 1.2 GPU hours. That is the point of the paper: high-quality cell search without the expensive search-time training loop. ImageNet ResultsThe ImageNet result is the headline claim in the title.
The paper reports two TE-NAS rows:
CIFAR-10 search: 26.2 top-1 error, 8.3 top-5 error, 6.3M parameters, and 0.05 GPU days of search. ImageNet search: 24.5 top-1 error, 7.5 top-5 error, 5.4M parameters, and 0.17 GPU days of search.
The ImageNet-searched cell reaches 24.5 top-1 error and 7.5 top-5 error with 0.17 GPU days of search. The paper describes this as roughly four GPU hours on one GTX 1080Ti. The strongest comparison in the same table is PC-DARTS searched on ImageNet: 24.2 top-1 error, 7.3 top-5 error, and 3.8 GPU days of search. TE-NAS is slightly worse in accuracy but dramatically cheaper in search time. What Did It Find?The appendix shows the cells found on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet.
The cells still look like DARTS-family artifacts: separable convolutions, dilated convolutions, skip connections, and pooling arranged inside a fixed DAG grammar. TE-NAS is not inventing arbitrary macro-architectures. It is choosing operations and edges inside the same style of cell search space used by DARTS. The paper also studies depth and width preference in the DARTS space.
The high-level reading is that both indicators prefer shallow and wide cells in this space. That matches a known tendency of DARTS-family searches: shallow and skip-heavy structures can have smoother optimization behavior. AblationsThe appendix checks whether both indicators are needed.
On CIFAR-100 in NAS-Bench-201:
Search rule Accuracy
Only NTK condition number 69.25
Only linear regions 70.48
TE-NAS combined rank 71.24
The combination rule also matters. Directly summing raw metric changes is worse than summing ranks, because the scales of NTK condition number and linear-region count are not comparable. Ranking makes the criterion less dependent on numeric magnitude. The rank-combination plot reinforces this:
Lower combined rank is better in this plot, so the negative correlation is the desired behavior. LimitationsTE-NAS is a strong zero-cost NAS baseline, but the assumptions are important.
The score is search-space dependent. It works in NAS-Bench-201 and DARTS cells, not necessarily in arbitrary spaces. It evaluates trainability and expressivity, not generalization directly. NTK computation needs Jacobians and eigenvalues, so numerical stability and batch choice matter. Linear-region counting depends on sampled inputs and activation-pattern diversity. The method still ends with a discrete cell that must be trained from scratch for final reporting. The found architectures are constrained by the DARTS cell grammar.
The paper is careful about this. It does not say NTK and linear regions are the only meaningful architecture indicators. It argues that theoretically motivated, training-free indicators can be strong enough to guide practical search. TakeawayTE-NAS is valuable because it turns deep-network theory into a usable NAS pruning rule. The method asks two cheap questions at initialization:
Does this architecture look trainable under gradient descent? Does it still have enough expressive capacity?
That combination is stronger than either signal alone. It also gives a useful lens for reading later zero-cost NAS work: a proxy should not only be cheap and correlated on one benchmark. It should expose what property of the architecture it is measuring, and it should be tested against the failure cases that property misses.

entry.title: TernaryBERT: Distillation-aware Ultra-low Bit BERT
entry.content:
Paper: TernaryBERT: Distillation-aware Ultra-low Bit BERT TernaryBERT is a training recipe for an ultra-low-bit BERT student. The core setting in the paper is written as W-E-A, meaning the number of bits used for Transformer weights, word embeddings, and activations. The interesting configuration is 2-2-8: Transformer weights are ternary, word embeddings are ternary, and activations entering linear or matrix-multiplication operators are quantized to 8 bits. This is not post-training quantization. At 2-bit weight precision, the student no longer has enough capacity to recover task behavior only from labels. The paper therefore treats quantization and distillation as one package:
keep full-precision latent weights during training; ternarize weights for the forward pass; quantize selected activations to 8 bits; train the quantized student with Transformer-layer and prediction-layer distillation from a full-precision teacher.
Why This Paper MattersThe paper is trying to occupy a difficult point on the size-accuracy curve: much smaller than 8-bit BERT and dense distillation-only models, but still close to full-precision BERT on GLUE and SQuAD.
Figure 1 from the paper. Red squares are the authors’ methods on MNLI-m. The key point is that TernaryBERT reaches Q-BERT-level or better accuracy with smaller model size. The most important number is not only the 2-bit weight format. It is the resulting model size. BERT-base is 418 MB in the paper’s accounting. TernaryBERT at 2-2-8 is 28 MB, or 14.9x smaller. TernaryTinyBERT at 2-2-8 is 18 MB, or 23.2x smaller. The paper also includes a 3-bit extension, but I read the 2-bit result as the main contribution. At 8 bits, BERT quantization is already relatively forgiving. At 2 bits, the training recipe becomes the method. What Is QuantizedThe paper quantizes the dominant dense parts of BERT:
attention projection weights W_Q, W_K, W_V, and W_O; feed-forward weights W_1 and W_2; word embedding weights; inputs to linear layers and matrix multiplication operations.
It does not quantize everything. Segment embeddings, position embeddings, linear biases, Softmax, LayerNorm, and the final task-specific layer are kept out of the low-bit path. The authors argue that these parameters are small, and quantizing the numerically sensitive operators can cause noticeable accuracy loss. This scope matters. TernaryBERT is aggressive about BERT’s large matrices, but it is not an integer-only Transformer in the I-BERT sense. Ternary Weight FormatThe weight representation is:
Here b is the ternary vector and alpha is a scaling parameter. The zero state is important. It lets small weights disappear instead of being forced into a positive or negative bucket. The paper evaluates two ternarization methods. TWN is approximation-based. It chooses alpha and b to keep the ternary tensor close to the latent full-precision weight:
The threshold can be solved exactly with sorting, but the practical TWN approximation uses a threshold proportional to the mean absolute weight:
Weights above Delta become positive, weights below -Delta become negative, and values in between become zero. The scale is computed from the surviving weights. LAT is loss-aware. Instead of minimizing plain weight reconstruction error, it uses a weighted norm based on curvature information. In the paper’s implementation, the diagonal curvature proxy comes from the second moment in BertAdam:
This makes LAT closer to “which weight error will hurt the loss?” than plain TWN. In the reported tasks, however, TWN and LAT are often close. That is useful because TWN is simpler and cheaper. GranularityTernaryBERT tests layer-wise and row-wise scaling. The final empirical choice is:
row-wise ternarization for word embeddings; layer-wise ternarization for Transformer-layer weights.
The reasoning is practical. Word embeddings contain word-specific semantic information, so a separate scale per row helps. Transformer weight matrices are highly redundant, and one scale per matrix is often enough. In the ablation, row-wise embedding plus layer-wise Transformer weights gives the best MNLI pair among the tested TWN settings: 83.3 on MNLI-m and 83.3 on MNLI-mm. Activation QuantizationWeights are ternary, but activations are 8-bit. The paper quantizes activations that feed linear layers and matrix multiplications. It compares symmetric 8-bit quantization with min-max 8-bit quantization and chooses min-max. The reason is visible in the hidden-state distributions.
Figure 3 from the paper. Hidden representations in early layers are skewed rather than cleanly symmetric around zero. Symmetric quantization wastes levels when the distribution is shifted. Min-max quantization allocates the 8-bit grid over the observed activation range:
The appendix shows the same issue across layers:
Figure 4 from the appendix. Early hidden states are visibly biased toward negative values, which supports the min-max activation quantizer. This is a small but important detail. If the activation distribution is not centered, the easy symmetric INT8 choice can be worse even when the bit-width is the same. Distillation-Aware TrainingThe framework is a teacher-student loop. The teacher is a full-precision BERT fine-tuned on the downstream task. The student starts from the same fine-tuned model, but each forward pass uses ternary weights.
Figure 2 from the paper. The quantized student is trained against a full-precision teacher through Transformer-layer and prediction-layer distillation. The full-precision latent weights are kept during training. At step t, the student weight w_t is ternarized to \hat{w}_t, the quantized model runs the forward pass, the distillation loss is computed, and the gradient is used to update the latent full-precision w_t. This is the usual straight-through style of ultra-low-bit training, but with a richer teacher signal. The Transformer-layer distillation loss has two pieces:
H_l denotes hidden representations, and A_l denotes attention scores. The prediction-layer loss uses soft cross-entropy between student and teacher logits:
The final loss is:
Algorithmically, the loop is simple: initialize: fixed full-precision teacher, trainable student initialized from fine-tuned BERTinput: downstream training set, optionally with data augmentationfor each training step: read a mini-batch ternarize the student's latent full-precision weights run the quantized student forward pass compute Transformer-layer and prediction-layer distillation losses backpropagate through the quantized student update the latent full-precision weights and learning rateoutput: TernaryBERT student
The important part is what is not happening: the ternary student is not trained only from hard task labels. It is repeatedly pulled toward the teacher’s hidden states, attention scores, and logits. GLUE Results Tables 1 and 2 from the paper. Development and test results on GLUE. Several rows are worth reading carefully:
BERT baseline: 32-32-32, 418 MB, dev MNLI 84.5/84.9. TernaryBERT-TWN: 2-2-8, 28 MB, dev MNLI 83.3/83.3. TernaryBERT-LAT: 2-2-8, 28 MB, dev MNLI 83.5/83.4. Q-BERT: 2-8-8, 43 MB, dev MNLI 76.6/77.0. Q2BERT: 2-8-8, 43 MB, dev MNLI 47.2/47.3. TernaryTinyBERT-TWN: 2-2-8, 18 MB, dev MNLI 83.4/83.8.
The surprising part is not that 2-bit BERT is slightly below fp32 BERT. That is expected. The surprising part is that TernaryBERT stays close while Q-BERT-style 2-bit baselines collapse much harder in the same table. On the GLUE test set, the full BERT baseline gets a score of 78.2. TernaryBERT-TWN at 2-2-32 gets 77.3, TernaryBERT-TWN at 2-2-8 gets 76.9, and TernaryTinyBERT-TWN gets 76.6. The Tiny version loses 1.6 points while being 23.2x smaller. SQuAD Results Table 3 from the paper. Development results on SQuAD v1.1 and v2.0. SQuAD is a useful stress test because span extraction depends on token-level representations, not just classification logits. The result pattern still holds:
BERT: 418 MB, SQuAD v1.1 81.5/88.7, SQuAD v2.0 74.5/77.7. Q-BERT: 43 MB, SQuAD v1.1 69.7/79.6. Q2BERT: 43 MB, SQuAD v2.0 50.1/50.1. TernaryBERT-TWN: 28 MB, SQuAD v1.1 79.9/87.4, SQuAD v2.0 73.1/76.4. TernaryBERT-LAT: 28 MB, SQuAD v1.1 80.1/87.5, SQuAD v2.0 73.3/76.6.
For SQuAD, LAT is slightly better than TWN. The paper also notes that the Transformer-layer loss is much larger than the prediction-layer loss, so SQuAD training is done in two stages: first with L_trm, then with the full loss. AblationsThe ablations are the most useful part of the paper because they show which pieces are load-bearing.
Table 5 from the paper. Min-max activation quantization beats symmetric activation quantization on SQuAD v1.1. With 2-2-8, symmetric activation quantization gets 79.0 EM and 86.9 F1 on SQuAD v1.1. Min-max activation quantization gets 79.9 EM and 87.4 F1. This matches the hidden-state distribution observation: the activations are not symmetric enough for the symmetric grid to be ideal.
Table 6 from the paper. Removing Transformer-layer distillation and logit distillation hurts, especially on CoLA, RTE, and SQuAD. The full TernaryBERT-TWN row gets 55.7 on CoLA, 72.9 on RTE, and 79.9/87.4 on SQuAD v1.1. Without Transformer-layer distillation, those become 52.7, 69.0, and 76.6/84.9. With both Transformer-layer and logit distillation removed, they fall to 45.4, 56.3, and 74.3/83.2. That is the central lesson: final labels alone are too weak for this bit-width.
Table 7 from the paper. Data augmentation and initialization from a fine-tuned BERT both matter. Initialization also matters. If the student is initialized from pre-trained BERT instead of the already fine-tuned BERT, CoLA drops from 55.7 to 46.0 and RTE drops from 72.9 to 66.4.
