Data augmentation also helps, especially on CoLA and RTE. Compression Comparison Table 8 from the paper. MNLI-m comparison against quantization and compression baselines. This table mixes several families of methods, so I read it as a size-accuracy map rather than a pure apples-to-apples benchmark:
DistilBERT: 250 MB, 81.6 MNLI-m. TinyBERT-4L: 55 MB, 82.8 MNLI-m. Quant-Noise: 38 MB, 83.6 MNLI-m. Q-BERT 2/4-8-8: 53 MB, 83.5 MNLI-m. 3-bit BERT: 41 MB, 84.2 MNLI-m. 3-bit TinyBERT: 25 MB, 83.7 MNLI-m. TernaryBERT: 28 MB, 83.5 MNLI-m. TernaryTinyBERT: 18 MB, 83.4 MNLI-m.
TernaryBERT is not always the highest-accuracy point. The 3-bit BERT row is higher on MNLI-m. But TernaryBERT and TernaryTinyBERT give a strong size-accuracy tradeoff with a simpler fixed low-bit setting than mixed-precision methods. Attention PatternsThe appendix checks whether ternarization destroys attention structure.
Figure 6 from the appendix. Attention maps from full-precision BERT and TernaryBERT on a CoLA example remain visually similar. I would not over-read this figure. Visual attention similarity is not a proof of functional equivalence. But it is a useful diagnostic: the ternary student is not merely matching logits while internally behaving randomly. The layer and attention distillation losses appear to preserve at least some internal structure. Relation To Q8BERT And BinaryBERTQ8BERT is the conservative baseline: use quantization-aware fine-tuning to put embedding and fully connected paths into INT8 while leaving numerically sensitive operations in FP32. TernaryBERT is more aggressive on weights and word embeddings, but it still keeps activations at 8 bits and leaves Softmax/LayerNorm out of the quantized path. BinaryBERT is the more extreme follow-up direction. It asks how to train 1-bit BERT weights, and it uses a ternary model as an intermediate bridge. From that angle, TernaryBERT is the boundary where BERT quantization starts to require serious training machinery, but still has a zero state that makes optimization manageable. The pattern across these papers is clean:
8-bit BERT can often be handled with QAT. 2-bit ternary BERT needs distillation and careful initialization. 1-bit binary BERT needs even more structure, such as ternary-to-binary splitting.
Reproduction ChecklistIf I were reproducing TernaryBERT, I would separate the moving parts:
Start from a task-fine-tuned full-precision BERT teacher. Define the exact quantized operator coverage before training. Do not silently quantize Softmax, LayerNorm, or the task head. Keep full-precision latent weights and ternarize only for the forward path. Implement TWN first; add LAT only after the TWN baseline is stable. Use row-wise scaling for word embeddings and layer-wise scaling for Transformer weights. Use min-max 8-bit activation quantization, not only symmetric activation quantization. Add distillation in stages: hidden states, attention scores, then logits. Run the ablations without L_trm, without logit distillation, without data augmentation, and without fine-tuned initialization. Report W-E-A, model size, and task metrics together. A bit-width claim without size accounting is ambiguous.
For deployment, I would also benchmark the actual runtime path. Ternary weights reduce model storage, but speedup depends on whether the inference backend has kernels that exploit ternary weights and 8-bit activations efficiently. LimitationsThe method is task-training heavy. It needs a fine-tuned full-precision teacher, distillation losses, and in some cases data augmentation. This is not the same convenience level as post-training quantization. The quantized scope is also partial. Activations are 8-bit, not ternary. Softmax, LayerNorm, biases, position/segment embeddings, and the task-specific layer are not quantized. That is a reasonable engineering choice, but it means the method should not be described as a fully ternary BERT inference graph. Finally, model size is not latency. A 28 MB TernaryBERT is attractive, but practical speed depends on packing, kernels, memory layout, and whether the hardware can turn ternary arithmetic into real throughput gains. TakeawayTernaryBERT is best read as a recipe for making 2-bit BERT trainable. The ternary format gives compression, but distillation gives the optimization signal that keeps the student close to the teacher. The paper’s strongest lesson is that ultra-low-bit Transformer compression is not just a quantizer choice. At 2 bits, initialization, activation quantization, scaling granularity, hidden-state distillation, attention distillation, and logit distillation all matter.

entry.title: TransNAS-Bench-101: Cross-Task NAS Benchmarking
entry.content:
Duan Y, Chen X, Xu H, et al. TransNAS-Bench-101: Improving Transferability and Generalizability of Cross-Task Neural Architecture Search. 2021.
Paper: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2105.11871.pdf Dataset: MindSpore TransNAS-Bench-101 VEGA docs: TransNAS-Bench-101
TransNAS-Bench-101 is a NAS benchmark for a question that older tabular benchmarks only partially answer: if an architecture is good on one vision task, does that tell us anything about another task? NAS-Bench-101 and NAS-Bench-201 are useful because they make architecture search queryable, repeatable, and cheap. But both are still classification-centered. TransNAS-Bench-101 shifts the benchmark target from “find a good cell for classification” to “understand how architecture choices behave across tasks.” The benchmark evaluates 7,352 backbones on seven vision tasks. That means 51,464 trained models, plus per-epoch metrics, inference time, FLOPs, parameter counts, and training time. The paper says the full generation cost was 193,760 V100 GPU hours, about 22.12 years on one V100. The point is not that everyone should reproduce this cost. The point is that the cost has already been paid once, so transfer-NAS algorithms can be tested without training tens of thousands of networks again. What It AddsThe main contribution is not simply a larger table. It is a benchmark design that makes task transfer explicit.
There are two search spaces:
Cell-level search space: 4,096 DAG cells following the NAS-Bench-201 style, with four operation candidates: zeroize, skip connection, 1x1 convolution, and 3x3 convolution. Macro-level search space: 3,256 residual-block skeletons where depth, downsampling locations, and channel-doubling locations vary.
This distinction matters. A lot of early NAS work searches cells while keeping the macro skeleton fixed. TransNAS-Bench-101 asks whether that is enough when the target task changes. Dense prediction, image reconstruction, and layout regression may care more about where resolution is lost, how channels expand, and how much capacity is allocated at each stage. Seven TasksThe benchmark uses Taskonomy-style indoor images and constructs seven tasks from the same visual source distribution.
The tasks cover several types of supervision:
Classification: object classification and scene classification. Point regression: room layout. Self-supervised learning: jigsaw puzzle and autoencoding. Pixel-level prediction: surface normal and semantic segmentation.
This choice is deliberate. If every task came from unrelated datasets, transfer failure could be blamed on dataset shift. Here, the images share a common source, so architecture-task interaction becomes easier to isolate. The paper uses 24 buildings from Taskonomy, about 120K images, split into 80K train, 20K validation, and 20K test. Every architecture is trained on every task. Task-Specific HeadsThe benchmark searches the backbone and plugs it into task-specific decoders.
Classification-like tasks use global average pooling plus a linear head. Pixel-level prediction tasks use convolution and deconvolution decoders. Losses and metrics also differ by task: accuracy for classification and jigsaw, SSIM for autoencoding and surface normal, mIoU for semantic segmentation, and L2 loss for room layout. This is important for reading the results. The benchmark is not forcing all tasks into a classification interface. The backbone is the common object being searched, but the task head and metric remain task-specific. Compared With NAS-Bench-101 And NAS-Bench-201The paper includes a short benchmark comparison.
TransNAS-Bench-101 is smaller than NAS-Bench-101 in raw search-space size, but broader in task coverage:
NAS-Bench-101: one dataset, one task domain, cell search. NAS-Bench-201: three datasets, one task domain, cell search. TransNAS-Bench-101: one image source, seven task domains, cell and macro search.
That is the right tradeoff for cross-task NAS. Exhaustively evaluating hundreds of millions of architectures across seven tasks would be impractical. A smaller but fully trained benchmark is more useful for diagnosing transfer behavior. Search-Space StatisticsThe aggregate statistics already show that the macro and cell spaces are not interchangeable.
The macro-level space reports better average performance on all seven tasks in the table. It also tends to cost more, especially for dense output tasks such as autoencoding, surface normal, and semantic segmentation. A few numbers are useful anchors:
Object classification average accuracy: 39.71 for cell-level vs 44.24 for macro-level. Scene classification average accuracy: 45.23 for cell-level vs 52.92 for macro-level. Semantic segmentation average mIoU: 19.95 for cell-level vs 24.47 for macro-level. Jigsaw average accuracy: 76.57 for cell-level vs 93.43 for macro-level.
This does not mean macro search is always the final answer. It means that benchmark conclusions can change when the search space changes. A transfer-NAS method that only works on a cell grammar may not be robust enough. Architecture LandscapeFigure 3 plots average task ranking against FLOPs and parameter count.
The macro space has a smoother spread of architectures across compute. The cell space is more clustered because the macro skeleton is fixed and only the cell operation choices vary. This makes the macro search space more expressive for compute allocation, but also creates a wider range of training costs. The paper observes that more FLOPs and longer training time often correlate with better average ranking, but only within a reasonable range. The largest networks are not automatically the best. This is exactly why the benchmark records compute information: an algorithm should not be rewarded only for discovering expensive architectures. Cross-Task CorrelationThe most useful part of the paper is the cross-task rank-correlation analysis.
The all-network correlations can look encouraging. Many task pairs have positive rank correlation, especially in the cell-level search space. But the top-half correlations shrink quickly. This is the hard NAS regime: after weak architectures are filtered out, the remaining candidates are all plausible, and task transfer becomes much less reliable. The paper gives a concrete example in the macro search space.
Scene classification and semantic segmentation have a high correlation in the macro-level space. Room layout and autoencoding are much weaker. This is not obvious from the task names alone. Both room layout and autoencoding use the same image source, but architecture ranking still behaves differently. The autoencoding example is even more revealing:
In the macro space, autoencoding has moderate correlation with semantic segmentation and surface normal. In the cell space, autoencoding has almost no correlation with semantic segmentation and only weak correlation with surface normal.
So transferability is not only a property of source and target tasks. It also depends on the search space. That is the core lesson of this benchmark. Cross-Task Performance StructureThe appendix gives a more detailed pairwise view of task performance.
The cell-level plots show more fragmented behavior. Some cell choices produce very poor networks on particular tasks, which creates larger gaps. The macro-level plots look smoother because changing downsampling and channel schedules affects the backbone more globally. This is useful when designing a transfer method. If the target task enters a part of the architecture space where source-task ranking is unstable, direct transfer can become negative transfer. Transfer BaselinesThe paper evaluates five transfer/search schemes:
Random search. Direct transfer of top architectures. Regularized evolution trained from scratch. Regularized evolution with transferred population initialization. PPO-style policy transfer and CATCH-style contextual policy transfer.
The REA curves are a good baseline because evolution is simple and robust.
REA-transfer gives small but stable improvements. It does not magically solve transfer, but it is less brittle than directly reusing the best architecture from another task. The transferred population gives the target-task search a better starting point while still allowing mutation to adapt. The policy-transfer result is more cautionary.
Plain PPO transfer can underperform PPO trained from scratch. That is classic negative transfer: the policy overfits to the source task and starts the target task with the wrong bias. CATCH helps by adding task context and an evaluator, and it can work very well on some settings such as macro-space object classification. But the paper is careful not to present policy transfer as universally solved. Overall Transfer ResultsThe full result table makes the baseline story concrete.
A few takeaways from the table:
Direct transfer is weak. Its percentile is 77.17 in the cell space and 83.59 in the macro space, far below random search. Random search is already strong: 97.91 percentile in the cell space and 98.18 in the macro space. REA-transfer is near the top: 99.02 percentile in the cell space and 99.11 in the macro space. PPO-transfer is fragile: it drops to 94.94 percentile in the cell space, below PPO trained from scratch. CATCH improves policy transfer in some cases, but it is not uniformly best.
This is a good benchmark behavior. It does not let a paper win by beating a weak baseline once. Random search is strong, direct transfer can fail, and the algorithm has to be robust across task families and search spaces. Ranking ConvergenceThe appendix also checks whether per-epoch rankings stabilize.
Most tasks trend upward: later-epoch rankings become more consistent with previous-epoch rankings. Some tasks stabilize quickly, while room layout and semantic segmentation are noisier. This matters if a NAS algorithm wants to use early training curves. Early signals may be useful, but the benchmark warns against treating early rank as exact final rank. How I Would Use ItTransNAS-Bench-101 is most useful as a diagnostic benchmark, not as a final claim that an architecture will transfer to all real systems. I would use it to answer questions like:
Does my search method beat random search consistently? Does it still work when the target task is dense prediction instead of classification? Does it depend on cell search, or can it handle macro skeleton choices? Does transfer help after the method is allowed to adapt, or is it just direct reuse? Does the method avoid negative transfer when the source and target task rankings disagree?
Those questions are closer to real NAS deployment than “did it win on one small classification dataset?” LimitationsThe benchmark is still controlled.
All tasks come from an indoor-scene image source. The search spaces are finite and handcrafted. The cell space has only four operation choices. The macro space searches a residual-block skeleton, not arbitrary modern backbones. Hardware measurements are tied to the benchmark setup. Querying the benchmark is much cheaper than real training, so algorithms can accidentally overfit to the tabular benchmark if evaluation protocol is loose.
The value is that these constraints are explicit. They make controlled transfer experiments possible. TakeawayTransNAS-Bench-101 is a good reminder that NAS transfer is not a free byproduct of finding a strong architecture on one task. Architecture rankings can change across tasks, and the amount of transfer depends heavily on the search space. A convincing NAS method should beat strong simple baselines, adapt after transfer, and survive both cell-level and macro-level search spaces.

entry.title: Transformer-XL: Attentive Language Models Beyond a Fixed-Length Context
entry.content:
Paper: Transformer-XL: Attentive Language Models Beyond a Fixed-Length Context Code: kimiyoung/transformer-xl Transformer-XL is an early long-context Transformer paper that is still worth reading carefully. The idea is not simply “make the context longer.” The paper identifies two concrete failures in fixed-length Transformer language models:
context fragmentation: training cuts a long corpus into short independent segments, so information cannot flow across segment boundaries; evaluation recomputation: a vanilla Transformer can use a sliding window at inference, but each shifted window has to be recomputed from scratch.
Transformer-XL fixes both with a recurrence over segment hidden states. The model caches hidden states from previous segments, reuses them as memory for the next segment, and changes positional encoding from absolute positions to relative distances so the cached states remain positionally meaningful. All crops below are taken from the original 2019 PDF. Fixed-Length Transformer LMA vanilla Transformer language model can only attend inside the segment it is currently processing. If the segment length is , the largest direct dependency visible to the model is bounded by , even if the original article is thousands of tokens long.
Figure 1. Vanilla Transformer LM training and evaluation with segment length 4. Training sees independent segments. Evaluation can slide the segment one token at a time, but that recomputes the whole segment repeatedly. This has two different costs. First, training loses cross-segment context. The first tokens of each segment are predicted with little left context even if the previous segment contained exactly the information needed. This is what the paper calls context fragmentation. Second, evaluation is expensive. To give each prediction the longest context seen during training, a vanilla model evaluates a full length- segment, predicts only the last position, shifts the window by one token, and evaluates another full segment. That procedure uses context, but it throws away almost all computation from the previous step. For a decoder-only model this is an unnatural use of self-attention. The hidden states for old tokens do not change when the next token arrives. Transformer-XL turns that observation into a recurrent state. Segment-Level RecurrenceTransformer-XL processes a stream as consecutive segments, but it does not discard the previous segment’s hidden states. For each layer, it stores the hidden state sequence from previous segments as a memory and concatenates that memory with the current segment when forming keys and values.
Figure 2. Transformer-XL reuses previous hidden states as fixed memory. During training the memory is stop-gradient. During evaluation the same mechanism gives an extended context without recomputing old segments. Let and be two consecutive segments of length . Let be the hidden state sequence of layer for segment . Transformer-XL builds an extended layer input for segment : h_tilde^{n-1}_{tau+1} = [SG(h^{n-1}_{tau}) ; h^{n-1}_{tau+1}]
where means stop-gradient and is concatenation along the sequence dimension. Queries come only from the current segment, while keys and values come from the concatenated memory plus current segment: q^n_{tau+1} = h^{n-1}_{tau+1} W_q^Tk^n_{tau+1} = h_tilde^{n-1}_{tau+1} W_k^Tv^n_{tau+1} = h_tilde^{n-1}_{tau+1} W_v^Th^n_{tau+1} = TransformerLayer(q^n_{tau+1}, k^n_{tau+1}, v^n_{tau+1})
The key detail is the layer index. Layer in the current segment attends to cached states from layer of the previous segment. Therefore, dependency across segments shifts one layer downward each time it crosses a segment boundary. With layers and segment length , the maximum dependency path grows on the order of rather than just . This is similar in spirit to truncated BPTT for RNNs, but the stored state is different:
Model family Reused state What is truncated
RNN-LM with truncated BPTT Usually the last hidden state Gradient through time
Transformer-XL A sequence of hidden states per layer Gradient across segments
Modern KV-cache decoding Projected keys and values per layer Usually no training gradient, inference only
Transformer-XL is not exactly the same abstraction as the modern KV cache. The paper describes caching hidden states and then using them to form keys and values for the next segment. But conceptually it is one of the clean ancestors of state reuse in decoder-only Transformers: do not recompute old token representations when the new segment only needs to attend to them. Training And Evaluation BehaviorDuring training, the previous memory is fixed. Gradients do not propagate into old segments: for segment in stream: h = embed(segment) for layer_id, layer in enumerate(layers): memory = stop_gradient(mems[layer_id]) kv_input = concat(memory, h) h = layer(query=h, key_value=kv_input, causal_mask=True) update_mems(hiddens_from_this_segment)
The stop-gradient choice is a practical compromise. It keeps training close to ordinary segment training in memory cost, while letting each segment condition on previous segments in the forward pass. During evaluation, the memory can be longer than one previous segment. The paper uses a memory length and a segment length , so each segment can attend over positions. The old representations are reused instead of recomputed. This is where the large evaluation speedup comes from: the model still attends to history, but it does not run all layers again for every shifted window. The causal mask has to cover two regions:
memory positions are always in the past, so current tokens may attend to them; inside the current segment, token may attend only to positions up to .
That mask is what makes chunked stream processing equivalent to autoregressive modeling rather than leaking future tokens. Why Absolute Position Breaks Memory ReuseCaching hidden states alone is not enough. If a Transformer uses absolute positional embeddings, then each segment reuses the same position indices . Token in the previous segment and token in the current segment both carry the same absolute position even though their relative distance to the query is different. For recurrence, the model needs to know where a memory token is relative to the current query, not where that token sat inside its original segment. The paper makes this precise by decomposing the absolute-position attention score: A_abs(i,j) = E[x_i]^T W_q^T W_{k,E} E[x_j]+ E[x_i]^T W_q^T W_k U[j]+ U[i]^T W_q^T W_{k,E} E[x_j]+ U[i]^T W_q^T W_k U[j]
The four terms can be read as:
Term Role in absolute attention
content-to-content addressing
content query to absolute key position
absolute query position to key content
absolute query position to absolute key position
Those and terms are tied to positions inside a segment. They do not survive state reuse cleanly. Relative Positional EncodingTransformer-XL replaces absolute positional dependence with relative distance dependence. The new attention score is: A_rel(i,j) = E[x_i]^T W_q^T W_{k,E} E[x_j]+ E[x_i]^T W_q^T W_{k,R} R[i-j]+ u^T W_{k,E} E[x_j]+ v^T W_{k,R} R[i-j]
Here is a sinusoidal relative positional encoding for the distance between the query position and the key position . The learned vectors and replace the absolute query-position terms with global content and position biases. The four relative terms have a useful interpretation:
Term Meaning
(a) content-based addressing Which token content should this query attend to?
(b) content-dependent positional bias Given this query content, which relative distances are useful?
(c) global content bias Which key contents are generally important?
(d) global positional bias Which relative distances are generally important?
The comparison to Shaw et al. (2018) is important. Shaw-style relative attention mainly keeps terms (a) and (b), and it uses learned relative embeddings. Transformer-XL keeps two additional bias terms and uses sinusoidal relative encodings. The paper argues that the sinusoidal structure helps the model generalize to longer memory at evaluation time than it saw during training. There is also an implementation issue. Naively computing for every pair would be quadratic in the number of pairwise distances. Appendix B shows the usual efficient trick: compute the relative logits as a matrix product over all possible distances, then shift rows so each query sees the correct relative offset. In later codebases this family of operations is often called a relative shift. What The Architecture Actually BuysIt is useful to separate the two proposed pieces:
Piece Main purpose Without it
Segment-level recurrence Reuse past hidden states and extend context beyond one segment Context is fragmented and evaluation recomputes old segments
Relative positional encoding Make cached states positionally coherent Memory states carry stale absolute positions
The recurrence solves the systems and context problem. The relative position scheme makes the recurrence mathematically usable. This is why the method is stronger than simply increasing segment length. A larger segment helps, but it increases attention cost and still imposes a hard boundary. Transformer-XL keeps the training segment manageable and adds a rolling memory that can be longer during evaluation. Main ResultsThe headline numbers are strong for the 2019 language modeling setting. Transformer-XL reports state-of-the-art or near state-of-the-art results on word-level and character-level benchmarks.
Table 1. On WikiText-103, the large Transformer-XL reaches 18.3 perplexity, improving over the contemporary adaptive-input result of 20.5. WikiText-103 is the benchmark that most directly matches the paper’s motivation. The articles are long enough that cross-segment dependencies matter. The paper uses attention length 384 during training and 1600 during evaluation for the standard word-level setting.
Table 2. On enwik8, the 24-layer Transformer-XL reaches 0.99 bits per character. The 12-layer 41M-parameter model already matches the 64-layer vanilla Transformer result from Al-Rfou et al. (2018).
Table 3. On text8, the 24-layer Transformer-XL reaches 1.08 bits per character. The character-level results show that the architecture is not only improving a word-level softmax setup. On enwik8, the paper trains with attention length 784 and evaluates with attention length 3800. That train/eval mismatch is exactly where relative positional encoding matters.
Table 4. On One Billion Word, the large Transformer-XL reports 21.8 perplexity. One Billion Word is shuffled at the sentence level, so it does not preserve long document dependencies. The improvement there is therefore not mainly about modeling thousand-token discourse. The paper uses it as evidence that recurrence also reduces context fragmentation for short sequences.
Table 5. On Penn Treebank, Transformer-XL reaches 54.52 perplexity without two-step finetuning, close to the best finetuned MoS result. Penn Treebank is much smaller, so this result is less central to the long-context argument. It is still useful because it shows the method does not only work when the dataset is large. Ablation: Recurrence And Position EncodingThe ablation table is the most important evidence in the paper. It asks whether the performance comes from recurrence, from the new positional encoding, or from both.
Table 6. WikiText-103 ablation. Recurrence plus the Transformer-XL relative position scheme gives the best result and can benefit from longer evaluation attention length. The pattern is clear:
using recurrence with the paper’s relative positional encoding gives the best perplexity; replacing it with Shaw et al. relative encoding is worse; removing recurrence is worse; absolute encodings do not generalize cleanly to longer attention length; increasing evaluation attention length helps only when the positional scheme can handle reused states.
The 151M setting is especially useful to read. The model is trained with a finite backpropagation length, but perplexity improves when the evaluation attention length is increased. That is the intended behavior: train on manageable segments, then reuse a longer memory at inference. One Billion Word And Evaluation SpeedThe paper also isolates context fragmentation using One Billion Word. Since the dataset is shuffled and lacks document-level long dependencies, an improvement from recurrence is harder to attribute to long-range discourse. It is more likely to come from not starting every segment cold.
Tables 7 and 9. On One Billion Word, recurrence improves perplexity even without document-level long dependency. The same state reuse gives very large evaluation speedups over the vanilla sliding-window Transformer. The table reports:
Variant One Billion Word PPL
Transformer-XL 25.2
With Shaw et al. encoding 25.7
Without recurrence 27.1
For evaluation speed, the paper compares against a vanilla Transformer that repeatedly evaluates shifted windows. The largest reported slowdown of the vanilla baseline is 1,874x relative to Transformer-XL. This number is not a claim that attention itself becomes 1,874x cheaper. It is a consequence of avoiding massive repeated full-window recomputation. Effective Context LengthThe paper introduces Relative Effective Context Length (RECL) because ordinary effective context length is hard to compare across models with different base perplexities. RECL asks whether increasing context still gives a relative improvement over a shared short-context baseline.
Table 8. Transformer-XL has longer RECL than QRNN, LSTM, and the vanilla Transformer baseline. The strongest 151M Transformer-XL reaches 900 words at . The table is compact but important:
Model RECL at RECL at RECL at
Transformer-XL 151M 900 800 700
QRNN 500 400 300
LSTM 400 300 200
Transformer-XL 128M 700 600 500
Transformer-XL 128M with Shaw encoding 400 400 300
Transformer-XL 128M without recurrence 300 300 300
Vanilla Transformer 128 128 128
The authors summarize this as Transformer-XL modeling dependencies 80% longer than RNNs and 450% longer than the vanilla Transformer under their RECL comparison. The supporting plots make the same point visually.
Figure 3. Relative perplexity gains remain useful over longer context spans for Transformer-XL than for the recurrent and Transformer baselines.
Figure 4. Perplexity keeps improving as context length grows, especially for Transformer-XL with recurrence and the proposed relative positional encoding. This is the strongest part of the paper for me. The benchmark tables show that the model is good, but the context-length analysis shows why it is good. The model is not just a larger Transformer with a better softmax; it is extracting measurable value from longer history. Attention VisualizationThe appendix visualizes attention behavior for the WikiText-103 model with 16 layers, 10 heads per layer, and memory length 640.
Figure 5. Average attention over the previous 640 tokens. Most heads prefer nearby tokens, but some heads spread attention over much longer ranges. The average heatmap is unsurprising at first: nearby context gets more attention. The useful detail is that a few heads maintain broad attention over the memory span. Those heads are the mechanism by which the model can keep long-range information accessible instead of collapsing entirely into local n-gram behavior.
Figure 6. Three wide-range heads selected from different layers. The low-level head is broad, while later heads become sparse and more token-specific. The paper interprets the three selected heads as different long-range behaviors:
an early-layer head scans broadly across memory; a middle-layer head picks sparse positions across the full range; a final-layer head gives each target token a distinct sparse focus.
That pattern is plausible: early layers gather candidate information, deeper layers decide which pieces matter for the current prediction.
Figure 7. The attention score decomposition shows different behavior for content addressing, content-dependent positional bias, and global positional bias. The score-term visualization is a useful sanity check for the relative attention formula. Term (a), the pure content-based term, is comparatively broad. Term (b), the content-dependent positional bias, resembles the final attention distribution more strongly. Term (d), the global positional bias, also favors nearby positions but is flatter. This supports the paper’s claim that the four-term decomposition is not just algebraic decoration; the terms learn different roles. Implementation NotesIf I were implementing Transformer-XL from scratch, these are the pieces I would treat as bug-prone:
Memory shape. Each layer needs its own memory tensor. The memory length can differ between training and evaluation. Stop-gradient. The memory used during training must be detached, otherwise the graph grows across segments. Causal mask. Current tokens can attend to all memory positions and to previous current-segment positions, but never to future current-segment positions. Relative shift. Relative attention logits need the correct distance alignment. An off-by-one error can silently preserve tensor shapes while corrupting position semantics. Position scheme. Absolute positional embeddings are not a drop-in choice when hidden states are reused across segments. Memory update. After each segment, append the new hidden states and keep only the latest states. Train/eval mismatch. If evaluation memory is longer than training memory, the relative position encoding must be able to represent those longer distances.
A minimal memory update looks like this: def update_memory(old_mem, new_hid, mem_len): if old_mem is None: cat = new_hid.detach() else: cat = torch.cat([old_mem, new_hid.detach()], dim=1) return cat[:, -mem_len:]
The real implementation has to do this for each layer and keep the hidden state list aligned with the layer stack. Relation To Later LLM SystemsTransformer-XL sits before the current LLM serving vocabulary, so it is easy to read it through later ideas:
XLNet directly builds on Transformer-XL’s recurrence and relative positions. Modern decoder inference uses KV cache rather than recomputing previous tokens; Transformer-XL is an earlier training-and-evaluation version of the same state-reuse instinct. T5-style relative bias, RoPE, and ALiBi are not the same method, but they belong to the same broader move away from fixed absolute position embeddings. Sliding-window and recurrent-memory Transformers keep revisiting the same tradeoff: finite memory is cheap enough to use, but it is still finite.
The limitation is equally important. Transformer-XL does not make arbitrary full-context attention cheap. For a segment length and memory length , attention still scales like per layer. The method avoids recomputing old segments and extends usable context, but it does not remove attention’s dependence on the visible memory size. The stop-gradient boundary is another limitation. The model can attend to old hidden states in the forward pass, but learning signals do not backpropagate through all historical tokens. That is the price paid to keep training feasible. TakeawayThe core lesson of Transformer-XL is that long-context modeling needs both a state mechanism and a position mechanism. Caching hidden states solves the fixed-window systems problem, but it only works if the model interprets cached states by relative distance rather than stale absolute indices. The paper’s strongest evidence is not just the perplexity table. It is the combination of:
better language modeling results on WikiText-103, enwik8, text8, One Billion Word, and PTB; ablations showing recurrence and the proposed relative encoding both matter; RECL analysis showing longer usable context; evaluation speedups from avoiding sliding-window recomputation; attention visualizations showing that some heads actually use long memory.
That combination is why Transformer-XL is still a useful reference point. It is not the final answer to long-context attention, but it is one of the cleanest demonstrations that Transformer language models need memory reuse and position handling to move beyond fixed-length segments.

entry.title: An Image is Worth 16x16 Words: Transformers for Image Recognition at Scale
entry.content:
Dosovitskiy A, Beyer L, Kolesnikov A, et al. An Image is Worth 16x16 Words: Transformers for Image Recognition at Scale. ICLR 2021.
Paper / Code ViT is important because it removes most of the CNN assumptions from the image classifier and then asks a very direct question: if an image is converted into a sequence, can the same Transformer stack used in NLP handle vision? The answer is yes, but with a condition. A plain Transformer is not a cheap drop-in replacement for a ResNet on small supervised image datasets. It has less locality and translation bias, so it needs large-scale pre-training to catch up. Once the pre-training dataset is large enough, the same lack of hard-coded visual bias becomes useful: the model scales cleanly, transfers well, and reaches strong accuracy with less pre-training compute than the large CNN baselines compared in the paper. This note reads ViT as an engineering recipe:
how the image is tokenized; what is actually standard Transformer and what is vision-specific; why patch size changes the compute profile; why JFT-300M changes the result compared with ImageNet-only training; what the figures say about learned position, attention distance, and scaling; what later work such as DeiT, Swin, and MAE had to fix or extend.
All figures and tables below are cropped from the official arXiv PDF. Core Idea Figure 1 from the paper. ViT turns an image into patch embeddings, prepends a learnable class token, adds position embeddings, and feeds the sequence into a standard Transformer encoder. For an image , ViT splits the image into non-overlapping patches of size . The number of image tokens is:
Each patch is flattened into a vector of length and projected into the Transformer hidden dimension :
ViT then prepends a learnable class token and adds position embeddings:
After this point, the model is intentionally boring. It is a pre-norm Transformer encoder:
The final representation is the output of the class token:
The classifier reads . During pre-training, the head is an MLP with one hidden layer. During fine-tuning, the paper removes the pre-training head and attaches a zero-initialized linear layer for the downstream label set. The main architecture choice is not a new attention variant. The main choice is to treat a 2D image as a 1D sequence of learned patch tokens and then rely on scale. What Is New And What Is NotViT keeps the following Transformer pieces almost unchanged:
multi-head self-attention; MLP block with GELU; residual connections; LayerNorm before each sub-layer; learned token embeddings; a BERT-style class token.
The vision-specific parts are small:
patch extraction at the input; a linear projection from flattened patch pixels to ; learned position embeddings for the patch sequence; interpolation of position embeddings when fine-tuning at a higher resolution.
That last point matters. The paper often pre-trains at resolution and fine-tunes at higher resolution, such as , , or . Patch size stays fixed, so the sequence becomes longer. The model can accept a longer sequence, but the learned position embedding table no longer has exactly the right spatial grid. ViT handles this by 2D interpolation of the pre-trained position embeddings. This is also where the paper is honest about inductive bias. A CNN has locality, translation equivariance, and a 2D neighborhood structure in every convolution. ViT uses the 2D structure only when cutting patches and when interpolating positions for a new resolution. Everything else has to be learned. Model Variants Table 1 from the paper. ViT-Base and ViT-Large mirror BERT-style model sizes, and ViT-Huge extends the family. The notation ViT-L/16 means:
L: Large variant; /16: patch size .
The patch size is more than a naming detail. It controls sequence length:
Input resolution Patch size Image tokens Tokens with class token
32 49 50
16 196 197
14 256 257
16 576 577
16 1024 1025
Self-attention has a pairwise token interaction term, so the attention matrix scales with roughly . Moving from to at the same resolution multiplies the image-token count by and the attention matrix size by about . This is why ViT-L/16 is much more expensive than ViT-L/32 even though the layer width and depth are the same. The same model sizes in working-note form:
ViT-Base: 12 layers, hidden size 768, MLP size 3072, 12 heads, 86M parameters. ViT-Large: 24 layers, hidden size 1024, MLP size 4096, 16 heads, 307M parameters. ViT-Huge: 32 layers, hidden size 1280, MLP size 5120, 16 heads, 632M parameters.
The model-size table looks simple, but it is one reason the paper was influential. Instead of designing a special vision attention block, the authors show that BERT-like scaling rules are already a strong baseline for image classification. Training And Fine-Tuning Recipe Table 3 from the appendix. The large-scale experiments use Adam, batch size 4096, 10k warmup steps, linear decay for most pre-training runs, and high weight decay. The training recipe is as important as the architecture. ViT is not trained from scratch on ImageNet and then declared better than CNNs. The paper evaluates transfer from large supervised pre-training datasets:
ImageNet-1K: 1.3M images; ImageNet-21k: 14M images; JFT-300M: about 303M high-resolution images and 18k classes.
The main pre-training setup:
Item Setting
Optimizer Adam
Batch size 4096
Warmup 10k steps
Weight decay usually 0.1 on JFT
Pre-training resolution 224
Fine-tuning optimizer SGD with momentum
Fine-tuning batch size 512
Typical fine-tuning resolution 384, higher for some ImageNet results
The high weight decay is not cosmetic. The paper states that strong regularization is key when training on smaller datasets, especially ImageNet. This fits the central ViT story: the architecture has fewer visual priors, so it overfits more easily when the data is not large enough. During transfer, the model removes the whole pre-training head and attaches a new zero-initialized linear head. This is a small implementation detail, but it avoids carrying a classifier whose output space was tied to the pre-training dataset. Main Results Table 2 from the paper. ViT-H/14 and ViT-L/16 pre-trained on JFT-300M outperform the BiT-L ResNet baseline on the reported transfer tasks while using less pre-training compute. The headline result is not just “ViT gets high ImageNet accuracy.” The more important result is the accuracy per pre-training compute. From Table 2:
ViT-H/14, JFT-300M: ImageNet 88.55, CIFAR-100 94.55, VTAB 77.63, 2.5k TPUv3-core-days. ViT-L/16, JFT-300M: ImageNet 87.76, CIFAR-100 93.90, VTAB 76.28, 0.68k TPUv3-core-days. ViT-L/16, ImageNet-21k: ImageNet 85.30, CIFAR-100 93.25, VTAB 72.72, 0.23k TPUv3-core-days. BiT-L ResNet152x4, JFT-300M: ImageNet 87.54, CIFAR-100 93.51, VTAB 76.29, 9.9k TPUv3-core-days. Noisy Student EfficientNet-L2: ImageNet 88.4/88.5, 12.3k TPUv3-core-days; the table does not report CIFAR-100 or VTAB.
The clean comparison is ViT-L/16 versus BiT-L. Both use JFT-300M. ViT-L/16 is slightly better on ImageNet, CIFAR-100, Pets, and VTAB, while using about TPUv3-core-days instead of . The paper is careful that pre-training efficiency also depends on optimizer and schedule, but the gap is large enough that the architecture is clearly competitive. ViT-H/14 improves further, especially on ImageNet, CIFAR-100, and VTAB. It also uses more compute than ViT-L/16, but still much less than the CNN baselines in the table. Low-Data Transfer Figure 2 from the paper. VTAB is split into Natural, Specialized, and Structured tasks with only 1000 training examples per task. VTAB is useful because it tests whether a pre-trained representation transfers to small downstream datasets. ViT-H/14 beats BiT-L on the overall VTAB score and does especially well on the Natural and Structured groups. The Specialized group is closer. This matters because the criticism of ViT is obvious: if it needs 300M images, is it only a brute-force ImageNet model? VTAB says the large supervised pre-training produces a representation that transfers to low-data settings. It does not mean ViT is data-efficient during pre-training. It means the pre-trained representation is useful after the expensive pre-training stage. Data Scale Is The Turning Point Figures 3 and 4 from the paper. Larger ViT models underperform or overfit more on small pre-training sets, but they improve strongly when the pre-training data reaches ImageNet-21k and JFT-300M scale. This is the most important figure in the paper for understanding why ViT initially looked risky. On ImageNet-only pre-training, large ViTs do not automatically win. ViT-L can underperform ViT-B even though it has more capacity. That is a sign of overfitting and weak data support, not a sign that the Transformer block cannot process images. As the pre-training dataset grows, the ordering changes:
On ImageNet, the CNN bias is helpful and the larger ViT variants do not shine. On ImageNet-21k, ViT becomes competitive and model scaling starts to help. On JFT-300M, larger ViT variants benefit clearly from scale.
The few-shot curve on the right is even more direct. ResNets are better at smaller JFT subsets, but their improvement flattens earlier. ViT is worse on small subsets and better when the subset grows to 90M or 300M images. The practical takeaway: ViT trades hand-coded visual priors for data. If data is scarce, that trade can be bad. If data is abundant, it becomes powerful. Full Transfer Table Table 5 from the appendix. The full transfer table makes the same trend concrete across CIFAR, ImageNet, ReaL, Flowers, and Pets. The appendix table is useful because it separates the three pre-training sources. A few patterns stand out:
ImageNet-only pre-training is not enough for the largest ViT-H/14 setting in this table. ImageNet-21k already gives strong transfer for ViT-L/16 and ViT-H/14. JFT-300M gives the best results for the large variants on the harder downstream sets.
For example, ViT-L/16 ImageNet accuracy moves from with ImageNet pre-training to with ImageNet-21k and with JFT-300M in the appendix setting. CIFAR-100 moves from to to . That scale sensitivity explains why the paper’s title includes “at Scale.” The architecture is simple, but the result depends on the training regime. Compute Scaling Figure 5 from the paper. ViT gives a better transfer-accuracy versus pre-training-compute frontier than the ResNet baseline in this controlled JFT-300M scaling study. The scaling study controls the pre-training data and compares three families:
pure ViT; ResNet BiT; hybrid models with a ResNet stem feeding a Transformer.
The paper reports that ViT uses roughly - less compute to reach the same transfer performance, averaged over five datasets. Hybrids help at small compute budgets, but the gap shrinks for larger models. This is an important nuance. The conclusion is not “CNNs are useless.” The hybrid result says local convolutional processing can help when the model or compute budget is smaller. The stronger claim is that at large scale, the pure Transformer is an excellent scaling target and does not saturate in the tested range. How To Scale The Transformer Figure 8 from the appendix. The paper varies depth, patch size, width, and MLP width under a small controlled setup. The appendix asks a practical scaling question: if compute increases, where should it go? The controlled experiment starts from a smaller ViT-like model and scales different dimensions. The paper’s observations:
increasing depth gives the clearest improvement up to a point; decreasing patch size helps because it increases token resolution; scaling width alone is weaker; scaling all dimensions together is robust.
This is close to how later ViT families are usually built. Larger models often combine more layers, enough width, and smaller patch sizes, but the sequence-length cost of small patches makes the compute tradeoff harsh. For an input resolution and patch size , the number of image tokens is:
The attention matrix is approximately:
This is why high-resolution dense prediction became a problem for plain ViT and why later models such as Swin introduced hierarchical features and window attention. What The Model Learns Figure 7 from the paper. The patch projection learns image-like basis filters, the learned position embeddings recover 2D spatial structure, and attention heads cover both local and global distances. This figure is useful because it answers a natural question: if the model is given only a flattened patch sequence and a learned 1D position embedding, does it recover image structure? The left panel shows principal components of the first patch projection. They look like low-level image filters. This is expected, but still important: the linear patch projection is not just a random tokenizer after training. It learns a useful local basis inside each patch. The center panel shows cosine similarity between position embeddings. Nearby patches tend to have similar embeddings, and row/column structure appears even though the default position embedding is learned as a 1D sequence. This supports the paper’s claim that explicit 2D-aware position embeddings did not improve much. The right panel shows mean attention distance by layer and head. Some heads attend globally even in early layers, while other early heads stay local. Later layers become more global. That is a different kind of receptive field from a CNN: the model can use image-wide information immediately, but it also learns localized heads when useful.
Figure 6 from the paper. Attention from the output token often highlights semantically relevant regions of the input image. These attention visualizations should not be over-interpreted as a full explanation, but they show that the class token is not just averaging the image uniformly. It can place high attention on discriminative regions such as the animal, aircraft, or object body. Position EmbeddingsThe paper uses standard learned 1D position embeddings. That choice looks suspicious for images, but the ablation in the appendix is surprisingly calm:
Position setting ImageNet 5-shot linear score
No position embedding 0.61382
1D position embedding 0.64206
2D position embedding 0.64001
Relative position embedding 0.64032
The exact numbers are from Table 8 in the appendix. The key point is not that 1D is theoretically best. The point is that learned position embeddings are enough for this classification setup, and explicit 2D position structure is not the bottleneck. The learned embedding similarity in Figure 7 already shows that the model recovers useful spatial organization. For transfer to higher resolution, however, the 2D layout comes back. The position embedding table must be interpolated as a grid. That is one of the few places where ViT manually uses image geometry. Class Token Versus PoolingThe main model uses a learnable class token, inherited from BERT. The appendix also tests global average pooling over patch tokens. The initial GAP attempt worked poorly, but the paper finds that the failure is mainly a learning-rate issue. With a better learning rate, GAP and class token work similarly. I still like the class-token design for the original paper because it keeps the model interface close to NLP Transformers. It makes the architecture easy to explain: [class] patch_1 patch_2 ... patch_N
The class token is the readout position. Patch tokens provide visual evidence. Self-attention decides how information moves between them. For later vision systems, pooling or task-specific heads often matter more. Dense prediction models cannot depend only on a final class token; they need spatial features at many positions. Real Hardware Cost Figure 12 from the appendix. On the paper’s TPUv3 timing setup, ViT has comparable speed to similar ResNets and large ViT variants fit larger per-core batches. The paper includes a useful hardware note. FLOPs do not perfectly predict runtime because memory layout, accelerator kernels, and batch size matter. In the TPUv3 measurements:
ViT speed is comparable to similar ResNet models across input sizes. Large ViT variants fit larger per-core batches than large ResNets. The expected bad scaling with image size becomes visible mostly at the largest models and highest resolutions.
This does not mean plain ViT is always hardware-efficient. On GPUs, in dense tasks, or at very high resolution, global attention can still become expensive. But the figure explains why the original ViT was practical at the paper’s training scale: it maps well enough to accelerator-friendly dense matrix operations. Self-Supervision In The Original PaperThe paper briefly tests masked patch prediction as a self-supervised objective, inspired by BERT’s masked language modeling. The setup corrupts 50% of patch embeddings:
80% are replaced with a learnable mask embedding; 10% are replaced with a random other patch embedding; 10% are kept unchanged.
The target is a coarse 3-bit mean color of each corrupted patch, so the target space has color classes. This is a preliminary experiment, not the final form of masked image modeling. The result is interesting historically: ViT-B/16 reaches ImageNet accuracy with self-supervised pre-training, about points better than training from scratch, but still about points behind supervised pre-training in the paper’s setup. Later work made this direction much more important. MAE, BEiT, DINO, and related methods showed that self-supervised or masked image pre-training can be a strong way to train ViT-style models without JFT-style supervised labels. Why The Paper Changed Vision BackbonesBefore ViT, attention in vision was often added carefully inside CNN-like structures or applied with specialized local/axial patterns. ViT made a different bet:
Keep the Transformer as standard as possible. Use patch tokens to make the sequence length manageable. Pre-train at large scale. Transfer to downstream datasets.
That recipe shifted a lot of vision research. The follow-up branches are easy to see:
Direction Problem it addresses Example papers
Data-efficient ViT training Plain ViT needs large supervised pre-training DeiT
Hierarchical backbones Plain ViT lacks multi-scale dense features Swin Transformer, PVT
Self-supervised pre-training JFT labels are not a scalable public recipe MAE, BEiT, DINO
Multimodal pre-training Patch tokens can share Transformer tooling with text tokens CLIP, ALIGN
Large-scale vision-language models ViT becomes the image encoder inside multimodal systems Flamingo, BLIP, GPT-4V-style systems
This is why ViT is more important than its first ImageNet number. It made “image as token sequence” a default abstraction. LimitationsThe paper’s own limitations are clear. First, plain ViT is not data-efficient from scratch. If the training set is small, CNN inductive bias helps. The paper needs ImageNet-21k or JFT-300M scale to make the strongest case. Second, the original model is mainly an image classification architecture. It does not naturally produce a feature pyramid. Detection, segmentation, and other dense tasks need additional design. This is exactly where Swin and other hierarchical ViTs became useful. Third, global self-attention becomes expensive as resolution grows. At with patches, there are tokens including the class token. At with the same patch size, there are tokens. The attention matrix grows from about entries to more than entries per head. Fourth, the best results depend on JFT-300M, which is not a public dataset. The ImageNet-21k results are strong, but the full “large scale training trumps inductive bias” claim is clearest with the in-house dataset. Implementation NotesFor a minimal ViT implementation, the patch embedding can be written as either:
explicit patch flattening followed by a linear layer; a convolution with kernel size P, stride P, and output channels D.
The convolution form is easier and faster in most frameworks: patch_embed = torch.nn.Conv2d( in_channels=3, out_channels=hidden_dim, kernel_size=patch_size, stride=patch_size,)
For a batch of images shaped [B, 3, H, W], this produces [B, D, H/P, W/P]. Then flatten the spatial grid and transpose: x = patch_embed(images) # [B, D, H/P, W/P]x = x.flatten(2).transpose(1, 2) # [B, N, D]
Then prepend the class token and add position embeddings: cls = cls_token.expand(batch_size, -1, -1)x = torch.cat([cls, x], dim=1)x = x + pos_embed
The two easy mistakes:
forgetting that changing image resolution changes N; forgetting to interpolate pos_embed when loading a checkpoint at a new resolution.
TakeawayViT is a simple paper with a large consequence. The architecture says: image patches -> token sequence -> standard Transformer encoder -> class token
The experiment says:
on small pre-training data, CNN inductive bias still matters; at ImageNet-21k and JFT-300M scale, ViT becomes very strong; the compute-accuracy frontier is favorable for large ViT models; the model learns spatial structure even with simple learned 1D position embeddings; dense prediction and data-efficient training require follow-up work.
My short version: ViT did not prove that convolution was obsolete. It proved that convolution was no longer the only reasonable default for visual representation learning once pre-training scale became large enough.

entry.title: ViTAS: Vision Transformer Architecture Search
entry.content:
Paper: ViTAS: Vision Transformer Architecture Search
Su X, You S, Xie J, Zheng M, Wang F, Qian C, Zhang C, Wang X, Xu C. ViTAS: Vision Transformer Architecture Search. ECCV 2022.
ViTAS is a Vision Transformer NAS paper, but the useful part is not only that it searches a better ViT backbone. The deeper point is about whether a one-shot Transformer supernet can rank candidate architectures fairly. The paper’s diagnosis is sharp:
one-shot NAS trains a large supernet and lets candidate architectures inherit weights from it; in width/dimension search, common ordinal sharing gives small dimensions the first channels; those early channels are trained more often than later channels; for ViTs, where token embeddings and FC projections dominate the block, this channel imbalance makes inherited accuracy a biased estimator; if inherited accuracy is biased, the search loop can select architectures that merely received better shared weights.
ViTAS attacks this with cyclic weight sharing for token embedding dimensions, then adds identity shifting and a weak superformer training recipe to stabilize search. All crops below are taken from the original PDF. Why ViT NAS Is Not Just CNN NASVision Transformers expose several architecture dimensions at once:
patch size or local/global attention granularity; number of attention heads; attention projection width; MLP hidden width; operation type in each layer; stage depth through identity operations.
In a one-shot setting, a superformer must contain many candidates and give each candidate a meaningful inherited evaluation. This is already hard for CNNs. It becomes more fragile for ViTs because changing token embedding dimension changes the FC projections used by attention and MLP blocks. The paper uses two search spaces:
Table 1. Twins-based ViTAS space. It searches patch size/head choices, attention dimensions, MLP dimensions, and depth through TBS layers. For the Twins-small based space, the paper reports a search-space size around 1.1e54, with FLOPs ranging from 0.02G to 11.2G and parameters from 0.16M to 86.1M.
Table 2. DeiT-based ViTAS space. It searches patch size, head number, attention/MLP dimensions, and depth through vanilla ViT block vs identity choices. For the DeiT-small based space, the paper reports around 5.4e34 candidates, with FLOPs ranging from 0.1G to 20.0G and parameters from 0.5M to 97.5M. The search problem is roughly: 1. Train a superformer over architecture choices A and dimension choices C.2. Evaluate sampled paths with inherited weights.3. Search for (architecture, dimensions) under a FLOPs budget.4. Retrain the selected architecture from scratch for final reporting.
The weak link is step 2. If the superformer trains some channels more than others, inherited validation accuracy is not a clean architecture score. The Channel Fairness ProblemThe core figure compares three ways to share channels when searching width.
Figure 1. Ordinal sharing over-trains early channels. Bilateral sharing reduces part of the imbalance but doubles the cost. Cyclic sharing aims to balance training time and channel influence with single-pass cost. In ordinal sharing, a candidate of width uses the first channels: ordinal(width = i): use channels [1, 2, ..., i]
If the maximum width is , channel 1 appears in every sampled width, while channel appears only when the widest candidate is sampled. The paper writes the training count for channel as C_A(i) = l - i + 1. That is the bias. This is dangerous in a supernet:
narrow candidates inherit heavily trained early channels; wide candidates inherit a mix of heavily trained and under-trained channels; the search algorithm may confuse weight quality with architecture quality.
BCNet-style bilateral sharing improves the picture by training from both sides, but it needs double training cost and still does not fully equalize the influence of each channel. ViTAS proposes cyclic sharing as a single-pass mapping. Cyclic Weight SharingViTAS designs an indicator matrix for channel use. In plain notation: beta[i, j] = 1 if channel i is used by dimension jbeta[i, j] = 0 otherwise
The mapping is chosen under two goals.
Goal Meaning
Training fairness Each channel should be selected about the same number of times.
Influence uniformity Each channel should contribute similar total gradient influence across the dimensions that use it.
The second condition is the more interesting one. In an FC layer, a dimension with more input channels distributes gradient contribution across more channels. The paper approximates the influence of a channel in a width- layer as proportional to 1 / j. Therefore, equal training count alone is not enough; the method also tries to equalize weighted influence. The final mapping is solved as a small quadratically constrained quadratic program over the binary assignment matrix. This sounds heavy, but it is not in the training loop. Once the mapping is selected, cyclic sharing is just an index mapping for channel slices. The appendix visualizes cyclic maps for different group counts:
Figure 10. Cyclic channel maps for group counts from 5 to 10. Red channels rotate across layer-width choices rather than staying fixed at the left side. For the blog-level takeaway, I read cyclic sharing as a fairness patch for width-search supernets: ordinal: small widths always see the same early channelscyclic: width choices rotate through channel groups
This matters because ViTAS is not trying to search from a randomly initialized subnetwork each time. It relies on inherited weights. Any systematic imbalance in inherited weights directly biases the search. Private Class TokenPure ViT and DeiT-style models use a class token. If patch size is searched, the number of patch tokens changes, and the class token interacts with different token layouts. ViTAS uses a private class token per patch-size setting.
Figure 2. Different patch sizes get private class tokens, avoiding interference between paths with different token counts. The point is small but practical. The class token has very few parameters, so privatizing it barely changes memory or compute. But it avoids forcing architectures with different token grids to share one class-token parameter. Identity ShiftingDepth search is implemented with identity operations. A layer can be a real operation or an identity, so the effective depth changes. The problem is that the same final architecture can be represented by multiple paths through the superformer. If identity operations are allowed anywhere, several path layouts can collapse to the same sequence of real operations. Those paths may train differently, which makes architecture evaluation noisy.
Figure 3. The original search space can map several superformer paths to the same architecture. ViTAS shifts identity operations deeper so each architecture has a cleaner path representation. ViTAS resolves this by arranging identity choices at deeper layers inside a stage. With three operation choices and twelve searched layers, the paper says this reduces the operation search space from 3^12 path layouts to 2^13 - 1 effective choices. The important part is not the exact count. The useful idea is that depth search should avoid many-to-one path encodings. Otherwise the superformer is asked to rank paths even when the final architecture is identical. Superformer Training RecipeThe authors found that a strong augmentation and regularization recipe can destabilize superformer training. That is slightly counterintuitive because strong recipes are usually helpful for final ViT training. For search, the superformer is not the final model. It is a ranking proxy. The paper therefore uses a weak recipe:
Table 4. Weakening augmentation and regularization improves the searched/retrained model. The best searched Twins 1.4G model reaches 79.4% after retraining. The selected superformer search recipe is simple:
Item Setting
Epochs 300
Batch size 1024
Optimizer AdamW
Learning rate 0.001
LR decay cosine
Warmup 5 epochs
The appendix clarifies that superformers for DeiT- and Twins-based spaces use the same search recipe. The final searched architectures are then retrained with the corresponding DeiT or Twins recipe. This separation is important:
superformer training should make ranking stable; final retraining should make the chosen architecture strong.
Treating those as the same objective can make the search proxy worse. Training Stability EvidenceThe loss curves are one of the most useful figures in the paper.
Figure 4. Cyclic sharing is slower in the first few epochs but reaches lower superformer loss later. Identity shifting also converges to a lower loss than the original path encoding. The paper’s interpretation:
ordinal sharing can look better early because a subset of channels gets trained heavily; after enough epochs, that imbalance hurts the superformer as a whole; cyclic sharing trains more evenly and ends with lower loss; identity shifting removes redundant path encodings and also improves convergence.
The text reports final training losses around 2.4 for the original identity setting and 1.5 with identity shifting on ImageNet-100. It also reports that searched architectures from the shifted setting reach 90.4%, compared with 88.3% from the original setting in that experiment. The ranking-correlation experiment is even closer to the NAS objective.
Figure 5. Cyclic sharing gives higher Pearson, Spearman, and Kendall correlation over sampled paths than ordinal or bilateral sharing. This is the evidence I care about most. A superformer can have a nice validation loss and still rank candidates poorly. ViTAS explicitly checks correlation over 2000 sampled paths across FLOPs groups, which directly tests whether inherited evaluation is a better search signal. ImageNet Results: Twins SpaceViTAS first searches in a Twins-based hierarchical transformer space.
Table 3. Searched Twins-based ViTAS models on ImageNet-1k under different FLOPs budgets. Key rows:
Model FLOPs Params Top-1
Twins-T reimplementation 1.4G 11.5M 77.8%
ViTAS-Twins-T 1.4G 13.8M 79.4%
Twins-SVT-S reimplementation 2.9G 24.0M 81.6%
ViTAS-Twins-S 3.0G 30.5M 82.0%
Twins-SVT-B reimplementation 8.6G 56.0M 83.2%
ViTAS-Twins-B 8.8G 66.0M 83.5%
ViTAS-Twins-L 16.1G 124.8M 84.0%
The tiny result is the cleanest gain: ViTAS-Twins-T improves the reimplemented Twins-T by 1.6 percentage points at roughly the same FLOPs. At larger scales the gains are smaller but still positive. There is a tradeoff: ViTAS-Twins models often use more parameters and lower throughput than the nearest baseline. The paper reports FLOPs, parameters, and throughput together, which is good. The result should not be read as “searched is always faster.” It is more accurate to say that ViTAS finds stronger accuracy/compute points inside the chosen transformer space. ImageNet Results: DeiT SpaceViTAS also searches a pure DeiT-style space, without the hierarchical/local attention biases of Twins.
Table 6. DeiT-based ViTAS results on ImageNet-1k. The small-budget case:
Model FLOPs Top-1
DeiT-T reimplementation 1.3G 72.3%
AutoFormer-T reimplementation 1.3G 74.7%
ViTAS-DeiT-A 1.4G 75.6%
The larger case:
Model FLOPs Top-1
DeiT-S reimplementation 4.6G 79.9%
AutoFormer-S reimplementation 5.1G 79.8%
ViTAS-DeiT-B 4.9G 80.2%
The result is useful because it separates ViTAS from Twins-specific priors. Cyclic sharing and the stabilized superformer recipe still help in a DeiT-style space. Transfer To Detection And SegmentationSearched ImageNet classifiers can fail to transfer. ViTAS evaluates the searched Twins backbones on COCO2017 and ADE20K.
Table 7. COCO2017 object detection and instance segmentation transfer with Mask R-CNN and RetinaNet. Representative Mask R-CNN box AP:
Backbone Mask R-CNN box AP Mask AP
Twins-SVT-S reimplementation 43.5 40.1
ViTAS-Twins-S 45.9 41.5
Twins-SVT-B reimplementation 45.5 41.4
ViTAS-Twins-B 47.6 42.9
Twins-SVT-L reimplementation 45.9 41.6
ViTAS-Twins-L 48.2 43.3
The RetinaNet side shows the same pattern: ViTAS backbones improve over the reimplemented Twins baselines across S/B/L sizes.
Table 8. ADE20K semantic segmentation transfer with Semantic FPN and UperNet. Representative mIoU:
Backbone Semantic FPN mIoU UperNet mIoU
Twins-SVT-S reimplementation 43.6 45.9
ViTAS-Twins-S 46.6 47.9
Twins-SVT-B reimplementation 45.5 47.7
ViTAS-Twins-B 49.5 50.2
Twins-SVT-L reimplementation 46.9 49.2
ViTAS-Twins-L 50.4 51.3
The transfer results matter because they weaken a common NAS criticism: maybe the architecture only fits ImageNet classification. Here the searched backbones remain strong for dense prediction. The appendix plots the same comparison as curves:
Figure 9. ViTAS transfer curves on ADE20K and COCO2017. Under similar FLOPs budgets, the searched backbones stay above the baseline curves. Ablation: What Actually MattersThe compact ablation table is the best summary of ViTAS as a method.
Table 9. Cyclic sharing improves over ordinal and bilateral sharing, and weak augmentation adds another large gain. The table can be read in two blocks. Without weak augmentation:
Sharing Top-1
Ordinal 77.2%
Bilateral 77.6%
Cyclic 77.9%
With weak augmentation:
Sharing Top-1
Ordinal + weak aug 78.1%
Bilateral + weak aug 78.5%
Cyclic + weak aug 79.4%
This says two things:
cyclic sharing is better than the two channel-sharing baselines under the same augmentation regime; the superformer training recipe is not a side detail, because weak augmentation contributes a large part of the final gain.
So I would not summarize ViTAS as only “cyclic weight sharing.” The method is a package: cyclic sharing, identity shifting, private class token for DeiT-style patch search, and a search-specific weak training recipe. Comparison With AutoFormerAutoFormer and ViTAS are close in time and motivation. Both are one-shot NAS methods for Vision Transformers. The difference is where they focus:
Paper Main issue Mechanism
AutoFormer Make inherited subnet evaluation reliable in a ViT supernet weight entanglement
ViTAS Make dimension/channel sharing fair in a ViT superformer cyclic channel sharing
The appendix compares the searched DeiT-T style architectures.
Figure 8. ViTAS and AutoFormer choose different DeiT-T width/head patterns. ViTAS keeps smaller dimensions in early layers and allocates more dimension/head budget later. The authors point out several patterns:
ViTAS keeps smaller dimensions in earlier layers and more dimensions later. Early layers tend to use smaller attention dimensions than MLP output dimensions. Attention dimensions become larger in later layers. ViTAS uses fewer blocks under the tight 1.4G budget, while AutoFormer stays closer to DeiT-T’s layer count.
This is not a universal design law, but it is a useful search result. Under a tight compute budget, the method prefers to save early-layer width and spend more capacity in later attention/head choices. Searched Architecture VisualizationThe appendix visualizes searched Twins architectures.
Figure 11. Visualization of searched ViTAS-Twins architectures and dimension percentages. The figure is dense, but it gives an intuition for why NAS can still be useful even after strong manual ViT designs. The searched models do not simply scale every stage uniformly. They vary local/global choices, depth, and layer dimensions stage by stage. The paper’s appendix makes three practical observations from the searched architectures:
in the last stage, local blocks can behave similarly to global blocks because the feature size is already small; dimension changes are more obvious in Twins-based architectures than in DeiT-based architectures; MLP and attention dimensions are not uniformly scaled together.
Again, these are clues, not laws. But they are the kind of clues that make a NAS paper more useful than just a leaderboard entry. Implementation NotesIf I were reproducing ViTAS, I would validate the proxy before trusting the final searched model.
Implement the search space and make sure every sampled path has valid head/dimension divisibility. Build ordinal sharing first as a baseline; measure whether early channels receive more updates. Add cyclic channel mapping and verify training-count fairness across channel groups. Approximate influence balance for FC layers; check that cyclic reduces the channel influence gap. Add identity shifting for depth search; confirm that multiple superformer paths no longer collapse to the same final architecture. For DeiT-style patch-size search, keep private class tokens per patch size. Train a small superformer and compare inherited ranking against a small set of retrained candidates. Only then scale to ImageNet and evolutionary search.
The paper uses evolutionary search under FLOPs constraints after superformer training. The appendix says it partitions dimensions into 10 groups, samples 50 architectures per budget range, and trains/retrains according to the reported recipes. The search details matter less than the estimator quality: if inherited accuracy is biased, a better evolutionary solver will still optimize the wrong signal. LimitationsViTAS is a strong paper, but the boundaries are clear.
The search space is still manually designed around DeiT and Twins. It does not discover entirely new attention operators or macro backbones. Cyclic sharing is designed for dimension search. It does not automatically solve every kind of operation-sharing bias. The influence calculation is a useful approximation for FC-heavy layers, not a full theory of supernet training dynamics. The compute budget is substantial: superformer training uses 300 ImageNet epochs, and the final architectures are retrained. Final results depend on the retraining recipe. The paper is careful to reimplement baselines under its recipe, but recipe sensitivity is always a concern in ViT comparisons. Throughput is not always better. Several ViTAS models trade more parameters or lower image/s for higher accuracy.
TakeawayViTAS is worth remembering for one sentence:
In Transformer NAS, inherited accuracy is only useful if the superformer trains dimensions fairly.
The paper’s main contribution is not just a searched ViT model. It is the argument that ordinal channel sharing makes the superformer itself biased, and that cyclic channel sharing gives a more reliable ranking signal for token embedding dimensions. The strongest evidence is the combination of:
Figure 1, which makes the channel imbalance visible; Figure 5, which tests ranking correlation directly; Table 9, which isolates cyclic sharing and weak augmentation; ImageNet results in both Twins and DeiT spaces; COCO/ADE transfer results showing the searched backbones are not ImageNet-only artifacts.
That makes ViTAS a useful bridge between AutoFormer and later ViT search-space work such as S3. AutoFormer makes weight sharing more structured; ViTAS makes dimension sharing fairer; S3 later asks how to evolve the search space itself. All three are really about the same hidden problem: the supernet is the measurement instrument, and if the instrument is biased, NAS optimizes noise.

entry.title: XLNet: Generalized Autoregressive Pretraining for Language Understanding
entry.content:
Reference Paper Code
XLNet is one of the most interesting papers in the immediate post-BERT period. It does not simply say “make BERT larger” or “train on more data”; it asks whether the pre-training objective itself can keep the clean likelihood factorization of autoregressive language modeling while still using bidirectional context like BERT. My short reading: XLNet is a carefully engineered answer to a very specific tension.
Autoregressive language modeling has a valid product-rule factorization, but a normal left-to-right factorization cannot deeply condition on right context. BERT’s masked language modeling can use bidirectional context, but it corrupts the input with [MASK] and predicts masked targets independently given the visible tokens. XLNet samples different factorization orders of the same sequence, not different token orders, and trains an autoregressive objective over those orders. This objective is only usable after solving a target-leakage problem, which is why the paper introduces two-stream attention. The final model is not only “permutation LM”; it is permutation LM plus Transformer-XL recurrence, relative position/segment encodings, partial prediction, span-based targets, and several training tricks.
MotivationThe paper frames pre-training objectives as a tradeoff between autoregressive (AR) language modeling and denoising autoencoding (AE). A standard forward AR language model factorizes a sequence as:
Equivalently, the training objective is:
This is a real likelihood factorization. There is no artificial corruption, and dependencies between predicted tokens can be modeled through the product rule. But the context is directional: a forward model sees only left context and a backward model sees only right context. Concatenating forward and backward models is not the same as deep bidirectional interaction. BERT changes the situation by using masked language modeling. Given a corrupted input and a mask indicator , it optimizes roughly:
The benefit is clear: can attend to both left and right context. The cost is also clear:
The model sees [MASK] during pre-training, but [MASK] does not appear during downstream fine-tuning. Multiple masked tokens are predicted independently under the usual MLM loss, so the model is not explicitly trained with a product-rule dependency among the targets. The objective is no longer a clean density estimation objective over the original sequence.
XLNet’s core question is therefore:
Can we keep the autoregressive product rule, avoid input corruption, and still let each position learn from bidirectional context?
