The answer is permutation language modeling. Permutation Language ModelingLet $\mathcal{Z}T[1, 2, \cdots, T]zz_ttz{1:t-1}$ denotes the indices that appear before it in that order. XLNet maximizes:
This is the key formula of the paper. The important subtlety is that XLNet permutes the factorization order, not the physical word order. The input sequence still has its natural order and still uses positional encodings from the natural order. The model changes only the attention mask, so a token can be predicted after tokens that are originally on its left, on its right, or both. The following appendix figure is the cleanest visualization of that point. In all four cases, the model predicts the same token , but the visible context changes because the factorization order changes.
This makes XLNet “bidirectional in expectation.” For a fixed target position, enough sampled permutations will place tokens from both sides before the target. The model still uses an autoregressive conditional probability for each sampled order, but across training it learns dependencies that a fixed left-to-right factorization would never expose. A concrete example from the paper is useful:
Suppose the target tokens are “New” and “York” and the visible non-target tokens are “is a city.” BERT’s MLM-style decomposition is:
XLNet can sample a factorization order where “New” is predicted before “York”:
This is the paper’s strongest conceptual criticism of BERT. BERT may learn the phrase “New York” indirectly through representation learning, but the MLM loss itself does not train the joint target dependency in this example. XLNet’s autoregressive factorization can make that dependency part of the loss. Why A Normal Transformer Is Not EnoughThe permutation objective sounds simple, but a naive Transformer parameterization has a hidden problem. If we try to predict the target token with a standard context representation:
then depends on the visible context but not on which position is being predicted. That is fatal under permutation LM. The same visible set can be used to predict different target positions under different permutations. Without target position information, the model is asked to emit the same distribution for different prediction targets. So XLNet re-parameterizes the distribution to be target-aware:
The new representation knows the target position , but it must not see the target content . Otherwise the pre-training task becomes trivial. This is exactly why the paper needs two-stream attention. Two-Stream Attention XLNet keeps two hidden states for each position:
The content stream plays the role of a normal Transformer hidden state. It can encode the token content and is used as context for future predictions. The query stream is target-aware but content-blind. It knows “I am predicting position ” but cannot look at itself.
At layer , the schematic update is:
The query stream can attend only to content states that are earlier in the sampled factorization order. It cannot attend to the content of the current target. The content stream update is:
The content stream is normal masked self-attention under the sampled order. It can see itself because it is not directly used to predict its own token; it is used to provide content to later prediction steps. Initialization is also different:
where is a trainable query vector. The query stream receives position information through the attention mechanism and positional encodings, not through the token embedding at that position. There is a practical detail I like: during fine-tuning, XLNet can drop the query stream and use the content stream like a normal Transformer-XL encoder. The complicated two-stream machinery is mainly a pre-training device needed to make the permutation objective valid. The appendix gives a more expanded view of the two streams. The content stream behaves like ordinary self-attention under a permutation mask:
The query stream uses the same factorization mask but with a self-exclusion constraint. The dashed vertical arrows in the paper figure emphasize that the query stream keeps location information while blocking same-position token content:
The implementation lesson is simple: if this mask is wrong, the whole pre-training objective collapses. A target token leaking into its own query state would let the model solve the task by copying, while a query state without position information would make different targets ambiguous. Partial PredictionPredicting every token under every sampled order is too hard and slow. XLNet therefore uses partial prediction. Split a sampled order into a non-target prefix and a target suffix . The objective becomes:
The target suffix is chosen because those positions have the longest context under the current factorization order. A hyperparameter controls the prediction rate:
So if , roughly one sixth of the tokens become prediction targets. This reduces optimization difficulty and saves memory because the query stream only needs to be computed for selected targets. The paper also uses span-based prediction for XLNet-Large: sample a span length , then select a consecutive target span inside a context window of about tokens. This makes the objective closer to predicting coherent local phrases instead of unrelated isolated tokens. Transformer-XL Inside XLNetThe name XLNet is not just branding. The model integrates two Transformer-XL ideas:
Segment recurrence, so the model can reuse hidden states from previous segments. Relative positional encoding, so attention depends on relative positions instead of only absolute indices.
Suppose the previous segment is and the current segment is . After processing the previous segment, XLNet caches content representations for each layer. For the current segment, the content-stream update with memory is:
The cached memory is content stream only. This is important because the content stream is a real representation of previous tokens, while query states are target-specific training devices. The memory can be reused without remembering the previous segment’s sampled factorization order, because after the previous content states are computed, the current layer only needs them as key/value memories. For multi-segment inputs such as [CLS, A, SEP, B, SEP], XLNet follows BERT’s input format but replaces absolute segment embeddings with relative segment encodings. For positions and :
When attends to , the segment contribution is:
This is added to the normal attention score. Instead of encoding “segment A” or “segment B” absolutely, the model encodes “same segment” versus “different segment.” That is more consistent with the relative-position philosophy and generalizes more naturally to tasks with more than two input segments. Training SetupThe reported XLNet-Large model has BERT-Large-like architecture scale, but the training stack is much heavier than a toy objective swap. The paper uses:
24 layers, hidden size 1024, 16 attention heads, head size 64, FFN hidden size 4096. Sequence length 512. Batch size 8192. 500K pre-training steps on 512 TPU v3 chips, taking about 5.5 days. Adam with linear learning-rate decay, warmup, weight decay, and dropout. Partial prediction with . No next-sentence prediction objective in the final XLNet-Large setting.
The fine-tuning hyperparameter table is also useful because it shows a pattern that was common in BERT-era models: small task-specific grids, short fine-tuning schedules, and layer-wise learning-rate decay for some tasks.
One practical note: this is not a cheap method. The objective is elegant, but two-stream attention, sampled masks, recurrence, and span-based partial prediction make the system more complex than vanilla MLM. That complexity matters when judging why the field later favored simpler objectives plus more data/compute in many settings. Results: Fair BERT ComparisonThe most important experimental table is not the biggest leaderboard table. It is the controlled comparison against BERT under the same BooksCorpus + Wikipedia setup and BERT-like hyperparameters.
This table tries to isolate the objective/architecture contribution from the “more data and more compute” contribution. XLNet-Large-wikibooks beats the best of three BERT variants across the listed tasks, including SQuAD, RACE, MNLI, QNLI, QQP, RTE, SST-2, MRPC, CoLA, and STS-B. The gains are especially striking on:
RACE: 75.1 to 77.4. RTE: 74.0 to 81.2. SQuAD2.0: 82.8/85.5 to 85.1/87.8.
This is the table that supports the paper’s claim that the objective is doing real work, not only benefiting from a larger corpus. Results: Scaling UpThe scaled-up model uses much more text: Wikipedia, BooksCorpus, Giga5, ClueWeb 2012-B, and Common Crawl after filtering. The paper reports roughly 32.89B subword pieces after SentencePiece tokenization. For RACE and ClueWeb09-B, XLNet improves over strong baselines:
The RACE result is a good stress test because the task is reading comprehension over longer contexts. The paper explicitly suggests that the larger gain there may come from Transformer-XL recurrence and better long-context handling, not only from permutation LM. On SQuAD, XLNet also improves over BERT and RoBERTa in the reported setting:
The text classification table is interesting because these datasets are not all tiny low-resource benchmarks. XLNet still improves on large supervised datasets such as Yelp and Amazon:
On GLUE, the paper reports both single-task dev results and multi-task ensemble leaderboard results:
My interpretation of these result tables:
XLNet is strongest when the task rewards long-context reasoning or target dependency modeling. Some gains probably come from the Transformer-XL backbone and relative encoding, not only from the permutation objective. The paper is careful to include a fair BERT comparison, but the full-data leaderboard comparisons still mix objective, data, training schedule, recurrence, and engineering. Later RoBERTa made the comparison more complicated by showing that a much better-tuned MLM baseline can close many gaps. That does not invalidate XLNet; it changes the conclusion from “MLM is fundamentally inferior” to “the objective matters, but optimization, data, and implementation details matter just as much.”
Ablation StudyThe ablation table is where the paper becomes most useful for implementation.
Rows 1-4 compare BERT-Base, a denoising-autoencoding Transformer-XL baseline, and two XLNet-Base variants. The important reading is:
DAE + Transformer-XL improves over BERT-Base on RACE and SQuAD2.0, suggesting the backbone/recurrence already helps. XLNet-Base improves further, suggesting permutation LM contributes beyond simply swapping the backbone. and are close; is an optimization knob rather than a semantic change.
Rows 5-8 are more diagnostic:
Removing memory hurts RACE clearly, which matches the long-context story. Removing span-based prediction hurts all four tasks mildly. Removing bidirectional data also hurts. Adding next-sentence prediction does not help and even hurts SQuAD2.0 in this setup.
This table is also a warning: reproducing XLNet by only coding the main PLM formula is not enough. The gains come from a bundle of choices, and the ablation shows several of them are measurable. Attention Pattern AnalysisThe appendix includes a qualitative attention analysis. First, XLNet and BERT share several intuitive attention patterns:
These include content stripes, local/self focus, two-segment patterns, and content-based symmetry. That is not surprising: both models are Transformer-based bidirectional representation learners during downstream use. The more interesting figure shows patterns that the authors say appear only in XLNet:
The “self exclusion” pattern is particularly tied to the query stream idea: the model often needs to use position without looking at same-position content. The “relative stride” and “one-side masked” patterns are plausibly related to relative attention and permutation masks. I would not over-interpret attention plots as causal proof, but they are useful sanity checks: XLNet is not only BERT with a different loss; the masking/relative-attention machinery changes what attention heads learn. Implementation ChecklistIf I were implementing or reviewing XLNet pre-training, these are the failure points I would check first. 1. Do not shuffle the token sequencePermutation LM samples a factorization order over indices. The actual sequence order remains natural:
The positional encodings still correspond to the original positions. Only the causal visibility mask changes according to . 2. Test target leakage directlyFor every selected target , the query stream for that target must not attend to the content state of the same position:
I would unit test the attention mask, not only rely on loss curves. A leakage bug can produce a deceptively good pre-training loss and a useless representation. 3. Compute query states only for targetsBecause partial prediction selects only a target suffix, query-stream computation for non-target positions can be skipped. That is not just an optimization; it is part of making the method practical. 4. Cache content memory, not query memoryTransformer-XL recurrence should cache content representations . Query states are target-specific and should not be treated as reusable segment memory. 5. Keep relative position based on original sequence positionsThe factorization order changes attention visibility, not physical distance. Relative positional encoding should still reflect natural sequence positions. 6. Separate the objective from the engineering bundleWhen comparing against BERT, isolate:
objective: MLM/DAE versus permutation LM; backbone: Transformer versus Transformer-XL; data: WikiBooks versus large web corpus; schedule: batch size, steps, sequence length; target selection: isolated tokens versus span-based partial prediction.
Otherwise the result is a leaderboard comparison, not an objective comparison. My TakeXLNet is valuable because it forces a precise distinction that is easy to blur:
“Autoregressive” does not have to mean left-to-right. “Bidirectional context” does not have to mean masked denoising. “No target leakage” is an architectural constraint, not just a loss-function slogan.
The paper is also a good reminder that elegant objectives often require awkward machinery. The permutation LM formula is simple. Making it train a Transformer without leaking the target is not simple. Two-stream attention is the price XLNet pays for combining autoregressive likelihood with bidirectional context. Historically, I would not read XLNet as the route that replaced BERT. RoBERTa, DeBERTa, T5-style denoising, and later decoder-only scaling all moved the field in different directions. But XLNet remains one of the cleanest papers for understanding the objective-level differences between GPT-style AR modeling and BERT-style MLM. The main technical takeaway for me:
XLNet turns bidirectionality into an expectation over autoregressive factorization orders, then uses two-stream attention to make that expectation trainable without target leakage.
That idea is still worth remembering even if the dominant modern LLM stack is no longer built around XLNet itself.

entry.title: Zen-NAS: A Zero-Shot NAS for High-Performance Deep Image Recognition
entry.content:
Reference Lin M, Wang P, Sun Z, et al. Zen-NAS: A Zero-Shot NAS for High-Performance Deep Image Recognition. ICCV 2021.
Paper: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2102.01063.pdf Code: https://github.com/idstcv/ZenNAS Related notes: Zero-Cost NAS, TE-NAS
Zen-NAS is a zero-shot NAS paper for CNN image recognition. It does not train a supernet, does not train sampled candidates, and does not learn an accuracy predictor. It scores each architecture at random initialization with Zen-Score, then uses evolutionary search to keep architectures with high score under latency / FLOPs constraints. The method is best read as a very practical proxy paper. The paper’s claim is not “initialization score fully explains generalization.” The useful claim is narrower: inside a constrained CNN macro search space, an expressivity score that is cheap, scale-corrected, and hardware-budget-aware can find strong ImageNet networks.
The headline plot is strong. On ImageNet with NVIDIA V100 FP16 latency, ZenNets sit on a better accuracy-latency frontier than common manual and NAS-designed CNN families. The largest ZenNet reports 83.6% top-1 and about 0.5 GPU day search cost. What Zen-Score MeasuresZero-cost NAS proxies often ask whether a randomly initialized architecture looks trainable. Zen-NAS instead frames the score as expressivity. The paper starts from a ReLU CNN as a piecewise-linear function. For a vanilla CNN , the paper defines a -score:
The short intuition: if the pre-classifier feature map changes strongly under input perturbations, the architecture has a richer input-output mapping at initialization. This is different from SNIP / GradNorm-style proxies, which differentiate the loss with respect to weights. Zen-NAS differentiates with respect to input, and it is not label-dependent. Why Plain Phi-Score BreaksThe score above is not immediately usable. If BatchNorm is removed, deep networks can overflow because feature magnitude grows with depth. If BatchNorm is kept, the raw score becomes rescaled by BN statistics and can flatten architecture differences.
Figure 2 is the key diagnostic:
without BN, -score grows with depth and overflows around 30 layers; with BN, overflow disappears, but the score is scaled down; for bottleneck-width changes, the BN version can become almost constant; Zen-Score restores a monotonic signal after compensating for BN scale.
This is the part that makes the paper more than “use gradient norm as a proxy.” The paper is explicitly debugging why a naive expressivity proxy becomes numerically useless in modern CNNs. Zen-ScoreThe practical Zen-Score uses a finite difference on the pre-GAP feature map and then adds a BN variance correction:
where is computed from the mini-batch standard deviation statistic of the -th BN layer.
Several implementation choices matter:
residual links are removed while computing the score; all neurons are re-initialized from ; the perturbation scale is fixed at ; finite difference is used instead of backpropagating directly; the score is computed on the pre-GAP feature map, not final logits.
This graph explains the BN correction. The score measures how much the feature map changes when the input mini-batch is perturbed, then multiplies in the per-BN channel deviation terms. The theorem in the paper argues that this recovers the scale of the corresponding no-BN vanilla network up to an approximation error. Search ProcedureZen-NAS uses evolutionary search as a simple architecture generator. The generator is not the main contribution; the score is. Still, the constraints are important:
Start from an initial structure. Mutate block type, kernel size, width, and depth. Reject candidates that violate latency / FLOPs budget or maximum depth. Compute Zen-Score for feasible candidates. Keep the population by removing the lowest-score network. Return the highest-score network after fixed iterations.
The search space is not arbitrary graph search. The paper uses CNN blocks inspired by ResNet / MobileNet families, with hardware or FLOPs constraints. This matters because a zero-shot score is only comparable when the architectures share enough grammar. I would not assume the same score ranks arbitrary DAG cells, Transformer blocks, or heavily skip-connected spaces without recalibration. Proxy ComparisonThe paper compares Zen-Score with FLOPs, gradient norm, SynFlow, TE-Score, NASWOT, and random search on CIFAR under the same architecture search loop.
The compact view:
Proxy C10 C100
Zen-Score 96.2 80.1
TE-Score 96.1 77.2
NASWOT 96.0 77.5
SynFlow 95.1 75.9
FLOPs 93.1 64.7
Random 93.5 71.1
The CIFAR-10 difference is small among stronger proxies. CIFAR-100 is more revealing: Zen-Score is several points ahead of TE-Score and NASWOT in this experiment. FLOPs and gradient norm are bad proxies here, even worse than random search on CIFAR-100. The speed comparison is also important because this paper is about search budget:
On 224x224 ResNet-18 / ResNet-50, Zen-Score is reported as roughly 20-28x faster than TE-Score. NASWOT is closer but still slower in these rows, and the authors note an Inf-score issue for the official NASWOT implementation on ResNet-18/50. ImageNet ResultsThe ImageNet experiments use two target constraints:
latency on NVIDIA V100 FP16, batch size 64; FLOPs for lightweight models, with SE blocks added.
The V100 latency result was the first figure. The paper reports that ZenNet-1.2ms reaches 83.6% top-1, between EfficientNet-B5 and B6, while being about 4.9x faster at the same accuracy level.
The FLOPs plot tells a similar story. ZenNet-900M-SE reaches 80.8% top-1, which the paper compares to EfficientNet-B3 with about 43-44% fewer FLOPs. OFANet is the closest competitor in this plot. Search Cost Table 3 is the reason Zen-NAS is interesting as a systems paper:
Method Top-1 Search cost
TE-NAS 74.1 0.2 GPU day
PC-DARTS 75.8 3.8 GPU days
OFANet 80.1 51.6 GPU days
EfficientNet-B7 84.4 3800 GPU days
Zen-NAS 83.6 0.5 GPU day
The comparison is not perfectly fair because NAS papers use different search spaces, training recipes, hardware, and accounting rules. The paper says this explicitly. Still, the contrast is useful: Zen-NAS is not merely saving a small constant factor. It tries to move ImageNet NAS from trained evaluation to initialization-time scoring. The paper estimates that scoring 96,000 ResNet-50-like networks takes about 4 GPU hours, or 0.17 GPU day; the full reported search cost is 0.5 GPU day after including the broader setup. How I Read ItZen-NAS is strongest when read together with its assumptions:
The score is an expressivity proxy, not a generalization theorem. The BN correction is essential; otherwise the proxy can overflow or lose ranking power. The search space is a CNN macro space with controlled block mutations. The final architectures still need full training for the reported accuracies. Hardware constraints are part of the search, not an afterthought.
The method also explains why “zero-cost NAS” is not one thing. NASWOT, SynFlow, TE-NAS, and Zen-NAS measure different properties at initialization: activation patterns, path saliency, NTK / linear regions, and input-feature sensitivity. A proxy can be cheap and still fail if it measures the wrong property for the search space. Reproduction NotesIf reproducing this paper, I would isolate the score from the search algorithm:
Fix the CNN search space and mutation ranges first. Implement Zen-Score with residual links removed only during scoring. Verify Figure 2-like behavior on toy depth / width sweeps before running NAS. Compare Zen-Score against SynFlow, NASWOT, and TE-Score using the same EA loop. Count the actual latency predictor and hardware benchmark cost separately from score computation. Train the final selected networks with the same augmentation and teacher setup before comparing ImageNet top-1.
The important sanity check is step 3. If the score does not increase with width/depth in the expected controlled setting, the full search result is hard to trust. TakeawayZen-NAS is a good example of a zero-shot NAS paper that pays attention to numerical details. The idea is not just “rank architectures without training”; it is “rank architectures with an expressivity proxy that survives BatchNorm and scale effects.” I would use Zen-Score as a first-stage filter or search signal in a CNN space where the candidates share a regular macro grammar. I would be more cautious using it outside that setting. The paper’s main practical lesson is that a zero-shot proxy needs to be designed together with the search space and the deployment constraint.

entry.title: Zero-Cost Proxies for Lightweight NAS
entry.content:
Reference Paper: Zero-Cost Proxies for Lightweight NAS Authors: Mohamed S. Abdelfattah, Abhinav Mehrotra, Lukasz Dudziak, Nicholas D. Lane Venue: ICLR 2021
This paper asks a practical NAS question: before training an architecture, can we compute a cheap signal at initialization that is correlated enough with its final accuracy? The answer is not “training is unnecessary.” The more useful answer is: a zero-cost score can be good enough to warm up a search algorithm, guide local mutations, or filter many bad candidates before spending real training budget. The name “zero-cost” is a little aggressive. These proxies still need model construction, initialization, sometimes a minibatch, and often a forward/backward pass. The cost is close to zero compared with training hundreds or thousands of candidate networks. One SentenceZero-cost NAS turns pruning-at-initialization signals such as snip, grasp, synflow, fisher, and jacob_cov into architecture-level scores by aggregating saliency over the whole network, then uses those scores to rank architectures without training them. My short reading: the paper is valuable because it treats zero-cost proxies as search tools, not as magic accuracy predictors. The best use case is not selecting one final model from a raw score. The best use case is spending a very cheap pass to bias a downstream NAS algorithm toward better regions of the search space. Why This Problem MattersClassical NAS spends most of its budget evaluating architectures. A candidate can be evaluated by full training, early stopping, reduced input resolution, fewer channels, fewer samples, weight sharing, or a learned surrogate. All of those proxies still have visible cost or bias. The paper uses EcoNAS as the conventional reduced-training baseline. EcoNAS reduces the training setting along axes such as resolution, channel width, dataset size, and epoch count. That is reasonable, but it still runs training loops. On a real GPU, the wall-clock time of small reduced models can also be much worse than their FLOP count suggests.
EcoNAS-style reduced training can produce useful rank correlation, but its theoretical FLOP reduction does not fully translate into wall-clock speedup. Figure 1 is a good warning. On NAS-Bench-201 CIFAR-10, the original EcoNAS-like setting r8 c4 e20 reaches only about rho = 0.61 when evaluated over all 15,625 architectures. The stronger econas+ configuration improves the rank correlation, but it needs more computation. The right plot is especially important: a point with FLOPs around one tenth of a full training epoch can still take time comparable to several full epochs because tiny models do not saturate the GPU well. This is where zero-cost scores become attractive. They replace reduced training with a minibatch-level diagnostic at random initialization. What A Proxy Score Is Trying To DoLet an architecture be , with randomly initialized parameters . A zero-cost proxy computes a scalar score:
where is usually one minibatch. For synflow, even is not needed. The scalar score should rank architectures in roughly the same order as final trained accuracy. The paper evaluates ranking quality with Spearman rank correlation. If there are no rank ties, a simple form is:
Here is the rank difference between the proxy ranking and the final-accuracy ranking for architecture . This is the right metric for NAS because the raw scale of the score does not matter. A proxy can be badly calibrated in value but still useful if it sorts candidates in a similar order. The important detail: global Spearman correlation is not the whole story. NAS mostly cares about top architectures and local decisions. A proxy with mediocre global correlation can still help if it keeps many good models near the top or chooses better neighbors during mutation. Turning Pruning Scores Into NAS ScoresMany zero-cost metrics start as pruning-at-initialization criteria. In pruning, the question is:
Which parameters or channels are least important and can be removed?
In NAS, the question becomes:
If I aggregate those importance scores over the whole network, does the total score tell me whether the architecture is promising?
A generic saliency-to-network-score pattern is:
where is a per-parameter saliency and is the number of parameters in architecture . This aggregation step is simple, but it is also dangerous: scores can become biased toward larger networks or networks with more active paths unless the search space controls model size. grad_normThe simplest proxy in the paper is the gradient norm. After one minibatch, compute gradients and sum their Euclidean norms:
The intuition is that a trainable network should produce useful gradients at initialization. If gradients are tiny, broken, or concentrated in a pathological way, the model may train poorly. But this metric is blunt. A large gradient norm can also mean unstable scale, more parameters, or bad normalization. So I read grad_norm as a cheap trainability diagnostic, not as a precise predictor. snipSNIP estimates how much the loss would change if a parameter were removed. The paper writes the per-parameter saliency in the form:
where is the Hadamard product. For architecture scoring, a useful scalar view is:
This is a first-order Taylor view. If setting to zero changes the loss a lot, then is salient. For NAS, the total saliency says: “this architecture has many parameters that already participate in the loss on a minibatch.” That can be useful, but it is still tied to the sampled data and labels. graspGraSP changes the target from preserving the current loss to preserving gradient flow. The paper gives the saliency form:
where is the Hessian of the loss with respect to parameters. In scalar architecture-score form:
The full Hessian is not explicitly built; the implementation can use Hessian-vector products. The extra second-order information tries to answer a subtler question than SNIP: if I remove this parameter, how much does the gradient norm, and therefore future learning dynamics, change? The tradeoff is clear. GraSP is still cheap compared with training, but it is less simple than SNIP and can be noisier. In the paper’s PyTorchCV experiment, GraSP has high variance and can fail badly across heterogeneous model families. synflowSynFlow is the most important metric in this paper. It has the same saliency shape as SNIP:
but is not cross-entropy on a labeled minibatch. A common implementation view is:
and the architecture score is:
The network is linearized through absolute weights and fed an all-ones input. This makes the score data-free. The intuition is path-based: a good architecture should have many live input-to-output paths capable of carrying signal. SynFlow was originally designed to avoid layer collapse in pruning. In NAS, that same property is useful because many search spaces contain skip, zero, or weak operations that can break signal flow. I would not interpret SynFlow as “accuracy without data.” It is closer to “does this randomly initialized architecture have healthy signal paths?” The paper’s empirical result is that this path signal is surprisingly correlated with final performance in several NAS spaces. fisherThe Fisher-style proxy scores activation saliency rather than parameter saliency. The paper writes:
Here is an activation and is the length of the vectorized feature map. The product measures how much the loss locally depends on that activation. Squaring makes it nonnegative and emphasizes large sensitivities. For channel pruning, this tells us which activation channels matter. For NAS, the paper aggregates this signal across layers to score the whole network. The limitation is that activation saliency can be heavily affected by normalization, activation scale, and batch statistics. jacob_covThe Jacobian covariance proxy comes from Mellor et al.’s “NAS without training” idea. For each input , consider the input-output Jacobian:
Then compare the vectorized Jacobians across different examples in a minibatch:
The score is based on the covariance/correlation structure of these Jacobians. The intuition is simple: if different inputs induce very similar Jacobians, the network is not separating them well at initialization. Lower correlation means the randomly initialized architecture is already more input-sensitive and potentially more expressive. This metric is more search-space dependent than it first appears. It works well inside NAS-Bench-201, but the paper shows it can fail when comparing unrelated PyTorchCV models or NAS-Bench-ASR models. voteThe paper also uses a small ensemble called vote. It takes a majority vote between synflow, jacob_cov, and snip when ranking two models:
Here is the pairwise preference from metric . This is useful because different proxies fail differently. synflow measures path saliency, jacob_cov measures input-Jacobian diversity, and snip measures minibatch loss sensitivity. The vote score is not a new theory; it is a practical way to reduce single-proxy brittleness. NAS-Bench-201: The Cleanest TestNAS-Bench-201 has 15,625 architectures in a compact cell search space. Each directed edge chooses one operation from zero, skip connection, 1x1 convolution, 3x3 convolution, or 3x3 average pooling. Because every architecture has tabulated training results on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet16-120, it is a natural place to test rank correlation.
Zero-cost proxy points are plotted against the cost and rank correlation of early validation accuracy and EcoNAS-style reduced training. Figure 2 is the main punchline. On NAS-Bench-201, zero-cost proxies sit far to the left of reduced-training curves because they need only minibatch-level computation. Yet synflow, jacob_cov, and especially vote reach competitive or better rank correlation.
Table 1: Spearman rank correlation on NAS-Bench-201. The table is worth reading carefully:
grad_norm and snip are around 0.58 to 0.64. They are useful, but not strong enough to trust alone. grasp is weaker on CIFAR-10 but becomes closer on CIFAR-100 and ImageNet16-120. fisher is poor here, around 0.33 to 0.39. synflow is consistently strong: 0.74, 0.76, and 0.75. jacob_cov is also strong: 0.73, 0.71, and 0.71. vote is best: 0.82, 0.83, and 0.82.
The cost comparison is the real result. The paper notes that the vote-style proxy costs about three minibatches, while econas+ is closer to a thousand minibatches. On this benchmark, a few initialization-time signals can beat a reduced-training proxy in rank correlation. Beyond NAS-Bench-201A proxy that works only on NAS-Bench-201 is not enough. NAS-Bench-201 is small, cell-based, and tightly controlled. The paper therefore tests a broader PyTorchCV model zoo and other tabular NAS spaces.
PyTorchCV is a heterogeneous setting: models differ in family, depth, width, and macro design. The PyTorchCV experiment is a good stress test because it compares unrelated model families such as ResNets, DenseNets, MobileNets, and EfficientNets. The ranking problem is less controlled than a cell search space. Two observations matter:
synflow, snip, fisher, and grad_norm remain usable across several datasets, with SynFlow especially strong on SVHN. grasp and jacob_cov become unstable in this heterogeneous setting, even though jacob_cov was strong inside NAS-Bench-201.
That suggests a useful rule: a proxy can be reliable inside a homogeneous search space but fail when architecture families change too much.
Table 2: correlations on NAS-Bench-101, NAS-Bench-NLP, and NAS-Bench-ASR. Table 2 makes the same point more sharply:
On NAS-Bench-101, grasp, synflow, and jacob_cov are all modest, around 0.37 to 0.45. On NAS-Bench-NLP, jacob_cov is best at 0.56, while synflow is 0.34. On NAS-Bench-ASR, synflow is best among reported metrics at 0.40, while jacob_cov becomes negative.
So the paper’s claim is not “SynFlow always wins.” The stronger claim is: SynFlow is the most consistently useful proxy across the tested NAS benchmarks. It may not be the best in every single table, but it rarely collapses as badly as some alternatives. How To Put A Zero-Cost Proxy Into NASThe paper studies two integration modes: warmup and move proposal. This is where the work becomes more practical than a plain correlation study. WarmupWarmup computes zero-cost scores for many random architectures before expensive training begins. If the training budget is , and the number of zero-cost scored models is , the intended regime is:
For aging evolution, score random models and use the best-ranked ones as the initial population. For reinforcement learning, use zero-cost scores as cheap rewards before true accuracy rewards are available. A simple normalized reward form is:
For a binary predictor, the paper uses zero-cost rankings to create pairwise supervision. With warmup points, the number of architecture pairs is:
This is a nice trick: one cheap ranking pass creates many pairwise training examples for a predictor. Move ProposalMove proposal uses a zero-cost proxy locally. Given a current architecture , define its edit-distance-one neighborhood . Instead of mutating randomly, score candidate neighbors and choose: $$a’ =\arg\max_{b \in \mathcal{N}1(a)}S{\mathrm{zc}}(b).$$ This is less dependent on global rank correlation. Even if the proxy cannot rank the whole search space well, it may still choose a better neighbor among a small mutation set. Search Results NAS-Bench-201 CIFAR-100: SynFlow warmup and move proposal improve random search, reinforcement learning, aging evolution, and binary predictor search. Figure 4 shows that adding SynFlow can speed up very different search algorithms. The improvement is most obvious for random search and reinforcement learning, but the paper also reports speedups for stronger methods such as aging evolution and binary predictors.
Table 7: tabulated NAS-Bench-201 CIFAR-100 search results. The table gives a more concrete view than the curves. It reports accuracy after 50 trained models and the number of trained models needed to reach 73.5% accuracy. For aging evolution and binary predictor, the paper reports about 5.6x and 2.3x speedups to the 73.5% target. The one caution is reinforcement learning with too much warmup. The paper notes that 15k warmup points can hurt RL because the controller starts overfitting to the SynFlow reward rather than learning the real objective.
NAS-Bench-ASR TIMIT: the same SynFlow idea also helps on a speech-recognition search space.
Table 8: NAS-Bench-ASR search summary. The ASR result is important because it is not just another image-classification cell benchmark. The target metric is phoneme error rate, and lower is better. To reach PER = 21.3%, the paper reports:
baseline random search and RL require more than 1000 trained models; baseline aging evolution needs 138 trained models; with 2000 SynFlow warmup points, those counts become 68, 173, and 87.
That is exactly how I would want a zero-cost proxy to behave: not perfect ranking, but a large reduction in the number of expensive evaluations.
Table 3: NAS-Bench-101 comparison with previous published methods. NAS-Bench-101 is larger and has weaker SynFlow correlation than NAS-Bench-201. Even there, the paper reports strong sample-efficiency gains. The random-search-with-warmup result reaches 94.22% test accuracy after training only 34 models, compared with prior results using 140 to 256 trained models. Why SynFlow HelpsThe discussion section is useful because it does not stop at global Spearman correlation. It asks whether SynFlow puts good architectures near the top and whether it chooses good local moves.
Table 4: how many top-5% architectures appear inside the top 64 models ranked by SynFlow. Randomly selecting 64 models would return about 5% top-5% models, roughly 3 models. SynFlow returns much more:
44, 54, and 56 on the three NAS-Bench-201 datasets; 12 on NAS-Bench-101; 16 on NAS-Bench-ASR.
This explains why warmup works. An initial evolution pool or predictor warmup set becomes much richer in good candidates.
Table 5: probability that SynFlow chooses the best model inside a local edit-distance-one cluster. For move proposal, the relevant question is local. In NAS-Bench-201, a random mutation has about a 1/25, or 4%, chance of selecting the best neighbor. SynFlow raises this to roughly 32% to 35%. On NAS-Bench-101, it is about 12%, close to the random cluster-size baseline but still useful. On NAS-Bench-ASR, the gain is smaller, from about 7.7% random chance to 10%. This makes the method feel less mysterious. SynFlow helps because it enriches the candidate set and makes local mutation less random. Top-Region And Local AnalysisThe appendix tables are worth including because they reveal where global correlation hides details.
Table 9: Spearman correlation restricted to the top 10% of points. Top-10% correlation is much harder than global correlation. Some metrics that look reasonable globally become negative or near zero at the top. SynFlow is not perfect, but it stays nonnegative and useful across the reported spaces: 0.18, 0.42, 0.55, 0.14, 0.10, and 0.40.
Table 10: percentage of truly top-10% models that also appear in each proxy’s top-10%. Table 10 uses overlap rather than rank correlation. This is often closer to what NAS needs. On NAS-Bench-201, SynFlow retrieves 46%, 50%, and 44% of the true top-10% models inside its top-10% set. It is also the strongest metric on NAS-Bench-101. But the ASR row is a reminder that proxy behavior is not universal: jacob_cov has high top-10% overlap there even though its global rank correlation is poor.
Table 12: local rank correlation inside edit-distance-one neighborhoods. Local correlation can differ from global correlation. On NAS-Bench-201, SynFlow and jacob_cov are both strong locally. On NAS-Bench-ASR, grad_norm and fisher have better local correlation than SynFlow. This means the best proxy for global warmup may not be the best proxy for local mutation in every search space.
Table 13: how often each proxy picks the best model in a local cluster. Table 13 is the most operational local metric. SynFlow picks the best local model about one third of the time on NAS-Bench-201, which is much better than random. On NAS-Bench-101 it is also the best among the listed metrics. On NAS-Bench-ASR, several metrics are close. Again, the practical lesson is to validate proxy choice on the target search space before relying on it. Failure ModesI would be careful with zero-cost NAS for several reasons. First, many scores are scale-sensitive. If an architecture has more parameters, more active paths, or different normalization behavior, a raw sum of saliencies can become a model-size proxy rather than an accuracy proxy. Second, minibatch-dependent scores depend on the minibatch. snip, grasp, grad_norm, fisher, and jacob_cov can change with batch size, labels, augmentation, BatchNorm mode, and random seed. That does not make them useless, but it means the scoring protocol must be fixed. Third, search-space homogeneity matters. jacob_cov is strong inside NAS-Bench-201 but weak across heterogeneous PyTorchCV models. A score that compares similar cell variants may not compare ResNet-like, MobileNet-like, and EfficientNet-like models fairly. Fourth, a proxy can be gamed by the search algorithm. The RL warmup failure with too many SynFlow points is a good example. The controller can optimize the proxy instead of the final objective. Finally, global rank correlation is not enough. A proxy should be checked on top-region overlap and local mutation decisions. Those are closer to the decisions a NAS algorithm actually makes. How I Would Use ItI would not use zero-cost scores to directly choose the final architecture. I would use them as a cheap prior. My practical workflow would be:
Sample a few hundred or a few thousand architectures from the target search space. Compute synflow, snip, grad_norm, and maybe jacob_cov under a fixed initialization and minibatch protocol. Train a small calibration subset to check direction, global Spearman correlation, top-k overlap, and local neighbor accuracy. Use the best proxy or a small vote ensemble for warmup. Keep final model selection based on real training or a stronger surrogate.
For a homogeneous cell space like NAS-Bench-201, SynFlow is a strong default. For a heterogeneous model zoo or a different task such as ASR, I would not assume the same proxy is best. I would spend a small budget to calibrate the proxy first. Implementation details I would keep fixed:
initialization scheme; train/eval mode for BatchNorm and dropout; minibatch size and labels for data-dependent scores; whether scores are normalized by parameter count, layer count, or operation type; random seed repetitions; score direction, because some metrics are better when lower and others when higher.
The last point matters. The paper’s tables report rank correlations after using each metric in its intended direction. In a new codebase, I would always verify whether larger score means better architecture before using it inside search. TakeawayZero-cost NAS is not a replacement for training. It is a way to buy a surprisingly informative ranking signal before training. The core insight is that an architecture’s initialization already exposes useful structure: gradient flow, path connectivity, activation saliency, and input-Jacobian diversity. Aggregated carefully, those signals can guide NAS algorithms with a tiny fraction of the evaluation cost. For me, the strongest result is not just Table 1’s high vote correlation on NAS-Bench-201. It is the combination of Figure 4, Figure 5, and the local-analysis tables: even when the proxy is imperfect, it can still improve the actual search loop by seeding better candidates and making better local moves.

entry.title: ZeroQ: Data-Free Post-Training Quantization
entry.content:
Paper: ZeroQ: A Novel Zero Shot Quantization Framework Code: amirgholami/ZeroQ
ZeroQ is an early and very clean formulation of data-free post-training quantization. The deployment setting is simple: the pretrained model is available, but the original training or calibration data is not. A normal PTQ pipeline would use calibration samples to choose activation clipping ranges and to estimate which layers are fragile. ZeroQ tries to recover those signals from the model itself. The key observation is that many CNN checkpoints contain BatchNorm layers, and BatchNorm stores running means and variances collected during training. Those statistics are not the original dataset, but they are a compact trace of the distribution that the model saw. ZeroQ turns that trace into synthetic calibration data. Problem SettingThe paper is not about quantization-aware training. It is a post-training method:
No access to training or validation data. No fine-tuning in the main results. Uniform quantization is supported, but the stronger results come from mixed precision. The target models are mostly BatchNorm-heavy CNNs: ResNet, MobileNetV2, ShuffleNet, SqueezeNext, InceptionV3, and RetinaNet with a ResNet50 backbone.
This matters because post-training quantization normally needs real samples. Without them, activation ranges are easy to misestimate, and layer sensitivity becomes guesswork. ZeroQ’s answer is to synthesize a small batch of “Distilled Data” and use it as a calibration probe. Distilled Data From BatchNormZeroQ starts from random Gaussian inputs and optimizes them so that their intermediate activations match the BatchNorm statistics stored in the model. The generated samples do not need to look like real images. They only need to excite the network in a way that exposes useful activation ranges and layer sensitivity.
Figure 3 from the paper. The left image is Gaussian input. The right image is optimized distilled data. The point is not semantic realism; the point is that the optimized sample has more local structure and better matches internal model statistics. For BatchNorm layer , let be the stored running mean and standard deviation, and let be the statistics measured when the synthetic input is forwarded through the model. The distilled-data objective is:
In practice, this gives ZeroQ two things that PTQ usually gets from a calibration set:
Activation clipping ranges. Inputs for estimating layer sensitivity under different bit widths.
Algorithm 1 from the paper. ZeroQ repeatedly forwards the synthetic input, measures intermediate statistics, and updates the input so that the model’s BatchNorm statistics are matched. The method is lightweight compared with training. The paper reports that generating 32 distilled images for ResNet50 on ImageNet takes about 3 seconds on an 8-V100 system. The complete ResNet50 quantization pipeline is reported as under 30 seconds. Sensitivity MeasurementThe next question is where to spend bits. Some layers can tolerate lower precision, while others cause large output drift if quantized aggressively. ZeroQ measures the sensitivity of layer at bit width by quantizing only that layer and comparing the output distribution with the full-precision model:
Here is not a real training image. It is distilled data. The metric is label-free, which is important because the zero-shot setting has neither labels nor input samples.
Figure 1 from the paper. The top branch is the original model; the bottom branch quantizes one layer. The KL divergence between the two outputs is used as the layer sensitivity. The sensitivity curves are the most convincing part of the method. Gaussian data produces a very different sensitivity ranking, especially in early ResNet50 layers. Distilled data tracks the real training-data sensitivity much more closely.
Figure 2 from the paper. On the left, distilled data is much closer to training data than Gaussian noise. On the right, sensitivity rises sharply as weights move from 8-bit to 4-bit and 2-bit. This explains why blindly using random Gaussian calibration is not enough. A synthetic batch is useful only if it produces the right internal activation behavior. Pareto Frontier For Mixed PrecisionFor a model with layers and possible precision choices per layer, exhaustive mixed-precision search has size . ZeroQ avoids that by treating layer sensitivities as additive and solving a constrained allocation problem:
is the parameter size of layer , is its selected bit width, and is the model-size budget. The paper describes this as a Pareto-frontier method and reports that the sensitivity computation scales as .
Figure 4 from the paper. Blue points are mixed-precision configurations. The selected configuration is the lowest-sensitivity point under a model-size constraint. This is the second core idea of ZeroQ: the distilled data is not just used for activation clipping. It also drives bit allocation.
Figure 5 from the appendix. Different layers can choose from 2-bit, 4-bit, and 8-bit settings instead of forcing the whole network to share one precision. ImageNet ResultsThe main ImageNet table covers ResNet50, MobileNetV2, and ShuffleNet. The strongest message is that ZeroQ is almost lossless at W8A8, while still usable in much more aggressive mixed-precision settings.
Table I from the paper. “No D” means no real data is used, and “No FT” means no fine-tuning. “MP” means mixed-precision weights. Some numbers worth remembering:
ResNet50 W8A8: 77.67 Top-1 versus 77.72 full-precision baseline. ResNet50 mixed weights with 6-bit activations: 77.43 Top-1, higher than the OCS comparison row at 74.80. ResNet50 aggressive mixed weights with 8-bit activations: 75.80 Top-1 at 12.17 MB. MobileNetV2 W8A8: 72.91 Top-1 versus 73.03 baseline, and above DFQ’s 71.20 row in the same table. ShuffleNet W8A8: 64.94 Top-1 versus 65.07 baseline.
The compact models are harder. MobileNetV2 and ShuffleNet lose more accuracy under aggressive average-4-bit weight compression, which is expected because there is less redundancy to absorb quantization noise. Detection And Low-Bit Uniform ResultsZeroQ also tests RetinaNet on COCO. This is useful because object detection has a more complicated model graph than classification, and some RetinaNet layers are not directly followed by BN. The paper handles this by extracting the ResNet backbone statistics and then feeding distilled data through RetinaNet for sensitivity and range estimation.
Table II from the paper. W8A8 reaches the same 36.4 mAP as the full-precision baseline; the mixed-weight rows trade mAP for model size. For RetinaNet, ZeroQ reports:
W8A8: 36.4 mAP, matching the full-precision baseline. Mixed weights with 6-bit activations: 35.9 mAP. Aggressive mixed weights with 8-bit activations: 33.7 mAP.
The ResNet18 table is also worth reading because it compares very low-bit uniform post-quantization settings against DFC and PACT.
Table III from the paper. ZeroQ remains competitive without fine-tuning, especially in the 6-bit and 8-bit rows. The W4A4 case is difficult. ZeroQ with percentile clipping reaches 69.05 Top-1, while DFC without fine-tuning reports 55.49 in the same row group. At 6-bit and 8-bit, ZeroQ is very close to the 71.47 full-precision baseline. Ablation: Why Distilled Data MattersThe distilled-data ablation asks whether BN-matched synthetic data is actually better than simple Gaussian data. It is.
Table IV from the paper. The quantized setting uses mixed weights and 8-bit activations. For ResNet50, Gaussian data gives 75.44, training data gives 75.95, and distilled data gives 75.80. That is a small gap. For MobileNetV2, the difference is larger: Gaussian data gives 66.73, training data gives 69.06, and distilled data gives 68.83. My read is that distilled data works because it recovers the statistics the quantizer actually needs. It is not a substitute for labels, and it is not a learned data generator. It is a calibration probe constructed from BN statistics. Ablation: Why Sensitivity Allocation MattersThe sensitivity ablation is even more direct. If the bit allocation is random, the average result collapses. If the sensitivity objective is inverted, it also collapses. ZeroQ’s Pareto allocation is stable across the selected top configurations.
Table V from the paper. Under the average 4-bit weight constraint, ZeroQ’s best, worst, and mean configurations are all around 75.7 Top-1, while random and inverse choices fail badly. This table is a good reminder that “mixed precision” is not automatically useful. It helps only when the allocation rule has a real signal. LimitationsZeroQ is not a generic answer to data-free quantization. Its strongest assumption is BatchNorm. A trained BN layer stores running statistics, and those statistics become the target for distilled-data optimization. LayerNorm-only Transformers do not provide the same dataset-level running mean and variance. That is why modern LLM PTQ methods usually rely on a small text calibration set, activation-aware heuristics, or reconstruction objectives instead of copying ZeroQ directly. There is also a practical boundary around very compact models and very low precision. The W8A8 results are almost lossless, but aggressive average-4-bit settings on MobileNetV2 and ShuffleNet still lose noticeable accuracy. That is not a failure of the paper; it is the real tradeoff. Finally, “zero-shot” does not mean “no information.” ZeroQ uses the weights, architecture, BatchNorm statistics, and the model’s own output distribution. It removes the data dependency, not the need for calibration signals. TakeawayZeroQ’s useful idea is narrow but important: if real calibration data is unavailable, a model may still contain enough internal statistics to synthesize calibration probes. For BN-heavy CNNs, matching BatchNorm statistics gives synthetic data that is much better than Gaussian noise, and that data can drive both activation range selection and mixed-precision sensitivity analysis. For LLMs, the direct recipe does not transfer cleanly because BatchNorm is absent. The broader lesson still transfers: quantization needs a distributional proxy. If the real calibration distribution is missing, the method must replace it with some trace that the model already carries, or with a carefully designed synthetic signal.

entry.title: ZeroQuant: Efficient and Affordable PTQ for Large Transformers
entry.content:
Paper: ZeroQuant: Efficient and Affordable Post-Training Quantization for Large-Scale Transformers Code: microsoft/DeepSpeed ZeroQuant is an important paper because it treats quantization as a modeling problem and a serving-system problem at the same time. The paper is not just saying “large Transformers can use INT8.” It asks a more practical question:
Can post-training quantization serve BERT-size and GPT-style models without full quantization-aware training, while still producing real GPU latency gains?
The answer is a system recipe:
use group-wise quantization for weights, because a single matrix scale wastes range on rows with small magnitude; use token-wise quantization for activations, because different tokens can have very different ranges; use layer-by-layer knowledge distillation when INT4 weights are involved; fuse quantization and dequantization around INT8 GEMM, otherwise fine-grained quantization can lose its latency benefit to memory traffic.
All crops below are taken from the original PDF. Why ZeroQuant MattersBefore ZeroQuant, there were already useful Transformer quantization papers. Q8BERT showed that BERT can tolerate 8-bit quantization with quantization-aware fine-tuning. Q-BERT pushed BERT weight precision down with Hessian information. But two gaps remained:
Full QAT or hidden-state distillation becomes expensive when the model has hundreds of millions or billions of parameters. Accuracy-only quantization results do not prove that the method is useful for serving, because token-wise scales and low-bit formats can introduce extra quantize/dequantize kernels and memory movement.
ZeroQuant sits exactly at that boundary. It tries to keep the user-facing behavior close to FP16, while making the quantization process cheap enough for large models. The paper evaluates:
Model family Examples in the paper Main benchmark
Encoder-only BERT-Base, BERT-Large GLUE development sets
Decoder-only GPT-3-style 350M and 1.3B 20 zero-shot tasks plus Wikitext-2
Larger open-source GPT models GPT-J 6B, GPT-NeoX 20B generation and zero-shot evaluation
The notation is WxAy: x bits for weights and y bits for activations. The paper also uses W4/8 for a mixed setting where multi-head self-attention weights stay INT8 and feed-forward weights are pushed to INT4. This is a sensible compromise because the feed-forward connection is a large fraction of Transformer parameters. The Failure Mode Of Naive PTQPost-training quantization is attractive because it does not retrain the model. A common PTQ flow is: 1. Run calibration data through the model.2. Estimate activation ranges.3. Quantize weights and activations with fixed scales.4. Evaluate the quantized model.
That is cheap, but it assumes that a small number of scales can represent the distributions well enough. ZeroQuant shows why this is fragile for Transformers.
Figure 1. GPT-3 350M has large variation across token activation ranges and across rows of the attention output matrix. A single coarse scale either clips large values or wastes representational levels on smaller values. The left plot is the activation problem. Token hidden states in the same layer can have very different max-absolute ranges. If all tokens share one activation scale, the largest token range determines the scale, and small-range tokens get a coarse quantization grid. The right plot is the weight problem. Rows in the attention output matrix do not share the same magnitude. A matrix-wide scale is again inefficient: rows with small ranges are represented by too few integer values, and this becomes much worse when weights are pushed to INT4. The first PTQ table makes the diagnosis concrete.
Table 1. Naive PTQ on GPT-3 350M. Activation quantization hurts more than INT8 weight quantization, and mixed INT4/INT8 weights can destroy generation quality. The useful read is not only the average score:
W8A16 is close to the FP16 baseline on the shown tasks. Weight-only INT8 is not the main problem here. W16A8 has a larger drop. Wikitext-2 perplexity moves from 21.5 to 24.6, so activation quantization is already painful. W8A8 is worse again on Wikitext-2, with perplexity 26.2. W4/8A16 collapses generation. Wikitext-2 becomes 1.76e5, which is effectively unusable.
This is why ZeroQuant is not a pure rounding paper. The method has to address the numerical range mismatch in both weights and activations. Fine-Grained QuantizationZeroQuant uses uniform symmetric scalar quantization. In plain notation: q = round(clamp(x / S, -2^(bit-1), 2^(bit-1)-1))
Here S is the scale. The important part is not the scalar quantizer itself; it is how the scale is chosen. Group-Wise Weight QuantizationFor a weight matrix W, ZeroQuant partitions the matrix into groups and quantizes each group separately. This gives each group its own scale. Compared with matrix-wise quantization, group-wise quantization reduces the penalty from rows or blocks with small magnitude. The group size is not arbitrary. The paper explicitly considers hardware constraints on NVIDIA Ampere GPUs, where Tensor Core throughput depends on WMMA tile shapes. This is the system-aware part of the design: very fine groups might improve accuracy, but if they do not map well to GPU kernels, the final model may not be faster. The appendix gives the concrete settings used in the experiments:
Model Group count used for weight quantization
BERT-Base 48 groups
BERT-Large 64 groups
GPT-3 350M 64 groups
GPT-3 1.3B 128 groups
I read this as a core ZeroQuant principle: choose quantization granularity where the model distribution needs it, but keep the layout friendly to the backend. Token-Wise Activation QuantizationThe activation side is different because activations are dynamic. A static calibration range can be too conservative for many tokens and too small for outlier tokens. ZeroQuant instead uses token-wise activation quantization. Each token has its own activation range during inference, so the quantizer can adapt to token-level variation. The benefit is accuracy. The cost is that dynamic token-wise quantization can introduce extra operations: FP16 activation -> compute per-token scale -> quantize -> INT8 GEMM -> dequantize
If those steps are implemented as separate kernels, the extra memory traffic can eat the speedup. That is why the method and the kernel design have to be read together. Layer-By-Layer Knowledge DistillationW8A8 is the moderate target. For the more aggressive W4/8 settings, ZeroQuant adds layer-by-layer knowledge distillation, abbreviated as LKD. The usual full-model distillation setup is expensive for large models:
it may need both teacher and student models in memory; optimizer states are kept for many student parameters; training is end-to-end, so memory and compute scale with the whole model; original training data may not be available.
ZeroQuant’s LKD makes the optimization local. For layer L_k, it compares the original FP layer with the quantized copy of the same layer. Only that layer is optimized. input_k = L_{k-1}(...L_2(L_1(X)))teacher_y = L_k(input_k)student_y = quantized_L_k(input_k)loss = MSE(teacher_y, student_y)update only quantized_L_kthen move to the next layer
This has three practical consequences. First, it does not need a separate full teacher model. The original layer acts as the teacher for the quantized layer. Second, optimizer memory is small because only one layer is being updated. Third, labels are not required. The objective is local feature reconstruction, not task supervision. This makes it possible to use alternative text data when the original pretraining corpus is unavailable. This local nature is also the limitation. LKD reconstructs one layer at a time. It can miss error accumulation across layers, and it is weaker than a fully tuned end-to-end student. But it is cheap enough to be practical, which is the whole point of the paper. Quantization-Optimized KernelsThe kernel section is easy to skip, but it is essential. Token-wise activation quantization and group-wise weight quantization add scale handling around GEMM. A naive implementation can perform extra reads, writes, and kernel launches.
Figure 2. The normal path pays separate quantize and dequantize costs. ZeroQuant fuses activation quantization with the preceding operator and fuses dequantization into the GEMM epilogue. The paper’s backend uses CUTLASS INT8 GEMM and fusion:
activation quantization is fused with preceding operations such as LayerNorm, GELU, or bias-add; INT32 GEMM accumulation is dequantized in the GEMM epilogue using activation and weight scales; the output is written back as FP16 when the next operator is still FP16; CUDA Graph support is used to reduce CPU launch overhead for small models such as BERT-Base.
This explains why ZeroQuant can claim both accuracy and speed. Without these fusions, token-wise activation quantization would be a nice accuracy trick but a questionable serving method. BERT ResultsBERT is the cleanest place to see the difference between naive PTQ, ZeroQuant, and QAT.
Table 2. BERT-Base GLUE results. ZeroQuant recovers most of the W8A8 PTQ loss without QAT, and LKD helps the mixed INT4/INT8 settings. The headline numbers:
Setting Average score Average quantization time
FP16 baseline W16A16 83.95 N/A
W8A8 PTQ 77.41 6 seconds
W8A8 QAT 83.37 2900 seconds
W8A8 ZeroQuant 83.75 0 seconds
W4/8A8 ZeroQuant 81.55 0 seconds
W4/8A8 ZeroQuant-LKD 82.71 31 seconds
For W8A8, ZeroQuant is almost at the FP16 average and slightly above the internal QAT row in this table, with no activation calibration cost. I would not over-read the small difference between 83.75 and 83.37; the important point is that ZeroQuant is in the same accuracy band as QAT without QAT’s retraining cost. For W4/8, naive PTQ is not usable. W4/8A16 PTQ averages 33.11, close to random behavior on several tasks. ZeroQuant raises it to 81.65, and LKD raises it again to 82.35. The same pattern holds for W4/8A8: ZeroQuant gives 81.55, and LKD improves it to 82.71. The BERT-Large table in the paper follows the same broad pattern:
W8A8 PTQ average drops to 73.54; W8A8 ZeroQuant reaches 84.81 against an FP16 baseline of 85.03; W4/8A8 ZeroQuant-LKD reaches 81.62; LKD costs about 550 seconds per task on one A100, far below the reported QAT cost.
The main caveat is RTE. Both QAT and ZeroQuant struggle more on RTE, which is a small dataset and often has high variance. This is a reminder that average GLUE scores can hide task-specific fragility. GPT-3-Style ResultsDecoder-only generation makes the quantization problem sharper. A classification task can sometimes tolerate small hidden-state perturbations, but autoregressive generation exposes accumulated errors token by token.
Table 4. GPT-3 350M results. ZeroQuant fixes most of the W8A8 PTQ damage, while LKD is needed for usable mixed INT4/INT8 generation. For GPT-3 350M, the W8A8 result is the strongest moderate-precision claim:
Setting Average over 19 accuracy tasks Wikitext-2 PPL
W16A16 38.9 21.5
W8A8 PTQ 37.8 26.2
W8A8 ZeroQuant 38.7 21.7
ZeroQuant nearly removes the generation penalty: Wikitext-2 moves from PTQ’s 26.2 back to 21.7, close to the FP16 baseline 21.5. The low-bit setting is more revealing:
Setting Average over 19 accuracy tasks Wikitext-2 PPL
W4/8A16 ZeroQuant 33.5 88.6
W4/8A16 ZeroQuant-LKD 37.0 30.6
W4/8A8 ZeroQuant 33.4 92.1
W4/8A8 ZeroQuant-LKD 36.6 31.1
LKD does not fully restore FP16 generation, but it changes the result from badly degraded to meaningfully usable. The paper reports that this LKD pass costs about 1.1 hours on one A100 for GPT-3 350M, which is tiny compared with pretraining. The GPT-3 1.3B table shows the same direction. W8A8 ZeroQuant gets Wikitext-2 PPL 15.7, close to FP16 15.3 and better than PTQ 18.9. For W4/8, LKD again improves both average accuracy and generation perplexity. LatencyAccuracy preservation is only half the story. ZeroQuant also reports end-to-end latency with the fused INT8 path.
Table 6. BERT latency on one A100. The W8A8 path gives roughly 2.27x to 5.19x speedup on BERT-Base and 2.47x to 5.01x on BERT-Large depending on sequence length and batch size. The speedup is larger at higher batch sizes because the integer GEMM path is better utilized and the fixed overhead is amortized. But the table also shows speedups at batch size 1, which matters for online serving. The paper also reports decoder-side speedups:
Model Quantized setting Reported latency result
GPT-3 350M W8A8 4.16x speedup over FP16
GPT-3 1.3B W8A8 4.06x speedup over FP16
GPT-J 6B W8A8 29.13 ms to 7.94 ms for first-50-token generation, 3.67x
GPT-NeoX 20B W8A8/16 2 x 65 ms on two A100s to 1 x 25 ms on one A100, reported as 5.2x better efficiency
The GPT-NeoX 20B result has an important qualification. The paper could not quantize all activation inputs to self-attention in pure W8A8 without accuracy loss, so it uses A8/16: FP16 activation for self-attention calculation and INT8 elsewhere. This is a practical result, but it also shows that extra-large decoder models can still have sensitive activation paths. Ablation: Which Component Matters?The ablation table is one of the most useful parts of the paper because it separates the three pieces: group-wise weight quantization, token-wise activation quantization, and LKD.
Table 9. BERT-Large ablation under W4/8A8. Group-wise weight quantization prevents collapse; token-wise activation quantization gives the largest additional gain; LKD adds a smaller but consistent improvement. The average score progression is clear:
Components Average score
no GQ, no TQ, no LKD 35.85
GQ only 66.52
GQ + TQ 81.06
GQ + TQ + LKD 81.62
My read:
group-wise weight quantization is the first gate. Without it, mixed INT4/INT8 weights are too destructive; token-wise activation quantization is the biggest BERT-Large jump in this ablation, from 66.52 to 81.06; LKD’s average gain is small on this BERT-Large table, but it matters more for GPT generation under W4/8.
So I would not summarize ZeroQuant as “LKD solves PTQ.” The stronger summary is: fine-grained quantization solves most of the W8A8 and W4/8A8 representation issue, and LKD repairs the remaining low-bit damage when the quantized layer needs local reconstruction. Distillation Without Original DataBecause LKD uses layer outputs rather than labels, it can use data from outside the original training set.
Table 10. GPT-3 350M W4/8A8 LKD with different data sources. Wikipedia data is close to original training data, and even random token data improves over no LKD. This table is interesting for deployment teams. The original pretraining data may be private, unavailable, or too large to reconstruct. ZeroQuant shows:
no LKD: Wikitext-2 PPL 92.1; random data LKD: PPL improves to 40.6; Wikipedia data LKD: PPL improves to 30.4; original data LKD: PPL 31.1.
The random-data result should not be overstated. It does not mean random data is as good as real text. But it does support the paper’s local-reconstruction argument: even random token sequences can provide enough layer input variation for the quantized layer to learn a better approximation of the FP layer. The Wikipedia result is more practically useful. A clean public text dataset can be enough for LKD when original data is not available. Relationship To Later LLM QuantizationZeroQuant is not the final word on LLM quantization. Later methods became more specialized:
Method Main idea Difference from ZeroQuant
LLM.int8() Keep outlier channels in higher precision Explicitly isolates activation outliers instead of relying mainly on token-wise quantization
SmoothQuant Move activation outlier difficulty into weights through equivalent scaling Cleaner W8A8 transform for serving large LLMs
GPTQ Weight-only second-order reconstruction Stronger local solver for low-bit weights, usually without activation quantization
AWQ Activation-aware weight quantization Protects salient weight channels based on activation statistics
ZeroQuant Fine-grained W8A8/W4/8A8 plus LKD and fused kernels Broader system recipe across BERT and GPT-style models
This is why ZeroQuant still matters. It makes the serving constraint explicit: a quantizer is not successful unless the backend can run it efficiently. It also shows that activation quantization is not a minor detail for generation models. W8A8 needs a real activation strategy, not just weight rounding. Reproduction NotesIf I were reproducing ZeroQuant, I would start smaller than the full paper:
Pick one Transformer block and implement symmetric quantization for its linear layers. Compare matrix-wise weight quantization with group-wise weight quantization using layer-output error. Compare static activation calibration with token-wise dynamic activation quantization. Evaluate both classification accuracy and generation perplexity. Perplexity is more sensitive to accumulated quantization error. Add LKD for one quantized layer and verify that the local MSE objective reduces output error. Stack quantized layers progressively and check where error accumulation becomes visible. Only after the numerical path works, optimize the kernels. Otherwise it is hard to tell whether failures come from quantization math or backend layout.
The kernel checks I would add:
Check Why it matters
Scale layout matches GEMM tiling Bad scale reads can erase Tensor Core gains
Quantization fused with LayerNorm/GELU/bias-add Separate kernels add memory traffic
Dequantization in GEMM epilogue Avoids writing and rereading INT32 outputs
Batch/sequence-specific schedules Small batch serving and large batch throughput have different bottlenecks
CUDA Graph path for small models Kernel launch overhead can dominate BERT-Base latency
The most important experiment is not only “does W8A8 match FP16?” It is: Does W8A8 match FP16 after measuring the real fused-kernel path,with the same sequence lengths and batch sizes used in serving?
Without that, a quantization paper can look good in accuracy tables and still fail as a deployment method. LimitationsZeroQuant has several clear limitations. First, W4/8 generation still needs LKD and remains worse than FP16. The paper makes the low-bit setting practical, but it does not make it free. Second, the local LKD objective does not directly optimize final task loss or long-range generation behavior. Layer-wise reconstruction can reduce local error while still allowing small errors to accumulate through the network. Third, the best results depend on custom kernels. Token-wise activation quantization is not automatically fast in a generic framework. The method assumes a backend that can fuse quantization and dequantization with GEMM-adjacent operators. Fourth, the GPT-NeoX 20B result uses W8A8/16, not pure W8A8 for every activation path. That is a useful engineering compromise, but it shows that some self-attention activations remain sensitive at larger scales. Finally, this paper predates the modern 4-bit LLM deployment stack. If the target is weight-only 4-bit serving for very large decoder-only models, GPTQ/AWQ-style methods may be closer baselines. If the target is true W8A8 serving with integer GEMM, ZeroQuant and SmoothQuant are more directly relevant. TakeawayZeroQuant’s main contribution is the combination: fine-grained quantization+ layer-by-layer distillation for aggressive low-bit settings+ fused INT8 Transformer kernels= affordable PTQ that can actually serve large Transformers
The paper is worth reading because it does not separate algorithm and system concerns. Token-wise activation quantization fixes a real numerical problem, but it only becomes deployable after fusion. Group-wise weight quantization fixes a real representation problem, but the group layout has to respect GPU kernels. LKD helps low-bit weights, but it is designed around the memory constraints of large models. That is the enduring lesson: for large Transformer quantization, accuracy tables, calibration cost, memory layout, and kernel fusion are one problem.

entry.title: BlockQNN: Efficient Block-wise Neural Network Architecture Generation
entry.content:
Paper BlockQNN is a follow-up to early RL-based NAS papers such as NAS-RL and MetaQNN. The difference is the search unit. Instead of generating a whole CNN layer by layer, BlockQNN searches for a reusable block, then stacks that block to build the final network. That sounds like a small modeling change, but it matters. Modern CNNs are already built from repeated motifs: residual blocks, inception blocks, dense blocks, inverted residual blocks. If the repeated motif is good, the full network can scale to different depths and input resolutions with much less search cost. MotivationThe original NAS-RL formulation is expensive because the controller emits an entire architecture and then trains a child model to get a reward. MetaQNN makes the controller simpler by using Q-learning, but it still searches over whole layer sequences. BlockQNN asks a more constrained question:
Can we search for a good network block, then reuse that block as the building unit?
The figure compares hand-crafted blocks, earlier auto-generated whole-network designs, and BlockQNN’s block-wise search. The red box is the key point: the agent only needs to construct the inside of one block. The final network is obtained by stacking the learned block. ContributionThe paper’s useful contributions are:
It formulates block generation as a Q-learning problem, where the agent sequentially chooses layer/component codes. It uses an early-stop reward so sampled blocks do not need full training during search. It adds a distributed asynchronous framework to train sampled candidates in parallel. It proposes Faster BlockQNN, which predicts block performance before full training and reduces search cost. It reports strong results: 2.35% error on CIFAR-10, 32 GPUs for 3 days for standard BlockQNN, and a faster version using 1 GPU for about 20 hours.
The headline ImageNet number is also notable for an early NAS paper: the depthwise BlockQNN variant reports 82.0% top-1 and 96.0% top-5 when trained at 224 x 224 and tested at 320 x 320. MethodologyNetwork structure codeBlockQNN describes a block as a sequence of network structure codes. Each code stores the information needed to build one component layer. The paper’s state includes:
layer index, layer type, kernel size, predecessor 1, predecessor 2.
The predecessor fields are what allow multi-branch connectivity. A new layer does not have to consume only the immediately previous layer; it can point to earlier components inside the block. That is how the search space can include residual-like and inception-like wiring. Q-learning loopThe Q-learning setup is straightforward:
The agent starts from an input state, samples actions to create a block, stacks the block into a network, trains/evaluates that network, and uses validation accuracy as reward. The Q-table is updated with the usual Bellman-style rule:
The search uses epsilon-greedy exploration. Early in search, random actions dominate. As epsilon decreases, the agent exploits blocks with higher learned Q-values. This is similar in spirit to MetaQNN, but the state-action graph is now about block construction rather than full CNN generation. Early-stop rewardTraining every sampled block to convergence would make the method too slow. BlockQNN therefore trains candidates briefly and uses an early-stop reward:
The left plot shows why shaped intermediate rewards help: the learning curve with shaped reward rises faster than the one that ignores intermediate reward. The right plot explains the early-stop correction. Raw early accuracy is not always aligned with final accuracy, so the paper subtracts FLOPs and density terms to make the reward less biased toward overly large or dense blocks.
