This reward is an engineering compromise. It is not a perfect estimate of final accuracy, but it is cheap enough to run many times. Faster BlockQNNThe paper then adds a predictor to avoid training every sampled architecture:
Faster BlockQNN encodes each layer, embeds the layer sequence, feeds it through an LSTM, concatenates an epoch embedding, and predicts accuracy with an MLP. The idea is to learn from partial training curves and architecture structure so the search can rank candidates before spending full training cost. This faster version is less accurate than the standard BlockQNN setting, but the compute reduction is large: the paper reports a comparable result with 1 GPU in 20 hours. ResultsSearch behavior The Q-learning curve rises as epsilon decreases, and the top block candidates appear in the final exploitation stage. The discovered blocks are not random chains. They contain short connections and multi-branch structures, which is exactly the kind of pattern hand-designed residual and inception networks also use. The figure also shows a smaller Block-QNN-S block. This matters because the unconstrained search can produce large models; once parameter limits are added, the discovered structure is simpler but still competitive. Block variants The paper explores several variants:
Block-QNN-Connection: searches the connection style between blocks instead of simply stacking them. Block-QNN-Faster: uses the performance predictor to reduce search time. Block-QNN-Depthwise: replaces convolution with a depthwise-style cell to reduce parameters.
The results are easiest to read as tradeoffs:
Model Params CIFAR-10 error CIFAR-100 error
Block-QNN-S 6.1M 3.30 17.05
Block-QNN-S more filters 39.8M 2.80 15.56
Block-QNN-Faster 3.9M 3.57 18.21
Block-QNN-Faster more filters 34.4M 3.15 16.74
Block-QNN-Connection 3.9M 3.01 16.07
Block-QNN-Connection more filters 33.3M 2.35 14.83
Block-QNN-Depthwise 3.3M 2.58 15.28
The 2.35% CIFAR-10 number comes from the larger connection-search version. The 2.58% depthwise model is interesting for a different reason: it is much smaller and transfers well to ImageNet. Search cost
Method Best CIFAR-10 error GPUs Time
MetaQNN 6.92 10 10 days
NAS 3.65 800 28 days
NASNet-A 2.65 450 3-4 days
BlockQNN 2.80 32 3 days
Faster BlockQNN 3.15 1 0.8 days
Depthwise BlockQNN 2.58 32 3 days
Connection BlockQNN 2.35 32 1 day
The exact comparison is not perfectly apples-to-apples, because these papers use different search spaces and training recipes. Still, the direction is clear: searching reusable blocks cuts the cost dramatically compared with whole-network NAS. ImageNet transfer
Model Input Params Top-1 error Top-5 error
ResNet-152 224 60M 23.0 6.70
DPN-131 320 80M 18.55 4.16
NASNet-A (6 @ 4032) 331 89M 17.30 3.80
Block-QNN-B 224 95M 24.3 7.40
Block-QNN-S 224 - 21.9 6.16
Block-QNN-Depthwise 224 91M 19.00 4.58
Block-QNN-Depthwise train 224 / test 320 91M 18.00 4.00
The transfer result is the main argument for block-wise search. The block is learned on CIFAR-style tasks, but the depthwise version can be scaled to ImageNet and remain competitive. TakeawayBlockQNN is best read as a search-space paper. The Q-learning itself is simple; the important move is narrowing the generation problem from “build a whole network” to “build a reusable block”. The method still inherits the limits of its search space and training proxy. The searched blocks are CNN motifs, not arbitrary computation graphs, and the best numbers depend on extra choices such as block connection search, more filters, and depthwise operations. But as an early NAS engineering paper, it makes a useful point: reducing the granularity of search can be just as important as changing the search algorithm.

[CUDA]reduce

DARTS: Differentiable Architecture Search
entry.content:
Liu H, Simonyan K, Yang Y. DARTS: Differentiable Architecture Search. ICLR 2019.
Paper / Code DARTS is the paper that makes NAS feel much less like black-box search. NASNet and AmoebaNet search over discrete cells with RL or evolution, which works but costs thousands of GPU days. DARTS keeps the cell-based search space, relaxes the operation choice into a continuous variable, and updates architecture parameters with gradients. The method is not magic. It still depends on a hand-designed search space and a discrete cell extraction step at the end. But as a baseline for differentiable NAS, it is a clean paper: one softmax relaxation, one bilevel objective, and a small set of experiments that show the speed/quality tradeoff clearly. MotivationEarlier NAS methods usually treat architecture search as a discrete optimization problem. A controller or evolutionary loop samples a cell, the child model is trained or partially trained, and the validation score becomes feedback. That gives a natural search loop, but it is expensive because the architecture itself is not differentiable. DARTS asks a narrower question:
Can the operation choice on each edge be relaxed so that the architecture is optimized with gradient descent?
This fits the NASNet-style cell search space very well. Instead of searching a whole network directly, DARTS searches for a normal cell and a reduction cell, then stacks the selected cells into a larger network for final evaluation. ContributionThe paper contributes:
A continuous relaxation of discrete operation choices in a cell-based NAS search space. A bilevel optimization formulation where network weights are trained on the training set and architecture parameters are trained on the validation set. First-order and second-order approximations for the architecture gradient. Experiments on both convolutional cells and recurrent cells, including transfer from CIFAR-10 to ImageNet and from PTB to WikiText-2.
The headline numbers are:
Task DARTS result Search cost
CIFAR-10 2.76 +/- 0.09% test error 4 GPU days
PTB 55.7 test perplexity 1 GPU day
ImageNet mobile setting 26.7% top-1 error 4 GPU days
WikiText-2 69.6 test perplexity 1 GPU day
The paper reports NASNet-A at 2000 GPU days and AmoebaNet-A at 3150 GPU days in the same CIFAR/ImageNet comparison context. That is the main reason DARTS became a common baseline: it makes gradient-based NAS cheap enough to iterate on. MethodologyContinuous relaxationThe cell is represented as a directed acyclic graph. Each node is a latent feature representation, and each edge contains an operation. Before relaxation, selecting an operation is a categorical decision.
DARTS replaces each categorical edge operation with a mixed operation:
Here is the learnable architecture vector for edge . The network weights are the usual operation parameters, such as convolution weights. After this relaxation, the search problem becomes continuous in . For convolutional cells, the candidate operation set contains:
3x3 and 5x5 separable convolutions, 3x3 and 5x5 dilated separable convolutions, 3x3 max pooling and 3x3 average pooling, skip-connect, zero.
The zero operation means “no connection”. Reduction cells are handled separately from normal cells; the architecture parameters for normal cells and reduction cells are shared across all cells of the same type. Bilevel optimizationDARTS separates the two roles of the data split. Network weights are optimized on the training set, while architecture parameters are optimized on the validation set:
The exact inner optimization is too expensive, so the paper uses a one-step approximation. The practical loop is:
There are two versions:
Second-order DARTS uses a one-step unrolled weight update when computing the architecture gradient. First-order DARTS sets the unrolled step size to zero, so the architecture update assumes the current weights are already good enough.
The first-order version is cheaper, but the paper’s tables show it is usually worse: on CIFAR-10, first-order DARTS reports 3.00 +/- 0.14% test error, while second-order DARTS reports 2.76 +/- 0.09%. Deriving the discrete cellThe continuous model is not the final architecture. After search, DARTS converts the mixed graph back into a discrete cell. For each node, it keeps the strongest non-zero incoming operations from distinct previous nodes. The paper uses for convolutional cells and for recurrent cells. This detail is easy to miss: zero operations are excluded during the final selection. Otherwise a cell could end up with fewer useful incoming edges, and the comparison with previous cell-based NAS methods would be unfair.
The learned convolutional normal cell is mostly separable convolution and skip-connect edges. The reduction cell uses more pooling. The recurrent cell is learned with a similar mixed-operation idea, but its candidate operations are linear transformations followed by tanh, relu, sigmoid, identity, or zero. ResultsSearch progress The search curve is useful because it shows how little time the method needs before it finds cells in the range of NASNet/AmoebaNet references. For convolutional cells, the validation error gets close to the NASNet-A and AmoebaNet-A reference lines after tens of GPU hours. For recurrent cells, the initialization sensitivity is more visible: some runs improve quickly, while one run stays flat. CIFAR-10 and PTB The compact comparison:
Model Metric Params / search
ENAS + cutout on CIFAR-10 2.89% error 4.6M / 0.5 GPU days
Random search on CIFAR-10 3.29 +/- 0.15% error 3.2M / 4 GPU days
DARTS first-order on CIFAR-10 3.00 +/- 0.14% error 3.3M / 1.5 GPU days
DARTS second-order on CIFAR-10 2.76 +/- 0.09% error 3.3M / 4 GPU days
ENAS on PTB 58.6 test perplexity 24M / 0.5 GPU days
Random search on PTB 59.4 test perplexity 23M / 2 GPU days
DARTS first-order on PTB 57.6 test perplexity 23M / 0.5 GPU days
DARTS second-order on PTB 55.7 test perplexity 23M / 1 GPU day
The CIFAR-10 result is competitive with much more expensive search methods, but not strictly the best number in the table. AmoebaNet-B + cutout reports 2.55 +/- 0.05% error, at 3150 GPU days. DARTS is more interesting because it reaches a strong cell with a few GPU days. The PTB result is stronger: second-order DARTS reaches 55.7 test perplexity, slightly better than the manually tuned LSTM + 15 softmax experts row at 56.0. Transfer The CIFAR-10 searched cell transfers to ImageNet mobile setting with 26.7% top-1 error, 8.7% top-5 error, 4.7M parameters, and 574M multiply-adds. This is close to NASNet-A’s 26.0% top-1 error and 8.4% top-5 error, but with 4 GPU days of search instead of 2000.
The recurrent-cell transfer to WikiText-2 is less impressive than the PTB result but still beats the ENAS transferred cell in the table: DARTS gets 69.6 test perplexity, while ENAS gets 70.4. TakeawayDARTS is important because it changes the unit of NAS optimization. Instead of sampling complete discrete cells and waiting for rewards, it trains a supernet-like relaxed cell and lets validation gradients shape the operation probabilities. My main notes:
The bilevel split is the core idea: weights learn from training data, architecture learns from validation data. The first-order approximation is a useful speed knob, but the second-order version gives better reported results. The final discrete architecture is still obtained by a heuristic top-k extraction step, so the relaxation and the final cell are not exactly the same object. The random-search baseline is not terrible, which means the search space itself is doing a lot of work.
That last point is the practical lesson. DARTS makes NAS cheaper, but it does not remove the need to design a good search space. Later differentiable NAS papers spend a lot of effort on exactly this weakness: how to make the supernet training signal match the final discrete model more reliably.

entry.title: Real-time Federated Evolutionary Neural Architecture Search
entry.content:
Paper : Real-time Federated Evolutionary Neural Architecture Search. I will call the method FedEvo below. The interesting part of this paper is not that it uses evolutionary NAS again, but that it tries to make NAS happen inside the normal communication loop of federated learning. A conventional evolutionary NAS setup evaluates many candidate networks after training them, while federated learning already pays a high price for every communication round. If we naively combine the two, each client would have to download, train, and upload too many models. The paper’s answer is simple: keep one shared master model, sample sub-models from it, train those sub-models on sampled clients, and use NSGA-II to select architectures under both accuracy and FLOPs constraints. MotivationFederated learning has two constraints that make centralized NAS awkward. First, clients are usually small devices. Training a whole population of candidate networks on every client is unrealistic. Second, communication is the bottleneck. Sending a full model population, or retraining every offspring from scratch, quickly dominates the cost. The paper also points out a less obvious issue: many NAS methods rely on transfer, proxy tasks, or centralized validation. In FL, data is distributed and often non-IID, so the architecture that looks good on one data split or one client group may not be stable globally. So the target problem is:
Requirement Why it matters in FL
Search during training Avoid an expensive offline NAS stage.
Train only small sampled models Reduce local compute and upload size.
Reuse model weights Avoid reinitializing every offspring.
Optimize model size too Edge clients care about FLOPs, not only accuracy.
ContributionsThe paper has three concrete contributions.
Double sampling. For every evolutionary generation, the server samples both architectures and participating clients. A client trains only one sub-model in that generation instead of a full population. Sub-model aggregation. Uploaded sub-models are reconstructed back into the master-model parameter space. Trained branches use client updates; missing branches are filled from the previous master model before aggregation. Online multi-objective search. One generation of NSGA-II is aligned with one communication round. The objectives are test error and FLOPs (the paper reports FLOPs as MACs).
The high-level loop looks like this: for each communication round / generation: sample parent choice keys from the population generate offspring choice keys with crossover and mutation sample clients and assign one sub-model to each client group train sampled sub-models locally aggregate uploaded branches into the master model evaluate error and FLOPs for parent + offspring sub-models run NSGA-II selection for the next generation
The key detail is that NAS is not a separate pre-processing step. In this design, architecture search and federated training share the same rounds. Search SpaceThe master network is a small CNN for CIFAR-10. It starts with a convolution block, then uses 12 choice blocks grouped by channel width: 64, 128, 256, and 512. Each choice block has four candidate branches.
Each choice block chooses one of four candidates:
identity block residual block inverted residual block depthwise separable block
Because each choice block has four options, it can be encoded with 2 bits. With 12 choice blocks, an architecture choice key has 24 bits. This is a small search space by modern NAS standards, but it is enough for the paper’s point: reduce federated compute and communication while still searching over meaningful CNN blocks. Double SamplingThe double-sampling step has two levels. First, the server samples one sub-model from the master model according to a choice key. Instead of sending the whole supernet, the client receives a concrete path through the choice blocks. Second, the server samples clients. If there are total clients and the client participation ratio is , then the round samples clients. These clients are split over the evolutionary population of size , so one candidate is trained by roughly clients. This matters because each client sees only one sub-model per generation. The local workload becomes bounded by a single sampled network, not by the population size. AggregationAggregation is the part I found most useful in this paper. A client only trains the branches that exist in its sampled sub-model, but the server still needs to update one master model. The paper handles this by reconstructing a full master-shaped model for each upload:
branches selected by the client use the trained client weights; branches not selected by that client are copied from the previous master model; reconstructed models are averaged, weighted by client data size.
This is basically weight sharing plus federated averaging, but applied at the branch level. It avoids random reinitialization of offspring models, which is one reason the real-time version is more stable than the offline evolutionary baseline in the paper. NSGA-II ObjectiveFedEvo uses NSGA-II to keep a Pareto set instead of choosing one scalar reward. The two objectives are:
Objective Meaning
Test error Lower is better. Used as the accuracy-side fitness.
FLOPs (MAC) Lower is better. Used as the efficiency-side fitness.
The paper then marks two representative solutions on the Pareto front:
High: the solution with the highest accuracy; Knee: the solution near the knee point, usually a better accuracy/FLOPs tradeoff.
One small caveat: the paper writes “test error” as the fitness. In a production FL setup, I would expect this to be a validation metric or a server-side held-out evaluation, otherwise the test set becomes part of model selection. ExperimentsThe experiments are on CIFAR-10 with 50,000 training images and 10,000 test images. The paper simulates 10, 20, and 50 clients under both IID and non-IID splits. For non-IID, each client has images from 5 classes. Important settings:
Item Value
Dataset CIFAR-10
Clients 10, 20, 50
Local epoch 1
Train batch size 50
NSGA-II population 10
Generations / rounds 500
Baseline ResNet18 for CIFAR-10
Baseline FLOPs 0.5587G MAC
The Pareto fronts after 500 rounds are shown below. Lower-left is better: lower test error and lower FLOPs.
The table in the paper is worth reading directly because it shows the tradeoff clearly.
A few rows are enough to see the pattern:
Setting ResNet18 High solution Knee solution
10 clients, IID 81.14%, 0.5587G 86.68%, 0.2796G 83.36%, 0.031G
10 clients, non-IID 80.29%, 0.5587G 81.27%, 0.2272G 78.94%, 0.0302G
20 clients, IID 82.50%, 0.5587G 85.16%, 0.2012G 83.65%, 0.0398G
20 clients, non-IID 79.91%, 0.5587G 83.01%, 0.3936G 81.58%, 0.1098G
50 clients, IID 80.78%, 0.5587G 77.10%, 0.3360G 71.46%, 0.0547G
50 clients, non-IID 77.63%, 0.5587G 75.10%, 0.1719G 69.22%, 0.0635G
For 10 and 20 clients, the best evolved model usually beats ResNet18 while using fewer FLOPs. The knee solution is more aggressive: it gives up some accuracy but cuts computation heavily. The 50-client case is weaker. The paper explains this as a data-per-client issue: when total data is fixed, more clients means less local data per client, so it becomes harder to find a stable global model. Real-time BehaviorThe real-time curves for 20 clients are the most convincing part of the experiments.
At the beginning, ResNet18 is better. That is expected: the searched models are still being optimized while the master model is changing. After about 200 communication rounds, the selected high-accuracy and knee solutions catch up and pass ResNet18 in the reported 20-client settings. The FLOPs curves also show the point of multi-objective search. The knee solution stays far below ResNet18 in compute, while the high-accuracy solution fluctuates more because it is chasing accuracy during the search. The paper also compares against an offline evolutionary federated NAS baseline. In that baseline, the selected model is trained from scratch for 500 communication rounds. The reported runtime is about 16.1 hours/GPU for real-time NAS over 500 generations, versus about 6.55 hours/GPU for only 50 offline generations before retraining cost. The paper summarizes this as roughly a 5x speedup per search round for the real-time method.
TakeawaysI like this paper because it treats communication rounds as the unit of NAS cost. Many NAS papers hide the search cost behind a centralized proxy task; here, the search loop is forced to live inside FL. What I would keep from this paper:
Represent architectures with compact choice keys. Do not ask each client to train a population. Aggregate partial sub-model updates back into a shared master model. Optimize compute explicitly, not as an afterthought.
What feels limited:
The search space is small and CNN-specific. The experiments are only on CIFAR-10. The 50-client results show that the method is sensitive to data fragmentation. Using “test error” as the search fitness is not ideal if interpreted literally.
Overall, FedEvo is a useful early design for federated NAS: it is not the most powerful NAS method, but it gives a concrete recipe for making evolutionary search compatible with FL communication constraints.

entry.title: Hierarchical Representations for Efficient Architecture Search
entry.content:
Liu, Simonyan, Vinyals, Fernando, and Kavukcuoglu. Hierarchical Representations for Efficient Architecture Search. ICLR 2018.
Paper This paper is a useful counterweight to early NAS papers that made the controller or optimizer look like the main story. The central claim here is simpler: if the architecture representation is well structured, even simple search methods such as random search and tournament evolution become strong. Instead of searching one flat graph of primitive operations, the paper builds networks from motifs. Low-level motifs combine primitive operations. Higher-level motifs combine lower-level motifs. A change to a lower motif can therefore propagate through many parts of the final architecture. Representation Figure 1 shows the key idea. The bottom level contains primitive operations. A level-2 motif is assembled from those primitives. A level-3 motif is assembled from level-2 motifs. The final network is therefore a recursively composed graph, not just a one-shot list of edge operations. In plain notation: level-1 motifs = primitive operationslevel-l motif = assemble(graph at level l, motifs from level l-1)full network = top-level motif
The primitive set is intentionally small:
1x1 convolution; 3x3 depthwise convolution; 3x3 separable convolution; 3x3 max pooling; 3x3 average pooling; identity.
The paper also uses a none operation to represent missing edges. Larger receptive fields and wider computations are meant to emerge from composing these primitives rather than adding many hand-designed primitives. Why Hierarchy MattersThe representation encodes a strong prior: good neural networks often reuse patterns. ResNet blocks, Inception modules, MobileNet inverted residuals, and Transformer layers are all examples of repeated structure. Hierarchical NAS makes that reuse part of the search space. The tradeoff is bias. A hierarchical representation can make search efficient when the true solution has reusable substructure. It can also hide architectures that do not fit the recursive grammar.
Representation Search bias
Flat graph flexible, but harder to search and can grow parameter count quickly
Cell-based graph reusable normal/reduction cells with a fixed macro skeleton
Hierarchical motif reusable substructures at multiple levels
This is why I read the paper as a search-space paper more than an evolution paper. Search Algorithm The search algorithm is asynchronous tournament evolution. A controller maintains a queue of unevaluated genotypes and a memory table of evaluated genotypes. Workers repeatedly pop genotypes, assemble the architecture, train it from scratch, evaluate validation fitness, and write the result back. There is no ENAS-style weight sharing and no inherited weights from parent to child. Every architecture evaluation trains a model from scratch for a fixed number of steps. That makes the fitness estimate cleaner than one-shot NAS, but it also means the method still spends serious compute. The mutation operator changes one edge in one motif:
sample a non-primitive level; sample a motif at that level; sample a successor node and predecessor node; replace the edge operation with another operation from the previous level, possibly none.
This single rule can add an edge, remove an edge, or change an existing edge. In the hierarchical case, changing a lower-level motif can affect all higher-level places where that motif is reused. Model Evaluation Setup The paper searches for a convolutional cell on CIFAR-10, then evaluates the found cell in larger CIFAR-10 and ImageNet models. The experimental setup has three model sizes:
a small CIFAR-10 model used during architecture search; a larger CIFAR-10 model used for final cell evaluation; an ImageNet model that transfers the searched cell to a larger-scale task.
This is similar in spirit to NASNet: search a small reusable component, then scale it. The difference is that the searched component itself is hierarchical. Search Curves The authors run evolution for 7000 steps using 200 GPU workers. The first 200 steps are random initialization; after that, tournament selection and mutation start. Figure 3 has an important nuance:
the flat representation can reach higher small-model fitness; the flat representation also tends to create larger models; when the flat representation is parameter-constrained, it becomes closer to the hierarchical representation.
So the hierarchy is not magic accuracy by itself. It is a way to bias the search toward reusable structures without letting the parameter count grow as freely.
The authors also check whether search progress on the small model transfers to the final larger model. The curve is not perfectly proportional, but improvement in the small fitness generally corresponds to improvement in the large model. That matters because NAS often fails when the proxy task ranking does not transfer. Main Results Table 1 is the most useful result in the paper. The best hierarchical evolution run reports:
Search method CIFAR-10 error ImageNet top-1/top-5 error
Hierarchical random architecture 4.21 +/- 0.11 21.5 / 5.8
Hierarchical random search, 200 samples 4.04 +/- 0.20 20.4 / 5.3
Hierarchical random search, 7000 samples 3.91 +/- 0.15 21.0 / 5.5
Hierarchical evolution, 7000 samples 3.75 +/- 0.12 20.3 / 5.2
Two points stand out. First, random search is surprisingly strong. With 200 samples, it is only 0.29 percentage points worse than the best hierarchical evolution result on CIFAR-10 and only 0.1 top-1 error worse on ImageNet. Because 200 samples can be evaluated in parallel, the paper reports this random-search setting as about 1 hour with 200 P100 GPUs. Second, evolution is still the best result in the table, but the paper’s own evidence says representation quality is doing a lot of the work. Comparison To Prior Models On CIFAR-10, the best hierarchical evolutionary architecture reaches 3.75 +/- 0.12% error with c0 = 64, and 3.63 +/- 0.10% with c0 = 128. In the paper’s 2018 context, this is competitive with early RL-based NAS results such as NAS v3, Block-QNN, and NASNet-A.
On ImageNet, the transferred hierarchical architecture reports 20.3% top-1 error and 5.2% top-5 error. That is behind NASNet-A in the table, but still competitive with strong manual convolutional baselines from that period. The paper notes that the ImageNet model has 64M parameters, which is larger than NASNet-A’s 22.6M. Found Cell The learned cell uses motifs as edges. The paper notes that only motifs 1, 3, 4, and 5 are used in the final cell, with motifs 3 and 5 dominating.
The motif visualization is a good reminder that hierarchical NAS does not just learn “which operation goes on this edge.” It learns small graphs that become operations for the next level. Several motifs contain direct skip-style paths, so the final cell inherits skip connections through the motif hierarchy. TakeawayThe strongest lesson is that search-space design can dominate optimizer design. A well-built representation makes random search a serious baseline. This paper shows that with a hierarchical motif space, even 200 random samples are competitive with a much longer evolutionary run. The limitations are clear:
the method still trains candidate models from scratch; the reported search uses 200 P100 workers; the ImageNet model is larger than NASNet-A; the hierarchical grammar is a strong prior and may exclude useful flat architectures; the final result is a convolutional cell search result, not a general architecture generator.
I would use this paper as a reminder before designing a new NAS optimizer: first ask whether the representation already makes good architectures easy to sample. If random search is strong, the optimizer needs to clear a much higher bar.

entry.title: Joint Neural Architecture Search and Quantization
entry.content:
Paper JASQ is a useful paper to read after NASNet, ENAS, DARTS, and early hardware-aware NAS. The question is simple: if the final model will be compressed before deployment, why search for a float architecture first and only quantize it afterwards? The paper joins the two decisions. A candidate model contains both a NASNet-style cell architecture and a per-cell quantization policy. The search objective is not raw validation accuracy. It is validation accuracy under a target storage budget. That is the main idea worth keeping. ProblemClassical NAS mainly optimizes topology. Quantization mainly optimizes how weights are represented. In deployment, these two decisions interact:
A large architecture may tolerate lower precision because it has more redundancy. A small architecture may need more bits in sensitive cells to avoid an accuracy collapse. A uniform 8-bit policy is easy to implement, but it assumes every layer has the same quantization sensitivity.
JASQ turns the quantization bit-width into a searchable design choice.
The framework has two modes:
Fix an existing architecture, such as ResNet, DenseNet, MobileNet, or SqueezeNet, and search only its quantization policy. Search both the architecture and the quantization policy, producing JASQNet and JASQNet-Small.
The important difference from a normal NAS pipeline is the evaluation point. The candidate is trained, quantized, evaluated, and then ranked. So the evolution does not merely search for a strong float model; it searches for a model that survives the target compression policy. Search SpaceThe architecture space follows NASNet. A network is built by stacking two searched cell types:
Normal cell: keeps the feature map resolution. Reduction cell: reduces height and width by a factor of two.
The macro layouts for CIFAR-10 and ImageNet are shown below. The same cell idea is reused, but the ImageNet network has additional cells and stem layers.
The searched architecture can be written as two cell definitions:
Here is the normal cell and is the reduction cell. A cell is a directed acyclic graph made of several combinations. Each combination chooses two previous nodes as inputs and applies one operation to each input:
I read this formula as the atomic edit unit of the NAS space. The two ’s say where the data comes from; the two ’s say how the data is transformed. The two transformed tensors are added, and the outputs of all combinations are concatenated to form the cell output. The operation set is small and NASNet-like:
Type Choices
Convolution 3x3 separable convolution, 5x5 separable convolution
Pooling 3x3 average pooling, 3x3 max pooling
Skip / drop identity, zero
The quantization policy is another string attached to the architecture:
Each is the quantization bit-width for one cell. The paper searches over three choices:
For CIFAR-10, the number of cells is:
where is the stacking number in the macro architecture. In the reported search setting, , so:
The quantization-policy space alone is therefore:
This is the first practical difficulty in the paper. JASQ does not replace NASNet’s architecture space with a smaller one; it multiplies the architecture space by an additional quantization policies. That makes brute-force enumeration impossible and motivates the evolutionary search. ObjectiveA quantized model is represented as:
where is the architecture and is the quantization policy. After quantization, the model has validation accuracy and storage size . The search maximizes:
The size target is . The exponent switches according to whether the model satisfies the storage target:
This small piecewise definition is the core of the method. If the model is within budget, then , so:
and the objective becomes:
In other words, JASQ does not reward making an already-small model even smaller. Once the candidate satisfies the storage target, the search uses accuracy as the deciding criterion. If the model is larger than the target, then , so:
Now an oversized model is penalized in proportion to how much it exceeds the budget. This is a pragmatic objective: do not minimize size forever, but punish the candidates that cannot meet the deployment constraint.
The surface in Figure 3 makes the behavior clear. When size is below , the objective only follows accuracy. When size is above , the surface falls quickly. This turns a two-objective problem, accuracy and size, into a scalar fitness value that tournament selection can rank. Evolution StrategyThe search algorithm is classical tournament selection.
The variables in Algorithm 1 are:
Symbol Meaning
#P population size
#S number of individuals sampled from the population at each step
training set used to train a mutated candidate
validation set used to evaluate fitness
#E search-loop budget in the pseudo-code
The loop is:
Sample #S candidates from the current population. Rank the sampled candidates by . Select the best candidate as the parent. Select the worst candidate as the one to remove. Mutate the parent’s architecture and quantization policy. Train, quantize, evaluate, and score the child. Insert the child and remove the worst sampled candidate.
The architecture mutation and quantization mutation happen separately:
For architecture , randomly choose one field from in a cell combination and replace it with another legal choice. For policy , randomly choose one bit assignment from and reset it to one of 4 bit, 8 bit, or 16 bit.
This matters because the search can make small local changes in either topology or precision. It does not have to redraw the whole architecture every time. The appendix reports the final hyperparameters as #P = 16 and #S = 16. The paper also uses parameter sharing for acceleration, so the one-GPU, three-day search cost in Table 2 should be read as an ENAS-like evolutionary search rather than independent training of every candidate from scratch. Quantization DetailsThe quantization section is short, but it contains several details that affect how to interpret the storage numbers. Given a weight vector and bit-width , the quantized weight is:
The linear transform is:
Here maps an arbitrary weight vector into , and maps the quantized value back. The paper does not rely on one global scaling range for the entire network. Instead, it applies the scaling function to fixed-length consecutive buckets. The reason is simple. If a tensor contains a few large outliers, one global range can waste most of the quantization levels. Bucketed scaling gives different local chunks their own scale parameters, so the quantizer can spend its limited levels more effectively. The actual quantization function accepts a scaled value :
where the rounding indicator is:
This is nearest-neighbor rounding on a grid with step size . The first term gives the lower grid point. The second term adds one grid step when the fractional part is greater than . In implementation terms, the formula says: scale to , round to the nearest -bit level, and rescale back. The bucket metadata changes the compression ratio. Suppose a weight vector has elements. Full precision with bits per value needs:
bits. With bucket size , quantization bit-width , and two full-precision scaling parameters per bucket, storage becomes:
So the compression ratio is:
This formula is a useful reminder that mixed precision is not free. Smaller reduces the per-weight cost, but small buckets increase metadata overhead because every bucket stores two scaling parameters. Two extra implementation details from the appendix:
On ImageNet, the first and last layers are not quantized, following earlier quantization work. The quantized values are Huffman encoded to save additional space.
Fixed-Architecture QuantizationBefore doing joint search, the paper tests whether the quantization-policy search is useful on fixed ImageNet architectures.
Table 1 compares three versions of each model:
Float model. Uniform 8-bit model. JASQ mixed-precision policy.
Some representative rows are:
Model Float acc / size Uniform 8-bit acc / size JASQ policy acc / size
ResNet18 69.76 / 46.76 MB 69.64 / 11.47 MB 70.02 / 7.21 MB
ResNet34 73.31 / 87.19 MB 73.23 / 21.32 MB 73.77 / 11.92 MB
ResNet50 76.13 / 102.23 MB 76.15 / 24.74 MB 76.39 / 14.91 MB
MobileNet-v1 69.57 / 16.93 MB 68.77 / 4.05 MB 70.59 / 4.10 MB
MobileNet-v2 71.81 / 14.02 MB 68.06 / 3.45 MB 72.19 / 4.25 MB
SqueezeNet 58.09 / 2.35 MB 57.93 / 1.20 MB 60.01 / 1.22 MB
The surprising part is not only compression. The searched quantization policy often improves top-1 accuracy over the float model. For ResNet18, the mixed policy is points higher than float while using MB instead of MB. For MobileNet-v1, it gains points while shrinking from MB to MB. I would interpret these gains carefully. Lower precision itself is not magic. The likely explanation is that quantization-aware retraining and the mixed policy act as a useful regularizer, while the search avoids over-compressing sensitive cells. The mobile models show why uniform 8-bit is not always enough. MobileNet-v2 drops from to under uniform 8-bit, but the searched policy reaches . The JASQ policy is slightly larger than the uniform 8-bit version, yet it recovers the lost accuracy.
Figure 4 visualizes the same point as size-error trade-off curves. The blue baseline points are uniform 2/4/8/16-bit quantization. The red star is the searched policy. For ResNets and DenseNets, the red point is much smaller than 8/16-bit while staying near the low-error region. For MobileNet and SqueezeNet, the red point avoids the severe accuracy damage of overly aggressive uniform precision. Joint Architecture And Quantization SearchThe full JASQ experiment searches on CIFAR-10 for:
Then the searched cells are retrained from scratch on CIFAR-10 and transferred to ImageNet. There is one extra complication: the ImageNet macro-architecture has additional cells, so the CIFAR-10 quantization policy cannot be copied directly. The paper uses the CIFAR-10 policy to initialize another evolution search for the ImageNet quantization policy. Two models are reported:
Model Search target
JASQNet MB
JASQNet-Small MB
The key rows are:
Model CIFAR-10 error / size ImageNet error / size
JASQNet float 2.94 / 13.2 MB 27.25 / 18.8 MB
JASQNet 2.90 / 2.5 MB 27.22 / 4.9 MB
JASQNet-Small float 3.08 / 7.2 MB 34.14 / 11.2 MB
JASQNet-Small 2.97 / 0.9 MB 34.10 / 2.5 MB
The distinction between #Params/M and Size/MB is important. Quantization does not remove parameters, so the parameter count stays the same between JASQNet float and JASQNet. What changes is the number of bits used to store those parameters. JASQNet is not the most accurate architecture in Table 2. NASNet-A and AmoebaNet-B have lower CIFAR-10 error. But their search costs are hundreds of GPU-days, and their model sizes are much larger. The JASQ row is closer to the deployment question: how much accuracy can we keep when the model must be around a few MB? The searched cells are shown in Figure 5.
The cells still look like NASNet-family cells: two inputs, several intermediate nodes, separable convolutions, pooling, and skip-like paths. The paper does not discover a completely new macro design. Its contribution is the combined topology-plus-precision search under the size objective. Joint Search Versus Single SearchFigure 7 is the most direct summary of the paper’s claim.
The red circles are fixed architectures with quantization search only. The blue squares are architecture-search baselines without joint quantization. The orange point is JASQNet. The blue pentagon is JASQNet float. The gap between JASQNet float and JASQNet is the quantization-policy effect: error is almost unchanged, but size moves far left. Compared with only architecture search, JASQNet is much smaller. Compared with only quantization search on existing architectures, it reaches a better size-error position. This plot is also a good warning about what the method does not prove. JASQNet is not strictly better than every architecture search baseline in accuracy. The claim is trade-off quality under a storage constraint, not absolute top accuracy. Search Process AnalysisMany NAS papers search on a smaller proxy network and then evaluate a wider or deeper final network. JASQ tests whether that proxy trick helps here.
The red curve uses a small proxy setting with . The blue curve searches with the same width and depth used for evaluation, . The mean population fitness rises faster for the non-proxy setting, and the standard deviation drops faster. The paper interprets this as faster convergence. The result is reasonable for joint search. If quantization sensitivity depends on width, depth, and cell placement, then a small proxy network may distort the precision policy. Searching architecture alone can sometimes tolerate a proxy gap; searching architecture plus quantization makes the proxy mismatch more damaging. Table 3 lists the search/evaluation width and depth used by several NAS methods.
Here is the initial number of convolution channels and is the cell stacking number. DARTS, for example, searches with and evaluates with . JASQ uses for both search and evaluation. That is more expensive per sampled candidate, but it avoids searching a quantization policy on a network that differs too much from the final one. The appendix also studies the population size and sample size.
The notation P16 S16 means population size 16 and sample size 16. The experiments are run at small scale with for 100 iterations. The best curve in this sweep is P16 S16, which is why the main experiments use #P = 16 and #S = 16. One detail I like here: increasing the population size does not automatically improve the mean fitness curve. With a limited iteration budget, a very large population may reduce selection pressure or spread updates too thinly. The result is empirical, but it is a useful reminder that evolutionary NAS hyperparameters are part of the method, not just implementation trivia. LimitationsJASQ is clean, but it is also narrower than later hardware-aware NAS.
The objective optimizes storage size, not measured latency, energy, or memory bandwidth. The quantization policy is per-cell, not a fully layer-wise or operator-wise policy. The bit choices are limited to 4/8/16 bits. The ImageNet first and last layers are left unquantized. The search space is constrained to NASNet-style cells. The ImageNet architecture is transferred from CIFAR-style search, while the ImageNet quantization policy needs another search because the macro layout changes. The paper mostly discusses weight storage. Activation quantization and real inference kernels are not the focus.
These limitations matter. A 4.9 MB model is not automatically faster if the deployment stack does not have efficient mixed-precision kernels. Storage-aware search is a useful proxy, but it is not the same as hardware-aware search. TakeawayThe part I would remember from JASQ is the objective design:
This is a simple way to make NAS respect a deployment budget. The search does not blindly minimize size; it asks the model to fit under a target and then uses accuracy to choose among feasible candidates. JASQ is not a complete hardware-aware NAS system. But as a bridge paper, it is valuable: it moves quantization from a post-processing step into the architecture search loop. That idea shows up again in later mixed-precision, hardware-aware, and co-design methods.

entry.title: Large-Scale Evolution of Image Classifiers
entry.content:
Real E, Moore S, Selle A, et al. Large-Scale Evolution of Image Classifiers. ICML 2017.
Paper This paper is an early large-scale neural architecture search result, but it does not look like later RL-controller NAS or differentiable NAS. The algorithm keeps a population of trained CNNs, repeatedly mutates selected parents, trains the children, and uses validation accuracy as the selection signal. The interesting part is how little algorithmic machinery is needed. The search is black-box, asynchronous, and almost embarrassingly parallel. The expensive part is that every child still has to be trained for real. Result PositioningThe paper reports 94.6% CIFAR-10 accuracy for a single evolved model, 95.6% for an ensemble, and 77.0% on CIFAR-100. At the time, this was not just a toy architecture search demo.
Table 1 compares the evolved model with hand-designed CNNs. The evolved CIFAR-10 model is below the strongest Wide ResNet and DenseNet numbers, but it is competitive with a much less human-designed starting point. The “Reachable?” column also matters: some hand-designed baselines live outside the search space.
Table 2 is the more relevant comparison. Against other automatically discovered architectures, the evolutionary run reaches 94.6% on CIFAR-10, 77.0% on CIFAR-100, and 95.6% with an ensemble. The starting point is deliberately weak: a single layer with zero convolutions. Search LoopThe evolutionary loop is pairwise tournament selection: repeat asynchronously on many workers: sample two individuals from the population kill the lower-fitness individual copy the higher-fitness individual mutate the copy train the child insert the child back into the population
Fitness is validation accuracy. The population size in the main experiments is 1000, and the paper reports running experiments over 250 parallel workers. Each child is trained for 25,600 SGD steps with momentum 0.9, batch size 50, and weight decay 0.0001. The search object is a full CNN graph plus training hyperparameters, not a neat repeated cell. Mutations can insert or remove convolutions, alter filter size, channel count, stride, learning rate, skip connections, and weight state. Some mutations preserve all weights, some preserve none, and many preserve only the compatible subset. What Evolution Finds Figure 1 shows a useful shape: many weak individuals appear early, then the population quickly moves into a high-accuracy band. The architecture sketches attached to lineage points are also instructive. The evolved networks are not clean human-designed templates; they contain stacked convolutions, skips, and repeated convolution-BN-ReLU patterns in places that a human probably would not draw first. This is why I would not summarize the paper as “evolution invents ResNet.” It is closer to: given a mutation grammar and enough training budget, local search can build competent CNN programs from very weak initial conditions. Controls The controls are important. Random search is much worse in the reported wall-clock comparison. Evolution without weight inheritance is close early on but stays lower later. That does not prove evolutionary search is always better, but it does show the result is not only coming from repeatedly sampling random architectures. The paper also makes a practical point about asynchronous search. Fast-training bad models can return early, enter the population, and get more chances to reproduce. That implicit bias is part of the system, so any reproduction should preserve the worker behavior instead of only copying the mutation list. Meta-Parameters The population-size and training-step sweeps explain why small NAS demos can be misleading. Larger populations explore more lineages, and longer child training gives the fitness estimate a better chance to reflect the architecture rather than just early optimization noise. The downside is direct: the main result costs a huge amount of compute. The paper reports the best CIFAR-10 run at about 4 x 10^20 FLOPs, with the five-experiment average around 9 x 10^19 FLOPs. This is not a cheap recipe. Local Optima Figure 4 is a good reminder that evolutionary search is not magic. Populations can plateau. The authors tried increasing the mutation rate and resetting weights to help populations escape local optima. Both can work, but both are blunt tools. The weight reset example is especially interesting. Weight inheritance helps make full-model evolution practical, but it can also make a mediocre architecture look good because it has accumulated more training. Resetting weights partially breaks that advantage and forces the population to re-evaluate architecture quality. TakeawayLarge-Scale Evolution is rough by modern NAS benchmark standards. The search space is broad, the compute budget is large, and the results are not directly comparable to later cell-based search spaces or tabular NAS benchmarks. The durable lesson is simpler: architecture search does not need a controller, relaxation, or differentiable proxy to be useful. If the evaluation loop is scalable and the mutation operators preserve enough structure, plain evolutionary pressure can discover strong trained models.

entry.title: Designing Neural Network Architectures using Reinforcement Learning
entry.content:
Paper / Project / Code MetaQNN is one of the early reinforcement-learning based NAS papers. It is worth reading together with Zoph & Le’s controller-RNN NAS paper, because the search strategy is different: instead of training an RNN controller to emit architecture strings, MetaQNN uses tabular Q-learning over a hand-designed state-action graph. The paper is not trying to discover arbitrary neural computation. The search space is deliberately limited to standard CNN components: convolution, pooling, fully connected layers, global average pooling, and softmax. That constraint is important. The interesting part of the paper is how the authors turn “choose a CNN architecture” into a finite-horizon Markov Decision Process that can be explored with a practical amount of computation. MotivationCNN design contains many coupled choices: layer type, ordering, filter size, number of channels, stride, pooling position, and termination point. Exhaustively enumerating this space is impossible even when every option is discretized.
Figure 1 summarizes the whole loop: sample a topology, train it, store its validation accuracy, and update the Q-values from replay memory. The paper’s framing is direct:
Let an agent build a CNN one layer at a time. Train the sampled CNN on the target dataset. Use validation accuracy as the reward. Update the agent so that future sampled architectures become better.
This is a clean formulation, but it only works if the architecture space is constrained enough. MetaQNN therefore spends a lot of effort on the state definition and action restrictions, not only on the reinforcement learning update. ContributionThe useful contributions are:
Formulate CNN architecture generation as a finite MDP, where a trajectory is a full network topology. Define a discrete state space for common CNN layers and use action constraints to avoid invalid or obviously degenerate networks. Use Q-learning with epsilon-greedy exploration and experience replay to search the architecture graph. Show that the discovered CNNs can outperform earlier networks that use only standard convolution, pooling, and fully connected layers. Release model definitions and code, although the original implementation is tied to an old Caffe/Python 2 stack.
The last point matters historically. MetaQNN is not only a conceptual NAS paper; it includes trained topologies, Caffe prototxt files, and a server-client training setup. MethodologyState and Action Space The MDP view is the core modeling choice. A path through this graph corresponds to one CNN, and the green path in the figure is one sampled architecture. Each state represents the current layer choice plus enough metadata to decide what layer can come next. The notation used in the paper is:
C(d, f, l): convolution with d filters, receptive field size f, and stride l. P(f, l): pooling with receptive field size f and stride l. FC(d): fully connected layer with d neurons. GAP / SM: global average pooling or softmax termination.
The experimental search space is small enough for tabular Q-learning but still large enough to contain useful CNNs:
Layer type Main choices
Convolution layer depth < 12, filter size {1, 3, 5}, stride 1, channels {64, 128, 256, 512}
Pooling layer depth < 12, (filter, stride) in {(5, 3), (3, 2), (2, 2)}
Fully connected layer depth < 12, at most two consecutive FC layers, neurons {512, 256, 128}
Termination global average pooling or softmax
The state also includes a binned representation size. This prevents the agent from repeatedly shrinking a feature map until later convolutions or pooling operations no longer make sense. For example, too many stride-2 pooling layers can reduce a 32 x 32 image to 1 x 1, so the action graph disallows transitions that would create invalid feature maps. This is one of the most practical pieces of the paper: NAS needs a search space, but it also needs guardrails. Without them, much of the budget would be wasted on architectures that are legal as strings but useless as CNNs. Q-learning LoopMetaQNN uses the standard Q-learning update:
where s_i is the current state, u is the action, s_j is the next state, and the reward r is the validation accuracy of the completed CNN. The paper sets:
alpha = 0.01 gamma = 1 initial Q-values to 0.5 final policy to epsilon = 0.1, not 0, so the final sampler can still generate several high-quality variants for ensembling
The search loop is:
Sample a CNN topology by walking through the state-action graph with epsilon-greedy exploration. Train the sampled topology with a short, aggressive schedule. Store the topology and validation accuracy in replay memory. Sample 100 previous models from memory and update Q-values backward along their trajectories. Anneal epsilon and repeat.
The epsilon schedule is deliberately exploration-heavy at the beginning:
Epsilon 1.0 0.9 0.8 0.7 0.6 0.5 0.4 0.3 0.2 0.1
Unique models trained 1500 100 100 100 150 150 150 150 150 150
So one full search run trains about 2700 unique models before the final fine-tuning stage. During exploration, each model is trained for only 20 epochs with Adam, batch size 128, initial learning rate 0.001, and dropout inserted after every two layers. The reported search cost is 8-10 days per dataset on 10 NVIDIA GPUs. Why Replay Memory Helps HereIn a normal supervised training loop, one minibatch update is cheap. In NAS, one “environment step” can mean training a CNN. MetaQNN therefore cannot afford to learn only from the most recent sampled architecture. The replay dictionary gives each trained architecture multiple chances to update the Q-table. If the same topology is sampled again, the paper does not retrain it; it reuses the stored validation accuracy. This is a simple engineering choice, but it matters because the expensive part is CNN training, not the Q-value update. ResultsSearch Behavior The Q-learning curves are the first sanity check. As epsilon decreases, the sampled models should become better on average. The paper reports that, for SVHN, mean model accuracy increases from 52.25% at epsilon = 1.0 to 88.02% at epsilon = 0.1. This does not prove that the agent found a globally optimal architecture. It does show that the Q-table learned useful preferences inside the constrained search graph. The learned preferences are also interpretable. In the appendix, the authors analyze Q-values by layer depth: convolution and pooling have higher Q-values early in the network, while fully connected and termination states become more likely deeper in the network. That matches the rough shape of hand-designed CNNs. Benchmark NumbersMetaQNN is strongest when compared with networks using similar layer types. The top CIFAR-10 model reaches 6.92% test error, better than the standard-layer baselines listed in the paper.
Method CIFAR-10 SVHN MNIST CIFAR-100
All-CNN 7.25 - - 33.71
MetaQNN ensemble 7.32 2.06 0.32 -
MetaQNN top model 6.92 2.28 0.44 27.14
ResNet-110 6.61 - - -
ELU network 6.55 - - 24.28
Tree+Max-Avg pooling 6.05 1.69 0.31 32.37
All numbers are test error percentages. The comparison against ResNet and more complex pooling methods is less flattering, but also less direct: those models use architectural ideas outside the MetaQNN search space. The more honest reading is that MetaQNN does well within a plain CNN search space, but the search space itself limits the ceiling. Discovered ArchitecturesThe top CIFAR-10 architecture reported in the appendix is: C(512,5,1) - C(256,3,1) - C(256,5,1) - C(256,3,1) -P(5,3) - C(512,3,1) - C(512,5,1) - P(2,2) - SM(10)
It reaches 6.92% test error with 11.18M parameters. The top five CIFAR-10 models range from 11.18M down to 1.10M parameters, but the error varies from 6.92% to 11.63%. That spread is a useful reminder: validation-guided architecture search can find good candidates, but the top architectures are not all equally strong. One design motif mentioned in the paper is the frequent use of 1 x 1 convolution near the input. The authors interpret it as a learned linear transformation of RGB channels, similar in spirit to preprocessing into another color space. I would treat that as an observation rather than a general rule, but it is a nice example of Q-value analysis producing inspectable architecture hints. TransferThe authors also test whether the best CIFAR-10 architecture transfers to other datasets. SOTA means the reference state-of-the-art number listed in the paper.
Target Scratch Fine-tune SOTA
CIFAR-100 27.14 34.93 24.28
SVHN 2.48 4.00 1.69
MNIST 0.80 0.81 0.31
The architecture transfers better than the weights. Fine-tuning from CIFAR-10 weights is worse than training from scratch in all three reported cases. That is not too surprising: the searched architecture can be reusable, but the learned filters from CIFAR-10 are not necessarily a good initialization for digit datasets or CIFAR-100. TakeawayMetaQNN is a good example of early NAS engineering. The paper’s main lesson is not that Q-learning is the final answer for architecture search. Later work moved toward controller RNNs, cell-based search, weight sharing, differentiable NAS, and hardware-aware search because training thousands of child models is too expensive. The lasting idea is the decomposition:
Define a searchable but valid architecture graph. Use a cheap policy representation over that graph. Evaluate sampled architectures with a consistent reward. Reuse expensive evaluations through replay or other performance-estimation tricks.
The limitation is equally clear. The method inherits the bias of its search space: only standard CNN layers, coarse discrete hyperparameters, and fixed training recipes. It can discover strong combinations inside that box, but it cannot invent residual blocks, depthwise separable convolutions, attention, or hardware-aware operators unless those choices are explicitly added to the state-action graph. For me, MetaQNN is most useful as a baseline mental model for NAS: before thinking about supernets or differentiable relaxations, first ask what the states are, which actions are legal, how much one reward costs, and whether the search space itself is the real bottleneck.

entry.title: MONAS: Multi-Objective Neural Architecture Search
entry.content:
Paper MONAS is not trying to invent a new cell search space. The paper is more about the objective: if a model is going to run under a power or energy budget, searching only for validation accuracy is the wrong optimization problem. The useful idea is straightforward: keep the usual controller-and-child-network NAS loop, but make the reward multi-objective. Accuracy is still there, but energy, peak power, or MAC operations can become part of the reward or a hard constraint. MotivationEarly NAS papers mostly asked one question: which architecture gives the best validation accuracy? That is fine for benchmark chasing, but less useful for deployment. A model with slightly better accuracy can be a bad choice if it burns too much energy or violates a device power budget. MONAS puts this deployment concern into the search loop instead of checking it after the fact. The paper evaluates this on CIFAR-10 using AlexNet-like and CondenseNet-like search spaces, then extends the idea with MONAS-S for a larger ENAS-style weight-sharing search space. ContributionThe paper makes three concrete contributions:
It formulates NAS as a multi-objective search problem, with reward functions that include accuracy, energy, peak power, or MAC constraints. It measures power and energy with NVIDIA nvprof, so the non-accuracy objective is tied to actual execution rather than only FLOPs. It extends the idea to MONAS-S, a weight-sharing version that searches a much larger space faster and biases the controller toward lower-MAC operations.
The paper’s most interesting claim is not that MONAS beats every classifier. It is that the controller can be steered toward a region of interest: under 70 W peak power, above 0.85 accuracy, or below a MAC threshold. MethodologyController loopMONAS keeps the classic NAS structure: an RNN controller samples a target CNN, the target CNN is trained/evaluated, and the measured objectives become the reward.
For the AlexNet-like search space, the controller predicts filter number, height, and width for each convolutional layer. For the CondenseNet-like search space, it predicts dense-block stage and growth values. This is a narrower space than later NAS cell-search papers, but it is enough to study objective design. Multi-objective rewardsThe paper discusses several reward shapes. The mixed reward trades off normalized accuracy and energy:
The hard-constraint versions are more deployment-like:
and:
For MONAS-S, MAC operations are used as a proxy constraint:
The exact reward is not the main point. The useful part is that the search can be aimed at the constraint users actually care about. MONAS-SMONAS-S borrows the weight-sharing idea from ENAS. Instead of training every sampled architecture from scratch, it trains a shared DAG and updates the controller from sampled subgraphs. This makes it practical to search a 12-layer space with roughly possible networks. The target network contains 12 layers. The first 4 layers have the largest feature maps, the next 4 are half-size, and the last 4 are half-size again. This detail matters because early-layer operations dominate MAC cost. ResultsConstraint steering The scatter plots show a useful sanity check. Random search spreads samples across the space. MONAS concentrates samples near the requested region:
Constraint Satisfied samples
Peak power < 70 W 340 / 600
Accuracy >= 0.85 498 / 600
This is the part I like: the controller is not just finding a high-accuracy model; it is learning where to spend search budget under a user-defined constraint. CondenseNet comparisonMONAS also finds CondenseNet-like configurations with better energy-accuracy tradeoffs than hand-picked baselines.
Model Error Energy / 1000 inf.
CondenseNet 122 4.48 129.37 J
CondenseNet 110 4.63 108.74 J
CondenseNet 74 5.28 56.35 J
CondenseNet-MONAS 4.34 92.16 J
CondenseNet-MONAS 5.07 42.46 J
CondenseNet-MONAS 5.60 34.88 J
This table is a reminder that “best” depends on where you are on the Pareto front. A 4.34% model is accurate but not the cheapest; a 5.60% model is much cheaper but gives up accuracy. MAC-aware search with MONAS-S When MONAS-S adds a MAC constraint, the sampled architectures move toward the lower-MAC region. The paper compares this against ENAS-like sampling without the MAC constraint, both trained for 600 epochs and then sampled for 1000 target networks.
The operation distribution explains where the saving comes from. MONAS-S uses more MAC-efficient operations, especially in early layers where feature maps are large. That is exactly the right place to reduce computation. TakeawayMONAS is an early reminder that NAS should optimize the real objective, not just the leaderboard metric. Accuracy-only NAS can easily produce architectures that are awkward for deployment. The limitation is that the paper’s search spaces are still relatively constrained, and the hardware measurements are tied to the tested GPU setup. But the main lesson transfers well: make the search reward reflect the target constraint, then look at the Pareto front instead of a single scalar “best model”.

entry.title: Neural Architecture Search with Reinforcement Learning
entry.content:
Zoph B, Le Q V. Neural Architecture Search with Reinforcement Learning. arXiv:1611.01578, 2016.
Paper This is the paper that made the phrase “Neural Architecture Search” concrete for a lot of people: use an RNN controller to generate a network description, train that child network, then use its validation accuracy as the reward for the controller. It is expensive and not how most practical NAS is done now. But the formulation is still worth reading because later papers either accelerate it, constrain it, or replace its controller/search space while keeping the same basic feedback loop. MotivationBefore NAS, architecture design was mostly manual: AlexNet, VGG, Inception, ResNet, DenseNet, and so on. The authors’ question is simple: if a neural network architecture can be serialized as a sequence of design decisions, can another neural network learn to emit that sequence? The proposed loop is:
The controller samples an architecture with probability . The child model with architecture is trained and evaluated. The resulting accuracy scales the gradient used to update the controller, so better architectures become more likely. ContributionThe paper contributes:
An autoregressive RNN controller that samples architecture tokens. A REINFORCE update using child validation accuracy as a non-differentiable reward. Extensions for skip connections, pooling, and recurrent-cell search. Large-scale distributed training to make the otherwise brutal search loop feasible.
The headline results are strong for the time:
Task Result
CIFAR-10 3.65% test error
PTB word-level LM 62.4 test perplexity
PTB character LM 1.214 bits/char
The cost is also very real: for CIFAR-10, the controller evaluated 12,800 architectures and the paper reports 800 child networks trained concurrently. MethodologyController as a token generatorFor a convolutional child network, the controller emits architecture tokens layer by layer: filter height, filter width, stride, number of filters, and so on.
This turns architecture design into a sequence modeling problem. After the controller emits a complete sequence, a child model is built from those tokens and trained. REINFORCE objectiveLet the sampled architecture decisions be , and let be the validation reward after training the child network. The controller maximizes:
The expectation is over architectures sampled from the controller distribution . Because is non-differentiable with respect to the architecture tokens, the paper uses a REINFORCE-style estimator:
Here is the moving-average baseline used to reduce variance. In practice, the update is estimated from a batch of sampled architectures. Distributed trainingThe expensive part is child training. One controller update needs feedback from many architectures, and every architecture may take hours to train.
The paper uses a parameter-server setup with many controller replicas. For CIFAR-10, it uses 20 parameter-server shards, 100 controller replicas, and 8 child replicas per controller replica. That is where the famous 800 concurrent networks number comes from. Skip connections and recurrent cellsA plain token list can describe sequential CNNs, but modern networks need skip connections. The controller therefore adds anchor-point decisions to select previous layers as inputs.
For language modeling, the controller searches over a recurrent cell instead of a CNN. The cell is built as a tree of operations combining , , and memory variables.
This part is important historically: the method is not tied to CNN layer hyperparameters. It is a general “emit a discrete architecture, train it, reward it” recipe. ResultsCIFAR-10
Model variant Depth Params Error
NAS v1, no stride/pooling 15 4.2M 5.50%
NAS v2, predicting strides 20 2.5M 6.01%
NAS v3, max pooling 39 7.1M 4.47%
NAS v3 + more filters 39 37.4M 3.65%
The best CIFAR result is 3.65% test error. The model is not tiny, but it shows that the controller can discover competitive CNNs from scratch. Penn Treebank
Model Params Test perplexity
Variational RHN, shared embeddings 24M 66.0
NAS cell, base 8 32M 67.9
NAS cell, shared embeddings 25M 64.0
NAS cell, larger shared embedding model 54M 62.4
The discovered recurrent cell beats the reported LSTM/RHN baselines in the paper, with the best word-level model reaching 62.4 test perplexity. The paper also reports 1.214 bits per character on PTB character modeling. RL versus random search The random-search comparison is a useful control. The controller does not just find one lucky architecture; the top-k average improves over random search as training progresses. TakeawayThe biggest contribution is the formulation: architecture search as policy learning over discrete design choices. It gave later NAS papers a common template to improve:
reduce search cost with weight sharing, design a more transferable search space, add hardware-aware objectives, or replace the RL controller with differentiable relaxation.
The obvious limitation is cost. Training thousands of child networks is too expensive for ordinary use. Reading this paper today, I treat it less as a practical recipe and more as the baseline that later NAS work is reacting to.

entry.title: Progressive Neural Architecture Search
entry.content:
Liu C, Zoph B, Shlens J, et al. Progressive Neural Architecture Search. ECCV 2018.
Paper PNAS is a practical answer to the main weakness of early NAS papers: the controller or evolution algorithm spends a huge amount of compute on complete cells before it has any useful knowledge about the space. The paper keeps the NASNet-style cell idea, but changes the search procedure. Instead of sampling a full 5-block cell directly, it grows cells from 1 block to 5 blocks. At each depth, a predictor ranks the expanded candidates, and only the top beam is actually trained. The key point is that PNAS is not differentiable NAS. It is closer to sequential model-based optimization: evaluate a small batch of candidates, fit a surrogate, use the surrogate to prune the next expansion, then spend real training only on the survivors. Why This Paper MattersBefore PNAS, the typical NAS story was expensive. NASNet uses an RNN controller trained by reinforcement learning, then performs an additional re-ranking stage. AmoebaNet improves the final model but still pays a large search budget. PNAS asks a narrower question: if the architecture is a graph built from small blocks, can we search the graph in an order that avoids most of the combinatorial explosion? The answer is yes, as long as three assumptions are good enough:
small cells contain signal about larger cells; the predictor ranks candidates well enough, especially near the top; the beam size is large enough to avoid pruning every promising partial design.
This is why I read PNAS as a sample-efficiency paper, not mainly as a new architecture paper. The final PNASNet cell is useful, but the more reusable idea is the search schedule. Cell Search SpacePNAS searches for a convolutional cell. A full CNN is built by stacking this cell many times. The paper deliberately learns only one cell type. A cell with stride 1 behaves like a normal cell, and a cell with stride 2 behaves like a reduction cell. This makes the search space smaller than the original NASNet space, which searches normal and reduction cells separately.
The left side of the figure is the best 5-block cell found by PNAS. The right side shows how the same cell is stacked for CIFAR-10 and ImageNet. This matters because the search itself is performed on small CIFAR-10 models, then the discovered cell is transferred into larger ImageNet networks. A cell receives two previous cell outputs, which I write as and . Inside cell , block can choose inputs from the two previous cell outputs and all earlier block outputs in the same cell:
The interpretation is simple: block 1 has only the two previous cell states, so it has 2 possible input tensors. Block 2 can also use the output of block 1, so it has 3 possible input tensors. This is why the number of possible input choices grows with the block index. Each block chooses two inputs, applies one operation to each, and combines the two branches. The paper writes a general block as:
Here and are input choices from , and are operations, and is the combiner. In this paper, is fixed to addition, so the effective block output is:
I like this formula because it makes the cell graph concrete. A block is not a layer in the usual sequential sense. It is a small two-branch DAG fragment. The final cell output is then formed by concatenating unused block outputs. The operation set has 8 candidates:
3x3 depthwise-separable convolution; 5x5 depthwise-separable convolution; 7x7 depthwise-separable convolution; 1x7 followed by 7x1 convolution; identity; 3x3 average pooling; 3x3 max pooling; 3x3 dilated convolution.
For one block at level , the raw number of choices is:
This formula says: choose the first input, choose the second input, choose the first operation, choose the second operation, and choose a combiner. Since PNAS fixes and uses , the first block has:
raw possibilities. The paper reports 136 unique one-block cells after removing symmetric duplicates caused by addition. That distinction is important later: the algebraic raw count is 256, but the actual number trained in the first stage is 136. For a 5-block cell, the unconstrained raw space is:
This is the first formula in the paper that really motivates PNAS. The cell has only 5 blocks and 8 operations, but the raw space is already hundreds of trillions. Even after symmetry pruning, the paper estimates roughly unique cells. Brute force is not a serious option. Progressive SearchThe algorithm below is the whole paper in one page. Start from all one-block cells, train them, fit a predictor, expand the current beam by one block, predict the expanded set, keep only top-, then repeat.
The core recurrence is:
I read it as three separate actions:
is the large child set produced by appending every possible block- choice to each surviving -block cell. is the predicted validation accuracy of those children. These predictions are cheap. is the beam that will actually be trained and evaluated. These evaluations are expensive.
The figure below shows this search tree view. PNAS does not expand the entire tree. It expands from the current beam, scores many children with the predictor, and pays training cost only for the selected layer of the tree.
For the main experiment, the paper uses blocks and . The number of trained models is:
This formula is easy to underestimate. PNAS still scores far more candidates than 1160 with the predictor, but it trains only 1160 CNNs. That is the expensive part. The rest is surrogate inference. Predictor DesignThe predictor is the fragile part of the method. If it ranks useful children too low, they disappear from the search tree permanently. The paper therefore evaluates the predictor with rank correlation, not just regression error. There are two predictors:
an RNN/LSTM predictor that reads the cell as a variable-length token sequence; an MLP predictor that embeds each block and averages block embeddings into a fixed-length cell representation.
For a cell with blocks, the RNN receives a token sequence of length :
The interpretation is that every block contributes four design tokens: two inputs and two operations. This representation naturally handles variable-depth cells, but it can overfit when the number of evaluated cells is small. The MLP predictor first embeds each token into a -dimensional vector and concatenates the four embeddings of each block:
Then it averages over blocks:
This loses some ordering information, but it creates a stable fixed-size representation for any . In the paper, this simple MLP ensemble works surprisingly well for the extrapolation setting. Both predictors are trained with loss. The paper also uses an ensemble of 5 predictors trained from scratch on 4/5 of the available data at each stage. This is not just an implementation detail: with so little data, ensembling reduces variance in the predicted ranking.
The scatter plots show the important failure mode. On the current level, the predictor can correlate well with observed performance. Predicting the next larger level is harder. At , extrapolating to 2-block cells has rank correlation only 0.142 in the MLP-ensemble plot. Later stages improve because the predictor has seen more and larger cells. The paper summarizes this with Spearman rank correlation:
measures ranking quality on the same block depth used for training. measures extrapolation to the next larger cell. The second number is more relevant for PNAS because the predictor is used before the new children are trained.
The table is a good reminder that a NAS predictor does not need perfect calibration. It needs the top candidates to be roughly right. In Table 1, MLP-ensemble has strong extrapolation at later stages: , , and . These are not huge correlations, but they are enough to beat random expansion when combined with a beam of 256. Search EfficiencyThe main efficiency plot compares PNAS, NAS, and random search under the same cell search space. Each sampled model is trained for 20 epochs on CIFAR-10, and the figure tracks the best top- validation accuracy found as the number of trained models grows.
The shape of the plot is the most important part. PNAS climbs quickly because each level uses the predictor to avoid most children. Random search is slower because it has no structure. NAS improves, but the curve is flatter because the controller still samples complete cells and has to learn through expensive feedback. The table below gives a compact speed comparison using the MLP-ensemble predictor.
For top-1 validation accuracy, PNAS reaches 0.9183 after training 1160 models. NAS needs 5808 trained models to reach the same mean accuracy. That is a 5.0x reduction by model count. The speedup by examples is 8.2x because NAS performs an additional re-ranking stage. The cost accounting formula is:
Here is the number of models trained during search, is the number of examples used per search model, is the number of models used in a re-ranking stage, and is the number of examples used per re-ranked model. PNAS has , while NAS and AmoebaNet-style methods often pay a second-stage cost. For PNASNet-5 on CIFAR-10, the paper reports:
For NASNet-A, the comparable cost is:
This is the concrete reason PNAS is interesting. The final error is similar to NASNet-A, but the search budget is much lower. CIFAR-10 Results The headline CIFAR-10 result is PNASNet-5 with 3.41 +/- 0.09 percent error, 3.2M parameters, and 1.0B search examples. NASNet-A has the same 3.41 percent error with 3.3M parameters, but its reported cost is 21.4B to 29.3B examples. AmoebaNet-A/B reach lower errors, but they pay substantially higher search cost. I would summarize Table 3 this way:
Model Error Params Search cost
NASNet-A 3.41 3.3M 21.4B-29.3B
AmoebaNet-B 3.37 +/- 0.04 2.8M 63.5B
