AmoebaNet-A 3.34 +/- 0.06 3.2M 25.2B
PNASNet-5 3.41 +/- 0.09 3.2M 1.0B
PNAS is not the absolute best accuracy row. Its selling point is the Pareto position: NASNet-level accuracy with a much smaller search budget. ImageNet Transfer The ImageNet transfer results are also competitive. In the mobile setting, PNASNet-5 uses 5.1M parameters and 588M multiply-adds, reaching 74.2 top-1 and 91.9 top-5. In the large setting, it uses 86.1M parameters and 25.0B multiply-adds, reaching 82.9 top-1 and 96.2 top-5. The important observation is not just the final ImageNet accuracy. The cell was searched on CIFAR-10, then scaled. This makes the search much cheaper, but it relies on CIFAR-10 being a useful proxy for ImageNet. The appendix checks this transfer assumption directly.
The rank correlation between CIFAR-10 and ImageNet accuracy is 0.727 for top-1 and 0.713 for top-5 over the tested architectures. That supports CIFAR-10 as a coarse proxy. The paper also notes that the correlation among high-CIFAR models is weaker: 0.505 for top-1 and 0.460 for top-5 when CIFAR accuracy is above 0.89. This is the expected regime where proxy search becomes noisy, because most candidates are already strong. What Happens Beyond 5 BlocksThe appendix extends progressive search to 10 blocks. The general raw search-space formula is:
For and :
The paper describes this as roughly possible model configurations. The point is not that PNAS fully solves this space. The point is that progressive search can continue exploring a narrow high-scoring beam even when the raw space becomes absurdly large.
The curve still improves as the search grows from 5 blocks to 10 blocks, although the gains are smaller. This is exactly what I would expect: more blocks increase expressiveness, but the predictor also has to extrapolate through a larger and noisier space. The appendix also shows the best intermediate cells.
These cells are useful because they show that PNAS is not simply waiting until block 5 to discover structure. PNASNet-1, 2, 3, and 4 are meaningful architectures along the way. The reported CIFAR-10 errors improve from 4.01 +/- 0.11 for PNASNet-1 to 3.50 +/- 0.10 for PNASNet-4, then 3.41 +/- 0.09 for PNASNet-5. My Reading NotesThe strongest part of PNAS is the way it turns an architecture into a growing object. A full cell is not sampled as a single opaque token. It is assembled in a curriculum from simple to complex graphs. That makes the search much more sample-efficient than a controller that starts by sampling full cells. The weakest part is also clear: pruning is irreversible. If the predictor assigns a low score to a partial cell, all descendants of that cell disappear. The paper reduces this risk with a fairly large beam, predictor ensembling, and repeated real evaluations at every depth, but the method still depends on a useful correlation between partial-cell promise and final-cell quality. This also explains why rank correlation is the right diagnostic. For search, calibrated accuracy prediction is less important than ordering. A predictor can have mediocre absolute error and still be useful if the top of its ranking is good enough. TakeawayPNAS is a pragmatic NAS paper. It keeps the cell-based search space from NASNet, but changes the expensive part: instead of evaluating many complete cells, it progressively grows cells and uses a learned predictor to decide which children deserve training. The result is not magic, but the cost comparison is convincing: about the same CIFAR-10 error as NASNet-A with roughly 1.0B search examples instead of more than 21B. The broader lesson still applies outside classic NAS: when the design space is compositional, do not score every full design from scratch. Grow partial designs, learn a cheap ranking model, and spend the expensive evaluation budget only where the ranking says it matters.

entry.title: ProxylessNAS: Direct Neural Architecture Search on Target Task and Hardware
entry.content:
Paper / Code ProxylessNAS is one of the NAS papers that is worth reading from an engineering angle. The main point is not just “NAS can find a good MobileNet-like model”. The more interesting part is that the search is done directly on the target task and the target hardware, while keeping GPU memory close to training a single compact network. MotivationEarlier NAS methods usually searched on a proxy task: fewer cells, fewer channels, smaller input resolution, or a smaller dataset. That made search affordable, but it also introduced a mismatch. A model that looks good on CIFAR or a tiny ImageNet setting may not be the best model after it is scaled and deployed on a phone/GPU/CPU. ProxylessNAS removes this extra transfer step:
The figure is simple but important. The left side learns an architecture on a proxy task, then transfers it to the real task. The right side learns the architecture with the target task and hardware in the loop. This matters especially for latency, because FLOPs and measured latency are not interchangeable once the hardware backend changes. ContributionThe paper contributes three things that are easy to mix together:
Search directly on large target tasks, including ImageNet, without shrinking the problem into a proxy task. Reduce the memory cost of differentiable NAS through path binarization, so only one candidate operation is active in each mixed operation during one forward/backward pass. Add hardware latency into the search objective, either through a differentiable latency regularizer or through a REINFORCE-style update for non-differentiable rewards.
The result is also practical: ProxylessNAS reports 74.6% ImageNet top-1 accuracy at 78 ms mobile latency, using about 200 GPU hours for search. For comparison, the paper reports MnasNet at 74.0% top-1, 76 ms latency, and 40,000 GPU hours. MethodologyPath-level pruningThe search space is represented as an over-parameterized network. Each learnable block contains several candidate operations, such as MBConv variants with different kernel sizes and expansion ratios. NAS then becomes a pruning problem: keep one path and remove the rest. For a mixed operation with candidates , the architecture parameters define the sampling probability:
A standard differentiable NAS implementation would keep all candidate paths in memory and compute a weighted sum. That is the expensive part. If every layer has multiple MBConv choices, keeping all activations quickly becomes much heavier than training the final compact model. Binarized pathsProxylessNAS samples a binary gate , where only one candidate path is active:
The training alternates between two updates:
Update weight parameters while freezing architecture parameters. Only the sampled active path is kept in memory. Update architecture parameters while freezing weight parameters. The gradient is estimated through the binary gate.
This is the key implementation trick. The supernet still contains all candidate operations as parameters, but a single minibatch only activates one path per mixed operation. So the peak activation memory is close to a normal compact network instead of a huge all-paths supernet. Hardware-aware objectiveThe latency term is built from a lookup table that measures the runtime of each operation on the target hardware. Let be the expected latency of block . It is computed by weighting each candidate’s measured latency by its probability:
The whole-network estimate is the sum over all learnable blocks:
Then the loss can include latency directly:
The paper also discusses a REINFORCE-based alternative. That route is useful when the target reward is not differentiable or when building a differentiable latency approximation is inconvenient. In practice, the lookup-table version is the easier one to reason about. ResultsCIFAR-10On CIFAR-10, ProxylessNAS reaches 2.08% test error with 5.7M parameters. The paper compares this with AmoebaNet-B at 2.13% test error and 34.9M parameters. I would not over-read this result because the paper’s bigger claim is ImageNet direct search, but it shows that the method is not only a hardware trick. ImageNet mobile setting
Model Top-1 Top-5 Mobile latency
MobileNetV2 72.0 91.0 75 ms
MnasNet 74.0 91.8 76 ms
Proxyless-G 71.8 90.8 83 ms
Proxyless-G+LL 74.2 91.9 79 ms
Proxyless-R 74.6 92.2 78 ms
MnasNet is hardware-aware but still proxy-based, with 40k GPU hours reported for search. The ProxylessNAS rows search directly on ImageNet with about 200 GPU hours; +LL adds the latency loss, and R uses the reinforcement-learning style architecture update.
The left plot is the result I care about most. At around the same top-1 accuracy, the searched model is much faster than a width-scaled MobileNetV2. The right plot is also important: the latency predictor is close enough to real mobile latency to be useful during search. ImageNet GPU setting
Model Top-1 Top-5 GPU latency
MobileNetV2 72.0 91.0 6.1 ms
MnasNet 74.0 91.8 6.1 ms
ProxylessNAS for GPU 75.1 92.5 5.1 ms
This is the part that supports the paper title. The best architecture is not a universal object. If the objective is GPU latency, the search picks a different network than it does for mobile latency. Hardware specialization
Optimized for Top-1 Target latency
GPU 75.1 5.1 ms
CPU 75.3 138.7 ms
Mobile 74.6 78 ms
The hardware-specific architectures are visibly different. The GPU model is shallower and wider, which exposes more parallel work. The CPU model becomes deeper and narrower. The mobile model tends to use larger MBConv blocks around downsampling stages. This is exactly why optimizing only FLOPs can be misleading. TakeawayMy main takeaway is that ProxylessNAS is less about finding one pretty architecture and more about making NAS deployable:
The search objective should include the real deployment target. Memory usage has to be controlled at the supernet level, not only in the final discovered network. Latency needs to be measured or modeled on the actual hardware backend.
The limitation is also clear. The method still depends on a predefined MobileNetV2-style search space, so it is not discovering arbitrary neural network structures. But within that constrained space, the paper gives a clean recipe: train the supernet directly on the real task, activate one path at a time, and let measured hardware latency shape the final architecture.

entry.title: Random Search and Reproducibility for NAS
entry.content:
Li L, Talwalkar A. Random Search and Reproducibility for Neural Architecture Search. UAI 2020.
Paper Code
This paper is useful because it attacks a boring but important question: when a NAS method looks good, how much of the gain comes from the search algorithm itself, and how much comes from the search space, the training recipe, the evaluation shortcut, or the final retraining protocol? The answer is uncomfortable. In the DARTS-style PTB and CIFAR-10 spaces, carefully implemented random search is a hard baseline. Random search with early stopping already reaches competitive results, and random search with weight sharing can match or beat several specialized NAS methods under similar budgets. NAS As Hyperparameter OptimizationThe paper frames NAS as a special case of hyperparameter optimization. There are three moving parts:
the search space, such as a cell DAG or a macro architecture; the search method, such as random search, RL, evolution, or gradient-based optimization; the evaluation method, such as full training, partial training, or weight sharing.
This split is the main mental model of the paper. If a new algorithm is evaluated with a stronger training recipe or cheaper evaluation oracle than the baseline, it is not clear whether the algorithm did the work. For NAS papers I think the minimum unit test should be:
Check What it catches
Same search space Avoids crediting a hand-designed space to the search method
Same evaluation budget Makes best-so-far comparisons meaningful
Same final training recipe Prevents retraining tricks from looking like search improvements
Multiple random seeds Measures variance instead of one lucky architecture
Released code and architecture Allows independent retraining and debugging
Reproducibility AuditThe authors first audit recent NAS papers. Their table checks whether a paper releases architecture-search code, model-evaluation code, random seeds, and hyperparameter-tuning details.
The important point is not that every paper is careless. NAS experiments are expensive, often multi-stage, and sensitive to implementation details. The problem is that missing seeds or missing hyperparameter logs make it impossible to separate an algorithmic contribution from a lucky or under-documented experimental setup. The paper distinguishes two levels:
Exact reproducibility: rerun the same code with the same seed and get the same result. Broad reproducibility: repeat the experiment with different seeds or equivalent code and get statistically similar conclusions.
Exact reproducibility is a low bar for a single-machine deterministic setup. Broad reproducibility is the bar that matters for judging whether a NAS method is robust. Method: Random Search With Weight SharingThe paper evaluates two random-search baselines:
Random search with early stopping. This uses ASHA to allocate more budget to promising architectures and stop poor ones early. Random search with weight sharing. This samples architectures uniformly, trains one shared-weight supernet by activating one architecture per minibatch, then scores many sampled architectures using the shared weights.
The second baseline is the most interesting one. It removes the sophisticated controller from methods like ENAS and keeps the cheap evaluation mechanism. If that baseline works, then the search controller may not be the main contribution. For PTB, the search space is a recurrent-cell DAG with (N=8) intermediate nodes. Each node selects a previous node as input and an operation from tanh, relu, sigmoid, or identity.
For CIFAR-10, the setup follows the DARTS normal-cell and reduction-cell space.
The search algorithm is simple, but the meta-hyperparameters are not. The result changes with the number of search epochs, batch size, network size, gradient clipping, number of sampled architectures, and final retraining length. PTB ResultsThe PTB table is the cleanest evidence that random search is not a strawman.
Key rows from the table:
Method Test perplexity Total search cost Search method
ENAS, published 56.3 N/A RL
DARTS second order, published 55.7 2 GPU days gradient-based
DARTS second order, reproduced 55.9 2 GPU days gradient-based
ASHA baseline 56.4 2 GPU days random
Random search WS 55.5 1.25 GPU days random
Random search with weight sharing gets 55.5 test perplexity, better than the reproduced DARTS run and the ASHA baseline in this setup. This does not prove that random search is universally better. It proves that the NAS comparison is weak if it does not include this baseline. The paper then digs into stage (2), where candidate architectures are retrained with a proxyless network for 300 epochs before choosing what to fully evaluate.
The table shows that the best Random (4) run has validation perplexity 63.8 after stage (2), close to the best published DARTS intermediate result. A second Random (4) run is worse, which is already a warning that a single search run is not enough. The ranking table makes that warning more concrete.
At 300 epochs, several methods are close. By 3600 epochs, Random (4) Run 1 becomes best, while Random (4) Run 2 ends fourth. Intermediate validation rank is a noisy selection signal. CIFAR-10 ResultsThe CIFAR-10 comparison is less one-sided, but it makes the same methodological point.
Key rows:
Method Best test error Average test error Total search cost Search method
ENAS, published 2.89 N/A N/A RL
DARTS second order, published N/A 2.76 +/- 0.09 5 GPU days gradient-based
DARTS second order, reproduced 2.62 2.78 +/- 0.12 10 GPU days gradient-based
ASHA baseline 2.85 3.03 +/- 0.13 9 GPU days random
Random search WS 2.71 2.85 +/- 0.08 9.7 GPU days random
Random search with weight sharing is competitive with the published DARTS/ENAS-style results, although the reproduced DARTS run still has the best average in this table. The important part is that the random baseline is in the same performance regime. The authors also tune the random-search-with-weight-sharing setup. This table is a good reminder that even a “random” baseline has important engineering choices.
The large proxyless setting, lower gradient clipping, and more evaluated architectures improve the random-search baseline. Without reporting those tuning choices, it would be easy to compare against a weak version of the baseline. Broad ReproducibilityThe paper repeats CIFAR-10 random search with weight sharing across six independent runs.
The six-run average is 2.92 test error. Runs 1 to 3 are around 2.85 to 2.88, while Runs 4 to 6 degrade to 2.95, 2.98, and 3.00. This is still competitive, but the spread is large enough that reporting only the best discovered architecture would be misleading. This is the most useful practical lesson for me: NAS results need distributions, not just a best architecture and a GPU-day number. Cost AccountingThe computational-cost section is short but important. The paper compares cost per architecture under three evaluation styles:
Evaluation style PTB cost per architecture CIFAR-10 cost per architecture
Full training 0.5 GPU days 4 GPU hours
ASHA partial training 9 minutes 19 minutes
Random search WS, amortized 0.2 minutes 0.8 minutes
Weight sharing makes each architecture extremely cheap to score, but that number can hide the real total cost. If many supernet trials, seed sweeps, and final retraining runs are needed to get a stable result, the headline search cost is not the whole story. TakeawaysRandom search is not the conclusion of NAS. It is the control experiment. My takeaways:
A NAS method should beat random search in the same search space and under the same final training recipe. Early stopping and weight sharing are evaluation methods, not search algorithms by themselves. Intermediate validation rankings can change after longer retraining, so short proxy evaluations need skepticism. Reproducibility requires seeds, code, architecture definitions, and hyperparameter-tuning logs. Best-run reporting is fragile. Average, variance, and rerun cost are part of the result.
The paper is a useful calibration point: before trusting a more complex NAS controller, first make the random baseline strong enough that beating it actually means something.

entry.title: SMASH: One-Shot Model Architecture Search through HyperNetworks
entry.content:
Brock A, Lim T, Ritchie J M, Weston N. SMASH: One-Shot Model Architecture Search through HyperNetworks. ICLR 2018.
Paper Code
SMASH is an early one-shot NAS paper, but it is not the same kind of one-shot method as ENAS or DARTS. It does not keep one shared supernet and select subgraphs. Instead, it trains a HyperNetwork that maps an architecture encoding to a set of generated weights. The core bet is:
where (c) is an architecture description, (H) is the HyperNetwork, and (W) is a subset of weights for the sampled CNN. If the validation error under (H(c)) correlates with the validation error after normal training, then architecture search becomes much cheaper: sample many architectures, score them with generated weights, keep the best, and train only the final architecture normally. SMASH LoopThe algorithm is short enough to fit in one figure.
The first loop trains the HyperNetwork. Each step samples a minibatch and a random architecture (c), generates weights (H(c)), evaluates the sampled network (f_c(H(c), x_i)), and updates (H). The second loop samples architectures on a validation set and ranks them by their SMASH score. The selected architecture is then fixed and trained from scratch with freely learned weights. This is important: generated weights are only a proxy. The final reported model is not deployed with HyperNetwork-generated weights. Memory-Bank Search SpaceThe paper needs a way to describe variable CNN topologies in a tensor form that a HyperNetwork can consume. The proposed answer is a memory-bank view of feed-forward networks.
Instead of thinking of a CNN as a simple chain of layers, SMASH treats each operation as reading from and writing to memory banks. This makes several connectivity patterns expressible with the same machinery:
Pattern Memory-bank behavior
ResNet-like read a bank, transform it, add/write back
DenseNet-like read many previous banks, write to a fresh bank
FractalNet-like use a more complex branching read/write pattern
The sampled network uses a normal CNN skeleton: stem, block 1, transition, block 2, transition, block 3.
Inside a block, each op starts with a generated (1 \times 1) convolution over the memory banks, followed by up to two parallel paths of two convolutions each. The (1 \times 1) weights are generated by the HyperNetwork; the other convolution weights are normally learned and shared across ops within a block. This design keeps the dynamic part manageable while still making connectivity and width variable. Architecture EncodingThe architecture (c) has to encode enough structure for (H(c)) to generate useful weights. SMASH encodes the read/write pattern, op choices, output units, dilation, and related settings into a tensor.
The paper uses a fully convolutional HyperNetwork so the output shape can change with the input architecture tensor. Conceptually, each spatial slice of the encoding corresponds to a slice of generated weights. The channel dimension stores one-hot architectural facts such as which memory banks are read, which banks are written, and what operation settings are active. This is a clever trick, but it also explains why SMASH is not a universal graph-to-weights solution. The search space has to be engineered so that the encoding is regular enough for a convolutional generator. Does The Proxy Rank Architectures?The key experiment is not the final CIFAR number. The key experiment is whether the SMASH score is correlated with true performance.
For SMASHv1, the authors train a SMASH network on CIFAR-100 for 300 epochs, sample 250 random architectures, rank them by SMASH validation error, and fully train every fifth architecture for 30 epochs. Figure 4 shows 50 architectures. Lower is better on both axes, and the positive correlation is what makes the method plausible. The authors are careful not to overclaim this. The correlation is one experimental condition, not a theorem. They then deliberately weaken the setup.
With a smaller “crippled” HyperNetwork, the relationship between generated-weight validation error and true validation error mostly breaks down. The rank plot also shows that scores from different HyperNetwork seeds have nontrivial spread. This is the main limitation in practice: one-shot evaluation is only useful if the proxy ranking is reliable. A cheaper proxy that changes the ordering of architectures is not just noisy; it can actively select the wrong model. Architectural Gradient By ProxySMASH also asks whether the architecture tensor itself can be optimized by gradient. Since (E = f(H(c), x)), one can in principle backpropagate to (c) and use (\frac{dE}{dc}) as a search signal. The paper tests whether the HyperNetwork actually uses the encoding by corrupting (c), for example by shuffling dilation values. The correct encoding gives better validation performance, suggesting that (H) has learned a real architecture-to-weight mapping. But the attempted gradient-descent-style update over discrete architecture choices did not beat random perturbations. This part reads more like a useful negative result than a complete algorithm. Benchmark ResultsSMASHv2 expands the search space with variable filter sizes, variable groups, and the full op structure from Figure 2. The best SMASHv2 models are then trained normally and compared with hand-designed and automatic methods.
Important rows from Table 1:

SMASHv2 is not state of the art against strong human-designed models. It is much closer to the automatic-design baselines of that period. The paper claims the discovered model is found with far less compute than Large-Scale Evolution, but the comparison is not perfectly symmetric: SMASH starts from a more structured search space and does not grow networks from trivial initial models. Transfer ResultsThe paper also transfers the best CIFAR-100 SMASHv2 architecture to STL-10 and ImageNet32x32.
The STL-10 result is not great against Wide ResNet: SMASHv2 has 41.52 +/- 2.10 error, while WRN-40-4 reports 35.02 +/- 1.14. A smaller 3x3 SMASHv2 variant improves to 37.76 +/- 0.58. On ImageNet32x32, SMASHv2 gets 38.62 top-1 and 16.33 top-5 error, better than the listed WRN baselines in the table. There is also an interesting earlier transfer observation in the text: the architecture found on CIFAR-100 beats the architecture found directly on STL-10 when both are trained on STL-10, suggesting that larger search datasets may produce architectures that generalize better. What The Found Architecture Looks LikeThe appendix visualization is messy, but that is part of the point. The discovered architecture is not a clean hand-designed motif.
This reinforces the engineering tradeoff in SMASH. The search space is flexible enough to produce long, irregular read/write graphs, but the method still depends on an encoding and HyperNetwork that can assign meaningful proxy weights to such graphs. TakeawaysSMASH is historically useful because it separates two ideas that later get blended in one-shot NAS:
Cheap architecture evaluation can be learned and amortized. The learned evaluator must be validated by ranking correlation, not only by final best accuracy. A HyperNetwork evaluator is different from a shared-weight supernet. Encoding design is part of the method; it constrains what the search can express. Generated weights are a proxy, not the final model parameters.
My read is that SMASH is less a production NAS recipe and more a clean early experiment in amortized model evaluation. The paper’s best contribution is not “HyperNetworks solve NAS”; it is the explicit question: can a learned weight generator rank architectures well enough to make search cheap?
